## 1.13 Loopback and tap paths

| Path | Endpoint | Domain | Format | Boards |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Base-domain serial loopback | `audio-mca-loopback`, `compatible = "audio-data,audio-loopback"` | base non-secure | 2 TX + 2 RX channels, **16-bit** | **every** board in scope |
| Low-power internal loopback | `audio-leap-internal-loopback`, `compatible = "audio-data,external"` | low-power non-secure | 2 TX + 2 RX channels, 32-bit | every board except j773g, j773s, j575c |
| Secure low-power loopback | `audio-secure-leap-loopback`, `device_type = "iop-audio-s"` | low-power **secure** (TX non-secure, RX secure) | 2 TX + 2 RX channels, 32-bit | **j714s, j714c, j716s, j716c only** |
| Speaker playback tap | `audio-speaker-tap`, `compatible = "audio-data,external"`, `clock-domain = "main"` | base non-secure | RX only, N channels (N = amplifier count) of **24-bit** samples in 32-bit slots | **A18 Pro and M5 only** — j700, j704, j813, j815, j714s, j714c, j716s, j716c |

The tap is new in this scope. It presents the speaker playback stream back to the
host as a capture stream with one channel per amplifier, at the amplifier sample
width, on a dedicated DMA receive channel (`base-ns-adma-rx-1`) that is otherwise
unused.

**The tap is not the sense return.** Its channel count equals the *playback* channel
count rather than 2 × N, its samples are 24-bit in 32-bit slots rather than 16-bit,
it is present on machines that have no sense path at all (j700) and absent on
machines that do (every t8132 and t604x board), and on j700 it cannot be
amplifier-sourced at all because the speaker link there has no return path. It is a
playback monitor / output reference. A driver must not feed it to a speaker
protection algorithm. **[Confirmed]** It is the only endpoint anywhere that declares `clock-domain`, and it
declares the base ("main") domain, which is significant on j700 where the speaker
stream itself lives in the low-power domain — i.e. **the tap crosses domains**.
**[Confirmed]**

The loopback endpoints have `device-uid` / `device-name` strings in the platform
description and a `data-sources` descriptor (§1.14.3). The base-domain loopback is
the only 16-bit path in the system, matching its dedicated DMA channel's
`max-bit-depth-bits = 16`. **[Confirmed]**

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 1.14 Low-power microphone and voice-trigger endpoints

### 1.14.1 Microphone capture

> **Naming trap.** The endpoint whose node name contains `hp-mic` is the **built-in
> digital microphone array**, not the headset microphone. It carries
> `device-name = "Digital Mic"`, `compatible = "audio-data,external"` and a data
> source naming the low-power audio processor's microphone input. The **headset**
> microphone is `audio-codec-input`, whose data node carries
> `audio-data,cs42l84-input` (or `audio-data,cs42l83-input` on t8140) — capture
> through the jack codec. Headset-microphone capture is in the normal world on
> **every** board in scope, bound to base non-secure receive channel 2; only the
> built-in array crosses the isolation boundary, and only on t8140, t8142 and
> t6050/t605x. **[Confirmed]**


| Element | M4 (t8132, t604x) | A18 Pro (t8140) | M5 (t8142, t6050, t605x) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Endpoint node | `audio-hp` | `audio-hp-mic` | `audio-hp-mic` |
| Data node | `audio-hp-mic` | `audio-hp-mic` | `audio-hp-mic` |
| `compatible` (data) | `audio-data,external` | `audio-data,external` | `audio-data,external` |
| `device_type` (endpoint) | `iop-audio-ns` | **`iop-audio-s`** | **`iop-audio-s`** |
| DMA | flat index 1 on `admac-leap-ns` | `leap-s-adma-rx-0` | `leap-s-adma-rx-0` |
| Channels | 3 | **2** | 3 |
| `device-uid` / `device-name` | "Digital Mic" | "Digital Mic" | "Digital Mic" |
| `input-data-selectors` | three 4-byte tags reading `imi1`, `imi2`, `imi3` | two tags, `imi1`, `imi2` | three tags |
| `default-input-data-selectors` | same list | same list | same list |
| `audio-stream-formatter` | FourCC `leap` | `leap` | `leap` |
| Extra | — | `function-input_power_enable` via the system power controller; `isolated-audio-service-input` phandle → `/arm-io/audio-hp-mic-proxy` | `isolated-audio-service-input` phandle → `/arm-io/audio-hp-mic-proxy` |

The migration of built-in microphone capture from the non-secure to the **secure**
low-power DMA domain, with a proxy node mediating it, is the single largest capture
path change in this scope. **[Confirmed]**

The boards with no built-in microphones (j773g, j773s, j575c) have **no**
`audio-hp`/`audio-hp-mic` endpoint, no `lp-mic-device`, no
`lp-mic-io-buffer-device`, no `siri-listening-device` and no
`/arm-io/iop-voicetrigger-controller` at all. **[Confirmed]**

### 1.14.2 Low-power microphone service nodes

| Node | `compatible` | `identifier` | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `lp-mic-device` | `iop-audio,lp-mic-device` | `lpai` | logical low-power microphone device; no DMA |
| `lp-mic-io-buffer-device` | `iop-audio,io-buffer-device` (M4) / `iop-audio,isolated-io-buffer-device` (A18 Pro, M5) | `adpx` | on M4: `io-buffer-size = 0xBB800` (768 000 bytes) and an `iommu-parent` phandle. On A18 Pro / M5: no `io-buffer-size`; instead `physical-descriptions` and a named external power provider, and the buffer is in the isolated execution environment |
| `siri-listening-device` | `iop-audio,client-manager-device` | `lai ` | `publish-user-client` boolean; no DMA |
| `lp-mic-injection-device` | `iop-adma-stream,mca` | `lpij` | **A18 Pro and M5 only**; TX only on `base-ns-adma-tx-5`; 3 channels (2 on j700) of 24-bit in 32-bit slots at **16 kHz**; `terminal-type-output` = FourCC `injm`; `device-name` "LPMic Injection" |

`physical-descriptions` on `lp-mic-io-buffer-device` is
`[64000, 16000, 'lpcm', 20, bytes-per-frame, X]`:

| Board | Value | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| j700 | 64000, 16000, `lpcm`, 20, 8, 536 | 16 kHz linear PCM, 8 bytes/frame = 2 channels |
| j704, j813, j815, j714*, j716* | 64000, 16000, `lpcm`, 20, 12, 792 | 12 bytes/frame = 3 channels |

Bytes-per-frame matches the microphone count; the trailing word scales as
256 × channels + 24 and is **[Unknown]**. **[Confirmed]** for the rate, format and
frame size.

### 1.14.3 `data-sources` descriptor

Endpoints that present a named logical device carry `data-sources`:

```
4-byte source tag (byte-reversed) │ u32 │ u16 flags │ u16 rate count │ u64 rate[…] │ name string
```

| Endpoint | Source tag | Rate count | Rates (Hz) | Name |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `audio-hp-mic` | `ap2a` | 1 | 48000 | "Leap Mic" |
| `audio-leap-internal-loopback` | `ap2a` | 1 | 48000 | "LEAP Internal Loopback" |
| `audio-mca-loopback` | `ap2c` | 1 | 48000 | "Loopback" |
| `audio-codec-input` (M4/M5) | `ap2c` | **4** | 48000, 44100, 88200, 96000 | "codecinput" |
| `audio-codec-input` (j700) | `ap2c` | 1 | 48000 | "codecinput" |
| `audio-speaker` (j700) | `ap2s` | 1 | 48000 | "Leap Speaker" |
| `audio-speaker-tap` | `ap2a` | 1 | 48000 | "SpeakerTap" |
| `lp-mic-injection-device` | `lpij` | 1 | **16000** | "LPMic Injection" |

The rate-count field is **[Confirmed]** (it predicts the number of u64 rate words
exactly in every case). The preceding u32 and the flags half-word are **[Unknown]**.

Note that rates in `data-sources` are plain little-endian u64 integers, whereas the
jack-codec node's `samplerate-default` and `samplerate-subset` use 32.32 fixed point
for the same quantity. Two different encodings of a sample rate coexist in the same
description; a driver must not use one decoder for both. **[Confirmed]**

Note the capture rate capability difference: the jack capture path advertises four
rates on every M4/M5 board but only 48 kHz on the A18 Pro board. **[Confirmed]**

### 1.14.4 Voice trigger

```
/arm-io/iop-voicetrigger-controller
    compatible  = "iop-audio,controller"
    device_type = "iop-voicetrigger-controller"
    iop-audio-service-name = <a second coprocessor service name>
  /audio-vt-device
    identifier  = FourCC `vtcm`
    device_type = "iop-nub"
    compatible  = "iop-audio,vt-device"            (t8132, t604x)
    compatible  = "iop-audio,isolated-vt-device"   (t8140, t8142, t6050/t605x)
```

On the A18 Pro and M5 boards the voice-trigger device is additionally marked
`exclave-assigned` and carries secure-world service names. It has **no DMA binding**
of its own; the voice-trigger audio path is entirely inside the always-on
coprocessor. `/product/audio` declares `voiceTriggerChannels = 1` on every board that
has it. **[Confirmed]**

A matching pair of service nodes exists under the always-on coprocessor's nub:
`/arm-io/aop/iop-aop-nub/aop-audio` (`compatible = "iop-audio,aop-service"`,
`device_type = "aop-audio"`) and `.../aop-voicetrigger` (same `compatible`,
`device_type = "aop-voicetrigger"`, plus a `name-override` naming the voice-trigger
service). On j773g, j773s and j575c only `aop-audio` is present. **[Confirmed]**

## 1.15 DisplayPort audio endpoints

| Board class | `dp-audio` nodes | DMA provider | Channel index | Channels | Buffer |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| t8132 (j604, j623, j624, j713, j715, j773g) | `dp-audio0…2` | `/arm-io/sio/iop-sio-nub/sio-dma` (shared) | 0x64, 0x66, 0x68 | 2 | 0x800 |
| t604x (j614s/c, j616s/c, j773s, j575c) | `dp-audio0…4` | `/arm-io/sio/iop-sio-nub/sio-dma` (shared) | as above, extended | 2 | 0x800 |
| t8140 (j700) | `dp-audio0…1` | `/arm-io/sio/iop-sio-nub/sio-dma` (shared) | 0x64, 0x66 | 2 | 0x800 |
| t8142 (j704, j813, j815) | `dp-audio0…2` | **one `admac-disp0` / `admac-dispext0` / `admac-dispext1` instance each** | 0 | 2 | 0x1000 |
| t6050/t605x (j714s/c, j716s/c) | `dp-audio0…4` | **one `admac-disp0` / `admac-dispext0…3` instance each** | 0 | 2 | 0x1000 |

Each `dp-audio` node also carries `power-gates`, `clock-gates` and
`function-device_reset_dpa` (tag `ARST`). The M5 generation additionally
instantiates a `…-ced-ssw` companion node next to each display audio DMA instance,
and an `admac-aop-ced-ssw` node next to the always-on side.

The move of DisplayPort audio off the shared serial-I/O DMA engine onto per-display
audio DMA instances, with the buffer size doubled, is an M5-generation change.
**[Confirmed]**

`/product/audio` is present on every board in scope and names where the per-unit

| `safety-offset-seed-us` | 500 | all 20 | 500 µs |

| `mach-time-audio-alignment` | 0 | all 20 | |
| `speaker-cpms-bgd_inst` / `_100ms` / `_1s` | see below | **j700 only** | inline speaker power limits |
| `supportedChannels` / `enabledChannels` / `historyChannels` | 0x7 (0x3 on j700) | all with microphones | microphone channel masks |
| `voiceTriggerChannels` | 1 | all with microphones | |
| `supports-secure-microphone` | 1 | all with microphones **except j623, j624** | |
| `supports-always-listening`, `supports-barge-in` | 1 | all with microphones | |

`acoustic-id` per board:

| Board | `acoustic-id` | Board | `acoustic-id` |
|---|---|---|---|
| j604 | 30 | j704 | 39 |
| j623, j624 | 31 | j714s, j714c | 40 |

Note that j773g and j773s share an `acoustic-id` (both Mac mini) and j623/j624 share
one (both 24-inch iMac), while every other machine has a distinct value.
**[Confirmed]**

`speaker-cpms-bgd_100ms` on j700 is two u32: 1363 and 5453; the `_inst` and `_1s`
variants are `0xFFFFFFFF, 0xFFFFFFFF` (no limit). Units **[Unknown]** — the
name suggests a continuous power metric with a 100 ms window.

`use-case-dsp-in-format` is a list of 32-byte records
`[format FourCC, sample rate, channels, 0x00040000, …]`:

| Board | Record 1 | Record 2 |
|---|---|---|
| j700 | `mtkd`, 48000, 2 channels | `hist`, 16000, 2 channels |
| j704, j813, j815, j714*, j716* | `mtkd`, 48000, **3 channels** | `hist`, 16000, **3 channels** |

`use-case-client-format` (A18 Pro and M5) holds three 32-byte records with source
tags `hist`, `siri` and `lpts`, all at 16000 Hz, 2 channels. **[Probable]**

## 1.17 Structural outliers

### 1.17.1 j700 (t8140, MacBook Neo) — fully documented difference

Every respect in which j700 differs from the rest of the scope:

| Aspect | Rest of scope | j700 |
|---|---|---|
| Amplifier part | `sn012776` (TAS2764 class) | **`max98360`** (MAX98360A class) |
| Amplifier control bus | I²C, 1/4/6 addresses | **none** — the amplifier node is a child of `/arm-io/iop-audio-controller`, not of an I²C bus |
| Amplifier count | 1, 4 or 6 | **2 channels on one part family with `num-channels = 2`** |
| Amplifier interrupt | shared GPIO | **none** |
| Amplifier reset/shutdown | shared GPIO | one GPIO (gpio0 pin 105), shared by both channels |
| `speaker-config`, `bop-config`, `amp-dcblocker-config`, `amp-tx-zd-config` | present | **all absent** |
| Speaker-ID straps | 2 pins (most boards) | **absent** |
| I/V sense return | present where protection is enabled | **absent — the part has no sense** |
| Speaker port format | slot-framed TDM, code `0x02` | **stereo I²S, code `0x13`** |
| Speaker sample format | 24-bit in 32-bit slots | **32-bit in 32-bit slots** |
| Speaker reference clock | 12 MHz, 250 cycles/frame | **12.288 MHz, 256 cycles/frame** |
| Speaker DMA domain | `admac-base-ns`, channel tx-0 | **`admac-leap-ns`, channel `leap-ns-adma-tx-0`** — the speaker path runs through the low-power audio processor, not the base domain |
| Speaker stream `compatible` | `iop-adma-stream,mca` | **`iop-adma-stream,leap`** |
| Speaker stream formatter | (none) | **`audio-stream-formatter` = FourCC `leap`** |
| Speaker mute behaviour | amplifier register controlled | `mute-ramp-sleep-ms = 20`, `enable-iop-ramp-down` — the ramp is done by the coprocessor |
| Jack codec | `cs42l84` at 0x4b | **`cs42l83` at 0x48** |
| Jack codec reset controller | always-on nub controller (M4, M5 base) | **main pin controller**, gpio0 pin 103 |
| Jack link reference clock | none (0), 64 bit clocks/frame | **24 MHz, 125 cycles/frame** |
| Jack capture rates | 48000, 44100, 88200, 96000 | **48000 only**, and `samplerate-subset` present on the codec node |
| Built-in microphones | 3 | **2** |
| Microphone power enable | (none) | **`function-input_power_enable` through the system power controller** |
| Speaker playback tap | present (A18 Pro and M5) | present, and it is the **only** endpoint crossing from the low-power speaker path into the base clock domain |
| DisplayPort audio | 3 or 5 instances | **2**, on the shared serial-I/O DMA engine |
| Second always-on coprocessor | absent on M4, present on M5 | **present** |
| `/product/audio` | no inline power limits | carries inline `speaker-cpms-bgd_*` limits |

Consequences for a driver: on j700 there is **no** amplifier register programming, no
brown-out configuration, no DC-blocker setting, no per-amplifier gain, no I/V sense,
and therefore no closed-loop speaker protection of the kind the rest of the scope
uses. Output level and channel assignment are fixed by board strapping and are not
described. The only host-visible controls are the shutdown GPIO and the DMA stream
itself, and even the mute ramp is delegated. **[Confirmed]**

### 1.17.2 The two 24-inch iMac boards (j623, j624)

`sn012776` amplifiers with I/V sense capability, but the speaker stream declares **no
receive channels** and `speaker-protection = 0`. `amp-tx-zd-config` is absent (no
bus-keeper duty, because nothing is transmitted). The amplifier output level is
higher than on any portable (code 0x12 = 20.0 dBV) and the DC-blocker value differs
(0x71 rather than 0x41). They also lack `supports-secure-microphone`. So these are
the only boards in scope that have a multi-amplifier array with the sense path
deliberately not wired up. **[Confirmed]**

### 1.17.3 The Mac mini and Mac Studio boards (j773g, j773s, j575c)

Single amplifier, no sense capture, `speaker-protection = 0`, no speaker-ID straps,
no `amp-tx-zd-config`, no microphones at all (no `audio-hp` endpoint, no
`lp-mic-device`, no voice-trigger controller, no `/product/audio` microphone
properties), but a full jack codec at 0x4b.

These three boards split on amplifier output level, and that split is the only
electrical change to an amplifier setting anywhere in this scope. **j773g and j773s
carry code 0x0f = 18.5 dBV**, where every earlier Mac mini board carries code
0x14 = 21.0 dBV; **j575c retains 0x14 = 21.0 dBV**, the maximum the field can
express, and is the only board in scope that does. The reduction is 2.5 dB of
full-scale output, 11.22 V rms → 8.41 V rms. A driver that carries a level value
forward from an earlier Mac mini will over-drive the M4 Mac mini. **[Confirmed]**

### 1.17.4 The two six-driver chassis families

The ten MacBook Pro 14/16-inch boards and the two 15-inch Air boards carry the same
six amplifiers at the same six addresses with the same slot geometry, but the
transducer at 0x39/0x3a and at 0x3c/0x3d is exchanged between them: the part at 0x39
is the left woofer 2 on the MacBook Pro chassis and the left tweeter on the 15-inch
Air. A single six-amplifier map applied to both would drive a tweeter with woofer
content on one of them. **[Confirmed]**, and it is the reason §1.3 states the role
table per chassis rather than per slot group.

### 1.17.5 j813 (M5 13-inch MacBook Air)

The only four- or six-amplifier board in scope with **no speaker-identification
mechanism** (`find-speaker-id`, `valid-speaker-ids`, `function-speaker-id0/1` all
absent) while still having `speaker-protection = 1`. Its M4 predecessor j713 has the
mechanism. A driver written against j713 will not find the straps on j813.
**[Confirmed]**

### 1.17.6 The M5 Pro/Max boards (j714s, j714c, j716s, j716c)

The only boards in scope with the secure low-power loopback endpoint
(`audio-secure-leap-loopback`, identifier `sllb`), its own DMA proxy and its own
stream proxy, and with `leap-ns-adma-tx-5` / `leap-s-adma-rx-5` channels. They are
also the only boards where the jack codec reset line is on the main pin controller
rather than the always-on nub controller, and the only ones with five display audio
DMA instances. **[Confirmed]**

| Amp GPIO pins | reset 15 / irq 14 / id 4,13 | reset 15 / irq 14 / id 4,13 | reset 15 / irq 14 / id 4,13 | reset 15 / irq 14 / id 4,13 | reset 15 / irq 14 / id 4,13 |

### Within t604x (M4 Pro/Max)

j614s, j614c, j616s and j616c are byte-identical in the audio tree except for

single-amplifier and differ from each other only in `acoustic-id` and the amplifier
output level — **18.5 dBV on the Mac mini, 21.0 dBV on the Mac Studio**, the Mac mini
having dropped 2.5 dB relative to its own predecessors. All six share amplifier GPIO pins
reset 54 / interrupt 55 / ID 52, 53 and jack codec interrupt pin 106, reset

|---|---|---|---|
| Amplifiers | 6, MacBook Pro chassis | 4, Air chassis | 6, **15-inch Air chassis** |

| Everything else | identical GPIO pins (reset 151, interrupt 150, jack interrupt 100, jack reset nub-gpio pin 18) |||

### Across generations, same chassis

| Chassis pair | What changed |
|---|---|
| j613 (M3) → j713 (M4) → j813 (M5) | slot map, addresses, amplifier level and DC-blocker all unchanged; cluster naming lost at M4; microphone capture moved to the secure domain at M5; **speaker-ID straps dropped at M5** |
| j615 (M3) → j715 (M4) → j815 (M5) | unchanged six-amplifier 15-inch Air map and addressing throughout, tweeters at slot groups 2 and 3; same changes as above, speaker-ID straps retained but **moved to pins 6 and 11** on j815 |
| j504 (M3) → j604 (M4) → j704 (M5) | unchanged six-amplifier MacBook Pro map and addressing, unchanged GPIO pins on j504/j604; j704 moved every audio GPIO. The tweeter slot group on this chassis is the subject of Open question 1 and is inherited unchanged from j504 |
| j514s (M3) → j614s (M4) → j714s (M5) | unchanged map and addressing; GPIO pins moved at every step; jack codec reset moved from the nub controller to the main controller at M5; secure loopback added at M5. Same open question on the tweeter slot group |
| j516c (M3) → j616c (M4) → j716c (M5) | as above |
| j433/j434 (M3) → j623/j624 (M4) | unchanged in every respect documented here, including the 20.0 dBV output level and the 0x71 DC-blocker value that are unique to the iMac chassis |
| M1/M2 Mac mini → j773g/j773s (M4) | **amplifier output level dropped from 21.0 dBV to 18.5 dBV**; everything else about the single-amplifier arrangement unchanged |

## Open questions

1. **Which slot groups the tweeters occupy on the MacBook Pro 14/16-inch chassis.**
   **Safety-critical, and unresolved.** The platform hardware description places the
   part at 0x39 (left woofer 2) in slot group 2 and the part at 0x3a (left tweeter) in
   slot group 4; the published, hardware-tested device trees for the M1 Pro/Max, M3
   and M3 Pro/Max boards of the same chassis place them the other way round. The two
   sources agree completely on the 15-inch Air chassis and on every four-amplifier
   machine, and they agree on this chassis about which *part* is the tweeter — the
   disagreement is only about which slot group it sits in, and it is therefore
   inherited by every MacBook Pro-chassis board in scope: j604, j614s, j614c, j616s,
   j616c, j704, j714s, j714c and j716s/j716c. This document follows the platform
   description. **Why it matters:** if the published trees are right, a driver built
   from these tables would route slot group 2's content, and apply slot group 2's
   excursion and thermal limits, to a tweeter — and woofer limits applied to a tweeter
   can destroy it. Because the amplifier's own thermal foldback is disabled on every
   machine in scope (§1.8.4), there is no in-part backstop. **Resolve by** muting one
   amplifier at a time over I²C while capturing the sense return and observing which
   capture channel pair falls silent; and independently by reading the receive-slot
   and sense-slot registers back from the parts at 0x39 and 0x3a after the platform
   has configured the link. Until then, per-transducer limits must not be applied on
   this chassis.

2. **Serial audio cluster identity.** Which of the six base-domain clusters
   (`AUDIO_MCA0_M` … `AUDIO_MCA5_M`) carries the left amplifier link, the right
   amplifier link, the jack codec link and the base loopback, and which port of the
   cluster each uses, is not expressed anywhere on any board in scope. A driver that
   wants to take the serialiser back from the coprocessor needs this. **Resolve by**
   toggling each cluster's power/clock domain in turn while a stream is running and
   observing which link stops, and by tracing the coprocessor's own accesses to the
   cluster apertures.

3. **The `0x21` / `0x22` selector in the M4 `dma-channels` blob.** Each endpoint's
   blob carries the same transmit and receive channel numbers twice, differing only
   in one word (0x21 versus 0x22). Candidate meanings include the two address
   translation contexts, the secure and non-secure views of the same channel, or two
   interrupt destinations. Until it is resolved a driver cannot know whether the two
   copies are alternatives or a pair that must both be programmed. **Resolve by**
   comparing with the A18 Pro / M5 named-channel form, which has no such duplication,
   and by tracing the channel registers touched when a single M4 stream starts.

4. **Bus-keeper polarity on four-amplifier machines.** The two masks in
   `amp-tx-zd-config` match the published transmit-slot idle masks for the
   equivalent M1 Pro/Max six-amplifier machines exactly, on the same two links, which
   confirms the property's meaning and the left/right link split from two independent
   sources. The published four-amplifier trees nevertheless assign the two masks to
   the opposite links. Driving zeros into slots another amplifier is driving would
   cause bus contention. **Stakes: moderate, and confined to j713, j813, j623 and
   j624.** **Resolve by** reading back the four transmit mask registers and the
   force-zero enable bit from each amplifier on a four-amplifier machine after the
   platform has started a stream.

5. **Bits 5 and 4 of the amplifier configuration word on the 24-inch iMac.** The
   word decodes to a 2 Hz sense high-pass with spread spectrum, the supply-measurement
   ADC filter and thermal foldback all off on every machine in scope (§1.8.4). j623
   and j624 carry `0x71` where every other board carries `0x41`, differing in bits 5
   and 4 only; thermal foldback is off on those boards too, so the difference lies in
   the spread-spectrum or supply-ADC-filter setting. Spread spectrum affects radiated
   emissions and the supply-ADC filter affects how quickly brownout protection reacts,
   so neither is cosmetic. **Resolve by** reading the register back on an iMac and on
   a portable and comparing against the public counterpart's field definitions, and by
   measuring the Class-D switching spectrum on both.

6. **GPIO flag bit 16.** The amplifier shutdown line carries flags `0x00010001` where
   the jack codec reset carries `0x00000001`; bit 16 also appears on SPI chip-select
   lines. If it means "park in a defined state at handover" a driver must honour it to
   avoid an audible click or an unprotected amplifier at shutdown. **Resolve by**
   observing the line's behaviour across sleep/wake and shutdown with a logic probe.

7. **Whether the PDM converter domain can ever carry speaker sense.** The
   `AUDIO_SENSE_PDMC` domain is a rename of the baseline generation's microphone PDM
   converter domain and is not a speaker-sense converter; every speaker endpoint in
   scope returns current and voltage sense as 16-bit PCM in TDM slots, and the domain
   is present identically on machines whose amplifiers have no sense capability at
   all (§1.5.3). **Stakes: low.** The residual question is only whether the hardware
   *could* be routed that way on a future machine, which matters for how rigidly a
   driver should assume the PCM-over-TDM sense path. **Resolve by** checking whether
   the domain is powered while a sense capture is running. Do not build a PDM sense
   path into a driver on the strength of the domain name.

8. **What the speaker ID code selects.** `valid-speaker-ids` is `{0, 3}` on every
   machine that has the mechanism, so there are exactly two module variants, but
   nothing in the platform description says what differs between them. This gates
   correct protection constants. **Resolve by** reading the two strap pins on
   physical machines of the same model and correlating with the per-unit calibration
   store, and by comparing the protection constants the reference implementation uses
   for each code. Cross-reference Section 9.

9. **Word 1 of the stream descriptor.** The low byte is the port channel width on
   every endpoint except the base-domain loopback, where it is a board-independent
   `0x0F`; the high byte takes three values (0x00, 0x10, 0x20) that group the speaker
   and loopback ports together and the jack ports together. Whether the high byte is
   a port-group index a driver must reproduce, or merely descriptive, is unknown.
   **Resolve by** tracing the coprocessor configuration message that carries this
   descriptor and observing which field ends up in which serialiser register.

10. **Words 2–4 of the stream descriptor on the A18 Pro jack link.** Every other port
    satisfies `word2 / word3 = 48 000` (12 000 000/250, 12 288 000/256). The A18 Pro
    jack link gives 24 000 000/125 = 192 000, while the codec node declares 48 kHz and
    48 kHz only. Either word 3 is not a simple frame divider, or the jack link runs a
    4× internal clock. **Resolve by** measuring the bit clock and frame clock on the
    jack link of that machine.

11. **`mic-config`.** The value `01 00 FF FF FF FF FF FF` is identical on every board
    and on both jack-codec variants, so nothing can be learned from correlation. It
    plausibly selects a microphone input and bias level with six unused entries, but
    the field boundaries are unverified. **Resolve by** comparing the codec's
    microphone-bias and input-select registers after the reference implementation has
    configured a headset with a microphone.

12. **j700 amplifier channel assignment.** With no control bus and one shared
    shutdown line, which of the two amplifier channels is left and which is right is
    determined by board strapping that the platform description does not carry, and
    the amplifier's fixed gain is likewise strapped. **Resolve by** playing a
    single-channel test signal and listening, and by reading the strap resistors.

13. **Second size field in the M4 DMA channel record.** It is exactly half the buffer
    size for every endpoint except the low-power internal loopback, where the
    transmit record has a quarter and the receive record two-fifths. If it is a FIFO
    watermark, the exception matters for latency. **Resolve by** correlating with the
    DMA controller's threshold registers during a running stream.

14. **`lp-mic-io-buffer-device` trailing descriptor word.** It scales as
    256 × channels + 24 across the two microphone counts observed, which suggests a
    per-channel block plus a header, but the block contents are unknown. **Resolve by**
    inspecting the shared buffer's layout while the low-power microphone path is
    running.

15. **Where in the chain the base-domain loopback and the playback tap take their
    signal.** Both observe the playback path — neither is the sense return (§1.13) —
    but the loopback is 16-bit and the tap 24-bit, and only the tap declares a clock
    domain. Whether each taps before or after the coprocessor's processing chain
    decides whether either can be used to verify what actually reaches the
    amplifiers. **Resolve by** playing a known signal and comparing both captures
    against it, with and without coprocessor processing enabled.


---

# 2. Clocking and power domains

## Baseline

Measured against the M1–M3 host-owned audio clock tree:

```
 numerically controlled oscillator (5 channels, 0x4000 stride)
        │  one channel per serial-audio cluster, programmed directly to the bit-clock rate
        v
 cluster master-clock gate ──> bit clock ──> cluster frame-sync generator ──> frame clock
                                              │                                  │
                                              v                                  v
                                       SERDES sync select                  I2S/TDM port
```

and against the M1–M3 power-domain set for audio: a host-side general audio
register-access domain, a host-side audio-DMA domain, and one host-side domain per
serial-audio cluster (`AUDIO_P`, `SIO_ADMA`, `MCA0`…`MCA3`/`MCA5`), all children of the
system-I/O domain; plus a functionally parallel, host-unreadable set inside the
always-on coprocessor island (`AOP_LEAP_CLK`, `AOP_ADMA0`, `AOP_LEAP`, `AOP_AUDIO_SHIM`,
`AOP_AUDIO_ADMA0`, `AOP_MCA0`…`AOP_MCA3`, `AOP_PDMC0`, `AOP_PDM0_REF`, `AOP_PDM1_REF`).

The public counterparts for the codec-side clocking are the CS42L42/CS42L83 family
(jack codec), the TAS2764/TAS2770 family (SN012776 speaker amplifier), and the
MAX98357/MAX98360 family (t8140 speaker amplifier).

## Summary of differences

| Item | M1–M3 | t8132 (M4) | t604x (M4 Pro/Max) | t8140 (A18 Pro) | t8142 (M5) | t605x (M5 Pro/Max) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Numerically controlled oscillator | present, host MMIO `0x14000`/5 channels, in the SoC clock-manager window | **present in hardware, no host aperture, node deleted** | same | **present in hardware, node retained with `compatible` + `clock-ids` but no `reg` and no `pmgr-nco-page-size`** | same as t8132 | same as t8132 |
| Oscillator owner | host | always-on coprocessor | coprocessor | coprocessor | coprocessor | coprocessor |
| Per-cluster master-clock cells | folded into the per-cluster domains `MCA0…MCAn` | **six explicit master-clock domains `AUDIO_MCA0_M`…`AUDIO_MCA5_M`** | same | same | same | same |
| Serial-audio cluster count (base domain) | 4 (6 on t8103/t8112) | 6 | 6 | 6 | 6 | 6 |
| Low-power-path serial-audio cluster | 1 (`AOP_LEAP`) | 1 (`AUDIO_LEAP_MCA`) + 5 RX + 1 TX stream domains | same | same | same | same |
| Audio-DMA power domains | 1 host (`SIO_ADMA`) + 1 coprocessor | **4: base/low-power × secure/non-secure** | same | same | same | same |
| Host-drivable audio power-state register | yes, and mainline Linux drives them | **none** (every audio entry carries the not-host-drivable flag bit) | none | none | none | none |
| Host audio-DMA power gate | real, two domains | **none** — only a virtual latency-tolerance vote | none | none | none | **none, and the vote is expressed as a named function instead** |
| Audio domain tree root | system-I/O domain (`SIO`) | always-on coprocessor filter domain | same | same | coprocessor IOMMU domain | coprocessor filter domain |
| Link clock descriptor (36-byte `reg` on `audio-data,*` nodes) | present under `mcaN/mcaNx` | **bit-identical, relocated under `/arm-io/iop-audio-controller`** | same | same, different values for the different codec/amplifier parts | same | same |
| Jack-codec master-clock source | external 6 MHz on M1; codec-internal from M2 on | codec-internal | codec-internal | codec-internal; link master clock 24 MHz ÷ 4 = 6 MHz bit clock | codec-internal | codec-internal |
| 44.1 kHz family | reachable | reachable | reachable | **not reachable (restricted to 48 kHz by `samplerate-subset`)** | reachable | reachable |
| Externally named power provider on the audio controller node | absent | absent | absent | **present** | **present** | **present** |

---

## 2.1 The numerically controlled oscillator

### 2.1.1 Presence and ownership

**The oscillator is present in hardware on every in-scope SoC but has no host MMIO
aperture; the bit, frame and master clocks it feeds are programmed on the host's
behalf by the always-on coprocessor.** **[Probable]**

On t8140 the node survives with the same two-element `compatible` value used from
t8103 through t6030 (`"nco,t8101"`, `"nco,s5l8960x"`), the same
`device_type = "nco"`, and a four-entry `clock-ids` array — but with **no `reg`
property and no `pmgr-nco-page-size` property**. A block that had been removed from
the die would not keep a `compatible`-bearing node; a block that is present but not
host-addressable is exactly what a node with a `compatible` and no aperture
describes. On t8132, t604x, t8142 and t605x the node is deleted outright, which in
this platform-description convention means only that no host driver is expected to
bind, not that the block is absent (the six serial-audio clusters it feeds are
likewise not described by any host-addressable node yet are still enumerated as power
domains — §2.6).

The set of audio power domains grew rather than shrank at this transition (§2.6), and
it grew by exactly the things an oscillator has to feed — six named per-cluster
**master-clock** domains `AUDIO_MCA0_M`…`AUDIO_MCA5_M`. On M1–M3 no domain carried a
master-clock-specific name. **[Confirmed]**

### 2.1.2 What this means for a host driver

- There is **no supported host path to the oscillator on any in-scope SoC**. No
  aperture is advertised, no clock gate referencing it is advertised, and on the one
  SoC where the node survives it also lacks the page-size property that a host driver
  would need to work out the channel count. **[Confirmed]**
- A host driver reaches the oscillator **only indirectly**: it asks the coprocessor,
  over the audio mailbox endpoint, for a stream on a named endpoint under
  `/arm-io/iop-audio-controller` at a given sample rate; the coprocessor programs the
  oscillator, the cluster master-clock cell, the cluster clock generator and the
  frame-sync generator on the host's behalf. The host keeps only the DMA endpoints of
  the path. **[Confirmed]** — the controller node carries no `reg`, only
  `iop-audio-service-name` (naming an audio service on the always-on coprocessor),
  and the clock parameters for each link are supplied to that service as platform
  data (§2.3).
- **Direct access at a fixed address is a probing question, not a driver strategy.**
  On M1–M3 the oscillator aperture sat inside the SoC clock/power-manager address
  window at window base + `0x44000`, size `0x14000` (five channels of `0x4000`), and
  the serial-audio switch node carried a second small window `0x4000` below it in the
  same block. The same offsets are plausible but unverified on M4 and later, and on
  M4 and later the block is very likely to have moved into the always-on island's
  clock-manager window instead, because that is where every audio power/clock cell
  now lives. **[Inferred]** — see Open questions 1 and 2. Even if the aperture
  responds, writing it from the host would race the coprocessor, which believes it
  owns the block.

### 2.1.3 Programming model

**Unchanged from the published M1–M3 model** — same register file, same Galois-LFSR
coarse-divisor coding, same two-increment phase accumulator. The full derivation is in
the public baseline and is not restated; what follows is only the formula, the ranges
and the contract a driver or a probe needs.
**[Probable]** — the block identity is asserted by an unchanged `compatible` on t8140;
no register-level evidence contradicts it, and none confirms it on M4 or later.

| Offset in channel | Name | Access | Fields | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | `CTRL` | R/W | `[31] ENABLE` | Runs the channel. |
| `0x04` | `DIV` | R/W | `[1:0] FINE`, `[12:2] COARSE` | Base divisor, coarse part LFSR-coded. |
| `0x08` | `INC1` | R/W | 32-bit | Accumulator increment used while the accumulator's top bit is clear. |
| `0x0c` | `INC2` | R/W | 32-bit (interpreted modulo 2³²; normally negative) | Increment used while the top bit is set. |
| `0x10` | `ACCINIT` | W | 32-bit | Accumulator preset; `0x8000_0000` is the neutral value. |

Channel stride `0x4000`; register file `20` bytes per channel.

**Divisor coding — unchanged from the baseline, not restated.** `FINE = D mod 4` and
`COARSE` is the LFSR encoding of `D div 4` published for the baseline block; the
representable range that follows from it is **`D ∈ [8, 8199]`**.

**Frequency.** For a desired output `f_out` from parent `f_par`:

```
D    = floor(2·f_par / f_out)
INC1 = 2·f_par − D·f_out
INC2 = INC1 − f_out            (stored modulo 2^32)
f_out(exact) = 2·f_par·(INC1−INC2) / (D·(INC1−INC2) + INC1)
```

Long-term frequency error is **0 ppm** relative to the parent for any `f_out` in range;
instantaneous period jitter is **±0.5 parent-clock periods**. **[Confirmed]** (public
model). Reachable band `2·f_par/8199 ≤ f_out ≤ f_par/4`: **219.5 kHz … 225 MHz** at the
baseline base-die parent of 900 MHz, **260.5 kHz … 267 MHz** at the baseline Pro/Max
parent of 1068 MHz. **[Confirmed]** for the baseline parts.

**Channel count and parent frequency on M4 and later: [Unknown].** The five-channel
figure and the 900/1068 MHz parents come from the baseline platform descriptions; the
in-scope descriptions carry neither. The six per-cluster master-clock domains
(`AUDIO_MCA0_M`…`_M5`) plus the low-power cluster (`AUDIO_LEAP_MCA`) imply **at least
seven** independently gated master clocks, which is more than five oscillator channels;
so either the channel count grew, or master clocks are shared between clusters as they
were on the six-cluster M1/M2 parts (where the cluster reference list was channels
0,1,2,3,4,4). **[Inferred]**

---

## 2.2 The audio clock tree on M4 and later

### 2.2.1 Chain

```
 reference clock(s) in the always-on island
        │
        ├─> numerically controlled oscillator channel        (fractional synthesis, §2.1)
        │
        v
 power-manager clock cell, one per cluster master clock      (domains AUDIO_MCAn_M,
   4 cascaded stages: pre-divider mux → divider → main → final mux/bypass,             AUDIO_LEAP_MCA)
   each stage: source-select, enable, auto-disable, bypass, and a "change pending" bit
        │
        v  cluster master clock
 cluster clock generator (per cluster, in the cluster's own register page)
   control register: reset bit
   config register:  clock-source select field, divisor field
        │
        v  bit clock
 cluster frame-sync generator (per cluster)
   control register: reset bit
   config register
   frame phase-0 count register, frame phase-1 count register
        │
        v  frame clock
 ├─> transmit SERDES: frame/bit-clock source-select field in the TX config register
 ├─> receive  SERDES: frame/bit-clock source-select field in the RX config register
 └─> I2S pad block: pad clock-select register with a "bit clock + frame clock" field
                    and a separate "master clock" field
```

**[Confirmed]** that this is the block decomposition on t8132, t604x, t8140, t8142 and
t605x; **[Confirmed]** that the cluster clock-generator and frame-sync-generator
register semantics are the same as the M1–M3 cluster page (master-clock enable +
divider at cluster offsets `0x000`/`0x004`; frame-sync enable, source select and two
period counters at `0x100`–`0x10c`), with two additions:

- the clock generator and the frame-sync generator each gained an explicit **reset**
  bit in their control register; on M1–M3 only the SERDES units had a self-clearing
  reset. **[Probable]**
- the pad-level clock select is now split into a **bit-clock-plus-frame-clock** field
  and an independent **master-clock** field, so a port can export a master clock to a
  codec without exporting bit and frame clocks and vice versa. The always-on-side
  instance already had this split on M1; the host-side instance did not expose it.
  **[Probable]**

The register offsets of these blocks within a cluster page on M4 and later are
**[Unknown]** — the pages are not host-addressable, so no aperture is available to
anchor them. The block *names* and *field* names are established; the addresses are not.

### 2.2.2 Constraints the clock tree enforces

- **A cluster's frame-sync generator must be sourced from the same cluster's clock
  generator.** Mismatched sync-generator and clock-generator identities are rejected.
  **[Confirmed]**
- **A link may not use a system-I/O-domain master clock as its clock source.** The
  audio path on M4 and later is confined to the always-on island's clock sources; the
  host system-I/O master clock, which was the M1–M3 source, is explicitly excluded.
  **[Confirmed]** This is the clocking counterpart of the ownership move in §2.1.
- **Ports carry a clock domain.** Routing a stream onto a port fails if the port is
  already driven from a different clock domain. Platform firmware names the domain on
  the nodes where it matters: on t8140, t8142 and t605x the speaker-tap endpoint
  carries `clock-domain` with the four-character value that reads `main`. **[Confirmed]**
  This is the same "one clock-driving cluster per port" rule as M1–M3, now expressed
  as a named domain rather than as a cluster index.
- Each power-manager master-clock cell stage must be polled until its **change-pending**
  bit clears before the next stage is touched. **[Confirmed]** No timeout value is
  established. **[Unknown]**

### 2.2.3 Parent clocks and frequencies

The always-on island exposes five selectable clock outputs (`AOP_CLK0`…`AOP_CLK4` on
M4 and later, `AOP_CLK_SEL_0`…`_4` on M1–M3) plus a fast low-power PLL
(`LPPLL_FST`/`LPPLL_FAST`) and a fixed always-on oscillator. The master-clock cell's
source-select field chooses among these and reports each candidate's frequency at
run time. **[Confirmed]** that this source set exists and is enumerable.

**The numeric frequencies are [Unknown].** The platform description's
`clock-frequencies` array on `/arm-io` is all zeroes on every in-scope board (it
is filled in by boot firmware at run time), and no in-scope description carries a
parent-frequency property for the audio path. This is Open question 3.

What *is* established is the **required** bit-clock frequency of every link, because
each link descriptor states the master-clock frequency and the frame length from which
it follows (§2.3, §11 §11.7.3): 12.000 MHz for the six-amplifier and low-power-path
links, 12.288 MHz for the t8140 speaker link, 3.072 MHz for the jack link at 48 kHz on
t8132/t604x/t8142/t605x, and **6.000 MHz** for the t8140 jack link — that link's
descriptor states a 24.000 MHz **master clock**, which the divider of 4 reduces to a
6.000 MHz bit clock. The 24.000 MHz figure is not a ceiling.

---

## 2.3 The per-link clock descriptor

Every leaf node with `compatible = "audio-data,…"` carries a **36-byte `reg`** that is
the complete clocking and framing contract for that link. On M1–M3 these nodes lived
under `mcaN/mcaNa`, `mcaN/mcaNb` and the always-on-side link nodes; on M4 and later
they live under `/arm-io/iop-audio-controller/<endpoint>/<endpoint>`. **The bytes are
identical across generations for the same part.** **[Confirmed]** — e.g. the jack-codec
output descriptor on t8122 and on t8132/t604x/t8142/t605x is the same 36 bytes.

### 2.3.1 Field layout — see §11 §11.7.3

> ☠ **The field layout of this descriptor is specified once, in §11 §11.7.3, and
> that subsection is the sole authority for it.** The decode this section
> previously carried is superseded and has been removed. It read bytes
> `0x08`–`0x0b` as a *bit-clock ceiling* (`BCLK_MAX_HZ`) rather than the
> **master-clock frequency**, and bytes `0x0c`–`0x0d` as a *bit-clock-to-frame
> ratio* (`BCLK_RATIO`) rather than the **frame length in bit clocks**, and it
> derived `max f_sample = BCLK_MAX_HZ / BCLK_RATIO`. **That derivation gives
> 24 000 000 ÷ 125 = 192 kHz on the A18 Pro jack link, where the correct answer
> is 48 kHz**, because the master-clock-to-bit-clock divider on that one link is
> 4, not 1 (§11 §11.7.3, §18 §18.4.5). It also left bytes `0x20`–`0x23`
> undecoded, losing the **direction mask** and the **receive data delay** that a
> key-`701` stream-configuration record requires (§18 §18.3.1).

The correct relations, from §11 §11.7.3 and §18 §18.4.2:

```
bit_clock  = master_clock_Hz / divider          divider ∈ 1…31, = 1 on every
                                                in-scope link but the A18 Pro
                                                jack link, where it is 4
frame_bits = phase0 + phase1                    = descriptor 0x0c
frame_rate = bit_clock / frame_bits             division must be exact
master_clock_Hz == frame_bits × frame_rate × divider      (checked, no remainder)
```

The descriptor states the master-clock frequency (`0x08`), the frame length in
bit clocks (`0x0c`), the frame-sync pulse length (`0x0e`) and the rate
numerator/denominator (`0x10`/`0x12`). It does **not** state the divider; a
driver derives it as `master_clock / (frame_bits × rate)` and the division must
be exact. Where `0x08` is zero the link has no stated master clock and the bit
clock is supplied by the cluster's clock generator (§2.2).

### 2.3.2 Values in scope

Column names below are the authoritative field names of §11 §11.7.3. **Master
clock** is descriptor `0x08`; **Frame (bclk)** is descriptor `0x0c`; **Rate num**
is descriptor `0x10`; **W8** is the four bytes `0x20`–`0x23` as a little-endian
u32, i.e. direction mask, receive data delay, transmit slot width, receive slot
width, lowest byte first.

| Link | Part | Machines | Interface class | Master clock (Hz) | Frame (bclk) | Rate num (kHz) | Divider | Bit clock | TX ch × width | RX ch × width | TX mask | RX mask | W8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| speaker, 6 amplifiers | SN012776 | j604 j614s j614c j616s j616c j715 j704 j815 j714s j714c j716s j716c | `0x02` | 12 000 000 | 250 | 48 | 1 | 12.000 MHz | 6 × 24 bit | 12 × 16 bit | `0x3f` | `0xfff` | `0x10200000` |
| speaker, 4 amplifiers + sense | SN012776 | j713 j813 | `0x02` | 12 000 000 | 250 | 48 | 1 | 12.000 MHz | 4 × 24 bit | 8 × 16 bit | `0x0f` | `0xff` | `0x10200000` |
| speaker, 4 amplifiers, no sense | SN012776 | j623 j624 | `0x02` | 12 000 000 | 250 | 48 | 1 | 12.000 MHz | 4 × 24 bit | — | `0x0f` | `0x00` | `0x00200000` |
| speaker, 1 amplifier | SN012776 | j773g j773s j575c | `0x02` | 12 000 000 | 250 | 48 | 1 | 12.000 MHz | 1 × 24 bit | — | `0x01` | `0x00` | `0x00200000` |
| speaker, 2 channels | MAX98360 | j700 | `0x13` | 12 288 000 | 256 | 48 | 1 | 12.288 MHz | 2 × 32 bit | — | `0x03` | `0x00` | `0x00200002` |
| speaker tap, 6 amplifiers | — | j815 j714s j714c j716s j716c | `0x02` | 12 000 000 | 250 | 48 | 1 | 12.000 MHz | — | 6 × 24 bit | `0x00` | `0x3f` | `0x20000101` |
| speaker tap, 6 amplifiers | — | **j704 only** | `0x02` | 12 000 000 | 250 | 48 | 1 | 12.000 MHz | — | 6 × 24 bit | `0x00` | `0x3f` | `0x20000001` |
| speaker tap, 4 amplifiers | — | j813 | `0x02` | 12 000 000 | 250 | 48 | 1 | 12.000 MHz | — | 4 × 24 bit | `0x00` | `0x0f` | `0x20000101` |
| speaker tap | — | j700 | `0x13` | 12 288 000 | 256 | 48 | 1 | 12.288 MHz | — | 2 × 24 bit | `0x00` | `0x03` | `0x20000201` |
| jack codec, playback | CS42L84 | all t8132 / t604x / t8142 / t605x boards | `0x13` | 0 (none stated) | 64 | 0 (agile) | n/a | from clock generator | 2 × 32 bit | — | `0x03` | `0x00` | `0` |
| jack codec, capture | CS42L84 | same | `0x13` | 0 | 64 | 0 | n/a | from clock generator | — | 1 × 32 bit | `0x00` | `0x01` | `0` |
| jack codec, playback | CS42L83 | j700 | `0x13` | 24 000 000 | 125 | 0 | **4** | **6.000 MHz** | 2 × 32 bit | — | `0x03` | `0x00` | `0` |
| jack codec, capture | CS42L83 | j700 | `0x13` | 24 000 000 | 125 | 0 | **4** | **6.000 MHz** | — | 1 × 32 bit | `0x00` | `0x01` | `0` |
| low-power microphone path | — | all with a low-power microphone endpoint | `0x42` | 12 000 000 | 250 | 48 | 1 | 12.000 MHz | — | 3 × 32 bit (2 on j700) | `0x00` | `0x07` (`0x03`) | `0x00000001` |
| low-power internal loopback | — | all | `0x42` | 12 000 000 | 250 | 48 | 1 | 12.000 MHz | 2 × 32 bit | 2 × 32 bit | `0x03` | `0x03` | `0x00000003` |
| secure low-power loopback | — | j714s j714c j716s j716c | `0x42` | 12 000 000 | 250 | 48 | 1 | 12.000 MHz | 2 × 32 bit | 2 × 32 bit | `0x03` | `0x03` | `0x00000003` |
| base-domain loopback | — | all | `0x12` | 12 000 000 | 250 | 48 | 1 | 12.000 MHz | 2 × 16 bit | 2 × 16 bit | `0x03` | `0x03` | `0` |

**[Confirmed]** for every value in the table (each appears on at least four boards
and, for the parts that also exist on M1–M3, identically on the baseline boards),
except the two divider values, which are **[Confirmed]** from the exact-division
invariant of §18 §18.4.2 and the coprocessor's own built-in records (§18 §18.7.1).

**The base-domain loopback's link channel count is `0x0f` = 15 on every board**,
which is neither direction's channel count (both are 2). It is **[Unknown]** and
is §11 open question 40. Every other endpoint's link channel count equals the
channel count of its wider direction.

☠ **The speaker tap's receive data delay is not the same on every M5-generation
board.** W8 byte `0x21` is **1** on j813, j815, j714s, j714c, j716s and j716c,
**0** on j704, and **2** on j700; every other field of the tap descriptor is
identical within a channel count. A driver must take the delay from the board's
own descriptor and must not carry it across boards. **[Confirmed]** — the value
differs between boards whose descriptors are otherwise byte-identical.

Two clocking facts follow directly and matter to a driver:

1. **The amplifier array link runs at a 12.000 MHz bit clock with a 250-bit frame at
   48 kHz**, and `12 000 000 ÷ 250 = 48 000` exactly. On t8132, t604x, t8142 and
   t605x that 12.000 MHz master clock is the **fixed 24 MHz reference divided by
   two**, not a synthesised frequency; the oscillator is not involved in the
   speaker link on those SoCs at all (§18 §18.4.1, §18 §18.7.1). **[Confirmed]**
   The oscillator is retained for the frequencies that are *not* reachable from
   the fixed reference: **12.288 MHz** for the t8140 speaker link, **3.072 MHz**
   for the codec links on t8132/t604x/t8142/t605x and for the injection link, and
   the whole **44.1 kHz family** on the jack link (§2.5.1). An earlier version of
   this subsection attributed the 12.000 MHz speaker clock to fractional
   synthesis; that rationale is withdrawn.
2. **The jack link states no master-clock frequency on M4 and M5** (descriptor
   `0x08` = 0) with a 64-bit-clock frame, so its clocking is limited only by the
   rate set (§2.5) and by the DMA channel: `64 × 96 kHz = 6.144 MHz` at the top of
   the advertised range, well inside the 26 MHz serial-clock limit of the public
   counterpart codec. On the A18 Pro jack link the descriptor **does** state a
   master clock — 24.000 MHz — and the divider is 4, so the bit clock is
   6.000 MHz and the frame 125 bit clocks: `6 000 000 ÷ 125 = 48 000` exactly.
   **A master-clock frequency is not a bit-clock ceiling**, and treating it as one
   gives 192 kHz here.

## 2.4 Jack-codec clock-source and rate properties

The jack codec's control node (`/arm-io/i2cN/audio-codec-output`,
`compatible = "audio-control,cs42l84"` or `"audio-control,cs42l83"`) carries:

| Property | Value in scope | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `internal-mclk-src` | `1` on **every** in-scope board | The codec derives its internal master clock from the link's **bit clock** using its own PLL; the SoC does **not** export a master clock *to the codec pin* on any in-scope board. **[Confirmed]** — corroborated by the M4/M5 jack link descriptor stating no master-clock frequency at all (`0x08` = 0), by the master-clock pad-routing mask being `0` in every built-in record (§18 §18.7.1), by the public counterpart codec's ability to lock its PLL to the serial clock, and by the fact that the property is **absent** on t8103, the one baseline machine whose jack link descriptor *does* state a 6.000 MHz clock. On t8140 the descriptor states a 24.000 MHz master clock, but that is the clock-generator input from which the 6.000 MHz bit clock is divided, not a clock driven to a pad. |
| `samplerate-default` | 8 bytes, `00 00 00 00 80 bb 00 00` on every in-scope board | A **32.32 fixed-point sample rate**, little-endian, i.e. the integer part is the high word. Decodes to **48 000.000 Hz**. **[Confirmed]** |
| `samplerate-subset` | absent on all in-scope boards **except j700**, where it is 16 bytes: `00 00 00 00 80 bb 00 00` followed by eight zero bytes | A **zero-terminated array of 32.32 fixed-point rates**. On j700 the list is exactly one entry, **48 000.000 Hz**. Absent = no restriction. **[Confirmed]** |
| `bits-per-sample-subset` | `24` on every in-scope board | 24-bit samples inside the 32-bit slots the link descriptor declares. **[Confirmed]** |

**Implications.**

- Because the codec makes its own clock from the bit clock, the SoC does not have to
  synthesise a codec-grade master clock for the jack path — only the bit clock. There
  is consequently **no master clock exported to any codec or amplifier on any in-scope
  board**: none of the link descriptors states a separate master-clock frequency, and
  the one amplifier part in scope that has no master-clock pin at all (t8140) is
  clocked from a 12.288 MHz bit clock. **[Confirmed]** The pad-level master-clock
  output described in §2.2.1 exists in the hardware but is not used by any in-scope
  board. **[Probable]**
- A driver must therefore bring the bit clock up **before** taking the codec out of
  reset and expecting it to respond to clock-dependent operations, and must keep the
  bit clock running for as long as the codec's PLL must stay locked (§2.7).
- `samplerate-default` establishes 48 kHz as the rate the link is configured to at
  probe time; it is not a limit except on j700, where `samplerate-subset` makes it one.

---

## 2.5 Sample rates

### 2.5.1 Are 44.1 kHz-family rates reachable in hardware?

**Yes — on t8132, t604x, t8142 and t605x. No — on t8140.** **[Confirmed]**

Evidence:

1. **Platform firmware enumerates them.** The jack-codec capture endpoint
   (`compatible = "audio-data,cs42l84-input"`) carries a `data-sources` property whose
   rate list is four entries long and reads, in 32.32 fixed point:
   **44 100 Hz, 48 000 Hz, 88 200 Hz, 96 000 Hz**. This is byte-identical on all twenty
   in-scope boards that use this codec, and byte-identical to the same property on the
   t8112, t602x, t8122 and t603x boards — i.e. the rate set has been unchanged since
   the M2 generation. On t8140, whose codec is the CS42L83 variant, the same property
   has a one-entry list: **48 000 Hz** only, and the codec control node additionally
   carries `samplerate-subset = {48 000 Hz}`.
2. **The clock hardware can produce them.** The jack link's bit-clock ratio is 64, so
   44.1 kHz needs 2.822 400 MHz and 88.2 kHz needs 5.644 800 MHz. A numerically
   controlled oscillator produces these exactly (0 ppm long-term error) from any parent
   in the band of §2.1.3; with a 900 MHz-class parent, 2.822 400 MHz needs base divisor
   `D = 637` (coarse 159, fine 1), comfortably inside the representable range
   `D ∈ [8, 8199]`. This is precisely what the retained oscillator is for.
3. **The codec supports them.** The public counterpart (CS42L42 family) locks its PLL
   to a 44.1 kHz-family serial clock natively.

So the answer to the reader's question is: **44.1 kHz and 88.2 kHz are reachable on the
headphone-jack link of every in-scope machine except the MacBook Neo (j700, t8140).**
They are **not** reachable on the internal-speaker link, the speaker-sense link, the
low-power microphone link or any loopback link on any machine — those all carry
a rate numerator of 48 (or 16 for the microphone-injection link) with denominator 1,
and a master clock, divider and frame length that give exactly 48 kHz (or 16 kHz).
**[Confirmed]**

### 2.5.2 The sample-rate subset property on a speaker node

j700 is the machine referred to: `/arm-io/iop-audio-controller/audio-speaker` carries

```
samplerate-subset = 00 00 00 00 80 bb 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
```

Decoded with the same 32.32 fixed-point, zero-terminated encoding as §2.4: a list of
**one** rate, **48 000.000 Hz**. It is not a "small list" of several rates — it is a
one-element list plus terminator, and its function is to *restrict* the link, which on
that machine is otherwise capable of 48 kHz only anyway
(12 288 000 Hz master clock ÷ divider 1 ÷ 256 bit clocks = 48 000 Hz). **[Confirmed]**

### 2.5.3 Complete reachable rate set, per link and per SoC

Three independent limits compose: the rate the link descriptor's master clock, divider
and frame length admit under the exact-division invariant (§11 §11.7.3, §18 §18.4.2), any
`samplerate-subset`, and the DMA channel's `max-sample-rate-hz`.

| Link | t8132 | t604x | t8140 | t8142 | t605x |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jack playback | 44.1 / 48 / 88.2 / 96 kHz | same | **48 kHz only** | 44.1 / 48 / 88.2 / 96 kHz, DMA-capped at 96 kHz | same as t8142 |
| Jack capture | 44.1 / 48 / 88.2 / 96 kHz | same | **48 kHz only** | same, DMA-capped at 96 kHz | same |
| Internal speakers | 48 kHz | 48 kHz | 48 kHz | 48 kHz | 48 kHz |
| Speaker sense (capture) | 48 kHz | 48 kHz | n/a (no sense on j700) | 48 kHz | 48 kHz |
| Speaker tap (capture) | n/a | n/a | 48 kHz | 48 kHz | 48 kHz |
| Low-power microphone path | 48 kHz | 48 kHz | 48 kHz | 48 kHz | 48 kHz |
| Low-power / secure loopback | 48 kHz | 48 kHz | 48 kHz | 48 kHz | 48 kHz |
| Base-domain loopback | 48 kHz | 48 kHz | 48 kHz | 48 kHz | 48 kHz |
| Low-power microphone injection | n/a | n/a | 16 kHz | 16 kHz | 16 kHz |

**[Confirmed]**, with one caveat: on t8132 and t604x the audio-DMA nodes carry **no
per-channel `max-sample-rate-hz`**, so the DMA-side limit on those two SoCs is
**[Unknown]** and only the link-descriptor limit applies.

The per-channel DMA limits on the SoCs that state them (`admac-evolution,*` on t8142 and
t605x, `admac,t8140` on t8140) are:

| DMA channel | Serves | t8140 | t8142 | t605x |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `base-ns-adma-tx-0` | speaker playback | — | 48 kHz, ≤6 ch, 32 bit | 48 kHz, ≤6 ch, 32 bit |
| `base-ns-adma-rx-0` | speaker sense | — | 48 kHz, ≤12 ch, 16 bit | 48 kHz, ≤12 ch, 16 bit |
| `base-ns-adma-rx-1` | speaker tap | 48 kHz, ≤2 ch, 32 bit | 48 kHz, ≤6 ch, 32 bit | 48 kHz, ≤6 ch, 32 bit |
| `base-ns-adma-tx-2` | jack playback | **48 kHz**, 2 ch, 32 bit | **96 kHz**, 2 ch, 32 bit | **96 kHz**, 2 ch, 32 bit |
| `base-ns-adma-rx-2` | jack capture | **48 kHz**, 1 ch, 32 bit | **96 kHz**, 1 ch, 32 bit | **96 kHz**, 1 ch, 32 bit |
| `base-ns-adma-tx-3` / `rx-3` | base-domain loopback | 48 kHz, 2 ch, 16 bit | 48 kHz, 2 ch, 16 bit | 48 kHz, 2 ch, 16 bit |
| `base-ns-adma-tx-5` | low-power microphone injection | 16 kHz, ≤2 ch, 32 bit | 16 kHz, ≤3 ch, 32 bit | 16 kHz, ≤3 ch, 32 bit |
| `leap-ns-adma-*`, `leap-s-adma-*` | low-power path | 48 kHz, 32 bit | 48 kHz, 32 bit | 48 kHz, 32 bit |

**[Confirmed]** Each channel node also carries `dma-stream-type` with the four-character
value that reads `ISOC` (isochronous), `max-channel-count` and `max-bit-depth-bits`.

### 2.5.4 Rate-to-divider relationship

For any link, given the desired sample rate `f_s` and the frame length in bit
clocks `frame_bits` from the link descriptor (§2.3, §11 §11.7.3):

```
f_bclk   = frame_bits × f_s
divider  = master_clock_Hz / (frame_bits × f_s)      must divide exactly; 1…31
oscillator: D = floor(2·f_par / f_bclk), INC1 = 2·f_par − D·f_bclk, INC2 = INC1 − f_bclk
cluster clock generator: DIVISOR field scales the cluster master clock to f_bclk
frame-sync generator:    phase 0 = 1
                         phase 1 = frame_bits − 1
                         (each register holds the phase count − 1, so
                          FRAME_PHASE_0 = 0 and FRAME_PHASE_1 = frame_bits − 2;
                          the message carries the phases themselves — §18 §18.3.1
                          bytes 0x2b/0x2f — and the minus one is applied at the
                          register — §18 §18.8.2)
```

☠ **The frame sync is a one-bit-clock pulse, not a 50 %-duty square wave.**
Every built-in record on every in-scope SoC carries phase 0 = 1 and
phase 1 = frame length − 1 (§18 §18.7.1). **[Confirmed]** An earlier version of
this subsection gave an evenly split recipe — `phase0 = floor(frame_bits/2) − 1`,
`phase1 = ceil(frame_bits/2) − 1`, worked as "124 and 124" for the 250-bit-clock
speaker frame — and that recipe is **withdrawn**. It is not merely a different
duty cycle: 124 + 124 = 248, so the frame length it implies is 248 rather than
250, the master-clock invariant `master_clock == frame_bits × rate × divider`
(§18 §18.4.2) leaves a remainder, and **a key-`701` stream-configuration record
built from it is refused before it reaches the hardware**.

Worked examples at 48 kHz, all with divider 1 except where stated:

| Link | Master clock | `frame_bits` | Bit clock | phase 0 | phase 1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| jack link, t8132 / t604x / t8142 / t605x | none stated | 64 | 3.072 MHz | 1 | 63 |
| jack link, t8140 | 24.000 MHz | 125 | 6.000 MHz (divider **4**) | 1 | 124 |
| amplifier link, `sn012776` machines | 12.000 MHz | 250 | 12.000 MHz | 1 | 249 |
| amplifier link, t8140 | 12.288 MHz | 256 | 12.288 MHz | 1 | 255 |
| low-power microphone injection | none stated | 192 | 3.072 MHz | 1 | 191 |

At 44.1 kHz the jack link's bit clock is 2.822 400 MHz; at 96 kHz, 6.144 MHz; the
frame length and therefore the two phases are unchanged, because a rate change on
a fixed-geometry link is a bit-clock change, not a frame-length change.
**[Confirmed]** for the phase encoding and for every row of the table; the
frame-sync generator's register offsets within a cluster block are given at §18
§18.8.2 (`FRAME_PHASE_0` at `+0x08`, `FRAME_PHASE_1` at `+0x0c`), **[Confirmed]**
for t8132 and t604x and **[Probable]** for t8142 and t605x.

---

## 2.6 Power domains

### 2.6.1 How the entries are laid out

The power manager's device list (`devices` under `/arm-io/pmgr`) is an array of
**48-byte** records, count = property length / 48. The fields below are the ones this
section relies on.

| Offset | Size | Field | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | 1 | Flags byte | Bit 4 (`0x10`) is decoded below. **[Confirmed]** |
| `0x04` | 4 | **Two** 16-bit parent domain indices (second is `0` when the domain has one parent) | Agrees with the `power-domains` lists mainline Linux publishes for t8103, t8112, t600x, t8122 and t6030 in 32 of 34 audio domains; the two exceptions are one domain where mainline lists a third parent the record has no room for and one where mainline omits a parent the record states. **[Confirmed]** |
| `0x0a` | 1 | Power-state slot index (register-block form) | See address derivation below. **[Confirmed]** |
| `0x0b` | 1 | Power-state register-block index (register-block form) | See address derivation below. **[Confirmed]** |
| `0x10` | 3 | Control-register byte offset, 24-bit little-endian (group form) | See address derivation below. **[Probable]** |
| `0x13` | 1 | Register-group index (group form) | See address derivation below. **[Probable]** |
| `0x1a` | 2 | 16-bit device index | Every `clock-gates` value elsewhere in the same tree resolves against it. **[Confirmed]** |
| `0x20` | 16 | Name, NUL-padded ASCII | **[Confirmed]** |

Bytes `0x01`–`0x03`, `0x08`–`0x09` and `0x14`–`0x19` are not interpreted here; see
Open question 13.

**Two address encodings exist**, and a driver must pick between them by testing whether
the power manager node carries a `ps-regs` property:

- **Register-block form** (`ps-regs` present — every M1/M2/M3 part, and t8132 in scope).
  `ps-regs` is an array of 12-byte triples `{u32 reg index, u32 byte offset, u32 word}`.
  Control-register address =
  `translate(pmgr.reg[ps-regs[entry[0x0b]].reg].addr) + ps-regs[entry[0x0b]].offset + entry[0x0a] × 8`.
  **[Confirmed]** — this reproduces mainline Linux's published per-domain register
  offset for **1266 of 1266 domains** across t8103, t8112, t600x, t602x, t8122, t6030
  and t6031, with zero mismatches.
- **Group form** (`ps-groups` present, `ps-regs` absent — t604x, t8140, t8142, t605x).
  `ps-groups` has the same triple layout. Control-register address =
  `translate(pmgr.reg[ps-groups[entry[0x13]].reg].addr) + u24le(entry[0x10..0x12])`.
  **[Probable]** — no mainline device tree exists for any SoC that uses this form, so it
  cannot be validated the same way. It is corroborated instead by the fact that on
  t8140 and t8142 it yields a strictly increasing, 8-byte-strided sequence of addresses
  in domain-id order, located `0x4000` into the same power-manager window and with the
  same internal structure that the *independently validated* register-block form yields
  on t8132.

Address translation through `/arm-io`'s `ranges` and the parsing of `reg` under
`#address-cells`/`#size-cells` are ordinary device-tree semantics.

**The flags byte.** Only one bit's meaning is established here, and it is the one that
matters:

> **Bit 4 (`0x10`) marks an entry that is not a host-drivable power-state register.**
> **[Confirmed]** — of the 532 domains that mainline Linux publishes as
> `power-controller` nodes across t8103, t8112, t8122 and t6030, **not one** has bit 4
> set. Every entry with bit 4 set is one mainline models no controller for, with a
> single class of exception: twelve DRAM-controller domains on t6030, which mainline
> does publish but marks always-on, i.e. never actually drives.

The remaining bits of the flags byte are **[Unknown]**. Observed values on audio and
neighbouring entries are `0x00`, `0x01`, `0x08`, `0x09`, `0x10`, `0x11`, `0x20`, `0x29`,
`0x30`, `0x50`. Bit 3 (`0x08`) correlates loosely with domains mainline marks
always-on (25 of 31 such domains on t8103 have it, but so do 2 domains that are not
marked always-on), which makes a "must not be powered down" reading plausible but
**[Probable]** at best. No reading is adopted for bits 0, 5 or 6.

**The power-manager device control register's bit layout.** One 32-bit register per
domain, domains spaced `8` bytes apart within a block, serving as both power-domain
control and reset control. The layout is published by mainline Linux, whose field names
are used here:

| Bits | Name | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `[31]` | `RESET` | RW | Device reset. Synchronous, and effective only while the device is powered **and** clocked, so it must be asserted before the domain is powered down and never while the domain is off. |
| `[28]` | `AUTO_ENABLE` | RW | Hardware auto power management: the domain follows its own activity rather than the target field. Not implemented on every domain; writing it is a no-op where it is not. |
| `[27:24]` | `PS_AUTO` | RW | Power state selected by the auto-enable mechanism. |
| `[19:16]` | `PS_MIN` | RW | Minimum power state the domain may drop to. |
| `[11]` | `PARENT_OFF` | RO | A parent domain of this one is off. |
| `[10]` | `DEV_DISABLE` | RW | Quiesce the device. Set before asserting `RESET`, cleared after deasserting it. |
| `[9]` | `WAS_CLKGATED` | sticky | The domain has been clock-gated since the flag was last cleared. Cleared by writing it back; the published driver clears both sticky flags on every write so as not to re-set them accidentally. |
| `[8]` | `WAS_PWRGATED` | sticky | As above, for power-gating. |
| `[7:4]` | `PS_ACTUAL` | RO | The state the domain is **actually** in. This is the field to poll. |
| `[3:0]` | `PS_TARGET` | RW | The state requested. |

State codes, in both `PS_ACTUAL` and `PS_TARGET`: **`0xF` = active**, **`0x4` = clock-gated**,
**`0x0` = power-gated**.

Sequencing published with the layout: write `PS_TARGET` (clearing `AUTO_ENABLE` and both
sticky flags in the same write), then poll `PS_ACTUAL` until it equals the requested state,
with a timeout of **100 µs**; set `AUTO_ENABLE` afterwards if wanted. A reset is
`DEV_DISABLE` set, `RESET` set, **1 µs**, `RESET` cleared, `DEV_DISABLE` cleared.
**[Confirmed]** — published by mainline Linux for these controllers, and consistent with
the eight-byte domain stride and single-word-per-domain structure the mainline device trees
carry.

**This layout is of limited use on the audio domains in scope and must not be used to try
to drive them**: every audio domain on every in-scope SoC carries the flag marking it as
having no host-drivable power-state register (§2.6.2). It is given because reading
`PS_ACTUAL` back is the cheapest way to observe what the coprocessor has done to the audio
island, and because the host does drive the I²C and GPIO domains the audio parts hang off.

### 2.6.2 The audio domains, per SoC

**All twenty-five audio domains are present, with identical names, on every in-scope
SoC.** **[Confirmed]** — checked on j604, j623, j624, j713, j715, j773g (t8132);
j614s, j614c, j616s, j616c, j773s, j575c (t604x); j700 (t8140); j704, j813, j815
(t8142); j714s, j714c, j716s, j716c (t605x).

The domain named for the sense path is
**`AUDIO_SENSE_PDMC`, unnumbered, on every in-scope SoC including t8132**. No in-scope
board carries `AUDIO_SENSE_PDMC0`. (The numbered form belongs to the M3 generation's
always-on-side domain `AOP_PDMC0`; M1 and M2 called it `AOP_PDMC_LPD`.) **[Confirmed]**
Those two are its direct ancestors and it is a **one-for-one rename of them**: this is
the **microphone** PDM converter domain, not a speaker-sense converter, despite the
name. See §8 §8.8 and §2.6.3 below. **[Confirmed]**

**Both secure domains exist on every in-scope SoC.** The description does **not** split
the DMA domains further into an `_ADMA_A` variant on any in-scope SoC; the four
DMA-aggregate domains are exactly `AUDIO_BASE_S_A`, `AUDIO_BASE_NS_A`,
`AUDIO_LEAP_S_A`, `AUDIO_LEAP_NS_A`. **[Confirmed]** — this is a correction to the
brief's expected list.

**Every audio entry on every in-scope SoC has flags-byte bit 4 set** (value `0x10`, or
`0x30` for six entries on t8132 — see below). By the correlation of §2.6.1 that means
**no audio power domain is a host-drivable power-state register on any in-scope SoC**.
On the M1–M3 parts, by contrast, `AUDIO_P`, `SIO_ADMA` and `MCA0`…`MCA5` all have
bit 4 **clear** and are published by mainline Linux as ordinary host-driven power
controllers. **[Confirmed]** This is the single most important power-domain fact in
this section.

Addresses below are produced by the derivation that reproduces mainline's published
offsets on 1266 of 1266 baseline domains; mainline publishes no t8132 device tree, so

|---|---|---|---|---|---|

Six of these entries — `AUDIO_A`, `AUDIO_LEAP_A`, `AUDIO_BASE_S_A`, `AUDIO_BASE_NS_A`,

flags byte is `0x30` rather than `0x10`, and bytes `0x08`–`0x09` of their record are
non-zero where every other audio entry has zero there. t8132 is also the only in-scope
SoC whose power-manager node carries a `perf-regs` property at all. Taken together these
say that those six domains carry an extra per-domain attribute the others do not.
**[Confirmed]** that the difference exists; **[Unknown]** what the attribute is and what
register, if any, it indexes — see Open question 15.
