#### t604x (M4 Pro/Max) and t605x (M5 Pro/Max) — group form, no address stated

On these two SoCs **every audio entry has bytes `0x08`–`0x13` entirely zero**, so under
either address encoding the description states **no control-register address for any
audio domain**. This is not a decoding artefact: on the same two boards the
serial-I/O processor, the I2C controllers and the storage controller all carry non-zero
bytes there (for example the serial-I/O processor's group-form offset is `0x120` on
t604x and `0x290` on t605x), and 353 of 485 entries on t604x and 487 of 656 on t605x do.
**[Confirmed]** that the description withholds the addresses; the registers themselves
must exist, because the coprocessor drives each cluster master-clock cell and the
low-power cluster cell as power-manager devices — but their addresses are **[Unknown]**
(Open question 4).

Structural notes for these two:

- **t604x** additionally omits the parent links on `AUDIO_BASE_S_A`,
  `AUDIO_BASE_NS_A`, `AUDIO_LEAP_S_A`, `AUDIO_LEAP_NS_A`, `AUDIO_LEAP_RX0…RX4` and
  `AUDIO_LEAP_TX0` — bytes `0x04`–`0x07` of those records are zero. Every other in-scope
  SoC, t605x included, states them. The hardware relationship is presumably the same as
  elsewhere. **[Inferred]**
- **t605x** replaces the virtual aliases `AUDIO-P-V`/`AUDIO-LLT-V` with a single
  `AUDIO_P_V` (underscores, not hyphens) and drops the latency-tolerance alias entirely
  (§2.7). **[Confirmed]**
- `AUDIO-P-V` is present on t604x and t8140, absent on t8132 and t8142. Its flags byte
  is `0x11` on t604x and t8140 — the only audio-tree entry in scope whose flags byte
  differs from `0x10`/`0x30` — while t605x's `AUDIO_P_V` has `0x10`. What bit 0
  signifies is **[Unknown]**. **[Confirmed]** that the difference exists.

### 2.6.3 Which domain gates which block

| Block | Gating domain(s) |
|---|---|
| Whole audio island, register access | `AUDIO_A` |
| Audio functional reference clock (feeds the low-power processor, the PDM converter domain, and the base peripheral domain) | `AUDIO_FR` |
| Base serial-audio controller, all six clusters' register access | `AUDIO_P` |
| Serial-audio cluster *n* master clock (*n* = 0…5) | `AUDIO_MCAn_M` |
| Low-power-path serial-audio cluster | `AUDIO_LEAP_MCA` |
| Host-addressable base audio DMA controller, non-secure aperture (`admac-base-ns`, `0x34000`) | `AUDIO_BASE_NS_A` |
| Base audio DMA controller, secure aperture | `AUDIO_BASE_S_A` |
| Low-power audio DMA controller, non-secure aperture (`admac-leap-ns`) | `AUDIO_LEAP_NS_A` |
| Low-power audio DMA controller, secure aperture (`admac-leap-s`, t8140/t8142/t605x only) | `AUDIO_LEAP_S_A` |
| Low-power audio processor core | `AUDIO_LEAP_C` (under `AUDIO_LEAP_A`) |
| Low-power receive stream *n* | `AUDIO_LEAP_RXn`, *n* = 0…4 |
| Low-power transmit stream 0 | `AUDIO_LEAP_TX0` |
| Microphone PDM converter (the domain named for the sense path — §8 §8.8) | `AUDIO_SENSE_PDMC` |
| PDM microphone reference clocks | `PDM0_AUDIO_REF`, `PDM1_AUDIO_REF` |

**[Confirmed]** for the tree shape; **[Probable]** for the block attributions, which
follow from the names and from the parent relationships.

**`AUDIO_SENSE_PDMC` is not a new block and not a sense converter — it is the
microphone PDM converter domain under a new name.** It is a one-for-one rename of the
baseline generation's microphone PDM converter domain (`AOP_PDMC_LPD` on M1/M2,
`AOP_PDMC0` on M3): the domain count is unchanged M1 → M5, its decimator input selector
takes a microphone index, it is grouped with the secure-microphone mute hardware, and it
is present identically on machines whose amplifiers have no sense capability at all.
Only the name changed. See §8 §8.8, where this is established exhaustively.
**[Confirmed]**

Structurally it hangs off `AUDIO_FR`, i.e. off the audio reference-clock domain and
*not* off `AUDIO_P`, so it is clocked independently of the base serial-audio controller.
A separate clock-enable control with its own change-pending bit exists for it in the
audio global configuration block, alongside a high-frequency-data input control.
**[Confirmed]**

Do **not** read the name as a capability statement about the sense path. Every in-scope
speaker link descriptor returns sense as 16-bit PCM slots on the same TDM link (§2.3.2),
and the sense return is PCM over TDM on every machine in scope; the domain is unused for
sense everywhere, and no PDM sense path exists on any machine in scope.
**[Confirmed]**

### 2.6.4 Required power-up ordering

The parent relationships impose:

```
AOP_FILTER (or AOP_DART on t8142)          ← always-on island, already up
   └─ AUDIO_A                               1. audio island
        └─ AUDIO_FR                         2. audio reference clock
             ├─ AUDIO_P                     3. base peripheral domain
             │    ├─ AUDIO_BASE_S_A         4a. secure DMA aggregate
             │    ├─ AUDIO_BASE_NS_A        4b. non-secure DMA aggregate
             │    ├─ AUDIO_LEAP_MCA         4c. low-power cluster
             │    └─ AUDIO_MCA0_M…MCA5_M    4d. per-cluster master clocks
             ├─ AUDIO_LEAP_A                3'. low-power processor root
             │    └─ AUDIO_LEAP_C           4'. low-power processor core
             │         ├─ AUDIO_LEAP_S_A / _NS_A   5'. its DMA aggregates
             │         ├─ AUDIO_LEAP_RX0…RX4       5'. its receive streams
             │         └─ AUDIO_LEAP_TX0           5'. its transmit stream
             └─ AUDIO_SENSE_PDMC            3''. microphone PDM converter
PDM0_AUDIO_REF, PDM1_AUDIO_REF              independent roots, any time
```

Power-down is the exact reverse. **[Confirmed]** from the parent fields.

Two ordering rules carry over from the baseline and remain load-bearing:

- **The reference clock must be running before a cluster domain is attached.** On the
  M1–M3 parts every cluster power domain is marked externally clocked, meaning it
  cannot complete a state transition while its reference clock is absent, and the
  published driver must enable the oscillator channel before attaching the cluster
  domain. The M4-and-later `AUDIO_MCAn_M` domains are literally the master-clock cells,
  so the same constraint applies with the dependency made explicit in the name.
  **[Probable]**
- **Every power-manager clock-cell stage must be polled to "not pending" before the
  next stage is written.** **[Confirmed]**

**Settling delays.** The only quantified delays that can be established are the
baseline ones, which are still the best available numbers for these parts:

| Delay | Value | What it covers |
|---|---|---|
| SERDES reset self-clear | wait **25 µs** (published upstream) or **50 µs** (published Asahi variant), then verify; observed clear time ~**1 µs** | Per-serialiser reset before every stream start. |
| Pre-DMA-start settle | **100 µs** after the serialiser's frame-sync source is reprogrammed, before the DMA channel is started | Empirically required; believed to be clock settling. |
| Power-manager state-change settle | **[Unknown]** | Any domain state change. No timeout or settle figure is available from any permitted source. |
| Amplifier mute ramp, t8140 only | `mute-ramp-sleep-ms = 20 ms` | Coprocessor-driven ramp-down before muting the MAX98360 (§2.7). |

**[Confirmed]** for the baseline values, **[Unknown]** whether the 25/50/100 µs figures
still apply on M4 and later — on these parts the sequence is executed by the
coprocessor and the host never observes it. No master-clock-cell settling time is
established. **[Unknown]**

### 2.6.5 Delta against the M3 generation

| M3 (t8122 / t603x) | M4 and later | Nature of change |
|---|---|---|
| `AUDIO_P` — host-managed, real register (e.g. `0x2_d070_0288` on j504), flags `0x00` | `AUDIO_P` — always-on island, virtual, no host register | **Ownership moved** |
| `SIO_ADMA` — host-managed, real register (`0x2_d070_0310`), flags `0x00`, parents `SIO` + a PWM domain | replaced by **four** domains `AUDIO_BASE_{S,NS}_A`, `AUDIO_LEAP_{S,NS}_A` | **Split 1 → 4, secure/non-secure added** |
| `MCA0`…`MCA3` — host-managed, real registers `0x2_d070_0398`/`03a0`/`03a8`/`03b8` (note the non-contiguous slot), flags `0x00` | `AUDIO_MCA0_M`…`AUDIO_MCA5_M` — always-on island, virtual | **4 → 6 clusters, renamed to master-clock cells** |
| `AOP_LEAP_CLK`, `AOP_LEAP`, `AOP_AUDIO_SHIM`, `AOP_AUDIO_ADMA0`, `AOP_ADMA0`, `AOP_MCA0`…`AOP_MCA3` | `AUDIO_LEAP_A`, `AUDIO_LEAP_C`, `AUDIO_LEAP_MCA`, `AUDIO_LEAP_{S,NS}_A`, `AUDIO_LEAP_RX0`…`RX4`, `AUDIO_LEAP_TX0` | **Renamed and expanded; per-stream domains are new** |
| `AOP_PDMC0` | `AUDIO_SENSE_PDMC` | **Renamed only; function unchanged.** Still the microphone PDM converter — the new name is misleading and does not indicate a repurposing (§8 §8.8) |
| `AOP_PDM0_REF`, `AOP_PDM1_REF` | `PDM0_AUDIO_REF`, `PDM1_AUDIO_REF` | Renamed; unchanged in function |
| — | `AUDIO_A`, `AUDIO_FR` | **New**: an audio island root and an audio reference-clock domain |
| Audio tree rooted at `SIO`, a domain mainline Linux drives and marks always-on | Audio tree rooted at the always-on coprocessor island | **Root moved off the host system-I/O domain** |
| DMA node `clock-gates` **and** `power-gates` = `{SIO_ADMA, AUDIO_P}` — real | DMA node `clock-gates` = one virtual latency-tolerance entry; **no `power-gates` at all** | **Host power management of audio DMA removed** |
| 6 host + 12 always-on-side audio domains | **25 always-on-island audio domains, 0 host** | |

## 2.7 Clock gating and idle behaviour

### 2.7.1 Must clocks keep running while a link is muted?

**Yes, on the amplifier links.** **[Confirmed]** Three properties in the platform
description and one hardware field establish the model:

- The transmit SERDES configuration word carries a **"disable output when idle"** bit.
  With it set the data pin is released during slots the serialiser owns but is not
  filling; with it clear the pin is driven. Both directions' slot masks are programmed
  as two independent sets — "slots this unit fills with data" and "slots this unit
  owns" — so a stream can be silent without releasing the bus. **[Confirmed]** The
  practical consequence is that **muting is a data-domain operation; it does not
  require stopping bit or frame clock**, and stopping the clocks is what produces a
  click.
- Platform data for the amplifier exposes **`amp-off-in-idle`** and
  **`amp-soft-shutdown-on-mute`** as per-machine switches, and the amplifier control
  path has an explicit "enable idle channel" operation. **[Confirmed]** These select
  between (a) leaving the amplifier enabled and silent, and (b) soft-shutting it down.
  Neither is expressed as a clock-gating decision — both keep the link clocked.
- The amplifier control path validates the **bit-clock-to-frame-sync ratio** and
  refuses an unsupported one. **[Confirmed]** The public counterpart part
  (TAS2764/TAS2770 family) raises a clock-error fault and mutes when the serial clock
  disappears or its ratio changes while the amplifier is out of shutdown; the same
  applies here. **A driver must therefore not stop or re-rate the bit clock while an
  amplifier is out of software shutdown.** **[Probable]**

**What may be gated while a stream is open but silent:**

| Item | May be gated? | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| DMA channel | Yes | The channel can be stopped and restarted; the published bring-up requires a 100 µs settle after the serialiser's frame-sync source is reprogrammed before starting it. |
| Transmit serialiser data (`STATUS.EN`) | Yes | Stopping the serialiser leaves the port clocks running if another direction or another cluster drives them. |
| Bit clock / frame clock | **No**, while any amplifier on the link is un-shut-down | Clock loss is a fault condition at the amplifier. |
| Cluster master clock (`AUDIO_MCAn_M`) | **No**, while the cluster drives any active port | The domain gates the master clock the whole cluster derives from. |
| `AUDIO_P`, `AUDIO_FR`, `AUDIO_A` | **No**, while any link is up | They are ancestors of everything. |
| Jack-codec bit clock | **No**, while the codec's PLL must stay locked | `internal-mclk-src = 1`: the codec's only clock source is the link's bit clock (§2.4). Stopping it unlocks the codec. |

**[Inferred]** except where noted.

The one machine with explicit ramp instrumentation is j700, whose speaker endpoint
carries **`enable-iop-ramp-down`** (a valueless flag) and **`mute-ramp-sleep-ms = 20`**.
Read together: on that machine the coprocessor performs a digital ramp-down before the
amplifier is muted and waits **20 ms** for it to complete. **[Confirmed]** No in-scope
board with the SN012776 amplifier carries either property, so on those machines the
ramp is either unconditional or handled inside the amplifier. **[Unknown]**

### 2.7.2 Always-on requirements implied by the flags

- **Every audio domain on every in-scope SoC carries flags-byte bit 4.** By the
  correlation of §2.6.1 that marks an entry the host does not drive as a power-state
  register: a host driver must neither write nor poll any of them, and attempting to do
  so races the coprocessor. **[Confirmed]** On M1–M3 the host-side audio domains had
  that bit clear and mainline Linux drives them as ordinary power controllers.
- **Nothing in the audio tree carries the flags-byte bit that correlates with
  "must not be powered down"** (bit 3) on any in-scope SoC; that bit appears on the
  serial-I/O domain on t8132 and t605x and on nothing in the audio tree. So the audio
  island is not declared unpowerable-down. **[Probable]** — the bit's meaning is itself
  only **[Probable]** (§2.6.1).
- The virtual alias `AUDIO-P-V` has flags byte `0x11` on t604x, on t8140 and on the
  M1–M3 parts — the only audio-tree entries in scope whose flags byte is neither `0x10`
  nor `0x30`. t8132 and t8142 have no such alias at all, and t605x's `AUDIO_P_V` has
  flags `0x10`. **[Confirmed]** that the difference exists; **what bit 0 signifies is
  [Unknown]** (Open question 13), so no "already on when the host starts" conclusion is
  drawn here.
- On t8132, six audio domains (`AUDIO_A`, `AUDIO_LEAP_A`, `AUDIO_BASE_S_A`,
  `AUDIO_BASE_NS_A`, `AUDIO_LEAP_S_A`, `AUDIO_LEAP_NS_A`) carry flags byte `0x30`
  instead of `0x10` and a non-zero pair of bytes at record offsets `0x08`–`0x09`; t8132
  is also the only in-scope SoC whose power-manager node carries a `perf-regs` property.
  On t604x, t8140, t8142 and t605x no audio entry differs from `0x10` and no such
  property exists. **[Confirmed]** that those six domains carry an extra per-domain
  attribute the others lack, and that it is a t8132-only feature; **[Unknown]** what the
  attribute is, what it indexes, and therefore whether the audio island's internal clock
  frequency is managed at run time on t8132 (Open question 15). No register address is
  derived for it here.

### 2.7.3 Relationship to the always-on coprocessor's own power state

- **The audio power tree is rooted inside the always-on coprocessor island on every
  in-scope SoC.** `AUDIO_A`'s parent is `AOP_FILTER` (t8132, t604x, t8140, t605x) or
  `AOP_DART` (t8142). On M1–M3, `AUDIO_P`'s parent was `SIO`. **[Confirmed]** The
  practical consequence: audio can run with the application processor asleep, and the
  host cannot power the audio block down by releasing its own domains — it has none.
- **The coprocessor node itself has empty `clock-gates`, `power-gates` and `clock-ids`
  properties** on M1–M3 and on all in-scope SoCs alike. It is not host-power-managed.
  **[Confirmed]**
- **The host DMA controllers have no real power gate.** On t8132, t604x, t8140 and
  t8142 each `admac-*` node carries `clock-gates` with exactly one entry,
  `AUDIO-LLT-V`, which is a virtual device, not a power domain — it is the audio
  **latency-tolerance** vote, paired on those SoCs with a latency-tolerance escalation
  detector service named in the DMA node's `ced-ssw-service` property. There is **no
  `power-gates` property at all** on any in-scope audio DMA node, whereas on M1–M3 the
  DMA node carried both, with two real domains. On **t605x** the vote is expressed
  differently again: the `admac-*` nodes carry **no `clock-gates` at all** and instead a
  `function-vote_crit_llt_mode` property (phandle + four-character tag reading `VCLM` +
  two zero arguments). **[Confirmed]**
- **Externally named power provider.** `/arm-io/iop-audio-controller` carries
  `external-named-power-provider` with the string value `HibernationAppUntrusted` on
  **t8140, t8142 and t605x**, and the property is **absent on t8132 and t604x**.
  **[Confirmed]** The low-power microphone I/O-buffer child carries a second such
  property naming a shared-IOMMU-mapper provider on the same three SoCs. Functionally
  this declares that the audio controller's power state is provided by an entity
  outside the device tree that survives hibernation — i.e. on the M5 generation and
  A18 Pro the audio path has a defined power relationship across the host's hibernate
  transition, and the host must wait on that named provider rather than on a power
  domain. **[Inferred]** A driver on those SoCs must expect the audio subsystem to be
  live across host suspend/resume without re-initialisation; on t8132/t604x no such
  relationship is declared. **[Probable]**
- Per-endpoint, the stream nodes under the controller carry
  **`external-power-provider`** as a phandle to their **DMA controller node**
  (`admac-base-ns` for the base-domain links, `admac-leap-ns` for the low-power links)
  on t8132 and t604x, together with a `function-admac_powerswitch` property (phandle +
  four-character tag reading `CSPa`). On t8140, t8142 and t605x these per-endpoint
  properties are replaced by `dma-provider-tx` / `dma-provider-rx` string references to
  named channels. **[Confirmed]** Either way the ordering constraint is the same: the
  DMA controller's domain is the power provider for the stream, so **the DMA controller
  must be up before a stream endpoint is opened**, and it is the last thing released.

### 2.7.4 The USB audio power domains — named for audio, not on the audio path

The power-manager device list carries a small group of domains whose names contain
`AUDIO` but which belong to the USB ports, not to the built-in audio subsystem. They are
documented here only so that a driver author searching the device list for `AUDIO` does not
mistake them for part of this subsystem.

| Domain | Parent | Flags | Present on |
|---|---|---|---|
| `USB-AUDIO-V` | none (root of its own small tree) | `0x10` | t8132, t8140, t8142 |
| `ATC0-USB-AUD-V` … `ATC3-USB-AUD-V` | `USB-AUDIO-V` | `0x10` | t8132, t8142 (four, one per port); t8140 (one, `ATC0-` only) |

**[Confirmed]** — checked on all twenty in-scope board descriptions; the per-port entries'
parent index resolves to `USB-AUDIO-V`'s own device index on every board that has them.

Three things follow.

- **They are absent on t604x and t605x**, i.e. on every Pro/Max die in scope. The port
  count on those machines is the same or higher, so this is a difference in how the die
  expresses the vote, not in how many ports exist. **[Confirmed]**
- **This is not an M4 delta.** The same pair of domains exists on the M3 generation
  (t8122) and on the M3 Pro die, and is likewise absent on the M3 Max die. **[Confirmed]**
- **They are votes, not power gates.** The `-V` suffix is the same convention as
  `AUDIO-LLT-V` in §2.7.3, and like it they carry flags-byte bit 4, so none of them is a
  host-drivable power-state register. **[Probable]** for the vote reading, from the naming
  convention and the flag; what is voted for is **[Unknown]**.

**Nothing in this document's audio path depends on them.** No audio node references them,
they are not in the `AUDIO_*` tree rooted on the coprocessor island (§2.6.2), and a driver
for the built-in audio subsystem should neither read nor write them.

## 2.8 Timebase apertures

Audio timestamping uses the audio DMA controller's own 54-bit local counter and the
always-on global timebase it is scaled against (Section 4 §4.1.3, §4.3.2). Two further
timebase nodes appear in the platform description and are recorded here because one of them
is an M4-generation-only node that a driver author will otherwise find unexplained.

Addresses are given both as the platform description's I/O-region-relative `reg` value and
as absolute addresses, using the per-SoC translation offset of Section 5 §5.2.7:
`0x2_0000_0000` on t8132, `0x2_1000_0000` on t8140.

| Node | SoC | `reg` (region-relative) | Size | Absolute | `device_type` | Boards |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `/arm-io/aic-timebase` | all in scope | `0x3_8118_0000` on t8132 | `0x1000` | `0x5_8118_0000` on t8132 | `timer` | every in-scope board |
| `/arm-io/siri-exclave-timebase` | t8132 | `0x3_C82A_8000` | `0x4000` | `0x5_C82A_8000` | none | **all six t8132 boards** |
| `/arm-io/siri-exclave-timebase` | t8140 | `0x3_482A_8000` | `0x4000` | `0x5_582A_8000` | none | **j700** |

**[Confirmed]** — the `reg` values are byte-identical across all six t8132 boards.

`siri-exclave-timebase` carries exactly three properties: `reg`, an empty
`exclave-assigned` boolean, and its phandle. The empty `exclave-assigned` marks the
aperture as belonging to the isolated execution environment (Section 11 §11.8), which is
the same marking the isolated mailbox nodes carry. It is **not** present on any t604x,
t8142 or t605x board, nor on any baseline board from M1 through M3 — so it appears at the
M4 generation and is gone again by the M5 generation. **[Confirmed]**

**Its relationship to audio is [Unknown].** A second timebase assigned to the isolated
environment is the kind of block that would timestamp isolated capture, and the built-in
microphone array is behind the isolation boundary on t8140 — but not on t8132, where six of
the seven boards carrying this node live and where no audio stream is isolated at all
(Section 11 §11.8.2). That mismatch is the reason no audio role is asserted here. A host
driver must not map or program this aperture: it is assigned to the isolated environment,
and nothing in the audio path references it. See Open question 18.

| Aspect | t8132 (j604, j623, j624, j713, j715, j773g) | t604x (j614s/c, j616s/c, j773s, j575c) | t8140 (j700) | t8142 (j704, j813, j815) | t605x (j714s/c, j716s/c) |

| Oscillator node | absent | absent | present, stub (no `reg`, no page size) | absent | absent |
| Power-manager address encoding | register-block form (`ps-regs`) | group form (`ps-groups`) | group form | group form | group form |
| Audio domain control registers stated | yes, `0x3_8828_4020`+ **[Probable]** | **no — bytes zero** | yes, `0x3_0828_4020`+ **[Probable]** | yes, `0x3_8828_4080`+ **[Probable]** | **no — bytes zero** |
| Extra per-domain attribute on 6 audio domains (flags `0x30`, non-zero bytes `0x08`–`0x09`, `perf-regs` property present) | yes | no | no | no | no |
| Audio tree root | `AOP_FILTER` | `AOP_FILTER` | `AOP_FILTER` | **`AOP_DART`** | `AOP_FILTER` |
| Parent links stated for the DMA-aggregate and low-power stream domains | yes | **no — bytes zero** | yes | yes | yes |
| Virtual alias of `AUDIO_P` | absent | `AUDIO-P-V`, flags `0x11` | `AUDIO-P-V`, flags `0x11` | absent | `AUDIO_P_V`, flags `0x10` |
| Latency-tolerance vote | `AUDIO-LLT-V` in `clock-gates` | same | same | same | **`function-vote_crit_llt_mode`, no `clock-gates`** |
| `external-named-power-provider` on the controller | absent | absent | present | present | present |
| Secure low-power DMA aperture (`admac-leap-s`) node | absent | absent | present | present | present |
| Per-display DMA instances | none | none | none | 3 (`admac-disp0`, `admac-dispext0/1`) | 5 (`admac-disp0`, `admac-dispext0…3`) |
| Per-DMA-channel rate metadata | absent | absent | present | present | present |
| Second always-on coprocessor instance (`/arm-io/aop2`) | no | no | yes | yes | yes |
| Jack codec | CS42L84, codec-internal clock, no master clock stated | same | **CS42L83**, codec-internal clock, 24 MHz master clock ÷ 4 = 6 MHz bit clock, 125-bit-clock frame | CS42L84 | CS42L84 |
| Jack rate set | 44.1 / 48 / 88.2 / 96 kHz | same | **48 kHz only** | same, DMA-capped 96 kHz | same, DMA-capped 96 kHz |
| Speaker amplifier link | SN012776 TDM, 12.000 MHz, 250-bit frame | same | **MAX98360, 12.288 MHz, 256-bit frame, 2 ch** | SN012776 as t8132 | SN012776 as t8132 |
| Speaker sense return | 12 ch × 16 bit (6 amps), 8 ch (4 amps), none on j623/j624/j773g | 12 ch × 16 bit; none on j773s/j575c | none | 12 ch (j704, j815) / 8 ch (j813) | 12 ch × 16 bit |
| Speaker tap endpoint | absent | absent | present, 2 ch | present, 4–6 ch | present, 6 ch |
| Amplifier ramp properties | none | none | `enable-iop-ramp-down`, `mute-ramp-sleep-ms = 20 ms` | none | none |
| `samplerate-subset` anywhere in the audio tree | no | no | yes, on both the jack control node and the speaker endpoint, `{48 kHz}` | no | no |
| Secure low-power loopback endpoint | no | no | no | no | yes |

Machine-level note: **Analog Devices SSM3515 does not appear on any in-scope board.**
Every in-scope speaker amplifier is either `audio-control,sn012776`/`audio-data,sn012776`
or, on j700 alone, `audio-control,max98360`/`audio-data,max98360`. **[Confirmed]**

## Open questions

1. **Where is the oscillator's register aperture on M4 and later, and does it respond to
   host reads?** *Why it matters:* it is the only fractional synthesiser in the audio
   path; if it is host-reachable, a host driver could observe (and in a bring-up
   scenario drive) the bit clock directly instead of trusting the coprocessor, and
   could verify computed divisors against hardware. *How to resolve:* on a baseline
   part the block sat in the SoC clock/power-manager window at base + `0x44000`, size
   `0x14000`. Map both the host clock-manager window
   and the always-on island clock-manager window and probe at + `0x44000` (and at
   + `0x44000` relative to the always-on block) for a five-or-more-channel pattern of
   `0x4000`-strided 20-byte register files whose word 0 has only bit 31 writable.
   Confirm by reading back `DIV`/`INC1`/`INC2` while a 48 kHz stream is running and
   checking `2·f_par·(INC1−INC2) / (D·(INC1−INC2)+INC1)` against the expected
   12.000 MHz.

2. **How many oscillator channels are there on M4 and later, and are master clocks
   shared between the six clusters?** *Why it matters:* it bounds how many links can run
   at mutually unrelated rates simultaneously — e.g. whether a 44.1 kHz jack stream and
   a 48 kHz speaker stream can coexist. *How to resolve:* size the aperture found in (1);
   or, behaviourally, open the jack link at 44.1 kHz and the speaker link at 48 kHz
   simultaneously and observe whether the coprocessor accepts both, then measure the
   two bit clocks on the test points.

3. **What is the oscillator's parent frequency on each in-scope SoC, and which
   always-on clock sources can the master-clock cells select?** *Why it matters:*
   without it no divisor can be computed, and the reachable rate band of §2.1.3 cannot
   be evaluated. *How to resolve:* read the boot-firmware-populated
   `clock-frequencies` array on `/arm-io` at run time (it is zero in the static board
   file but is filled in before the kernel runs); cross-check by reading the
   oscillator's `DIV`/`INC1`/`INC2` for a link whose bit clock is known from its
   descriptor (12.000 MHz on the amplifier link) and solving for the parent.

4. **What are the audio power-domain control-register addresses on t604x, t8142 and
   t605x?** *Why it matters:* they are needed to observe (not drive) the state of the
   six cluster master clocks and the DMA aggregates while debugging a stream that will
   not start. *How to resolve:* on those SoCs the description gives group 0 / offset 0.
   Trace the coprocessor's own bus accesses: watch the always-on
   power-manager window while opening and closing each endpoint under
   `/arm-io/iop-audio-controller`, and correlate the touched offsets with the endpoint
   opened. t8132 and t8140 give the addresses directly and can be used to predict the
   layout (stride `0x8`, in domain-id order).

5. **What is the settling time of a cluster master-clock cell, and of the audio island
   root domain?** *Why it matters:* it sets the minimum stream-start latency and whether
   the published 100 µs pre-DMA-start delay is still sufficient. *How to resolve:* trace
   the coprocessor's writes to the master-clock cell and time the interval between the
   final stage's enable write and the first serialiser enable; separately, measure the
   time from the change-pending bit being set to its clearing.

6. **Settled — `AUDIO_SENSE_PDMC` is the microphone PDM converter domain, not a
   speaker-sense converter, and no in-scope machine returns sense as PDM.** The domain
   is a one-for-one rename of `AOP_PDMC_LPD` / `AOP_PDMC0` (§2.6.3, §8 §8.8) and the
   sense return is 16-bit PCM in TDM slots everywhere. **[Confirmed]** *Retained as a
   confirmation only:* capture on the `base-ns-adma-rx-0` channel and check that the
   returned data is 16-bit PCM, as the link descriptor says, rather than a 1-bit
   stream; and confirm that the domain's clock-enable follows microphone capture
   rather than speaker sense.

7. **Does the jack link actually run at 44.1 kHz, and what does the coprocessor do to
   the oscillator when it does?** *Why it matters:* this is the one place where the
   fractional synthesiser is load-bearing, and it is the difference between resampling
   everything to 48 kHz and passing 44.1 kHz through. *How to resolve:* request a
   44.1 kHz stream on the jack endpoint, measure the bit clock (expect
   2.822 400 MHz ±0 ppm), and read back the oscillator divisor/increment registers if
   (1) succeeds.

8. **Confirm the frame-sync generator and cluster clock-generator register offsets
   within a cluster block on M4 and later by reading them back.** The offsets are
   **established** at §18 §18.8.1 and §18 §18.8.2 — `CLOCK_GEN_CONTROL` `+0x00`,
   `CLOCK_GEN_CONFIG` `+0x04` (`CLOCK_SELECT` bits 2:0, `DIVISOR` bits 12:8);
   `SYNC_GEN_CONTROL` `+0x00`, `SYNC_GEN_CONFIG` `+0x04`, `FRAME_PHASE_0` `+0x08`,
   `FRAME_PHASE_1` `+0x0c` — **[Confirmed]** for t8132 and t604x, **[Probable]** for
   t8142 and t605x, and the presence of the two reset registers is **[Unknown]** on
   t8132, t604x and t8140 (§18 open question 8). What remains is confirmation on a
   live part. *Why it matters:* a host driver that ever takes the serial-audio
   controller back (for a bare-metal bring-up) needs them, and they are the only way
   to verify the frame phases against the 250-bit-clock frame.
   *How to resolve:* with the six-amplifier speaker link running, read the cluster
   block of §3 §3.4.2 and expect `FRAME_PHASE_0` = **0** and `FRAME_PHASE_1` = **248**
   — the registers hold the phase count minus one, and the phases are 1 and 249, not
   the evenly split pair an earlier version of this section predicted (§2.5.4).
   Expect `DIVISOR` = 1 on that link and 4 on the t8140 jack link.

9. **Settled for the last four bytes; still open for descriptor bytes `0x02`,
   `0x03` and `0x07`.** What this entry used to call "word 8" is bytes
   `0x20`–`0x23` and is decoded at §11 §11.7.3 as direction mask, receive data
   delay, transmit slot width and receive slot width — which is why the value
   differs between otherwise identical machines with and without speaker sense
   (the receive slot width is 16 with sense and 0 without) and why the speaker
   tap's differs between M5-generation boards (its receive data delay is 1 on
   j813/j815/j714s/j714c/j716s/j716c, 0 on j704 and 2 on j700). **[Confirmed]**
   What remains **[Unknown]** is byte `0x07`, which is `0` on every instance of
   every board of every generation, and bytes `0x02`–`0x03`, which are `0`
   everywhere and which the second candidate reading of §11 §11.7.3 assigns to a
   master-clock mode selector and a per-direction bit-order byte. *Why it
   matters:* under that second reading byte `0x01` also carries link framing —
   frame-sync edge and polarity, serialiser clock-edge mode — that a driver must
   reproduce, and under the first reading it does not. *How to resolve:* this is
   §18 open question 16 and is settled the same way: read property key `701`
   back from a configured endpoint and compare the framing bytes of the returned
   record against the descriptor's bytes `0x00`–`0x03`.

10. **Settled — the 250-bit amplifier frame really is 250 bit clocks.** The link
    descriptor's frame field is a count of **bit clocks**, the bit clock is
    **12.000 MHz**, and 12 000 000 ÷ 250 = **48 000 Hz** exactly.
    **[Confirmed]** on three lines: the platform hardware description carries the
    12 000 000 Hz reference and the 250-cycle frame directly (§11 §11.7.3); the
    coprocessor's built-in record for this stream family carries frame-sync
    phase 0 = 1, phase 1 = 249 and divider 1 (§18 §18.7.1); and the amplifier's own
    bit-clock-to-frame-rate register has a code for 250, one of three
    non-power-of-two entries that exist so a 12 MHz reference can be used at
    96 / 48 / 24 kHz (§18 §18.4.4). The objection recorded here — that 250 is not a
    multiple of the declared slot widths — is answered: **the frame is longer than
    the data.** Six 32-bit playback slots occupy 192 bit clocks and twelve 16-bit
    sense slots occupy 192 in the opposite direction, leaving **58 idle bit clocks**
    in each; on a four-amplifier machine 128 data bits and 122 idle, on a
    single-amplifier machine 32 and 218. *Retained as a confirmation measurement:*
    count bit-clock edges per frame on the amplifier link with a logic analyser.

11. **What does the `external-named-power-provider` relationship require of a host
    driver on t8140, t8142 and t605x?** *Why it matters:* it is the only declared
    dependency between the audio controller and anything outside the device tree, and
    getting it wrong most likely shows up as audio that does not resume after
    hibernate. *How to resolve:* suspend and resume with a stream open and observe
    whether the coprocessor re-runs the clock bring-up sequence, by tracing the
    always-on power-manager and cluster windows across the transition.

12. **What clock-gating is applied automatically?** *Why it matters:* the master-clock
    cells have an **auto-disable** bit per stage; if it is set, the clock may stop on
    its own when no consumer is active, which is exactly the pop/click hazard of §2.7.
    *How to resolve:* read back each stage's configuration while a link is open but
    silent and check the auto-disable bit; then mute and watch whether the bit clock
    stops.

13. **What do the remaining bits of the power-manager entry flags byte, and entry bytes
    `0x01`–`0x03`, `0x08`–`0x09` and `0x14`–`0x19`, encode?** *Why it matters:* one of
    them distinguishes `AUDIO-P-V` (flags `0x11`) from every other audio entry. The
    meaning of that bit is **[Unknown]**. A driver that assumes the audio peripheral
    domain is already up at hand-off, and is wrong, will open a stream on a dead
    block. *How to resolve:* correlate each candidate bit against mainline Linux's
    `apple,always-on` and `apple,min-state` annotations across all seven baseline SoCs
    (bit 3 already correlates at 25/31 on t8103 and is the leading candidate for a
    "do not power down" bit); then confirm behaviourally by reading the domain's
    control register at hand-off on a machine whose entry has bit 0 set and one whose
    entry does not.

14. **Does the published control-register bit layout hold on the in-scope SoCs?**
    *Closed for the layout itself* — the field map, state codes, sequencing and timeouts
    are published by mainline Linux and are reproduced at §2.6.1. **[Confirmed]** What
    remains open is only whether the same layout holds on t8132, t604x, t8140, t8142 and
    t605x, for which no mainline controller description exists. *Why it matters:* reading
    `PS_ACTUAL` back is the only cheap way to observe what the coprocessor has done to the
    audio island, and a driver that misreads the field would draw the wrong conclusion
    about whether audio is powered. *How to resolve:* read the register of a **host-driven**
    domain whose state is known (the I²C controller carrying the amplifiers, which is up
    whenever the host is running) and check that `PS_ACTUAL` reads `0xF`; then transition
    it and check that `PS_ACTUAL` follows `PS_TARGET` through `0x4` and `0x0` within
    100 µs. Do **not** attempt this on an audio domain: none is host-drivable in scope.

15. **What is the extra per-domain attribute that six t8132 audio domains carry?**
    *Why it matters:* if it is a run-time frequency or voltage state, then on t8132 —
    and only on t8132 — the audio island's internal clock can change under the
    coprocessor's control while a stream is open, which a driver computing DMA timing
    must know about. *How to resolve:* the six entries are `AUDIO_A`, `AUDIO_LEAP_A`,
    `AUDIO_BASE_S_A`, `AUDIO_BASE_NS_A`, `AUDIO_LEAP_S_A` and `AUDIO_LEAP_NS_A`; their
    records differ from the other nineteen only in the flags byte (`0x30` vs `0x10`)
    and in bytes `0x08`–`0x09`, and t8132 is the only in-scope SoC carrying a
    `perf-regs` property on the power-manager node. Trace the always-on power-manager
    window on a t8132 machine while starting and stopping a stream and see whether any
    word outside the `0x…284000` block changes in step; correlate the changing offset
    against those two bytes.

16. **Does the group-form address encoding used by t604x, t8140, t8142 and t605x mean
    what it is read to mean here?** *Why it matters:* the t8140 and t8142 audio-domain
    addresses in §2.6.2 rest on it, and no mainline device tree exists for any SoC that
    uses that encoding, so unlike the register-block form it could not be validated
    against 1266 published domains. *How to resolve:* read the derived addresses on a
    t8140 or t8142 machine and check that each holds a plausible power-state word that
    changes when the corresponding endpoint is opened; a wrong base or stride will show
    as reads of unrelated or unmapped words.

17. **What do the `USB-AUDIO-V` and `ATC<n>-USB-AUD-V` pseudo-devices vote for, and why do
    the Pro/Max dies not have them?** (§2.7.4.) The vote reading follows from the naming
    convention and the flag byte and is **[Probable]**; the quantity voted for is
    **[Unknown]**, as is what expresses the same requirement on t604x and t605x. *Why it
    matters:* only to rule them out. If they turn out to place a latency or clock floor on
    a shared fabric that the audio DMA controllers also sit behind, they stop being
    irrelevant to this subsystem. *How to resolve:* compare the audio DMA controller's
    measured memory-access latency (`CHAN_MAX_MEM_READ_LATENCY`, Section 4 §4.3.3) with a
    USB audio device streaming and with none, on a t8132 machine and on a t604x machine.

18. **What is `/arm-io/siri-exclave-timebase`, and does it have any audio role?** (§2.8.)
    It appears at the M4 generation on all six t8132 boards and on j700, is absent
    everywhere else including the whole M5 generation and the entire M1–M3 baseline, is
    assigned to the isolated execution environment, and carries no `device_type` and no
    properties beyond `reg`. **[Unknown]** throughout. *Why it matters:* if it is the
    timebase against which isolated capture is timestamped, a driver correlating isolated
    microphone frames with host time needs to know it exists and that it is unreachable; if
    it is unrelated to audio, it can be ignored, and saying so removes an unexplained
    aperture from the map. *How to resolve:* it cannot be probed directly from the normal
    world — the aperture is assigned away. Resolve it indirectly: compare the timestamps
    on isolated microphone capture with the always-on global timebase on j700, and check
    whether the relationship is the same on a t8142 machine, which has isolated capture but
    no such node.

# 3. Serial audio controller (I2S/TDM transceiver)

## Baseline

The closest documented equivalent is the M1–M3 multi-cluster serial audio
controller: an array of identical clusters, each with one master-clock gate, one
frame-sync generator, four serialiser/deserialiser units (TXA, RXA, TXB, RXB) and
one I2S/TDM port, plus a separate "switch" region holding per-cluster DMA/slot
adapters and the cross-connect between cluster clocks, cluster serialisers and
periphery ports. Each cluster occupies one `0x4000` page in a cluster region and
two `0x4000` pages in a switch region. On those parts the host owns the block:
platform firmware publishes one node per cluster with three apertures, a switch
node with the aggregate windows, one interrupt per cluster, one reference clock
per cluster from the numerically controlled oscillator, and one power domain per
cluster plus a common register-access domain. That register map, its programming
order and its timings are the project baseline and are not restated here.

Every M1-generation and later SoC also carries a **second instance of the same
block inside the always-on (low-power) audio island**, with its own cluster power
domains, its own audio DMA controller and its own PDM converter. On M1–M3 that
instance is invisible in the platform description except for a few endpoint nodes
with no MMIO.

## Summary of differences

| Aspect | M1–M3 | t8132 (M4) | t604x (M4 Pro/Max) | t8140 (A18 Pro) | t8142 (M5) | t605x/t6050 (M5 Pro/Max) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Block present in silicon | yes, two instances | **yes, merged into one** | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Host MMIO aperture published | yes | **no** | no | no | no | no |
| MMIO base given here | published | **yes, §3.4** | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Register map | cluster pages of `0x4000`, switch pages of `0x8000` | **redesigned: one compact block with `0x100`-strided per-unit arrays** | same | same | same | same |
| Base-domain clusters | 4 or 6 host + 2/4/6 low-power | **6** | 6 | 6 | 6 | 6 |
| Low-power-domain clusters | separate instance, 2–6 clusters | **1** | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| Serialiser addressing | 4 per cluster, addressed within the cluster page | **flat array of 17 transmit and 17 receive units** | same | same | same | same |
| Atomic multi-unit start | none | **new aligned-enable trigger with set/clear registers** | same | same | same | same |
| Serialiser → DMA-channel binding | implicit (fixed) | **explicit programmable map register** | same | same | same | same |
| Cluster power domains | `MCA0`…`MCA3/5` under the host serial-I/O island | `AUDIO_MCA0_M`…`AUDIO_MCA5_M` + `AUDIO_LEAP_MCA` under the **always-on** island | same | same | same | same |
| Power-state registers host-addressable | yes | **yes** (§3.4.1) | **no — not enumerated** | yes | yes | **no — not enumerated** |
| Per-cluster interrupt in host interrupt controller | yes | **none claimed** | none | none | none | none |
| Numerically controlled oscillator node | node with `reg` | **absent** | absent | present, **no `reg`** | absent | absent |
| Audio DMA controllers | one shared serial-I/O instance | **four** (base / low-power × secure / non-secure) | same | same | same | same |
| Fabric inbound address-protection filter over audio addresses | absent | absent | absent | **present, 8 ranges** | **present, 7 ranges** | **present, enabled and locked, no range table published** |
| Control ownership | host | **always-on coprocessor** | coprocessor | coprocessor | coprocessor | coprocessor |
| Internal loopback | present | present | present | present | present | present + a second, security-crossing one |
| Link "tap" (capture of a transmitted link) | not exposed | **not exposed** | not exposed | **exposed** | **exposed** | **exposed** |
| Microphone PDM converter domain | `AOP_PDMC_LPD` (M1/M2), `AOP_PDMC0` (M3) | **renamed `AUDIO_SENSE_PDMC`** — the name is misleading; count and function unchanged (§8 §8.8) | same | same | same | same |

---

## 3.1 Does the block still exist in hardware?

**Yes. [Confirmed].** The block is enumerated, addressed and fed as follows:

1. **The power manager still enumerates the per-cluster power/clock domains** on
   every in-scope SoC, in the block's characteristic one-domain-per-cluster
   shape: `AUDIO_MCA0_M`, `AUDIO_MCA1_M`, `AUDIO_MCA2_M`, `AUDIO_MCA3_M`,
   `AUDIO_MCA4_M`, `AUDIO_MCA5_M`, plus `AUDIO_LEAP_MCA`. All seven are children
   of one common domain, `AUDIO_P` — the "register access + common logic" domain
   the block has always had. On the base dies these entries carry real gating
   register addresses (§3.4.1).
2. **The block has a recoverable MMIO address and an internal structure that
   matches the domain list**: a register region whose per-cluster array has
   exactly six entries (§3.4.2).
3. **The audio DMA controllers are host-addressable and their channel counts
   match a six-cluster controller**: the base-domain controller declares 13
   transmit and 13 receive channels with channel 12 explicitly marked skipped,
   leaving 12 usable in each direction — six clusters × two serialiser pairs.
4. **Every audio stream endpoint is typed by which serial-audio domain serves
   it** (`compatible = "iop-adma-stream,mca"` or `"iop-adma-stream,leap"`) and is
   bound to a numbered DMA channel of the matching controller.
5. **The per-endpoint link descriptors are serial-audio frame formats** — TDM
   channel counts, sample widths and slot widths, with a per-amplifier slot map
   supplied separately (§3.7).

What has gone is not the block but its host-visible *description*: the
per-cluster nodes, the switch node, their `reg`, `interrupts` and `clocks`
properties, and the `numClusters` / `regStride` parameters. **[Confirmed]**

---

## 3.2 Topology

### 3.2.1 Cluster count and placement

| Domain | Clusters | Power domains | DMA controllers |
|---|---|---|---|
| Base audio domain | **6** | `AUDIO_MCA0_M` … `AUDIO_MCA5_M`, children of `AUDIO_P` | `admac-base-s`, `admac-base-ns` |
| Low-power audio processor domain | **1** | `AUDIO_LEAP_MCA`, **also a child of `AUDIO_P`** | `admac-leap-s`, `admac-leap-ns` |

Identical on t8132, t604x, t8140, t8142 and t605x. **[Confirmed]** — the same
seven domain names, in the same order, with the same parent, in the power-manager
device list of every in-scope board, and the
register region's per-cluster array has exactly six entries.

The arrangement is therefore six base clusters plus one low-power cluster, with
one refinement: the low-power cluster's *serial-audio* half is
not in the low-power island's power hierarchy. `AUDIO_LEAP_MCA` hangs off
`AUDIO_P` alongside the six base clusters, whereas everything else belonging to
the low-power audio processor (`AUDIO_LEAP_C`, its two DMA apertures
`AUDIO_LEAP_S_A` / `AUDIO_LEAP_NS_A`, and its per-link domains
`AUDIO_LEAP_RX0`…`RX4` and `AUDIO_LEAP_TX0`) hangs off `AUDIO_LEAP_A`, a sibling
of `AUDIO_P`. **[Confirmed]**

The reading is that the low-power cluster is a **cluster of the same controller**,
sharing its common logic, register region and port cross-connect, with its
DMA-facing side wired to the low-power processor's DMA controllers instead of the
base ones. **[Probable]** — supported independently by the cross-domain routing
evidence in §3.8.3.

### 3.2.2 Serialisers

The register region contains **two peer arrays of 17 serialiser units** (one
transmit, one receive) and a third array of 17 smaller per-unit blocks
(§3.4.2). **[Probable]** that the two peer arrays are transmit and receive;
**[Unknown]** which array is which.

Seventeen units admits two readings, and a driver author must not commit to
either without probing:

- **12 + 5.** Six base clusters × two serialisers = 12 (indices 0–11), followed by
  the low-power cluster's five receive links (indices 12–16). This matches the
  low-power domain list (`AUDIO_LEAP_RX0`…`RX4`) exactly and explains why the
  low-power cluster shares `AUDIO_P`. **[Inferred]**
- **16 + 1.** Sixteen per-unit slots filling a `0x1000` window, plus a broadcast
  or aggregate alias immediately after the array. **[Inferred]**

The base-domain DMA channel number used by each stream endpoint equals the
cluster index on every in-scope endpoint — speaker on channel 0, link tap on
channel 1, headphone codec on channel 2, loopback on channel 3, low-power
microphone injection on channel 5 — and the base DMA controller reserves channel
12 for the coprocessor's own use, which is exactly why the platform description
marks channel 12 as skipped. **[Confirmed]** The binding of serialiser index to
DMA channel is **programmable** through a dedicated map register (§3.6.8), so
this correspondence is a configuration, not a wiring constant. **[Probable]**

### 3.2.3 Low-power cluster links

The per-link power domains name **five receive links and one transmit link**
(`AUDIO_LEAP_RX0`…`RX4`, `AUDIO_LEAP_TX0`). Both low-power DMA controllers
declare 9 transmit and 9 receive channels, none skipped. Observed channel use is
receive 0, 4 and 5 and transmit 0, 4 and 5. **[Confirmed]** that receive link 0
is the low-power microphone capture link and receive link 4 the internal
loopback: those are the two links the M1–M3 platform description exposed as
always-on-side endpoints with `alc-number = 0` and `alc-number = 4`, and they use
the same DMA channel indices 0 and 4 on t8122, t603x and every in-scope SoC.
**[Unknown]** why nine DMA channels exist for six named links, and what receive
link 5 (used on M5 Pro/Max) corresponds to in the domain list.

### 3.2.4 Ports

The number of I2S/TDM pad groups is **[Unknown]**. On M1–M3 the port namespace is
six regardless of populated cluster count. The in-scope parts have six base
clusters plus one low-power cluster, and §3.8.3 shows a base deserialiser
capturing a link driven by the low-power cluster, so at least seven port
identities must be reachable inside the cross-connect. **[Unknown]** whether the
port count grew or whether the low-power cluster shares a port.

---

## 3.3 Power, clock and reset structure

### 3.3.1 Domain tree

Identical on all five in-scope SoCs except where noted:

```
AOP_FILTER  (always-on island root; on t8142/t605x the parent is AOP_DART)
  └── AUDIO_A                      audio island root
        └── AUDIO_FR               audio free-running domain
              ├── AUDIO_P                  serial audio controller common / register access
              │     ├── AUDIO_BASE_S_A     base audio DMA controller, secure aperture
              │     ├── AUDIO_BASE_NS_A    base audio DMA controller, non-secure aperture
              │     ├── AUDIO_LEAP_MCA     low-power serial audio cluster
              │     └── AUDIO_MCA0_M … AUDIO_MCA5_M   six base clusters
              ├── AUDIO_LEAP_A             low-power audio processor root
              │     └── AUDIO_LEAP_C
              │           ├── AUDIO_LEAP_S_A     low-power DMA controller, secure
              │           ├── AUDIO_LEAP_NS_A    low-power DMA controller, non-secure
              │           ├── AUDIO_LEAP_RX0..RX4 five receive link domains
              │           └── AUDIO_LEAP_TX0     one transmit link domain
              └── AUDIO_SENSE_PDMC         microphone PDM converter (misleading name — §8 §8.8)
PDM0_AUDIO_REF, PDM1_AUDIO_REF                   two PDM reference-clock domains, no parent
```

**[Confirmed]** on all five SoCs.

**This is the single most important structural change.** On M1–M3 the host block's
common domain `AUDIO_P` is a child of the host serial-I/O coprocessor domain
`SIO`, and its cluster domains are children of both `AUDIO_P` and the serial-I/O
DMA domain. On every in-scope SoC `AUDIO_P` has been reparented underneath the
**always-on island root**. The block did not move in function; it moved in
*ownership*, out of the host's power hierarchy into the coprocessor's.
**[Confirmed]**

Bring-up dependency order: `AOP_FILTER` (or `AOP_DART`) → `AUDIO_A` → `AUDIO_FR`
→ `AUDIO_P` → cluster domain. The low-power cluster additionally needs
`AUDIO_LEAP_A` → `AUDIO_LEAP_C` → the per-link domain before its data path works.
**[Inferred]** from the parent links, following the power manager's standard
child-after-parent rule.

### 3.3.2 Reference clocks

- **t8132, t604x, t8142, t605x**: no oscillator node in the platform description.
  **[Confirmed]**
- **t8140**: the oscillator node exists with its `compatible` value and a
  `clock-ids` list of **four** entries, but **no `reg`** and no page-size
  property — four oscillator channels described as existing, with no host
  aperture. **[Confirmed]**

Per-cluster clocking is still expressed as a clock generator with a **source
select** and an integer **divisor**, feeding a frame-sync generator programmed
with a source, an edge, a pulse length and two phase-period counts. **[Probable]**
That is the M1–M3 model with one addition: the frame-sync generator now has its
own control register with a **self-clearing reset bit that is polled**
(§3.6.4). **[Probable]**

Per-link master clocks carried in the platform description: 12.000 MHz on
machines with the Apple-exclusive speaker amplifier family, 12.288 MHz on the
t8140 speaker link, 24.000 MHz on the t8140 headphone codec link, and none
(field zero) on the headphone codec link elsewhere. **[Confirmed]**

### 3.3.3 Reset

**[Unknown]** whether a whole-block reset line exists and how it is reached; no
reset is bound to anything audio-related in the in-scope platform descriptions
because no node carries the block. Per-unit resets do exist and are exercised
(§3.6.4, §3.6.5, §3.6.9). The power manager's own per-domain reset bit is
available on the base dies through the power-state registers of §3.4.1.
**[Probable]**

---

## 3.4 Address map

### 3.4.1 Audio power-state registers

On the **base dies** the power manager enumerates a control-register address for
every audio domain, in the always-on island's power-manager aperture, 8 bytes
apart in domain order.

**t8132 (M4)** — identical on j604, j623, j624, j713, j715, j773g:

| Domain | Power-state register |
|---|---|
| `AUDIO_A` | `0x3_8828_4020` |
| `AUDIO_FR` | `0x3_8828_4090` |
| `AUDIO_P` | `0x3_8828_40B8` |
| `AUDIO_LEAP_A` | `0x3_8828_40C0` |
| `AUDIO_SENSE_PDMC` | `0x3_8828_40C8` |
| `AUDIO_BASE_S_A` / `AUDIO_BASE_NS_A` | `0x3_8828_40D0` / `0x3_8828_40D8` |
| `AUDIO_LEAP_MCA` | `0x3_8828_40E0` |
| `AUDIO_MCA0_M` … `AUDIO_MCA5_M` | `0x3_8828_40E8`, `…40F0`, `…40F8`, `…4100`, `…4108`, `…4110` |
| `AUDIO_LEAP_C` | `0x3_8828_4118` |
| `AUDIO_LEAP_S_A` / `AUDIO_LEAP_NS_A` | `0x3_8828_4120` / `0x3_8828_4128` |
| `AUDIO_LEAP_RX0` … `RX4` | `0x3_8828_4130`, `…4138`, `…4140`, `…4148`, `…4150` |
| `AUDIO_LEAP_TX0` | `0x3_8828_4158` |
| `PDM0_AUDIO_REF` / `PDM1_AUDIO_REF` | `0x3_8828_4160` / `0x3_8828_4168` |

**t8140 (A18 Pro)** — same order, starting at `0x3_0828_4020` for `AUDIO_A`:
`AUDIO_FR …40A8`, `AUDIO_P …40D0`, `AUDIO_LEAP_A …40D8`, `AUDIO_SENSE_PDMC …40E0`,
`AUDIO_BASE_S_A …40E8`, `AUDIO_BASE_NS_A …40F0`, `AUDIO_LEAP_MCA …40F8`,
`AUDIO_MCA0_M`…`MCA5_M` `…4100`…`…4128`, `AUDIO_LEAP_C …4130`,
`AUDIO_LEAP_S_A …4138`, `AUDIO_LEAP_NS_A …4140`, `AUDIO_LEAP_RX0`…`RX4`
`…4148`…`…4168`, `AUDIO_LEAP_TX0 …4170`, `PDM0_AUDIO_REF …4178`,
`PDM1_AUDIO_REF …4180`.

**t8142 (M5)** — same order, starting at `0x3_8828_4080` for `AUDIO_A`:
`AUDIO_FR …40B8`, `AUDIO_P …40D8`, `AUDIO_LEAP_A …40E0`, `AUDIO_SENSE_PDMC …40E8`,
`AUDIO_BASE_S_A …40F0`, `AUDIO_BASE_NS_A …40F8`, `AUDIO_LEAP_MCA …4100`,
`AUDIO_MCA0_M`…`MCA5_M` `…4108`…`…4130`, `AUDIO_LEAP_C …4138`,
`AUDIO_LEAP_S_A …4140`, `AUDIO_LEAP_NS_A …4148`, `AUDIO_LEAP_RX0`…`RX4`
`…4150`…`…4170`, `AUDIO_LEAP_TX0 …4178`, `PDM0_AUDIO_REF …4180`,
`PDM1_AUDIO_REF …4188`.

**[Confirmed]** — reproduced identically on every board of each SoC. The
address derivation itself is established independently: each domain's entry in
the power-manager device list names a register block and an index within it, the
block table gives an aperture index and a base offset, and the resulting address
is `aperture + block_offset + 8 × index`. Applied to the M1, M2, M3 and M3 Pro
platform descriptions this rule reproduces **544 of 544** power-domain register
offsets published for those SoCs in mainline Linux, with no mismatch. On the
in-scope SoCs that carry a **block table** (t8132) the same rule applies directly;
on those that carry a **group table** (t8140, t8142, t604x, t605x) the entry
carries a 24-bit offset and a group index instead, and the address is
`aperture + offset`. The group form has **no external ground truth** — it appears
on no SoC for which published register offsets exist — so the t8140 and t8142
addresses above are **[Probable]**, not Confirmed, resting on: every decoded
address being unique, 8-byte aligned and inside the declared aperture (225 of 296
and 301 of 386 domains respectively, zero collisions); the audio domains landing
in the same aperture, in the same order and at the same 8-byte stride as on the
externally validated t8132; and `AUDIO_A` landing at the identical in-aperture
offset `0x4020` on t8132 and t8140.

On t8140 and t8142 the always-on island root itself is also addressable
(`AOP_FILTER` at `0x3_0828_4000` and `0x3_8828_4000` respectively, and on t8142
`AOP_DART` at `0x3_8828_4020`); on t8132 it is not. **[Probable]**

**t604x and t605x/t6050: no address at all.** On these SoCs *every* always-on
island device entry carries a null power-state register offset, while host-side
devices in the same list carry valid ones. **[Confirmed]** The reading is that on
the Pro/Max dies the always-on island's power state is managed exclusively by the
coprocessor and is not gateable from the application processor. **[Inferred]**
On t604x the two base DMA domains additionally carry a null parent reference,
where on t605x they name `AUDIO_P`; the domain tree of §3.3.1 is otherwise
identical on both. **[Confirmed]**

### 3.4.2 Serial audio controller register region — map

The block occupies **one contiguous region of about `0x9014` bytes** (map
`0x10000`), laid out as a small global block followed by three `0x100`-strided
arrays of per-unit blocks. Offsets relative to the region base:

| Offset | Count | Stride | Size of each | Content |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `0x0000` | 1 | — | `0x230` | **Global block** — whole-controller control and status, including the aligned multi-unit enable trigger (§3.6.3) and the interrupt aggregation. |
| `0x2000 + 0x100·n`, n = 0…5 | **6** | `0x100` | `0xA0` | **Per-cluster block** — clock generator, frame-sync generator, port/pad configuration (§3.6.4). One per base cluster. |
| `0x4000 + 0x100·n`, n = 0…16 | **17** | `0x100` | `0x60` | **Serialiser array 1** (§3.6.5). |
| `0x6000 + 0x100·n`, n = 0…16 | **17** | `0x100` | `0x60` | **Serialiser array 2** (§3.6.5). |
| `0x8000 + 0x100·n`, n = 0…16 | **17** | `0x100` | `0x14` | **Per-unit adapter/status block** (§3.6.7). |

**[Confirmed]** for the structure — the same relative offsets, counts and block
sizes hold on all five in-scope SoCs, and the six-entry per-cluster array matches
the six cluster power domains derived independently.

Region base addresses:

| SoC | Serial audio controller base |
|---|---|
| t8132 (M4) | `0x3_9360_0000` |
| t604x (M4 Pro/Max) | `0x5_1360_0000` |
| t8140 (A18 Pro) | `0x3_1360_0000` |
| t8142 (M5) | `0x3_9360_0000` |
| t605x / t6050 (M5 Pro/Max) | `0x2_9360_0000` |

**[Probable]** for the base addresses; **[Confirmed]** for the region layout.
Each address falls on the audio island's `0x10_0000` grid where the island's
other blocks place it (§3.4.3), and the six-entry per-cluster array matches the
six cluster power domains. **It has not been verified by a read.** A single 32-bit read at the region base, with
`AUDIO_P` powered, settles it — see Open questions 1.

The old two-region layout (`0x4000` per cluster in a cluster region, `0x8000` per
cluster in a switch region) is **gone**. A driver ported from the M1–M3 map must
be rewritten, not re-based. **[Confirmed]**

### 3.4.3 The audio island

All audio blocks lie in one contiguous island on a `0x10_0000` grid. The low 32
bits of every block address are identical across all five SoCs; only the upper
bits differ.

| Block | Low 32 bits | t8132 | t604x | t8140 | t8142 | t6050 | Size |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Low-power audio DMA controller, secure | `0x1320_0000` | `0x3_9320_0000`† | `0x5_1320_0000`† | `0x3_1320_0000` | `0x3_9320_0000` | `0x2_9320_0000` | `0x34000` |
| Low-power secure DMA channel-buffer memory (§3.4.5) | `0x1324_0000` | **[Unknown]**§ | **[Unknown]**§ | `0x3_1324_0000` | `0x3_9324_0000` | `0x2_9324_0000`¶ | `0x1_2000` |
| Low-power audio DMA controller, non-secure | `0x1330_0000` | `0x3_9330_0000` | `0x5_1330_0000` | `0x3_1330_0000` | `0x3_9330_0000` | `0x2_9330_0000` | `0x34000` |
| **PDM converter group** (§3.10) | `0x1350_0000` | `0x3_9350_0000` | `0x5_1350_0000` | `0x3_1350_0000` | `0x3_9350_0000` | `0x2_9350_0000` | `0x14000` |
| **Serial audio controller** | `0x1360_0000` | `0x3_9360_0000` | `0x5_1360_0000` | `0x3_1360_0000` | `0x3_9360_0000` | `0x2_9360_0000` | `0x9014` |
| Base audio DMA controller, secure | `0x1370_0000` | `0x3_9370_0000` | `0x5_1370_0000` | `0x3_1370_0000`‡ | `0x3_9370_0000`‡ | `0x2_9370_0000`‡ | `0x34000` |
| Base secure DMA channel-buffer memory (§3.4.5) | `0x1374_0000` | **[Unknown]**§ | **[Unknown]**§ | `0x3_1374_0000` | `0x3_9374_0000` | `0x2_9374_0000`¶ | `0x1_C000` |
| Base audio DMA controller, non-secure | `0x1380_0000` | `0x3_9380_0000` | `0x5_1380_0000` | `0x3_1380_0000` | `0x3_9380_0000` | `0x2_9380_0000` | `0x34000` |
| Audio island global configuration (§3.6.8) | `0x13C0_0000` | `0x3_93C0_0000` | `0x5_13C0_0000` | `0x3_13C0_0000` | `0x3_93C0_0000` | `0x2_93C0_0000` | `0x244` |
| Second global block | `0x13C1_0000` | `0x3_93C1_0000` | `0x5_13C1_0000` | `0x3_13C1_0000` | `0x3_93C1_0000` | `0x2_93C1_0000` | `0x468` |
| DMA low-latency escalation detector (M5 only) | `0x13C8_0000` | — | — | — | `0x3_93C8_0000` | `0x2_93C8_0000` | 2 × `0x4000` |

† not described on t8132/t604x; address by generational consistency, the domain
`AUDIO_LEAP_S_A` exists on both. **[Inferred]**
‡ the base secure DMA aperture is not described on any SoC. It is established on
t604x and, through a secure-world alias, on t8132, and independently on t8140 and
t8142 by the fabric filter of §3.4.5, three of whose protected ranges decode as
per-channel registers of a `0x34000` audio DMA aperture based at `0x…_1370_0000`;
extended to t605x by the low-32-bit invariance. Two independent lines of evidence:
**[Confirmed]**
§ no protected-range table is published on t8132 or t604x and no other source places
a channel-buffer memory window there; presence and address on those two SoCs are
**[Unknown]**.
¶ t605x publishes no protected-range table; address by the low-32-bit invariance.
**[Inferred]**

Everything without a footnote is **[Confirmed]** (the four DMA controller
addresses are published apertures, translated through the `/arm-io` `ranges`
mapping and identical across all boards of each SoC) or **[Probable]** (the PDM
group, serial audio controller and global blocks, on the same basis as §3.4.2).

The whole island is also visible through a **secure-world alias**. On t8132 that
alias is at **+`0x4000_0000`** (the base secure DMA controller appears at both
`0x3_9370_0000` and `0x3_D370_0000`, and the power-manager aperture likewise).
**[Probable]** On other SoCs the platform description exposes an aliased view of
the low-power secure DMA aperture at a different per-SoC offset: +`0x4000_0000`
on t8140, +`0x2_5000_0000` on t8142, +`0x2_4000_0000` on t6050. **[Confirmed]**
Do not assume a single alias constant.

For reference, the island base sits at a fixed +`0x320_0000` from the always-on
island base on every in-scope SoC. **[Probable]**

### 3.4.4 Interrupts

No interrupt in any in-scope platform description is bound to the serial audio
controller. **[Confirmed]** The audio interrupt numbers that are bound belong to
the DMA controllers and sit in a short run with one or two unclaimed numbers,
consistent with those belonging to the DMA controllers' secure apertures:

| SoC | base non-secure DMA | unclaimed | low-power secure DMA | low-power non-secure DMA |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| t8132 | 475 | 476, 477 | — | 478 |
| t8140 | 449 | 450 | 451 | 452 |
| t8142 | 549 | 550 | 551 | 552 |
| t605x | 637 | — | 638 | 639 |

**[Confirmed]** for the assigned numbers. The controller aggregates its own
interrupt sources into a wrapper-level enable that separates DMA, serial-audio
and PDM sources (§3.6.8). **[Probable]** **[Unknown]** whether any resulting line
reaches the application processor's interrupt controller; on M1–M3 there is one
line per cluster and none of those has a counterpart here. The plausible reading
is that the lines now go to the coprocessor only. **[Inferred]**

### 3.4.5 Fabric inbound address-protection filter

A fabric-boundary access-control block guards the inbound edge of the always-on
island. Its protected ranges lie inside the audio island of §3.4.3 — the on-chip
channel-buffer memories of the two **secure** audio DMA controllers, and five of those
controllers' per-channel buffer-configuration registers — with two exceptions on t8140,
noted below. Platform firmware
describes it as `/arm-io/aop/iop-aop-nub/aop-gapf-filters`. It is an instance of a
general fabric-boundary filter type that these SoCs instantiate at several subsystem
ingress points; this section documents only the always-on instance, which is the one
that bears on audio.

**Delta.** There is **no M1–M3 counterpart**. The M1–M3 always-on complex describes a
single access-control structure, an address-protection filter table attached to the
always-on IOMMU (`dapf-instance-0`, a list of 52-byte `{start, end, stream-mask}`
records; a 24-byte form under a different property name on the M1 generation). That
table constrains what the coprocessor reaches **through the IOMMU**, and its ranges
name the power manager, the always-on GPIO block, the system management controller
and the sensor hub — never an audio block. On exactly the SoCs where the block
described here appears, `dapf-instance-0` disappears from the always-on IOMMU node
and `allow-dram-apf-slices-0 = 0` appears there instead. Address protection for the
always-on complex thus moves **out of the IOMMU and into the fabric**, and its targets
change from power and sensor blocks to audio blocks. **[Confirmed]**

The hardware itself is not new: the power manager enumerates an always-on filter
domain on every generation from M1 through M5, including t604x where no such node is
described. What changed at A18 Pro / M5 is that platform firmware now describes the
block's configuration. **[Confirmed]**

**Presence, per SoC and per board.**

| SoC | Boards | Node present | Range table |
|---|---|---|---|
| t8132 (M4) | j604, j623, j624, j713, j715, j773g | no | — |
| t604x (M4 Pro/Max) | j614s, j614c, j616s, j616c, j773s, j575c | no | — |
| t8140 (A18 Pro) | j700 | yes | 8 entries |
| t8142 (M5) | j704, j813, j815 | yes, all 3 | 7 entries, byte-identical on all three |
| t605x / t6050 (M5 Pro/Max) | j714s, j714c, j716s, j716c | yes, all 4 | **none published** |

**[Confirmed].** Every property of the node is **per-SoC, not per-machine** — all
boards of a given SoC carry byte-identical values — so a driver needs no per-machine
table for it.

**The M5 Pro/Max case is the one a driver must not misread.** On t605x the node
carries the enable, lock, lock-declaration and agent-list properties but **no
`fabric-slices` range table and no `device_type`**. The filter is enabled and locked
on that die with its protected ranges not published. **An absent range table does not
establish that the filter is absent**, and no reasoning about M5 Pro/Max reachability
may rest on the assumption that it is. **[Confirmed]**

**Ownership.** The node carries `sptm-locks-gapf`, a zero-length property whose
presence is the assertion, on all eight boards that have the node: the block is
programmed, enabled and locked by pre-kernel firmware, not by the host. A host driver
**inherits** the configuration and cannot change it. Treat the enable bit and the
entry table as read-only by the time any host driver runs, on t8140, t8142 and t605x.
**[Probable]**

**Per-entry hardware fields.** A violation is reported to the owning block as an
interrupt carrying the offending master identifier, the offending address and the
access direction, together with the index and valid flag of the entry that fired. The
per-entry fields are therefore:

| Field | Width | Description |
|---|---|---|
| entry index | — | selects one filter entry |
| `VALID` | 1 | entry participates in matching |
| `MASTER_ID` | ≥ 17 bits | fabric master identifier the entry applies to |
| `RW` | 1 | access direction the entry applies to |
| `START` | 64-bit physical | first byte of the protected range |
| `END` | 64-bit physical | last byte, **inclusive** |

**[Confirmed]** that these six fields exist and are per-entry. Their register offsets,
bit positions, the number of entry slots in hardware, the violation-status register
and the filter's allow/deny polarity are all **[Unknown]**.

**Node property layout.**

| Property | Size | Encoding | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `device_type` | 17 B | ASCII `aop-gapf-filters` | present on t8140 and t8142; **absent on t605x**. **[Confirmed]** |
| `fabric-slice-fmt-ver` | u32 | `1` on every board that carries it | format version of `fabric-slices`; a driver or verifier must refuse any other value. **[Confirmed]** |
| `fabric-slices` | 32 B × N | see the record layout below | N = 8 on t8140, 7 on t8142; **absent on t605x**. **[Confirmed]** |
| `sptm-gapf-enable-reg` | 16 B | `u64 address ‖ u32 value ‖ u32 mask` | see the control registers below |
| `sptm-gapf-lock-reg` | 16 B | `u64 address ‖ u32 value ‖ u32 mask` | see the control registers below |
| `sptm-locks-gapf` | 0 B | present-or-absent boolean | present on all eight boards with the node; declares that pre-kernel firmware, not the host, owns programming and locking. **[Confirmed]** |
| `sram-t-agents-count` | u32 | count | number of 8-byte records in `sram-t-agents` |
| `sram-t-agents` | 8 B × count | `u32 identifier ‖ u32 match mask` | **trusted** agent list for the protected on-chip memory windows |
| `sram-ut-agents-count` | u32 | count | number of records in `sram-ut-agents` |
| `sram-ut-agents` | 8 B × count | `u32 identifier ‖ u32 match mask` | **untrusted** agent list; the property is omitted entirely when the count is 0 |

**Control registers.** Each 16-byte control-register record decodes as a 64-bit
absolute physical address, a 32-bit value and a 32-bit write mask. The 64-bit reading
is not a guess: the upper half of each address (`0x3` on t8140 and t8142, `0x2` on
t605x) reproduces the per-SoC die prefix that every other absolute address on that SoC
carries. Both registers lie in an otherwise undescribed 16 KiB page at **always-on
island base + `0x82_8000`**, the page immediately above the always-on GPIO aperture at
always-on island base + `0x82_4000`. **[Confirmed]**

| Offset in page | Name | Access | Reset | Fields | Value programmed | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `+0x20` | `FABRIC_FILT_ENABLE` | RW until locked, then RO | **[Unknown]** | `[1:0]` enable; `[31:2]` **[Unknown]** | `0x0000_0003`, mask `0x0000_0003` | Enables the filter. Two enable bits are set on every SoC; what each of the two selects is **[Unknown]**. |
| `+0x24` | `FABRIC_FILT_LOCK` | RW1S | **[Unknown]** | `[0]` lock; `[31:1]` **[Unknown]** | `0x0000_0001`, mask `0x0000_0001` | Locks the enable bit and the entry table. Write-once; cleared only by reset. **[Probable]** |

| SoC | `FABRIC_FILT_ENABLE` | `FABRIC_FILT_LOCK` |
|---|---|---|
| t8140 | `0x3_1082_8020` | `0x3_1082_8024` |
| t8142 | `0x3_9082_8020` | `0x3_9082_8024` |
| t605x / t6050 | `0x2_9082_8020` | `0x2_9082_8024` |

**[Confirmed]** for the addresses, values and masks; **[Probable]** for the field split
and the write-once behaviour.

**`fabric-slices` record layout.** 32 bytes per record, four little-endian 64-bit
words:

| Word | Offset | Name | Observed | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | `0x00` | `ATTR` | `0x1F` on every record of every board | Attribute / permission word. Which bits are which is **[Unknown]**. It is *not* a master identifier — real master identifiers on this fabric are ≥ 17-bit values such as `0x1_A8C2`. **[Inferred]** |
| 1 | `0x08` | `START` | see below | first protected byte, absolute physical |
| 2 | `0x10` | `END` | see below | last protected byte, **inclusive** |
| 3 | `0x18` | `VALID` | `1` on every record | entry is live |

**[Confirmed]** for the record size and the start/end/valid fields; **[Inferred]** for
word 0 being a permission word rather than an identifier.

**What is protected — t8142 (j704, j813, j815), 7 entries, byte-identical on all
three boards:**

| # | Start | End | Size | Identification |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | `0x3_9324_0000` | `0x3_9325_1FFF` | `0x1_2000` | Low-power **secure** audio DMA controller's on-chip channel-buffer memory (controller base + `0x4_0000`) |
| 1 | `0x3_9374_0000` | `0x3_9375_BFFF` | `0x1_C000` | Base **secure** audio DMA controller's on-chip channel-buffer memory (controller base + `0x4_0000`) |
| 2 | `0x3_9320_CA50` | `0x3_9320_CA53` | 4 B | Low-power secure DMA, `CHAN_BUF_CFG` of **receive channel 5** |
| 3 | `0x3_9320_C050` | `0x3_9320_C053` | 4 B | Low-power secure DMA, `CHAN_BUF_CFG` of **receive channel 0** |
| 4 | `0x3_9370_DA50` | `0x3_9370_DA53` | 4 B | Base secure DMA, `CHAN_BUF_CFG` of **receive channel 13** |
| 5 | `0x3_9370_D850` | `0x3_9370_D853` | 4 B | Base secure DMA, `CHAN_BUF_CFG` of **receive channel 12** |
| 6 | `0x3_9370_9850` | `0x3_9370_9853` | 4 B | Base secure DMA, `CHAN_BUF_CFG` of **transmit channel 12** |

**What is protected — t8140 (j700), 8 entries.** The same addresses with the t8140 die
prefix (`0x3_13…` in place of `0x3_93…`), **minus** the low-power receive-channel-5
entry, **plus** two 16 KiB windows that are the only protected ranges anywhere outside
the audio island:

| # | Start | End | Size | Identification |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6 | `0x3_1085_0000` | `0x3_1085_3FFF` | `0x4000` | Undescribed 16 KiB page in the always-on peripheral block. **[Unknown]** — the additional always-on serial-bus controllers fitted to this part are the candidates. |
| 7 | `0x3_1084_0000` | `0x3_1084_3FFF` | `0x4000` | Undescribed 16 KiB page, same block, one page lower. **[Unknown]** |

**Why the four-byte entries are `CHAN_BUF_CFG`.** Under the direction-separated
channel layout of §4 §4.3.1 — transmit channel *n* at `+0x8000 + n × 0x200`, receive
channel *n* at `+0xC000 + n × 0x200` — and the per-channel offset `+0x50` for
`CHAN_BUF_CFG` (§4 §4.3.3):

| Offset within the `0x34000` aperture | Decode | In range? |
|---|---|---|
| `+0xC050` | receive channel 0 | yes — the low-power instance has 9 receive channels |
| `+0xCA50` | receive channel 5 | yes |
| `+0x9850` | transmit channel 12 | yes — the base instance has 13 transmit channels |
| `+0xD850` | receive channel 12 | yes — 14 receive channels |
| `+0xDA50` | receive channel 13 | yes — 14 receive channels |

All five land exactly on the per-channel buffer-configuration register and all five
channel indices fall inside the declared channel counts. Under the interleaved
numbering of the M1–M3 baseline the same offsets decode to channels 32, 37, 12, 44 and
45, three of which do not exist on these instances. This independently confirms the
direction-separated channel block layout and the asymmetric 13-transmit /
14-receive count of the base secure instance (§4 §4.2.1). **[Confirmed]**

**Why the two large windows are on-chip channel-buffer memory.** Three lines converge:
the node's own agent lists are named for on-chip static memory and the only other
things the table protects are the registers that carve that memory up; each window
sits at its controller's base + `0x4_0000`, inside the controller's `0x10_0000` slot on
the audio island grid but outside its `0x34000` register aperture; and the sizes are
exactly `0x2000 × max(#transmit, #receive)` for each instance — `0x2000 × 9 =
0x1_2000` for the low-power instance (9/9 channels) and `0x2000 × 14 = 0x1_C000` for
the base instance (13/14 channels), on both t8140 and t8142. Identification
**[Probable]**; addresses and sizes **[Confirmed]**. The two windows are tabulated in
§3.4.3. Whether the **non-secure** instances have equivalent windows at their own base
+ `0x4_0000` (`0x…_3340_0000`, `0x…_3840_0000`) is **[Unknown]** — no filter entry
names them, which is consistent with their existing but not needing protection.

**Agent lists.** Each record is `u32 identifier ‖ u32 match mask`. The mask is
`0xFFFC_0FFF` on every record on every board, so **bits 12–17 of the identifier are
wild-carded**. Those six bits carry a per-SoC value (`0x19` on t8140, `0x1A` on t8142,
`0x1B` on t605x) that is masked out, so the same table matches an agent regardless of
which fabric node it is reached through.

| SoC | Trusted agents (masked identifier) | Untrusted agents (masked identifier) |
|---|---|---|
| t8140 | `0x896`, `0x882` | none — `sram-ut-agents-count = 0`, property absent |
| t8142 | `0x8C2` | `0x8DC`, `0x8DD`, `0x8DE`, `0x8DF` |
| t605x / t6050 | `0x8C2` | `0x8DC`, `0x8DD`, `0x8DF` |

**[Confirmed]** for the values and the mask. The four untrusted identifiers on t8142
form a contiguous run of four and there are exactly four audio DMA controller
instances in the island, so the untrusted list plausibly enumerates the DMA
controllers' master ports with the single trusted identifier belonging to the
coprocessor core — **[Inferred]**, low confidence. t605x lists only three of the four,
so one master is on neither list there, and the two trusted identifiers on t8140
(`0x882`, `0x896`) are from a different numeric neighbourhood than the t8142 and t605x
ones.

**Access-control semantics — summary.**

| Question | Answer | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| What is filtered? | Inbound accesses at the always-on complex's fabric boundary, matched on address range, master identifier and direction. | [Confirmed] |
| Which addresses? | Exactly the seven (t8142) or eight (t8140) ranges tabulated above; nothing else on any board that publishes a table. | [Confirmed] |
| Which agents? | One or two trusted masters and zero to four untrusted masters, by masked identifier. | [Confirmed] |
| What permissions? | A per-entry read/write direction exists in hardware; the published table carries a constant `0x1F` attribute word whose bit meanings are unresolved. | [Confirmed] / [Unknown] |
| Allow-list or deny-list? | **[Unknown].** The small, highly specific range set argues for a protect-list — deny by default *for the listed ranges*, permit the trusted master — rather than a whole-map allow-list. | [Inferred] |
| Lockable? | Yes — a dedicated lock register one word above the enable register, written `1` with mask `1`. | [Confirmed] |
| When locked? | Before the host kernel runs; the node carries an explicit boolean declaring that pre-kernel firmware performs the lock. | [Probable] |
| Can the host change it? | No. | [Probable] |

**Consequences for a driver.** On t8140, t8142 and t605x the fabric protects the
*secure* audio DMA instances' channel-buffer memory and five of their per-channel
buffer-configuration registers, and classifies the audio DMA master ports into trusted
and untrusted sets. **The secure DMA instances' buffer allocation must be treated as
unavailable to a normal-world driver on the A18 Pro and M5 generations.** **[Probable]**
Nothing in the published table touches the non-secure instances, the serial audio
