controller, the PDM converter group or the island global blocks; what that omission
means depends on the filter's polarity, which is **[Unknown]** — see §11 §11.6.2(c) and
Open questions 28–33. The other always-on access-control block, which sits on the
register rather than the DMA path, is described in §11 §11.6.3.

---

## 3.5 Host reachability, and the driver-design consequence

**"Not described" and "not accessible" are different, and the answer differs per
SoC.**

- **Register apertures.** Not described on any in-scope SoC; addresses are
  given in §3.4.2. **[Unknown]** whether the application processor's fabric answers a
  read there. There is no positive evidence of a firewall: the DMA controllers in
  the same island, on the same `0x10_0000` grid, answer host reads normally.
- **Power.** On **t8132, t8140 and t8142** the host can address the audio power
  domains directly and can therefore raise `AUDIO_P` and any cluster domain
  without the coprocessor's cooperation. **[Probable]** — the addresses are
  established; whether the write is honoured while the island is owned by the
  coprocessor is **[Unknown]**. On **t604x and t605x/t6050** no address is
  published for any always-on-island domain, so there is **no host mechanism to
  power the block** other than asking the coprocessor. **[Confirmed]** that no
  address is published; **[Inferred]** that no mechanism exists.
- **Secure paths.** Both DMA domains are split secure / non-secure, and the
  secure instances are deliberately not host-mapped: the secure low-power DMA
  controller carries an empty `iommu-parent` and is reached through a proxy node
  (`compatible = "admac-ec-proxy"`, with per-stream
  `"iisaudio,isolated-stream-proxy"` nodes). The headphone-microphone capture
  link and, on M5 Pro/Max, one loopback capture link are bound to the **secure**
  low-power DMA controller. **[Confirmed]** Any link whose capture side is secure
  is not host-reachable by design, whatever the controller's registers allow.
  The island's global configuration additionally carries an explicit
  **secure-link-to-DMA-channel map** and a hardware-triggered microphone disable
  (§3.6.8), so the security boundary is enforced in the audio hardware itself,
  not only in the IOMMU. **[Probable]**
- **Arbitration.** There is none. The block has exactly one configuration
  authority — the coprocessor's audio service — and nothing exposes a lock, a
  claim register or a per-cluster ownership bit to the host. The coprocessor
  reprograms clock generators, frame-sync generators, serialiser configuration
  and routing on its own schedule, including at power transitions. It also keeps
  per-cluster capability state: a cluster may be marked as not under master-clock
  control, as not subject to routing validation, or as **immutable**, in which
  case configuration changes are rejected. **[Probable]** **[Unknown]** which
  clusters carry which flags on which machine.

**Driver-design consequence.** Treat the serial audio controller as **not host
owned**. The supported control interface is the coprocessor audio service named
by `iop-audio-service-name` on `/arm-io/iop-audio-controller`; the host owns the
audio DMA controllers and nothing else on the coprocessor-side control path. A driver that
programs the block directly must (a) use the addresses in §3.4.2, which are
derived rather than published, (b) power the domains itself — impossible on the
Pro/Max dies — and (c) race the coprocessor on every register with no arbitration
primitive and no way to make it stand down. Direct MMIO is a legitimate bring-up,
tracing and fallback technique; it is not a basis for a production driver.
Concretely: implement the coprocessor transport, and use the register path only
from a bring-up environment that can trap MMIO, and only on t8132 / t8140 /
t8142 where the power domains are reachable.

Second consequence: because the cluster domains descend from the always-on island
root, **the block cannot be powered without the coprocessor island being
powered**, and any host sequence must hold `AOP_FILTER`/`AOP_DART`, `AUDIO_A`,
`AUDIO_FR` and `AUDIO_P` up for the whole life of a stream. **[Confirmed]**

---

## 3.6 Register interface

### 3.6.1 Overall assessment

The **functional design is the same** — per-cluster clock generator, per-cluster
frame-sync generator, transmit and receive serialisers with slot masks, a port
cross-connect, DMA/slot adapters — but the **register map is a redesign, not a
revision**. Three changes make a baseline-derived driver unusable without rework:

1. **The geometry changed.** One compact region with `0x100`-strided per-unit
   blocks replaces two regions of `0x4000`/`0x8000` pages. **[Confirmed]**
2. **Serialisers are a flat, independently addressed array** rather than four
   fixed sub-blocks inside a cluster page. **[Confirmed]**
3. **Serialiser-to-DMA-channel binding is now an explicit programmable map**
   (§3.6.8) rather than implicit in the cluster/adapter wiring. **[Probable]**

**Individual register offsets within each per-unit block are established, in
§18 §18.8.** They were **[Unknown]** when this section was first written and are
not any more, and the field inventory below is to be read together with them:

| Block | Offsets established | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Bit-clock generator (one per cluster) | `+0x00` `CLOCK_GEN_CONTROL`; `+0x04` `CLOCK_GEN_CONFIG` (`CLOCK_SELECT` bits 2:0, `DIVISOR` bits 12:8, 5 bits, range 1…31) | §18 §18.8.1 |
| Frame-sync generator (one per cluster) | `+0x00` `SYNC_GEN_CONTROL`; `+0x04` `SYNC_GEN_CONFIG` (`CLOCK_SELECT` bits 3:0, `BIT_CLOCK_POLARITY` bit 9, `FRAME_SYNC_POLARITY` bit 10); `+0x08` `FRAME_PHASE_0`; `+0x0c` `FRAME_PHASE_1` — each phase register holds the phase count **− 1** | §18 §18.8.2 |
| Pad clock routing (one per I2S pad group) | `+0x64` `PAD_CLOCK_SELECT` (`MASTER_CLOCK_SELECT` bits 2:0, `BIT_AND_FRAME_CLOCK_SELECT` bits 11:8) | §18 §18.8.3 |
| Serialiser (one block per unit) | `+0x00` `CONTROL`; `+0x04` `CONFIG` (full bit table); `+0x08` `DATA_DELAY`; `+0x0c`/`+0x10` `CHANNEL_MASK` high/low, written **inverted**; `+0x14`/`+0x18` transmit `OUTPUT_ENABLE_MASK` high/low, receive `DATA_SELECT.DIN_SELECT` and `LOOPBACK_DATA_SELECT.SERDES_SELECT` | §18 §18.8.4 |

**[Confirmed]** for t8132, t604x and t8140; **[Probable]** for t8142 and t605x.
Two registers named in the tables above are **[Unknown]** as to existence on
t8132, t604x and t8140 — the two per-cluster reset registers at `+0x00`
(§18 open question 8).

What is still **[Unknown]** inside a per-unit block is the remainder of the
`0x60`-byte block beyond the seven serialiser registers above: the FIFO depth
control (§3.6.6), the interrupt status and mask (§3.6.9), and the shift-buffer
bank (§18 §18.8.6). Those are open questions 5, 6, 7 and §18 open question 10.

### 3.6.2 Field inventory by functional group

All names below are functional. Where a field has an established M1–M3 counterpart
in the public baseline, it is named so the correspondence is visible.

**Clock generator (per cluster).**

| Field | Meaning | Baseline counterpart |
|---|---|---|
| `CLOCK_SELECT` | Source of the cluster's reference clock. | the unknown `[3:0]` of the baseline's `MCLK_CONF` |
| `DIVISOR` | Integer divider from reference clock to bit clock. | `MCLK_CONF[11:8] DIV` |
| `ENABLE`, `PENDING` | Gate enable and a status bit indicating the change has not yet taken effect. | `MCLK_STATUS[0] MCLK_EN` |

**[Probable]**. This resolves the baseline's open question about `MCLK_CONF[3:0]`:
it is a **clock source selector**, not an unused field.

**Frame-sync generator (per cluster).**

| Field | Meaning | Baseline counterpart |
|---|---|---|
| `SYNC_GEN_CONFIG` | Frame-sync generator configuration word. | `SYNCGEN_STATUS`/`SYNCGEN_MCLK_SEL` region |
| `SYNC_GEN_CONTROL.RESET` | **Self-clearing reset, polled until it reads back clear.** | not in the baseline |
| `FRAME_PHASE_0` | Bit-clock count of the frame clock's first phase, programmed as *count − 1*. | `SYNCGEN_HI_PERIOD` |
| `FRAME_PHASE_1` | Same for the second phase, programmed as *count − 1*. | `SYNCGEN_LO_PERIOD` |

**[Probable]**. Frame length in bit clocks = `(PHASE_0 + 1) + (PHASE_1 + 1)`,
unchanged. The **frame-sync generator reset is new relative to the baseline** and
must be polled to completion before the generator is used.

**Port / pad configuration (per cluster).**

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `CLOCK_SELECT.BCLK_AND_LRCK` | Which source drives this port's **bit clock and frame clock together**. |
| `CLOCK_SELECT.MCK` | Which source drives this port's **master clock**, selected **independently**. |
| `OUTPUT_ENABLE.MCLK` | Master clock pad output enable. |
| `OUTPUT_ENABLE.SYNC_CLOCKS` | Bit clock + frame clock pad output enable, as one group. |
| `OUTPUT_ENABLE.DOUT` | Transmit data pad output enable. |

**[Probable]**. This corrects and completes the baseline's `PORT_ENABLES`
(`[3] TX_DATA`, `[2:1] CLOCKS` written together, `[0]` unknown) and
`PORT_CLOCK_SEL` (a single `[11:8]` selector): there are **three independently
maskable output groups**, not two or four, and the clock selector is **two
independent fields**, one for the bit/frame clock pair and one for the master
clock. The baseline's "`[2:1]` always written together" is explained: bit clock
and frame clock are one group in hardware.

**Serialiser configuration (per unit, both directions unless noted).**

| Field | Meaning | Baseline counterpart |
|---|---|---|
| `CHANNELS_PER_FRAME` | Slots per frame. | `CONF[3:0] NSLOTS` |
| `BITS_PER_CHANNEL` | Slot width in bits. | `CONF[8:4] SLOT_WIDTH` |
| `CLOCK_EDGE` | Bit-clock edge on which data is driven/sampled: rising or falling. | `CONF[10] BCLK_POL` |
| `DATA_ENDIAN` | Bit order within a slot: most-significant-bit-first or least-significant-bit-first. | `CONF[11] LSB_FIRST` |
| `SYNC_AND_BCLK_SELECT` | Which cluster's frame-sync generator and bit clock gate this unit. | `CONF[18:16] SYNC_SEL` |
| `AUTO_RESTART` | The unit restarts itself after an error/stall rather than staying stopped. | one of `CONF[12]`/`CONF[13]` |
| `SKIP_MASKED` | Masked slots are skipped rather than consuming/producing FIFO data. | the other of `CONF[12]`/`CONF[13]` |
| `DISABLE_OUTPUT_WHEN_IDLE` *(transmit only)* | Release the data pad during slots this unit does not own. | `CONF[14]`, set on transmit units and clear on receive units in the published baseline programming |
| `DISABLE_MASTER_MODE_LOOPBACK_CLKSEL` *(receive only)* | Suppresses the clock-select path used when the unit is receiving an internally looped-back stream. **New; no baseline counterpart.** | — |
| `DATA_DELAY` | Bit clocks between the frame edge and the first data bit; `1` for I2S, `0` for left-justified. Must be **strictly less than** the frame length. | `BIT_DELAY` |
| `CHANNEL_MASK` (low and high words) | 64-bit mask of the slots this unit carries data in. | `SLOT_MASK[0..1]`, "mask 1" |
| `OUTPUT_ENABLE_MASK` (low and high words) *(transmit only)* | 64-bit mask of the slots this unit **drives** at all, whether or not they carry data. | `SLOT_MASK[2..3]`, "mask 2" |
| `DATA_SELECT.DIN_SELECT` *(receive only)* | Which I2S data-in pad this unit samples. | `PORT_SEL` at receive-block `0x04` |
| `LOOPBACK_DATA_SELECT.SERDES_SELECT` *(receive only)* | **Which transmit serialiser this unit samples instead of a pad** — the internal loopback source selector. **New as a distinct register; no baseline counterpart.** | — |
| `CONTROL.RESET` | Self-clearing reset. | `STATUS[1] RST` |
| `CONTROL` enable | Run the unit. | `STATUS[0] EN` |

**[Probable]** throughout.

Three of the baseline's open questions are resolved by this inventory:

- **`CONF[12]` and `CONF[13]`** — set unconditionally on both directions by the
  public driver, meaning unknown — are `AUTO_RESTART` and `SKIP_MASKED` (order
  **[Unknown]**).
- **The two 64-bit slot masks** are not "mask 1 / mask 2" of unclear purpose: the
  first is the **channel mask** (which slots carry data) and the second the
  **output-enable mask** (which slots the transmit unit drives). The baseline's
  inference was correct; this names it. Receive units have only a channel mask,
  which is why the published baseline programming leaves the second pair alone on capture.
- **Internal loopback has its own selector register**, separate from the data-in
  pad selector. On the baseline map the two unwritten receive registers at
  block offsets `0x18`/`0x1c` are the most likely home of that selector.
  **[Inferred]**

### 3.6.3 Global block — aligned multi-unit enable (new)

The global block carries a **synchronised enable facility with no M1–M3
counterpart**:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `RX_ENABLE_SET` / `RX_ENABLE_CLR` | Set/clear-only bitmask registers arming receive units for a synchronised start. |
| `TX_ENABLE_SET` / `TX_ENABLE_CLR` | Same for transmit units. |
| `SYNC_OMUX_ENABLE_SET` / `SYNC_OMUX_ENABLE_CLR` | Set/clear-only bitmask registers enabling the frame-sync output multiplexer per unit or per port. |
| `SYNC_OMUX_SEL` | Selects the frame-sync source that the output multiplexer forwards. |
| `ALIGNED_ENABLE_TRIGGER` | **One write starts every armed unit on the same frame boundary.** |

**[Probable]**. Functional consequence: multiple serialisers — including
serialisers of different clusters — can be started **sample-aligned**, which the
M1–M3 block cannot do (there, each serialiser is enabled by an individual
read-modify-write, with the 100 µs settle the baseline records). A driver that
must keep a six-amplifier playback link, its sense capture and its tap capture
phase-locked should arm all three and issue one trigger rather than enabling them
in sequence. **[Inferred]**

Set/clear-only registers also remove the read-modify-write hazard that makes
concurrent host/coprocessor access on M1–M3 unsafe — but they do not remove the
configuration race described in §3.5.

### 3.6.4 Reset and start sequence

Three self-clearing resets exist and are polled: the **frame-sync generator
reset** (per cluster), the **serialiser reset** (per unit), and a **PDM converter
software reset** (§3.10). **[Probable]**

The serialiser reset retains the M1–M3 shape — manipulate the unit's frame-sync
source selection, assert reset, wait, confirm the bit self-cleared — and
additionally has a **selectable reset type**, chosen independently for transmit
and receive, one variant of which is **synchronised to the bit clock**.
**[Probable]** A bit-clock-synchronous reset cannot complete while the bit clock
is stopped, which is the most likely explanation for the baseline's unexplained
pre-DMA-start settle delay. **[Inferred]**

The reset operation behaves differently on the **low-power cluster**; resetting
it is an exceptional case. **[Probable]**; **[Unknown]** how it differs. Do not
assume the base-cluster sequence applies there.

Timing values for in-scope parts are **[Unknown]**. Use the baseline's 25–50 µs
reset settle and 100 µs pre-DMA-start settle as starting points, but poll the
self-clearing bits rather than relying on fixed delays: all three are documented
as polled conditions, not timed ones.

Established start-order failure conditions, all of which a driver must respect:
the transmit FIFO depth must be configured before a transmit unit is enabled;
enabling a transmit unit whose FIFO is not yet full raises a distinct
**start-underflow** condition; and a receive unit is only (re)started with its
FIFO empty. **[Probable]**

### 3.6.5 The two serialiser arrays

Both arrays have 17 entries of `0x60` bytes at `0x100` stride, at region offsets
`0x4000` and `0x6000`. **[Confirmed]** for the geometry. **[Probable]** that one
is transmit and the other receive; **[Unknown]** which. The discriminator is the
field inventory: the transmit array's units carry an `OUTPUT_ENABLE_MASK` pair
and `DISABLE_OUTPUT_WHEN_IDLE`; the receive array's units carry
`DATA_SELECT.DIN_SELECT`, `LOOPBACK_DATA_SELECT.SERDES_SELECT` and
`DISABLE_MASTER_MODE_LOOPBACK_CLKSEL` and no output-enable mask.

`0x60` bytes is 24 registers, against the baseline's 7 (transmit) or 8 (receive).
**[Unknown]** what the additional registers hold; candidates are the FIFO depth
and status (§3.6.6), per-unit interrupt status and mask, and the reset-type
selector.

### 3.6.6 FIFOs

Each serialiser has a **FIFO with a programmable depth**, an "empty" status, an
explicit start trigger, a zero-fill operation, and a pre-start reserve check.
**[Probable]** The depth appears to be a per-stream configurable quantity on
in-scope SoCs. Whether the M1–M3 serial audio controller has an equivalent
serial-side depth control is **[Unknown]**: the published baseline records
FIFO depth and watermark behaviour as unknown on the serial-audio side and names
no depth register there, so nothing establishes that this control is a
carry-over, and its baseline semantics cannot be borrowed. The only comparable
quantity that *is* established on M1–M3 is on the **DMA** side — the per-channel
buffer carve-out and transfer threshold of Section 4 §4.3.3 — which is a
different control in a different block. See Open question 26.

☠ **[Unknown], and it blocks a legal transmit start**: the register offset
within the per-unit block, the units (entries, bytes or frames), the legal range,
the reset value, and whether a receive-side depth control exists distinct from
the transmit one.

**No value and no bound is established anywhere in this document, and none can
be borrowed.** The published M1–M3 baseline records serial-side FIFO depth and
watermark behaviour as unknown and names no depth register, so there is no
baseline figure to carry forward; the DMA-side per-channel buffer carve-out and
transfer threshold of §4 §4.3.3 are a different control in a different block and
must not be substituted; and the value is not in the platform description, which
exposes no aperture for this block at all (§3.2). It is **[Unknown]**, not
merely unstated. See Open questions 5 and 6.

**What this costs a driver, precisely.** §3.6.4's start sequence requires a
pre-start reserve check — the unit will not start legally until the FIFO holds
enough data — and a driver that does not know the depth cannot compute how much
"enough" is. On every SoC in scope this is moot in the ordinary case, because
**the host does not start the transmit unit: the coprocessor does** (§3.5,
§11 §11.6), and the coprocessor supplies the depth from its own configuration.
The depth is needed only in the two cases where the host drives the block
directly:

1. A bare-metal or bring-up driver programming the serial audio controller over
   MMIO on t8132, t8140 or t8142 (impossible on t604x and t605x, where no
   power-domain address is published — §3.5).
2. Reasoning about how much DMA-side slack absorbs a scheduling gap before the
   serialiser starves. **A driver must not assume the FIFO absorbs anything.**
   §3.6.11 already requires treating any host-side DMA underrun as proof the
   serialiser starved, and the unknown depth is exactly why: there is no basis
   for a smaller assumption. Until the depth is established, the only safe
   figure is **zero bytes of absorption**.

Under/overrun is reported as four distinct conditions per adapter pair and four
per serialiser pair (§3.6.9), plus two refinements of transmit underflow —
**underflow at stream start** and **frame-aligned underflow**. **[Probable]**
**[Unknown]** whether the two refinements are separate status bits or a decode of
one bit plus context.

Watermark control exists on the PDM converter as an explicit high-water /
low-water pair (§3.10) but has **no established counterpart** on the serial audio
side. **[Unknown]**

### 3.6.7 The per-unit adapter array

Seventeen blocks of `0x14` bytes (five registers) at region offset `0x8000`,
`0x100` stride. **[Confirmed]** for the geometry. These are in the position the
M1–M3 DMA/slot adapters occupy functionally — between the DMA channel's word
stream and the serialiser's slot stream — and one of the five registers is a
status register. **[Probable]** On M1–M3 the adapter is a single register whose
field semantics are explicitly not understood; here there are five, so the
baseline's field layout for it must be treated as **superseded, not ported**.
**[Unknown]** for all five registers' contents.

The baseline's sample-format quantities — transmit least-significant padding,
receive most-significant padding, channel counts — must be programmed somewhere,
and this array is the most likely home. **[Inferred]**

### 3.6.8 Audio island global configuration

Two further register blocks sit at the top of the audio island, at
`0x…13C0_0000` (`0x244`) and `0x…13C1_0000` (`0x468`) (§3.4.3). Established
fields in the island's global configuration:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `MCA_TO_ADMA_CH_MAP` | **Maps serial-audio units to audio DMA channels.** This is what makes the observed "DMA channel number equals cluster number" correspondence a configuration rather than a wiring constant. |
| `SECURE_LEAP_TO_ADMA_CH_MAP` | The same mapping for the low-power cluster's **secure** links. Separating the secure map is what keeps a secure capture link out of reach of a non-secure DMA channel. |
| `PDM_SCRAMBLE_DESCRAMBLE_CONFIG` | Scrambling of the PDM microphone data path, presumably so that a capture cannot be read in the clear outside the secure domain. |
| `PDM_SECURE_MIC_DISABLE` + `HW_TRIGGER_CONFIG` | **Hardware-enforced microphone disable**, with a hardware trigger source — i.e. a microphone kill that does not depend on software. |
| `SENSE_PDMC_CLK_ENABLE` | Clock enable for the PDM converter domain named for the sense path — in fact the microphone PDM converter (§3.10.2). |
| `SENSE_PDMC_INPUT_CTL` | Input control for the same; its input selector takes a microphone index (§3.10.2). |

**[Probable]** for all six. **[Unknown]** which of the two blocks holds which, and
all bit assignments.

A wrapper-level control and status block also exists with **separate interrupt
enables for the DMA, serial-audio and PDM source groups**, per-group FIFO
interrupt enable and status registers, control/status registers for each of the
three, and a **frame-generator multiplexer** selecting which frame generator
drives which consumer. **[Probable]**

### 3.6.9 Interrupt sources

Twelve sources, named functionally:

| Source | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `TXA_UNDERFLOW`, `TXB_UNDERFLOW` | transmit serialiser ran out of data |
| `RXA_OVERFLOW`, `RXB_OVERFLOW` | receive deserialiser overran |
| `TXA_FRAME_ERROR`, `TXB_FRAME_ERROR` | frame-sync timing violation seen by a transmit unit |
| `RXA_FRAME_ERROR`, `RXB_FRAME_ERROR` | frame-sync timing violation seen by a receive unit |
| `ADAPTER_A_RX_UNDERFLOW`, `ADAPTER_B_RX_UNDERFLOW` | DMA adapter underflow, capture direction |
| `ADAPTER_A_TX_OVERFLOW`, `ADAPTER_B_TX_OVERFLOW` | DMA adapter overflow, playback direction |

plus the two transmit-underflow refinements of §3.6.6. **[Probable]** for the
source inventory; **[Unknown]** for bit positions, latching and clearing rules,
and whether the status lives per unit, per cluster or in the global block. No
public driver programs, reads or services the block's interrupt registers on any
generation, so nothing about latching or clearing is established anywhere.

The A/B suffixes reflect the M1–M3 two-serialiser-pairs-per-cluster structure. On
in-scope parts, with a flat serialiser array, the same twelve conditions most
plausibly appear per serialiser unit rather than per cluster. **[Inferred]**

### 3.6.10 Register access width and endianness

**[Probable] unchanged**: 32-bit aligned reads and writes, little-endian. The
set/clear-only registers of §3.6.3 are write-1-to-act. Read side effects are
**[Unknown]**; on M1–M3 the interrupt status register has them.

### 3.6.11 What a serial-side underflow means for a host driver

This is the practical consequence of §3.6.9, and it is not a small one.

**A serial-side underflow is not host-detectable on any SoC in scope.** The status and
interrupt registers of §3.6.9 live in the serial audio controller's register file, and on
t8132, t604x, t8140, t8142 and t605x platform firmware describes **no host MMIO aperture
for that block at all** (§3.2). The host cannot read the condition, cannot mask it, and
cannot clear it. **[Confirmed]** — from the absence of the aperture, not from the block's
behaviour.

**It is not host-recoverable either.** Every control that would clear or restart the
serialiser — unit enable, FIFO reset, zero-fill, clocking — is behind the same aperture and
is the coprocessor's (Section 11 §11.6). The host's only reset is the per-channel DMA ring
reset (Section 4 §4.10.1), which does not touch the serialiser. **[Confirmed]**

**Whether the coprocessor reports it to the host is [Unknown].** The audio service does
have an unsolicited-report path — a framed call of category `0x00`, subtype `0xc4`, on the
service's own (endpoint, channel) — but its payload layout for the audio service is
**[Unknown]**, so no message carrying an underflow, overflow or frame-error notification is
established (Section 11 §11.4.5, Open question 35). A driver must not assume one exists,
and must not wait for one.

**What the serialiser emits during an underflow is [Unknown].** The block has a zero-fill
operation and a pre-start reserve check (§3.6.6), which is consistent with zero-fill on
starvation, but nothing establishes that zero-fill is what an underflow triggers as opposed
to slot repetition or stale FIFO contents. **This matters because the transmit serialiser
feeds the speaker amplifiers directly**: if an underflow repeats stale FIFO contents, the
output is an uncontrolled, potentially full-scale transient into a transducer, not silence.
Until it is established, an underflow on a speaker link must be treated as a **potentially
destructive event, not a glitch**. See Open question 27.

**Therefore, what a driver must actually do.**

1. **Prevent it.** The only underflow evidence the host ever sees is on its own side of the
   link: `CHAN_INT_STATUS[i]` bit 1, the data-buffer underrun/overrun cause (Section 5
   §5.2.4). Keep the DMA channel fed with margin; do not run the buffer close to empty.
2. **Treat a host-side DMA underrun as proof that the serialiser also starved.** The
   serialiser is downstream of the channel with only the FIFO of §3.6.6 between them, whose
   depth is **[Unknown]**, so the host has no basis for assuming the FIFO absorbed the gap.
3. **Silence the amplifiers before investigating.** The shared shutdown line is host-owned
   on every machine in scope (Section 6), and asserting it is the only action that is
   guaranteed to stop output regardless of what the serialiser is emitting.
4. **Recover by tearing the stream down and re-opening it through the coprocessor**, not by
   resetting anything locally — Section 15 §15.5, re-entering at S9 for a DMA fault and at
   S5 if the coprocessor itself is implicated.

---

## 3.7 Frame format

### 3.7.1 The programming quantities and their constraints

| Quantity | Where | Constraint |
|---|---|---|
| Slots per frame | serialiser `CHANNELS_PER_FRAME` | — |
| Slot width | serialiser `BITS_PER_CHANNEL` | independently settable per direction |
| Sample width | adapter padding | must be ≤ slot width; violating this is rejected |
| Channel count | serialiser + adapter | must equal the channel mask's population count |
| Channel mask | serialiser `CHANNEL_MASK`, **64-bit per direction** | the bits it requires must fit inside the frame |
| Which slots are driven | transmit `OUTPUT_ENABLE_MASK`, 64-bit | — |
| Bit-clock edge | serialiser `CLOCK_EDGE` | per direction |
| Frame-clock polarity | **no field — fixed in hardware** | unchanged from baseline |
| Frame delay / justification | serialiser `DATA_DELAY` | **strictly less than the frame length**; `1` = I2S, `0` = left-justified |
| Bit order | serialiser `DATA_ENDIAN` | per direction |
| Frame-sync pulse length | frame-sync generator | must not exceed the frame length |
| Frame length in bit clocks | `FRAME_PHASE_0` + `FRAME_PHASE_1`, each *count − 1* | must be ≥ the bits each direction's channel mask requires |
| Master clock | clock generator `CLOCK_SELECT` + `DIVISOR` | divisor has a bounded range; the master-clock count per frame must exceed the frame's bit count and be an exact multiple of the frame rate; a zero-frequency master clock is rejected; only fixed (not derived) master clocks are used in practice |

**[Probable]** throughout. Material differences from the baseline:

- **Transmit and receive are configured independently** for slot width, sample
  width, channel count, channel mask, data delay and clock edge, and each is
  validated separately against the frame. This contradicts the baseline's finding
  that format is a per-cluster rather than per-direction property. On in-scope
  parts a link routinely carries, for example, six 32-bit transmit slots and
  twelve 16-bit receive slots in one frame — every machine with speaker
  current/voltage sense does exactly that (§3.7.3). **[Confirmed]** that such
  asymmetric links exist; **[Probable]** that the asymmetry is expressed in
  independent register fields.
- **What still ties the directions together** is the frame: both share the
  cluster's bit clock and frame-sync generator, so frame length and frame rate are
  common, and each direction's mask must fit inside that frame.
- **A legacy two-channel I2S mode** exists as a distinct mode from TDM, with two
  extra constraints: the frame size must be even and must be large enough for two
  channels of the configured slot width. **[Probable]**
- The bit-clock source may be of a **per-frame-rate** type, for which an
  explicitly specified bit-clock frequency is rejected — the bit clock is then
  derived from the frame rate. **[Probable]**
- The 64-bit channel mask raises the slot ceiling well above the baseline's
  16-slot `NSLOTS` field. **[Probable]** **[Unknown]** what
  `CHANNELS_PER_FRAME`'s width is now.

### 3.7.2 The per-link format descriptor

Every stream endpoint under `/arm-io/iop-audio-controller` carries a `reg`
property that is **not an address** — it is a nine-word link format descriptor:

| Word | Content | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | master clock frequency in Hz, or 0 if the link has none | **[Probable]** |
| 3 | master-clock-to-frame-rate ratio (low byte), or the bit-clock-to-frame-rate ratio when word 2 is 0 | **[Probable]** |
| 4 | nominal frame rate in kHz (low byte), or 0 for a rate-agile link | **[Probable]** |
| 5 | transmit channel mask | **[Confirmed]** |
| 6 | receive channel mask | **[Confirmed]** |
| 7 | byte 0 transmit channel count, byte 1 receive channel count, byte 2 transmit sample width in bits, byte 3 receive sample width in bits | **[Confirmed]** |
| 8 | byte 2 transmit slot width in bits, byte 3 receive slot width in bits | **[Probable]** |
| 0, 1 | link class and frame-geometry bytes | **[Unknown]** |

Words 5–8 are corroborated independently by the `max-channel-count` and
`max-bit-depth-bits` properties of the bound DMA channel node on every machine
where per-channel nodes are published, and by the per-amplifier slot map.
**[Confirmed]**

Resulting link table (identical for every board of the same machine family):

| Link | Endpoint node | Cluster / DMA channel | TX ch × sample/slot | RX ch × sample/slot | Rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Speaker, 6 amplifiers (j604, j715, j614s/c, j616s/c, j704, j815, j714s/c, j716s/c) | `audio-speaker` | base 0 | 6 × 24 bit in 32-bit slots | 12 × 16 bit in 16-bit slots | 48 kHz |
| Speaker, 4 amplifiers (j713, j813) | `audio-speaker` | base 0 | 4 × 24/32 | 8 × 16/16 | 48 kHz |
| Speaker, 4 amplifiers, no sense (j623, j624) | `audio-speaker` | base 0 | 4 × 24/32 | none | 48 kHz |
| Speaker, single amplifier (j773g, j773s, j575c) | `audio-speaker` | base 0 | 1 × 24/32 | none | 48 kHz |
| Speaker, t8140 (j700) | `audio-speaker` | **low-power TX 0** | 2 × 32/32 | none | 48 kHz, 12.288 MHz master clock |
| Speaker link tap (t8140/t8142/t605x) | `audio-speaker-tap` | base 1 | none | 6 / 4 / 2 × 24 bit in 32-bit slots | 48 kHz |
| Headphone codec playback | `audio-codec-output` | base 2 | 2 × 32/32 | none | ≤ 96 kHz; ≤ 192 kHz on t8140 |
| Headphone codec capture | `audio-codec-input` | base 2 | none | 1 × 32/32 | same |
| Base-domain loopback | `audio-mca-loopback` | base 3 | 2 × 16/16 | 2 × 16/16 | 48 kHz |
| Low-power microphone injection (t8140/t8142/t605x) | `lp-mic-injection-device` | base 5 | 3 × 24/32 (2 on t8140) | none | **16 kHz** |
| Low-power microphone capture | `audio-hp` / `audio-hp-mic` | low-power RX 0, **secure** | none | 3 × 32/32 (2 on t8140) | 48 kHz |
| Low-power internal loopback | `audio-leap-internal-loopback` | low-power TX 4 / RX 4 | 2 × 32/32 | 2 × 32/32 | 48 kHz |
| Secure low-power loopback (t605x) | `audio-secure-leap-loopback` | low-power TX 5 non-secure / RX 5 **secure** | 2 × 32/32 | 2 × 32/32 | 48 kHz |

**[Confirmed]** for every row.

### 3.7.3 Speaker link frame geometry

`speaker-config` gives the slot map as one four-byte record per amplifier,
`index | 0x0f | slot A | slot B`, with slots in **16-bit units**. On a
six-amplifier machine:

```
0 0f 00 02   1 0f 04 06   2 0f 08 0a   3 0f 0c 0e   4 0f 10 12   5 0f 14 16
```

Amplifier *k* owns 16-bit units `4k`,`4k+1` (one 32-bit playback slot, slot A)
and units `4k+2`,`4k+3` (two 16-bit sense slots, from slot B). On a
six-amplifier machine that is **192 data bits in the transmit direction** (six
24-bit playback channels in 32-bit slots) and **192 data bits in the receive
direction** (twelve 16-bit sense channels) — two separate wires, each carrying
192 bits. **[Confirmed]** — the record layout, the channel counts (6 transmit,
12 receive), the widths (24-in-32, 16-in-16) and the bound DMA channels'
`max-channel-count` (6, 12) and `max-bit-depth-bits` (32, 16) all agree.

**Those are counts of data bits per direction. They are not the frame length.**
The frame is **250 bit clocks long at a 12.000 MHz bit clock**, giving
12 000 000 ÷ 250 = **48 000 Hz** exactly, on every `sn012776` machine in scope
and irrespective of amplifier count; 192 of those bit clocks carry data in each
direction and the remaining **58 are idle**. **[Confirmed]** — the link
descriptor in the platform hardware description carries the 12 000 000 Hz
reference and the 250-cycle frame directly (§11 §11.7.3); the coprocessor's own
built-in record for this stream family carries frame-sync phase 0 = 1, phase 1 =
249 and divider 1; and the amplifier's bit-clock-to-frame-rate register takes
code `0x30`, the table entry for 250, on the same machines (§18 §18.4.4,
§18 §18.7.1).

An earlier version of this subsection added the two directions' data bits
together into a "384-bit frame" and derived an 18.432 MHz bit clock from it.
Both figures are withdrawn: the two directions do not share a wire, and the
frame length is 250 bit clocks, not a data-bit count.

Four-amplifier machines carry **128 data bits in each direction** (four 32-bit
playback slots; eight 16-bit sense slots) in the **same 250-bit-clock frame at
12.000 MHz**, with 122 idle bit clocks. Single-amplifier machines use one
playback slot and no sense return (`txm = 0x1`, `rxm = 0`) — 32 data bits in a
250-bit-clock frame. The iMac machines use four playback slots and no sense
return at all. **[Confirmed]**

The A18 Pro machine is the exception: two 32-bit playback slots, no sense
return, and a **256-bit-clock frame at a 12.288 MHz bit clock** derived from the
oscillator rather than the fixed reference. **[Confirmed]** (§18 §18.7.1)

---

## 3.8 Routing, loopback and tap

### 3.8.1 The cross-connect model

The switch is a graph over four kinds of endpoint, and the M1–M3 platform
description states routes as (source, destination) pairs over exactly this
namespace:

- **audio clients** — the DMA-fed stream endpoints;
- **transmit serialisers** and **receive deserialisers**, indexed over the whole
  block;
- **ports** (pad groups), indexed separately.

Three route kinds are used: *client → port*, *serialiser → port*, and
**serialiser → deserialiser with no port**, an internal loopback entirely inside
the switch. **[Confirmed]** for M1–M3; **[Probable]** that the same three kinds
exist in scope.

On in-scope parts the selection state is expressed as **pin masks** — a
transmit-serialiser pin mask, a receive-deserialiser pin mask, a clock-generator
output pin mask — plus a **loopback pin mask**. The receive unit has two separate
source selectors: `DATA_SELECT.DIN_SELECT` picks a pad, and
`LOOPBACK_DATA_SELECT.SERDES_SELECT` picks a transmit serialiser (§3.6.2). The
internal loopback is therefore a first-class, explicitly selected path, not a
special case of the port selector. **[Probable]**

### 3.8.2 The exposed loopback endpoints

| Endpoint | Domain | Format | What it loops |
|---|---|---|---|
| `audio-mca-loopback` | base cluster 3, transmit and receive DMA channel 3 | 2 ch, 16-bit in 16-bit slots | a base serialiser back into a base deserialiser |
| `audio-leap-internal-loopback` | low-power link 4, both directions | 2 ch, 32-bit | a low-power serialiser back into a low-power deserialiser |
| `audio-secure-leap-loopback` (t605x only) | low-power link 5: transmit non-secure, receive **secure** | 2 ch, 32-bit | a non-secure playback into a secure capture |

**[Confirmed]** All three have transmit and receive bound to the same link index
with no external part attached, and the base one declares
`compatible = "audio-data,audio-loopback"`.

The third is a hardware capability statement: the cross-connect can carry data
from a **non-secure** transmit unit to a **secure** receive unit. **[Confirmed]**
that the binding crosses the security boundary; the island's separate
secure-link-to-DMA-channel map (§3.6.8) is where that crossing is authorised.
**[Probable]**

Loopback links see **only the two channels their own serialiser carries** — their
masks are `0x3`/`0x3` on every machine regardless of speaker channel count. They
are not a monitor of another link. **[Confirmed]**

### 3.8.3 The speaker link tap — new on t8140, t8142, t605x

`audio-speaker-tap` is a **receive-only** endpoint on **base cluster 1**, bound to
base receive DMA channel 1, with no transmit side and no external device. Its
receive channel mask and count track the speaker link's **transmit** side exactly:

| Machine | Speaker transmit | Tap receive |
|---|---|---|
| j704, j815, j714s/c, j716s/c | 6 ch, 24 bit in 32-bit slots, mask `0x3f` | 6 ch, 24/32, mask `0x3f` |
| j813 | 4 ch, 24/32, mask `0xf` | 4 ch, 24/32, mask `0xf` |
| j700 | 2 ch, 32/32, mask `0x3` | 2 ch, 24 bit in 32-bit slots, mask `0x3` |

**[Confirmed]**. What this establishes:

1. **A receive unit can capture what a transmit unit is driving**, and it is a
   *per-slot* capability: the tap's mask covers the playback slots only, and it
   does not see the twelve sense slots that the same link's other deserialiser
   (base receive channel 0) reads. Two independent receive units therefore read
   **disjoint slot sets of the same frame simultaneously**. **[Confirmed]**
2. **The tap unit belongs to a different cluster from the serialiser it listens
   to** (cluster 1 vs cluster 0), so a deserialiser of one cluster can sample a
   link driven by another — the M1–M3 behaviour of the deserialiser source
   selector, unchanged. **[Confirmed]**
3. **On t8140 the tap crosses the base / low-power boundary.** The speaker link
   there is driven from the *low-power* cluster's transmit unit
   (`leap-ns-adma-tx-0`), yet the capturing deserialiser is a *base* cluster unit
   (`base-ns-adma-rx-1`). The two clusters therefore share one register region
   and one cross-connect. **[Confirmed]** for the bindings; **[Probable]** for
   the shared cross-connect — no other mechanism is consistent with it, and the
   shared `AUDIO_P` parent (§3.2.1) and the single 17-unit serialiser array
   (§3.2.2) point the same way.

Functionally the tap is a playback monitor giving a bit-exact copy of what is sent
to the amplifiers, independent of the sense return. It is available on t8140,
t8142 and t605x and **not** on t8132 or t604x. **[Confirmed]**

### 3.8.4 Low-power microphone injection — new on t8140, t8142, t605x

`lp-mic-injection-device` is a **transmit-only** endpoint on base cluster 5, three
channels (two on t8140) of 24-bit samples in 32-bit slots at **16 kHz** — the only
16 kHz link in the system and the only one whose channel count matches the
low-power microphone capture link. **[Confirmed]** The reading is an injection
path driving synthetic microphone data into the low-power capture chain.
**[Inferred]**

---

## 3.9 The low-power serial audio cluster

### 3.9.1 What it is

One serial audio cluster whose register/common logic is in the base audio domain
(`AUDIO_LEAP_MCA` under `AUDIO_P`) but whose DMA side, per-link clocking and
per-link power gating are in the low-power audio processor's domain
(`AUDIO_LEAP_C` and below). It presents **five receive links and one transmit
link**. **[Confirmed]**

It is the successor of the always-on-side serial audio instance of M1–M3, where
the platform description exposes the same links as separate nodes with an
`alc-number` property, no `reg`, and an always-on-device control function; two of
those links are populated, number 0 (low-power microphone capture) and number 4
(an internal loopback, from the M3 generation). **The link numbering and DMA
channel numbering of those two links are unchanged from M3 through M5.**
**[Confirmed]**

The change at M4 is that the always-on-side instance shrank from a multi-cluster
block (six clusters on t8103/t8112, two on t600x/t602x, four on t8122/t603x) to a
**single** cluster with six links, merged into the base block's register region.
**[Confirmed]** — on M1–M3 the always-on island enumerates `AOP_MCA0`…`AOP_MCA5`
(or `…MCA1`, or `…MCA3`) plus its own DMA and shim domains; on M4 and later it
enumerates exactly one serial-audio domain.

The low-power audio processor itself is a **programmable engine with its own
loadable firmware image**, powered and reset independently of the serial audio
controller. **[Probable]** Its serial-audio cluster is one of its peripherals, not
the engine itself.

### 3.9.2 What it connects to

| Link | Use | Machines |
|---|---|---|
| receive 0 | low-power microphone capture, 3 channels at 48 kHz (2 on t8140), on the **secure** low-power DMA controller | all in-scope |
| receive 4 / transmit 4 | internal loopback, 2 ch 32-bit, non-secure | all in-scope |
| receive 5 / transmit 5 | second loopback, transmit non-secure, receive secure | t605x only |
| transmit 0 | **speaker playback** | **t8140 only** |
| receive 1, 2, 3 | not bound on any in-scope machine | — |

**[Confirmed]**

### 3.9.3 The t8140 speaker path

On the A18 Pro machine the speaker playback stream is bound to
`leap-ns-adma-tx-0` — the low-power processor's non-secure DMA transmit channel 0
and hence the low-power cluster's single transmit link. Every other in-scope
machine binds speaker playback to `base-ns-adma-tx-0`. **[Confirmed]**

Read with the rest of that machine's description this is coherent:

- The t8140 speaker amplifier is a publicly documented part with **no control bus
  and no current/voltage sense return** (`num-channels = 2`). There is no sense
  capture to pair with playback, so the speaker link is a plain two-channel,
  32-bit, 48 kHz transmit-only link with a 12.288 MHz master clock — well within
  one transmit serialiser.
- Putting the loudspeaker path on the low-power cluster lets the base audio
  domain — `AUDIO_P`'s six clusters and both base DMA apertures — stay gated
  during ordinary playback, leaving only the `AUDIO_LEAP_*` branch and the
  amplifier powered. **[Inferred]**; it is the only functional reason to prefer
  the low-power cluster for the machine's primary output.
- The monitoring a sense return would have given is replaced by the **tap** on
  base cluster 1 (§3.8.3), enabled on demand, which needs the base domain only
  while monitoring.

**Driver consequence for t8140**: speaker playback requires the low-power
processor's non-secure DMA controller and the low-power cluster's transmit link,
not the base path, and the base domain is not required for playback at all. Code
that assumes the speaker is on base transmit channel 0 is wrong on this machine.
**[Confirmed]**

### 3.9.4 Host reachability of the low-power cluster

Worse than the base clusters. Its registers are presumably in the same region
(§3.2.2), but its per-link power domains are under `AUDIO_LEAP_C`, its most
interesting link (receive 0) is bound to a DMA controller that is deliberately not
host-mapped and is reached through an isolated-stream proxy, and on t604x and
t605x none of its power domains has a host-addressable control register.
Additionally, its reset behaves differently from a base cluster's (§3.6.4).
**[Confirmed]** Treat it as coprocessor-only.

---

## 3.10 The PDM converter group and the domain named for the speaker-sense path

### 3.10.1 The PDM converter group

A block of `0x14000` sits immediately below the serial audio controller in the
audio island (§3.4.3), structured as a `0x114`-byte wrapper block followed by
**five `0x4000` per-channel units**, each containing a register block and a large
(`0x2000`–`0x3000`) coefficient memory. **[Probable]** Five `0x4000` units is
exactly the size and shape of the always-on PDM region on M1. **[Confirmed]** for
the geometry.

Established per-channel fields:

| Group | Fields |
|---|---|
| Decimator | `DECIMATOR_RATE_1`, `_2`, `_3`, `DECIMATOR_TOTAL_RATE`; `FILTER1_LEN`, `FILTER2_LEN`, `FILTER3_LEN`; `DIN_POL_SEL`, `DIN_PHASE_SEL`; per-stage clock-gating force bits; a status-clear field; a coefficient memory |
| PDM controller | `CFG` with per-channel enables, `START`, `STOP`; `SW_RESET` (self-clearing); `STATUS.RX_RUNNING`; `FIFOCTL.FLUSH_RX_FIFO`; `FIFOSHIFT.RX_FIFO_SHIFT`; `RXFIFOCFG.HIGH_WATER` / `.LOW_WATER`; `IRQ_MASK.RX_HIGH_WATER` / `.RX_OVERFLOW` / `.RX_UNDERFLOW`; `RXCFG.DMA_EN`, `RXCFG.RX_AUTO_RESTART` |
| Synchronisation | **`SYNC_MCA.ENABLE` and `SYNC_MCA.SELECT` — the PDM converter can be phase-locked to a selected serial-audio cluster.** |

**[Probable]**. The high-water/low-water pair is programmed from the DMA burst
size, with high water one below low water. **[Probable]**

The `SYNC_MCA` pair is the architecturally important one: it is the mechanism by
which a PDM capture can be made sample-aligned with a TDM link — relevant to
microphone capture running alongside a TDM playback link. It is **not** evidence
of a PDM sense path (§3.10.2). **[Inferred]**

M5 and A18 Pro add a **PDM-side loopback** (enable plus source select) and a
**PDM transmit scrambler** that do not exist on M4. **[Probable]**

### 3.10.2 `AUDIO_SENSE_PDMC` — a renamed microphone PDM converter, not a sense converter

`AUDIO_SENSE_PDMC` is a **one-for-one rename of the baseline generation's
microphone PDM converter domain** (`AOP_PDMC_LPD` on M1/M2, `AOP_PDMC0` on M3),
**not a new block and not a speaker-sense converter**: the domain count is
unchanged M1 → M5, its decimator input selector takes a microphone index, it is
grouped with the secure-microphone mute hardware, and it is present identically on
machines whose amplifiers have no sense capability at all. Only the name changed.
See §8 §8.8, where this is established exhaustively. **[Confirmed]**

Structurally it is a child of `AUDIO_FR` and a sibling of both `AUDIO_P` and
`AUDIO_LEAP_A`. Two PDM reference-clock domains (`PDM0_AUDIO_REF`,
`PDM1_AUDIO_REF`) sit alongside with no parent. **[Confirmed]** Its clock enable
and input control are registers in the audio island's global configuration
(§3.6.8). **[Probable]**

The name must not be read as a capability statement about the sense path. Nothing
establishes that the SoC can accept the speaker current/voltage sense return as a
PDM bitstream; do not infer a PDM sense path from the domain name. **[Confirmed]**

On every in-scope machine the sense return is carried as **PCM in TDM slots on
the speaker link** — twelve 16-bit channels on a six-amplifier machine, eight on a
four-amplifier machine, on base receive DMA channel 0 (§3.7.2). **[Confirmed]** No
machine binds a stream to a PDM sense path, and the domain is unused for sense on
every machine in scope. **[Confirmed]**

**[Unknown]**: whether it is one of the five channels of the PDM group above or a
sixth instance elsewhere, its register block address, and which machine uses it.

---

## Per-SoC / per-machine differences

**t8132 (M4)** — six base clusters plus one low-power cluster. Serial audio
controller at `0x3_9360_0000`; base DMA at `0x3_9380_0000` (non-secure) and
`0x3_9370_0000` (secure, not described); low-power DMA at `0x3_9330_0000`
(non-secure), secure not described. Audio power-state registers host-addressable
at `0x3_8828_4020`…`0x3_8828_4168`. **No link tap** and **no low-power microphone
injection endpoint**. Speaker on base cluster 0: j604 and j715 six amplifiers with
12-channel sense; j713 four amplifiers with 8-channel sense; j623/j624 four
amplifiers with no sense; j773g one amplifier, no sense, and no low-power
microphone or loopback endpoints at all. No oscillator node.

**t604x (M4 Pro/Max)** — identical block structure. Serial audio controller at
`0x5_1360_0000`; base DMA at `0x5_1380_0000` / `0x5_1370_0000`; low-power DMA at
`0x5_1330_0000`. **No audio power domain carries a host-addressable control
register**; the whole always-on island is host-ungateable. No link tap, no
injection endpoint. Six-amplifier link with 12-channel sense on j614s/c and
j616s/c; single-amplifier no-sense link on j773s and j575c, which also omit the
low-power microphone and loopback endpoints. No oscillator node.

**t8140 (A18 Pro, j700)** — the outlier. Serial audio controller at
`0x3_1360_0000`. Speaker playback on the **low-power** cluster's transmit link
(two channels, 32-bit, 12.288 MHz master clock, no sense return); **link tap
present** on base cluster 1; **low-power microphone injection present** on base
cluster 5 with two channels; low-power microphone capture is two channels rather
than three; the headphone codec link runs to 192 kHz with a 24 MHz master clock
against 96 kHz and no master clock elsewhere. Three DMA controllers described
(base non-secure, low-power secure, low-power non-secure). Audio power-state
registers host-addressable at `0x3_0828_4020`…`0x3_0828_4180`. The **oscillator
node is present with four clock identifiers but no aperture** — the only in-scope
SoC where it is described at all.

**t8142 (M5)** — as t8132 plus: the low-power **secure** DMA controller is
described (`0x3_9320_0000`), the link tap is present on base cluster 1, the
low-power microphone injection endpoint is present on base cluster 5 with three
channels, and a low-latency escalation-detector block appears at
`0x3_93C8_0000`. Serial audio controller at `0x3_9360_0000`. Audio power-state
registers at `0x3_8828_4080`…`0x3_8828_4188`; note `AUDIO_A`'s parent here is the
always-on island's IOMMU domain rather than its filter domain. j704 and j815 are
six-amplifier machines with 12-channel sense and a 6-channel tap; j813 is a
four-amplifier machine with 8-channel sense and a 4-channel tap.

**t605x / t6050 (M5 Pro/Max)** — as t8142 for structure; serial audio controller
at `0x2_9360_0000`, DMA at `0x2_9320_0000` / `0x2_9330_0000` / `0x2_9380_0000`.
**No audio power domain carries a host-addressable control register**, as on
t604x. Uniquely, a **second low-power loopback link** on link 5 whose transmit
side is non-secure and whose receive side is secure. All four machines (j714s/c,
j716s/c) are six-amplifier with 12-channel sense and a 6-channel tap.

---

## Open questions

Each item states what is unknown, why a driver author needs it, and the probe that
settles it. Probes assume a bring-up environment able to trap and pass through
MMIO accesses from the application processor, and, where a domain must be raised,
either the power-state registers of §3.4.1 (t8132, t8140, t8142) or a machine
where the coprocessor has already brought the block up.

1. **Confirm the serial audio controller base address.** Everything else rests on
   §3.4.2 and no read has been done. *Probe*: with `AUDIO_P` powered (read back
   its power-state register first), read 32 bits at the region base
   (`0x3_9360_0000` on t8132/t8142, `0x5_1360_0000` on t604x, `0x3_1360_0000` on
   t8140, `0x2_9360_0000` on t6050). A non-aborting read is confirmation; then
   verify the structure by reading the six per-cluster blocks at `base + 0x2000 +
   0x100·n` and confirming that the seventh (`n = 6`) reads as zero or aborts
   while `n = 0…5` do not. **An abort proves nothing on its own** — retry with
   the domain confirmed on, and then at `base + 0x4000` and `base + 0x8000`.
2. **Which of the two 17-entry arrays is transmit and which receive?** A driver
   that gets this backwards writes slot masks into the wrong direction. *Probe*:
   start the six-amplifier speaker link through the coprocessor and read both
   arrays. The array whose unit 0 holds a 64-bit mask with six bits set and a
   second 64-bit mask is transmit; the array whose unit 0 holds a mask with
   twelve bits set and only one mask pair is receive. Cross-check the tap: on
   t8142 the receive array's unit 1 should hold a six-bit mask.
3. **What does index 16 of each array address — a 17th unit or a broadcast
   alias?** This decides whether the low-power cluster's links are units 12–16 of
   the base array (§3.2.2, reading "12 + 5") or whether index 16 is an aggregate.
   *Probe*: write a distinctive value into unit 16's configuration and read units
   0–15 back. If they all change, index 16 is a broadcast alias. If nothing
   changes, it is a real 17th unit — then start the low-power microphone capture
   and see whether unit 12 of the receive array becomes configured.
4. **Confirm the established per-unit register offsets, and place the ten or so
   words of each block that remain unassigned.** The first seven serialiser
   registers (`+0x00` … `+0x18`) and the per-cluster clock-generator and
   frame-sync registers are **established** at §18 §18.8.1–§18 §18.8.4 and are
   summarised in §3.6.1; `0x60` bytes is 24 words, so roughly two thirds of each
   block is still unassigned. *Probe*: with the speaker link running, diff a
   unit's 24 words against a stopped unit's; then change one quantity at a time
   through the coprocessor (slot count 2 → 6, slot width 16 → 32, data delay
   0 → 1, channel mask) and record which word moves — confirming that the moving
   words are the ones §18 §18.8.4 names, at the offsets it gives. In the
   per-cluster block the **frame length in bit clocks — 250 on every `sn012776`
   machine at 48 kHz, whatever the amplifier count, and 256 on t8140** — should
   appear as `FRAME_PHASE_0 + FRAME_PHASE_1 + 2`, i.e. `0 + 248 + 2` on a
   `sn012776` machine, because each register holds its phase count minus one and
   the phases are 1 and 249 (§2 §2.5.4, §18 §18.7.1). The figure of 384 this
   entry previously carried was a sum of the two directions' data-bit counts and
   is **withdrawn** (§18 §18.4.4).
5. **Where is the transmit FIFO depth, in what units, and what is its maximum?**
   Without it a transmit unit cannot legally be started (§3.6.4). *Probe*: bring
   up two streams of very different channel count (1 and 6) and diff the unit
   blocks; the depth field should scale with per-frame byte count. Then find the
   maximum by raising it until the start-underflow condition stops appearing at
   the smallest DMA burst.
6. **Is there a receive-side FIFO depth or watermark control?** The PDM converter
   has an explicit high/low water pair; the serial audio side has no established
   equivalent. *Probe*: on the base loopback link, whose two directions can be
   driven independently, vary the capture burst size and diff the receive unit's
   block.
7. **What is the interrupt status/mask bit assignment, and where does it live?**
   Twelve sources are named (§3.6.9) but not located, and it is unknown whether
   status is per unit, per cluster or global. A driver that cannot detect
   underflow cannot recover a stream. *Probe*: run a transmit stream and starve
   the DMA channel (stop the descriptor queue, leave the serialiser enabled);
   diff the unit block, the cluster block and the global block. Repeat for
   capture overflow and, with a deliberately short frame-sync count, for the
   frame-error sources. Separately determine whether write-1 clears, whether read
   clears, and whether the mask gates the status bit or only the output line.
8. **Does the block raise any interrupt into the application processor's
   interrupt controller?** §3.4.4 lists the unclaimed numbers. *Probe*: unmask
   everything, provoke an underflow, and watch numbers 476–477 (t8132), 450
   (t8140), 550 (t8142). If nothing fires, a host driver must poll.
9. **How is the aligned multi-unit enable used, and what exactly does the trigger
   align to?** This is the block's most useful new facility (§3.6.3) and there is
   no prior art. *Probe*: arm two transmit units on different clusters, trigger,
   and measure the phase relationship of the two links on a logic analyser
   against the same two units started by individual enables. Establish whether
   the trigger waits for a frame boundary, a bit-clock edge, or fires
   immediately, and whether arming a unit whose clock is stopped hangs the
   trigger.
10. **What are the five registers of the per-unit adapter block?** The baseline's
    single-register DMA adapter layout is superseded (§3.6.7), and the sample
    padding and channel-count fields must be in here somewhere. *Probe*: change
    the sample width from 16 to 24 to 32 bits at constant slot width and diff; the
    padding fields should track `32 − width`. Then change the channel count at
    constant slot count.
11. **Where is the serialiser-to-DMA-channel map, and what is its encoding?**
    (§3.6.8.) This determines whether a driver can move a link to a different DMA
    channel, and it is the enforcement point for secure links. *Probe*: read
    `0x…13C0_0000` and `0x…13C1_0000` with the speaker stream running and again
    with it stopped; look for a field whose value is the cluster index of each
    active link. Then bring up the tap and check that a second entry appears
    naming channel 1.
12. **How does a receive unit select an internal loopback source?** (§3.8.1.)
    *Probe*: start `audio-mca-loopback` and read the receive unit's two source
    selectors; compare with the values seen when the same unit captures the
    headphone codec. The differing register is the loopback selector, and its
    value identifies the transmit unit index being looped.
13. **How does the tap deserialiser attach to the speaker link — through a pad or
    through the internal loopback path?** This decides whether a driver can build
    its own monitor of any link (pad path, generalisable) or only where the
    cross-connect wires allow (loopback path, not generalisable). *Probe*: on
    t8142 start the speaker stream and the tap, then read the tap unit's
    `DATA_SELECT.DIN_SELECT` and `LOOPBACK_DATA_SELECT.SERDES_SELECT`. Whichever
    is non-zero answers it.
14. **On t8140, how does a base-cluster deserialiser see a low-power-cluster
    serialiser?** The strongest evidence for a single shared cross-connect
    (§3.8.3). *Probe*: on j700, start speaker playback and the tap, then read the
    tap unit's source selectors. A serialiser index of 12 or above, or a pad index
    outside the base clusters' range, settles how the low-power cluster is
    addressed.
15. **Which slots does the tap read, and is that reprogrammable?** A driver
    wanting a 12-channel sense capture and a 6-channel monitor simultaneously
    needs to know the two receive units are independently maskable. *Probe*:
    rewrite the tap unit's channel mask to select the sense slots and confirm the
    captured data changes.
16. **What is the reset-type selector, and how does the low-power cluster differ?**
    (§3.6.4.) *Probe*: trap the unit control register during a
    coprocessor-initiated restart on a base cluster and on the low-power cluster;
    compare written values and self-clear latency with the bit clock running and
    stopped. If the reset never self-clears with the bit clock stopped, the
    bit-clock-synchronous type is confirmed and the baseline's unexplained 100 µs
    settle is explained.
17. **Are the block's registers reachable from the application processor on t604x
    and t605x?** There is no host-addressable power domain there (§3.4.1), so the
    block can only be powered by the coprocessor. *Probe*: start any stream
    through the coprocessor, then read `0x5_1360_0000` / `0x2_9360_0000`. If they
    answer, only power is coprocessor-gated; if they abort while a stream is
    plainly running, there is a fabric firewall and direct MMIO is impossible on
    those parts.
18. **What are the reset values of every register?** None is known on any
    generation. *Probe*: read the whole region immediately after taking `AUDIO_P`
    and one cluster domain from off to on, before the coprocessor touches them —
    i.e. with the coprocessor held in reset or before its audio service starts.
19. **How many I2S/TDM pad groups exist, and how are base and low-power clusters
    numbered within that space?** (§3.2.4.) *Probe*: write each value into a
    cluster's bit/frame-clock source selector and read back; the field saturates
    or ignores values above the implemented count. Cross-check against the number
    of distinct pad groups the board wiring uses.
20. **Is the frame format really per-direction?** (§3.7.1.) *Probe*: on a
    six-amplifier machine with the speaker stream running, read the transmit and
    receive units' `BITS_PER_CHANNEL` and confirm they differ (32 vs 16). If they
    are equal, the asymmetry lives in the adapter and must be programmed there
    instead.
21. **Is the channel mask really 64 bits, and what is `CHANNELS_PER_FRAME`'s
    width now?** The baseline's 4-bit slot-count field caps at 16 slots, but the
    six-amplifier speaker frame already uses 24 16-bit units. *Probe*: read the
    running speaker link's `CHANNELS_PER_FRAME` and see what value 24 slots is
    encoded as; then program a slot above 31 on the loopback link and observe
    which mask word changes.
22. **Is `AUDIO_SENSE_PDMC` one of the five PDM channels at `0x…1350_0000` or a
    sixth block?** (§3.10.2.) *Probe*: raise `AUDIO_SENSE_PDMC` with
    `AUDIO_LEAP_A` down and sweep the audio island for a block that becomes
    readable; check whether any of the five known PDM channels responds. Also
    determine whether `PDM0_AUDIO_REF` or `PDM1_AUDIO_REF` must be on first.
23. **What do `SYNC_MCA.ENABLE`/`SYNC_MCA.SELECT` align the PDM converter to, and
    with what latency?** It aligns a PDM capture to a selected serial-audio
    cluster; its use in scope is microphone capture alongside a TDM link, not a
    sense path (§3.10.1, §3.10.2). *Probe*: enable the low-power microphone capture with
    and without the sync fields set while a TDM link runs, and measure the
    sample-phase relationship between the two captures.
24. **What do words 0 and 1 of the per-link format descriptor mean?** (§3.7.2.)
    Word 1's low byte tracks the receive channel count on speaker links but not on
    the tap, and its second byte is the receive slot width on speaker links and
    zero elsewhere. *Probe*: compare descriptors across j623/j624 (no sense), j713
    (4+8), j604 (6+12) and j773g (1+0) against the frame geometry actually
    programmed into the cluster and unit blocks.
25. **Validate the group-form power-state register decode.** On t8140, t8142,
    t604x and t605x the power-manager device list encodes each domain's control
    register differently from the SoCs for which published register offsets
    exist, so the addresses in §3.4.1 for t8140 and t8142 rest on internal
    consistency only, and the "no address at all" finding for t604x and t605x
    rests on the same decode. A driver author must not write into a power-state
    register on those parts until this is settled. *Probe*: on t8140 read
    `0x3_0828_40D0` (`AUDIO_P`) and `0x3_0828_4100` (`AUDIO_MCA0_M`) while the
    coprocessor has a speaker stream running, and again with audio idle. A
    power-state register reads back a running/settled state field that differs
    between the two, and its neighbours at ±8 bytes must belong to the adjacent
    domains in §3.3.1's order. If the values look like unrelated registers, the
    group-form decode is wrong and every §3.4.1 address for t8140 and t8142 must
    be treated as **[Unknown]**.
26. **Does the serialiser FIFO depth control exist on the M1–M3 baseline, and what
    are its register offset, units and range here?** (§3.6.6.) The control is
    **[Unknown]** on the baseline and its offset, units (entries, bytes or frames),
    legal range, reset value and receive-side counterpart are **[Unknown]** in scope
    as well. *Why it matters:* a driver cannot size a serial-side FIFO, cannot
    compute the reserve a stream start needs, and cannot tell a genuine underflow
    from an under-sized FIFO until this is known; and it must not assume the
    baseline's DMA-side threshold semantics apply to it. *Probe*: with a link
    running, sweep the candidate per-unit register through its legal values and
    watch the "empty" status and the transmit-underflow causes of §3.6.9 for the
    threshold at which a fixed DMA feed rate starts to underflow; the depth in
    frames follows from the feed rate and the time to first underflow.

27. **What does the transmit serialiser emit when its FIFO underflows, and is the condition
    reported to the host at all?** (§3.6.9, §3.6.11.) Both are **[Unknown]**: zero-fill,
    slot repetition and stale FIFO contents are all consistent with what is known, and no
    coprocessor message carrying the condition is established. *Why it matters:* it decides
    whether an underflow on a speaker link is an audible glitch or a full-scale transient
    into a transducer, and therefore whether a driver may continue a stream after one or
    must silence the amplifiers. *Probe:* on a machine with a speaker tap or loopback
    endpoint, starve a transmit channel deliberately (stop feeding descriptors while the
    link runs) and capture what the link carries during the gap; repeat with the FIFO
    pre-loaded and with it empty at stream start, and watch for any coprocessor-originated
    message arriving in the same interval.

28. **Is the fabric inbound address-protection filter an allow-list or a deny-list?**
    (§3.4.5.) The polarity is **[Unknown]** and nothing in the platform description
    distinguishes the two readings. *Why it matters:* an address the table omits is
    "permitted" under one reading and "denied" under the other, and the two give
    opposite answers for every audio block the table does not name — the serial audio
    controller among them (§11 §11.6.2(c)). It also decides whether the audio island is
    reachable at all from the normal world on the M5 generation. *Probe*: with the
    coprocessor running, read a protected address — the low-power secure instance's
    `CHAN_BUF_CFG` for receive channel 0, `0x3_9320_C050` on t8142 — and an unprotected
    address in the same aperture, both from the normal world. A fault on the first and a
    value on the second proves a protect-list.

29. **What is the register map of the fabric filter's entry array?** (§3.4.5.) Only the
    enable and lock registers have addresses. The per-entry registers — valid, master
    identifier, direction, start, end — have no established offsets, no bit positions,
    no entry count, and no violation-status register is located. *Why it matters:* a
    driver cannot read the live table back and check it against the published one, which
    is the only way to characterise the t605x case, where the filter is enabled and
    locked with no table published. *Probe*: dump the whole 16 KiB page at always-on
    island base + `0x82_8000` and correlate the published range values against its
    contents.

30. **Is the fabric filter already locked when a host driver first runs, and what
    happens on a violation?** (§3.4.5.) The lock declaration is a present-or-absent
    boolean in the platform description; the timing is **[Inferred]** and the violation
    behaviour — abort, read-as-zero, silent drop — is **[Unknown]**. *Why it matters:*
    if the block is not yet locked at hand-off a driver could in principle widen it; if
    it is, the protected addresses are off-limits until reset, and a driver must know
    whether touching one faults or merely returns nothing. *Probe*: read the lock
    register early in boot, then attempt a write to the enable register and read it
    back; separately, access a protected address and record the failure mode.

31. **What do the bits of the `0x1F` attribute word mean?** (§3.4.5.) The word is
    constant across every entry on every board, so the platform description carries no
    differential signal for it. *Why it matters:* it is the only place a per-range
    read/write permission could be encoded, and without it a driver cannot tell whether
    a protected range is closed to reads, to writes or to both. *Probe*: after Open
    question 29, correlate the published word against the live per-entry registers.

32. **What are the two protected 16 KiB pages on t8140 at `0x3_1084_0000` and
    `0x3_1085_0000`?** (§3.4.5.) No node describes them and their contents are
    **[Unknown]**. *Why it matters:* they are the only protected ranges outside the
    audio island on any in-scope board, and t8140 is the machine whose audio topology is
    least understood, so a block the fabric protects alongside the audio DMA controllers
    may yet turn out to be on an audio path. *Probe*: read them with the coprocessor
    running and compare against the known always-on serial-bus controller layouts one
    and two pages below.

33. **What do the trusted and untrusted master identifiers name?** (§3.4.5.) The
    untrusted run of four on t8142 matches the four audio DMA controller instances in
    count, but the mapping is unverified and t605x lists only three. *Why it matters:* a
    driver that knows which master identifier its DMA channel presents to the fabric can
    predict which of its accesses will be refused, instead of discovering it as a fault.
    *Probe*: provoke a violation from a known master and read the reported identifier out
    of the violation-status register located by Open question 29.


---

# 4. Audio DMA controller

## Baseline

The closest documented equivalent is the **audio DMA controller of the M1–M3 generations**
(t8103 / t600x / t8112 / t602x / t8122 / t603x), documented publicly by the mainline Linux
driver and its binding: a `0x34000`-byte MMIO aperture; global start/stop registers and
four per-interrupt-destination state registers in the first `0x100` bytes; a per-channel
register block at `0x8000 + channel × 0x200`; and two 4-byte FIFO ports per channel — a
write-only descriptor port and a read-only completion port — at `0x10000` / `0x10100` for
transmit and `0x14000` / `0x14100` for receive. Up to 24 channels have been seen; channels
are hardwired to endpoints, even-numbered channels transmit and odd-numbered receive. Four
interrupt outputs exist, of which usually one is wired to the host. Descriptors and
completion entries are four 32-bit words each, pushed and popped through the FIFO ports;
the ports are four slots deep. A per-channel byte-granular carveout of an on-chip buffer
memory, a per-channel FIFO limit/threshold pair, and a per-channel bus-width/frame-size
control complete the published picture. Two further global registers at `0x0028` and
`0x002C` must be written `0x0020_0000` on the M3 generation.

On every in-scope SoC the block is **still host-addressable and still `0x34000` bytes**,
and the global register layout is largely recognisable — but the **M4 generation
introduced a new controller revision**: per-channel register blocks are re-addressed and
split by direction, the per-channel timestamp port (which first appeared on M2 and lay
dormant on M2 Pro/Max–M3) is put into service, AXI attribute/error/telemetry registers
appear, a per-destination global interrupt-enable array appears, and the always-on
coprocessor gains its own direct ownership path. The **M5 generation** flags a further
revision in platform firmware and in the coprocessor-side implementation. This section
documents that delta.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Summary of differences

| Topic | M1–M3 | t8132 / t604x (M4) | t8140 (A18 Pro) | t8142 / t605x (M5) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Aperture size | `0x34000` | `0x34000` **unchanged** | `0x34000` | `0x34000` |
| Second aperture | 8 B, shared | 8 B, shared — **always-on global timebase** | same | same |
| Instances | `admac-sio` (shared with general I/O), `admac-aop-audio` | `admac-base-ns`, `admac-leap-ns` | + `admac-leap-s` | + per-display instances of a second controller type |
| Platform identifier | `admac,t8103` … `admac,t6030` | `admac,t8132` / `admac,t604x` | `admac,t8140` | **`admac-evolution,t8142` / `admac-evolution,t6050`** |
| `admac-evolution` property | absent | **absent** | **present, = 1** | **present, = 1** |
| Per-channel block addressing | `0x8000 + pair × 0x400`, receive half at +`0x200` | **TX `0x8000 + n × 0x200`, RX `0xC000 + n × 0x200`** | same | same |
| FIFO ports per channel | 2 on M1; **3 from M2** (timestamp port unused on M2 Pro/Max–M3) | **3, all used** | 3 | 3 |
| Fourth mapped aperture `0x18000 + n × 0x40` | present, never dereferenced | **gone** | gone | gone |
| Per-channel AXI attribute / error / telemetry registers | not documented | **present** | present | present |
| Global per-destination interrupt **enable** array | not documented | **present** (`0x0060 + 4i`) | present | present |
| Global stream-class bitmaps | absent | **present** (`0x0100`, `0x0104`) | present | present |
| Channel-buffer carveout granularity | bytes | **16-byte units** | 16-byte units | 16-byte units |
| Global `0x0028`/`0x002C` write | required on Pro/Max dies | **not written** | not written | not written |
| Host interrupt output index | 1 (general I/O instance), 2 (always-on instance) | **0** | 0 | 0 |
| Channel count declaration | `#dma-channels` (pairs) | `#dma-channels` + `skip-channels-tx/-rx` | `#dma-channels` | **`#dma-channels-tx` / `#dma-channels-rx`** |
| Channels named in platform description | no | no (bound by number) | **yes, child nodes with their own `reg`** | **yes** |
| Memory-latency escalation block | absent | **declared, no implementation** | declared, no implementation | **present and implemented** |
| Display-port audio DMA | general-purpose I/O DMA controller | general-purpose I/O DMA controller | general-purpose I/O DMA controller | **own instance per display**, older controller type, `0x24000` aperture |
| Secure instance | none host-visible | none | `admac-leap-s` | `admac-leap-s` (+ `admac-base-s` in hardware) |
| Externally owned channels | none | none | 1 proxy node | 1–2 proxy nodes |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4.1 Instances

### 4.1.1 Inventory and naming

Platform firmware instantiates the controller with functional node names; all audio
instances carry `device_type = "admac"`. Each carries a four-character `role` code (stored
byte-reversed, as all such values are):

| Node | `role` reads | Function |
|---|---|---|
| `admac-base-ns` | `BANS` | Base audio domain, non-secure |
| `admac-base-s` | `BASS` | Base audio domain, secure — **exists in hardware but has no node** on any in-scope board |
| `admac-leap-ns` | `LENS` | Low-power audio-processor domain, non-secure |
| `admac-leap-s` | `LESS` | Low-power audio-processor domain, secure |
| `admac-disp0`, `admac-dispext0…3` | `DAI0`, `DAX0`/`DX00`… | Display-audio instances (M5 generation only) |

**[Confirmed]** — the node set is identical across every board of a generation.

The secure base instance is asserted by the M5-generation memory-latency escalation node,
whose `dma-controllers` property lists four controller roles (`BASS`, `BANS`, `LESS`,
`LENS`) with matching channel-count arrays, while only three have device nodes.
**[Confirmed]**

### 4.1.2 MMIO apertures, sizes and interrupts

Every audio instance declares exactly **two** `reg` entries: the `0x34000`-byte control
aperture and an **8-byte** auxiliary window. The display-audio instances declare a
`0x24000`-byte control aperture plus the same 8-byte window.

Addresses below are absolute — the platform description's I/O-relative values translated
through the `/arm-io` `ranges` table. **[Confirmed]** — the translation was validated by
reproducing a publicly documented M1 address (`0x2_3820_0000`) from the same board description.

**t8132 (M4)**

| Instance | Control aperture | Size | Aux window | Interrupt |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `admac-base-ns` | `0x3_9380_0000` | `0x34000` | `0x3_882A_8000` (8 B) | 475 |
| `admac-leap-ns` | `0x3_9330_0000` | `0x34000` | `0x3_882A_8000` (8 B) | 478 |

**t604x (M4 Pro / M4 Max)**

| Instance | Control aperture | Size | Aux window | Interrupt |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `admac-base-ns` | `0x5_1380_0000` | `0x34000` | `0x5_0832_8000` (8 B) | 754 |
| `admac-leap-ns` | `0x5_1330_0000` | `0x34000` | `0x5_0832_8000` (8 B) | 757 |

**t8140 (A18 Pro)**

| Instance | Control aperture | Size | Aux window | Interrupt |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `admac-base-ns` | `0x3_1380_0000` | `0x34000` | `0x3_082A_8000` (8 B) | 449 |
| `admac-leap-s` | `0x3_1320_0000` | `0x34000` | `0x3_082A_8000` (8 B) | 451 |
| `admac-leap-ns` | `0x3_1330_0000` | `0x34000` | `0x3_082A_8000` (8 B) | 452 |

**t8142 (M5)**

| Instance | Control aperture | Size | Aux window | Interrupt |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `admac-base-ns` | `0x3_9380_0000` | `0x34000` | `0x3_882A_8000` (8 B) | 549 |
| `admac-leap-s` | `0x3_9320_0000` | `0x34000` | `0x3_882A_8000` (8 B) | 551 |
| `admac-leap-ns` | `0x3_9330_0000` | `0x34000` | `0x3_882A_8000` (8 B) | 552 |
| `admac-disp0` | `0x2_8614_0000` | `0x24000` | `0x3_882A_8000` (8 B) | 822 |
| `admac-dispext0` | `0x5_0614_0000` | `0x24000` | `0x3_882A_8000` (8 B) | 894 |
| `admac-dispext1` | `0x3_AA14_0000` | `0x24000` | `0x3_882A_8000` (8 B) | 969 |
| Latency-escalation block (audio) | `0x3_93C8_0000` + `0x3_93C8_4000` | 2 × `0x4000` | — | 569 |

| `admac-leap-s` | `0x2_9320_0000` | `0x34000` | `0x2_8832_8000` (8 B) | 638 |
| `admac-leap-ns` | `0x2_9330_0000` | `0x34000` | `0x2_8832_8000` (8 B) | 639 |
| `admac-disp0` | `0x4_8A14_0000` | `0x24000` | `0x2_8832_8000` (8 B) | 1012 |
