Each display instance has its own escalation block (two `0x4000` windows at
`…2F4_0000` and `…1A0_0000` relative to the same display region) with an interrupt two
above the controller's: 824 / 896 / 971 on t8142; 1014 / 1094 / 1166 / 1238 / 1310 on
t605x. **[Confirmed]**

No audio DMA instance appears on die 1 of a multi-die part. **[Probable]**

The secure base instance's aperture address is **[Unknown]** — firmware describes its
power domain, IOMMU stream and channel counts but never its registers.

### 4.1.3 Purpose of the 8-byte second aperture

The 8-byte window is **identical for every audio DMA instance on a given SoC, and is the
same window the always-on coprocessor node declares as one of its own apertures**. It lies
inside the always-on-side power-manager register block (it falls within the power
manager's own `reg` range on every generation back to M1). **[Confirmed]**

Functionally it is the **always-on global timebase**: every audio DMA controller reads it
in order to relate its own local counter (§4.3.2) to system time, deriving an integer
clock scaler and an averaged signed offset between the two. A host driver must map it and
must treat it as read-only shared state. **[Confirmed]** — the aperture is shared by the
coprocessor node and by all audio DMA nodes across six SoC generations, and relating the
two counters requires reading this window and the channel's local counter together.

On t605x the coprocessor node's corresponding aperture has grown to `0x24` bytes while the
audio DMA nodes still claim only the first 8. **[Confirmed]**

### 4.1.4 Power and clock domains

The audio power domains are enumerated by the platform power manager. From the M4
generation the audio island's domains live in the **always-on-side power-manager block**,
not the main one. **[Probable]**

Domain tree, identical on t8132, t604x, t8140, t8142 and t605x (derived from each entry's
parent-domain index): **[Confirmed]**

```
AOP_FILTER  (t8142: AOP_DART)
└─ AUDIO_A
   └─ AUDIO_FR
      ├─ AUDIO_P
      │  ├─ AUDIO_BASE_S_A      ← admac-base-s
      │  ├─ AUDIO_BASE_NS_A     ← admac-base-ns
      │  ├─ AUDIO_LEAP_MCA
      │  └─ AUDIO_MCA0_M … AUDIO_MCA5_M
      ├─ AUDIO_LEAP_A
      │  └─ AUDIO_LEAP_C
      │     ├─ AUDIO_LEAP_S_A   ← admac-leap-s
      │     ├─ AUDIO_LEAP_NS_A  ← admac-leap-ns
      │     └─ AUDIO_LEAP_RX0 … AUDIO_LEAP_RX4, AUDIO_LEAP_TX0
      └─ AUDIO_SENSE_PDMC
PDM0_AUDIO_REF, PDM1_AUDIO_REF   (no parent)
```

Domain indices differ per SoC; on t8132 `AUDIO_BASE_NS_A` is 241 and `AUDIO_LEAP_NS_A` 251,
on t8140 184 and 194, on t8142 252 and 262, on t605x 306 and 316. **[Confirmed]**

Every audio domain carries flags byte `0x10`; on t8132 the six domains that directly back
a controller or a cluster group (`AUDIO_A`, `AUDIO_LEAP_A`, `AUDIO_BASE_S_A`,
`AUDIO_BASE_NS_A`, `AUDIO_LEAP_S_A`, `AUDIO_LEAP_NS_A`) carry `0x30` instead; on t8140,
t8142 and t605x all of them carry `0x10`. The display-audio domains carry `0x00`.
**[Confirmed]** — the meaning of the extra bit is **[Unknown]**.

**The power-state register addresses are established, and none of them is the host's to
write.** §2 §2.6.1 derives the per-domain control-register address from the power-manager
entry and validates the rule against mainline Linux's published offsets for **1266 of 1266**
baseline domains; §2 §2.6.2 gives the resulting per-SoC addresses. Two caveats carry over
here: on **t604x and t605x the device list states no control-register address at all** for
any audio domain, and on **t8140 and t8142** the addresses come from the group-form decode,
which has no mainline ground truth and is **[Probable]** on internal consistency alone
(§3 Open question 25 owns that validation). Either way, **flags-byte bit 4 is set on every
audio domain on every in-scope SoC**, which marks it as having no host-drivable power-state
register: a host driver does not raise, lower or reset any audio domain, and the audio
island's power is the coprocessor's. **[Confirmed]** See Open question 8 for what does
remain open here.

The display-audio instances sit in ordinary display power domains named `DISP_ADMA` and
`DISPEXT0_ADMA` … `DISPEXT3_ADMA`, parented to the corresponding display-subsystem domain.
**[Confirmed]**

On t8132, t604x, t8140 and t8142 every audio DMA node's `clock-gates` property points at a
power-manager pseudo-device named **`AUDIO-LLT-V`** — a *vote*, not a clock gate (LLT =
low-latency-transaction memory-system mode; see §4.10.4); it has no parent domain. On
**t605x that pseudo-device does not exist**; each node instead carries
`function-vote_crit_llt_mode`, a power-manager function call with tag `VCLM` and two zero
arguments. A second pseudo-device `AUDIO-P-V` (parent `AUDIO_P`) exists on t604x, t8140 and
t605x but not on t8132 or t8142. **[Confirmed]**

From **t8140** onwards the power manager's performance-counter table additionally carries
per-instance energy-measurement domains named `AUDIO_BASE_NS_ADMA_A`,
`AUDIO_BASE_S_ADMA_A`, `AUDIO_LEAP_NS_ADMA_A`, `AUDIO_LEAP_S_ADMA_A`, absent on t8132 and
t604x. These are measurement domains, not power-state domains. **[Confirmed]**

### 4.1.5 Proxy nodes for externally owned channels

On t8140 and the M5 generation, firmware describes channels of the **secure low-power
instance** that belong to another agent (the isolated execution environment). They appear
as separate nodes with `compatible = "admac-ec-proxy"`, `device_type = "admac-proxy"`, a
`dma-channel` property giving the receive-channel index, an `exclave-assigned` marker, and
a `function-iommu_handler` property whose tag reads `sdpr` and whose phandle points at the
shared-mapper node of §4.9.3.

| SoC | Node | `dma-channel` | Aperture claimed |
|---|---|---|---|
| t8140 | `admac-leap-s-rx-0-proxy` | 0 | `0x34000` at `0x5_6320_0000` |
| t8142 | `admac-leap-s-rx-0-proxy` | 0 | `0x34000` at `0x5_E320_0000` |
| t605x | `admac-hp-mic-ec-proxy` (built-in microphone array — the node name misleads, see note ² in §4.2.4) | 0 | `0x34000` at `0x4_D320_0000` |
| t605x | `admac-sllb-ec-proxy` | 5 | `0x34000` at `0x4_D320_0000` (same window) |

The proxy aperture is a **second physical alias of the whole secure low-power instance**,
at an address not related by a constant offset to the one the host sees. **[Probable]**
The corresponding channel child node under `admac-leap-s` carries a `service-exclave_proxy`
property naming the proxy. The t605x secure-loopback proxy and its channel additionally
carry `proxy-is-development-only` / `channel-is-development-only`, so that path is not
present on shipping configurations. **[Confirmed]**

A host driver cannot own a channel that has a proxy node: an IOMMU mapper and an isolated
proxy are mutually exclusive on one instance. **[Probable]**

## 4.2 Channels, numbering and the per-machine channel map

### 4.2.1 Counts

| Instance | TX channels | RX channels |
|---|---|---|
| `admac-base-ns` | 13 | 13 |
| `admac-base-s` | 13 | **14** |
| `admac-leap-ns` | 9 | 9 |
| `admac-leap-s` | 9 | 9 |
| Display-audio instance | 1 | 0 |

**[Confirmed]** for every row. The secure base instance's asymmetric 13-transmit /
14-receive count is corroborated independently of its declaration by the M5 escalation
node: a fabric filter entry protects that instance's `CHAN_BUF_CFG` for **receive
channel 13**, which exists only if the receive count is 14 (§3 §3.4.5).

The controller's per-direction channel-enable masks are **13 bits wide** (`0x1FFF`), which
caps a direction at 13 channels and matches the base instance's declared count exactly.
This mask does not exist on the M1–M3 controllers. **[Confirmed]**

On **t8132 / t604x** the count appears as a single `#dma-channels = 13` (or `9`) counting
**transmit/receive pairs**, together with `skip-channels-tx = <12>` and
`skip-channels-rx = <12>` on `admac-base-ns`. These are *lists* of channel indices present
in the address map but not to be used; here each list has one entry, index 12.
**[Probable]**

On **t8140 and the M5 generation** the count appears as two independent 64-bit properties,
`#dma-channels-tx` and `#dma-channels-rx`. The asymmetry of the secure base instance is
only expressible in this form. **[Confirmed]**

`channels-offset` is `0` on every in-scope instance. On M1–M3 the shared general-I/O
instance used `0x28`, because audio occupied a window inside a larger channel space.
**[Confirmed]**

### 4.2.2 Numbering and how channels are named

Two numbering schemes coexist:

* **Interleaved global number** `c`: `c = 2n` for transmit channel *n*, `c = 2n + 1` for
  receive channel *n*. This is what M1–M4 platform descriptions put in the `dma-channels`
  property of a stream endpoint; a consumer reduces it to a direction-local index by
  `n = c >> 1` with direction `c & 1`. **[Confirmed]**
* **Direction-local index** `n`: used by the register map (§4.3), by the
  `dma-provider-tx` / `dma-provider-rx` strings, and by the channel child nodes.

That `#dma-channels` counts *pairs* is established independently: the mainline binding
gives the M1 controller 24 channels while the same board's platform description declares
`#dma-channels = 12`. **[Confirmed]**

From **t8140** onwards the stream endpoints stop carrying `dma-channels` and instead carry
**string** properties `dma-provider-tx` / `dma-provider-rx` naming a channel, e.g.
`base-ns-adma-tx-2`, `leap-s-adma-rx-0`. The name encodes instance role, direction and
direction-local index and resolves against **named child nodes of the controller**
(`device_type = "adma-ch"`, `compatible = "audio-dma-channel,v4p0"`). **[Confirmed]**

Each channel child node carries its own `reg` with **four** sub-apertures — the per-channel
register block and the three FIFO ports (§4.3.4) — plus:

| Property | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `max-channel-count` | maximum number of audio slots the stream may carry |
| `max-bit-depth-bits` | 16 or 32 |
| `max-sample-rate-hz` | 16000, 48000 or 96000 |
| `dma-stream-type` | four-character stream class; only `ISOC` observed |
| `direction`, `index`, `channel-buffer-size` | present but **zero-length** (markers) |
| `role` | inherited instance role |
| `service-exclave_proxy` | only on externally owned channels |
| `channel-is-development-only` | only on the secure loopback capture channel |

**[Confirmed]**

Further per-channel properties are defined but not populated on any in-scope board: `max-fifo-depth-bytes`, `initial-trigger-bytes`,
`max-fifo-depth-us`, `initial-trigger-us`, `axi-burst-size-bytes`. **[Probable]** — these
give a driver the option of expressing FIFO depth and trigger point either in bytes or in
microseconds.

### 4.2.3 The `dma-channels` record layout (M1–M4 stream endpoints)

`dma-channels` is **128 bytes = four 32-byte records** on every board that has it (47 of 56
boards; absent on t8140 and all M5 boards). Field layout: **[Confirmed]**

| Word | Bytes | Field | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0–3 | Interleaved global channel number | `0xFFFFFFFF` = direction not present |
| 1 | 4–7 | Stream-class code | `0x21` and `0x22` on audio endpoints; `0x02` on display-audio endpoints; `0x00` on general I/O peripherals |
| 2 | 8–11 | zero in every instance observed | reserved/flags |
| 3 | 12–15 | FIFO **limit**, bytes | bits 31:16 of the channel threshold register |
| 4 | 16–19 | FIFO **transfer threshold**, bytes | bits 15:0 of the same register |
| 5–7 | 20–31 | zero in every instance observed | |

Record order is **[TX, class A], [RX, class A], [TX, class B], [RX, class B]**. The two
classes carry identical channel numbers and identical FIFO values on every board,
so the pair describes one channel under two stream classes. The controller distinguishes
**isochronous** streams from **bulk** (memory-to-memory) streams, and the successor
property `dma-stream-type` on the M5 channel nodes carries that code space (`ISOC`
observed; `BULK` is the other value the controller knows). Mapping `0x21` / `0x22` onto
those two classes is **[Inferred]**; the direction of the mapping is **[Unknown]**.

Corroboration for words 3 and 4: the mainline driver programs the channel threshold
register as limit = `0x30 × word_size`, threshold = `0x18 × word_size`, and the loopback
endpoint on every in-scope M4 board carries exactly `0xC0` / `0x60` — the 32-bit-word case.
**[Confirmed]**

#### Display-audio channels (M5 generation)

(`#dma-channels-tx = 1`; the matching escalation node declares tx = 1, rx = 0). The
corresponding `dp-audioN` node's `dma-channels` record gives channel number **0**, class
code `0x02`, FIFO limit **4096 B**, threshold **2048 B**, and its `dma-parent` phandle
points at `admac-dispN`. On M4 the same `dp-audioN` nodes point at the **general-purpose
I/O DMA controller** with channel numbers `0x64`, `0x66`, `0x68`, … and FIFO limit 2048 B,
threshold 2048 B (t8132) or 1536 B (t604x). **[Confirmed]** — this is the clearest single
expression of the display-audio change.

t8142 has three display instances; t605x has five. **[Confirmed]**

## 4.3 Register map

Throughout, *n* is the direction-local channel index and *i* the interrupt-destination
index (0…3), matching the notation of §5 §5.2. Register names below are coined
functional names, used consistently and identically to §5 (see the naming note in
§4.3.3).

### 4.3.1 Region layout of the aperture

**M1–M3 (baseline, for contrast).** Per channel *pair* the controller exposes four
sub-apertures — a `0x400`-byte register block at `0x8000 + pair × 0x400` whose receive half
starts at +`0x200`; the descriptor and completion ports at `0x10000 + 4n` / `0x10100 + 4n`
(transmit) and `0x14000 + 4n` / `0x14100 + 4n` (receive); and, **from the M2 generation
only, a fifth**: a timestamp port at `0x10200 + 4n` / `0x14200 + 4n`. All generations
M1–M3 additionally map a region at **`0x18000 + n × 0x40`** which no observed access
pattern ever dereferences. **[Probable]**

**M4, A18 Pro and M5.**

| Range | Contents |
|---|---|
| `0x00000`–`0x00FFF` | Global register block |
| `0x08000`–`0x0BFFF` | **Transmit** channel register blocks, stride `0x200`, up to 32 |
| `0x0C000`–`0x0FFFF` | **Receive** channel register blocks, stride `0x200`, up to 32 |
| `0x10000`–`0x13FFF` | Transmit FIFO ports (three arrays of 4-byte ports) |
| `0x14000`–`0x17FFF` | Receive FIFO ports (three arrays of 4-byte ports) |
| `0x18000`–`0x33FFF` | Not accessed by any observed access pattern — **[Unknown]** |

The `0x18000 + n × 0x40` region of the baseline is **no longer mapped**. **[Probable]**

**Change from the baseline:** per-channel blocks are no longer interleaved. Baseline placed
a channel pair at `0x8000 + pair × 0x400`; from the M4 generation transmit channel *n* is
at `0x8000 + n × 0x200` and receive channel *n* at `0xC000 + n × 0x200`. **[Confirmed]** —
the explicit per-channel `reg` entries in the t8140 and M5 platform descriptions place
transmit index 2 at aperture +`0x8400` and receive index 2 at +`0xC400`, and the three
region bases `0x8000`, `0xC000`, `0x10000` are the ones in use from the M4 generation on,
none of which exists on M1–M3.

The display-audio controller type has a `0x24000` aperture. Which region is absent is
**[Unknown]**.

### 4.3.2 Global register block

| Offset | Name | Access | Reset | Fields | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `0x0000` | `TX_EN_SET` | RW | **[Unknown]** | bit *n* per transmit channel, 13 bits | Start transmit channel *n*. Programmed read-modify-write with a `0x1FFF` mask from the M4 generation. **[Confirmed]** |
| `0x0004` | `TX_EN_CLR` | RW | **[Unknown]** | bit *n* | Stop transmit channel *n*. **[Confirmed]** |
| `0x0008` | `RX_EN_SET` | RW | **[Unknown]** | bit *n* | Start receive channel *n*. **[Confirmed]** |
| `0x000C` | `RX_EN_CLR` | RW | **[Unknown]** | bit *n* | Stop receive channel *n*. **[Confirmed]** |
| `0x0010` | `GLB_CTL` | RW | Unknown | bits 4, 5, 6 | Cleared (masked with `0xFFFFFF8F`) once during bring-up on every generation. Meaning **[Unknown]**. **[Probable]** |
| `0x0028` | `GLB_UNK_28` | RW | Unknown | — | Written `0x0020_0000` on the M1 Pro/Max, M2 Pro/Max and M3 Pro/Max dies only. **Not written on any in-scope SoC.** **[Probable]** |
| `0x002C` | `GLB_UNK_2C` | RW | Unknown | — | as above |
| `0x0030 + 4i` | `TX_INT_STATE[i]` | RO | **[Unknown]** | bit *n* per transmit channel | Which transmit channels assert output *i*. Unchanged from baseline. **[Confirmed]** |
| `0x0040 + 4i` | `RX_INT_STATE[i]` | RO | **[Unknown]** | bit *n* | Unchanged. **[Confirmed]** |
| `0x0050 + 4i` | `GLOBAL_INT_STATE[i]` | W1C | **[Unknown]** | Unknown | Controller-level (non-channel) interrupt status for output *i*; all four written all-ones during set-up. **[Confirmed]** |
| `0x0060 + 4i` | `GLOBAL_INT_ENABLE[i]` | RW | **[Unknown]** | Unknown | **New from the M4 generation.** A second four-entry per-destination array; the entry selected by `irq-destination-index` is written all-ones at the end of interrupt set-up. **[Confirmed]** |
| `0x0070` | `TIMEBASE_LO` | RO | — | counter[31:0] | Local free-running counter, low half. **[Confirmed]** |
| `0x0074` | `TIMEBASE_HI` | RO | — | `[21:0]` counter[53:32]; `[31]` VALID | **The counter is 54 bits wide**; bit 31 is a validity flag that must read 1 before the counter is used. **[Confirmed]** |
| `0x0080` | `REVISION` | RO | fixed | `[23:0]` revision | Controller revision, read once at bring-up and masked to 24 bits. **The register that distinguishes the generations.** **[Confirmed]** |
| `0x0090` | `IMPRINT` | RO | fixed | Unknown | Identification word named by the mainline baseline; **not read by any in-scope access pattern**. **[Probable]** |
| `0x0094` | `TX_BUF_SIZE` | RO | fixed | bytes | Transmit-side channel buffer memory size. Present per the baseline; **in scope the size is taken from `channel-buffer-allocation` in firmware instead**. **[Probable]** |
| `0x0098` | `RX_BUF_SIZE` | RO | fixed | bytes | as above |
| `0x0100` | `TX_STREAM_CLASS` | RW | Unknown | bit *n*, 13 bits (`0x1FFF`) | **New from the M4 generation.** Per-transmit-channel stream-class bitmap selecting bulk (memory-to-memory) versus isochronous behaviour. **[Probable]** |
| `0x0104` | `RX_STREAM_CLASS` | RW | Unknown | bit *n*, 13 bits | **New from the M4 generation.** **[Probable]** |

The counter's clock frequency is **[Unknown]**; the controller derives an integer *clock
scaler* (≥ 1) by comparing it against the always-on global timebase of §4.1.3, which
implies a fixed integer ratio rather than an assumed rate. **[Probable]**

### 4.3.3 Per-channel register block (stride `0x200`)

Transmit and receive blocks have the **same internal layout**; direction-specific fields
(AXI read versus write attributes, almost-full versus almost-empty threshold) simply follow
the block. **[Confirmed]**

> **Naming.** Register and bit names for the interrupt block, the FIFO status registers and
> the bus-error capture registers follow **one** coined scheme throughout this document —
> the one set out in §5 §5.2.4/§5.2.5, which is where the per-bit acknowledgement rules and
> the mainline anchors are. The names used there are used here; the only exception is
> `+0xA4`, whose name is the one coined in this section (§4.3.3) and adopted by §5. Nothing
> below reintroduces a second name for a register named there.

| Offset | Name | Access | Reset | Fields | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `+0x00` | `CHAN_CTL_STATUS` | RW | **[Unknown]** | `[0]` RESET | Set bit 0 then clear it to reset the channel's FIFOs. **[Confirmed]** for bit 0 (the published `REG_CHAN_CTL` ring-reset bit). Every other bit of this register is **[Unknown]**, including whether it carries a DMA-engine-idle status bit at all: no position is established for one, and no public source names one. See §4.10.1 and Open question 24. |
| `+0x04` | `CHAN_ENABLE` | RW | Unknown | `[1]` DMA engine enable, `[2]` peripheral-controller enable, `[29:16]` 14-bit value | Programmed immediately before every transfer; the 14-bit field is written `0x29B` (667) in one configuration and left clear in another. **New relative to the baseline.** Field meaning of `[29:16]` **[Unknown]**. **[Probable]** |
| `+0x10 + 4i` | `CHAN_INT_STATUS[i]` | W1C | **[Unknown]** | §4.3.5 | Per-destination interrupt status; cleared by writing all-ones. **[Confirmed]** |
| `+0x20 + 4i` | `CHAN_INT_MASK[i]` | RW | **[Unknown]** | same layout | Per-destination interrupt enable. **[Confirmed]** |
| `+0x30` | `CHAN_CFG` | RW | Unknown | `[3:0]` 4-bit field; `0x2` is the only value observed in service and it reads back; `[9:8]` 2-bit timestamp-capture-mode field | **New relative to the baseline.** See §4.8.4 for the competing identifications of the 4-bit field. Further fields belong to this register's map but are not yet placed at a bit position: an audio-channel-rate field, a pseudo-memory-access enable, a transfer-counter automatic-reset enable, and a **descriptor-FIFO repeat** enable. **[Probable]** |
| `+0x34` | `BUS_ERROR_INFO0` | RW | **[Unknown]** | Unknown | AXI master error status; read on an error interrupt, written all-ones to clear, and written all-ones during channel reset. **[Probable]** |
| `+0x38` | `BUS_ERROR_INFO1` | RW | **[Unknown]** | Unknown | Companion capture register; read on an error interrupt and written 0 to clear. **[Probable]** |
| `+0x40` | `CHAN_BUS_WIDTH` | RW | Unknown | `[3:0]` word size 0 = 8-bit, 1 = 16-bit, 2 = 32-bit; `[7:4]` frame size 0 = 1 word, 1 = 2 words, 2 = 4 words | Baseline register. Only word-size values 0–2 are used in scope; bits [3:2] are reserved. **[Probable]** The same register carries a peripheral transfer-request-mode field on receive channels. **[Confirmed]** |
| `+0x50` | `CHAN_BUF_CFG` | RW | **[Unknown]** | `[31:16]` size, `[15:0]` base | The channel's slice of the controller's on-chip buffer memory. Both fields are written **in 16-byte units placed at the top of their field** — equivalently, byte values whose low four bits are always zero. Bit positions unchanged from the baseline. **[Confirmed]** |
| `+0x54` | `CHAN_XFER_THRESH` | RW | Unknown | `[31:16]` almost-full threshold (transmit) / almost-empty threshold (receive); `[15:0]` transfer threshold | Baseline register. Firmware values per stream in §4.2.3/§4.2.4. Reset value **[Unknown]**; the smallest firmware-supplied value is `0x00C0_0060`. **[Confirmed]** |
| `+0x60` | `CHAN_AXI_OUTSTANDING` | RO | **[Unknown]** | Unknown | Count of outstanding AXI read (transmit) or write (receive) transactions. Sampled on the telemetry interrupt and before each transfer. **[Probable]** |
| `+0x64` | `CHAN_RESIDUE` | RO | **[Unknown]** | bytes | Baseline register — bytes remaining in the descriptor currently executing. **Not read by any in-scope access pattern**, which derives position from the completion FIFO instead. **[Probable]** |
| `+0x70` | `DESC_FIFO_STATUS` | RW | Unknown | `[1:0]` write slot, `[5:4]` read slot, `[8]` EMPTY, `[9]` FULL, `[10]` ERR (W1C) | Descriptor-FIFO status. Bit 9 is tested before every push; bit 8 before every pop; bit 10 is written back to clear and is also written during channel reset. Bits 31:11 and 13:12 **[Unknown]**. **[Confirmed]** |
| `+0x74` | `REPORT_FIFO_STATUS` | RW | Unknown | same layout | Completion-FIFO status. Bit 8 gates every pop. **[Confirmed]** |
| `+0x80` | `DATA_FIFO_STATUS` | RO | Unknown | Unknown | Data-buffer status, reported together with the maximum-latency and outstanding-transaction values. **[Probable]** |
| `+0xA0` | `CHAN_LATENCY_CTL` | RW | **[Unknown]** | `[0]`, `[1]` single-bit controls | **New.** Written 0 on channel reset and read-modify-written before each transfer. Arms the measurement at `+0xA4`. **[Probable]** |
| `+0xA4` | `CHAN_MAX_MEM_READ_LATENCY` | RW | **[Unknown]** | latency in interconnect clock cycles | **New.** A latched maximum memory-access latency; **read then cleared by writing 0**. Cleared before every transfer and sampled on the per-transfer completion interrupt (bit 10, §5 §5.2.4). **[Probable]** — the register lies outside the published baseline aperture, and the identification rests on its pairing with `+0xA0` and on the registers sampled alongside it. The name is provisional; confirm by probe (Open question 18). |
| `+0xB0` | `CHAN_TS_FIFO_STATUS` | RO | Unknown | `[8]` EMPTY; an overrun-error bit; an underrun-error bit | **New.** Timestamp-FIFO status. Bit 8 gates every pop; separate overrun and underrun error bits belong to this register, whose positions are **[Unknown]**. **[Confirmed]** for bit 8. |
| **[Unknown]** — see below | `CHAN_XFER_COUNT` | RW | **[Unknown]** | bytes | A transferred-byte counter, read during operation and written 0 on channel reset. **[Probable]** |
| **[Unknown]** — see below | `CHAN_AXI_SW_ERR_STATUS` | RW | — | 4 bits | A software-visible AXI error status written `0xF` to clear. **[Probable]** |

☠ **The last two rows have no offset and are therefore not programmable as
written.** Both registers are established as existing and their access patterns
are established; **their offsets within the `0x200`-byte per-channel block are
[Unknown]** and are not derivable from anything in this document or from the
published baseline, which describes neither register. Open question 5.

What *is* established is where they are not. The offsets assigned above account
for `+0x00`, `+0x04`, `+0x10`–`+0x1c`, `+0x20`–`+0x2c`, `+0x30`, `+0x34`,
`+0x38`, `+0x40`, `+0x50`, `+0x54`, `+0x60`, `+0x64`, `+0x70`, `+0x74`, `+0x80`,
`+0xa0`, `+0xa4` and `+0xb0`. The two unplaced registers therefore lie somewhere
in the unassigned remainder of the block — `+0x08`, `+0x0c`, `+0x3c`,
`+0x44`–`+0x4c`, `+0x58`–`+0x5c`, `+0x68`–`+0x6c`, `+0x78`–`+0x7c`,
`+0x84`–`+0x9c`, `+0xa8`–`+0xac`, and `+0xb4` upward — which is the search space
the probe in Open question 5 covers. **[Inferred]** from the assignment above;
nothing establishes that either register is inside the block at all rather than
in a global window.

**What a driver must do meanwhile.** Neither register is required to run a
stream. `CHAN_XFER_COUNT` is a second, cheaper source of stream position;
**derive position from the completion FIFO instead** (§4.6.3), which is fully
specified and needs no unplaced register. `CHAN_AXI_SW_ERR_STATUS` is a
diagnostic; **the error is already signalled** by `CHAN_INT_STATUS` and captured
by `BUS_ERROR_INFO0`/`BUS_ERROR_INFO1` at `+0x34`/`+0x38` (§4.10.3), both of
which have offsets. A driver that simply does not touch either register loses no
function. **Do not guess an offset**: a stray write into an unassigned offset of
a live channel block has no defined effect and is not recoverable by anything
short of a channel reset.

**Correspondence with the published names.** Where a register in the two tables above is
also described by the mainline audio DMA controller driver, that driver's published name
is the preferred one and is given here; the coined name is retained in this document only
so that one scheme spans the registers mainline does not describe.

| Offset | Name used here | Published mainline name |
|---|---|---|
| `0x0000` / `0x0004` | `TX_EN_SET` / `TX_EN_CLR` | `REG_TX_START` / `REG_TX_STOP` |
| `0x0008` / `0x000C` | `RX_EN_SET` / `RX_EN_CLR` | `REG_RX_START` / `REG_RX_STOP` |
| `0x0030 + 4i` | `TX_INT_STATE[i]` | `REG_TX_INTSTATE` |
| `0x0040 + 4i` | `RX_INT_STATE[i]` | `REG_RX_INTSTATE` |
| `0x0050 + 4i` | `GLOBAL_INT_STATE[i]` | `REG_GLOBAL_INTSTATE` |
| `0x0090` | `IMPRINT` | `REG_IMPRINT` |
| `0x0094` / `0x0098` | `TX_BUF_SIZE` / `RX_BUF_SIZE` | `REG_TX_SRAM_SIZE` / `REG_RX_SRAM_SIZE` |
| `+0x00` | `CHAN_CTL_STATUS` | `REG_CHAN_CTL` (bit 0 = `REG_CHAN_CTL_RST_RINGS`) |
| `+0x10 + 4i` | `CHAN_INT_STATUS[i]` | `REG_CHAN_INTSTATUS` |
| `+0x20 + 4i` | `CHAN_INT_MASK[i]` | `REG_CHAN_INTMASK` |
| `+0x40` | `CHAN_BUS_WIDTH` | `REG_BUS_WIDTH` (`BUS_WIDTH_WORD_SIZE`, `BUS_WIDTH_FRAME_SIZE`) |
| `+0x50` | `CHAN_BUF_CFG` | `REG_CHAN_SRAM_CARVEOUT` (`CHAN_SRAM_CARVEOUT_SIZE` / `_BASE`) |
| `+0x54` | `CHAN_XFER_THRESH` | `REG_CHAN_FIFOCTL` (`CHAN_FIFOCTL_LIMIT` / `_THRESHOLD`) |
| `+0x64` | `CHAN_RESIDUE` | `REG_RESIDUE` |
| `+0x70` | `DESC_FIFO_STATUS` | `REG_DESC_RING` (`RING_WRITE_SLOT`, `RING_READ_SLOT`, `RING_EMPTY`, `RING_FULL`, `RING_ERR`) |
| `+0x74` | `REPORT_FIFO_STATUS` | `REG_REPORT_RING` (same field names) |
| `0x10000 + 4n` / `0x14000 + 4n` | descriptor push port | `REG_DESC_WRITE` |
| `0x10100 + 4n` / `0x14100 + 4n` | completion pop port | `REG_REPORT_READ` |

Registers with no published counterpart — `GLB_CTL`, `GLB_UNK_28/2C`,
`GLOBAL_INT_ENABLE[i]`, `TIMEBASE_LO/HI`, `REVISION`, `TX_STREAM_CLASS`,
`CHAN_ENABLE`, `CHAN_CFG`, `BUS_ERROR_INFO0/1`, `CHAN_AXI_OUTSTANDING`,
`DATA_FIFO_STATUS`, `CHAN_LATENCY_CTL`, `CHAN_MAX_MEM_READ_LATENCY`,
`CHAN_TS_FIFO_STATUS`, `CHAN_XFER_COUNT`, `CHAN_AXI_SW_ERR_STATUS` and the
timestamp pop port — keep the coined names of this document.

### 4.3.4 FIFO ports

Three arrays of 4-byte ports per direction, addressed by the direction-local channel index:

| Port | Transmit address | Receive address | Access | Words per entry |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Descriptor push | `0x10000 + 4n` | `0x14000 + 4n` | write-only | 4 × 32-bit |
| Completion pop | `0x10100 + 4n` | `0x14100 + 4n` | read-only | 4 × 32-bit |
| **Timestamp pop** | `0x10200 + 4n` | `0x14200 + 4n` | read-only | **2 × 32-bit** |

The first two are the baseline ports at unchanged addresses. The third **first appears on
the M2 generation**, is mapped but unused on the M2 Pro/Max and M3 generations, and is in
service again from the M4 generation. **[Confirmed]** — the port addresses appear verbatim
as the third and fourth sub-apertures of every channel child node on t8140 and the M5
boards, and each channel exposes all three ports independently.

### 4.3.5 Per-channel interrupt status / enable bit layout

Status and enable share one layout. **Ten bits are placed**; the complete layout, the
per-bit acknowledgement rules and the enable-mask constants actually programmed are given
in §5 §5.2.4 and are not repeated here. In summary:

- Bits **0** (`COMPLETION_REPORT_AVAILABLE`) and **6** (`RING_ERR`) are **[Confirmed]** —
  both position and meaning are published in the mainline audio DMA controller driver.
- Bits **1, 5, 8, 9, 10, 12, 16** are **[Confirmed]** as positions the hardware raises and
  that are unmasked in service, with their functional names **[Probable]**.
- Bit **4** is **[Unknown]** (§5 Open question 5).
- Bit **10** is the **per-transfer completion** cause (`TRANSFER_COMPLETE`), enabled per
  channel only while that channel is transferring. The telemetry registers of §4.10.4 are
  read and re-armed while servicing it; that is a property of the servicing sequence, not
  of the bit.

The controller enumerates **eight distinct per-channel exception causes**, each with its
own identifier: **underrun/overrun**, **descriptor/completion-FIFO error**, **data-buffer
full**, **data-buffer empty**, **AXI read/write error**, **completion-FIFO full**,
**excessive jitter**, and an **unknown-interrupt** catch-all. *Excessive jitter*,
*data-buffer full/empty* and *completion-FIFO full* have no counterpart in the published
baseline. The exception set first appears on the M2 generation. Mapping the eight causes
onto bit numbers: of the eight, the ones still unplaced are **excessive jitter** and the
**unknown-cause catch-all**; the remainder correspond to the placed bits of §5 §5.2.4.
**[Confirmed]** for the cause list; **[Probable]** for the cause-to-bit correspondence.

The interrupt-destination index is chosen by `irq-destination-index`. On every in-scope
instance it is **0**, and `irq-destinations` reads `AIC `, `ACPU`, `GTN `, `UNSD` — output 0
to the host interrupt controller, 1 to the always-on coprocessor, 2 to a third agent,
3 unused. On M1–M3 the host output was index 1 (general-I/O instance, destinations
`SCPU`, `AIC `, `UNSD`, `SCLK`) or index 2 (always-on instance, destinations
`ACPU`, `SCPU`, `AIC `, `SCLK`). **A driver must use destination 0, not 1.** **[Confirmed]**

Only one `interrupts` value is given per instance, matching the single valid output.

## 4.4 The evolved controller generation on the M5 SoCs

### 4.4.1 What the platform identifier separates

| Identifier | SoCs | `admac-evolution` |
|---|---|---|
| `admac,t8132`, `admac,t604x` | M4 | absent |
| `admac,t8140` | A18 Pro | **present, = 1** |
| `admac-evolution,t8142`, `admac-evolution,t6050` (+ `admac,t605x`) | M5 audio instances | **present, = 1** |
| `admac,t8142`, `admac,t6050`/`admac,t605x` | M5 **display-audio instances only** | absent |

The "evolution" marker therefore first appears on **t8140**, one generation before the
identifier string changes; and on the M5 SoCs the **display-audio instances are explicitly
the non-evolution type**. **[Confirmed]**

`admac-evolution` is a u32. Value **1** selects the evolved register/ownership contract;
absence of the property selects the legacy one. The two contracts differ at least in how
the controller-level interrupt enables are programmed and in whether the instance may be
driven through an isolated proxy rather than a host IOMMU mapper. **[Confirmed]**

### 4.4.2 What is common to M4, A18 Pro and M5, and what is not

The register map, field set and behaviour of the controller are identical on t8132,
t604x, t8140, t8142 and t605x, and differ from the M3 generation. **[Confirmed]**

Consequently everything in §4.3 marked "new relative to the baseline" — direction-separated
channel blocks, the third FIFO port in service, `CHAN_CFG`, the AXI error and latency
telemetry registers, the 54-bit timebase, the second global per-destination array, the
stream-class bitmaps, the 13-bit channel mask, the 16-byte carveout granularity —
**first appears in the M4 generation, not the M5 generation.**

The firmware-visible deltas that **are** established for the M5 generation:

1. **Independent transmit and receive channel counts.** `#dma-channels-tx` /
   `#dma-channels-rx` replace the single pair count, and are used: the secure base instance
   has 13 transmit and **14** receive channels. A driver assuming symmetry will mis-size
   the receive channel array. **[Confirmed]**
2. **Per-channel capability description in firmware.** Every usable channel is a named
   child node carrying its own four apertures plus slot count, sample width, rate ceiling
   and stream class — replacing the `dma-channels` record of §4.2.3. **[Confirmed]**
3. **`channel-buffer-allocation` collapses from two values to one**, equal to the former
   transmit value. **[Confirmed]**

   | Instance | t8132 / t604x / t8140 (TX, RX) | t8142 / t605x |
   |---|---|---|
   | `admac-base-ns` | 7680 B, 7680 B | 7680 B |
   | `admac-leap-ns` | 3584 B, 4352 B | 3584 B |
   | `admac-leap-s` (t8140) | 768 B, 3776 B | 768 B |
   | Display instance | — | 6400 B |

   `channel-buffer-alloc-base-tx` / `-rx` give the starting byte offset of the instance's
   slice: **256** for `admac-base-ns`, **0** for every other instance, on every generation.
   **[Confirmed]**
4. **The coprocessor-driven contract for the low-power instance steps from revision 4.0
   to revision 4.1.** This is where the real M4 → M5 hardware delta lives. Established
   changes:
   * The per-channel buffer carve-out is allocated per channel rather than as one fixed
     block, and the per-channel buffer base address is programmed explicitly. **[Probable]**
   * `REVISION` (global `0x0080`) reads a different value on the M5 generation than on the
     M4 generation; the values themselves are **[Unknown]** and must be read back.
     **[Probable]**
   * The burst size must be **1, 2 or 4**; no other value is legal. **[Confirmed]**
   * The controller exposes per-channel secure/non-secure assignment and a secure and a
     non-secure channel mask; a buffer may additionally request the **non-secure**
     controller explicitly. **[Probable]** — register locations **[Unknown]**.
5. **The memory-latency escalation block becomes real.** See §4.10.4. **[Confirmed]**
6. **`skip-channels-tx` / `skip-channels-rx` disappear.** **[Confirmed]**
7. **The low-latency-transaction vote moves** from a power-manager pseudo-device to a
   power-manager function call, on t605x only. **[Confirmed]**
8. **No `clock-gates` property at all** on t605x audio DMA nodes. **[Confirmed]**

What did **not** change on the M5 generation: aperture size, region layout, global
start/stop registers, per-channel block stride, FIFO port addresses, descriptor format,
completion format, interrupt destination arrangement. **[Confirmed]**

One further architectural note, relevant to who owns the block: from the **M4
generation** the secure low-power DMA instance is driven by the always-on coprocessor
rather than by the host. This is a change of **ownership and exposure, not of
silicon**. The always-on coprocessor already had its own audio DMA engine and its own
serial audio controller on the M1 generation, each with its own power domains and
address ranges; what changed at M4 is which instances platform firmware gives the host
a path to, and which instance the coprocessor drives on the host's behalf. No audio
DMA hardware was added to the coprocessor at the M4 generation. **[Probable]**

### 4.4.3 The second controller type used for display audio

On t8142 and t605x each display pipe gains its own audio DMA instance. These are **not** the
evolved type:

* `compatible` is the plain `admac,<soc>` form with no `admac-evolution` property.
* The control aperture is **`0x24000`**, `0x10000` smaller than the audio instances'.
* Exactly **one transmit channel, no receive channel**; a `self-actuated` property marks
  the instance as driving itself rather than being driven by a stream endpoint. An instance
  so marked may carry exactly one channel in total. **[Probable]**
* `channel-buffer-allocation` = 6400 B, allocation base 0.
* Its IOMMU parent is the display pipe's own isochronous translation unit, stream 30.
* Its power domain is `DISP_ADMA` / `DISPEXT<n>_ADMA`, parented to the display subsystem.
* It has its own latency-escalation companion node, but with `#ssw-register-count = 4`
  rather than 157 — a four-register snapshot instead of a 157-register one.

On M4 the equivalent display-port audio streams are channels `0x64`, `0x66`, `0x68`, … of
the **general-purpose I/O DMA controller**, FIFO limit 2048 B (t8132) or 1536 B (t604x). On
M5 they become channel 0 of a dedicated instance with FIFO limit 4096 B, threshold 2048 B.
**[Confirmed]**

Which `0x10000` region the display type omits is **[Unknown]**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4.5 Descriptor format

**Unchanged from the baseline** on every in-scope SoC. **[Confirmed]** — the descriptor is
assembled in memory as a 16-byte structure and pushed as **four consecutive 32-bit writes
to the same descriptor-FIFO port address**, in the order word 0, 1, 2, 3.

| Word | Bits | Field | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 31:0 | Buffer address, low 32 bits | IOMMU (device) address |
| 1 | 31:0 | Buffer address, high 32 bits | |
| 2 | 31:0 | Transfer length in bytes | |
| 3 | 7:0 | **Descriptor identifier** | Propagated verbatim into the completion and timestamp entries; allocated modulo 256 |
| 3 | 15:8 | **Attribute byte** | Per-descriptor attributes; meaning **[Unknown]** |
| 3 | 16 | NOTIFY | Raise the descriptor-done interrupt on completion of this descriptor. **[Confirmed]** |
| 3 | 31:17 | Unknown | **[Unknown]** |

Word 3 therefore splits into a low identifier byte and a high attribute byte, with the
remaining bits as tabulated. **[Confirmed]**

There is **no** descriptor chain or ring in memory: descriptors are pushed individually into
a hardware FIFO **four slots deep**. A pusher must test `DESC_FIFO_STATUS` bit 9 (FULL)
before each push and must not push a partial descriptor. **[Confirmed]**

Repeat behaviour is **not** a descriptor flag in scope: the per-channel configuration
register carries a **descriptor-FIFO repeat** enable instead. **[Probable]**

**Minimum transfer length: 16 bytes.** A shorter request is rejected before any descriptor
is built. **[Probable]**

**Maximum transfer length per descriptor: [Unknown].** The length field is a full 32-bit
word; no smaller ceiling was established. The number of descriptors assembled for one
client request is capped at **64**. **[Probable]**

**Required address alignment: [Unknown].** No alignment mask is applied to the buffer
address in any observed path; the 16-byte minimum length and the 16-byte channel-buffer
granularity make 16-byte alignment the conservative assumption. **[Inferred]**

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4.6 Completion FIFO and derivation of position and residue

### 4.6.1 Entry format

A completion entry is **four 32-bit words**, popped by four consecutive reads of the same
completion-port address, only while `REPORT_FIFO_STATUS` bit 8 (EMPTY) is clear.

| Word | Bits | Field |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 31:0 | Timestamp, low 32 bits |
| 1 | 21:0 | Timestamp, bits 53:32 |
| 1 | 31:22 | Unknown |
| 2 | 15:0 | 16-bit count — bytes transferred or remaining for the completed descriptor |
| 2 | 25 | Status flag |
| 2 | 27 | Status flag |
| 2 | 31:24 | Status/error field (bits 25 and 27 are extracted individually) |
| 3 | 7:0 | Descriptor identifier, echoing the descriptor's identifier byte |
| 3 | 31:8 | Unknown |

**[Probable]** — single line of evidence, but internally consistent: the timestamp is
assembled exactly as the global counter is (32 + 22 bits), and the identifier is matched
against the identifier of the descriptor that was submitted. A completion carrying a
non-zero status field is treated as an error completion. **[Confirmed]**

The mainline baseline treats words 2 and 3 as opaque, so this is a refinement rather than a
contradiction.

### 4.6.2 Counter width and wrap

The completion timestamp is **54 bits** in the controller's local timebase — the same
counter that `TIMEBASE_LO`/`TIMEBASE_HI` expose, and `TIMEBASE_HI` bit 31 must read 1
before it is trusted. The clock rate is **[Unknown]**, so the wrap interval is
**[Unknown]**; at any plausible audio-domain rate a 54-bit counter does not wrap within
the life of a boot. **[Confirmed]** for the width.

### 4.6.3 Deriving position and residue

Two methods are available.

**(a) Completion-driven — the method the in-scope controller uses.** Each descriptor's
completion entry carries the descriptor identifier and a 16-bit count. The consumer keeps
the byte position of the descriptor stream, advances it by the length of each descriptor
whose completion has been popped, and uses the 16-bit field of the newest entry as the
sub-descriptor correction. Position is exact at descriptor granularity; the four-deep FIFO
is the only source of latency. A transferred-byte counter also exists in the channel block
(offset **[Unknown]**) and is read during operation. **[Probable]**

**(b) Residue register — the published baseline method. Unchanged, and unused in scope.**
`CHAN_RESIDUE` (`+0x64`) and `REPORT_FIFO_STATUS` (`+0x74`) keep their baseline offsets,
widths and field layouts (§4.3.3), so the baseline's residue-based position calculation —
paired status/residue reads to resolve the descriptor-load race between them, occupied
completion slots from the write/read slot fields and the FULL/EMPTY bits, and the residue
subtracted from the reclaimed position — remains available exactly as published, and is
not restated here. No in-scope access pattern uses it. **[Confirmed]** as a baseline
method.

Whether the FIFO status registers also carry overrun/underrun counters is **[Unknown]**;
bits 31:11 of those registers are unplaced.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4.7 Timestamp FIFO

The third per-channel port delivers hardware timestamps. Entry format — **two 32-bit
words**, popped only while `CHAN_TS_FIFO_STATUS` (`+0xB0`) bit 8 (EMPTY) is clear:

| Word | Bits | Field |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 31:0 | Timestamp, low 32 bits |
| 1 | 21:0 | Timestamp, bits 53:32 |
| 1 | 23 | Flag |
| 1 | 31:24 | Descriptor identifier |

**[Probable]**

The timestamp is in the controller's 54-bit local timebase, the same domain as the
completion timestamp and the global counter. Its purpose is to give the audio pipeline a
hardware capture instant for a descriptor, converted to system time using the scale factor
and offset derived against the always-on global timebase of §4.1.3.

Timestamp capture is a **per-channel capability, enabled per direction by a channel
bitmask** — the controller maintains separate transmit and receive "use timestamps" masks
and reports a transmit and a receive "timestamp engage" word per channel. Two
instance-wide switches can force it on per direction. **[Probable]**

☠ **The MMIO field that carries the per-channel enable is [Unknown], so the
timestamp path is not programmable from this document.** Two candidates are
named — `CHAN_CFG` bits 9:8 (`+0x30`, programmed from a timestamp-capture-mode
selector) and `CHAN_ENABLE` bits 1–2 (`+0x04`) — and nothing distinguishes them.
Open question 10.

**What a driver must do meanwhile.** Do not depend on the timestamp FIFO. Every
function it serves has a specified alternative: stream position and residue come
from the completion FIFO two independent ways (§4.6.3); the completion entry
carries its own timestamp in the same 54-bit local timebase; and the local-to-
system-time relation is derived from the always-on global timebase window
(§4.1.3) without the FIFO. A driver may **read** the FIFO opportunistically —
`CHAN_TS_FIFO_STATUS` bit 8 gates the pop and is **[Confirmed]** — and use
whatever it finds, but must behave correctly when it stays empty, which is what
happens if the enable was never set. It must not block on a timestamp.

The timestamp FIFO has its **own overrun and underrun error bits** in its status register,
distinct from the data-path underrun/overrun cause. Their bit positions are
**[Unknown]** (§4.3.3). **[Probable]**

The controller measures **timestamp jitter** against a threshold, with a configurable
panic-on-excess behaviour and a dedicated *excessive jitter* exception cause, plus
per-direction workaround masks. Both the threshold and the panic mask are per-channel
configuration words. **The unit of the threshold is [Unknown]** — the plausible
candidates are ticks of the controller's own 54-bit local counter and ticks of the
always-on global timebase of §4.1.3, and the two differ by the integer scaler a driver
derives between them, so a threshold written in the wrong one is wrong by that factor.
Until the unit is established a driver must not program this threshold; leaving the
excessive-jitter cause masked is the safe default, and the cause's bit position is in
any case **[Unknown]** (§5 §5.2.4). **[Probable]** for the mechanism, **[Unknown]**
for the unit — Open question 9.

The timestamp path exists in hardware from the **M2** generation, is not used on the M2
Pro/Max and M3 generations, and is used from **M4** onwards. **[Probable]**

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4.8 Transfer parameters

### 4.8.1 Bus width and frame size

`CHAN_BUS_WIDTH` (`+0x40`): bits 3:0 select 8-, 16- or 32-bit words (encodings 0, 1, 2);
bits 7:4 select 1, 2 or 4 words per frame (encodings 0, 1, 2). The frame-size control is
out-of-band signalling to the peripheral of a word's position within a frame.
**[Confirmed]** The same register carries a peripheral transfer-request-mode selector on
receive channels. **[Probable]**

Per-stream sample widths in scope are 16-bit and 32-bit only; no 8-bit stream is declared
on any in-scope board. **[Confirmed]**

### 4.8.2 FIFO thresholds and channel buffer allocation

`CHAN_XFER_THRESH` (`+0x54`): bits 31:16 hold the **almost-full threshold** on a transmit
channel and the **almost-empty threshold** on a receive channel; bits 15:0 the **transfer
threshold**, the occupancy at which a memory transfer is triggered. The controller enforces

```
transmit:  0 < transfer_threshold < almost_full_threshold  ≤ channel_buffer_size
receive:   0 < almost_empty_threshold < transfer_threshold ≤ channel_buffer_size
```

and rejects a configuration that violates it. **[Confirmed]**

Per-stream firmware values range from 192 B / 96 B (loopback) to 1152 B / 576 B (six-slot
speaker playback) on audio instances, and 4096 B / 2048 B on display-audio instances.
**[Confirmed]** Reset value **[Unknown]**.

`CHAN_BUF_CFG` (`+0x50`) allocates the channel's slice of the controller's on-chip buffer
memory: bits 31:16 size, bits 15:0 base, **both in 16-byte units** (equivalently, byte
values with the low four bits zero). The instance's total budget and starting offset come
from `channel-buffer-allocation` and `channel-buffer-alloc-base-tx` / `-rx`. A request that
would run past the budget is rejected, and a later request larger than the one already
granted for that channel is rejected. The 16-bit fields cap the buffer memory at 64 KiB per
direction. **[Confirmed]**

The FIFO depth may also be expressed in **microseconds** rather than bytes — the controller
accepts `max-fifo-depth-us` and `initial-trigger-us` alongside the byte forms and converts
using the stream's rate, slot count and sample width. **[Probable]**

The on-chip memory this register carves up is located for the two **secure** instances
on t8140 and t8142: it lies at each controller's base + `0x4_0000`, outside the
`0x34000` register aperture, and is sized `0x2000 × max(#transmit, #receive)` —
`0x1_2000` for the low-power instance and `0x1_C000` for the base instance. Both
windows are tabulated in §3 §3.4.3 and are fabric-protected (§3 §3.4.5), so a
normal-world driver must treat the secure instances' buffer allocation as unavailable.
Whether the **non-secure** instances have equivalent windows at their own base +
`0x4_0000` is **[Unknown]** — see Open question 25.

### 4.8.3 Burst size and DMA address width

A per-channel **AXI burst-size** field exists in the channel's AXI control register; an
`axi-burst-size-bytes` property and an instance-wide override switch feed it. The only
stated constraint is a legality check on the **M5** generation admitting the values
**1, 2 and 4**; no such check exists on the M4 generation, so the assertion is established
for M5 and not for the controller generally.

**The unit is [Unknown] and the property name is misleading.** `axi-burst-size-bytes`
implies a byte count, but a burst *length* of 1, 2 or 4 bytes is not a usable AXI
quantity. The set is consistent with AXI `AxSIZE` — bytes **per beat**, i.e. 8-, 16- or
32-bit beats, matching exactly the three word sizes `CHAN_BUS_WIDTH` (`+0x40`) supports —
**[Inferred]**; it is equally consistent with a beat count or with an opaque three-value
selector. The field's offset and encoding are **[Unknown]**. **[Probable]** for the legal
value set itself: one line of evidence, M5 only. See Open question 17.

**DMA address width: 64 bits** — the descriptor carries a full 64-bit address in two words,
and the transfer path handles 64-bit segment addresses. Whether the IOMMU restricts the
usable range further is a property of the translation unit. **[Confirmed]**

Descriptor physical-contiguity is checked before submission, so a scatter/gather list
becomes one descriptor per contiguous segment. **[Probable]**

### 4.8.4 Bus-attribute / cache-attribute control

There is a per-channel, per-direction **AXI cache attribute**: an `ARCACHE` field in a
transmit channel block and an `AWCACHE` field in a receive channel block, whose **required
value is `0x2`** — AXI `AxCACHE` encoding `0b0010` = *Normal, Non-cacheable, Modifiable,
Non-bufferable* (bit 0 bufferable, bit 1 modifiable/cacheable, bit 2 read-allocate, bit 3
write-allocate). The value is **checked by read-back after programming**, so the hardware is
expected to return what was written and a mismatch is treated as a fault. **[Confirmed]**

The only per-channel register masked to four bits, set to `0x2` and then compared against
`0x2` before a transfer is **`CHAN_CFG` at `+0x30`**. Two identifications of that 4-bit
field are therefore in play — the AXI cache attribute, and an audio-channel rate selector
named in the controller's register map but not yet placed at an offset. **[Probable]** The
bit operations are **[Confirmed]**; which name belongs to `+0x30[3:0]` is **[Unknown]** and
is Open question 4.

**This ambiguity does not block a driver, and here is why.** Only one value,
`0x2`, has been observed in the field on any in-scope machine, in every
configuration, and the hardware is expected to read it back unchanged. A driver
that writes `0x2` is correct under **both** identifications: it is the required
cache attribute under the first, and it is the value every in-scope stream uses
under the second. **Write `0x2` and do not attempt to vary it.** The reason to
settle the question is that under the second identification the field would have
to change for a stream at a rate other than 48 kHz — which no in-scope speaker,
loopback or low-power link uses, but which the jack link does at 44.1, 88.2 and
96 kHz (§2 §2.5.1). **[Inferred]** A driver offering those jack rates should
treat a 44.1 kHz or 96 kHz jack stream as the case that tests this, and should
verify the field reads back `0x2` after configuring one.

**Four further fields belong to this register's map and have no bit position.**
An audio-channel-rate field, a pseudo-memory-access enable, a transfer-counter
automatic-reset enable and a descriptor-FIFO repeat enable are named in the
register map and are all **[Unknown]** as to position (§4.3.3, Open questions 4
and 16). A driver must therefore **preserve every bit of `CHAN_CFG` it does not
own**: read the register, clear bits 3:0 and 9:8 only, OR in its own values, and
write back. Writing the register as a whole word from a constant would clear
whatever those four fields hold.

The read-modify-write sequence is: mask off bits 3:0, OR in `0x2`, store; then insert a
2-bit field at bits 9:8 taken from a timestamp-capture-mode selector. **[Confirmed]**

If the cache attribute is indeed *non-cacheable and non-bufferable*, audio DMA buffers are
**not** coherent with CPU caches by hardware snooping, and a host driver must map them
non-cacheable or perform explicit maintenance. **[Inferred]**

A per-channel AXI control register also belongs to the controller's register map, carrying
the maximum burst size; whether it is `+0x30` or a further, unplaced offset is
**[Unknown]**. **[Probable]**

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4.9 IOMMU

### 4.9.1 Which translation unit serves which instance

All four audio DMA instances are served by the **always-on translation unit**
(`/arm-io/dart-aop`, `compatible = "dart,t8110"`) through four dedicated mapper nodes, with
**identical stream indices on every in-scope SoC**: **[Confirmed]**

| Mapper node | Stream index | Serves | `allow-subpage-mapping` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mapper-admac-base-ns` | **8** | `admac-base-ns` | yes |
| `mapper-admac-base-s` | **9** | `admac-base-s` (no device node) | no |
| `mapper-admac-leap-ns` | **10** | `admac-leap-ns` | yes |
| `mapper-admac-leap-s` | **11** | `admac-leap-s` | no |

Streams 0 and 1 of the same unit belong to the always-on coprocessor and its isolated
counterpart; stream 3 to a further client; streams 16/17 to the second always-on
coprocessor instance present on t8140 and the M5 generation. **[Confirmed]**

The **display-audio instances** are served by the corresponding display pipe's
*isochronous* translation unit (`dart-disp0-isoc`, `dart-dispext0-isoc`, …) at **stream
index 30**, with `allow-subpage-mapping`. **[Confirmed]**

`admac-leap-s` carries an **empty** `iommu-parent` property on t8140 and the M5 generation —
the host is given no mapper for the secure instance directly (§4.9.3). **[Confirmed]**

The always-on translation unit's `dart-options` value changes from `0x25` on M1–M4 to
`0x65` on t8140 and the M5 generation. **[Confirmed]** — the bit meanings belong to the
IOMMU section, but a driver must program the unit correctly before any audio DMA is safe.

### 4.9.2 How a driver establishes mappings

A host driver binds to the mapper node named by its instance's `iommu-parent` phandle, maps
its audio buffers into that stream, invalidates the stream, and writes the resulting device
addresses into descriptor words 0 and 1. The mapper index above is the stream identifier,
and the controller reads it back from the mapper to tag its own accesses. **[Confirmed]**

Non-secure audio streams are allocated `allow-subpage-mapping`, so their buffers need not
be page-aligned; secure streams are not. **[Confirmed]**

### 4.9.3 The shared-mapper arrangement for isolated buffers

On t8140, t8142 and t605x a separate node `/arm-io/audio-shared-dart-proxy` expresses how
the **secure** streams are shared between use cases. It has no `reg`; instead:

* `iommu-parent` — a list of **two** mapper phandles. On t605x these resolve to
  `mapper-admac-base-s` (stream 9) and `mapper-admac-leap-s` (stream 11).
* `usecase-dart-map` — an array of (four-character use-case code, index into that list):

| SoC | Map entries |
|---|---|
| t8140, t8142 | `hpai` → 1, `adpx` → 0 |
| t605x | `adpx` → 0, `hpai` → 1, `sllb` → 1 |

So on t605x the built-in-microphone-array capture use case (`hpai`) and the secure loopback
use case (`sllb`) **share one translation stream** (the secure low-power one), while the
low-power-microphone buffer use case (`adpx`) has the secure base stream to itself.
**[Confirmed]**

The node is marked `exclave-assigned` and names an isolated-world service; the host does not
own these mappings, it requests them, and the request path supports *set up use case*,
*suspend* and *resume* operations. A host driver that wants the built-in microphone array
must go through this path rather than mapping the secure instance itself. **[Probable]**

The `admac-ec-proxy` nodes of §4.1.5 each carry `function-iommu_handler` referencing this
node with tag `sdpr`, confirming that the proxy channels' mappings are made by the shared
proxy. **[Confirmed]**

## 4.10 Reset and error recovery

### 4.10.1 Channel reset sequence

1. Stop the channel: set bit `1 << n` in `TX_EN_CLR` (`0x0004`) or `RX_EN_CLR` (`0x000C`),
   read-modify-write with the 13-bit channel mask. **[Confirmed]**
2. Drain pending descriptors and wait for the channel to quiesce. **The idle indication
   itself is [Unknown]** — see "Quiescing a channel" below; do not assume a polled idle
   bit in `CHAN_CTL_STATUS`.
3. Assert `CHAN_CTL_STATUS` bit 0 (RESET), then deassert it. **[Confirmed]**
4. Clear latched error state: write the ERR bit (bit 10) into `DESC_FIFO_STATUS` and
   `REPORT_FIFO_STATUS`; write all-ones into `BUS_ERROR_INFO0`; write 0 into
   `BUS_ERROR_INFO1`, `CHAN_LATENCY_CTL`, `CHAN_MAX_MEM_READ_LATENCY` and the
   transferred-byte counter; write `0xF` into the software AXI error status. **[Probable]**
5. Re-arm interrupts: write all-ones to `CHAN_INT_STATUS[i]` to clear, then the desired
   cause mask to `CHAN_INT_MASK[i]`. **[Confirmed]**

**Quiescing a channel — the idle indication is [Unknown].** A drain deadline of
**5000 ms** is associated with this step, after which the channel is declared unusable and
the failure reported as a timeout distinct from other errors. **[Probable]** — this is a
*drain* deadline, not a hardware reset settling time, which remains **[Unknown]**.

What is **[Unknown]** is what the drain polls. This document does not establish a
DMA-engine-idle status bit: no bit position is given anywhere for one, and no public source
names one in `CHAN_CTL_STATUS` (§4.3.3, and §5 §5.2.6, which states the negative). The two
readings cannot both be right and neither is supported, so the position adopted throughout
this document is the **[Unknown]**.

Until it is settled, quiesce a channel this way instead:

1. Clear the channel's enable bit (`TX_EN_CLR` / `RX_EN_CLR`) and do not push further
   descriptors.
2. Poll `CHAN_AXI_OUTSTANDING` (`+0x60`) until it reads **0** — no outstanding AXI read
   (transmit) or write (receive) transaction remains — and check that the completion FIFO
   has stopped advancing (`REPORT_FIFO_STATUS` `+0x74`, read slot stable and EMPTY set).
   **[Inferred]** — both registers are established (§4.3.3) and both are direct evidence
   of in-flight work; neither is a documented quiesce handshake.
3. Bound the wait. A **bounded timeout is mandatory**, because step 2 is not a documented
   handshake: on expiry, proceed to the reset of step 3 regardless. The reset itself clears
   the FIFOs, so a channel that never reports quiet is recovered by resetting it, not by
   waiting longer.

The outer deadline of 5000 ms above is a fault deadline, not a latency target: a channel
carrying a normal audio period quiesces within one descriptor period.

See Open question 24.

### 4.10.2 What survives a reset, what must be reprogrammed

Resetting the channel clears the descriptor, completion and timestamp FIFOs and their slot
pointers. The following are re-programmed on every transfer set-up and must be treated as
not surviving: `CHAN_BUS_WIDTH` (`+0x40`), `CHAN_BUF_CFG` (`+0x50`), `CHAN_XFER_THRESH`
(`+0x54`), `CHAN_CFG` (`+0x30`), `CHAN_ENABLE` (`+0x04`), `CHAN_LATENCY_CTL` (`+0xA0`) and
`CHAN_MAX_MEM_READ_LATENCY` (`+0xA4`, cleared). Interrupt enables are re-programmed after a
resume. **[Probable]**

The channel buffer carveout is instance-global bookkeeping and should be kept stable across
resets: a re-allocation larger than the one already granted is rejected. **[Confirmed]**

### 4.10.3 Underrun and overrun

Underrun (transmit starvation) and overrun (receive overflow) are reported as a **single
combined exception cause**. A FIFO error sets the ERR bit (bit 10) of the offending FIFO
status register, cleared by writing that bit back; the controller reports the descriptor and
completion FIFO status words together on that path. If neither FIFO reports ERR and an error
interrupt is nonetheless asserted, the only safe recovery is to mask the error cause for
that channel. **[Probable]**

Separate causes exist for **data-buffer empty**, **data-buffer full** and **completion-FIFO
full**, distinct from underrun/overrun; the data-buffer status register is `+0x80` and the
controller reports the buffer's configuration and its base/size alongside it on that path.
A completion-FIFO-full condition is additionally tracked as a duration, so the hardware
tolerates it transiently. **[Probable]**

An AXI read or write error is its own cause, reported with `BUS_ERROR_INFO0` and
`BUS_ERROR_INFO1` plus both FIFO status words. **[Probable]**

### 4.10.4 Excessive-latency detection and escalation

Two related mechanisms exist.

**(a) Per-channel latency telemetry.** `CHAN_MAX_MEM_READ_LATENCY` (`+0xA4`) latches the
maximum memory-access latency observed on the channel, in interconnect clock cycles, and is
cleared by writing 0. It is cleared before each transfer and sampled on the per-transfer
completion interrupt (bit 10, §5 §5.2.4) together with `DATA_FIFO_STATUS`
(`+0x80`) and `CHAN_AXI_OUTSTANDING` (`+0x60`). `CHAN_LATENCY_CTL` (`+0xA0`) bits 0 and 1
arm it. Present from the M4 generation. **[Probable]** — the identification of `+0xA4`
and its name are provisional (§4.3.3, Open question 18).

**(b) A separate escalation-detector block.** Firmware describes it as a peer device with
`device_type = "ced-ssw"` and `compatible = "admacled,<soc>"`, carrying:

* **two `0x4000` apertures** — a control/tunable window and a snapshot window;
* its own interrupt;
* an `identity` string (at most 16 characters) naming the group it covers;
* `dma-controllers`, listing the four-character roles of the controllers it watches, with
  `#dma-controllers` and parallel `#dma-channels-tx` / `#dma-channels-rx` arrays;
* **`#ssw-register-count`** — the number of registers captured in a snapshot: **157** for
  the audio group, **4** for each display group;
* `ced-tunables` and `ssw-tunables`, one blob per aperture.

Audio DMA nodes point at it with a `ced-ssw-service` property; only the M5-generation audio
nodes have one. **[Confirmed]**

**Tunable blob format.** Each blob is an array of **24-byte entries**:
`{ u32 register offset; u32 size (must be 4); u64 mask; u64 value }`. The block applies
`mask & value` to `aperture_base + offset` for each entry. Index 0 of the two apertures is
the detector, index 1 the snapshot window. **[Probable]**

**Behaviour.** The block watches the audio DMA channels' memory-access latency and, when a
channel is at risk, **escalates the memory system into a critical low-latency-transaction
mode**. The vote is expressed through the power manager: on t8132, t604x, t8140 and t8142
through a pseudo-device named `AUDIO-LLT-V`; on t605x through the
`function-vote_crit_llt_mode` platform function (tag `VCLM`, two zero arguments). Failure to
raise or drop the vote is reported as a distinct error. **[Probable]**

**Configuration surface and defaults**, from the block's tunable set: **[Probable]**

| Control | Default | Overridable |
|---|---|---|
| Rack configuration enabled | off | yes |
| Detector enabled | on | yes (a disable switch) |
| Mode | **panic** (the alternative is telemetry-only) | yes |
| Absolute latency-tolerance override | **`0x7F` (127)** | yes |
| Escalation-duration override | **`0x7F` (127)** | yes |
| Trigger-threshold override | **`0x1C20` (7200)** | no — fixed |
| Panic when clients are active at the deepest power state | off | yes |

☠ **Units for the latency tolerance, the escalation duration and the trigger
threshold are [Unknown]**, and the three raw defaults above are therefore not
usable as a starting configuration on their own. No in-scope board supplies
`ced-tunables`, so there is no platform-supplied default to copy either. The
plausible candidates are interconnect clock cycles (the unit
`CHAN_MAX_MEM_READ_LATENCY` at `+0xa4` uses), ticks of the controller's 54-bit
local counter, and ticks of the always-on global timebase — which differ from
one another by the integer scalers of Open question 9. Open question 3 in §13,
and §13 §13.5.6.

**What a driver must do meanwhile.** The escalation detector is **optional**:
it is a stub on t8132, t604x and t8140, where audio runs without it at all, and
on t8142 and t605x it improves behaviour under memory-bandwidth load rather than
enabling anything (§13 open question 6). **Leave it disabled** until the units
are established. Writing a wrong value is worse than leaving it off in both
directions: too large a threshold never escalates, and too small a one escalates
permanently, holding the memory system in its critical low-latency mode for as
long as audio runs — which is a system-wide effect, not an audio one. **Do not
write the three raw defaults as if they were dimensionless.**

On escalation the block **captures its snapshot registers** into a **ring of 8 snapshot
records** (each a 16-byte header plus `#ssw-register-count` 32-bit register values, with an
acknowledge word the consumer writes 1 into). In the panicking configuration it emits the
group identity, the snapshot-window name, the list of active transmit and receive channels
(four of each) and the captured register data. **[Probable]**

**Which SoCs have a real implementation.** **[Confirmed]**

| SoC | Escalation nodes in firmware | Implementation |
|---|---|---|
| t8132 (M4) | none | **stub — registers a service and does nothing else** |
| t604x (M4 Pro/Max) | none | **stub** |
| t8140 (A18 Pro) | none | **stub** |
| t8142 (M5) | audio + one per display | **real** |
| t605x (M5 Pro/Max) | audio + one per display | **real** |

On t8132, t604x and t8140 the escalation block is declared but inoperative — no
thresholds, no timers and no configuration properties exist for it; only on t8142 and
t605x is it functional. **[Probable]** So the mechanism is *architecturally present* from M4 (the per-channel latency telemetry registers
exist and are used on all in-scope parts) but the *escalation block* is only instantiated on
the M5 generation. A driver on t8132/t604x/t8140 has the telemetry but no escalation peer
and no `ced-ssw-service` property to bind to. **[Confirmed]**

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4.11 Secure versus non-secure instances

At the hardware level the four instances are **four physically separate controllers**, each
with its own `0x34000` aperture, its own interrupt, its own power domain
(`AUDIO_BASE_S_A` / `AUDIO_BASE_NS_A` / `AUDIO_LEAP_S_A` / `AUDIO_LEAP_NS_A`) and its own
IOMMU stream (9 / 8 / 11 / 10). "Secure" and "non-secure" denote **ownership and isolation
domain**, not a mode bit inside one controller. **[Confirmed]**

In addition, the audio fabric carries **secure channel-map registers** — one mapping serial
audio cluster streams to DMA channels and one mapping low-power-processor streams to DMA
channels — together with per-channel *make secure* / *make non-secure* operations and
readable secure and non-secure channel masks. A channel may not appear in both masks. So
individual channels can be moved between the secure and non-secure domains at run time by
the owning agent, and the host cannot do this itself. **[Probable]**

What a host driver can and cannot do:

* **`admac-base-ns` and `admac-leap-ns`** — fully host-owned. The host maps their apertures,
  owns streams 8 and 10, and drives them directly. **[Confirmed]**
* **`admac-base-s`** — **no device node on any in-scope board**. Its stream (9) exists and is
  referenced by the shared-mapper node, and its channel counts are declared by the M5
  escalation node, but the host is given no aperture. Not host-drivable. **[Confirmed]**
* **`admac-leap-s`** — has a node and an aperture on t8140 and the M5 generation, but an
  **empty `iommu-parent`**: the host may reach the registers but cannot make its own
  translations. Its used channels carry a `service-exclave_proxy` property naming a proxy
  node, and the proxy claims a *second* aperture of the same instance at a different
  physical address. Buffers for those channels are mapped by the isolated world through the
  shared-mapper node of §4.9.3. **[Confirmed]**
* A single instance may **not** have both a host IOMMU mapper and an isolated proxy.
  **[Probable]**

Which streams use which instance, in scope:

| Stream | Instance | SoCs |
|---|---|---|
| Speaker playback + amplifier sense capture | `admac-base-ns` | t8132, t604x, t8142, t605x |
| Speaker playback | `admac-leap-ns` | **t8140 only** |
| Speaker tap (monitor capture) | `admac-base-ns` | t8140, t8142, t605x |
| Headset playback and **headset-microphone capture** (jack codec) | `admac-base-ns` — transmit index 2 and **receive index 2**, on every board without exception | all |
| Serial-audio loopback | `admac-base-ns` | all |
| Low-power-microphone injection | `admac-base-ns` | t8140, t8142, t605x |
| Low-power-processor internal loopback | `admac-leap-ns` | all |
| **Built-in digital microphone array capture** (the endpoint misleadingly named `audio-hp` / `audio-hp-mic`) | `admac-leap-ns` on t8132/t604x; **`admac-leap-s`** on t8140, t8142, t605x | — |
| **Secure low-power loopback capture** | `admac-leap-s` (development-only) | t605x only |

The migration of **built-in digital microphone array** capture from the non-secure to the
**secure** low-power instance at the A18 Pro / M5 boundary is the most consequential
ownership change for a host driver: on t8132 and t604x that capture path is directly
host-drivable (low-power non-secure receive index 0), and from t8140 onward it is not.
**[Confirmed]**

**Headset-microphone capture is unaffected.** It is bound to `base-ns-adma-rx-2` — the base
**non-secure** instance — on every in-scope board without exception, and remains fully
host-drivable on all five SoCs. The endpoint that carries "hp-mic" in its node name is the
built-in array, not the headset microphone; see note ² in §4.2.4. **[Confirmed]** — verified
across j604, j713, j614s, j700, j704, j813 and j714s.

Per-machine:

* **j604 / j715** (MacBook Pro 14 M4, MacBook Air 15 M4) — speaker playback and sense
  capture, FIFO 1152 B / 576 B.
* **j713** (MacBook Air 13 M4) — same topology, FIFO 768 B / 384 B.
* **j623 / j624** (iMac 24 M4) — speaker playback only, no sense capture, FIFO 768 B / 384 B.
* **j773g** (Mac mini M4) — speaker playback only, FIFO 192 B / 96 B; **no built-in

* **j614s / j614c / j616s / j616c** (MacBook Pro 14/16 M4 Pro/Max) — as j604.
* **j773s** (Mac mini M4 Pro) and **j575c** (Mac Studio 2025) — speaker playback only,
  FIFO 192 B / 96 B, **no low-power-instance endpoints at all**.
* **j700** (MacBook Neo, t8140) — unique: speaker playback on the **low-power** instance
  (`leap-ns-adma-tx-0`, 2 slots, 32-bit, 48 kHz); no base-instance channel pair 0; speaker
  tap on `base-ns-adma-rx-1`; built-in microphone array (two internal inputs) on the
  **secure** low-power instance; headset-microphone capture on `base-ns-adma-rx-2` through a
  different jack codec part from the rest of the scope.
* **j704 / j815** (MacBook Pro 14 M5, MacBook Air 15 M5) — 6-slot speaker playback, 12-slot
  sense capture.
* **j813** (MacBook Air 13 M5) — **4-slot speaker playback, 8-slot sense capture**; every
  other channel identical to j704.
* **j714s / j714c / j716s / j716c** (MacBook Pro 14/16 M5 Pro/Max) — as j704, plus the
