## Open questions

1. **What occupies `0x18000`–`0x33FFF` of the aperture, and why is the display-audio variant
   `0x24000`?** 112 KiB of the aperture is never touched by any observed access pattern; the
   baseline generations mapped a region at `0x18000 + n × 0x40` there and never dereferenced
   it, and the M4 generation stopped mapping even that. *Why it matters:* a driver must know
   whether this region holds the channel buffer memory (which would let it inspect FIFO
   contents) or further register banks. *Probe:* map the full aperture under a hypervisor
   with the audio power domain on and read the whole range in 4-byte steps, logging
   non-zero and non-aliasing responses; repeat with a channel running to see whether any
   window tracks FIFO occupancy; compare against the buffer sizes at global `0x0094`/`0x0098`.

2. **Confirm the direction-separated channel block layout by probing.** *Why it matters:*
   every per-channel access depends on it, and a wrong base silently writes another
   channel's control register. *Probe:* with all channels stopped, write a recognisable
   pattern to `CHAN_XFER_THRESH` at `0x8000 + n × 0x200` and at `0xC000 + n × 0x200` for
   several *n*, then start one transmit channel and see which copy the hardware honours by
   observing the transfer trigger point. **Narrowed.** All five per-channel addresses
   protected by the fabric inbound filter on t8140 and t8142 decode to valid, in-range
   channels **only** under the direction-separated layout; under the interleaved
   numbering of the M1–M3 baseline three of the five name channels that do not exist on
   those instances (§3 §3.4.5). The probe remains worth doing but is now confirmatory.

3. **The eight exception causes' bit positions in `CHAN_INT_STATUS`.** Ten bits are placed
   (§5 §5.2.4); what remains unplaced is the **excessive-jitter** cause and the meaning of
   **bit 4**. *Why it matters:* a driver cannot distinguish an underrun from a bus error
   without them, and an unhandled cause that is enabled will live-lock a level-triggered
   line. *Probe:* enable all 32 bits in
   `CHAN_INT_MASK[0]`, provoke each condition individually (starve a transmit FIFO;
   overflow a receive FIFO; point a descriptor at an unmapped IOMMU address; stop popping
   completions until the completion FIFO fills; assert a reset while running) and record
   which bit sets.

4. **Is `CHAN_CFG[3:0]` the AXI cache attribute or an audio-channel-rate selector?** The
   field is four bits wide, carries `0x2` in service, and reads back what is written; the
   controller's register map defines both an AXI cache attribute that must equal `0x2`
   and an audio-channel-rate field. *Why it matters:* if it is the cache attribute, buffer
   coherency and the required value follow from it; if it is a rate selector, the cache
   attribute lives at an offset a driver has not yet found and would be left at reset.
   *Probe:* write each value 0–15 with a channel stopped and read back which stick; then run
   a stream at two different sample rates and see whether the field must change. Separately,
   dump the whole channel block while varying only the requested sample rate.

5. **Offsets of the transferred-byte counter, the software AXI error status, and the AXI
   maximum-burst-size field.** All three belong to the controller's register map but are
   not yet placed at an offset. *Why it matters:* the byte counter is a second, cheaper source
   of stream position, and burst size affects memory-system behaviour under load.
   *Probe:* diff a full channel-block dump taken before and after a known number of bytes
   has transferred (isolates the counter); diff before and after provoking a bus fault
   (isolates the software error status); diff after changing the burst-size property.

6. **Maximum single-descriptor transfer length and required buffer alignment.** *Why it
   matters:* a driver must know when to split a period into multiple descriptors. *Probe:*
   binary-search the length field with a single descriptor against a known-good buffer,
   checking the completion entry's 16-bit count and the FIFO ERR bit; then walk the buffer
   address across every offset in a 64-byte window and find the smallest alignment that
   completes without error.

7. **Global `0x0010` bits 4–6, `0x0060 + 4i`, `0x0100`/`0x0104`, and the `REVISION` value per
   SoC.** *Why it matters:* `0x0060 + 4i` is most likely the controller-level interrupt
   enable, which a driver must set for global error reporting to work; the stream-class
   bitmaps decide whether a channel behaves isochronously or as memory-to-memory; and the
   revision word is what distinguishes the M4 and M5 generations. *Probe:* read `0x0080` on
   each of t8132, t604x, t8140, t8142 and t605x and tabulate — the value must differ at the
   M4/M5 boundary. Then set and clear bits of `0x0060 + 4i` and `0x0010` and observe which
   global conditions reach the host.

8. **When does the audio DMA aperture become readable, and what must the host do to make
   it so — which is *not* raising a power domain.** The power-domain side of this is
   settled and is **not** an open question: the domain names, indices, parents and flag
   bytes are established, the control-register address rule is established and reproduces
   mainline Linux's published per-domain offsets for 1266 of 1266 baseline domains
   (§2 §2.6.1), and **every audio domain on every in-scope SoC carries the flag that marks
   it as having no host-drivable power-state register** (§2 §2.6.2, §14). The host therefore
   **cannot** raise the audio island; the always-on coprocessor owns device power for the
   whole audio complex. Two things do remain open for this section. *(a)* Whether the audio
   DMA aperture faults, reads as zero, or reads back normally while the coprocessor has the
   relevant domain down, and therefore whether a host driver may touch the controller
   before the coprocessor has opened the stream at all. *(b)* On t604x and t605x the device
   list states **no** control-register address for any audio domain, and on t8140 and t8142
   the addresses come from the group-form decode, which has no mainline ground truth
   (§2 §2.6.1; §3 Open question 25 owns the validation). *Why it matters:* it fixes where in
   the bring-up order the host's first controller access may legally sit, and it removes
   any temptation to write a power register that is not the host's to write. *Probe:* read
   `REVISION` (global `0x0080`) on each instance with no audio stream open and again with
   one open, on each SoC, and record whether the first read faults, returns zero, or
   returns the same value as the second.

9. **The clock frequency of the controller's 54-bit local counter, the integer ratio to
   the always-on global timebase, and which of the two the jitter threshold of §4.7 is
   expressed in.** *Why it matters:* every timestamp reported to userspace depends on the
   conversion, and a jitter threshold written in the wrong one of the two units is wrong
   by exactly that ratio — silently, because the excessive-jitter cause would then simply
   fire at the wrong rate rather than fail. *Probe:* read both counters alternately over
   several seconds and fit the ratio; check that it is an exact integer. Then program the
   jitter threshold to a value that is unambiguous under only one of the two readings
   (a value whose interpretation in the other unit lies outside the observable jitter
   range entirely) and observe whether the excessive-jitter cause fires.

10. **Is the timestamp FIFO enabled by default, and what enables it?** *Why it matters:* if
    it fills and is never drained the controller raises an error. *Probe:* run a channel
    with `CHAN_CFG` bits 9:8 and `CHAN_ENABLE` bits 1–2 each clear and set, and observe
    whether `CHAN_TS_FIFO_STATUS` bit 8 ever clears; correlate popped timestamps against the
    global counter sampled at known instants. Also find the FIFO's own overrun and underrun
    bit positions by deliberately not draining it.

11. **The completion FIFO status registers' upper bits (31:11, 13:12).** The baseline places
    only slots, empty, full and error. *Why it matters:* if bits 31:16 are an
    overrun/underrun counter, a driver gets free error accounting; if not, it must count in
    software. *Probe:* provoke a controlled number of underruns and read the register before
    and after; then set `CHAN_CTL_STATUS` bit 1 and see whether the field zeroes.

12. **The escalation block's register map, the units of its latency-tolerance, escalation
    duration and trigger threshold, and the content of its 157-register snapshot.** *Why it
    matters:* on M5 machines a driver that leaves this block unconfigured may see the memory
    system fail to escalate, producing underruns at high memory load. *Probe:* dump both
    `0x4000` windows before and after provoking a high-latency condition (heavy memory load
    plus a low-threshold audio stream), diff them, and correlate the changed words against
    per-channel `CHAN_MAX_MEM_READ_LATENCY` values. The tunable blobs in firmware name the
    exact offsets the block expects to be written, so parsing `ced-tunables` and
    `ssw-tunables` on a live machine gives the register list directly.

13. **What is the third interrupt destination (`GTN `)?** *Why it matters:* to be sure a host
    driver's use of destination 0 cannot be pre-empted. *Probe:* enable a cause in
    `CHAN_INT_MASK[2]` and observe whether anything acknowledges it.

14. **The `0x21` / `0x22` stream-class codes and which is isochronous and which is bulk.**
    *Why it matters:* it decides which of the two FIFO-threshold profiles a driver should
    adopt on M4 machines, and whether memory-to-memory operation is available on a channel.
    *Probe:* set and clear the corresponding bit in the global stream-class bitmaps at
    `0x0100`/`0x0104` for one channel and observe whether the channel still honours a
    peripheral transfer request or instead runs free as a memory-to-memory copy.

15. **Whether the display-audio instances are usable by a host driver at all.** They are
    marked `self-actuated` and have no stream endpoint. *Why it matters:* display-port audio
    output on M5 machines depends on them. *Probe:* bring up one instance's single transmit
    channel with the display power domain on and a buffer mapped in stream 30 of the display
    isochronous translation unit, and see whether descriptors complete.

16. **Is the descriptor-FIFO repeat control per-channel (in `CHAN_CFG`) rather than
    per-descriptor, and is it cleanly revocable?** *Why it matters:* a cyclic audio stream is
    the normal case, and a repeat mode that cannot be cleared without a power-domain reset
    would force a different driver design. *Probe:* enable the repeat control, submit a
    single descriptor, confirm it repeats, then clear the control and confirm the channel
    stops after the current descriptor.

17. **What unit the AXI burst-size field is in.** The legality check admits 1, 2 and 4
    (M5 firmware only), which is not a usable byte count; the set is equally consistent
    with AXI `AxSIZE` (bytes per beat), with a beat count, and with an opaque three-value
    selector. **[Unknown]** (§4.8.3). *Why it matters:* it decides how the field must be
    derived from a stream's word size, and it affects memory-system behaviour under load.
    *Probe:* program 1, 2 and 4 in turn on a transmit channel and observe the AXI beat
    width and burst length on the memory interface; cross-check against `CHAN_BUS_WIDTH`
    word size.

18. **What `+0xA4` actually is.** The access pattern is established — cleared before each
    transfer, read and re-cleared while servicing bit 10 alongside `DATA_FIFO_STATUS`
    (`+0x80`) and `CHAN_AXI_OUTSTANDING` (`+0x60`) — but the published baseline aperture
    stops at `+0x74`, so no public source names it. The maximum-memory-read-latency
    identification is **[Probable]** and the name is provisional (§4.3.3). *Why it
    matters:* if it is instead a completion counter or a captured position, a driver
    could use it as a cheap stream-position source; if it is a latency measurement it is
    diagnostic only. *Probe:* run a channel under controlled memory contention and see
    whether the value tracks induced latency (in interconnect clock cycles) or the bytes
    transferred since the last clear.

19. **Reset values of the per-channel and global registers — every one of them.** No
    reset value in §4.3.2 or §4.3.3 is established. The registers whose reset value is
    **[Unknown]** are: `TX_EN_SET`/`TX_EN_CLR` (`0x0000`/`0x0004`),
    `RX_EN_SET`/`RX_EN_CLR` (`0x0008`/`0x000C`), `GLB_CTL` (`0x0010`),
    `GLB_UNK_28`/`GLB_UNK_2C`, `TX_INT_STATE[i]` (`0x0030 + 4i`), `RX_INT_STATE[i]`
    (`0x0040 + 4i`), `GLOBAL_INT_STATE[i]` (`0x0050 + 4i`), `GLOBAL_INT_ENABLE[i]`
    (`0x0060 + 4i`), `TX_STREAM_CLASS`/`RX_STREAM_CLASS` (`0x0100`/`0x0104`),
    `CHAN_CTL_STATUS` (`+0x00`), `CHAN_ENABLE` (`+0x04`), `CHAN_INT_STATUS[i]`
    (`+0x10 + 4i`), `CHAN_INT_MASK[i]` (`+0x20 + 4i`), `CHAN_CFG` (`+0x30`),
    `BUS_ERROR_INFO0`/`BUS_ERROR_INFO1` (`+0x34`/`+0x38`), `CHAN_BUS_WIDTH` (`+0x40`),
    `CHAN_BUF_CFG` (`+0x50`), `CHAN_XFER_THRESH` (`+0x54`), `CHAN_AXI_OUTSTANDING`
    (`+0x60`), `CHAN_RESIDUE` (`+0x64`), `DESC_FIFO_STATUS` (`+0x70`),
    `REPORT_FIFO_STATUS` (`+0x74`), `DATA_FIFO_STATUS` (`+0x80`), `CHAN_LATENCY_CTL`
    (`+0xA0`), `CHAN_MAX_MEM_READ_LATENCY` (`+0xA4`), `CHAN_TS_FIFO_STATUS` (`+0xB0`),
    `CHAN_XFER_COUNT`, and the channel-buffer allocation registers of §4.8.2.
    *Why it matters:* a driver that assumes zero where the hardware resets non-zero will
    leave a field set that it never wrote, and a driver that assumes zero where it is
    entitled to expect hardware to have initialised the field will skip a step it must
    perform. The concrete hazard is `CHAN_BUF_CFG` (`+0x50`), the per-channel staging
    buffer configuration register: a driver that treats its reset value as zero will
    conclude that no on-chip buffer is allocated to the channel, or conversely that a
    zero-size allocation is the reset state it can leave alone, and **skip the
    staging-memory allocation entirely** — the channel then runs with no buffer carve-out
    and underruns immediately. The buffer-allocation and stream-class registers are
    instance-global, so a stale value there affects other channels as well. *Probe:* with
    the audio power domain just brought up and before any write, dump the global block and
    one channel block of each direction on each SoC and tabulate; repeat after a channel
    reset (`CHAN_CTL_STATUS` bit 0) to separate power-on reset from channel reset. Until
    that is done, a driver must write every field it depends on rather than relying on any
    reset state.

20. **The descriptor attribute byte and the reserved fields of the descriptor and
    completion entries.** Descriptor word 3 bits 15:8 (attribute byte) and bits 31:17,
    and completion-entry word 1 bits 31:22 and word 3 bits 31:8, are **[Unknown]**
    (§4.5, §4.6.1). *Why it matters:* the attribute byte is the most likely home of
    per-descriptor cache or priority attributes, and an unknown reserved field cannot be
    safely written as zero if the hardware expects otherwise. *Probe:* submit descriptors
    with each bit of the attribute byte set in turn against a known buffer and watch for a
    change in bus attributes or completion status; and read back completion entries for
    descriptors of known length, identifier and error state to see which reserved bits
    ever become non-zero.

21. **Contents of the bus-error capture registers `BUS_ERROR_INFO0` (`+0x34`) and
    `BUS_ERROR_INFO1` (`+0x38`).** Both are read on an error interrupt and cleared, but
    their layouts are **[Unknown]** on every generation, in this section and in §5
    §5.2.4. *Why it matters:* they are the only per-channel diagnostic for a bus fault,
    and without a layout a driver can only report "an error occurred". *Probe:* point a
    descriptor at an unmapped IOMMU address, then at a read-only mapping, then at an
    address that faults mid-burst, and diff both registers after each; repeat on a
    receive channel to separate read from write reporting.

22. **The channel reset settling time.** The drain deadline is established, but the time
    the hardware needs after `CHAN_CTL_STATUS` bit 0 is set and cleared before the channel
    may be reprogrammed is **[Unknown]** (§4.10.1). *Why it matters:* a driver that
    reprograms too early may write registers the reset is still clearing, which shows up
    as a rare, load-dependent failure to start. *Probe:* assert and release the reset and
    poll the idle-status bit and the FIFO status registers, recording the worst-case delay
    over many iterations and across the M4, A18 Pro and M5 controllers.

23. **The meaning of the extra flags bit in the audio power-domain entries.** On t8132 six
    audio domains carry flags byte `0x30` where every other in-scope SoC carries `0x10`
    for the same domains, and the display-audio domains carry `0x00`. The meaning of the
    extra bit is **[Unknown]** (§4.1.4). *Why it matters:* the `0x10` bit already means
    "no host-drivable power control", so a second bit set only on the base M4 die may
    indicate a different control path or an additional constraint on bring-up order.
    *Probe:* compare the same domains' behaviour on t8132 and t8142 when the coprocessor
    brings the audio island up, and correlate the bit against which domains have a stated
    control-register address.

24. **Does `CHAN_CTL_STATUS` (`+0x00`) carry a DMA-engine-idle status bit, and at which
    position?** (§4.3.3, §4.10.1; §5 §5.2.6 states that no polled idle bit exists.) The
    question is unresolved in both directions and no bit position is established.
    *Why it matters:* teardown ordering depends on knowing the channel is quiet before the
    coprocessor removes the clock that drains the serialiser (Section 15 §15.4). Without an
    idle indication a driver must fall back on the outstanding-transaction and completion-FIFO
    evidence above plus a bounded timeout, which is weaker and slower. *Probe:* with a channel
    running a long descriptor, read `+0x00` repeatedly and compare the word against the same
    read taken with the channel stopped and drained, on each SoC; any bit that is set in
    exactly one of the two conditions, and that tracks `CHAN_AXI_OUTSTANDING` reaching zero,
    is the candidate. Repeat on both directions and on a `leap-*` instance to confirm the
    position is not instance-specific.

25. **Do the non-secure instances have on-chip channel-buffer memory windows at their
    own base + `0x4_0000`, and how large are they?** The two **secure** instances' windows
    are located and sized (§4.8.2, §3 §3.4.3, §3 §3.4.5); the equivalent windows for
    `admac-base-ns` (`0x…_3840_0000`) and `admac-leap-ns` (`0x…_3340_0000`) are
    **[Unknown]** in both existence and size, because no protected-range entry names
    them. *Why it matters:* a host driver programming `CHAN_BUF_CFG` on a non-secure
    instance is allocating out of a pool whose total size it currently cannot read, and
    the carve-out bookkeeping of §4.8.2 — where a request past the budget is rejected —
    depends on knowing it. *Probe:* read `TX_BUF_SIZE` / `RX_BUF_SIZE` (global `0x0094`
    and `0x0098`) on each non-secure instance and compare against
    `0x2000 × max(#transmit, #receive)`; then read the window itself at base + `0x4_0000`
    and see whether it responds and whether its contents track a running channel's FIFO.


---

# 5. Interrupts

## Baseline

Measured against the M1–M3 audio subsystem as documented in section 0 of the public
baseline (serial audio controller §A.4, audio DMA controller §B.9/§B.10, device-tree
interrupt conventions §E.2) and, for the codec and amplifier interrupt pins, against
the public counterpart parts (TAS2764/TAS2770 `IRQZ`, CS42L42/CS42L83 `INT`) as
documented in section 0 of the baseline codec document (§A.10, §B.10).

The relevant baseline facts are: the audio DMA controller has **four independent
interrupt outputs**, every per-channel status/mask register is replicated once per
output, and platform firmware names the four destinations and selects one with
`irq-destination-index` (1 for the host-side instance, 2 for the always-on-side
instance on every M1–M3 SoC). The serial audio controller exposes **one interrupt per
cluster** to the application-processor interrupt controller, which no public driver
services. Codec and amplifier interrupt pins are active-low, level-sensitive, and are
routed to the application-processor GPIO controller, with all amplifiers sharing one
line.

## Summary of differences

| Topic | t8132 (M4) | t604x (M4 Pro/Max) | t8140 (A18 Pro) | t8142 (M5) | t605x / t6050 (M5 Pro/Max) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Serial audio controller cluster interrupts (host-visible) | **absent** | **absent** | **absent** | **absent** | **absent** |
| Numerically controlled oscillator interrupt | absent (node absent) | absent (node absent) | absent (node has no `reg`, no `interrupts`) | absent (node absent) | absent (node absent) |
| Audio DMA controller: number of interrupt outputs per instance | unchanged (4) | unchanged (4) | unchanged (4) | unchanged (4) | unchanged (4) |
| Audio DMA controller: destination index selected for the host | **changed** 1 → **0** | **changed** 1 → **0** | **changed** → **0** | **changed** → **0** | **changed** → **0** |
| Audio DMA controller: destination name list | **changed** | **changed** | **changed** | **changed** | **changed** |
| Audio DMA controller instances described / host lines reserved | **changed** 2 → 2 described, 4 reserved | 2 described, 4 reserved | 3 described, 4 reserved | 3 described, 4 reserved | 3 described, 3 contiguous reserved |
| Per-channel interrupt status/mask offsets and bit meanings | offsets unchanged; bit meanings newly established, see body | offsets unchanged; bit meanings newly established, see body | offsets unchanged; bit meanings newly established, see body | offsets unchanged; bit meanings newly established, see body | offsets unchanged; bit meanings newly established, see body |
| Per-channel status bit 12 (timestamp-report source) | **new** | **new** | **new** | **new** | **new** |
| Channel-summary register bit → channel mapping | **changed** (direction-local) | **changed** | **changed** | **changed** | **changed** |
| Display-audio DMA interrupts | unchanged (coprocessor-owned, no host line) | unchanged | unchanged | **new** — 3 host-visible instances | **new** — 5 host-visible instances |
| Audio DMA latency-escalation detector interrupt | absent | absent | absent | **new** (4 lines) | **new** (6 lines) |
| Coprocessor mailbox interrupt lines described | 4 | **8** | 4 + 2 + 4 + 2 | 4 + 2 + 4 | 4 + 2 + 4 |
| Second always-on coprocessor instance | absent | absent | **new** | **new** | **new** |
| Amplifier interrupt pin | unchanged (shared, active-low) | unchanged | **absent** (amplifier has no control bus) | unchanged | unchanged |
| Jack-codec interrupt pin | unchanged (active-low, own pin) | unchanged | unchanged (different codec part) | unchanged | unchanged |
| Audio wake sources | **changed** (+1 trusted mailbox) | **changed** (two numbered outboxes) | **changed** (two coprocessors × 2 mailboxes) | **changed** | **changed** |
| Any audio interrupt shared with a non-audio block | no | no | no | no | no |

## 5.1 Interrupt-specifier conventions in the platform description

Three distinct interrupt parents appear on the audio path. A driver must decode the
`interrupts` property according to which one `interrupt-parent` names.

| Parent | Cells per interrupt | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `/arm-io/aic` (application-processor interrupt controller) | 1 | Interrupt number. Trigger is fixed level-high. **[Confirmed]** — every audio node on every board carries exactly one word per line, and the equivalent in-tree description for the baseline generations declares `IRQ_TYPE_LEVEL_HIGH`. |
| A GPIO controller (`gpio0`, `aop-gpio`/`aop-gpio0`, `nub-gpio`/`nub-gpio0`, `smc-gpio`) | 2 | `<pin, trigger>`; see below. |
| A serial-power-management-interface controller (`aop-spmi0`, `aop-spmi1`) | 1 | Not on the audio path on any in-scope board. |

### GPIO interrupt specifier, second word (trigger type)

| Value | Trigger | Where it appears on in-scope boards |
|---|---|---|
| `0x00000001` | **level, active low** | every audio amplifier and jack-codec node, every in-scope and baseline board |
| `0x00000002` | level, active high | non-audio (wireless) |
| `0x00000003` | edge, both | non-audio (touch) |
| `0x05000004`, `0x06000002`, `0x06000004`, … | variants with a non-zero upper byte | non-audio; the upper byte is **[Unknown]** and never non-zero on an audio node |

**[Confirmed]** that `1` means active-low level for the audio nodes: the same board
files that carry `1` for the amplifier and jack-codec pins correspond, on the M1–M3
generations, to in-tree descriptions that declare `IRQ_TYPE_LEVEL_LOW` for exactly
those devices, and the public counterpart parts drive their interrupt pins active-low
open-drain. The upper-byte variants are **[Unknown]**; they do not occur on audio.

A GPIO controller exposes **seven interrupt groups** to the application-processor
interrupt controller (`#gpio-int-groups = 7`, seven entries in its own `interrupts`
list). Which group a given pin is steered into is a per-pin hardware configuration and
is not expressed in the platform description. This is unchanged from M1–M3.
**[Confirmed]**

### Coprocessor mailbox interrupt specifier ordering

A mailbox node's `interrupts` list is **not** in ascending numeric order. For a
four-entry list beginning at base line *n* the order is:

| Position | Line | Function |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | `n+1` | outbound (host → coprocessor) queue **not empty** |
| 1 | `n+0` | outbound queue **empty** |
| 2 | `n+3` | inbound (coprocessor → host) queue **not empty** |
| 3 | `n+2` | inbound queue **empty** |

**[Confirmed]** — the ordering is fixed on every board from M1 to M5, and on
the baseline generations the same four lines appear in the in-tree description in
ascending order with the names *outbound-empty, outbound-not-empty, inbound-empty,
inbound-not-empty*, which pins the mapping exactly. The line a host driver actually
needs for message reception is position **2** of the list. Unchanged from M1–M3.

## 5.2 Audio DMA controller interrupts

### 5.2.1 Instances and host interrupt lines

Two controller variants exist in scope. Platform firmware distinguishes them by
`compatible`:

| `compatible` family | Aperture size | Channel blocks | Instances |
|---|---|---|---|
| `admac,<soc>` (t8132, t604x) / `admac-evolution,<soc>` (t8140, t8142, t6050) | `0x34000` | separate transmit and receive arrays | `admac-base-ns`, `admac-base-s`, `admac-leap-ns`, `admac-leap-s` |
| `admac,<soc>` (t8142, t6050 only) | `0x24000` | one transmit channel | `admac-disp0`, `admac-dispext0…N` |

Host-visible lines, byte-exact from the platform description. All are on the
application-processor interrupt controller, all one line per instance, all with
`irq-destination-index = 0`.

Aperture bases below are **absolute**, i.e. the platform description's
I/O-region-relative `reg` value plus the `/arm-io` `ranges` parent base. That base is
**not uniform**: `0x2_0000_0000` on t8132, t604x and t605x, and `0x2_1000_0000` on
t8140 and t8142. A figure taken straight from `reg` is 8 GiB or 8.25 GiB below the
hardware. **[Confirmed]** — the parent base is the second cell of the `/arm-io`
`ranges` triple, whose child base is zero, on every board in scope.

| SoC | Node | Aperture base | Host line | Channels (tx/rx) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| t8132 | `admac-base-ns` | `0x3_9380_0000` | **475** | 13 / 13 (index 12 marked skipped) |
| t8132 | `admac-leap-ns` | `0x3_9330_0000` | **478** | 9 / 9 |
| t8132 | *(`admac-base-s`)* | **[Unknown]** | **476** *(inferred)* | **[Unknown]** |
| t8132 | *(`admac-leap-s`)* | **[Unknown]** | **477** *(inferred)* | **[Unknown]** |
| t604x | `admac-base-ns` | `0x5_1380_0000` | **754** | 13 / 13 (index 12 skipped) |
| t604x | `admac-leap-ns` | `0x5_1330_0000` | **757** | 9 / 9 |
| t604x | *(`admac-base-s`)* | **[Unknown]** | **755** *(inferred)* | **[Unknown]** |
| t604x | *(`admac-leap-s`)* | **[Unknown]** | **756** *(inferred)* | **[Unknown]** |
| t8140 | `admac-base-ns` | `0x3_1380_0000` | **449** | 13 / 13 |
| t8140 | *(`admac-base-s`)* | **[Unknown]** | **450** *(inferred)* | **[Unknown]** |
| t8140 | `admac-leap-s` | `0x3_1320_0000` | **451** | 9 / 9 |
| t8140 | `admac-leap-ns` | `0x3_1330_0000` | **452** | 9 / 9 |
| t8142 | `admac-base-ns` | `0x3_9380_0000` | **549** | 13 / 13 |
| t8142 | *(`admac-base-s`)* | **[Unknown]** | **550** *(inferred)* | 13 / 14 |
| t8142 | `admac-leap-s` | `0x3_9320_0000` | **551** | 9 / 9 |
| t8142 | `admac-leap-ns` | `0x3_9330_0000` | **552** | 9 / 9 |
| t605x / t6050 | `admac-base-ns` | `0x2_9380_0000` | **637** | 13 / 13 |
| t605x / t6050 | `admac-leap-s` | `0x2_9320_0000` | **638** | 9 / 9 |
| t605x / t6050 | `admac-leap-ns` | `0x2_9330_0000` | **639** | 9 / 9 |
| t605x / t6050 | *(`admac-base-s`)* | **[Unknown]** | **[Unknown]** — no adjacent gap | 13 / 14 |

Notes:

- The numbers are **per SoC, not per board**: every board of a given SoC carries
  identical values. **[Confirmed]** on every in-scope board.
- **Four instances exist in silicon on every SoC in scope**, whether or not they are
  described as nodes. The power-manager device list of every in-scope board enumerates
  exactly four per-instance register-access power domains — `AUDIO_BASE_NS_A`,
  `AUDIO_BASE_S_A`, `AUDIO_LEAP_NS_A`, `AUDIO_LEAP_S_A` — and the always-on IOMMU of
  every in-scope board carries exactly four matching mapper nodes
  (`mapper-admac-base-ns`, `-base-s`, `-leap-ns`, `-leap-s`). Neither name appears on
  any M1–M3 board. **[Confirmed]** — two independent structures in the same
  platform-supplied description.
- On t8132, t604x, t8140 and t8142 the described instances leave **gaps** in an
  otherwise contiguous run of four interrupt lines, and the gaps fall exactly where the
  secure-domain instances would sit in the order *base non-secure, base secure, leap
  secure, leap non-secure*. **[Inferred]** that four consecutive lines are reserved for
  the four instances, one each; the secure instances simply have no node. On t605x the
  three described instances are contiguous with no gap, so the secure base instance's
  line is **[Unknown]** there.
- The transmit/receive channel counts of the two secure instances on t8142 and t605x
  are given by the `#dma-channels-tx` / `#dma-channels-rx` arrays of the
  latency-escalation detector node (§5.2.7), which enumerates all four instances.
  **[Confirmed]** for those two SoCs; **[Unknown]** for t8132/t604x/t8140.
- On t8132 and t604x each direction declares `skip-channels-tx = 12`,
  `#skip-channels-tx = 1` and the receive equivalents: of the 13 channels per
  direction, index 12 is reserved and not available to the host. On t8140/t8142/t605x
  no skip list is present. **[Confirmed]** **[platform description]**
- The baseline `channels-offset` convention (40 for the host-side instance, 0 for the
  always-on-side instance) is gone: every in-scope instance declares
  `channels-offset = 0`, and channel numbering is per-instance and per-direction.
  **[Confirmed]**

### 5.2.2 The four interrupt outputs (destinations)

Unchanged in count and in mechanism: the controller has four interrupt outputs, and
`TX_INT_STATE`, `RX_INT_STATE`, `GLOBAL_INT_STATE`, `GLOBAL_INT_ENABLE`,
`CHAN_INT_STATUS` and `CHAN_INT_MASK` are each replicated four times, once per output.
A driver must read `irq-destination-index` and use **only** that output's register
copy throughout. **[Confirmed]** — the platform description carries a four-entry
`irq-destinations` list plus `irq-destination-index` on every instance, and the
in-silicon bound is four (index values are range-checked against 4).

What **changed** is the destination list and which index the host gets:

| Index | M1–M3 host-side instance | M1–M3 always-on-side instance | **All in-scope SoCs, all instances** |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | a coprocessor | a coprocessor | **application-processor interrupt controller** ← selected |
| 1 | **application-processor interrupt controller** ← selected | a coprocessor | always-on coprocessor |
| 2 | unused | **application-processor interrupt controller** ← selected | a third on-chip agent; the platform tag reads `GTN ` — **[Unknown]**, most plausibly the clock/power-gating manager, which occupied the analogous slot (tag `SCLK`) on M1–M3 **[Inferred]** |
| 3 | a clock/power-manager consumer | a clock/power-manager consumer | explicitly marked unused (tag `UNSD`) |

The list is **byte-identical on every in-scope SoC and every instance**, including the
display-audio instances. **[Confirmed]**

Practical consequence, and the single most likely source of a silent failure: on
M1–M3 a driver had to use register copy **1** (host-side) or **2** (always-on-side);
on every SoC in scope it must use copy **0**. Code that hard-codes the baseline index
will arm and poll a register set that the wired output never asserts, and will see no
interrupts at all.

### 5.2.3 Global (controller-level) interrupt registers

Offsets from the aperture base; *i* is the interrupt-destination index.

| Offset | Name | Access | Reset | Fields | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `0x0030 + 4i` | `TX_INT_STATE[i]` | R | **[Unknown]** | bit *n* = **transmit channel *n*** | Summary: which transmit channels currently assert output *i*. Read-only summary of the per-channel status registers; not itself acknowledgeable. **[Confirmed]** |
| `0x0040 + 4i` | `RX_INT_STATE[i]` | R | **[Unknown]** | bit *n* = **receive channel *n*** | Same for receive. **[Confirmed]** |
| `0x0050 + 4i` | `GLOBAL_INT_STATE[i]` | **R/W1C** | **[Unknown]** | **[Unknown]** bit meanings | Non-channel interrupt causes. Cleared by writing all-ones. **[Confirmed]** — cleared with `0xFFFFFFFF` for all four copies during controller bring-up on every in-scope SoC, exactly as on M1–M3. |
| `0x0060 + 4i` | `GLOBAL_INT_ENABLE[i]` | R/W | **[Unknown]** | same layout as `GLOBAL_INT_STATE` | **Not defined by any public driver.** Written `0xFFFFFFFF` once per destination after per-channel enables are programmed, i.e. "enable every global cause". Present and written identically on the M1–M3 controllers as well, so this is a **gap in the public record, not a delta**. **[Probable]** that it is the mask for `GLOBAL_INT_STATE` — the pairing of offset, width, replication factor and programming order is exact; no read-back is available. |

**Delta — summary-register bit mapping.** On M1–M3 channel numbering was global and
interleaved: `TX_INT_STATE` bit *k* meant channel `2k` and `RX_INT_STATE` bit *k*
meant channel `2k+1`. On every in-scope SoC the two directions are numbered
independently and **bit *n* of `TX_INT_STATE` is transmit channel *n***, bit *n* of
`RX_INT_STATE` is receive channel *n*. For the `base-*` instances the meaningful width
is 13 bits (`0x00001FFF`); for the `leap-*` instances 9 bits. **[Confirmed]** — the
summary word is masked to thirteen bits on t8132, t604x, t8140, t8142 and t6050
alike, matching the declared `#dma-channels-tx`/`#dma-channels-rx` of the base
instances exactly.

**Delta — per-channel register block addressing.** Following from the same change:

| | M1–M3 | In scope |
|---|---|---|
| Transmit channel *n* block | `0x8000 + (2n) × 0x200` | `0x8000 + n × 0x200` |
| Receive channel *n* block | `0x8000 + (2n+1) × 0x200` | `0xC000 + n × 0x200` |

**[Confirmed]** for t8140, t8142 and t605x — the platform description enumerates each
stream's channel block as an explicit aperture (for example a base-domain non-secure
transmit channel 2 at aperture base `+0x8400`, receive channel 1 at `+0xC200`).
**[Probable]** for t8132 and t604x, which do not enumerate per-channel apertures but
use the same controller family and the same separate transmit/receive block structure.

The descriptor and report FIFO port addresses are **unchanged**, with one addition:

| Port | Address | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Transmit descriptor write, channel *n* | `0x10000 + 4n` | unchanged |
| Transmit completion-report read, channel *n* | `0x10100 + 4n` | unchanged |
| **Transmit timestamp-report read, channel *n*** | `0x10200 + 4n` | **new** |
| Receive descriptor write, channel *n* | `0x14000 + 4n` | unchanged |
| Receive completion-report read, channel *n* | `0x14100 + 4n` | unchanged |
| **Receive timestamp-report read, channel *n*** | `0x14200 + 4n` | **new** |

**[Confirmed]** — each stream node's `reg` carries exactly four apertures: the
`0x200`-byte channel block and three 4-byte FIFO ports at these offsets.

### 5.2.4 Per-channel interrupt status and mask

| Offset (from channel block) | Name | Access | Reset | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `+0x10 + 4i` | `CHAN_INT_STATUS[i]` | **R/W1C** | **[Unknown]** | Per-channel, per-destination interrupt status. |
| `+0x20 + 4i` | `CHAN_INT_MASK[i]` | R/W | **[Unknown]** | Per-channel, per-destination enable. A cause is delivered to output *i* only if the corresponding bit is set here. |
| `+0x34` | `BUS_ERROR_INFO0` | R | — | Captured on a bus error (bit 16). Contents **[Unknown]**. Present on M1–M3 as well. |
| `+0x38` | `BUS_ERROR_INFO1` | R | — | Second bus-error capture word. Contents **[Unknown]**. |
| `+0x80` | `DATA_FIFO_STATUS` | R | — | Captured on the data-buffer empty/full causes (bits 8, 9). Contents **[Unknown]**. |
| `+0xA4` | `CHAN_MAX_MEM_READ_LATENCY` | R/W (write-zero to clear) | **[Unknown]** | Latched maximum memory-access latency in interconnect clock cycles (§4 §4.3.3). Read, then written with zero, on the completion/telemetry path. Name and contents **[Probable]** — the published baseline aperture stops at `+0x74`, so no public source names it. |

Offsets `+0x10`/`+0x20` and the replication factor of four are **unchanged from
M1–M3**. **[Confirmed]**

#### Bit layout of `CHAN_INT_STATUS[i]` / `CHAN_INT_MASK[i]`

| Bit | Name (functional) | Meaning | Acknowledgement | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | `COMPLETION_REPORT_AVAILABLE` | A completion report is waiting in the channel's completion-status FIFO. Raised only for descriptors whose notify flag was set. | write 1 to this bit | unchanged (baseline `DESC_DONE`) |
| 1 | `DATA_FIFO_UNDERRUN_OVERRUN` | Channel data buffer underran (transmit) or overran (receive). | write 1 to this bit | unchanged in position; **name newly established** — mainline Linux does not name this bit |
| 4 | **[Unknown]** | **[Unknown]**. The bit exists but is not unmasked in service on any in-scope or baseline part, and is not described by any public driver. | presumed write 1, **[Unknown]** | see Open question 5 |
| 5 | `REPORT_FIFO_FULL` | Completion-status FIFO is full. | write 1 to this bit | unchanged |
| 6 | `RING_ERR` | Descriptor FIFO and/or completion-status FIFO reported an error. | **indirect** — see below | unchanged |
| 8 | `DATA_FIFO_EMPTY` | Channel data buffer is empty. | write 1 to this bit | unchanged in position; **name newly established** |
| 9 | `DATA_FIFO_FULL` | Channel data buffer is full. | write 1 to this bit | unchanged in position; **name newly established** |
| 10 | `TRANSFER_COMPLETE` | Per-transfer completion. **This is the interrupt a running stream actually raises**, and it is enabled per channel only while that channel is transferring. | write 1 to this bit | unchanged in position; **name newly established** |
| 12 | `TIMESTAMP_REPORT_AVAILABLE` | A report is waiting in the channel's **timestamp** FIFO. Used instead of bit 0 when the channel is configured for timestamped reports. | write 1 to this bit | **new** |
| 16 | `BUS_ERROR` | Bus (AXI) read or write error. Diagnostic capture in `BUS_ERROR_INFO0/1`. | write 1 to this bit | unchanged in position; **name newly established** |
| others | **[Unknown]** | Bits outside the above have no established meaning; write-1 clears them like the rest. | write 1 | — |

**[Confirmed]** for bits **0** and **6**: both position and meaning are stated by the
mainline audio DMA controller driver (`drivers/dma/apple-admac.c`, which defines the
descriptor-done cause at bit 0 and the error cause at bit 6 and services both).

**[Confirmed]** that bits **1, 5, 8, 9, 10** and **16** are raised by the in-scope
hardware and are unmasked in service on t8132, t604x, t8140, t8142 and t605x.
**[Probable]** for their functional names. The block defines exactly eight interrupt
causes: underrun/overrun, descriptor-or-report FIFO error, data buffer full, data buffer
empty, bus read/write error, completion-status FIFO full, excessive jitter, and an
unrecognised-cause catch-all; the cause set is identical on the M3 and M5 controllers.
**[Probable]** for the name-to-bit mapping. Mainline Linux names none of these six.

**[Confirmed]** for bit **12** being new: it does not exist in the M1–M3 programming and
has no corresponding FIFO aperture there.

**[Unknown]** for bit **4**. It is not described by mainline Linux and is not unmasked
in service on any generation. Nothing establishes what it means. See Open question 5.

**The excessive-jitter cause is [Unknown] in bit position.** The cause exists on both M3
and M5, with a companion "high jitter threshold" configuration value expressed in
memory-access-timer units, but no enable-mask bit is associated with it. See Open
questions.

#### Enable masks actually programmed

Identical on t8132, t604x, t8140, t8142 and t605x, and identical to M1–M3:

| When | Value written to `CHAN_INT_MASK[irq-destination-index]` | Bits |
|---|---|---|
| Controller bring-up, per channel, normal mode | `0x0001_0063` | 0, 1, 5, 6, 16 |
| Controller bring-up, per channel, timestamped-report mode | `0x0001_1062` | 1, 5, 6, 12, 16 |
| Channel start (read-modify-write, OR) | `+ 0x0000_0400` | adds 10 |

**[Confirmed]** — the same two constants and the same per-transfer OR of bit 10 appear
in the bring-up of every in-scope SoC and of the M3 baseline. Note that the normal and
timestamped masks differ **only** in bit 0 versus bit 12: the two bits are alternative
notifications of the same event, selected by which report FIFO the channel is
configured to use.

The mainline Linux audio DMA controller driver enables only bits 0 and 6 and never
bit 10, which is why bit 0 is the completion interrupt as far as public documentation
goes. On the in-scope controllers a driver that enables only bit 0 will still receive
report-available interrupts, but will not receive the per-transfer completion interrupt
that is unmasked in service. **[Inferred]** that bit 0 alone remains
sufficient to drive a stream; this needs probing (Open question 2).

### 5.2.5 Acknowledgement semantics — exact rules

Getting these wrong produces an interrupt storm. Stated per register:

| Register | Semantics | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| `CHAN_INT_STATUS[i]` | **write-one-to-clear**, level-latched | Write a word with the bits you have handled set. Writing `0xFFFFFFFF` clears everything. **The bits are independent per destination copy**: clearing copy 0 does not clear copies 1–3. **[Confirmed]** — bring-up clears all four copies with `0xFFFFFFFF` on every generation. |
| `CHAN_INT_STATUS[i]` bit 6 (`RING_ERR`) | **not clearable by writing bit 6** | Bit 6 is a *level* reflection of the error bits in the two FIFO status registers. To clear it: read `DESC_FIFO_STATUS` (`+0x70`) and `REPORT_FIFO_STATUS` (`+0x74`); for each whose bit 10 (`ERR`) is set, write that register back **with bit 10 set**; only then does bit 6 drop. Writing bit 6 into the status register alone leaves the condition asserted and the line will re-assert immediately. **[Confirmed]** — this is the documented baseline behaviour and the in-scope error path performs exactly the read-modify-write-with-bit-10 on both FIFO status registers. Unchanged. |
| `CHAN_INT_MASK[i]` | plain read/write | Not a status register; no clearing semantics. Read-modify-write when adding bit 10 at channel start. |
| `TX_INT_STATE[i]`, `RX_INT_STATE[i]` | **read-only, level** | Pure summary of the per-channel status registers gated by the per-channel masks. There is nothing to acknowledge; they fall of their own accord when the underlying `CHAN_INT_STATUS` bits are cleared. **[Confirmed]** |
| `GLOBAL_INT_STATE[i]` | **write-one-to-clear** | Cleared with `0xFFFFFFFF`. **[Confirmed]** |
| `GLOBAL_INT_ENABLE[i]` | plain read/write | Written `0xFFFFFFFF`. |
| `DESC_FIFO_STATUS` (`+0x70`), `REPORT_FIFO_STATUS` (`+0x74`) | bit 10 write-one-to-clear; the rest read-only status | Unchanged from baseline. |
| `CHAN_MAX_MEM_READ_LATENCY` (`+0xA4`) | **write-zero to clear** | Read, then written with `0`. **[Probable]** |
| The application-processor interrupt controller line itself | **level, active high** | The line stays asserted until every contributing `CHAN_INT_STATUS[i]` bit under a set mask bit has been cleared. A handler that returns without clearing will be re-entered immediately. **[Confirmed]** |

**Correct handler order** (derived, **[Inferred]** as a whole, each step
**[Confirmed]** individually):

1. Read `TX_INT_STATE[i]` and `RX_INT_STATE[i]`; mask to the declared channel counts.
2. For each set bit, read `CHAN_INT_STATUS[i]` of that channel and AND with
   `CHAN_INT_MASK[i]`.
3. Handle bit 10 (and/or bit 0 / bit 12) by draining the relevant report FIFO.
4. Handle bit 6 by clearing `ERR` in `DESC_FIFO_STATUS`/`REPORT_FIFO_STATUS` first.
5. Write the handled bits back to `CHAN_INT_STATUS[i]` (or `0xFFFFFFFF`).
6. Read `GLOBAL_INT_STATE[i]`; if non-zero, write `0xFFFFFFFF`.

There is **no** read-to-clear register anywhere in this block, and **no** edge-triggered
status bit. **[Confirmed]**

### 5.2.6 Whole-block and per-channel recovery

Unchanged: stop the channel through the controller's transmit- or receive-stop
register, pulse bit 0 (ring reset) of the channel control register at channel-block
offset `+0x00`, then resubmit from an empty FIFO — the sequence the mainline audio DMA
controller driver performs. No new abort handshake is described by any source.
**[Confirmed]** for the sequence.

**Whether a polled idle bit exists is [Unknown], not settled.** No bit position for a
DMA-engine-idle status is established here or in any public source, and §4 §4.10.1
describes a drain step that would need one. The two readings cannot both be right and
neither is supported, so the position adopted throughout this document is the
**[Unknown]**, together with the outstanding-transaction fallback and the mandatory
bounded timeout set out in §4 §4.10.1. See §4 Open question 24.

### 5.2.7 Audio DMA latency-escalation detector — **new on the M5 generation**

A companion block, one per audio DMA controller group, with its own interrupt.

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| `device_type` | `ced-ssw` |
| `compatible` | `admacled,t8142` / `admacled,t6050` |
| `reg` | two `0x4000` apertures |
| `interrupts` | one line, application-processor interrupt controller |
| `dma-controllers` | list of the controllers it monitors, by their `role` tag |
| `#dma-channels-tx`, `#dma-channels-rx` | one entry per monitored controller |
| `identity` | a printable identity string, e.g. `ADMAC-A` for the base/leap group, `DISP-I-ISOC` for a display instance |
| `#ssw-register-count` | number of snapshot registers captured on an escalation event |

Aperture bases below are **absolute**, i.e. the platform description's
I/O-region-relative `reg` value plus the `/arm-io` `ranges` parent base. That base is
**not uniform**: `0x2_0000_0000` on t8132, t604x and t605x, and `0x2_1000_0000` on
t8140 and t8142. A figure taken straight from `reg` is 8 GiB or 8.25 GiB below the
hardware. **[Confirmed]** — the parent base is the second cell of the `/arm-io`
`ranges` triple, whose child base is zero, on every board in scope.

| SoC | Node | Aperture bases | Line | Monitors |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| t8142 | `admac-aop-ced-ssw` | `0x3_93C8_0000`, `0x3_93C8_4000` | **569** | all four base/leap instances (tx 13, 13, 9, 9; rx 14, 13, 9, 9) |
| t8142 | `admac-disp0-ced-ssw` | `0x2_862F_4000`, `0x2_861A_0000` | **824** | `admac-disp0` |
| t8142 | `admac-dispext0-ced-ssw` | `0x5_062F_4000`, `0x5_061A_0000` | **896** | `admac-dispext0` |
| t8142 | `admac-dispext1-ced-ssw` | `0x3_AA2F_4000`, `0x3_AA1A_0000` | **971** | `admac-dispext1` |
| t605x | `admac-aop-ced-ssw` | `0x2_93C8_0000`, `0x2_93C8_4000` | **652** | all four base/leap instances |
| t605x | `admac-disp0-ced-ssw` | `0x4_8A2F_4000`, `0x4_8A1A_0000` | **1014** | `admac-disp0` |
| t605x | `admac-dispext0-ced-ssw` | `0x2_B22F_4000`, `0x2_B21A_0000` | **1094** | `admac-dispext0` |
| t605x | `admac-dispext1-ced-ssw` | `0x3_922F_4000`, `0x3_921A_0000` | **1166** | `admac-dispext1` |
| t605x | `admac-dispext2-ced-ssw` | `0x3_022F_4000`, `0x3_021A_0000` | **1238** | `admac-dispext2` |
| t605x | `admac-dispext3-ced-ssw` | `0x3_062F_4000`, `0x3_061A_0000` | **1310** | `admac-dispext3` |

**Function.** Every audio DMA controller node in scope carries a
`function-vote_crit_llt_mode` entry — a call into the power manager that raises the
controller's *critical low-latency-traffic* vote on the memory system. This block
watches that vote and raises its interrupt when the escalation actually fires,
capturing a snapshot of which transmit and receive channels were active at the moment
of escalation together with a configurable number of block registers. It is a
quality-of-service / latency-observability block, **not** a data-path interrupt: no
audio sample flow depends on servicing it. **[Probable]** The block's interface
comprises an escalation event, an active-client list, a per-direction active-channel
snapshot, a configurable absolute latency-tolerance override, an escalation-duration
threshold and a trigger threshold; the register offsets of all six are **[Unknown]**.

Status and mask register layout of this block: **[Unknown]**. Acknowledgement
semantics: **[Unknown]**.

**Absent on t8132, t604x and t8140** — no such node exists on any board of those
SoCs. **[Confirmed]**

## 5.3 Display-audio DMA interrupts

This is the largest structural change in this section.

**M1–M3, t8132, t604x, t8140.** The `dp-audio0…N` nodes carry no `reg` and no
`interrupts`. Their `dma-parent` points at the general-purpose I/O coprocessor's DMA
engine (`/arm-io/sio/iop-sio-nub/sio-dma`), with `dma-channels` naming global channel
100, 102, 104, 106, 108 for display 0…4. Display audio therefore raises **no
host-visible interrupt at all**; completion is signalled through that coprocessor's
mailbox. **[Confirmed]** — identical structure on j504/j514s (M3) and on every t8132,
t604x and t8140 board.

**t8142 and t605x.** Each display audio stream gets its **own audio DMA controller
instance**, host-addressable, with its own host interrupt, its own IOMMU and its own
latency-escalation detector. `dp-audio<N>`'s `dma-parent` now points at that instance
and its `dma-channels` entry is channel 0.

Aperture bases below are **absolute**, i.e. the platform description's
I/O-region-relative `reg` value plus the `/arm-io` `ranges` parent base. That base is
**not uniform**: `0x2_0000_0000` on t8132, t604x and t605x, and `0x2_1000_0000` on
t8140 and t8142. A figure taken straight from `reg` is 8 GiB or 8.25 GiB below the
hardware. **[Confirmed]** — the parent base is the second cell of the `/arm-io`
`ranges` triple, whose child base is zero, on every board in scope.

| SoC | Display node | DMA node | Aperture base | Size | Audio DMA line | IOMMU line | Escalation line |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| t8142 | `dp-audio0` | `admac-disp0` | `0x2_8614_0000` | `0x24000` | **822** | 823 | 824 |
| t8142 | `dp-audio1` | `admac-dispext0` | `0x5_0614_0000` | `0x24000` | **894** | 895 | 896 |
| t8142 | `dp-audio2` | `admac-dispext1` | `0x3_AA14_0000` | `0x24000` | **969** | 970 | 971 |
| t605x | `dp-audio0` | `admac-disp0` | `0x4_8A14_0000` | `0x24000` | **1012** | 1013 | 1014 |
| t605x | `dp-audio1` | `admac-dispext0` | `0x2_B214_0000` | `0x24000` | **1092** | 1093 | 1094 |
| t605x | `dp-audio2` | `admac-dispext1` | `0x3_9214_0000` | `0x24000` | **1164** | 1165 | 1166 |
| t605x | `dp-audio3` | `admac-dispext2` | `0x3_0214_0000` | `0x24000` | **1236** | 1237 | 1238 |
| t605x | `dp-audio4` | `admac-dispext3` | `0x3_0614_0000` | `0x24000` | **1308** | 1309 | 1310 |

**[Confirmed]** — byte-exact and identical across all boards of each SoC, and
corroborated independently by the power-manager device list, which carries a
`DISP_ADMA` domain plus `DISPEXT0_ADMA`…`DISPEXT<N>_ADMA` domains on exactly these two
SoCs (three in total on t8142, five on t605x) and **no such domain on t8122, t6030,
t8132, t604x or t8140**.

Properties of the display instances that matter for interrupt handling:

- `compatible = "admac,t8142"` / `"admac,t6050"` + `"admac,t605x"` — the **classic**
  controller family, *not* `admac-evolution`. The interrupt-output structure, the
  `irq-destinations` list and `irq-destination-index = 0` are identical to the
  base/leap instances. **[Confirmed]**
- `#dma-channels-tx = 1`, no receive channels. Only bit 0 of `TX_INT_STATE[0]` can be
  set. **[Confirmed]**
- Aperture is `0x24000`, not `0x34000`. The receive-side FIFO port window at `0x14000`
  is inside that range; what occupies `0x18000`–`0x24000` is **[Unknown]**.
- `self-actuated` (an empty flag property) is present on the display instances and on
  no other audio DMA instance. Meaning **[Unknown]**; plausibly it indicates the
  instance is started by the display pipeline rather than by an explicit host write.
  **[Inferred]**
- Each display instance has its own IOMMU (`dart-disp0-isoc`, `dart-dispext<N>-isoc`)
  with its own translation-fault interrupt, one line below the DMA line.
  **[Confirmed]**

So the count of host-visible audio-DMA-related interrupt lines per SoC:

| SoC | base/leap DMA | display DMA | escalation detectors | display IOMMU | total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| t8122 / t6030 (baseline) | 2 | 0 | 0 | 0 | **2** |
| t8132 | 2 | 0 | 0 | 0 | **2** |
| t604x | 2 | 0 | 0 | 0 | **2** |
| t8140 | 3 | 0 | 0 | 0 | **3** |
| t8142 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 3 | **13** |
| t605x | 3 | 5 | 6 | 5 | **19** |

## 5.4 Serial audio controller interrupt

**Absent on every SoC in scope.** On M1–M3 the platform description exposed one
`interrupts` entry per serial-audio cluster node (`mca0`, `mca1`, `mca2`, …) bound to
the application-processor interrupt controller — for example lines 772–774 on t8122,
881–883 on t6030, 1318–1320 on t603x. On t8132, t604x, t8140, t8142 and t605x there is
**no cluster node, no switch node and no interrupt** for this block anywhere in the
platform description. **[Confirmed]** on every in-scope board.

The hardware still exists: the power-manager device list of every in-scope board
enumerates six base-domain serial-audio cluster master-clock domains
(`AUDIO_MCA0_M`…`AUDIO_MCA5_M`) plus one in the low-power audio processor domain
(`AUDIO_LEAP_MCA`), on t8132, t604x, t8140, t8142 and t605x alike. **[Confirmed]**
Whether the block's per-cluster interrupt outputs are still wired to the
application-processor interrupt controller and simply undeclared, or are now wired only
to the always-on coprocessor, is **[Unknown]**. Nothing in the host-visible interrupt numbering settles it: the
audio DMA lines are the only audio lines in their neighbourhood and the surrounding
numbers are occupied by unrelated blocks.

The numerically controlled oscillator likewise has no interrupt: the node is absent on
t8132, t604x, t8142 and t605x, and on t8140 it is present with `compatible` and
`clock-ids` but **no `reg` and no `interrupts`**. **[Confirmed]**

## 5.5 Codec and amplifier interrupt pins

### 5.5.1 Routing, per board

All of these are on the **application-processor GPIO controller** (`gpio0`), with
specifier `<pin, 1>` = **level, active low**.

| Board | SoC | Amplifier line node | GPIO ctrl | Pin | Trigger | Jack-codec node | GPIO ctrl | Pin | Trigger | Amps on the shared line |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| j604 | t8132 | `i2c3/audio-speaker` | `gpio0` | 14 | level low | `i2c1/audio-codec-output` | `gpio0` | 98 | level low | 6 |
| j623 | t8132 | `i2c3/audio-speaker` | `gpio0` | 14 | level low | `i2c1/audio-codec-output` | `gpio0` | 98 | level low | 4 |
| j624 | t8132 | `i2c3/audio-speaker` | `gpio0` | 14 | level low | `i2c1/audio-codec-output` | `gpio0` | 98 | level low | 4 |
| j713 | t8132 | `i2c3/audio-speaker` | `gpio0` | 14 | level low | `i2c1/audio-codec-output` | `gpio0` | 98 | level low | 4 |
| j715 | t8132 | `i2c3/audio-speaker` | `gpio0` | 14 | level low | `i2c1/audio-codec-output` | `gpio0` | 98 | level low | 6 |
| j773g | t8132 | `i2c3/audio-speaker` | `gpio0` | 14 | level low | `i2c1/audio-codec-output` | `gpio0` | 98 | level low | 1 |
| j614s/j614c/j616s/j616c | t604x | `i2c1/audio-speaker` | `gpio0` | 55 | level low | `i2c2/audio-codec-output` | `gpio0` | 106 | level low | 6 |
| j773s | t604x | `i2c1/audio-speaker` | `gpio0` | 55 | level low | `i2c2/audio-codec-output` | `gpio0` | 106 | level low | 1 |
| j575c | t604x | `i2c1/audio-speaker` | `gpio0` | 55 | level low | `i2c2/audio-codec-output` | `gpio0` | 106 | level low | 1 |
| **j700** | **t8140** | **none — amplifier has no control bus** | — | — | — | `i2c0/audio-codec-output` | `gpio0` | 104 | level low | 0 |
| j704 | t8142 | `i2c3/audio-speaker` | `gpio0` | 150 | level low | `i2c1/audio-codec-output` | `gpio0` | 100 | level low | 6 |
| j813 | t8142 | `i2c3/audio-speaker` | `gpio0` | 150 | level low | `i2c1/audio-codec-output` | `gpio0` | 100 | level low | 4 |
| j815 | t8142 | `i2c3/audio-speaker` | `gpio0` | 150 | level low | `i2c1/audio-codec-output` | `gpio0` | 100 | level low | 6 |
| j714s/j714c/j716s/j716c | t605x | `i2c1/audio-speaker` | `gpio0` | 106 | level low | `i2c2/audio-codec-output` | `gpio0` | 134 | level low | 6 |

**[Confirmed]** — byte-exact from each board's own description; the pin numbers are
per-SoC constants across boards of the same SoC.

Note the collision hazard for anyone building a cross-SoC table: pin **106** is the
jack codec on t604x and the **amplifier** line on t605x.

### 5.5.2 Decoding the two-word specifier

```
interrupts        = <u32 pin, u32 trigger>
interrupt-parent  = <u32 phandle-of-GPIO-controller>
```

- Word 0 is the **GPIO pin number within that controller's own numbering**, not a
  global line number and not an interrupt-controller line. It is the same numbering
  space used by the `function-<name>` properties on the same node (which have the
  shape `phandle | 4-byte tag | arg0 = pin | arg1 = flags`).
- Word 1 is the trigger encoding of §5.1. For every audio device on every in-scope
  board it is `1` = **level, active low**.
- The interrupt reaches the application-processor interrupt controller on the line
  corresponding to whichever of the GPIO controller's seven interrupt groups the pin
  is steered into. That steering is **not** in the platform description, so a driver
  must program it. Which group a given audio pin belongs to is **[Unknown]**.

Worked example, j714s amplifier: `interrupt-parent` → `/arm-io/gpio0`;
`interrupts = <0x6a, 0x01>` → pin 106, level active low. `/arm-io/gpio0` itself
declares `interrupts = <486 487 488 489 490 491 492>`, its seven groups; pin 106's
interrupt will emerge on exactly one of those seven lines.

### 5.5.3 Sharing, polarity and source identification

**Unchanged from the M1–M3 baseline in every respect.**

- **Amplifier line is shared.** Only the first amplifier node (the one that also
  carries `speaker1`…`speakerN` phandles to its siblings, i.e. amplifier index 0)
  carries `interrupts`; every other amplifier node on the board has no `interrupts`
  and no `interrupt-parent`. All amplifiers' interrupt pins are wired together to that
  single pin. **[Confirmed]** — this pattern holds on every in-scope board
  and on every baseline board.
- **Polarity: active low, level.** Open-drain wired-OR; any amplifier holding the line
  low keeps it asserted. A handler must be level-triggered and one-shot.
  **[Confirmed]**
- **Source identification when shared: there is no hardware arbiter.** The line gives
  no indication of which amplifier asserted it. The only method is to poll each
  amplifier's own latched fault registers over I²C and, for each device that has a
  latched bit set, issue that device's own interrupt-pin-release write. A device whose
  latch is read but whose release bit is not written will continue to hold the shared
  line low. This is the classic storm source on this platform. **[Confirmed]** — see
  the baseline codec document §B.10 for the register-level detail of the counterpart
  part; nothing about it changed.
- **Jack codec has its own dedicated pin**, not shared with the amplifiers, on every
  board. **[Confirmed]** Its interrupt structure (three status registers and three
  masks, plus a headset-detect status/mask pair) is unchanged from the baseline.
- **t8140 is the exception:** the amplifier part on that machine has no control bus
  and therefore no interrupt pin, no shared line and no fault reporting path. Speaker
  protection on that machine cannot be interrupt-driven. **[Confirmed]** — the speaker
  node on j700 lives under `/arm-io/iop-audio-controller`, not under an I²C bus, and
  carries no `interrupts`.

### 5.5.4 Wake capability of codec interrupts

**None.** On every in-scope board the audio codec and amplifier pins are on `gpio0`,
the application-processor-domain GPIO controller, and `gpio0` carries **no
`wake-events` property on any board of any generation**, nor does any entry of the
system wake-source list name an application-processor-domain GPIO group (§5.7). Only
the always-on-domain and nub-domain GPIO controllers declare `wake-events`
(`0x06 0x16 0x06 0x1a 0x04 0x1a 0x00 0x00` on the always-on controller, byte-identical
on every board from M1 to M5; `0x02 0x04` on the nub controller), plus
`wake-no-interrupt-group = 4`. The exact encoding of `wake-events` is **[Unknown]**;
it is a small table of (interrupt-group, pin) pairs that matches the
`…GPIO.IRQ4`/`…GPIO.IRQ6` wake-source entries. **[Inferred]**

Consequence for a driver: headphone insertion/removal cannot wake the machine through
the jack codec's own interrupt pin. Wake on an audio event must come through the
always-on coprocessor mailbox. **[Confirmed]** by the absence of any
application-processor GPIO wake source.

---

## 5.6 Coprocessor-side interrupts

### 5.6.1 What raises a host interrupt on the coprocessor-side control path

The audio controller node `/arm-io/iop-audio-controller`
(`compatible = "iop-audio,controller"`) has **no `reg`, no `interrupt-parent` and no
`interrupts`** on any in-scope board, and neither do any of its per-stream children
(`compatible = "iop-adma-stream,mca"` / `"iop-adma-stream,leap"`). Everything the
coprocessor-side control path needs to tell the host — stream state, jack events routed through the
coprocessor, low-power microphone events, voice-trigger events — arrives as a mailbox
message on the always-on coprocessor's inbound queue, i.e. on that coprocessor's
**inbound-not-empty** line. **[Confirmed]**

Corollary for interrupt budgeting: a host audio driver on these SoCs needs exactly
**two** kinds of interrupt to run a stream — the audio DMA controller's line for data
movement, and the always-on coprocessor's inbound-not-empty line for control. On
M1–M3 it needed the DMA line only, because the control path was host MMIO and polled.

### 5.6.2 Always-on coprocessor mailbox lines, per SoC

Node `compatible = "iop,ascwrap-v6"` in every case. Order as §5.1.

| SoC | Node | `interrupts` (as listed) | Decoded: outbound-NE / outbound-E / inbound-NE / inbound-E |
|---|---|---|---|
| t8122 (baseline) | `aop` | 372, 371, 374, 373 | 372 / 371 / 374 / 373 |
| t6030 (baseline) | `aop` | 420, 419, 422, 421 | 420 / 419 / 422 / 421 |
| **t8132** | `aop` | 434, 433, 436, 435 | 434 / 433 / **436** / 435 |
| **t604x** | `aop` | 711, 710, 713, 712, **715, 714, 717, 716** | first mailbox 711 / 710 / **713** / 712; second mailbox 715 / 714 / **717** / 716 |
| **t8140** | `aop` | 391, 390, 393, 392 | 391 / 390 / **393** / 392 |
| **t8140** | `aop-exclave-mailbox` | 397, 394 | see below |
| **t8140** | `aop2` | 399, 398, 401, 400 | 399 / 398 / **401** / 400 |
| **t8140** | `aop2-exclave-mailbox` | 405, 402 | see below |
| **t8142** | `aop` | 491, 490, 493, 492 | 491 / 490 / **493** / 492 |
| **t8142** | `aop-exclave-mailbox` | 497, 494 | see below |
| **t8142** | `aop2` | 499, 498, 501, 500 | 499 / 498 / **501** / 500 |
| **t605x** | `aop` | 579, 578, 581, 580 | 579 / 578 / **581** / 580 |
| **t605x** | `aop-exclave-mailbox` | 585, 582 | see below |
| **t605x** | `aop2` | 587, 586, 589, 588 | 587 / 586 / **589** / 588 |

**[Confirmed]** — identical for every board of each SoC.

**Each coprocessor instance owns eight consecutive interrupt lines**, arranged as two
mailbox quadruples: lines `n`…`n+3` are the ordinary (non-secure) mailbox, lines
`n+4`…`n+7` are a second, secure mailbox. **[Inferred]**, with strong support:

- On t604x the single `aop` node claims all eight in two consecutive quadruples.
- On t8140, t8142 and t605x the second quadruple is broken out as a separate node
  `aop-exclave-mailbox` (`compatible = "iop,secure-rtbuddy-proxy"`, a single `0x4000`
  aperture) which claims exactly **two** of those four lines — `n+7` and `n+4` — i.e.
  its inbound-not-empty and its outbound-empty.
- On t8132 only the first quadruple is described; `n+4`…`n+7` (437–440) are not bound
  to anything in the platform description.

The second (`aop2`) coprocessor instance is **new** on t8140, t8142 and t605x, and is
absent on t8132 and t604x and on all baseline SoCs. **[Confirmed]** On t8140 both
instances get a secure-mailbox node; on t8142 and t605x only the first does.

Which of the two mailboxes carries audio traffic is **[Unknown]**; the audio service
named by `iop-audio-service-name` is a service of the first coprocessor instance, so
the ordinary mailbox (`aop` line *n+3*) is the **[Probable]** answer.

`aop2` has no audio-named children in the platform description on any board — its nub
(`iop-aop2-nub`) carries no audio node — so no audio interrupt is known to arrive on
its mailbox. **[Confirmed]** — no such binding is declared on any in-scope board;
**[Unknown]** what it does carry.

### 5.6.3 IOMMU fault interrupts on the audio path

Not audio interrupts strictly, but they fire on audio DMA misprogramming and belong in
a driver's fault-handling story. All four base/leap audio DMA instances are mapped
through the always-on IOMMU (`dart-aop`), which has a single translation-fault line:

| SoC | `dart-aop` fault line | Mapper nodes for audio DMA |
|---|---|---|
| t8122 (baseline) | 391 | — |
| t6030 (baseline) | 439 | — |
| t8132 | **457** | `mapper-admac-base-ns`, `-base-s`, `-leap-ns`, `-leap-s` |
| t604x | **734** | same four |
| t8140 | **428** | same four |
| t8142 | **528** | same four |
| t605x | **616** | same four |

**[Confirmed]**. Note that all four audio DMA instances share this one fault line, so
a fault gives no immediate attribution to an instance; the fault-status registers of
the IOMMU must be read. The display-audio instances on t8142/t605x each have their own
IOMMU and their own fault line (§5.3).

## 5.7 System wake sources

The platform description carries an explicit wake-source list at
`/arm-io/pmgr : ap-wake-sources`. Its encoding is an array of **36-byte records**:

```
u32  wake-source index
char name[32]   (NUL-padded)
```

**[Confirmed]** — the length of the property is an exact multiple of 36 on every board
and every record decodes to a printable name.

The index is the bit position of that source in the power manager's wake-status
register set. **[Inferred]**

### Audio-relevant entries, per SoC

| SoC | Audio-relevant wake sources (index : name) | Relevance |
|---|---|---|
| t8122 / t6030 (baseline) | 3 : `AOP.CPUWakeupAP`; 51 : `AOP.OutboxNotEmpty` | the always-on coprocessor's only mailbox |
| **t8132** | 5 : `AOP.CPUWakeupAP`; 42 : `AOP.OutboxNotEmpty`; **229 : `AOP.TrustedOutboxNotEmpty`** | **new**: the secure mailbox of the same coprocessor is now a wake source |
| **t604x** | 25 : `AOP.Outbox0_NotEmpty`; **27 : `AOP.Outbox1_NotEmpty`**; 28 : `AOP.CPUWakeupAP` | the two mailboxes are named by number rather than by trust level |
| **t8140** | 0 : `AOP.AICWakeupAP`; 5 : `AOP.CPUWakeupAP`; 42 : `AOP.OutboxNotEmpty`; 211 : `AOP.TrustedOutboxNotEmpty`; **227 : `AOP2.OutboxNotEmpty`**; **231 : `AOP2.TrustedOutboxNotEmpty`**; **236 : `AOP2.CPUWakeupAP`** | both coprocessor instances, both mailboxes each |
| **t8142** | 5 : `AOP.CPUWakeupAP`; 44 : `AOP.OutboxNotEmpty`; 237 : `AOP.TrustedOutboxNotEmpty`; 256 : `AOP2.TrustedOutboxNotEmpty`; 261 : `AOP2.CPUWakeAP` | |
| **t605x** | 28 : `AOP.Outbox0_NotEmpty`; 30 : `AOP.Outbox2_NotEmpty`; 38 : `AOP2.Outbox2_NotEmpty`; 39 : `AOP.CPUWakeupAP`; 290 : `AOP2.CPUWakeupAP` | |

GPIO wake entries present on every in-scope SoC — `AOP.GPIO.IRQ4`, `AOP.GPIO.IRQ6`,
`NUB.GPIO.IRQ2`, `NUB.GPIO.IRQ6` (exact set varies, see the per-SoC section) — refer
to interrupt **groups** of the always-on-domain and nub-domain GPIO controllers. **No
audio device's interrupt pin is on either of those controllers on any in-scope
board**, so none of these is an audio wake source. **[Confirmed]**

**Reading for a driver.** The only audio-capable wake path is a mailbox message from
the always-on coprocessor. In practice that means: voice-trigger detection, low-power
microphone activity, and any jack or accessory event the coprocessor chooses to
report. There is no wake source anywhere in the list corresponding to the audio DMA
controller, the serial audio controller, the display audio path, or an
application-processor GPIO pin. **[Confirmed]**

Deltas worth restating: the *number* of coprocessor mailbox wake sources went from one
on M1–M3 to two on t8132 and t604x, and to four on t8140 (two coprocessors × two
mailboxes). The naming convention also changed twice — `AOP.OutboxNotEmpty` /
`AOP.TrustedOutboxNotEmpty` on t8132, t8140 and t8142 versus numbered
`AOP.Outbox0_NotEmpty` / `AOP.Outbox1_NotEmpty` / `AOP.Outbox2_NotEmpty` on t604x and
t605x. Whether "Outbox2" on t605x is the same physical queue as "TrustedOutbox" on
t8142 is **[Probable]** but not established.

---

## 5.8 Sharing with non-audio blocks

**No audio interrupt line is shared with a non-audio block on any in-scope SoC.**
**[Confirmed]** — every application-processor interrupt controller line bound by an
audio node on any in-scope board is bound by exactly one node. (Shared
lines do occur elsewhere on these SoCs — for example the nub GPIO controller's seven
group lines are also claimed by a secure-repair block on t8142 — but never on an audio
node.)

Two qualifications a driver author must not overlook:

1. **Within audio, sharing is pervasive at the GPIO level.** The amplifier interrupt
   pin is one wired-OR line shared by up to six amplifiers (§5.5.3), and it emerges on
   one of the application-processor GPIO controller's seven group lines — a line that
   is shared with **every other pin steered into the same group**, audio or not. Which
   pins those are is not in the platform description, so a driver must claim that line
   as shared and must never assume an assertion is its own. **[Confirmed]** in
   principle; the specific group membership is **[Unknown]**.
2. **The always-on IOMMU fault line is shared by all four audio DMA instances** and by
   every other consumer of that IOMMU. **[Confirmed]**

---

## Per-SoC / per-machine differences

**t8132 (M4)** — j604, j623, j624, j713, j715, j773g.
Two described audio DMA instances (lines 475, 478) of four reserved; no display audio
DMA (display audio is on the I/O coprocessor's DMA engine); no latency-escalation
detector; one coprocessor with one described mailbox quadruple (433–436) and a second,
undeclared quadruple at 437–440; amplifier line `gpio0` pin 14, jack codec `gpio0` pin
98, on all six boards; amplifier count 6 (j604, j715), 4 (j623, j624, j713) or 1
(j773g); wake sources add a trusted-mailbox entry over the baseline.

**t604x (M4 Pro/Max)** — j614s, j614c, j616s, j616c, j773s, j575c.
As t8132 but lines 754 and 757; the coprocessor node claims **all eight** mailbox
lines (710–717) in one node rather than four; wake sources use the numbered
`Outbox0`/`Outbox1` naming; amplifier line `gpio0` pin 55, jack codec `gpio0` pin 106;
amplifier count 6 on the notebooks, 1 on j773s and j575c.

**t8140 (A18 Pro)** — j700 only.
Three described audio DMA instances (449, 451, 452) including the low-power secure
instance, which no other M4-class SoC describes; `admac-evolution` compatible and
per-channel apertures present; no display audio DMA and no latency-escalation
detector; **two** coprocessor instances, each with both an ordinary mailbox node and a
secure mailbox node (390–393 / 394+397, 398–401 / 402+405); a numerically controlled
oscillator node that exists but has neither `reg` nor `interrupts`. **The machine has
no amplifier interrupt at all** — its amplifier part has no control bus — so the
jack codec on `gpio0` pin 104 is the *only* audio GPIO interrupt on the board. Its
jack codec is also a different part from the rest of the scope.

**t8142 (M5)** — j704, j813, j815.
Three described audio DMA instances (549, 551, 552); **three display-audio DMA
instances** (822, 894, 969) each with its own IOMMU fault line and its own escalation
detector line; one escalation detector for the whole base/leap group (569); two
coprocessor instances, the first with a secure mailbox node; amplifier `gpio0` pin 150,
jack codec `gpio0` pin 100; amplifier count 6 (j704, j815) or 4 (j813).

**t605x / t6050 (M5 Pro/Max)** — j714s, j714c, j716s, j716c.
Three described audio DMA instances (637, 638, 639) with **no gap** for the secure base
instance — the only SoC in scope where the four-line reservation pattern does not hold;
**five display-audio DMA instances** (1012, 1092, 1164, 1236, 1308) with matching IOMMU
and escalation lines; base/leap escalation detector at 652; amplifier `gpio0` pin 106,
jack codec `gpio0` pin 134, six amplifiers on all four boards; wake sources use the
numbered `Outbox0`/`Outbox2` naming and include an `AOP2.Outbox2_NotEmpty` entry that
t8142 does not have.
