## Open questions

1. **Which interrupt-destination index is really wired on each instance — verify by
   provocation.** The platform description says 0 for every in-scope instance, a change
   from 1/2 on M1–M3, and a driver that gets this wrong sees nothing. *Experiment:*
   with the audio DMA power domain up, set `CHAN_INT_MASK[i]` for all four *i* on one
   transmit channel to `0x00011FFF`, run a short cyclic transfer, and read all four
   copies of `CHAN_INT_STATUS`, `TX_INT_STATE` and `GLOBAL_INT_STATE`. Confirm that
   copy 0 asserts, that the application-processor line fires, and record whether copies
   1–3 also latch (they should, since the outputs are independent routes of the same
   causes).

2. **Bit 10 versus bit 0 as the completion notification.** In service bit 0 (or bit 12)
   is unmasked permanently and bit 10 is added only while a channel runs. It
   is not established whether bit 10 is a distinct hardware cause or a gated duplicate
   of bit 0. *Experiment:* submit a descriptor **with** the notify flag and one
   **without**, with only bit 0 unmasked, then repeat with only bit 10 unmasked, and
   record which of the two bits sets in each case and whether a report appears in the
   completion FIFO.

3. **Bit 12 and the third FIFO.** Confirm that bit 12 is raised by data becoming
   available in the per-channel timestamp FIFO at `0x10200 + 4n` / `0x14200 + 4n`, what
   a timestamp record contains, and how many words it is. *Experiment:* enable bit 12,
   run a transfer, and read the timestamp port repeatedly, watching
   `REPORT_FIFO_STATUS`-style slot/empty/full fields for a third ring if one exists at
   an offset near `+0x78`.

4. **Bit positions of the underrun/overrun, data-buffer and bus-error causes.** Bits 1,
   8, 9 and 16 are unmasked in service; the name-to-bit mapping for bits 1 and 16 is
   **[Probable]**.
   *Experiment:* provoke each condition individually — starve a running transmit
   channel by not refilling its descriptor FIFO (expect underrun), stop draining a
   receive channel (expect overrun), point a descriptor at an unmapped address (expect
   bus error, then read `+0x34` and `+0x38`) — and record which bit sets each time,
   plus the contents of `+0x80` and `+0x34`/`+0x38`.

5. **What bit 4 of the per-channel status register means.** It is the one bit in the
   register that nothing characterises: mainline Linux neither names nor services it,
   and it is not unmasked in service on any generation. A driver that unmasks the whole
   register will take it and be unable to attribute it. *Experiment:* unmask bit 4 alone on an idle channel, then (a) start the
   channel with an empty descriptor FIFO, (b) let a running channel drain its descriptor
   FIFO without refill, and (c) reset the rings while the channel is stopped, recording
   in each case whether bit 4 sets and whether writing 1 to it clears it.

6. **The excessive-jitter cause.** An excessive-jitter cause exists on both M3 and M5,
   with a companion high-jitter threshold expressed in memory-access-timer units; its
   bit position is **[Unknown]** and no enable-mask bit is associated with it. *Experiment:* unmask
   all 32 bits of `CHAN_INT_STATUS[0]` on a running channel, introduce large memory
   latency (contend the fabric), and record which bits outside the known set assert.

7. **`GLOBAL_INT_ENABLE[i]` at `0x60 + 4i` and the bit meanings of
   `GLOBAL_INT_STATE[i]`.** Both are entirely uncharacterised on every generation.
   *Experiment:* write `0` to `GLOBAL_INT_ENABLE[0]`, provoke a controller-level error
   (for example a descriptor write to a channel that is not started, or a bus error on
   a stopped channel), and see whether `GLOBAL_INT_STATE[0]` still sets while the line
   stays quiet; then write `0xFFFFFFFF` and repeat.

8. **Acknowledgement of the ring error bit.** The indirect clear (write bit 10 of the
   descriptor and report FIFO status registers) is inherited from the baseline and
   assumed unchanged. *Experiment:* force a ring error (over-submit into a full
   4-deep descriptor FIFO), then (a) write bit 6 into `CHAN_INT_STATUS[0]` alone and
   observe whether the line re-asserts, and (b) do the indirect clear and observe that
   it drops. This directly tests the storm case.

9. **Per-channel block addressing on t8132 and t604x.** Those two SoCs do not enumerate
   per-channel apertures, so the transmit-at-`0x8000`/receive-at-`0xC000` split is
   inferred from t8140/t8142/t605x. *Experiment:* start transmit channel 1, then read
   `CHAN_INT_STATUS[0]` at both `0x8000 + 1×0x200` and `0x8000 + 2×0x200` and see which
   tracks; equivalently read `RESIDUE` at both candidates during a transfer.

10. **The identity of interrupt destination 2 (tag `GTN `).** Unknown on every in-scope
   SoC. It matters because a driver that sets mask bits in copy 2 may be injecting
   interrupts into another agent. *Experiment:* set a single mask bit in copy 2 on an
   idle channel, provoke the cause, and watch for secondary effects (power-state
   changes, clock-gate transitions) while confirming no application-processor line
   fires.

11. **Which GPIO interrupt group carries the amplifier and jack-codec pins.** The
    platform description gives the pin but not the group, and the group determines
    which of the seven application-processor lines to claim and who else shares it.
    *Experiment:* read the per-pin configuration register of `gpio0` for the amplifier
    and codec pins before touching anything (firmware has already configured them), and
    record the group field; then enumerate every other pin steered into the same group.

12. **Whether the serial audio controller's cluster interrupts still reach the
    application-processor interrupt controller.** The nodes are gone but the hardware
    is present. If those lines are still wired and are left unmasked by firmware, a
    driver that brings the block's power domain up could take an unclaimed interrupt.
    *Experiment:* enumerate application-processor interrupt controller lines that no
    platform-description node claims in the neighbourhood of the audio DMA lines, then
    bring up an audio cluster power domain and watch for spurious lines.

13. **Latency-escalation detector register map and acknowledgement.** Entirely
    unknown, and it is a live interrupt on M5 machines. *Experiment:* with the block's
    two `0x4000` apertures mapped, run a high-channel-count stream while contending
    memory bandwidth, dump both apertures before and after the line asserts, and
    determine which word changed and which write clears it. Also determine whether the
    line can be left permanently masked with no effect on audio.

14. **Which coprocessor mailbox carries audio, and whether the secure mailbox does
    too.** Needed to know which line to claim on t8140/t8142/t605x. *Experiment:*
    claim all mailbox lines of both instances, start a playback stream through the
    coprocessor-owned control path, and record which inbound-not-empty line fires and
    with what message identifiers.

15. **The undeclared secure audio DMA instances.** On t8132 and t604x neither secure
    instance is described, and on t605x the base secure instance has no obvious
    reserved line. Their apertures, channel counts and interrupt lines are all unknown.
    *Experiment:* probe the address one `0x100000` step below `admac-base-ns`'s base
    (the spacing between the described instances is regular) for a responding
    `0x34000` window, and correlate with the reserved application-processor lines.

16. **`wake-events` encoding and `wake-no-interrupt-group`.** The eight-byte
    always-on-domain table is byte-identical on every board from M1 to M5, which makes
    it easy to check but leaves its field layout unproven. *Experiment:* correlate the
    table's bytes against the per-pin group configuration of the always-on GPIO
    controller for the pins it names, and confirm the (group, pin) reading against the
    `AOP.GPIO.IRQ4` / `AOP.GPIO.IRQ6` wake-source entries.

17. **Whether a display-audio DMA instance on M5 can be driven without its
    escalation detector.** A driver that ignores the detector line entirely may take
    an unserviced level interrupt. *Experiment:* claim only the display audio DMA line,
    run an HDMI audio stream at maximum channel count, and observe whether the
    detector line asserts and stays asserted.

18. **The contents of the three per-channel capture registers read by the interrupt
    path.** `BUS_ERROR_INFO0` (`+0x34`), `BUS_ERROR_INFO1` (`+0x38`) and
    `DATA_FIFO_STATUS` (`+0x80`) are read (and, for the first two, cleared) when their
    causes fire, but their bit layouts are **[Unknown]** on every generation, here and
    in §4 §4.3.3. *Why it matters:* they are the only per-channel diagnostic a handler
    has for a bus fault or a data-buffer condition; without a layout the handler can
    only report that something happened. *Experiment:* provoke each cause in isolation
    — an unmapped IOMMU address, a read-only mapping, a fault part-way through a burst,
    a starved transmit FIFO and an overflowing receive FIFO — and diff all three
    registers after each, on both a transmit and a receive channel. Shared with §4 Open
    question 21.


---

# 6. Control bus and GPIO

## Baseline

The control-plane hardware measured against here is the M1–M3 arrangement: a set of
host-addressable I2C master controllers of the PASemi-derived family (device-tree
`compatible = "i2c,t8101", "i2c,s5l8940x", "iic,soft"`, upstream Linux binding
`apple,t8103-i2c`), one 32-bit-per-pin GPIO/pin-mux controller per power island
(application-processor, always-on, "nub", system-management), and, hanging off two
or three of the I2C buses, discrete speaker amplifiers and a headphone-jack codec
whose reset, shutdown, interrupt and module-identification lines are ordinary GPIO
pins. The public counterparts are the TAS2764 (for the `sn012776` amplifier family)
and the CS42L42/CS42L83 (for the `cs42l84`/`cs42l83` jack codec). On M1–M3 every
speaker amplifier in a machine shares one software-shutdown GPIO and one interrupt
GPIO, and the jack codec's reset line sits on the nub GPIO controller.

**Headline result for this section: none of that changed.** The migration of the
serialiser/clocking/routing control path behind the always-on coprocessor on M4 and
later did **not** move the I2C control buses. The host still owns the amplifier and
codec I2C buses directly, with no arbitration, no ownership token and no handoff
protocol.

## Summary of differences

| Item | t8132 (M4) | t604x (M4 Pro/Max) | t8140 (A18 Pro) | t8142 (M5) | t605x (M5 Pro/Max) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| I2C controller block (register map, tunable scheme) | unchanged from M2/M3 | unchanged | unchanged | unchanged | unchanged |
| Audio I2C bus ownership | host | host | host | host | host |
| Number of audio I2C buses | 2 | 3 | 1 | 2 | 3 |
| Amplifier on I2C | yes (`sn012776`) | yes | **absent** — `max98360`, no control bus | yes | yes |
| Jack codec | `cs42l84` @0x4b | `cs42l84` @0x4b | **`cs42l83` @0x48** | `cs42l84` @0x4b | `cs42l84` @0x4b |
| Shared amplifier shutdown GPIO | unchanged (one line, all amps) | unchanged | **repurposed**: single enable line for the control-bus-less amplifiers | unchanged | unchanged |
| Shared amplifier interrupt GPIO | unchanged | unchanged | **absent** | unchanged | unchanged |
| Codec reset GPIO controller | nub (unchanged) | nub (unchanged) | **application-processor** | nub (unchanged) | **application-processor** |
| Speaker-ID GPIO pair | unchanged | unchanged | **absent** | present except j813 | unchanged |
| System-management GPIO controller node | present | present | present (6 pins only) | present | **absent** |
| Extra GPIO controller instances | — | — | **multi-touch-processor GPIO** | — | — |
| Microphone supply enable | none | none | **present**, via system-management controller | none | none |
| Codec clock-master arbitration function target | moved to coprocessor stream endpoint | same | same | same | same |

---

## 6.1 The host I2C master controller

### 6.1.1 Block identity — unchanged

Every audio-bearing I2C controller on every in-scope board carries
`compatible = "i2c,t8101", "i2c,s5l8940x", "iic,soft"` and `device_type = "i2c"`,
identical to M1–M3, and matches the mainline Linux binding `apple,t8103-i2c` /
`apple,i2c`. The programming interface is the PASemi-derived master documented by
the mainline Linux driver for this family: master transmit FIFO at offset 0x00,
master receive FIFO at 0x04, transfer status at 0x0c, status at 0x14, interrupt
mask at 0x18, control at 0x1c, revision at 0x28. The aperture is 0x4000 bytes on
every instance, on every SoC in scope and in the baseline. **[Confirmed]** —
aperture size and compatible string identical on every board from M1 to M5, and the
register map is the mainline one.

Per the delta rule, the register map is **not** re-documented here; take it from the
mainline Linux driver for this controller family. The fields that matter to the
rest of this section are the control register at 0x1c — enable bit 11, master
receive FIFO reset bit 10, master transmit FIFO reset bit 9, auto-unjam enable
bit 8, clock divider bits 7:0 — and the status register at 0x14, whose jam
(bit 24), jam-detected (bit 25), master-timeout (bit 23), arbitration-lost
(bit 22) and NACK (bit 21) indications are the ones a host must watch on a shared
board-level bus. **[Confirmed]** — mainline Linux.

Registers at offsets 0x08, 0x10, 0x20 and 0x44 exist in the 0x4000 aperture but
their function is **[Unknown]**; mainline does not describe them and nothing in the
platform description names them. See Open question 15.

### 6.1.2 Instance map, MMIO, interrupts, clock domain

`reg` on these nodes is two 64-bit cells (address, size) expressed in the
`/arm-io` child address space; the `/arm-io` `ranges` entry that covers them maps
child 0x0…0x3c0000000 onto parent 0x200000000 on t605x and analogous windows
elsewhere. Absolute addresses below are post-translation and were cross-checked
against the published in-tree platform descriptions for t8103, t6030 and t6031,
which they reproduce exactly. **[Confirmed]**

Interrupts are routed to the top-level interrupt controller (`interrupt-parent`
points at the `aic` node), one level-high line per controller. The clock domain is
given by `clock-gates` (a power-manager device index) plus `clock-ids = 4`
(a functional-clock selector, constant across every I2C instance on every board,
baseline and in-scope). **[Confirmed]**

| SoC | Instance | MMIO base | Size | Interrupt | Power-manager device index | SCL pin | SDA pin | Audio role |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| t8132 | i2c0 | 0x3ad010000 | 0x4000 | 1062 | 0x3e | 0x68 (104) | 0x67 (103) | — |
| t8132 | **i2c1** | **0x3ad014000** | 0x4000 | **1063** | 0x3f | 0x6a (106) | 0x69 (105) | jack codec |
| t8132 | i2c2 | 0x3ad018000 | 0x4000 | 1064 | 0x40 | 0x2c (44) | 0x2b (43) | — |
| t8132 | **i2c3** | **0x3ad01c000** | 0x4000 | **1065** | 0x41 | 0x2a (42) | 0x29 (41) | speaker amplifiers |
| t8132 | i2c4 | 0x3ad020000 | 0x4000 | 1066 | 0x42 | 0x6c (108) | 0x6b (107) | — |
| t604x | **i2c1** | **0x429014000** | 0x4000 | **1576** | 0xad | 0x3a (58) | 0x3b (59) | left amplifiers |
| t604x | **i2c2** | **0x429018000** | 0x4000 | **1577** | 0xae | 0x3c (60) | 0x3d (61) | jack codec |

| t605x | **i2c2** | **0x505018000** | 0x4000 | **1377** | 0xc0 | 0x3e (62) | 0x3f (63) | jack codec |

Baseline for comparison: t8122 i2c1 = 0x2a1014000 (irq 781), i2c3 = 0x2a101c000
(irq 783); t6030 i2c1/2/3 = 0x289014000/0x289018000/0x28901c000 (irq 890/891/892);
t6031 i2c1/2/3 = 0x391014000/0x391018000/0x39101c000 (irq 1327/1328/1329). The
instance-to-role assignment is therefore **unchanged in shape**: base dies put the
codec on i2c1 and all amplifiers on i2c3; Pro/Max dies split the amplifiers
left/right across i2c1 and i2c3 and put the codec alone on i2c2. **[Confirmed]**

Note the aperture stride: instances are 0x4000 apart with instance *n* at
`base + 0x4000·n`, and i2c5/i2c7 exist only on the Pro/Max dies. **[Confirmed]**

### 6.1.3 SCL/SDA pin descriptors and bus recovery

Each controller node carries `gpio-iic_scl` and `gpio-iic_sda`, twelve bytes each,
laid out as `u32 pin | u32 flags | 4-byte controller-role tag`. The role tag is
stored byte-reversed and reads `AP` on every audio bus of every board — i.e. both
lines are pins of the **application-processor** GPIO controller, never of the
always-on or system-management ones. The flags word is 0x00010102 on every I2C
pin descriptor on every board. **[Confirmed]**

Decoding the flags word against the other observed GPIO function flag words
(see §6.4.3): bit 1 selects the peripheral (alternate) function — required, since
in normal operation SCL/SDA are driven by the I2C block and not by the GPIO
block — and bit 8 enables the input buffer so the line can be read back.

The practical significance is bus recovery. The controller has a hardware
auto-unjam machine, enabled by bit 8 of the control register at 0x1c, and reports
a jammed bus in bit 24 of the status register at 0x14, with a jam-detected latch in
bit 25 and a transaction-in-progress indication in bit 28. **[Confirmed]** —
mainline Linux.
When the auto-unjam machine fails, the fallback available to a host is to reassign
the two named pins from peripheral function to GPIO output (§6.4.2) and clock out
recovery pulses by hand; the platform description names the pins precisely so that
this is possible. **[Inferred]** — from the pin descriptors plus the mainline GPIO
register map; no board property states it.

Whether the controller additionally offers a direct-drive mode that bit-bangs SCL
and SDA from within its own register file, and whether it exposes the instantaneous
line levels, is **[Unknown]**. Mainline does not describe such a facility. See Open
question 16.

### 6.1.4 Bus clock

`clock-ids = 4` selects the controller's functional clock. The mainline Linux
driver for this family computes the control register's 8-bit divider field
(bits 7:0) as `ceil(f_ref / (16 × f_SCL))` and rejects any result below 4 (bus too
fast) or above 0xff (bus too slow). **[Confirmed]** — mainline Linux. Taking the
reference at 24 MHz, as the mainline device trees do for this controller family on
prior Apple SoCs:

| Target SCL | Minimum SCL period (from the child `reg`, see §6.1.6) | Divider | Actual SCL |
|---|---|---|---|
| 400 kHz | 2500 ns | 4 | 375 kHz |
| ~355 kHz | 2816 ns | 5 | 300 kHz |
| 100 kHz | 10000 ns | 15 | 100 kHz |

**Every audio device on every board, baseline and in-scope, asks for 2500 ns, i.e.
400 kHz Fast-mode, divider 4, effective 375 kHz.** **[Confirmed]** — the 2500 ns
value appears on every audio and audio-adjacent I2C child of every board; 24 MHz is
**[Probable]**, inherited from the published binding.

The usable divider range is 4…0xff, so with a 24 MHz reference this controller
cannot exceed 375 kHz — the 400 kHz the platform description requests is a ceiling,
not an achieved rate — and cannot go below ≈5.9 kHz. **[Confirmed]** — mainline
Linux.

The revision register at offset 0x28 gates one control-register bit: parts
reporting revision ≥ 6 require the enable bit (bit 11) of the control register at
0x1c to be set together with the divider and the FIFO-reset and auto-unjam bits.
**[Confirmed]** — mainline Linux. The revision value the in-scope parts report is
**[Unknown]** and must be read on hardware; assume ≥ 6 until measured.

The hardware clock-stretch timeout is approximately 25 ms. **[Probable]** —
mainline Linux states this.

### 6.1.5 Timing/tuning properties on the controller node

Three properties appear on every I2C controller node of every M3, M4, A18 Pro and M5
board, and on most M2-generation controllers. Each is exactly two 32-bit words: **`u32 mask, u32 value`**, applied as
a read-modify-write `new = (old & ~mask) | (value & mask)` to one fixed
configuration register. The register each one targets:

| Property | Target register offset | Meaning of the register |
|---|---|---|
| `trigger-level-tunable` | **0x2c** | FIFO service trigger/watermark configuration |
| `tbuf-tunable` | **0x30** | bus-free time between STOP and the next START (t_BUF) |
| `filter-tunable` | **0x38** | input spike/glitch filter configuration |

Only two distinct value sets exist on any board, and they correlate
exactly with the bus speed requested by the devices on that bus:

| Bus speed | `filter-tunable` (mask, value) | `tbuf-tunable` | `trigger-level-tunable` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 400 kHz (2500 ns) — **all audio buses** | `0xfffff3ff, 0x433343a9` | `0xffff0000, 0x44340000` | `0xffff0000, 0x44330000` |
| 100 kHz (10000 ns) | `0xfffff3ff, 0x476673a9` | `0xffff0000, 0x46340000` | `0xffff0000, 0x46330000` |

Readings:

- The filter register is written almost wholesale; **bits 10 and 11 are explicitly
  preserved** from whatever the register already holds. A host must therefore
  read-modify-write rather than store the literal. **[Confirmed]**
- The two trigger/bus-free registers are written only in bits 31:16; bits 15:0 are
  preserved. **[Confirmed]**
- Between the 100 kHz and 400 kHz variants exactly one nibble of the upper half
  differs in the trigger and bus-free words (bits 27:24: 0x4 at 400 kHz, 0x6 at
  100 kHz), and seven bits differ in the filter word (bits 26, 22, 20, 18, 16, 13,
  12). The internal field decomposition, and therefore the conversion of these
  values into nanoseconds, is **[Unknown]**. What is certain is that they are
  bus-speed-dependent analogue/timing trim, not board-dependent: the same two value
  sets appear on 41 different machines spanning four SoC generations.
  **[Confirmed]**
- These are **not** a delta. The identical property set and the identical 400 kHz
  values are already present on the M2 and M3 generations. The M1 base generation
  omits all three entirely. The M1 Pro/Max generation, and some controllers of the
  M2 Pro/Max generation, instead carry a two-word `filter-tunable` of
  `0x000003a0, 0x000003a0` and no `tbuf-tunable` or `trigger-level-tunable` at all —
  a different, earlier scheme in which mask and value are equal, i.e. a plain
  set-these-bits operation. **[Confirmed]**
- No board carries the generic `iic-tunables` array, nor
  `use-table-div`, `force-polling`, `idle-off-delay-us` or `service-gates`; only the
  three named tunables above are supplied. **[Confirmed]**

Bring-up ordering: read the revision register at 0x28 → write 0 to the interrupt
mask at 0x18 → write the control register at 0x1c with the FIFO-reset bits (10 and
9), the auto-unjam bit (8), the divider in bits 7:0 and, if the revision is ≥ 6,
the enable bit (11) → clear the status register at 0x14 → apply the three tunables
at 0x2c, 0x30 and 0x38. The first four steps are the mainline sequence
**[Confirmed]**; the placement of the tunables after them is **[Probable]**.

### 6.1.6 The controller's own reset function

Every I2C controller node carries
`function-device_reset = u32 phandle | 4-byte tag | u32 arg`, where the phandle is
the power-manager node, the tag is stored byte-reversed and reads **`ARST`**, and the
single argument is the **same power-manager device index that appears in
`clock-gates`** for that controller (e.g. 0xbf for t605x i2c1, 0x41 for t8132 i2c3,
0x58 for t8142 i2c3). Reset is therefore not a GPIO: it is a
power-manager-mediated block reset of the controller's own device entry. This is
unchanged from M1–M3. **[Confirmed]**

The power-manager device list resolves those indices to named domains `I2C0`…`I2C8`
(`I2C0`…`I2C4` on t8140), and the index-to-name mapping is self-validating: every
`clock-gates` value anywhere in a given tree resolves to a domain whose name matches
the node that carries it. **[Confirmed]**

Each device entry also carries a 32-bit field whose high byte is an index into the
power-manager node's own `reg` aperture list and whose low 24 bits are a byte offset
within that aperture — i.e. the address of that domain's control register. This
reading was correlated against the aperture list itself: on t604x, t8142 and t8140
every non-zero field in the entire device list lands inside the aperture it names
(341/341, 302/302, 226/226 entries respectively), and on t605x 440 of 451 do. The
resulting control-register addresses for the audio I2C controllers, after
translation through the `/arm-io` `ranges`:

| SoC | Domain | Device index | Control register |
|---|---|---|---|
| t604x | `I2C1` / `I2C2` / `I2C3` | 0xad / 0xae / 0xaf | 0x508300158 / 0x508300160 / 0x508300168 |
| t8140 | `I2C0` | 0x43 | 0x3007002c8 |
| t8142 | `I2C1` / `I2C3` | 0x56 / 0x58 | 0x380700350 / 0x380700360 |
| t605x | `I2C1` / `I2C2` / `I2C3` | 0xbf / 0xc0 / 0xc1 | 0x2809002c8 / 0x2809002d0 / 0x2809002d8 |
| t8132 | `I2C1` / `I2C3` | 0x3f / 0x41 | **[Unknown]** |

Domains are spaced 8 bytes apart in the ascending instance order, so the whole
`I2C0`…`I2C8` block is contiguous. **[Confirmed]**

On **t8132 this field is zero for every one of the 392 entries in the list**, so the
control-register address is either carried in a different field of the entry on that
SoC or is not carried at all. A host targeting t8132 must locate the I2C power
domain registers another way. **[Confirmed]** that the field is zero; the
alternative encoding is **[Unknown]**. See Open question 17.

### 6.1.7 The I2C child `reg` encoding — resolved

The controller node declares `#address-cels = 1` (note the spelling — the property
is **`#address-cels`**, not `#address-cells`, on every I2C controller node of every
board — the misspelling is in the platform description itself, so match the string
exactly) and
`#size-cells = 3`. A child `reg` is therefore four 32-bit words:

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | **7-bit I2C target address**, right-aligned (the R/W bit is not included) |
| 1 | **minimum SCL period in nanoseconds** — the fastest the bus may be clocked for this device |
| 2 | 0 on every I2C child of every board |
| 3 | 0 on every I2C child of every board |

Only three values of word 1 exist anywhere: 2500 (400 kHz), 2816 (≈355 kHz, used
only by USB4 retimer devices), and 10000 (100 kHz). The controller must run at the
slowest period any device on that bus demands. **[Confirmed]** — the interpretation
is pinned by the correlation with the per-bus tunable values in §6.1.5: every bus
whose children say 10000 carries the 100 kHz tunable set and every bus whose
children say 2500 carries the 400 kHz set, without exception on any board.

## 6.2 Bus-to-device map, per in-scope board

All addresses are 7-bit. "amp" = `compatible = "audio-control,sn012776"`,
"codec" = `compatible = "audio-control,cs42l84"` (or `cs42l83` on t8140).
The node named plainly `audio-speaker` is always amplifier index 0 and is the node
that carries `speaker-config`, the `speaker1`…`speakerN` phandles, the shared
shutdown line, the shared interrupt and the speaker-ID pins.

### t8132 (M4)

| Board | Machine | i2c1 | i2c3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| j604 | MacBook Pro 14" M4 | codec 0x4b | 6 amps: 0x38 (L woofer 1), 0x39 (L woofer 2), 0x3a (L tweeter), 0x3b (R woofer 1), 0x3c (R woofer 2), 0x3d (R tweeter) |
| j623 | iMac 24" M4 | codec 0x4b | 4 amps: 0x38, 0x39 (L tweeter), 0x3b (R woofer), 0x3c (R tweeter) |
| j624 | iMac 24" M4 | codec 0x4b | 4 amps: 0x38, 0x39, 0x3b, 0x3c |
| j713 | MacBook Air 13" M4 | codec 0x4b | 4 amps: 0x38, 0x39, 0x3b, 0x3c |
| j715 | MacBook Air 15" M4 | codec 0x4b | 6 amps: 0x38, 0x39 (L tweeter), 0x3a (L woofer 2), 0x3b, 0x3c (R tweeter), 0x3d (R woofer 2) |
| j773g | Mac mini M4 | codec 0x4b | 1 amp: 0x38 |

Note the address-to-position assignment differs between j604 and j715 even though
both have six amplifiers: on j604 0x39 is the second left woofer and 0x3a the left
tweeter, on j715 0x39 is the left tweeter and 0x3a the second left woofer, and on
the right side 0x3c/0x3d are likewise swapped. A driver must take the mapping from
the node names and `speaker-config`, never from the address ordering.
**[Confirmed]**

### t604x (M4 Pro / M4 Max)

| Board | Machine | i2c1 | i2c2 | i2c3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| j614s / j614c | MacBook Pro 14" M4 Pro / Max | 3 amps: 0x38, 0x39 (L woofer 2), 0x3a (L tweeter) | codec 0x4b | 3 amps: 0x3b, 0x3c, 0x3d |
| j616s / j616c | MacBook Pro 16" M4 Pro / Max | same | codec 0x4b | same |
| j773s | Mac mini M4 Pro | 1 amp: 0x38 | codec 0x4b | — |

## 6.3 Bus ownership and arbitration

**Finding: on every in-scope board the host owns every audio I2C bus outright.
There is no arbitration mechanism, no ownership token, no handoff protocol, and
nothing a host driver must negotiate before driving the bus.** **[Confirmed]**

This is a positive finding and it is load-bearing, because the serialiser, clock
generation and stream routing *did* move behind the always-on coprocessor on these
SoCs. Control of the amplifiers and the codec did not follow them.

Supporting facts, each independent of the others:

1. **Topology.** The amplifier and codec nodes are children of `/arm-io/i2cN`
   controller nodes whose `interrupt-parent` is the top-level application-processor
   interrupt controller (`aic`), whose SCL/SDA pin descriptors name pins of the
   application-processor GPIO controller (role tag `AP`), and whose clock/reset
   domain is an ordinary power-manager device entry. Nothing in that path passes
   through the coprocessor or the system-management controller. **[Confirmed]**
2. **The other agents have their own, separate I2C master hardware.** The
   power-manager device list in the same platform description enumerates four
   distinct families of I2C master power domain per SoC — the host's, the always-on
   coprocessor's, the system-management controller's, and the multi-touch
   processor's:

   | SoC | Host | Always-on coprocessor | System-management controller | Multi-touch processor |
   |---|---|---|---|---|
   | t8132 | `I2C0`…`I2C8`, indices 0x3e…0x46 | `AOP_I2CM0`…`AOP_I2CM2`, 0xde…0xe0 | `SMC_I2CM0`…`SMC_I2CM4`, 0x109…0x10d | `MTP_I2CM0`, 0x11f |
   | t604x | `I2C0`…`I2C8`, 0xac…0xb4 | `AOP_I2CM0`…`AOP_I2CM2`, 0x13a…0x13c | `SMC_I2CM0`…`SMC_I2CM6`, 0x166…0x16c | `MTP_I2CM0`, 0x17c |
   | t8140 | `I2C0`…`I2C4`, 0x43…0x47 | `AOP_I2CM0`…`AOP_I2CM3`, 0xa2…0xa5 | `SMC_I2CM0`…`SMC_I2CM2`, 0xd0…0xd2 | `MTP_I2CM0`, 0xe3 |
   | t8142 | `I2C0`…`I2C8`, 0x55…0x5d | `AOP_I2CM0`…`AOP_I2CM3`, 0xe2…0xe5 | `SMC_I2CM0`…`SMC_I2CM4`, 0x114…0x118 | `MTP_I2CM0`, 0x12a |
   | t605x | `I2C0`…`I2C8`, 0xbe…0xc6 | `AOP_I2CM0`…`AOP_I2CM3`, 0x119…0x11c | `SMC_I2CM0`…`SMC_I2CM6`, 0x14a…0x150 | `MTP_I2CM0`, 0x162 |

   **Only the host's `I2C0`…`I2C8` have device nodes in the tree, and the audio
   codecs and amplifiers hang off those.** The coprocessor's and the
   system-management controller's masters have power domains but no nodes, no
   apertures and no children anywhere in the description. **[Confirmed]** — the
   device indices are the same ones that `clock-gates` resolves against, and every
   `clock-gates` value in each tree resolves to a domain whose name matches its node.
3. **The peripherals the coprocessor reaches over its own masters are described as
   unaddressable.** The ambient-light sensor, accelerometer and gyroscope appear
   under the coprocessor's nub as bare nodes with no `reg`, no bus parent and no
   address — the pattern the description uses for a device the host cannot address.
   No audio device appears in that form on any in-scope board. **[Confirmed]**
4. **The always-on coprocessor's I2C domains are marked as belonging to the
   coprocessor island**, carrying the same flags byte (0x10) as the audio power
   domains, whereas every host `I2Cn` domain carries 0x00. On t605x the
   coprocessor's four I2C domains additionally carry **no host control-register
   address at all** (the control-register field of their device entries is zero,
   while all nine host `I2Cn` entries carry real addresses), so the host cannot even
   gate them. **[Confirmed]**
5. **The system-management controller touches no audio I2C bus on any in-scope
   board.** Its only audio-adjacent role anywhere is the microphone
   supply enable on one machine (§6.9), which is a power rail, not a bus.
   **[Confirmed]**
6. **The second always-on coprocessor instance (`/arm-io/aop2`) has no I2C power
   domain of its own** in any in-scope tree. **[Probable]**

### What a host driver must do before touching an audio I2C bus

No coprocessor handshake. The required sequence is entirely local:

1. Enable the controller's clock/power domain — the power-manager device index in
   `clock-gates` (table in §6.1.2).
2. Optionally reset the controller via its `function-device_reset` (same
   power-manager device index, tag `ARST`).
3. Program the clock divider for the slowest device on the bus (§6.1.4), apply the
   three tunables (§6.1.5), clear status, mask interrupts.
4. **For an amplifier bus: release the shared shutdown line first** and wait — the
   amplifiers do not acknowledge their addresses while it is asserted (§6.5).
5. **For the codec bus: release the codec reset line first** and wait (§6.7).
6. On a machine with speaker-ID pins, sample them before assuming a calibration set
   (§6.8).

### What the coprocessor *does* own

For completeness, so the boundary is unambiguous: the property that binds the jack
codec to its clock master, `function-codecinput_master`, has changed target. On
M1–M3 its phandle resolves to a port of the host serial audio controller
(a port node of the host serial audio controller). On every in-scope SoC it resolves to a
coprocessor-mediated stream endpoint
(`/arm-io/iop-audio-controller/audio-codec-input/audio-codec-input`). The tag
(`AUD1`) and argument (a byte-reversed four-character code reading `ap2c`) are
unchanged. Likewise `function-codecinput_active` and `external-power-provider`,
which on M1–M3 appear on the codec and amplifier nodes and point at serial-audio-
controller cluster nodes, are **absent from the codec and amplifier nodes on every
in-scope board** — those clusters no longer have host-visible nodes to point at.
**[Confirmed]**

So the boundary is: **clocking and streaming — coprocessor. Register-level device
control over I2C, reset, shutdown, interrupt and identification GPIOs — host.**

## 6.4 GPIO controllers

### 6.4.1 Instances

Every instance carries `compatible = "gpio,t8101"`, `device_type =
"interrupt-controller"`, `#interrupt-cells = 2`, `#gpio-int-groups = 7` and a
`role` string naming the island it belongs to (`AP` = application-processor island,
`AOP` = always-on island, `NUB` = nub island, `SMC` = system-management island,
`MTP` = multi-touch island). `#gpio-pins` gives the pin count.
`interrupts` lists seven top-level interrupt lines, one per interrupt group.

| SoC | Node | Role | MMIO base | Aperture | Pins | Interrupt group lines | Carries audio lines? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| t8132 | `/arm-io/gpio0` | `AP` | 0x39a000000 | 0x100000 | 224 | 0x12f…0x135 | **yes** — amp shutdown, amp IRQ, codec IRQ, speaker-ID |
| t8132 | `/arm-io/aop-gpio` | `AOP` | 0x390824000 | 0x4000 | 57 | 0x1a7…0x1ad | no |
| t8132 | `/arm-io/nub-gpio` | `NUB` | 0x3881f0000 | 0x4000 | 32 | 0x1f3…0x1f9 | **yes** — codec reset |
| t8132 | `/arm-io/smc-gpio` | `SMC` | 0x38c820000 | 0x4000 | 18 | 0x228…0x22e | no |
| t604x | `/arm-io/gpio0` | `AP` | 0x51c000000 | 0x4000 | 200 | 0x1de…0x1e4 | **yes** — amp shutdown, amp IRQ, codec IRQ, speaker-ID |
| t604x | `/arm-io/aop-gpio0` | `AOP` | 0x510824000 | 0x4000 | 85 | 0x2bc…0x2c2 | no |
| t604x | `/arm-io/nub-gpio0` | `NUB` | 0x5081e4000 | 0x4000 | 61 | 0x333…0x339 | **yes** — codec reset |
| t604x | `/arm-io/smc-gpio0` | `SMC` | 0x50c824000 | 0x4000 | 24 | 0x3d9…0x3df | no |
| t8140 | `/arm-io/gpio0` | `AP` | 0x31a000000 | 0x100000 | 216 | 0x107…0x10d | **yes** — amplifier enable, codec reset, codec IRQ |
| t8140 | `/arm-io/aop-gpio` | `AOP` | 0x310824000 | 0x4000 | 57 | 0x17c…0x182 | no |
| t8140 | `/arm-io/nub-gpio` | `NUB` | 0x3081f0000 | 0x4000 | 30 | 0x1d9…0x1df | no |
| t8140 | `/arm-io/smc-gpio` | `SMC` | 0x30c820000 | 0x4000 | **6** | 0x23c…0x242 | no (but see §6.9) |
| t8140 | `/arm-io/mtp-gpio` | `MTP` | 0x314838000 | 0x4000 | 10 | 0x468…0x46e | no |
| t8142 | `/arm-io/gpio0` | `AP` | 0x39a000000 | 0x100000 | 224 | 0x15b…0x161 | **yes** — amp shutdown, amp IRQ, codec IRQ, speaker-ID |
| t8142 | `/arm-io/aop-gpio` | `AOP` | 0x390824000 | 0x4000 | 77 | 0x1e0…0x1e6 | no |
| t8142 | `/arm-io/nub-gpio` | `NUB` | 0x3881f0000 | 0x4000 | 40 | 0x23e…0x244 | **yes** — codec reset |
| t8142 | `/arm-io/smc-gpio` | `SMC` | 0x38c820000 | 0x4000 | 18 | 0x270…0x276 | no |
| t605x | `/arm-io/gpio0` | `AP` | 0x29c000000 | **0x44000** | 221 | 0x1e6…0x1ec | **yes** — amp shutdown, amp IRQ, codec reset, codec IRQ, speaker-ID |
| t605x | `/arm-io/aop-gpio0` | `AOP` | 0x290824000 | 0x4000 | 85 | 0x238…0x23e | no |
| t605x | `/arm-io/nub-gpio0` | `NUB` | 0x2881e4000 | 0x4000 | 61 | 0x2c2, 0x2c4, 0x2c6, 0x2c8, 0x2ca, 0x2cc, 0x2ce (**stride 2**) | no |

Baseline for comparison: t8122 application-processor island 0x2c7100000 / 224 pins,
always-on island 0x2f4824000 / 54, nub island 0x2e41f0000 / 32, system-management
island 0x2ec820000 / 18. t6030 application-processor island 0x347100000 / 224, nub
island 0x3641f0000 / 37. t6031 application-processor island 0x2b3000000 (0x4000) /
200, always-on island 0x2a8824000 / 102, nub island 0x2a01f0000 / 59,
system-management island 0x2a4820000 / 30. **[Confirmed]**

Deltas worth flagging to a driver author:

- **t605x has no system-management GPIO controller node at all.** Its predecessor
  t604x has one with 24 pins. Any code that assumes four GPIO controllers must
  tolerate three. **[Confirmed]**
- **t605x nub GPIO controller interrupt lines are spaced 2 apart**, not 1, unlike
  every other GPIO controller on every other SoC. **[Confirmed]**
- **t605x AP GPIO aperture is 0x44000**, a third size distinct from the 0x100000
  used by base dies and the 0x4000 used by t604x/t603x. **[Confirmed]**
- **t8140 adds a fifth controller** (`mtp-gpio`, role `MTP`, 10 pins) for the
  multi-touch processor island, and its system-management controller exposes only
  6 pins. **[Confirmed]**
- Always-on and nub GPIO pin counts grew with each generation (always-on island
  54 → 57 → 77 → 85; nub island 32 → 40 → 61). **[Confirmed]**

### 6.4.2 Pin-to-register mapping

Identical to M1–M3 and to the mainline Linux pinctrl/GPIO driver for this SoC
family, and unchanged on every in-scope SoC. **[Confirmed]** — mainline Linux.

| Address | Contents |
|---|---|
| `base + 4·pin` | 32-bit configuration/data register for that pin |
| `base + 0x800 + 0x40·group + 4·(pin >> 5)` | interrupt pending/acknowledge, one bit per pin (bit `pin % 32`), write-1-to-clear; `group` is the value in bits 18:16 of that pin's own register |

Per-pin register fields **[Confirmed]** — mainline Linux:

| Bits | Field |
|---|---|
| 0 | data (output level when driving; input level when reading) |
| 3:1 | mode — 1 = output; 2 = input, interrupt on high level; 3 = input, interrupt on low level; 4 = input, interrupt on rising edge; 5 = input, interrupt on falling edge; 6 = input, interrupt on either edge; 7 = input, interrupt disabled (also the value used for a plain input, and the value used to mask the interrupt) |
| 6:5 | peripheral (alternate function) select |
| 8:7 | pull — 0 = off, 1 = pull-down, 2 = strong pull-up, 3 = pull-up |
| 9 | input buffer enable |
| 11:10 | drive strength (low half) |
| 15 | Schmitt trigger |
| 18:16 | interrupt group (selects which of the seven top-level lines this pin's interrupt raises) |
| 21 | lock |
| 23:22 | drive strength (high half) |

So: **a pin number quoted in a `function-*` property is an index into the pin space
of the GPIO controller named by that property's phandle, and the register that
controls it is at that controller's MMIO base plus four times the pin number.**
There is no global pin numbering; pin 0x6b on the AP controller and pin 0x6b on the
nub controller are unrelated pins on different blocks at different base addresses.

### 6.4.3 `function-*` property encoding

`function-<name>` = `u32 phandle | 4-byte tag (stored byte-reversed) | u32 arg0 | u32 arg1 …`.
Tags observed on audio-relevant nodes:

| Tag (readable) | Provider | Argument layout |
|---|---|---|
| `GPIO` | a GPIO controller node | `arg0` = pin number, `arg1` = flags word |
| `ARST` | the power-manager node | `arg0` = power-manager device index to reset |
| `AUD1` | a coprocessor audio stream endpoint | `arg0` = four-character stream selector, byte-reversed |
| `aPSC` | an audio DMA controller node | no arguments |
| `pKW4` | the system-management controller's power service | `arg0` = four-character key naming one managed line, `arg1` = command template |
| `pKW8` | the system-management controller's power service | `arg0` = four-character key (`pcIO`), `arg1` = command template, `arg2` = line selector, bits 23:16 = index, bits 27:24 = flag |

Flags words that occur on `GPIO`-tag functions, on any board of any generation:

| Flags | Where it appears | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| `0x00000000` | bus reset lines with no host drive requirement | no drive, no read-back |
| `0x00000001` | **jack codec reset**, and other simple outputs | output |
| `0x00000002` | clock-request and receive lines | peripheral function |
| `0x00000003` | one receive line on t8140 | output + peripheral |
| `0x00000100` | **speaker-ID 0 and 1**, hot-plug detect, panic notify | input only |
| `0x00000101` | debug and power-enable lines | output + input read-back |
| `0x00000102` | transmit lines | peripheral + input read-back |
| `0x00010001` | **shared amplifier shutdown line**, SPI chip-selects | output, plus one further attribute |
| `0x00010102` | **every I2C SCL and SDA descriptor** | peripheral + input read-back, plus that same further attribute |

Bit 0 = the line is driven by the host as an output. Bit 1 = the line is assigned to
the block's peripheral function rather than to the GPIO block. Bit 8 = the input
buffer is enabled so the level can be read back. **[Probable]**
Bit 16 appears only on the shared amplifier shutdown line, on SPI chip-selects and
on I2C bus pins — three cases that share the property of being a *bus-level or
multi-consumer* line rather than a point-to-point one. Its exact meaning is
**[Unknown]** and it is not needed to drive the pin.

---

## 6.5 The shared amplifier shutdown line

**Still true, unchanged, on t8132, t604x, t8142 and t605x: every speaker amplifier
in the machine shares one software-shutdown GPIO.** **[Confirmed]**

The platform description declares `function-reset` **only on amplifier index 0**
(the node named `audio-speaker`). The other amplifier nodes — reached through the
`speaker1`…`speakerN` phandles on that node — carry no `function-reset` of their
own, no interrupt and no interrupt parent. There is exactly one line, and it goes to
every amplifier's shutdown pin, including amplifiers on a *different* I2C bus: on
t604x and t605x the left-side amplifiers sit on i2c1 and the right-side ones on
i2c3, and both groups are gated by the single line declared on the i2c1 node's
amplifier index 0. **[Confirmed]**

The public counterpart's pin is `SDZ`, active-low: low = shutdown, high = operating.
The flags word is `0x00010001` (host-driven output) on every board, and the
published upstream binding for the counterpart declares this line
`GPIO_ACTIVE_HIGH` for the logical "enable" sense, i.e. logical 1 on the pin means
the amplifier is out of shutdown.

| SoC | GPIO controller | Pin | Consumers |
|---|---|---|---|
| t8132 (j604, j623, j624, j713, j715, j773g) | `AP` | **0x0f (15)** | all amplifiers on i2c3 (1, 4 or 6 devices depending on board) |
| t604x (j614s/c, j616s/c, j773s, j575c) | `AP` | **0x36 (54)** | all amplifiers on i2c1 **and** i2c3 |
| t8142 (j704, j813, j815) | `AP` | **0x97 (151)** | all amplifiers on i2c3 |
| t605x (j714s/c, j716s/c) | `AP` | **0x6b (107)** | all amplifiers on i2c1 **and** i2c3 |
| t8140 (j700) | `AP` | **0x69 (105)** | the control-bus-less amplifiers — see §6.6 |

Baseline, for the A/B chassis pairs: j613/j504 (t8122) pin 0x0d (13) → j713/j604
(t8132) pin 0x0f (15); j514s (t6030) pin 0xab (171) and j516c (t6031) pin 0x1c (28)
→ j614s/j616c (t604x) pin 0x36 (54) → j714s/j716c (t605x) pin 0x6b (107). The
*mechanism* is unchanged; only the pin number moves. **[Confirmed]**

### Required ordering and hold times

The line is shared, so **every operation on it is machine-wide**. Asserting it puts
every amplifier in the machine into shutdown simultaneously and their register
contents are lost; a host must therefore treat it as a global resource and
re-initialise all amplifiers after any assertion.

| Step | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Before any I2C transaction to any amplifier | the line must be deasserted (amplifiers enabled). While asserted the amplifiers do not acknowledge their addresses. **[Confirmed]** |
| After deassertion, before the first register access | **≥ 1 ms** settle. The public counterpart's published flow uses 1–2 µs-resolution sleep of 1000–2000 µs at exactly this point. **[Confirmed]** — these machines are operated with the same ≥ 1 ms wait between releasing the line and the first transaction |
| Assertion hold time, when cycling the line to force a clean state | **≥ 10 ms** asserted before deassertion, on these machines. The public counterpart's published flow uses 20 ms. Use 20 ms to satisfy both. **[Confirmed]** |
| On entering system sleep | assert the line, then allow **≥ 6 ms** before removing supplies (the public counterpart's published suspend flow waits 6–7 ms) **[Probable]** |
| Register state across an assertion | **not retained.** All amplifier registers must be rewritten after the line is deasserted. **[Confirmed]** — the public counterpart specifies the register file as undefined after an SDZ low period |
| After deassertion, before relying on the amplifier | issue the part's software-reset register write and wait a further **1–2 ms** **[Probable]** |

There is a second, distinct reset concept on the public counterpart — a hardware
`RESET` pin separate from `SDZ`. **No in-scope board declares a second GPIO for the
amplifiers**; only the one shutdown line exists. **[Confirmed]**

---

## 6.6 The control-bus-less amplifier machine (t8140 / j700)

This is the largest per-machine difference in the section.

On j700 the speaker amplifier node is **not a child of any I2C controller**. It sits
at `/arm-io/iop-audio-controller/audio-speaker` with
`compatible = "audio-control,max98360"` and no `reg`, no address, no interrupt and
no interrupt parent. Its public counterpart is the MAX98360A/B/C/D family: a digital
input Class-D amplifier with **no I2C or SPI control interface whatsoever**.
**[Confirmed]**

Everything the host can do to this amplifier it does through **one GPIO line**:

| Property | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `function-reset` | AP GPIO controller, pin **0x69 (105)**, flags `0x00010001` | the amplifier's enable line |
| `num-channels` | 2 | two amplifier channels are gated by this one line |
| `mute-ramp-sleep-ms` | **20** (0x14) | 20 ms |
| `enable-iop-ramp-down` | present, empty | the coprocessor performs a digital ramp-down before the line is dropped |

### What the line does

On the public counterpart the `EN` pin is a hard enable: driven low the part is fully
powered down and draws quiescent current only; driven high it powers up. The part
has no register state, so there is nothing to lose and nothing to restore — the only
consequence of toggling it is an audible transient if the digital audio input is not
already silent. Gain and (in TDM mode) which slot the part consumes are set by a
resistor network on a separate `GAIN_SLOT` pin and are **not host-controllable**;
the host cannot read or change amplifier gain on this machine. **[Confirmed]** —
public datasheet.

The part also auto-enters standby when the serial-audio input goes idle and exits it
when the input toggles, so the enable line is not the only thing gating output.
**[Probable]**

### Timing requirements

| Requirement | Value | Source / confidence |
|---|---|---|
| Turn-on time after `EN` rises, A/B variants | ~1 ms | public datasheet **[Confirmed]** |
| Volume ramp during turn-on and turn-off, C/D variants | 13 ms | public datasheet **[Confirmed]** |
| **Mute/ramp settle before the enable line may be dropped** | **20 ms** | carried by the platform description as `mute-ramp-sleep-ms`; consistent with the 13 ms C/D ramp plus margin **[Confirmed]** |
| Ordering on stop | silence or digitally ramp the stream → wait 20 ms → drive `EN` low | **[Confirmed]** |
| Ordering on start | drive `EN` high → wait ≥ 20 ms (covers both the 1 ms A/B and the 13 ms C/D ramps with margin) → unmute the stream | **[Probable]** |
| Which variant (A/B vs C/D) is fitted | not determined | **[Unknown]** — the platform description names only the family; the 20 ms value implies C or D but does not prove it |

Because `enable-iop-ramp-down` is present, the digital ramp is performed by the
coprocessor-side stream, not by the host; the host's obligation is the 20 ms wait
and the correct ordering. **[Probable]**

### Consequences for a driver

- No speaker-protection telemetry is possible on j700: there is no current/voltage
  sense return path from this part and no registers to read. `speaker-protection`,
  `speaker-config`, `bop-config`, `amp-dcblocker-config` and `amp-tx-zd-config` are
  all **absent** from the j700 amplifier node. **[Confirmed]**
- There is **no amplifier interrupt line** on j700. **[Confirmed]**
- There are **no speaker-ID pins** on j700. **[Confirmed]**
- Excursion/thermal limits must come from a fixed per-machine table, not from the
  part.

---

## 6.7 Codec and amplifier interrupt lines

### Specifier encoding

On a node whose `interrupt-parent` is a GPIO controller, `interrupts` is two 32-bit
words: **`u32 pin | u32 flags`**. The pin is an index into that controller's pin
space, exactly as in a `function-*` property. This decoding is pinned by comparison
with the published in-tree platform descriptions of baseline machines, where the
same pin numbers appear explicitly: j274 codec interrupt pin 0xb7 = 183, published
as `<183 IRQ_TYPE_LEVEL_LOW>`; j613 amplifier interrupt pin 0x0c = 12 and codec
interrupt pin 0xad = 173, published as 12 and 173 with the same type.
**[Confirmed]**

The flags word is **`0x00000001` on every audio interrupt on every board**,
baseline and in-scope. Against the published descriptions of the same
machines, that value corresponds to **active-low, level-triggered**. **[Confirmed]**
Non-audio nodes use other values (e.g. `0x02000002`, `0x03000002`, `0x05000004`, and
`0x02000000` on the M1/M2 touch blocks). **How the remaining bytes are partitioned is
[Unknown].** Two readings fit the platform description and they disagree about the audio pins: low
byte = trigger type with the upper byte selecting the interrupt group, which places the
audio pins in **group 0**; or upper byte = trigger type with the low byte the group,
which places them in **group 1**. The `0x02000000` words on j293 pin 194 and j493
pin 174 — published upstream as `IRQ_TYPE_EDGE_FALLING` — are consistent only with the
second, since under the first they decode to a trigger type 0 that is not defined above.
Nothing else in the platform description discriminates. **The interrupt group an audio pin is steered
into is therefore [Unknown] and must be read back from bits 18:16 of the pin's own
configuration register (§6.4.2), which is where the steering actually lives** — the
platform description does not state it and a driver must program it. See Open question 19
and §5 Open question 11.

### Lines

| SoC | Amplifier interrupt (AP GPIO pin) | Codec interrupt (AP GPIO pin) | Codec reset (controller, pin) |
|---|---|---|---|
| t8132 | 0x0e (14) | 0x62 (98) | **nub**, 0x11 (17) |
| t604x | 0x37 (55) | 0x6a (106) | **nub**, 0x3a (58) |
| t8140 | — (none) | 0x68 (104) | **AP**, 0x67 (103) |
| t8142 | 0x96 (150) | 0x64 (100) | **nub**, 0x12 (18) |
| t605x | 0x6a (106) | 0x86 (134) | **AP**, 0x8b (139) |

Baseline: t8122 (j613/j504) amplifier 0x0c (12), codec 0xad (173), codec reset nub
0x11 (17); t6030 (j514s) amplifier 0xc3 (195), codec 0xc4 (196), codec reset nub
0x15 (21); t6031 (j516c) amplifier 0x1d (29), codec 0x1e (30), codec reset nub 0x3a
(58). **[Confirmed]**

### Shared vs dedicated

- **The amplifier interrupt is shared and is declared only on amplifier index 0**,
  exactly as the shutdown line is, and exactly as on M1–M3. One pin serves every
  amplifier in the machine, across both I2C buses on the Pro/Max dies.
  **[Confirmed]**
- **The codec interrupt is dedicated** — one codec, one pin. **[Confirmed]**
- The two are always on the **application-processor** GPIO controller, never on the
  always-on or system-management ones, on every board. **[Confirmed]**

### Identifying the source of a shared amplifier interrupt

Because the line is level-triggered active-low and wired-OR across up to six
devices, the host cannot learn the source from the GPIO block. It must poll each
amplifier's latched interrupt status registers over I2C — reading the latched
registers is also what clears them and releases the line. The public counterpart
exposes three latched interrupt status registers and three corresponding masks; at
bring-up the masks must be programmed before the line is unmasked at the GPIO, or
the level-triggered line may already be asserted and will storm. **[Probable]**

The practical sequence, per interrupt: read latch registers on every amplifier on
every audio bus in turn → act → re-read the GPIO pin's data bit to confirm the line
has released → acknowledge the GPIO interrupt by writing 1 to the pin's bit in the
group pending register. If the line is still low after servicing all devices, a
device is stuck and the shared shutdown line must be cycled (§6.5), which affects
all amplifiers. **[Inferred]**

### Delta

Two changes, both trivial to accommodate but both fatal if assumed away:

1. **On t8140 and t605x the codec reset moved from the nub GPIO controller to the
   application-processor GPIO controller.** On t8132, t8142 and the whole M1–M3
   baseline it is on the nub controller. A driver must read the phandle, not assume
   the controller. **[Confirmed]**
2. **On t8140 there is no amplifier interrupt at all**, because the amplifier has no
   control bus and nothing to report. **[Confirmed]**

---

## 6.8 Speaker module identification GPIOs

Unchanged in mechanism from M1 Pro/Max onward; only the pin numbers move.
**[Confirmed]**

Amplifier index 0 carries, when the machine supports it:

| Property | Content |
|---|---|
| `find-speaker-id` | `1` — the machine has an identification mechanism and it must be read |
| `function-speaker-id0` | GPIO controller phandle, tag `GPIO`, pin, flags `0x00000100` (input only) |
| `function-speaker-id1` | as above, second pin |
| `valid-speaker-ids` | two 32-bit words: **`0x00000000` and `0x00000003`** |

**Encoding: two pins, both inputs on the application-processor GPIO controller, read
as a 2-bit value. Of the four possible codes only two are valid — 0b00 and 0b11.**
The `valid-speaker-ids` value is byte-for-byte identical (`0000000003000000`) on
every board that carries it, from M1 Pro/Max through M5 Max.
**[Confirmed]**

The two valid codes correspond to two speaker-module suppliers/variants fitted to
the same chassis. The identity selects **which calibration and protection parameter
set applies** to the amplifiers — excursion limits, thermal model coefficients and
the tuning tables the machine's amplifier configuration properties feed. It does
**not** change bus addresses, slot allocation or any control-path behaviour.
**[Probable]**

Reading order: the pins are inputs with the input buffer enabled by the flags word;
set mode 7 (input, interrupt disabled), read bit 0 of each pin register, and form
`id = (id1 << 1) | id0`. A value other than 0 or 3 indicates a hardware fault or a
pin not yet settled and must not be used to select a calibration set.
**[Inferred]**

| SoC / board | id0 pin (AP GPIO) | id1 pin (AP GPIO) |
|---|---|---|
| t8132 — j604, j623, j624, j713, j715 | 0x04 (4) | 0x0d (13) |
| t8132 — j773g | **absent** | **absent** |
| t604x — j614s/c, j616s/c | 0x34 (52) | 0x35 (53) |
| t604x — j773s, j575c | **absent** | **absent** |
| t8140 — j700 | **absent** | **absent** |
| t8142 — j704 | 0xc6 (198) | 0xc7 (199) |
| t8142 — j813 | **absent** | **absent** |
| t8142 — j815 | 0x06 (6) | 0x0b (11) |
| t605x — j714s/c, j716s/c | 0x88 (136) | 0x89 (137) |
| *baseline* t8122 — j613, j504 | 0x9b (155) | 0x9c (156) |
| *baseline* t6030 — j514s | 0x03 (3) | 0x04 (4) |
| *baseline* t6031 — j516c | 0x1a (26) | 0x1b (27) |

Pattern: **machines without a portable-chassis speaker module** — the Mac mini
(j773g, j773s), the Mac Studio (j575c), the iMacs (j623, j624), the MacBook Air 13"
(j813) and the MacBook Neo (j700) — omit the mechanism entirely and carry no
`find-speaker-id`. Note that j813 omits it while its 15-inch sibling j815 has it,
so this is per-board, not per-SoC. **[Confirmed]**

## 6.9 Regulators, supplies and enable ordering

### On t8132, t604x, t8142, t605x: none

**No supply-enable GPIO or regulator is associated with any audio device on any of
these boards.** The codec and amplifier nodes carry no supply phandle, no regulator
reference, and no power-enable function of any kind. Their rails are brought up
unconditionally by the power-management chain before the host runs; the only
"enable" a driver performs is releasing the reset/shutdown GPIOs of §6.5 and §6.7.
**[Confirmed]** — no such property exists on any audio node of any in-scope board.

The M1–M3 `external-power-provider` property that appeared on codec and amplifier
nodes is **absent** on all in-scope boards (§6.3); it was a binding to a
serial-audio-controller cluster's power domain, not a supply rail, and that
cluster no longer has a host-visible node.

### On t8140 (j700): the microphone array supply

One machine in scope does carry an input-power enable. The internal digital
microphone stream node
`/arm-io/iop-audio-controller/audio-hp-mic/audio-hp-mic`
(`compatible = "audio-data,external"`, `device-name = "Digital Mic"`, sources
`imi1`/`imi2` — internal microphone 1 and 2) carries:

```
function-input_power_enable = <phandle-of /arm-io/smc/iop-smc-nub/smc-pmu>
                              'pKW8'          (tag, stored byte-reversed)
                              'pcIO'          (arg0, stored byte-reversed)
                              0x00000000      (arg1, command template)
                              0x00190000      (arg2, line selector)
```

Decoding:

- The provider is the **system management controller's power service**, not a GPIO
  controller. The supply is switched by the system-management controller, not by the
  host.
- The tag `pKW8` denotes an 8-byte write to the key named by `arg0`; `pKW4` (used by
  the same service on t8132 and t8142) denotes a 4-byte write to a key that itself
  names a single line.
- `arg0` = `pcIO` is the aggregate line-control key used on t8140 and t605x. On
  t8132/t8142 the equivalent functions instead name one key per line (`gP0f`,
  `gP19`, `gP1a`, `gP1c`, `gP1d`, `gp0e`, `gP13`).
- `arg2` bits 23:16 select **line index 0x19 (25)**; bits 27:24 are a flag, 0 here.
  Cross-checking the same service's other functions on the same and adjacent SoCs
  confirms the index: line 0x19 on t8140/t605x corresponds to key `gP19` on
  t8132/t8142, line 0x0f to `gP0f`, 0x1a to `gP1a`, 0x1c to `gP1c`, 0x1d to `gP1d`,
  0x0e to `gp0e`. **[Confirmed]**
- `arg1` = 0 appears to be a **command template** into which the desired level is
  merged, rather than the value itself. Template values that occur elsewhere in the
  platform description are `0x00000000`, `0x00010000` and `0x00800000`, and they track the
  *function* of the line rather than the machine — power-enable lines carry
  `0x00800000` or `0x00000000`, reset lines carry `0x00010000` — which is what one
  would expect of a template. **[Inferred]** The exact command word a host must send
  to assert the line is **[Unknown]**; see Open question 18.

**Ordering:** the microphone supply must be enabled — one command to the
system-management controller's power service naming line 25 — **before** the
low-power microphone path is started. Nothing on the I2C control buses depends on
it, and the jack codec on j700 is unaffected by it. **[Confirmed]** that the
dependency exists and that it gates the microphone path; **[Unknown]** what the
settling delay is — the platform description carries no delay value for it, and none
of the other lines driven through the same service on any board carries one either.
Budget the system-management controller's own command turnaround (which is not
instantaneous — this is a message to a separate processor, not an MMIO write) plus a
microphone-array power-on time that must be measured. See Open question 9.

### Ordering summary for a full audio bring-up

1. Enable the I2C controller clock/power domains (§6.1.2, §6.3).
2. j700 only: ask the system-management controller to enable the microphone supply
   (line 25) if capture is wanted.
3. Deassert the jack codec reset GPIO (§6.7); wait, then the codec answers on I2C.
4. Deassert the shared amplifier shutdown GPIO (§6.5); wait ≥ 1 ms; every amplifier
   then answers on I2C, on both buses where there are two.
5. Sample the speaker-ID pins (§6.8) and select the calibration set.
6. Program the amplifiers; unmask their interrupt sources; only then unmask the
   shared interrupt pin at the GPIO controller.
7. j700 only: drive the amplifier enable line high and wait ≥ 20 ms before
   unmuting (§6.6).

---

## Per-SoC / per-machine differences

**t8132 (M4) — j604, j623, j624, j713, j715, j773g.** Two audio I2C buses (i2c1
codec, i2c3 amplifiers), both at 400 kHz. Shared amplifier shutdown AP pin 15,
shared amplifier interrupt AP pin 14, codec interrupt AP pin 98, codec reset **nub**
pin 17. Speaker-ID AP pins 4 and 13 on all boards except j773g. Four GPIO
controllers. Amplifier count 6 (j604, j715), 4 (j623, j624, j713), 1 (j773g). No
supply enables. Every one of these numbers is constant across all six boards —
the only per-board variation on this SoC is the amplifier count, the
address-to-position mapping, and the presence of speaker-ID.

**t604x (M4 Pro/Max) — j614s, j614c, j616s, j616c, j773s, j575c.** Three audio I2C
buses; amplifiers split left (i2c1) / right (i2c3) with the codec alone on i2c2.
Shared shutdown AP pin 54 gates amplifiers on **both** buses. Shared amplifier
interrupt AP pin 55, codec interrupt AP pin 106, codec reset **nub** pin 58.
Speaker-ID AP pins 52 and 53 on the notebooks only. Four GPIO controllers, AP
aperture 0x4000 with 200 pins. j773s and j575c have a single amplifier on i2c1 and
no i2c3 audio.

**t8140 (A18 Pro) — j700.** One audio I2C bus (i2c0) carrying one device, the
`cs42l83` jack codec at **0x48** — a different part and a different address from
every other in-scope machine. No amplifier on any bus; the `max98360` amplifier pair
is enabled by AP pin 105 and nothing else (§6.6), with a mandatory 20 ms mute-ramp
wait. Codec reset is on the **AP** controller (pin 103), not the nub controller.
Codec interrupt AP pin 104. No amplifier interrupt, no speaker-ID, no
speaker-protection data. **Five** GPIO controllers — the extra one serves the
multi-touch processor — and the system-management controller exposes only 6 pins.
The only audio supply enable anywhere in scope is here: the internal microphone
array rail, switched by the system-management controller on line 25.

**t8142 (M5) — j704, j813, j815.** Two audio I2C buses (i2c1 codec, i2c3
amplifiers). Shared shutdown AP pin 151, shared amplifier interrupt AP pin 150,
codec interrupt AP pin 100, codec reset **nub** pin 18. Speaker-ID present on j704
(AP 198/199) and j815 (AP 6/11) but **absent on j813**. Four GPIO controllers; the
always-on controller grew to 77 pins and the nub controller to 40. Amplifier count 6
(j704, j815), 4 (j813).

**t605x (M5 Pro/Max) — j714s, j714c, j716s, j716c.** Three audio I2C buses, same
left/right split as t604x. Shared shutdown AP pin 107 gating both buses, shared
amplifier interrupt AP pin 106, codec interrupt AP pin 134. **Codec reset moved to
the AP controller, pin 139.** Speaker-ID AP pins 136 and 137. **Only three GPIO
controllers — the system-management GPIO controller node is gone.** AP aperture is
0x44000 with 221 pins; the nub controller's seven interrupt lines are spaced 2 apart
rather than 1. All four boards are identical in every audio respect.

---

## Open questions

1. **Prove host ownership on live hardware.** Attach a logic analyser or an I2C
   sniffer to SCL/SDA of the amplifier bus (SoC pins listed in §6.1.2) and boot to a
   fully running system, then play audio and change volume. *What to look for:* every
   transaction on that bus should be preceded, within a few microseconds, by a write
   to the host controller's transmit FIFO at `base+0x00`, observable by trapping the
   controller aperture. If any transaction appears on the wire with no corresponding
   host FIFO write, a second master exists and this section is wrong. Also watch for
   arbitration-lost (bit 22) and bus-jam (bits 24/25) indications in the status
   register at `base+0x14` during heavy playback — a second master would show up
   there. This single experiment settles items 1 and 2 below and is the highest-value
   test in the section.
2. **Does the coprocessor ever drive the amplifier bus during low-power or
   voice-trigger playback?** Repeat experiment 1 with the host suspended and a
   voice-trigger or alarm playback path active. *What to look for:* any I2C traffic
   to addresses 0x38–0x3d while the host controller aperture is quiescent or its
   power domain is gated. If such traffic exists, the amplifiers are reachable by
   some second agent and a host driver must not assume exclusive access across
   suspend.
3. **Decode the three tuning registers into nanoseconds.** Read the registers at
   `base+0x2c`, `base+0x30` and `base+0x38` on a 400 kHz audio bus and on a 100 kHz
   bus before and after applying the published values, then sweep candidate fields
   while measuring SCL/SDA on a scope. *What to look for:* which field changes the
   measured STOP-to-START bus-free time (register 0x30), which changes the minimum
   glitch width the controller rejects on SDA (register 0x38, inject 10–200 ns
   glitches), and which changes the FIFO service point (register 0x2c, observe the
   gap between bytes with a partially filled FIFO). Until this is done a driver must
   copy the literals and preserve the masked bits.
4. **Confirm the controller revision and the meaning of control-register bit 11.**
   Read `base+0x28` on each in-scope SoC. *What to look for:* whether the value is
   ≥ 6, and whether clearing bit 11 of `base+0x1c` after bring-up breaks transfers.
   A host that omits this bit on a revision that needs it may see silent corruption
   rather than an error.
5. **Confirm the I2C reference clock is 24 MHz on M4/M5.** Program divider values 4,
   8 and 15 and measure SCL with a scope. *What to look for:* SCL = f_ref/(16·n).
   If f_ref is not 24 MHz, every audio bus is running at the wrong speed when a
   driver computes the divider from the 2500 ns period.
6. **Measure the real minimum hold time on the shared amplifier shutdown line.**
   Drive the line low for 1, 2, 5, 10 and 20 ms and, after each, attempt an I2C read
   of an amplifier identification register. *What to look for:* the shortest
   assertion after which every amplifier on both buses comes back with default
   register contents, and the shortest post-deassertion delay after which the first
   read acknowledges. The 10 ms / 1 ms figures in §6.5 are what the machines use,
   not what the part requires.
7. **Confirm the shutdown line really is common to both I2C buses on the Pro/Max
   dies.** Assert the line and attempt transactions to the amplifiers at 0x3b–0x3d on
   i2c3 while the line declared on the i2c1 amplifier node is low. *What to look
   for:* NAK from all six devices. If the i2c3 group still answers, there is a second
   undeclared line and the platform description is incomplete.
8. **Determine the MAX98360 variant fitted to j700 and its true enable timing.**
   Drive the enable line with a known digital input present and capture the speaker
   terminals. *What to look for:* a ~1 ms hard turn-on (A/B variants) versus a 13 ms
   volume ramp (C/D variants), and whether audible artefacts appear if the 20 ms wait
   is shortened. Also measure the auto-standby entry and exit thresholds by idling
   the serial input — a driver that relies on the enable line alone may find the part
   already in standby.
9. **Measure the j700 microphone supply enable latency.** Issue the
   system-management controller write for line 25 and capture the microphone supply
   rail together with the first valid PDM data. *What to look for:* the total delay
   from command to valid data — command turnaround plus rail rise plus microphone
   start-up. No value for this exists anywhere in the platform description and a
   capture path started too early will return silence or a click.
10. **Verify the polarity and level sense of the shared amplifier interrupt.** Force
    an amplifier fault (over-temperature is the easiest to provoke) and watch the AP
    GPIO pin. *What to look for:* that the line is level-low while any device asserts,
    that it releases only after every device's latch registers have been read, and
    that it is safe to unmask at the GPIO before all amplifiers are configured. A
    level-triggered wired-OR line unmasked too early will livelock the host.
11. **Read the speaker-ID pins on both module variants of the same chassis.** *What
    to look for:* that only 0b00 and 0b11 ever occur, that the value is stable from
    cold boot with no settling time, and which calibration set each code selects. A
    machine read as the wrong variant will be driven with the wrong excursion limits.
12. **Determine the meaning of bit 16 in the GPIO function flags word.** Compare the
    pin register contents at boot for a pin whose function flags have bit 16 set
    (the amplifier shutdown line, an SPI chip-select) against one that does not (the
    codec reset line). *What to look for:* a difference in pull configuration, drive
    strength or lock bit that firmware applies only to the bit-16 pins. It is not
    needed to drive the pin but it may encode a required pull that a host must not
    clear.
13. **Confirm that t605x genuinely has no system-management GPIO controller** rather
    than one omitted from the description. *What to look for:* probe the address
    where the t604x instance sits relative to its island base (0x…c824000 pattern)
    and see whether a controller responds. If one exists but is undescribed, some
    board-level line may be unreachable to a host driver that trusts the tree.
14. **Confirm the audio buses are never put into bit-bang recovery by firmware
    before the host starts.** Read the pin registers for the SCL/SDA pins named in
    §6.1.3 at the earliest possible point after taking over. *What to look for:*
    whether they are in peripheral mode (expected) or GPIO mode, which would indicate
    firmware left a recovery attempt in progress and the host must complete it.
15. **Identify the registers at I2C aperture offsets 0x08, 0x10, 0x20 and 0x44.**
    These are inside the 0x4000 window but are not described by mainline and are not
    named by the platform description, so their function is Unknown. *What to look
    for:* dump the whole 0x4000 window at reset, mid-transfer and after a transfer,
    and note which of the four change and how they track transfer progress. A host
    driver does not need them for ordinary transfers, but one of them may be the only
    way to halt a runaway transfer.
16. **Determine whether the controller has a direct-drive (bit-bang) mode and
    line-level read-back.** *What to look for:* with the bus idle, walk single bits
    through the undocumented registers of question 15 and watch SCL and SDA on a
    scope for a line that follows a written bit, and a bit that follows an externally
    driven line. If such a facility exists it is the clean way to recover a jammed
    audio bus without disturbing the pin mux; if it does not, the GPIO-reassignment
    fallback in §6.1.3 is the only route and must be validated instead.
17. **Recover the I2C power-domain control-register addresses on t8132.** The
    power-manager device entry field that carries them on the other four SoCs is zero
    for every entry on t8132. *What to look for:* compare the remaining bytes of a
    t8132 device entry against the corresponding entry on t8142 for a domain present
    on both, and test candidate addresses by reading them and checking that the
    running/disabled state of a known-idle block matches. Without this a host cannot
    gate or reset the audio I2C controllers on M4 base-die machines.
18. **Determine the exact command word for a system-management-controller line.**
    Needed only on j700, for the microphone supply (§6.9). *What to look for:* with
    the microphone rail on a scope, send the 8-byte payload naming line 25 with the
    template as given and with the low bit set, and see which turns the rail on;
    then measure the command turnaround and the rail rise time together, which also
    answers question 9.

19. **Which interrupt group the amplifier and jack-codec pins are steered into, and
    how the `interrupts` flags word is partitioned.** The audio value `0x00000001`
    decodes to group 0 under one reading of the word and group 1 under the other,
    and the platform description does not discriminate (§6.5 "Specifier encoding"). **[Unknown].**
    *Why it matters:* the group selects which of the seven top-level GPIO interrupt
    lines the pin raises, the platform description does not carry it, and a driver
    that registers a handler on the wrong top-level line will never see the
    amplifier fault interrupt. *What to look for:* read bits 18:16 of the
    configuration register of each audio pin (§6.4.2) on a running machine — that
    field is the steering — and cross-check by masking each top-level GPIO line in
    turn while provoking an amplifier interrupt. Shared with §5 Open question 11.

# 7. Speaker amplifiers

## Baseline

Two amplifier families appear on in-scope machines.

1. **The Apple-exclusive Texas-Instruments-family mono digital-input Class-D
   amplifier with speaker I/V sense**, identified in platform firmware by
   `compatible = "audio-control,sn012776"` (control node) and
   `"audio-data,sn012776"` (stream node). It is fitted on every t8132, t604x,
   t8142 and t605x machine. Its closest public counterpart is the **TAS2764**
   (TI datasheet SLOS998A); the older Apple variant of the **TAS2770** is not
   present on any in-scope board. The public baseline for both counterparts, the
   already-published Apple deviations and the speaker-protection data model are
   established by the public TAS2764 and TAS2770 datasheets, by the deviations
   published for the Apple variant of this part, and by the published
   speaker-protection data model; this section is a delta against those.
2. **The publicly documented control-less Class-D amplifier family**
   (`compatible = "audio-control,max98360"` / `"audio-data,max98360"`, public
   counterpart **MAX98360A**, ADI document 19-100665 Rev 3), fitted only on the
   t8140 machine j700, with `num-channels = 2`. It has no control bus, no
   registers, no telemetry and no fault path to the host. Baseline: the
   MAX98360A datasheet cited above.

**No Analog Devices SSM3515 appears on any in-scope board.** [Confirmed — the
part is present only on the 24-inch iMac M1 (j456/j457); no `audio-control,ssm3515`
node exists on any t8132, t604x, t8140, t8142 or t605x board.] Nothing replaced it; the machines that would have used it
(the M4 iMac j623/j624) use the TI-family part instead.

## Summary of differences

| Item | M1 Pro – M3 Max baseline | t8132 (M4) | t604x (M4 Pro/Max) | **t8140 (A18 Pro)** | t8142 (M5) | t605x (M5 Pro/Max) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Amplifier part | `sn012776` | **unchanged** | **unchanged** | **absent — `max98360`** | **unchanged** | **unchanged** |
| Register map, paging, hidden pages | see 7.3 | unchanged | unchanged | none (no control bus) | unchanged | unchanged |
| Revision ID read back | 0x3x at page 0 / 0x7D | unchanged | unchanged | not readable | unchanged | unchanged |
| I²C addresses | 0x38…0x3D | unchanged | unchanged | n/a | unchanged | unchanged |
| `speaker-config` (level + slot map) | see 7.5.1 | byte-identical | byte-identical | absent | byte-identical | byte-identical |
| `bop-config` (24 bytes) | see 7.5.2 | byte-identical | byte-identical | absent | byte-identical | byte-identical |
| `amp-dcblocker-config` | see 7.5.3 | byte-identical | byte-identical | absent | byte-identical | byte-identical |
| `amp-tx-zd-config` | see 7.5.4 | byte-identical | byte-identical | absent | byte-identical | byte-identical |
| Configuration sequence and delays | see 7.6 | unchanged | unchanged | different (7.9) | unchanged | unchanged |
| Output level per machine | 16.0 / 18.5 / 20.0 / 21.0 dBV | **Mac mini drops to 18.5 dBV** | unchanged | fixed by strap | unchanged | unchanged |
| Sense path fitted | multi-driver machines only; **iMac never** | 4/6-amp portables yes, **iMac no — unchanged from the M3 iMac (j433/j434), not an M4 change** | yes | **impossible** | yes | yes |
| Echo-reference tap endpoint | absent | absent | absent | **present** | **present** | **present** |

**Headline finding: the Apple-exclusive amplifier did not change.** On the
in-scope generations it is the same part, with the same register map, the same
undocumented registers, the same hidden second-level paging, the same
initialisation sequence and byte-for-byte the same per-machine configuration
blobs as on M1 Pro through M3 Max. [**Confirmed**:
(a) every amplifier configuration blob in platform firmware
(`speaker-config`, `bop-config`, `amp-dcblocker-config`, `amp-tx-zd-config`)
is byte-identical on every board from M1 Pro to M5 Max, with
the single exception of a four-amplifier-machine transmit-mask change that had
already happened by the M3 generation; (b) the complete register-programming
sequence required on the M4 and M5 generations is the same as the M3-generation
one, register for register, value for value and in the same order;
(c) the part identification, the I²C addresses, the shared-shutdown/shared-
interrupt topology and the slot map are unchanged.] Anything that a driver
author does correctly for an M1 Pro/M2/M3 machine carries over unchanged.

The two substantive contents of this section are therefore (i) the **complete
specification of what the part is actually programmed with**, which the public
record covers only in part, and (ii) the **A18 Pro machine**, which replaces the
part entirely.
