## 9.8 What the amplifier does if the host does nothing

This is the question of how much protection is left when host software is
absent, wedged or bypassed. The answer, for the speaker, is **none, on every
machine in scope**. What follows is what the silicon *does* do, so that a
driver author does not mistake any of it for speaker protection.

### 9.8.1 SN012776 / TAS2764-class amplifier (every machine except j700)

| Autonomous protection | What it protects | Trigger | Response | Does it protect the speaker? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Graduated thermal foldback** | the amplifier die | die temperature above the first graduated flag | **disabled on every machine in scope** — `TFB_EN = 0` in the platform-supplied `amp-dcblocker-config` (§7 §7.5.3). [Confirmed] | **No — and it is not even running.** The amplifier does not reduce gain as its die heats; only the hard over-temperature shutdown below remains |
| Die over-temperature | the amplifier die | die temperature above an internal threshold (the part family's thermal-foldback threshold range is 100–150 °C, with a recommended maximum operating die temperature of 140 °C — but the graduated foldback that would act on that range is **switched off**, see the row above) | shuts the output stage down; auto-retry when the die cools | **No.** Voice-coil temperature and die temperature are unrelated; the coil reaches 130 °C while the die is barely warm |
| Output over-current | the amplifier output stage | output current beyond the internal limit | output disabled; latch-or-retry selectable | **No.** The limit is a short-circuit threshold, far above any thermally damaging continuous current |
| Supply brown-out prevention | the system supply rail | PVDD/VBAT sagging | fast gain reduction ahead of the limiter | **No.** It tracks the supply, not the load |
| Supply-tracking limiter | the supply rail and output clipping | output approaching the available headroom | gain reduction — **but the limiter is disabled on every machine in scope**: no platform-supplied configuration writes registers 0x0B, 0x1B or 0x1C, and `LIM_CFG0` resets with `LIM_EN = 0`. **[Probable]** — counterpart datasheet reset value, single source, not yet read back; assume no limiter until `LIM_CFG0` has been read from a live part (§7 §7.7) | **No**, twice over: it is switched off, and even when running it limits to the supply, which is set well above the coil's thermal rating |
| Supply over/under-voltage | the part | rail out of range | fault, reported | No |
| Clock-error detection | the part | bit clock or frame sync lost | Class-D output halted after a timeout | Incidentally yes — loss of clock mutes. **Do not rely on it as a safety mechanism** |

There is **no voice-coil thermal model, no excursion limiter, no
sense-driven gain reduction and no user-settable output power cap** in this
part. Its own protection is entirely self-preservation. [Confirmed — the
register map contains no parameter that could express a coil thermal model,
and the entire parameter set of §9.4 lives in host software.]

The one host-settable, persistent constraint that does bound the output is the
analogue level field (§9.4.6) — but that comes out of reset at **maximum**, so
it is a constraint only after the host has written it.

Additionally note the platform-supplied brown-out configuration: a 24-byte
preset that the machine writes into the amplifier's 24-register brown-out
block, byte-identical on every in-scope machine and on every M2-and-later
baseline machine:

```
bop-config = 01 32 02 22 83 2d 80 02 06 32 46 30 02 06 38 40 30 02 06 3e 37 30 ff e6
```

This is supply protection, not speaker protection. Its threshold-to-volts
encoding is **[Unknown]** and is Open question 8.

### 9.8.2 MAX98360A-class amplifier (j700, MacBook Neo)

This part has **no control interface and no sense return**. The platform
description gives it only:

| Property | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `compatible` | `audio-control,max98360` / `audio-data,max98360` | part family |
| `num-channels` | 2 | two mono amplifier instances gated together |
| `function-reset` | GPIO pin 105, flags 0x00010001 | the shutdown/enable pin — the **only** control the host has |
| `samplerate-subset` | 48 000 Hz only | |
| `mute-ramp-sleep-ms` | 20 | ramp settling time before/after the enable pin is toggled |
| `enable-iop-ramp-down` | (flag, empty) | coprocessor performs a ramp-down on stop |
| `iboot-audio-volume` | (placeholder, empty) | boot-chime level |
| `identifier` | `spkr` | |

Its autonomous protection, from the public datasheet family:

| Protection | Threshold | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| Thermal shutdown | **150 °C** die, **18 °C** recovery hysteresis | output disabled until the die cools |
| Short-circuit / over-current | internal | output protected |
| Under-voltage lockout | **1.5 – 2.3 V** | part disabled |
| Supply range | 2.5 – 5.5 V | — |
| Output capability | 3.2 W into 4 Ω at 5 V | — |
| Gain | pin-strapped, one of −3 / 3 / 6 / 9 / 12 dB (fixed at 12 dB in TDM mode) | not host-changeable |

[Confirmed for the part family from the vendor datasheet; the specific
GAIN_SLOT strap fitted on this board is **[Unknown]** — the platform-supplied
full-scale figure of **7.34 V peak (5.19 V RMS, 14.3 dBV)** is the only
statement of it available here, and is [Probable].]

**Speaker protection on j700, stated plainly: there is none in hardware, and
the host has exactly one lever — the enable pin.** There is no digital volume
in the amplifier, no level register, no sense return and no fault reporting
back to the host. Everything protecting those speakers is upstream of the DMA,
in host software. The protection data that exists for this machine is:

- the feed-forward loudspeaker model with the Thiele/Small set in §9.4.4
  (Re 4.43 Ω, Bl 0.70 T·m, Mms 2.147e-4 kg, Kms 1489.8 N/m, Rms 0.1643 N·s/m,
  front port 258 854 N/m / 1.711e-4 kg / 3.279 N·s/m), with excursion control
  **active** (unlike every other in-scope machine);
- a per-model output volume curve, 17 points from −69.53 dB to −0.31 dB;
- a neural-network mitigation stage, 48 kHz, 480-sample blocks, 480-sample
  look-ahead (10 ms), mono in / mono out, **declared to run on the CPU**;
- the factory `SpTS` / `SpGa` objects, present as on every other machine;
- a platform-supplied **peak-power budget** for the speaker path (§9.8.3).

The runtime loudspeaker-model processor on this machine — the same family used
on the 13-inch MacBook Air, but here **without** the system-identification
stage, because there is no sense return to identify from — exposes the
following limits. This is the complete set of constraints that stand between
the host's samples and the transducer on j700:

| Limit | Unit | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Displacement limit | mm | Peak cone excursion |
| Passive-radiator displacement limit | mm | Peak port/radiator excursion |
| Velocity limit (three bands) and maximum velocity attenuation | m/s, dB | Cone velocity, per frequency band |
| Amplitude limit | — | Output amplitude clamp |
| Temperature hard limit / soft limit / headroom | °C | Coil temperature thresholds |
| Maximum temperature attenuation | dB | Ceiling on thermal gain reduction |
| Power hard limits 1–4, power soft limits 1–4, with four time scales | W, s | A **four-tier** power/time limiter — short-term through long-term |
| Maximum power attenuation | dB | Ceiling on power-limiter gain reduction |
| Volts full scale | V | Amplifier full-scale output (7.34 V peak here, §9.4.6) |
| Parasitic resistance | Ω | Series resistance between amplifier and coil |
| Power-amplifier model; low/mid/high rail idle power, ratio, crossover voltage, holdover time | W, —, V, ms | Supply-rail model of the Class-D stage |
| Use battery voltage; battery telemetry gain | — | Optional supply-voltage input to the model |
| Band centres 0–4, mask band minimum/maximum, mask attack/release | Hz, s | Per-band masking of the limiter |

[Confirmed for the limit set and units; the **numeric values** for this
machine are held in a packed parameter vector whose identifier-to-name mapping
is **[Unknown]** — see Open question 14.]

Note what this list implies. Because there is no sense return, **every one of
these limits is evaluated feed-forward from the samples the host writes**,
using the Thiele/Small model. If the host writes the samples without running
the model, not one of these limits exists anywhere in the system.

### 9.8.3 Peak-power budgeting — unique to j700

j700 alone among every board of every generation carries speaker peak-power
budget properties on `/product/audio`:

| Property | Raw value | Decoded |
|---|---|---|
| `speaker-cpms-bgd_inst` | `ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff` | no instantaneous limit |
| `speaker-cpms-bgd_100ms` | `53 05 00 00 4d 15 00 00` | two u32: **1363** and **5453** |
| `speaker-cpms-bgd_1s` | `ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff` | no 1-second limit |

and its power-manager node registers **"speaker"** as a peak-power-management
client with weight 0.95 alongside the package at weight 0.80 — the only board
that does so.

Units: properties of this shape carry a *peak-power range*, so the pair is most
likely a **{minimum, maximum} peak-power budget in milliwatts over a 100 ms
window** (1.363 W to 5.453 W for the two speakers together) [Inferred — the
exact 4.000 ratio between the two values is unexplained and the units are
**[Unknown]**]. **[Probable]**

**This is a system power-delivery budget, not speaker protection.** It bounds
what the speaker path may draw from the battery so that the platform does not
brown out. It does not know about the voice coil. Do not treat it as a safety
limit.

---

## 9.9 Where the protection maths runs — and what happens if the host bypasses the coprocessor

### 9.9.1 The answer

**Protection has not moved to the coprocessor. It runs on the host CPU, in
software, on every machine in scope, including the A18 Pro machine.**
Speaker protection is not performed anywhere in the audio hardware path:
neither the amplifier — whose autonomous protection is die-temperature,
over-current and brown-out only (§8.7.1) — nor the always-on coprocessor, nor
the low-power audio processor holds a voice-coil thermal or excursion model.
**[Confirmed]** It must therefore be implemented by the driver's host-side
modelling.

- **The low-power audio processor is a filter engine, not a protection
  engine.** Its coprocessor-side interface consists of clock control, DMA
  channel configuration, serial-audio and PDM agent configuration, and a
  **coefficient cache with a fixed coefficient element size**. Coefficients
  come from the host. There is no speaker-parameter object, no temperature
  state and no gain-reduction control in its interface. **[Probable]**
- **The protection input is a host-side stream.** A speaker-protection
  telemetry stream is an input to the host's processing chain, and exactly one
  such input is required. The per-unit calibration block is read from the audio
  device's properties and converted into floating-point model parameters there.
  **[Probable]**

The 2 ms look-ahead, 4.6 s gain attack and 20 s gain release in §9.4.2 are
consistent with host-side block processing, not with a sample-rate hardware
limiter.

### 9.9.2 What the coprocessor *does* own

The coprocessor-side control path: the serial-audio cluster, its clocking, and stream routing.
On all in-scope machines except j700 the speaker stream endpoint is
`iop-adma-stream,mca` with playback on `base-ns-adma-tx-0` and the sense return
on `base-ns-adma-rx-0` — both channels of the **host-addressable, non-secure**
audio DMA controller.

**j700 is the exception, and it is the reason this question was asked.** Its
speaker stream endpoint is `iop-adma-stream,leap`, its playback channel is
`leap-ns-adma-tx-0`, its data node carries
`audio-stream-formatter` = `leap` and its device is named "Leap Speaker". Its
speaker path is bound to the low-power audio processor's DMA rather than the
base DMA. **But** the protection maths for that machine is still in the host
tuning set and still runs on the host — the coprocessor binding changes *which
DMA controller instance carries the samples*, not *who computes the limit*.
[Confirmed for the location of the maths; **[Unknown]** whether the low-power
processor applies any additional processing to that stream in transit — see
Open question 1.]

### 9.9.3 Does the host still need the calibration data?

**Yes, unconditionally.** Nothing downstream of the host consumes it. If the
host does not read the calibration and run the model, no other agent will.

### 9.9.4 Does the host need to supply the calibration to the coprocessor?

**No.** There is no message, endpoint or property through which speaker
calibration is handed to the coprocessor, on any machine, in any generation.

### 9.9.5 What the host can and cannot reach — and why that matters here

The ownership split is sharply asymmetric, and it is the heart of
the answer to the bypass question. Restated for the speaker path only:

| Speaker-path capability | Host-reachable? |
|---|---|
| Move sample bytes (audio DMA controller MMIO, interrupts, IOMMU) | **Yes** — full host MMIO, unchanged aperture |
| Amplifier registers: analogue level, digital volume, mute, power mode, slot assignment, sense enables, high-pass corner, over-current policy, brown-out preset, fault status | **Yes** — host-owned I²C, complete M1–M3 property set intact (not on j700) |
| Amplifier shutdown / reset GPIO | **Yes** — host GPIO, **on every machine including j700** |
| Speaker-ID strap | **Yes** — host GPIO |
| Sense-return data | **Yes** — lands in host memory via host DMA |
| Sense-return *capture setup* | **No** — coprocessor only |
| Bit clock, frame clock, master clock | **No** — coprocessor only |
| TDM slot geometry, routing, format, sample rate | **No** — coprocessor only |
| Any volume or mute upstream of the amplifier | **No** — coprocessor only; no host mixer exists |
| Device power state; the audio power and clock domains | **No** — coprocessor only. Every audio power domain on every in-scope SoC carries the flag meaning *no host-drivable power control*, and hangs off the coprocessor's domain tree. On M1–M3 the host-side audio domains carried the opposite flag |

### 9.9.6 **What happens if the host bypasses the coprocessor and drives the DMA directly**

This is the most important question in this document, so it is answered in
parts, each with its own confidence.

**(a) You cannot actually bypass the coprocessor for the speaker signal.**
The host has no aperture for the serialiser, cannot generate the bit, frame or
master clock, cannot choose the slot geometry, and — decisively — **cannot
power the audio complex at all**. A host that programs the DMA controller with
no prior coprocessor stream setup moves bytes into an unpowered, unclocked
serialiser and produces silence. **The coprocessor must bring the stream up on
every in-scope machine.** [Confirmed]

**(b) So the real configuration, and it is the one an independent driver
reaches first, is a hybrid.** The coprocessor brings the stream up — clocks,
slots, format, power — and then the host owns two things outright: the DMA
ring the samples come from, and (on every machine except j700) the amplifier's
own registers over I²C. **In that configuration nothing between the host's
buffer and the voice coil inspects, attenuates or limits the samples.**
[Confirmed for M4 and M5 machines: the whole protection model is host-side
software (§9.9.1), the amplifier has no coil model (§9.8.1), and there is no
host-reachable mixer anywhere in the path.]

**(c) Answer the conditional directly: *if* protection and limiting did run in
the coprocessor's DSP, what would be lost and what would remain?**

- **Nothing would be lost by "driving the DMA directly", because you cannot
  route around the coprocessor.** Any fixed processing the coprocessor-owned
  path applies is applied to your samples whether you like it or not — you
  cannot reach the serialiser to avoid it, and you cannot power the complex
  without it. This is the one genuinely reassuring structural fact in this
  section.
- **What would still be lost is the host-side protection software**, which is a
  different thing from the coprocessor, and which is where the protection
  actually is.
- **What would remain available to a host driver in that configuration** is
  precisely the two mechanisms below. It is worth being exact about them,
  because one of them is sufficient and the other is not.

**(d) Mechanism 1 — host-side modelling from sense data. Available, and
sufficient, on every machine that has a sense return.**

The sense return is 2 × N channels of S16 landing in host memory through the
host-owned DMA controller, and the amplifier's digital volume is writable over
host-owned I²C. That is a complete closed loop: measure `V × I`, run the
two-stage thermal model of §9.4.2 with the per-model constants of §9.4.2 and
the per-unit resistance of §9.2.2, and apply gain reduction by writing the
amplifier's digital volume register. **This is exactly the architecture of the
published open-source protection daemon, and it is available unchanged on
every in-scope machine with `speaker-protection = 1`** — that is, on
j604, j713, j715, j614s/c, j616s/c, j704, j813, j815, j714s/c, j716s/c.
Nothing about the M4 architecture change takes it away. [Confirmed]

It is **not** available on j623, j624, j773g, j773s or j575c, which have no
sense return at all; those machines must be protected feed-forward from the
known output signal using the open-loop parameter sets of §9.7.1. It is **not**
available on j700 in any form (see (f)).

**(e) Mechanism 2 — amplifier-autonomous limiting. Available, and worthless
for this purpose.**

Every register of the amplifier's own protection block is host-reachable and
programmable. None of it protects the speaker. Restating §9.8.1 because it is
the thing most likely to be mistaken for a safety net: die over-temperature
protects the die; over-current protects the output stage against a short;
brown-out prevention protects the supply rail — and the supply-tracking limiter,
which would also protect the supply rail, is **disabled on every machine in
scope** (`LIM_EN = 0` at reset and not set by any platform-supplied
configuration; **[Probable]**, §7 §7.7 and §9.8.1).
The part contains no voice-coil thermal model, no excursion limiter and no
sense-driven gain reduction — it physically cannot, because there is nowhere in
its register map to put a thermal parameter. Programming every protection
register in the amplifier to its most conservative value **does not move the
continuous-power limit at all**; the coil will still reach 130 °C while the die
is barely warm and no fault bit will ever set.

**Therefore: amplifier-autonomous protection is NOT sufficient. It is not
partially sufficient. It provides zero protection for the transducer, on every
machine in scope.**

**(f) j700 is worse than the others and must be called out separately.**

On the A18 Pro machine the host has **neither** mechanism:

- No sense return exists, so Mechanism 1 is impossible.
- The amplifier has no control bus, so Mechanism 2 does not exist either — and
  neither does *any* host-reachable gain or mute. Every speaker control on that
  machine other than the enable pin is upstream of the amplifier and therefore
  coprocessor-only.

The **only** things standing between a host driver and the transducer on j700
are (i) the numerical values the host writes into the DMA ring, and (ii) the
amplifier enable GPIO. The entire feed-forward loudspeaker model of §9.8.2 is
host software operating on (i). **A host driver on j700 that writes samples
without running that model has no protection whatsoever and no way to reduce
level after the fact except to shut the amplifier down.**

**(g) The fail-safe that does work, everywhere.**

The amplifier shutdown/reset GPIO is host-owned and host-reachable on **every**
in-scope board, including j700 (pin 105 there). It is the only actuator that is
available on all machines and that cannot be taken away by the coprocessor.
A driver's error, timeout, panic and shutdown paths must drive it to the
inactive state. Note that asserting it is equivalent to a power cycle of the
amplifier's digital core: the full register configuration is lost and must be
replayed, and the amplifier will come back at **maximum analogue level and
0 dB digital volume** (§9.4.6). Never re-release it without reprogramming.

Note also what is *not* available as a fail-safe: the host **cannot** power the
audio complex down, because every audio power domain is coprocessor-owned.
Recovery by power-cycling the audio block is not an option a host driver has.

**(h) What a naive first bring-up actually produces.**

Worse than the protected case, not better. If the host asks the coprocessor for
a stream and then writes samples without programming the amplifier, the
amplifier is at its reset defaults: analogue level **21.0 dBV** — 2.5 dB above
the platform's intended level on every portable in scope and on the M4 Mac
mini — digital volume 0 dB, high-pass corner at the default rather than the
per-model value (so a tweeter receives low-frequency content it is not built to
survive), and voltage-sense transmit already enabled and pointed at slot 2 out
of reset, which will collide on the shared sense line with whichever amplifier
legitimately owns that slot.

**(i) Stated as plainly as it can be stated.**

> Driving the audio DMA on these machines gives you **zero** speaker
> protection unless you implement it yourself. You cannot bypass the
> coprocessor — but the coprocessor was never protecting the speaker. There is
> no hardware limiter, no coprocessor-side coil model, and no watchdog. The
> amplifier's own protections will let the voice coil reach destruction
> temperature and will not report anything while it does. On a 14-inch MacBook
> Pro the margin between what the amplifier can deliver and what the woofer can
> survive continuously is **15.4 dB**; on a MacBook Air 15-inch tweeter it is
> **19.5 dB**. The coil time constant is **1.8 to 5.5 seconds** and the magnet
> time constant is **28 to 197 seconds**, so damage accumulates on a human
> timescale and is not preceded by any audible warning.
>
> The good news, and it is real: **on every machine with a sense return, the
> complete closed loop is host-reachable** — sense data arrives via host DMA
> and the amplifier's digital volume is writable over host I²C. An independent
> driver can build exactly the protection the platform builds. **The bad news
> is that it must, because nothing else will**, and on the A18 Pro machine it
> cannot even do that: there the only levers are the samples themselves and the
> enable pin.
>
> **If you are not certain your protection loop is running and is being fed
> real sense data, mute — and if you cannot mute, assert the shutdown GPIO.
> There is no safe "just test it quickly".**

**(j) What is still uncertain, and it is not a small thing.**

Whether the coprocessor-owned serialiser path inserts *any* attenuation,
soft-clip or ramp of its own has not been established and cannot be established
from the interface description at all; it must be resolved by probing. It
matters less than it would if the path were bypassable
— it is not — but it matters for calibrating how loud "full scale in the ring"
actually is, and on j700, where the platform explicitly asks the coprocessor to
perform a ramp-down on stop and where the stream carries a coprocessor stream
formatter, there is clearly *some* coprocessor-side signal handling. **Assume
it provides no protection.** A driver must be written so that it is safe if the
coprocessor does nothing to the samples, and this must be resolved by tracing
before anyone drives these speakers hard. This is Open question 1 and it is the
highest-priority item in this section.

---

## Per-SoC / per-machine differences

**t8132 (M4), base die**

- j604: six amplifiers, closed-loop protection, **woofer temperature limit
  reduced to 130 °C** — the only in-scope machine other than its M5 successor
  and the Pro/Max 14-inch to do so. 18.5 dBV. Speaker-ID strap on GPIO 4/13.
- j713: four amplifiers, closed-loop but with a different processor;
  carries the strap but nothing consumes it; Thiele/Small set unchanged from
  the M2-generation 13-inch Air.
- j715: six amplifiers, **tweeters at amplifier indices 2 and 3**, not 4 and 5.
  `z_shunt` = 0. Tweeter continuous limit 0.42 W — the lowest in scope.
- j623, j624: four amplifiers, **no sense return**, open-loop only, temperature
  limit **120 °C** — the lowest limit in scope. 20.0 dBV.
- j773g: one amplifier, no sense, open-loop, **18.5 dBV — down 2.5 dB from the
  M2/M3 Mac mini**.

**t604x (M4 Pro / M4 Max)**

- j614s/c, j616s/c: six amplifiers, closed-loop. The 16-inch uses a **2.7 Ω**
  woofer and a 140 °C limit; the 14-inch a 3.2 Ω woofer and a 130 °C limit.
  Speaker-ID strap on GPIO 52/53.
- j773s: identical speaker configuration to j773g.
- j575c: one amplifier, no sense, open-loop, **21.0 dBV** — the loudest
  amplifier setting in scope, on the machine with the least protection.

**t8140 (A18 Pro) — j700, the outlier**

Everything about this machine's protection story is different:

- Amplifier family with **no control bus and no sense return**; two instances
  gated by one enable pin (GPIO 105).
- The speaker stream is the **only** one in the population bound to the
  low-power audio processor's DMA, with a stream formatter naming that
  processor.
- No `speaker-protection` property, no `speaker-config`, no `bop-config`, no
  `amp-dcblocker-config`, no `amp-tx-zd-config`, no speaker-ID strap.
- 48 kHz only; 20 ms mute ramp; coprocessor-performed ramp-down on stop.
- The factory calibration objects (`SpTS`, `SpGa`) are present exactly as on
  every other machine — the per-unit calibration mechanism is **unchanged**
  even though there is no amplifier to calibrate against.
- Protection is a **feed-forward loudspeaker model** with a full Thiele/Small
  set, **with excursion control active** (the only in-scope machine where it
  is), plus a neural-network stage on the CPU, plus a 17-point volume curve,
  plus a platform-supplied peak-power budget registered with the system power
  manager (the only board in the population to do so).
- **What applies it: the host CPU, in userspace, and nothing else.** If that
  software is not running, these speakers have no protection of any kind
  beyond the amplifier's own 150 °C die thermal shutdown.

**t8142 (M5), base die**

- j704: parameters byte-identical to j604. Strap moved to GPIO 198/199.
  Gains a speaker-tap capture stream that j604 does not have.
- j813: **drops the speaker-ID strap** its M4 predecessor carries, and
  correspondingly ships a single tuning variant. One module variant only.
- j815: parameters identical to j715; strap on GPIO 6/11; retains two variants.

**t605x / t6050 (M5 Pro / M5 Max)**

- j714s/c, j716s/c: parameters byte-identical to their M4 counterparts. Strap
  on GPIO 136/137. Speaker-tap capture stream added.

**The M4 → M5 delta for this section is, in one sentence: nothing changed
except the speaker-ID strap pin assignments, the addition of a speaker-tap
capture stream, and the removal of the strap on the 13-inch Air.**

---

## Open questions

Numbered. Items marked **☠** must be resolved before speakers are driven on the
affected machine; the marker is defined in the introduction.

1. **Does the coprocessor-owned serialiser path alter the samples between the
   DMA ring and the amplifier — attenuate, soft-clip, limit or ramp?**
   *Why it matters:* the path is not bypassable (§9.9.6a), so whatever it does
   is always applied; but a driver needs to know how loud "full scale in the
   ring" really is before it calibrates a limiter against it, and if the
   coprocessor *does* apply a fixed limiter then the measured headroom on a
   reference machine will be misleading. On j700 the platform explicitly asks
   the coprocessor for a ramp-down on stop and the stream carries a coprocessor
   stream formatter, so there is certainly some coprocessor-side signal
   handling there. *How to resolve:* with the machine under a hypervisor, bring
   the stream up through the normal coprocessor path, inject a known full-scale
   sequence into the DMA ring, and capture the TDM bus with a logic analyser;
   compare sample-for-sample, and repeat with a signal designed to trip a
   limiter. Repeat on j700, where the capture point is the amplifier's own input
   pins. **Until this is answered, assume no attenuation and design the driver
   to be safe without one.** **[Unknown] — highest priority.**

2. **Byte-level layout of the per-unit calibration record.** The envelope
   (§9.2.1) and the field set with units (§9.2.2) are established; the offsets,
   widths and scaling of the individual fields are not, nor is which of the
   optional fields is actually populated on these machines. *Why it matters:*
   the pair (coil DC resistance, calibration temperature) is the only per-unit
   quantity in the system, and mis-parsing it yields a wrong coil-temperature
   estimate in the direction that under-protects. *How to resolve:* read the
   `speaker-thiele-small` property from a live machine and correlate against a
   four-wire resistance measurement of each transducer at a known ambient;
   repeat on two units of the same model to separate per-unit fields from
   constants; check every candidate decode against the per-model acceptance
   windows of §9.4.3, which bracket both values tightly. Cross-check the
   version byte against §9.2.1's accepted set. **[Unknown]**

   *Until then:* §9.2.2 gives the two things a driver may do — decline to
   consume the record, or identify the two fields at run time from the per-model
   acceptance windows and refuse the record unless the identification is unique
   across every record in the block. **Neither is a substitute for the layout,
   and guessing an offset is not a third option.** This is the same question as
   §8 open question 6, which carries the ☠ marker; it is a blocker for every
   closed-loop protection model and for nothing else.

3. **Behaviour when the factory calibration key is absent.** The property
   descriptor has no fallback clause. *Why it matters:* a driver must
   distinguish "no calibration, use conservative defaults" from "calibration
   present and zero", and the two may be indistinguishable if the boot
   firmware emits an empty or zero-filled property. *How to resolve:* observe
   the property on a machine with a replaced or unprogrammed speaker module;
   or compare against the microphone trim-gain property on the 13 boards that
   lack it. **[Unknown]**

4. **☠ The trim-gain index mapping.** The trim-gain array is indexed by a
   per-device selector whose transducer-to-index mapping is not in the
   platform description. *Why it matters:* applying a per-unit trim to the
   wrong transducer mis-balances the array and mis-scales one driver.
   *How to resolve:* read `speaker-trim-gains` from a live machine alongside a
   per-transducer acoustic measurement; or trace the property reads at probe.
   **[Unknown]**

5. **☠ Which sense slot is current and which is voltage — [Probable], not
   settled.** **[Confirmed]** and naming-independent: the lower slot of each
   pair (0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20) is written into amplifier register `0x0E` and the
   upper (2, 6, 10, 14, 18, 22) into `0x0F`; the published upstream trees write
   the two **exchanged** into the same two registers. Which register carries
   voltage rests on the mainline driver headers for the counterpart part and its
   sibling — one family of sources sharing one convention, not two independent
   lines — and the coprocessor cannot distinguish the two channels at all
   (§18 §18.5.5), so the question cannot be settled from the controller side.
   See §8 §8.2.1 and §7 §7.5.1. *Why it matters here in particular:* the thermal
   model uses only the product `V × I`, in which the two full-scale constants
   commute, so a power-based model **cannot detect the mistake**; but any
   resistance-based coil-temperature estimate — which is what the per-unit
   calibration is *for* — is wrong by a factor of (14/3.75)² ≈ 13.9, i.e.
   11.4 dB, in the under-protecting direction if reversed. And the per-unit
   Thiele–Small parameters every in-scope board carries only earn their place in
   an excursion/impedance model, which is exactly the sensitive kind.
   **[Inferred]** *Resolution, assuming neither convention:* drive one amplifier
   into **two different known load resistances** and observe which of the two
   captured channels changes; the current channel scales inversely with load
   impedance, the voltage channel does not. ☠ **Do not adopt this document's
   slot map together with the channel labels of an existing published
   speaker-protection configuration** — they come from different stacks; see the
   third hazard in §00.

6. **☠ Per-transducer thermal parameters for the 13-inch MacBook Air M4 and M5.**
   Their closed-loop processor's parameter vector is not self-describing and
   the thermal resistances and time constants could not be located in it.
   *Why it matters:* it is one of only two in-scope chassis for which the
   thermal model cannot be reconstructed. *How to resolve:* measure — drive
   each transducer with a known step power and fit the two-stage thermal model
   from the sense-derived resistance; or use the M2-generation values for the
   same chassis, whose Thiele/Small set is byte-identical, as a conservative
   starting point. **[Unknown]**

7. **Units of the peak-power budget on the A18 Pro machine**, and the exact
   factor-of-four relationship between its two values. *Why it matters:* it
   constrains system power delivery on a machine where the speaker is a
   registered power client; misreading it risks brown-out, not speaker damage.
   *How to resolve:* measure supply current into the amplifier while sweeping
   output level, and correlate with the power manager's granted budget.
   **[Unknown]**

8. **Brown-out preset threshold-to-volts encoding.** The 24-byte preset is
   byte-identical everywhere and is written into the amplifier's brown-out
   register block, but the encoding of its threshold fields is not published.
   *Why it matters:* only for a driver that wants to change it; the shipped
   value can be used verbatim. *How to resolve:* vendor datasheet section, or
   sweep the supply on a bench board and observe the trip point. **[Unknown]**

9. **☠ The GAIN_SLOT strap value on the A18 Pro machine.** The platform states a
   full-scale figure of 7.34 V peak but the part's gain is set by a resistor
   strap that is not described anywhere in the platform data. *Why it matters:*
   it is the *only* thing bounding output level on that machine, and it cannot
   be changed or read by software. *How to resolve:* board inspection, or
   measure the output for a known digital full-scale input. **[Unknown]**

10. **Whether the speaker tap stream on the M5 and A18 Pro machines is
    intended as a protection input.** It carries one channel per amplifier,
    not two, and is in the main clock domain. *Why it matters:* if it is a
    post-processing monitor it could be used by a driver as an independent
    check that the limiter is actually attenuating. *How to resolve:* capture
    it while driving a known signal and compare with what was written to the
    playback ring. **[Unknown]**

11. **Whether the per-unit calibration is used at all on the machines with no
    sense return.** The objects are present in the factory store on every
    machine including the single-amplifier desktops, but their open-loop
    models contain no field that obviously consumes a measured resistance.
    *Why it matters:* it determines whether a driver for those machines needs
    to read the factory store at all. *How to resolve:* trace the property
    reads at probe on a Mac mini or Mac Studio. **[Unknown]**

12. **☠ Whether the displacement/excursion model is ever enabled at runtime on
    the closed-loop machines.** It ships disabled, with internally inconsistent
    parameters. *Why it matters:* excursion damage is mechanical and instant,
    unlike thermal damage; if excursion is genuinely unprotected on these
    machines then low-frequency content is bounded only by the equalisation
    curve. *How to resolve:* measure cone displacement, or drive a swept
    low-frequency tone at full scale and observe whether gain reduction occurs
    ahead of the thermal model engaging. **[Unknown]**

13. **☠ Numeric limit values for the A18 Pro machine's loudspeaker model.** The
    limit set is established (§9.8.2) but the values sit in a packed
    parameter vector whose identifier-to-name mapping is not recoverable from
    the data alone. *Why it matters:* these are the **only** limits protecting
    that machine's speakers, and there is no sense return to catch an error.
    *How to resolve:* correlate the vector against the same processor's vector
    on the 13-inch MacBook Air, where the system-identification stage's
    parameters can be anchored to measurable impedance quantities; or measure
    directly — sweep level and frequency and observe where gain reduction
    begins. **[Unknown]**

14. **The 13-inch MacBook Air's adaptive model, and its cached state.** Those
    two machines re-identify the transducer model at runtime and cache it in
    mutable per-machine storage rather than relying on the factory record.
    *Why it matters:* a driver must decide whether to implement the adaptive
    loop, seed a fixed model from the factory record, or fall back to the
    M2/M3-generation constants for the same chassis; and it must know whether
    the cached state is safety-relevant (i.e. whether a cold machine with no
    cache is protected). *How to resolve:* observe the cache directory on a
    running machine across cold boot, first playback and sustained playback;
    and check whether the per-unit calibration input to the model manager is
    connected at all on the M5 member of the pair. **[Unknown]**

15. **Whether the richer factory calibration object exists on these machines
    and what its relationship to the device-tree-mirrored one is.** The
    consumer prefers an object that is not mirrored into the platform
    description and falls back to the one that is. *Why it matters:* a driver
    that can only read the device tree gets the fallback; it needs to know
    whether that is the same data, a subset, or stale. *How to resolve:* read
    both from a live machine and compare. **[Unknown]**

16. **The remaining bytes of both factory objects** — the 4-byte trailer on the
    trim-gain object and the trailer on the calibration object. A checksum is
    the obvious candidate but its algorithm is not established. *Why it
    matters:* a driver should validate the objects before trusting them.
    *How to resolve:* read both from several machines and fit. **[Unknown]**

# 10. Headphone jack codec

## Public sources

Mainline Linux `sound/soc/codecs/cs42l42.c`, `include/sound/cs42l42.h`,
`include/dt-bindings/sound/cs42l42.h`, `sound/soc/codecs/cs42l83-i2c.c`,
`sound/soc/codecs/cs42l84.{c,h}`,
`Documentation/devicetree/bindings/sound/cirrus,cs42l84.yaml`,
`sound/soc/apple/macaudio.c`; and Apple platform firmware device trees.

---

## Baseline

The public counterpart for both parts in scope is the **Cirrus Logic CS42L42**
headset codec: stereo Class-H headphone DAC, mono headset-microphone ADC,
I²S/TDM serial port, integrated tip/ring-sense jack detection, headset-type
(CTIA/OMTP) auto-detection, four-level headset-button detection, headset bias
generator, and headphone load detection. Its complete register map is published
in mainline Linux (`include/sound/cs42l42.h`).

Two derivatives appear on Apple machines:

- **CS42L83** — same register map, same page-based addressing and (with one
  exception) the same reset values as CS42L42. Mainline carries it as a thin
  reset-value override over the CS42L42 core. Used on all M1 machines and on the
  A18 Pro machine (j700).
- **CS42L84** — an Apple-exclusive part with a *different* register map: flat
  16-bit register addressing, no page register, a different interrupt structure,
  no S/PDIF, no SoundWire, and an added DC impedance-measurement block. Used on
  every other in-scope machine (M1 Pro/Max through M5 Max). Mainline carries a
  dedicated driver.

Baseline behaviour of the CS42L84 on M1 Pro–M3 Max is published (mainline
`cs42l84.c`/`cs42l84.h`). This section documents the M4/A18 Pro/M5 delta against
that, plus everything the published driver does not cover.

---

## Summary of differences

| Item | M1–M3 baseline | t8132 / t604x (M4) | t8140 (A18 Pro) | t8142 / t605x (M5) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Part | CS42L83 (M1 base) / CS42L84 (M1 Pro onward) | CS42L84 | **CS42L83** | CS42L84 |
| Silicon revision behaviour | — | **unchanged** vs M1 Pro–M3 Max [Confirmed] | **unchanged** vs M1 [Confirmed] | **unchanged** [Confirmed] |
| Register map | as published | **unchanged** | **unchanged** | **unchanged** |
| I²C address | 0x48 (L83) / 0x4B (L84) | 0x4B | **0x48** | 0x4B |
| I²C bus rate | 400 kHz | 2500 ns requested = 400 kHz nominal; **375 kHz** achieved (§6 §6.1.4) | same | same |
| Serial-link descriptor | per-part | **unchanged** from M1 Pro | **changed**: link clock 24.000 MHz vs 6.000 MHz on M1 | **unchanged** |
| Codec-node property set | 12–14 properties | **`function-codecinput_active` removed**, `external-power-provider` removed | same removals; **gains** `enable-dcid`, `internal-mclk-src`, `mic-config` vs M1 CS42L83 | same as M4 |
| `samplerate-subset` | present only on CS42L83 boards | absent | **present, = {48 kHz}** | absent |
| Capture rates offered by platform | 48/44.1/88.2/96 kHz (L84), 48 kHz (L83) | 48/44.1/88.2/96 kHz | **48 kHz only** | 48/44.1/88.2/96 kHz |
| Serial-port mux selection | explicit platform function onto a host-owned switch | **absent** (moved behind the always-on coprocessor) | **absent** | **absent** |
| Capture-master selection | platform function on the capture stream endpoint | **unchanged in form**, target is now a coprocessor stream endpoint | same | same |

The headline result: **the jack codec silicon did not change at the M4 boundary.**
What changed is (a) which part is fitted on the A18 Pro machine, and (b) the
platform plumbing around the codec, which lost the host-visible serial-port mux
selector and the host-visible "serial port is my power provider" link.

---

## 10.1 Part identification, bus and address

### 10.1.1 Bus and address, per in-scope board [Confirmed — platform firmware, every in-scope board]

`reg` on a codec node is four u32 words: `address | clock-period-ns | 0 | 0`.
The second word is the **I²C bit period in nanoseconds**: 2500 ns, i.e.
**400 kHz** fast-mode nominal, for every jack codec on every in-scope board.
That is the requested ceiling, not the achieved rate — the controller's divider
yields **375 kHz** actual (§6 §6.1.4). (The same field reads 10000 ns
= 100 kHz on slow peripherals and 2816 ns ≈ 355 kHz on some retimers elsewhere
in the same trees, which is what establishes the unit. [Confirmed])

| SoC | Boards | Node | I²C controller | Controller aperture (**absolute**) | 7-bit address | Bus rate | Other devices on that bus |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| t8132 | j604, j623, j624, j713, j715, j773g | `/arm-io/i2c1/audio-codec-output` | `i2c,t8101`-compatible | 0x3_AD01_4000 + 0x4000 | **0x4B** | 375 kHz (400 kHz nominal) | none |
| t604x | j614s, j614c, j616s, j616c, j773s, j575c | `/arm-io/i2c2/audio-codec-output` | same | 0x4_2901_8000 + 0x4000 | **0x4B** | 375 kHz (400 kHz nominal) | none |
| t8140 | j700 | `/arm-io/i2c0/audio-codec-output` | same | 0x3_8501_0000 + 0x4000 | **0x48** | 375 kHz (400 kHz nominal) | none |
| t8142 | j704, j813, j815 | `/arm-io/i2c1/audio-codec-output` | same | 0x3_A501_4000 + 0x4000 | **0x4B** | 375 kHz (400 kHz nominal) | one further device at 0x10 |
| t605x | j714s, j714c, j716s, j716c | `/arm-io/i2c2/audio-codec-output` | same | 0x5_0501_8000 + 0x4000 | **0x4B** | 375 kHz (400 kHz nominal) | none |

Apertures above are **absolute**, and match §6 §6.1.2 controller for controller.
They are the platform description's I/O-region-relative `reg` value plus the
`/arm-io` `ranges` parent base, which is **not uniform**: `0x2_0000_0000` on
t8132, t604x and t605x, `0x2_1000_0000` on t8140 and t8142. A figure taken
straight from `reg` is 8 GiB or 8.25 GiB below the hardware. **[Confirmed]**

The public counterpart's I²C address is strapped by two pins as
`1 0 0 1 0 AD1 AD0`, giving **0x48 / 0x49 / 0x4A / 0x4B** [Confirmed,
datasheet]. In-scope CS42L83 boards therefore strap AD1 = AD0 = 0 and the
CS42L84 boards strap AD1 = AD0 = 1 (if the CS42L84 retains the same strapping
scheme — [Probable]). The bus rate — 400 kHz nominal, 375 kHz achieved — is well
inside the part's **1 MHz** fast-mode-plus maximum either way.

The `compatible` strings are `audio-control,cs42l84` / `audio-control,cs42l83`
on the control (I²C) node, and `audio-data,cs42l84` / `audio-data,cs42l84-input`
(resp. `…cs42l83…`) on the playback and capture serial-link nodes.

### 10.1.2 Register addressing

| | CS42L83 | CS42L84 |
|---|---|---|
| I²C transaction | 1 address byte + data | **2 address bytes (big-endian) + data** |
| Paging | page-select register at offset 0x00 of every page; pages 0x10–0x30 | **none — flat 16-bit space** |
| Address space | 0x1001 … 0x3014 expressed as (page ≪ 8) \| offset | 0x0000 … 0x73FE flat |
| Register width | 8 bits | 8 bits |

[Confirmed — mainline register-map configurations for both parts, corroborated
by the parts' decoded register ranges (§10.2.2(a)).]

### 10.1.3 Device ID and revision

| | CS42L83 | CS42L84 |
|---|---|---|
| Device-ID registers | 0x1001, 0x1002, 0x1003 (3 bytes, MSB first) | **0x0000, 0x0001, 0x0002** (3 bytes, MSB first) |
| Device-ID value | **0x04 0x2A 0x83** → 0x42A83 | **0x04 0x2A 0x84** → 0x42A84 |
| Fabrication ID | 0x1004 | 0x0004 [Probable — by position within the 0x0000–0x0008 block] |
| Revision ID | 0x1005 | 0x0005 [Probable] |
| Second revision register | 0x3014 (sub-revision) | **0x73FE** — a one-register block at the very top of the address space, read at initialisation [Confirmed] |

Probe-time discrimination for a driver:

1. The two parts are never both present on a machine, and platform firmware
   names the part in `compatible`. Trust that first.
2. Otherwise: the CS42L84 answers a 2-byte-address read at 0x0000 with
   `04 2A 84`; the CS42L83 does not decode 2-byte addressing at all and answers
   a 1-byte-address read at 0x01 of page 0x10 with `04 2A 83`.
3. The addresses differ (0x4B vs 0x48) on every observed board, which is by
   itself sufficient.

**Revision.** No revision constant is compared anywhere in the host-side
configuration of either part on any generation: the revision registers are read
and reported but never branched on. Together with §10.2.4 this establishes that
**no revision-dependent workaround exists for either part on any generation in
scope** [Confirmed]. The actual revision byte values are **[Unknown]** — see
Open questions.

---

## 10.2 CS42L84: precise differences from CS42L42, and what the M4+ generations add

### 10.2.1 Already published

The following are documented in mainline and are not restated here beyond the
summary table in the Baseline section: flat 16-bit addressing; device ID at
0x0000 and revision at 0x73FE; a three-register interrupt status/mask structure
at 0x0400–0x0402 / 0x0418–0x041A; tip/ring-sense control at 0x1282–0x1283 and
status at 0x1288; the headset-detect/mic-detect block at 0x1470–0x148x; block
enables at 0x1800–0x1802; headset switch matrix at 0x1812; ADC at 0x2000–0x2003;
DAC and headphone at 0x3000–0x3020; routing at 0x4000–0x4001; serial port at
0x5000–0x506E; clocking at 0x0600–0x0608 and PLL at 0x0800–0x0808. Sample-rate
codes 4/5/6 (48/96/192 kHz) and 12/13/14 (44.1/88.2/176.4 kHz).

### 10.2.2 Further deviations established here

**(a) Complete extent of the populated register space.** The CS42L84 address
space is sparse. The populated/decoded ranges are, exhaustively
[Confirmed — the part decodes these 28 ranges and no others]:

```
0x0000-0x0008   0x0203          0x0400-0x041F   0x0600-0x0610
0x0800-0x0808   0x0C00-0x0C02   0x1200-0x1288   0x1470-0x14B6
0x1600          0x1800-0x1836   0x2000-0x2003   0x2400
0x2600-0x2612   0x3000-0x3020   0x3068          0x30D4
0x3123          0x31A1          0x3400-0x3401   0x3600
0x3800          0x3826          0x4000-0x4004   0x4200-0x4203
0x4400-0x4444   0x4800-0x4844   0x5000-0x506E   0x73FE
```

This is a substantially larger and better-delimited map than the published
driver uses (which declares only `max_register = 0x73FE` and touches ~35
registers). Six of these ranges (0x0203, 0x0C00–0x0C02, 0x1600, 0x2400,
0x2600–0x2612, 0x3400–0x3401, 0x3600, 0x3800, 0x3826, 0x4200–0x4203,
0x4400–0x4444, 0x4800–0x4844) contain registers the published driver never
touches.

**(b) A software-reset register that the published driver does not use.**
Offset **0x0203**, write **0x5A** — a magic-key soft reset. Settling time after
the write is **500 µs** before any further access [Confirmed]. This is a
functional equivalent of the CS42L42 "soft reset / reboot" register at page
0x27, but at a different address and with a key value rather than a single bit.

**(c) A pad-interface block at 0x0C00–0x0C02.** Offset **0x0C01** is a
slew-rate / drive-strength control carrying at least two fields: an I²C-SDA
drive selector and an ASP-SDOUT drive selector. The value programmed on every
in-scope machine is **0x0B**, which selects **SDA drive 2 mA** and
**ASP SDOUT drive 8 mA** [Confirmed].

**(d) A charge-pump LDO reference trim at 0x3826.** Programmed to **0x25** to
select the **5 V** charge-pump rail [Confirmed]. The register is also read back.
This is the control behind the headphone output-voltage boost (see (g)).

**(e) An undocumented per-mode analogue trim group in the 0x30xx–0x31xx region.**
These registers are *outside* the decoded-range table in (a) — i.e. they are
hidden registers in the same sense as the hidden pages of the Apple speaker
amplifier variant. Three groups are written:

| Group | Offset | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Common (always) | 0x31E8 | 0x77 |
| | 0x31E9 | 0x02 |
| | 0x31F4 | 0x77 |
| | 0x31F5 | 0x02 |
| | 0x31B0 | 0xE6 |
| | 0x31B1 | 0x05 |
| | 0x31BC | 0xE6 |
| | 0x31BD | 0x05 |
| | 0x31C8 | 0xE6 |
| | 0x31C9 | 0x05 |
| | 0x31D4 | 0xE6 |
| | 0x31D5 | 0x05 |
| | 0x31AE | 0xAB |
| High-capacitance load mode | 0x317B | 0x0F |
| | 0x317F | 0x0F |
| | 0x3064 | 0x81 |
| All other load modes | 0x317B | 0x0C |
| | 0x317F | 0x0C |
| | 0x3064 | 0x01 |

[Confirmed — identical on every generation from M1 Pro to M5 Max.] The four
repeating `0xE6 / 0x05` pairs at 0x31B0/0x31BC/0x31C8/0x31D4 and the two
`0x77 / 0x02` pairs at 0x31E8/0x31F4 have the shape of per-band or per-stage
bias/slew trims. Field semantics **[Unknown]**.

**(f) Headphone output-stage controls the published driver does not use.**

| Offset | Function | Fields established |
|---|---|---|
| 0x3000 | DAC control 1 | bit 0 = DAC un-mute (published); mask **0x74** carries **HP load select**, **HP capacitive-load select**, **HP high-voltage enable** |
| 0x3001 | DAC control 2 | headphone pull-down selection, including a **1.1 kΩ** setting |
| 0x3068 | Headphone force control | bit 4 = force headphone output stage on |
| 0x30D4 | Headphone full-scale compensation | bit 0 = full-scale compensation enable; bit 1 = **0 dBFS ⇒ 3.5 V RMS** mode enable |
| 0x3123 | Headphone clamp control | bit 0 = override the headphone negative-clamp |
| 0x181C | FILT+ charge control | bit 0: 0 = FILT+ un-clamped (charging), 1 = FILT+ clamped (discharge) |

[Confirmed for the field names and bit masks; the *encoding* of the load-select
and capacitive-load-select sub-fields inside mask 0x74 is **[Unknown]**.]

**(g) A load-dependent output-level table.** Six headphone load-impedance bands
are recognised, each mapping to an output-level code:

| Load range | Code |
|---|---|
| 0 Ω … 70 Ω | 0x00 |
| 70 Ω … 100 Ω | 0x0F |
| 100 Ω … 200 Ω | 0x12 |
| 200 Ω … 400 Ω | 0x13 |
| 400 Ω … 1000 Ω | 0x15 |
| ≥ 1000 Ω | 0x00 |

[Confirmed — a 6-entry `{u16 min_ohms, u16 max_ohms, u8 code}` table.] The code
is applied as a headphone volume boost together with the full-scale-compensation
register at 0x30D4 and the charge-pump trim at 0x3826. Two per-machine
properties gate it (`headphone-volume-boost`, `headphone-volume-boost-range`);
**neither is present on any in-scope board**, so on all in-scope machines the
boost path runs on its built-in defaults [Confirmed].

**(h) PLL reference-clock range.** The PLL accepts a reference between
**0.973 MHz and 25.851 MHz** [Confirmed]. Decision thresholds inside that range
are at **2.8224 MHz** and **5.6448 MHz** (see §10.6).

**(i) Clock-source register value for the internal oscillator.** The published
driver parks the codec on its internal oscillator by writing **0x00** to the
clock-source register 0x0600. The host writes **0x08**, i.e. source = internal
RC oscillator with the *nominal-frequency* field set to the 12.288 MHz bin
rather than the 12 MHz bin [Confirmed]. Since the field feeds the internal
sample-rate divider chain, 0x08 is the better-founded value for a driver to use.

**(j) Sample rates below 44.1 kHz are reachable.** The sample-rate register
0x0601 accepts at least the codes 1, 2, 3, 10 in addition to the published
4/5/6/12/13/14 — see §10.6.2.

**(k) A DC impedance-measurement block at 0x1200–0x1215.** See §10.8.6.

### 10.2.3 What is unchanged

Everything not listed in 10.2.2 is as the published CS42L84 description: the
tip/ring-sense debounce encoding, the interrupt bit assignments, the headset
switch matrix bit assignments, the block-enable bit assignments, the ADC and DAC
volume scalings, the serial-port slot/width encodings, and the PLL divider
layout. The CS42L84's *jack-detection and button-detection field layout* is
CS42L42's, relocated to different addresses.

### 10.2.4 Generation delta (the central question)

The complete host-side configuration sequence for the CS42L84 — every register
address, every mask, every literal value, in order — is **byte-for-byte
identical** across all seven generations that carry the part
(M1 Pro/Max, M2, M2 Pro/Max, M3, M3 Pro/Max/Ultra, M4, M4 Pro/Max, M5,
M5 Pro/Max). The register and field set is likewise identical.
No register, field, value, threshold, delay or revision constant is added,
removed or changed at the M4 or M5 boundary.

**Conclusion: the CS42L84 on t8132, t604x, t8142 and t605x is the same silicon,
at the same revision level as far as anything observable is concerned, as the
part on M1 Pro through M3 Max.** [Confirmed — identical on all seven SoCs.]

The same holds for the CS42L83: its configuration sequence on the A18 Pro
machine is identical to the M1 one [Confirmed].

minimum headphone load **15 Ω**; maximum load capacitance **1 nF** or **10 nF**
depending on the load-mode bit; headphone output current limit
**80 / 115 / 160 mA** (min / typ / max).

LSB/MSB pairs, range **−256 … +24** in **0.5 dB** steps ⇒
**−128.0 dB … +12.0 dB**, with the minimum code acting as mute. Both channels
must be written inside a freeze window (0x0006 bit 0 set, then cleared).

touched; by size and stride they have the shape of coefficient banks.

| 0x5010 | `ASP_FSYNC_CTL2` | RW | — | `[7:1] BCLK_PERIOD_LO` | Frame period in bit clocks, bits 6:0 |
| 0x5011 | `ASP_FSYNC_CTL3` | RW | — | `[4:0] BCLK_PERIOD_HI` | Frame period in bit clocks, bits 11:7 |
| 0x5018 | `ASP_DATA_CTL` | RW | — | `ASP_DOUT_HIZ_DLY`, `ASP_DOUT_HIZ_EN`, `ASP_DOUT_SLOT_HIZ_EN`, `ASP_FSYNC_FRAME_START_PHASE`, `ASP_FSYNC_FRAME_START_DLY` | Programmed to **0x3A** = SDOUT tri-state delayed, SDOUT tri-stated outside its slot, frame start on the low→high frame-sync edge, data delayed **1 bit clock** after the frame edge (i.e. I²S framing) [Confirmed] |
| 0x5020 | `ASP_RX_EN` | RW | — | `[0] CH1_EN`, `[1] CH2_EN` | |
| 0x5024 | `ASP_TX_EN` | RW | — | `[0] CH1_EN` | |
| 0x5028 | `ASP_RX_CH1_CTL1` | RW | — | `[7:1] SLOT_START_LSB`, `[0] SLOT_PHASE` | `SLOT_PHASE` 0 = first (rising-edge) half-frame, 1 = second half-frame |
| 0x5029 | `ASP_RX_CH1_CTL2` | RW | — | `[2:0] SLOT_START_MSB` | |
| 0x502A | `ASP_RX_CH1_WIDTH` | RW | — | `[7:0]` | Slot width − 1, in bits. Legal widths **8, 16, 24, 32** |
| 0x502C–0x502E | `ASP_RX_CH2_*` | RW | — | as ch1 | |
| 0x5068 | `ASP_TX_CH1_CTL1` | RW | — | as RX | |
| 0x5069 | `ASP_TX_CH1_CTL2` | RW | — | as RX | |
| 0x506A | `ASP_TX_CH1_WIDTH` | RW | — | as RX | |
| 0x506C–0x506E | `ASP_TX_CH2_*` | RW | — | as ch1 | |

Frame configuration used on every in-scope machine: channel 1 in the first
half-frame (`SLOT_PHASE = 0`, slot start 0), channel 2 in the second half-frame
(`SLOT_PHASE = 1`, slot start 0), frame period **64 bit clocks**, slot width
**24 bits** (from `bits-per-sample-subset`) inside 32-bit half-frames
[Confirmed].

## 10.4 CS42L83: differences from CS42L42

This is new ground; the only previously published deviation is a single reset
value.

### 10.4.1 Published deviation

| Item | CS42L42 | CS42L83 |
|---|---|---|
| Device ID (0x1001–0x1003) | 0x42A42 | **0x42A83** |
| Reset value of the clock control register 0x1009 | 0x02 | **0x00** |
| Every other published reset value | — | identical |
| SoundWire variant | offered | not offered |

The single reset-value difference concerns `INTERNAL_FS` (0x1009 bit 1), i.e.
the two parts come out of reset assuming different internal sample-rate
families. [Confirmed — mainline.]

### 10.4.2 Deviations established here

**(a) The decoded register space is CS42L42's, plus three registers, minus two
pages.** The populated ranges are exactly [Confirmed — a 20-entry
`{start, length}` table]:

| Range | Length | Corresponds to published CS42L42 block |
|---|---|---|
| 0x1001–0x1010 | 16 | Global: device ID, revision, freeze, SRC control, MCLK status/control, soft-ramp rate, slow-start enable, I²C debounce/stretch/timeout |
| 0x1101–0x1129 | 41 | Power control, ring/tip sense, headset detect, headset switch, clamp |
| 0x1201–0x120C | 12 | Clocking: MCLK source, frame-sync period/pulse width, ASP clock and frame config, sample-rate enables, ASRC clock selects, PLL pre-divider |
| 0x1301–0x1320 | 32 | Interrupt status and mask block |
| **0x1401** | **1** | **Not in the published map** |
| 0x1501–0x151B | 27 | PLL |
| 0x1925–0x1927 | 3 | Headphone load detect (result, done, enable) |
| 0x1B70–0x1B7C | 13 | Headset bias autocontrol, wake, ADC mute, tip-sense, misc-detect, mic-detect 1/2, detect status 1/2, detect interrupt masks 1/2, **plus 0x1B7B and 0x1B7C which are not in the published map** |
| 0x1C03 | 1 | Headset bias control |
| 0x1D01–0x1D04 | 4 | ADC |
| 0x1F01–0x1F06 | 6 | DAC |
| 0x2001 | 1 | Headphone control |
| 0x2101 | 1 | Class-H control |
| 0x2301–0x2303 | 3 | Mixer volumes |
| 0x2401–0x240E | 14 | EQ |
| 0x2501–0x2507 | 7 | Audio-port / S/PDIF channel select and rates |
| 0x2601–0x2609 | 9 | Sample-rate converter |
| 0x2801–0x2804 | 4 | S/PDIF |
| 0x2901–0x290B | 11 | Serial-port transmit |
| 0x2A01–0x2A13 | 19 | Serial-port receive |

Three registers are therefore present on the CS42L83 that the published CS42L42
map does not list: **0x1401**, **0x1B7B**, **0x1B7C**. Their function is
**[Unknown]**. Two published CS42L42 areas are absent from the decoded set:
**page 0x27** (the alternate soft-reset/reboot register) and **page 0x30**
(sub-revision). [Probable — these pages are absent from the part's decoded
register range, which is strong but not conclusive evidence of absence in
silicon.]

**(b) A register on page 0x11 that the published map does not list is
programmed at run time: 0x1117**, written with **0x09** in one path and
**0x08** in another [Confirmed]. Page 0x11 offset 0x17 lies in the gap between
the oscillator-switch status register (0x1109) and the ring-sense control
register (0x1112) in the published map. Its function is **[Unknown]** — the
two values differ in bit 0 only, and the writes bracket the sequence that brings
the serial port up and down, so it is most likely an analogue-path enable tied
to clock presence [Inferred].

**(c) The EQ block is used.** 0x2401–0x240E are programmed and polled
(coefficient input words 0x2401–0x2404, coefficient read/write strobe 0x2406,
coefficient output words 0x2407–0x240A, initialisation status 0x240B, filter
start 0x240C, EQ mute 0x240E), with an explicit timeout on EQ initialisation
[Confirmed]. The mixer/EQ power-down bit (0x1101 bit 4) is cleared around it.
This is a functional block the CS42L84 does not expose in the same form.

**(d) Headphone load detection (0x1925–0x1927) is decoded but never triggered**
in any observed path [Confirmed]. The mechanism exists in the silicon — a
0→1 transition of `HP_LD_EN` (0x1927 bit 0) drives a **24 kHz** tone on the
left headphone output and measures the load, returning a coarse result in
`LOAD_DET_RCSTAT` (0x1925): `[1:0]` = **0b00 ⇒ 15 Ω, 0b01 ⇒ 30 Ω, 0b10 ⇒
3 kΩ**, and `[4]` = **0 ⇒ high capacitance (≈ 2 nF), 1 ⇒ low capacitance**,
with `LOAD_DET_DONE` (0x1926 bit 0) as the completion flag. It requires the ADC
and headphone powered down, both analogue mutes asserted, the DAC high-pass
off, the bias in high-impedance and the Class-H rail pinned to its lowest
setting. **The A18 Pro machine does not use it**, so headphone output level is
not matched to the load on that machine — unlike the CS42L84 machines, which
have the finer measurement block of §10.8.6.

**(e) The sample rates the part is driven at are enumerated as nine values**
(§10.6.3) and do not include any rate above 48 kHz.

**(f) Everything else is unchanged from CS42L42**: page layout, field layouts,
interrupt structure, jack-detection mechanism, button-detection mechanism,
serial-port configuration, PLL programming, and all remaining reset values.

### 10.4.3 CS42L83 register map

Because the map is CS42L42's, it is not restated in full. The table below gives
only the registers actually exercised on an in-scope machine, with the values
programmed. Addresses are in the (page, offset) form `0xPPOO`. Reset values are
the published CS42L83 reset values [Confirmed — mainline].

#### Clocking, PLL, sample rate

| Offset | Name | Access | Reset | Fields | Description / observed programming |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0x1007 | `SRC_CTL` | RW | 0x10 | `[4] SRC_BYPASS_DAC`, `[1:0]` | Sample-rate-converter control. Bit 4 cleared/set around DAC path changes; low bits set to 0b11 |
| 0x1009 | `MCLK_CTL` | RW | **0x00** | `[1] INTERNAL_FS` | Written **0x02** to select the non-12/24 MHz internal family. **This is the one published CS42L83 deviation** |
| 0x100B | `SLOW_START_ENABLE` | RW | 0x70 | `[6:4] SLOW_START_EN` | Written **0x00** to disable slow start and **0x70** to re-enable it — see §10.11 |
| 0x1201 | `MCLK_SRC_SEL` | RW | 0x00 | `[1] MCLKDIV`, `[0] MCLK_SRC_SEL` | Bit 0 selects the serial bit clock as the master-clock source; bit 1 halves a 24 MHz input |
| 0x1205 | `FSYNC_P_LOWER` | RW | 0xF9 | `[7:0]` | Frame period, bits 7:0. The 12-bit field is **bit clocks per frame minus 1**; reset 0x0F9 = 249 ⇒ 250 bit clocks per frame |

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0x1101 | `PWR_CTL1` | RW | 0xFF | `[7] ASP_DAO_PDN`, `[6] ASP_DAI_PDN`, `[5] MIXER_PDN`, `[4] EQ_PDN`, `[3] HP_PDN`, `[2] ADC_PDN`, `[0] PDN_ALL` | Whole-device and per-block power-down. #### Audio path

| Offset | Name | Access | Reset | Fields | Description / observed programming |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0x1D03 | `ADC_VOLUME` | RW | 0x00 | `[7:0]` signed | Digital ADC volume, **1.0 dB per step**: 0x00 = 0 dB; 0x01…0x0B = +1 … +11 dB; 0x0C…0x7F clamp at **+12 dB**; 0xFF…0xA0 = −1.0 … **−96.0 dB**; **0x80…0x9F = mute**. Written with mask 0xFF; note 0x80 is a *mute* code, not "minimum gain" [Confirmed, datasheet] |
| 0x1D04 | `ADC_WNF_HPF_CTL` | RW | 0x71 | `[6:4] WNF_CF`, `[3] WNF_EN`, `[2:1] HPF_CF`, `[0] HPF_EN` | Written 0x08 = wind-noise filter enabled, high-pass **disabled**. WNF −3 dB corners 160/180/200/220/240/260/280/**300 Hz** for codes 0…7 at 48 kHz; HPF corners **1.86 / 120 / 235 / 466 Hz**. Note the datasheet warns the ADC high-pass "must remain asserted for proper functionality"; the host clears it |
| 0x1F01 | `DAC_CTL1` | RW | 0x00 | `[1] DACB_INV`, `[0] DACA_INV` | Written 0x00 |
| 0x1F06 | `DAC_CTL2` | RW | 0x02 | `[7:4] HPOUT_PULLDOWN`, `[3] HPOUT_LOAD`, `[2] HPOUT_CLAMP`, `[1] DAC_HPF_EN`, `[0] DAC_MON_EN` | Written 0x02; also updated with mask **0xF4** (pull-down + load + clamp). `HPOUT_PULLDOWN`: 0b1000 = none, 0b1001 = **9.3 kΩ**, 0b1010 = **5.8 kΩ**, every other code = **0.9 kΩ** (±20 %). `HPOUT_LOAD`: 0 = 1 nF mode, 1 = 10 nF mode. `DAC_HPF_EN` corner **0.935 Hz at 48 kHz** |
| 0x2001 | `HP_CTL` | RW | 0x0D | `[3] HP_ANA_BMUTE`, `[2] HP_ANA_AMUTE`, `[1] HP_FULL_SCALE_VOL` | Written **0x0C** = both channels analogue-muted, full-scale 0 dB. Both mute bits are **set at reset**. `HP_FULL_SCALE_VOL`: **0 = 0 dB, 1 = −6 dB** (the −6 dB setting is the datasheet's recommendation for ≈15 Ω loads); the host **clears** it, selecting full swing |
| 0x2101 | `CLASSH_CTL` | RW | 0x07 | `[2:0] ADPTPWR` | Class-H rail selection: 0b001 = fixed ±2.5 V, 0b010 = fixed ±VCP, 0b011 = ±VCP/2, 0b100 = ±VCP/3, **0b111 = adapt-to-signal (reset)**. The host writes **0x01**, pinning the charge pump to the fixed ±2.5 V rail instead of letting it track the signal — a deliberate departure from the part's default [Confirmed]. In adaptive mode a rail step takes **≈20 µs** to ramp upward and carries **≈5.5 µs** of hysteresis downward; the fixed setting avoids that artefact at the cost of idle power |
| 0x2301 | `MIXER_CHA_VOL` | RW | 0x3F | `[5:0]` | 0x00 = 0 dB, **−1.0 dB per step**, 0x3E = −62 dB, **0x3F = mute (reset value)** |
| 0x2302 | `MIXER_ADC_VOL` | RW | 0x3F | `[5:0]` | Written **0x3F** = **mute** — the microphone is *not* mixed into the headphone output (no analogue sidetone) [Confirmed] |
| 0x2303 | `MIXER_CHB_VOL` | RW | 0x3F | `[5:0]` | as channel A |
| 0x2901 | `ASP_TX_SZ_EN` | RW | 0x00 | `[0]` | 0/1 |
| 0x2902 | `ASP_TX_CH_EN` | RW | 0x00 | `[1] CH2`, `[0] CH1` | 0/1 |
| 0x2903 | `ASP_TX_CH_AP_RES` | RW | 0x0F | `[7] CH1_AP`, `[6] CH2_AP`, `[3:2] CH2_RES`, `[1:0] CH1_RES` | Written **0x0F** |
| 0x2905 | `ASP_TX_CH1_BIT_LSB` | RW | 0x00 | `[7:0]` | Transmit slot start |
| 0x2A01 | `ASP_RX_DAI0_EN` | RW | 0x00 | `[5:2] CH4..CH1_EN` | Written **0x0C** = receive channels 1 and 2 enabled |
| 0x2A02 | `ASP_RX_DAI0_CH1_AP_RES` | RW | 0x03 | `[6] AP`, `[1:0] RES` | |
| 0x2A04 | `ASP_RX_DAI0_CH1_BIT_LSB` | RW | 0x00 | `[7:0]` | Channel-1 slot start |
| 0x2A05 | `ASP_RX_DAI0_CH2_AP_RES` | RW | 0x03 | `[6] AP`, `[1:0] RES` | |
| 0x2A07 | `ASP_RX_DAI0_CH2_BIT_LSB` | RW | 0x00 | `[7:0]` | Channel-2 slot start |

Slot-resolution encoding (`*_RES`) [Confirmed, mainline]: 1 = 16 bit,
3 = 32 bit; `AP` selects the second half-frame.

## 10.5 Platform-firmware properties on the codec node

All values below are byte-exact from platform firmware.

| Property | Bytes | Decoded | Present on |
|---|---|---|---|
| `reg` | `4b 00 00 00 c4 09 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00` | I²C address 0x4B, bit period 2500 ns = 400 kHz | all CS42L84 boards |
| `reg` | `48 00 00 00 c4 09 …` | I²C address 0x48, 400 kHz | j700 and all M1 CS42L83 boards |
| `samplerate-default` | `00 00 00 00 80 bb 00 00` | 32.32 fixed-point ⇒ **48000.0 Hz** | all in-scope boards |
| `samplerate-subset` | `00 00 00 00 80 bb 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00` | list of 32.32 rates: **{48000.0}**, zero-terminated | **j700 only** in scope (and all M1 CS42L83 boards) |
| `bits-per-sample-subset` | `18 00 00 00` | **24 bits per sample** | all in-scope boards |
| `mic-config` | `01 00 ff ff ff ff ff ff` | 8-byte array, one byte per microphone index, 0xFF = slot unused; two entries populated (0x01, 0x00) | all in-scope boards |
| `enable-ringsense` | `01 00 00 00` | ring-sense detection enabled | all in-scope boards |
| `ringsense-inverted` | `01 00 00 00` | ring-sense comparator polarity inverted | all in-scope boards |
| `enable-dcid` | `01 00 00 00` | DC impedance-detection block enabled | all in-scope boards |
| `internal-mclk-src` | `01 00 00 00` | the codec's internal master clock is generated internally (PLL from the bit clock, or the internal oscillator) rather than taken from an external master-clock pin | all in-scope boards |
| `PowerOffAtSleep` | `01 00 00 00` | the codec is fully powered off at system sleep | all in-scope boards |
| `function-codecinput_master` | `<phandle> "AUD1" "ap2c"` | platform function `codecinput_master`, implemented by the **capture stream endpoint** node, invoked with the FourCC argument `ap2c` — this is the selector that makes the capture direction clock master | all in-scope boards |
| `function-reset` | `<phandle> "GPIO" <pin> <flags>` | hardware reset pin, see §10.12 | all in-scope boards |
| `interrupts` | `<irq> 01` | see §10.12 | all in-scope boards |
| `interrupt-parent` | `<phandle>` | GPIO block, see §10.12 | all in-scope boards |
| `private` | `31 00` | ASCII `"1"` | all in-scope boards |
| `device_type` | `"audio-control"` | | all |
| `function-codecinput_active` | `<phandle> "i2sR" "pin2"` / `"pin3"` | **ABSENT on every in-scope board.** On M1–M3 it selects, on the host-owned serial-port switch node, which serial-port pin the codec's data-out is routed to (`pin2` for CS42L84 machines, `pin3` for CS42L83 machines) | M1–M3 only |
| `external-power-provider` | `<phandle>` | **ABSENT on every in-scope board.** On M1–M3 it points at the serial-audio cluster sub-node that must be powered for the codec link to work | M1–M3 only |

Two properties that the part supports but that **no in-scope board carries**:
`headphone-volume-boost` and `headphone-volume-boost-range` (a per-machine
override of the load-versus-output-level table in §10.2.2(g)). The CS42L83 also
recognises `force-vcp-mode` and `mclk-src-sel-sclk`, and neither is present on
j700 [Confirmed].

The M1 CS42L83 boards carry `enable-ringsense` and `ringsense-inverted` as
**zero-length boolean** properties and carry neither `enable-dcid` nor
`internal-mclk-src`. **On j700 all four are present as u32 = 1** — i.e. the A18
Pro machine's CS42L83 node uses the modern property encoding and explicitly
enables DC impedance detection, which no M1 CS42L83 board does. [Confirmed]
Whether the CS42L83 silicon actually implements a DC-impedance block, or the
property is simply ignored for this part, is **[Unknown]** — see Open questions.
