## 10.6 Sample rates

### 10.6.1 Rates reachable in hardware vs rates the host configures

| | CS42L84 | CS42L83 |
|---|---|---|
| Rates the sample-rate register can encode | at least 8 codes beyond the published six — see 10.6.2 | CS42L42's full set |
| Rates the host enumerates | 8, 11.025, 12, 16, 22.05, 24, 32, 44.1, 48, 88.2, 96, 176.4, 192 kHz [Probable] | **8, 11.025, 12, 16, 22.05, 24, 32, 44.1, 48 kHz** — nine values, nothing above 48 kHz [Confirmed] |
| Rates the platform offers on the link | 48, 44.1, 88.2, 96 kHz (capture endpoint `data-sources`) | **48 kHz only** |
| Default | 48 kHz | 48 kHz |
| 44.1 kHz family reachable? | **Yes** — dedicated register codes and a dedicated internal master clock of 11.2896 MHz | **Yes** — CS42L42 mechanism, internal master clock 11.2896 MHz |

`samplerate-default = 48000.0` and `bits-per-sample-subset = 24` are **policy**,
not hardware limits: the serial port supports 8/16/24/32-bit slots and the
sample-rate register supports the whole family. `samplerate-subset = {48000}` on
j700 is **also a policy restriction**, but it is consistent with the hardware
capability actually enumerated for the CS42L83 (no rate above 48 kHz), so for
that part it is close to a hardware limit. [Confirmed]

### 10.6.2 CS42L84 sample-rate register (0x0601) encoding

| Rate | Code | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| 48 kHz | 4 | [Confirmed] — published upstream |
| 96 kHz | 5 | [Confirmed] |
| 192 kHz | 6 | [Confirmed] |
| 44.1 kHz | 12 | [Confirmed] |
| 88.2 kHz | 13 | [Confirmed] |
| 176.4 kHz | 14 | [Confirmed] |
| 22.05 kHz | 10 | [Confirmed] — host only; **not exposed by the published driver** |
| 12 kHz / 16 kHz / 24 kHz | 1, 2, 3 in some order | [Probable] |
| 8 kHz, 11.025 kHz, 32 kHz | further codes in the same two families | [Inferred] |

The encoding is two families of six: a 48 kHz family in the low nibble and a
44.1 kHz family at +8. **A driver that needs only 44.1/48 kHz and their
multiples can use the six published codes; the low-rate codes are a bonus that
the published driver does not expose.**

### 10.6.3 CS42L83 rate set

The nine rates enumerated for the CS42L83, as 32.32 fixed-point values, are
exactly: **8000, 11025, 12000, 16000, 22050, 24000, 32000, 44100, 48000 Hz**
[Confirmed]. This list is identical on the M1 boards and on j700.

### 10.6.4 PLL configuration

**CS42L84.** The PLL reference is either the MCLK pin or the serial bit clock,
selected in 0x0602. The reference must lie between **0.973 MHz and
25.851 MHz** [Confirmed]. Internal decision thresholds sit at **2.8224 MHz**
and **5.6448 MHz**; the PLL target is **12.288 MHz** for the 48 kHz family and
**11.2896 MHz** for the 44.1 kHz family [Confirmed].

Published divider settings, indexed by bit-clock frequency [Confirmed,
mainline]:

| Bit clock | Reference source | Reference pre-div | Integer div | Fractional div | Mode | Output div | Resulting internal master clock |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2.8224 MHz | PLL | 0 | 0x40 | 0x000000 | 3 | 0x10 | 11.2896 MHz |
| 3.072 MHz | PLL | 0 | 0x40 | 0x000000 | 3 | 0x10 | 12.288 MHz |
| 5.6448 MHz | PLL | 0 | 0x40 | 0x000000 | 3 | 0x10 | 11.2896 MHz |
| 6.144 MHz | PLL | 1 | 0x40 | 0x000000 | 3 | 0x10 | 12.288 MHz |
| 11.2896 MHz | direct (no PLL) | — | — | — | — | — | 11.2896 MHz |
| 12.288 MHz | direct (no PLL) | — | — | — | — | — | 12.288 MHz |
| 24.576 MHz | PLL | 3 | 0x40 | 0x000000 | 3 | 0x10 | 12.288 MHz |

At 64 bit clocks per frame, the bit clock is 3.072 MHz at 48 kHz and
2.8224 MHz at 44.1 kHz — both rows are present, so **both families are
reachable with the frame format the platform actually uses** [Confirmed].

After programming, the sequence is: enable the reference clock (0x0603 bit 0),
set `PLL_EN` (0x0800 bit 0), poll the lock status (0x040E bit 4) every
**250 µs** with a **1250 µs** timeout, then switch the clock source in 0x0600
and wait **150 µs** for the glitchless switch. The PLL must be running before
the source is switched to it. Tearing down runs in reverse: park 0x0600 on the
internal oscillator, wait **150 µs**, clear `PLL_EN`, clear the reference-clock
enable. [Confirmed — the order and the 150 µs are published upstream.]

**CS42L83.** CS42L42's published PLL table applies unchanged. The PLL reference
(the serial bit clock) must be **2.8224 – 25 MHz**, and the bit-clock pin itself
is specified **0.973 – 25.81 MHz** — the latter is numerically the same window
the CS42L84 states for its PLL reference, so the two parts' clock front ends
are dimensioned alike [Confirmed]. Two rows of the published table matter here:

| Bit clock | Pre-div | Integer div | Frac | Mode | Divout | Cal ratio | Internal master clock |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6.000 MHz | 0x01 | 0x40 | 0x000000 | 0x03 | 0x10 | 128 | 12.000 MHz |
| 24.000 MHz | 0x03 | 0x40 | 0x000000 | 0x03 | 0x10 | 128 | 12.000 MHz |

These are exactly the two link-clock values platform firmware supplies for the
CS42L83 (6.000 MHz on M1, **24.000 MHz on j700** — see §10.7.2), which is the
strongest evidence that the field is the serial bit clock and that the part is
operated from it through the PLL [Confirmed].

---

## 10.7 Master/slave role and clocking requirements

### 10.7.1 The two role-selecting properties

**`function-codecinput_master`** — present on every in-scope board. It is a
platform-function reference of the standard shape
`u32 provider-phandle | 4-byte tag | u32 arg…`, with tag `AUD1` and a single
FourCC argument `ap2c`. The provider is **the capture (codec-input) serial
stream endpoint node**, not a GPIO. Invoking it selects the clock-provider role
for the capture direction. On M1–M3 the provider is the serial-audio cluster's
capture sub-node (`…/mca2b/audio-codec-input`); on every in-scope machine it is
the corresponding coprocessor stream endpoint
(`/arm-io/iop-audio-controller/audio-codec-input/audio-codec-input`). The
argument `ap2c` is the same FourCC that heads the `data-sources` property on
that endpoint, i.e. it names the route the role applies to. [Confirmed for the
encoding and the target; the semantics of "master" here — whether it means the
codec drives the clocks or the SoC does — is **[Inferred]**, see below.]

**`internal-mclk-src = 1`** — present on every in-scope board (and on no M1
CS42L83 board). It selects an **internal** master-clock source for the codec, as
opposed to an externally supplied master clock on a dedicated pin. The codec has
four possible internal master-clock sources (0x0600 `MCLK_SRC`): the internal
RC oscillator, the MCLK pin, the serial bit clock, and the PLL. With
`internal-mclk-src = 1` the part is run from the RC oscillator when idle and
from the PLL (referenced to the serial bit clock) when streaming.

### 10.7.2 What the hardware actually requires in each role

**Slave / clock-consumer (the configuration on every in-scope machine).**
The serial-port clock-role register 0x0608 is programmed to **0x00** on every
in-scope machine: bit clock **external**, serial port in **slave** mode, bit
clock **non-inverted**, frame-sync not aligned. The frame-sync generator is
disabled (0x5000 `ASP_FSYNC_EN` = 0) and only the bit-clock input is enabled
(`ASP_BCLK_EN` = 1). [Confirmed]

Requirements in this role:

1. The SoC must drive both the bit clock and the frame sync.
2. Frame length must be programmed into the codec as a bit-clock count
   (0x5010/0x5011); the value must be even and must divide the bit clock exactly
   by the sample rate. The value used is **64**.
3. The bit clock must be one of the frequencies in the PLL table (§10.6.4), or
   the PLL cannot lock.
4. The bit clock must be running **before** un-mute and must stay running until
   after mute; the published driver and the host both park the codec on its
   internal oscillator before stopping the clock.
5. The published driver additionally rejects any format other than I²S with
   inverted bit clock and inverted frame clock (`IB_IF`) and any role other than
   clock-consumer/frame-consumer, so a driver should assume the part is only
   validated in this configuration.

**Master / clock-provider.** The hardware supports it: 0x0608 carries an
`ASP_MASTER_MODE` field and an `ASP_BCLK_SEL` field that selects an internally
generated bit clock, and 0x5000 carries an `ASP_FSYNC_EN` bit that enables
frame-sync generation. In that role the codec would derive the bit clock from
its internal master clock, which must therefore come from the MCLK pin, the PLL
or the RC oscillator. **No in-scope machine uses it**, and the exact divider
that produces the bit clock from the internal master clock in that mode is
**[Unknown]**. The `function-codecinput_master` property is therefore best read
as selecting which end drives the *capture* link's clocks — and since the codec
is programmed as a slave on every board, it must be requesting that the **SoC
side** be the clock provider for that direction [Inferred].

### 10.7.3 Link clock supplied per machine

The `audio-data,*` serial-link descriptor node carries a 9-word `reg` whose
third word is the link clock frequency in hertz and whose fourth word carries a
clock ratio in its low 16 bits:

| Board set | Part | Link clock (word 2) | Ratio field (word 3, low 16) |
|---|---|---|---|
| All M1 Pro … M5 Max CS42L84 machines, including every in-scope CS42L84 board | CS42L84 | **0** (derived; no fixed clock supplied) | **64** |
| M1 CS42L83 machines (j274/j293/j313/j456/j457) | CS42L83 | **6 000 000 Hz** | **125** |
| **j700** | CS42L83 | **24 000 000 Hz** | **125** |

For the CS42L84 the ratio 64 is corroborated independently: it is the frame
length the codec is programmed with, and it is the bit-clock ratio the mainline
machine-level driver uses for the headphone link. [Confirmed]

For the CS42L83 on M1, 6 000 000 / 125 = 48 000 — self-consistent. **On j700 the
same ratio field with a 24 MHz clock does not reproduce 48 kHz**, so either the
ratio field is stale boilerplate on that board or it does not mean bit-clocks
per frame for this part. Marked **[Unknown]**; see Open questions. What is solid
is that **the A18 Pro machine's codec link runs at four times the M1 CS42L83
clock**, and that 24.000 MHz is a first-class entry in the published PLL table
for this part family.

## 10.8 Jack detection and type detection

### 10.8.1 Mechanism

Both parts detect insertion with two independent comparators on the jack
conductors:

- **Tip sense** — a comparator on the tip contact, with programmable polarity
  inversion and independent rise/fall debounce. It is the primary
  insert/remove event source.
- **Ring sense** — a second comparator on the ring/sleeve contact, with
  programmable polarity inversion, a programmable pull-up, and independent
  rise/fall debounce. It reports whether the plug is *fully* seated: a plug part
  way in asserts tip sense but not ring sense.

Each comparator's debounced state is exposed as a 2-bit code:
**0b00 = unplugged, 0b11 = plugged, 0b01 = in transition** (0b10 reserved).

Electrical thresholds of the two comparators, from the public counterpart and
[Probable] for both Apple variants:

| Comparator | Parameter | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Tip sense | input-high threshold | **0.87 × VP** |
| Tip sense | pull-up current in short-detect mode | **1.00 – 2.91 µA** |
| Ring sense | trim code 0: high / low threshold | **0.15 × VP / 0.03 × VP** |
| Ring sense | trim code 1: high / low threshold | **0.40 × VP / 0.28 × VP** |
| Ring sense | pull-up, mid-impedance setting | **16.2 kΩ** (12.15 – 20.25 kΩ) |
| Ring sense | pull-up, high-impedance setting | **2.25 MΩ** (trim 0) or **1.125 MΩ** (trim 1) |
| Ring sense | discrimination impedance (metal vs plastic barrel) | **≈ 1 kΩ** |

VP is the high-voltage interface rail (2.50 – 5.25 V; performance guaranteed
only above 3.0 V). **Caveat:** the public counterpart's datasheet states the
ring-sense trim thresholds twice with different numbers — 0.15/0.03 · VP and
0.40/0.28 · VP in its electrical-characteristics table, but 0.10/0.05 · VP and
0.35/0.30 · VP in the register description. The table values are quoted above;
treat the ring-sense threshold as **known only to about ±0.05 · VP** until it is
measured, and see Open questions.

A separate 2-bit tip-sense *unplug* debounce also exists
(`TIPSENSE_CTL2[1:0]` on the CS42L84, `TIPSENSE_CTL[1:0]` on the CS42L83):
**0 = none, 1 = 200 ms, 2 = 500 ms, 3 = 1000 ms**; it is distinct from the
3-bit rise/fall debounce fields of §10.8.3.

### 10.8.2 Ring sense — the platform properties

`enable-ringsense = 1` on every in-scope board turns the ring-sense comparator
on. `ringsense-inverted = 1` inverts its polarity. The hardware they configure:

- **CS42L84**: the tip/ring-sense block enable is `MSM_BLOCK_EN3` (0x1802)
  bit 3; the polarity-inversion bit is `RING_SENSE_CTL` (0x1282) bit 7; the
  pull-up enable is bit 6 of the same register. Both bits are set together
  (mask 0xC0) [Confirmed].
- **CS42L83**: the ring-sense block is powered by `PWR_CTL3` (0x1103) bit 1;
  the polarity-inversion and pull-up bits are `RSENSE_CTL3` (0x1112) bits 7
  and 6, again set together with mask 0xC0 [Confirmed].

The purpose of the inversion is board-dependent: on these machines the ring
contact is pulled to the opposite rail from the part's default assumption, so
without the inversion a fully-seated plug would read as unplugged.

### 10.8.3 Debounce settings actually used

Encoding (both parts, identical to CS42L42): 0 = 0 ms, 1 = 125 ms, 2 = 250 ms,
3 = 500 ms, 4 = 750 ms, 5 = 1000 ms, 6 = 1250 ms, 7 = 1500 ms.

| Comparator | Edge | Published driver | **Host-programmed value on in-scope machines** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tip sense | rise (insert) | 500 ms | **250 ms** |
| Tip sense | fall (remove) | 125 ms | **125 ms** |
| Ring sense | rise | 125 ms | **1000 ms** |
| Ring sense | fall | 125 ms | not programmed separately |

[Confirmed.] The host writes `TIP_SENSE_CTL` (CS42L84 0x1283) with mask 0xBF and
value **0x8A** — inverted, fall 125 ms, rise 250 ms — and `RING_SENSE_CTL`
(0x1282) with mask 0x07 and value **0x05** — ring rise debounce 1000 ms.

The long ring-sense rise debounce is deliberate: it gives the user a full second
to push a partially-inserted plug home before the machine commits to a
detection result.

### 10.8.4 Type detection (headphone vs headset, CTIA vs OMTP)

Both parts implement the CS42L42 comparator-based type detector:

- Two reference comparators whose thresholds are set in `HSDET_CTL1`
  (CS42L83 0x111F; CS42L84 0x1810 [Inferred]) as two 4-bit codes, each linear
  with a **0.05 V** step [Confirmed, datasheet]:
  **comparator 1 = 0.65 V + 0.05 V × code** (0.65 V … 1.40 V) and
  **comparator 2 = 1.65 V + 0.05 V × code** (1.65 V … 2.40 V).
  Reset for both fields is code 7 ⇒ **1.00 V** and **2.00 V**. The manual-probe
  overrides used by the published driver are code 12 ⇒ **1.25 V** and code 2 ⇒
  **1.75 V**.
- `HSDET_CTL2` (CS42L83 0x1120; CS42L84 0x1811) sequences the measurement:
  `CTRL` starts it, `SET` selects which of four switch configurations is
  applied, `REF` selects the bias reference, and `AUTO_TIME` sets the
  settling time per step.
- `HS_SWITCH_CTL` (CS42L83 0x1121; CS42L84 0x1812) is an 8-bit analogue switch
  matrix: for each of the two sleeve conductors (HS3, HS4) it independently
  connects **reference**, **filtered headset bias**, **raw headset bias**, or
  **ground**.
- `HS_DET_STATUS` (CS42L83 0x1124; CS42L84 0x1836) returns the two comparator
  outputs and a 2-bit plug type: **0 = CTIA, 1 = OMTP, 2 = headphone (no
  microphone), 3 = invalid**.

The four switch configurations and their register values, published for the
counterpart and byte-identical on the CS42L84 [Confirmed]:

| Configuration | Switch register value | HS3 | HS4 | Comparator result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Type 1 — AHJ / **CTIA** | **0xA6** | reference + filtered bias + ground | raw bias | comp 1 high, comp 2 low |
| Type 2 — **OMTP** | **0x59** | raw bias | reference + filtered bias + ground | comp 1 low, comp 2 high |
| Type 3 — headphone, no microphone | **0xF3** | ground + filtered bias + reference | ground + filtered bias + reference | both low |
| Type 4 — optical / S/PDIF plug | **0xA6** | reference + filtered bias + ground | raw bias | both high |

`HS_DET_CTL2.SET` in manual mode assigns the pins directly: 0b00 = HS3 ground /
HS4 bias, 0b01 = HS3 bias / HS4 ground, 0b10 = both ground. `HS_DET_CTL2.CTRL`:
0b00 = manual disabled, 0b01 = manual active, 0b10 = automatic disabled (switch
bits ignored, switches hold), 0b11 = automatic active — **entering 0b11 starts
the sequence**, and `CTRL` must be returned to 0b10 when the auto-done
interrupt fires.

**On the in-scope machines the auto-detect sequencer is not used for CTIA/OMTP
discrimination.** Instead the switch matrix is written directly to **0xA6** —
exactly the published Type-1/CTIA value — and a single microphone-presence
measurement is taken (§10.8.5). [Confirmed — the value the host programs is
bit-identical to the published CTIA configuration, which is what establishes
that the CS42L84's switch matrix bit assignment is unchanged.] A driver that
wants OMTP support must run the full sequencer, or the two-hypothesis manual
probe (write 0xA6, settle, read; write 0x59, settle, read), itself.

### 10.8.5 Microphone-presence measurement and the detection state machine

Sequence as implemented in hardware, on insertion:

1. Tip-sense plug interrupt fires after the tip rise debounce (250 ms).
2. Raise the headset bias: `MISC_DET_CTL` (CS42L84 0x1474) `HSBIAS_CTL` ← **3
   (2.7 V)**, `DETECT_MODE` ← 0.
3. Power up the microphone-level detector: same register, `PDN_MIC_LVL_DET` ← 0.
4. Wait for the bias to settle — **50 ms** [Confirmed, published driver].
5. Connect the bias in the assumed (CTIA) wiring via `HS_SWITCH_CTL` ← 0xA6 and
   set `HS_DET_CTL2.SET` ← 0.
6. `MISC_DET_CTL.DETECT_MODE` ← 3 to arm the level comparator.
7. Wait **50 ms**.
8. Read `DET_STATUS2` (CS42L84 0x147D) bits [1:0]:
   **0b10 = a load is present ⇒ headset with microphone**;
   **0b00 = open circuit ⇒ headphones only**;
   **0b11 = shorted ⇒ headphones only**.
9. Power the level detector back down.
10. If the result was open or shorted, drop the bias to the 0 V setting.
11. Re-read the tip-sense status. If it is no longer "plugged", the plug moved
    during the measurement: discard the result and revert.
12. Un-mask the ring-sense interrupts so that a plug that seats fully later
    re-triggers the measurement.

On removal: mask the ring-sense interrupts, drop the bias to 0 V, set
`DETECT_MODE` ← 0, and return the switch matrix to **0xF3** — both conductors on
reference + filtered bias + ground, i.e. the published Type-3 / reset
configuration — with `HS_DET_CTL2.SET` ← 2.

The host adds two behaviours the published driver does not have: it reports
"ring fully plugged, re-run microphone detection if headphones" as an explicit
state, and it maintains a multi-state machine with the states
*detached*, *headphones-only*, *headphones-waiting*, *waiting-for-microphone*,
*microphone-open*, *headset*, plus "will notify"/"no notify" variants
[Confirmed]. It also recognises a "**microphone connector reversed**"
condition — i.e. an OMTP plug — and carries per-machine properties to invert
headphone detection (`hp-detect-invert`), to force a headset-switch
configuration (`hp-switch-force-config`), to ramp the headset switch
(`hp-switch-ramp`), to apply a reverse bias (`reverse-bias`), and to apply
pop-suppression work-arounds (`hp-pop-workaround`,
`headphone-pop-workaround`, `hs-switch-workaround`). **None of those properties
appears on any in-scope board**, so all in-scope machines use the default
behaviour [Confirmed].

### 10.8.6 DC impedance detection (CS42L84), and the `enable-dcid` property

The conversion from the measurement result to ohms is **[Unknown]**.

`enable-dcid = 1` on every in-scope board enables a dedicated DC
impedance-measurement block that the CS42L42 does not have (the CS42L42 has only
a coarse 2-bit load-detect result, §10.4.2(d)). The block:

| Element | Register | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Block enable | 0x1802 bit 4 | |
| Measurement range | 0x1200 `[2:0]` | 8 ranges |
| Ground selection | 0x1201 `[6:4]` | none / HS3 / HS4 |
| Start trigger | 0x1202 bit 0 | one-shot |
| Analogue front-end force | 0x1215 | manual vs automatic |
| Pull-down reference reading | 0x120B | read back before the measurement |
| Result | 0x120C … 0x120F | four bytes |

Supporting controls used around a measurement: the headphone clamp override
(0x3123 bit 0), the headphone output-stage force (0x3068 bit 4), and the
headphone pull-down selection (0x3001, including the **1.1 kΩ** setting).

Four measurement modes are distinguished by the hardware configuration applied:
**low impedance**, **high impedance**, **high capacitance**, and a
**1 V RMS** mode. Each selects a different analogue trim group (§10.2.2(e)) and
a different charge-pump/full-scale configuration. The result is used to pick an
output-level code from the load table in §10.2.2(g).

Ordering constraint: **a measurement cannot be started while the DAC is
running.** If a measurement is requested during playback it must be deferred
until the DAC stops. [Confirmed]

**The numeric conversion from the four result bytes to ohms is [Unknown].**
The conversion is known to involve the raw converter code, a differential term,
a trim offset, a gradient/slope term and the measured pull-down reference, but
the exact arithmetic and the calibration constants are not established here.
See Open questions.

Whether the CS42L83 implements anything equivalent is **[Unknown]**: j700's node
carries `enable-dcid = 1`, but no impedance-measurement register block is
decoded anywhere in the CS42L83 address space, and the part's coarse load-detect
registers (0x1925–0x1927) are never triggered. The most likely reading is that
the property is inherited boilerplate and is ignored for this part [Inferred].

### 10.8.7 Interrupt sources

**CS42L84**

| Source | Status register | Mask register | Bit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ring-sense plug | 0x0400 | 0x0418 | 0 |
| Ring-sense unplug | 0x0400 | 0x0418 | 1 |
| Tip-sense plug | 0x0400 | 0x0418 | 2 |
| Tip-sense unplug | 0x0400 | 0x0418 | 3 |
| PLL lock / lock error | 0x040E | 0x041A [Inferred] | 4 / 5 |
| Second and third status groups | 0x0401, 0x0402 | 0x0419, 0x041A | contents **[Unknown]** |
| Headset-bias sense | 0x1484 | 0x1480 | 7 |
| Tip-sense plug (detect block) | 0x1484 | 0x1480 | 6 |
| Tip-sense unplug (detect block) | 0x1484 | 0x1480 | 5 |
| Detect true→false | 0x1485 | 0x1481 | 7 |
| Detect false→true | 0x1485 | 0x1481 | 6 |
| Headset bias high-Z | 0x1485 | 0x1481 | 2 |
| Short release | 0x1485 | 0x1481 | 1 |
| Short detect | 0x1485 | 0x1481 | 0 |

Note that **tip plug/unplug is reported twice**, once by the general interrupt
controller at 0x0400 and once by the detection block at 0x1484. Both masks are
manipulated together, and the tip-unplug mask in particular is swapped between
the two as the state machine advances [Confirmed]. All status registers are
sticky and are cleared by reading.

**CS42L83** uses CS42L42's structure unchanged: eleven status registers at
0x1301–0x130F with masks at 0x1316–0x1320. The ones actually read are 0x1301
(ADC overflow), 0x1302 (mixer), 0x1303 (SRC), 0x1304 (ASP RX), 0x1305 (ASP TX),
0x1308 (codec: power-down-done, auto-detect-done), 0x130B (SRC phase lock),
0x130D (VP monitor), 0x130E (PLL lock), 0x130F (tip/ring plug) plus the detect
block at 0x1B77/0x1B78 [Confirmed].

## 10.9 Headset button detection

### 10.9.1 What the hardware provides

**The silicon implements one button directly**, plus one programmable
comparator that software uses to synthesise more [Confirmed]:

| Detector | Register | Threshold | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| **S0 short detect** — the headset shorts its microphone conductor to ground through the centre button | fixed, not programmable | **100 mV min / 150 mV typ / 200 mV max** on the bias node | `DET_STATUS2` bit 0 `SHORT_TRUE` (**not debounced**); edges as `SHORT_DETECTED` / `SHORT_RELEASE` |
| **Programmable DC level detect** | `MIC_DET_CTL1[5:0] HS_DET_LEVEL` (CS42L84 0x1475; CS42L83 0x1B75) | **(code + 1) × 1.5625 % of the headset bias**, i.e. 1.5625 % … 100 % in 64 steps; reset code 0x1F = **50 %** | `DET_STATUS2` bit 1 `HS_TRUE`; edges as `DETECT_FALSE_TRUE` / `DETECT_TRUE_FALSE` |

Against the 2.7 V bias used on these machines, one code of `HS_DET_LEVEL` is
**42.2 mV** and the full range is **42 mV … 2.70 V**. The threshold the host
programs, code 0x2C, is 70.31 % ⇒ **1.898 V** [Confirmed].

Timing: the DC level detector needs **11 ms** to settle after being powered up
(`PDN_MIC_LVL_DET` ← 0); total group delay for S0 detection is **5 ms typ**.
The hardware debounce for the level detector, `MIC_DET_CTL2[7:5]`
(CS42L84 0x1476; CS42L83 0x1B76), encodes **10 / 20 / 30 / 40 / 50 / 60 / 70 /
80 ms**, reset code 1 = **20 ms**. The datasheet warns that the DC level
detector "should not be continuously enabled if the headset input is enabled
because the noise performance is degraded".

### 10.9.2 How more than one button is distinguished

There is **no hardware resistor-ladder decoder**. Additional buttons are
distinguished by **sweeping the programmable threshold and re-reading
`HS_TRUE`**: a button with a larger series resistance pulls the bias node down
less, so it trips only the more sensitive thresholds. The published driver
sweeps four descending threshold codes — default **15, 8, 4, 1** (i.e. **25.0 %,
14.06 %, 7.81 %, 3.125 %** of the bias, or 675 mV / 380 mV / 211 mV / 84 mV at
2.7 V) — and reports the level at which `HS_TRUE` goes false:

| Sweep level at which `HS_TRUE` clears | Button reported |
|---|---|
| 1 | button C |
| 2 | button B |
| 3 | button D |
| 4 | button A (a hard short, i.e. S0) |

**Four buttons are therefore distinguishable** [Confirmed], but only because
four thresholds are tried; the number is a software choice and the hardware
limit is the 6-bit threshold resolution.

On the in-scope machines the surrounding model recognises three distinct
reports — **S0** (centre / play-pause), **volume up** and **volume down** — and
distinguishes a "single button" headset from a "multiple buttons" headset
[Confirmed]. Headsets are additionally classified by earpiece design,
microphone design and a "third party" / "sound isolating" / "transmitter tone
id" attribute, read out of the accessory rather than measured.

### 10.9.3 Interrupt behaviour

- A press or release raises `DETECT_FALSE_TRUE` / `DETECT_TRUE_FALSE` in the
  second detect-interrupt pair (CS42L84 0x1485 status / 0x1481 mask; CS42L83
  0x130A status / 0x1B7A mask).
- Those two, together with `SHORT_DETECTED`, `SHORT_RELEASE` and
  `HSBIAS_HIZ`, **must be masked for the duration of the threshold sweep** and
  unmasked afterwards, with the status register read once to clear spurious
  edges before unmasking [Confirmed].
- `SHORT_RELEASE` has a **shadow register that captures up to two button
  events**; reading the status register once transfers the shadow in, so it can
  usefully be read twice per interrupt. The shadow is unavailable in wake mode
  [Confirmed, datasheet].
- Two software debounce intervals surround the sweep: an **initial** debounce
  after enabling button detection (default **100 ms**, range 0–200 ms) and a
  **per-event** debounce before each sweep (default **10 ms**, range 0–20 ms)
  [Confirmed, published binding].
- In short-detect-only mode (`DETECT_MODE` = 0b01) the interrupt line is
  dedicated to the S0 comparator and **no other source can assert it**
  [Confirmed, datasheet].

## 10.10 Capture path for a headset microphone

**Bias voltage.** `MISC_DET_CTL.HSBIAS_CTL` (CS42L84 0x1474 `[2:1]`;
CS42L83 0x1B74 `[2:1]`) selects the headset bias [Confirmed]:

| Code | Setting | Output at 500 µA load (min / typ / max) |
|---|---|---|
| 0b00 | high-impedance (low-power reference) | — |
| 0b01 | **0.0 V** weak ground — the reset value and the park value | — |
| 0b10 | **2.0 V** | 1.80 / **2.00** / 2.10 V in normal detect mode |
| 0b11 | **2.7 V** — the value used on every in-scope machine | 2.61 / **2.75** / 2.86 V in normal detect mode |

Only 0b10 or 0b11 gives a functional headset interface. In normal detect mode
the generator uses a high-performance reference; otherwise a low-power one, and
the 2.7 V setting then only guarantees 1.75 / 2.30 / 2.70 V. Output resistance
is **2.19 – 2.23 kΩ**, integrated output noise ≤ **4 µV RMS** (100 Hz – 20 kHz),
DC output current **0.91 mA typ** (2.0 V) / **1.2 mA typ** (2.7 V). The bias
must be changed only with the headset path muted.

**Bias generator and ramp.** `HS_BIAS_CTL` (CS42L84 0x1600; CS42L83 0x1C03)
carries a capless-mode bit (set by default — no external reservoir capacitor
assumed), a 60 kΩ pull-down enable, and a 2-bit ramp selector [Confirmed]:

| Code | Ramp | Rise (to 95 %) | Fall (95 → 5 %) | Ramp-delay before the bias may be reprogrammed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0b00 | fast rise, slow load-dependent fall | 0.002 ms | 3 ms | ≈ **10 ms** |
| 0b01 | fast | 10 ms | 15 ms | ≈ **40 ms** |
| 0b10 | slow (reset) | 25 ms | 37 ms | ≈ **90 ms** |
| 0b11 | slowest | 50 ms | 75 ms | ≈ **170 ms** |

Rise/fall figures assume a 4.7 µF bias filter capacitor. **Neither `HS_TRUE`
nor `SHORT_TRUE` is valid until the ramp-delay has elapsed after powering the
bias up**, and the ramp field itself must not be changed inside that window.
Transition times between levels are 1 – 23 µs for small steps and ≈ 92 µs to or
from high-impedance.

**Short-circuit / current-sense autocontrol.** `HSBIAS_SC_AUTOCTL`
(CS42L84 0x1470; CS42L83 0x1B70) carries a sense enable (bit 7), an
automatic-high-impedance-on-trip bit (bit 6), a tip-sense-driven enable
(bit 5), and a 3-bit trip threshold. The trip current, sensed through the
2.21 kΩ bias output resistance [Confirmed]:

| Code | Trip | Code | Trip |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 12 µA | 4 | 64 µA |
| 1 | 23 µA | 5 | 75 µA |
| 2 | 41 µA | 6 | 93 µA |
| **3** | **52 µA** — the value programmed | 7 | 104 µA |

The automatic-high-impedance behaviour is the part's named mechanism for
suppressing the transient produced when a plug is withdrawn slowly; to
disengage it, the bit must be cleared before being set again. The sense enable
**must be off in short-detect-only mode**, because the open circuit would
otherwise force a permanent trip.

**Gain stages** (CS42L84) [Confirmed, mainline]:

| Stage | Register | Codes | Scale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Analogue pre-amplifier | 0x2000 `[7:6]` | 0, 1, 2 | **0 dB, +10 dB, +20 dB** |
| Analogue PGA | 0x2000 `[4:0]` | 0 … 24 | **−12.0 dB … 0.0 dB in 0.5 dB steps** |
| Digital ADC volume | 0x2001 | signed 8-bit | **1.0 dB per step** by analogy with the public counterpart: 0x00 = 0 dB, up to +12 dB, down to −96 dB, 0x80–0x9F mute [Probable] |

Both analogue stages are programmed from per-machine values
(`adc-pre-amp-gain`, `adc-pga-vol`); **neither property is present on any
in-scope board**, so the built-in defaults apply [Confirmed]. On the CS42L83 the
corresponding digital control is `ADC_VOLUME` (0x1D03), written with a full
8-bit mask, scaled 1.0 dB per step from +12 dB down to −96 dB with 0x80–0x9F as
mute codes. Note that the CS42L83 has **no analogue programmable-gain
amplifier at all** — the public counterpart explicitly contrasts itself with
designs that use selectable gain stages, and switches internally between a
high-amplitude and a low-noise path instead. Its only gain controls are the
digital volume above and a **+20 dB digital boost** bit (`ADC_CTL` 0x1D01
bit 0). The CS42L84's two analogue stages are therefore an addition.

**Filters.** `ADC_CTL4` (CS42L84 0x2003; CS42L83 `ADC_WNF_HPF_CTL` 0x1D04)
carries a wind-noise filter and a high-pass filter, each with an enable and a
2-bit corner selection. The corners programmed on the in-scope machines are
**wind-noise 300 Hz** and **high-pass 3 Hz** [Confirmed].

**Format on the serial link.** The microphone occupies **serial transmit
channel 1 only** — mono. Routing is `BUS_ASP_TX_SRC` (0x4000) `[3:0]` ← 0b0111
(ADC) [Confirmed]. The transmit channel is placed in the **first half-frame**
(`ASP_TX_CH1_CTL1.SLOT_PHASE` = 0, slot start 0) at **24 bits** wide, inside the
same 64-bit-clock frame as playback, and SDOUT is tri-stated outside its slot
(`ASP_DATA_CTL` = 0x3A). Playback uses receive channels 1 and 2, channel 1 in
the first half-frame and channel 2 in the second. [Confirmed]

**Security domain — the headset microphone is reachable by a normal-world
driver on every in-scope machine.** The capture stream endpoint that the jack
codec feeds carries `device_type = "iop-audio-ns"` (non-secure) on **all** of
t8132, t604x, t8140, t8142 and t605x, and on t8140/t8142/t605x it names its DMA
channel explicitly as `dma-provider-rx = "base-ns-adma-rx-2"` — the **base
non-secure** receive channel 2. On t8132 and t604x the same endpoint binds its
channel by `dma-parent` phandle plus a `dma-channels` mask instead of by name,
but is likewise `iop-audio-ns`. [Confirmed — read directly from the platform
description on j713, j614s, j700, j813 and j714s.]

This matters because it is **not** true of the machine's other capture path: the
built-in digital microphone array sits behind the isolation boundary on t8140,
t8142 and t605x. Note also that the node whose *name* contains "hp-mic" is the
built-in array, not the headset microphone — it carries
`compatible = "audio-data,external"` and a low-power-processor data source. The
headset microphone is the node whose child carries
`compatible = "audio-data,cs42l84-input"` (or `"…cs42l83-input"` on t8140).
A driver author should not infer anything about the jack codec from the "hp-mic"
node name.

**`mic-config`.** An 8-byte array on the codec node, identical on every board
that carries it: `01 00 ff ff ff ff ff ff`. It is read as a fixed 8-byte blob
and indexes a per-microphone configuration table with a documented maximum
count; 0xFF marks an unused slot. Two slots are populated, with values 0x01 and
0x00. The meaning of the two populated values is **[Unknown]** — see Open
questions.

---

## 10.11 Power sequencing and pop/click suppression

### 10.11.1 Cold start (CS42L84)

1. Drive the reset pin low, then high. Allow **3000 µs** for boot before the
   first register access [Confirmed, published driver]. The counterpart's own
   figure for the post-reset internal-initialisation wait is **2.5 ms**, so
   3 ms is the same number rounded up. **The minimum reset-pin low pulse width
   is not published** — see Open questions.
2. Optionally issue the soft reset: write **0x5A** to 0x0203 and wait **500 µs**
   [Confirmed].
3. Read the device ID at 0x0000–0x0002 and the revision at 0x73FE.
4. Set pad drive strength: 0x0C01 ← **0x0B**.
5. Set the charge-pump LDO reference trim: 0x3826 ← **0x25** (5 V).
6. Program the analogue trim group (§10.2.2(e)).
7. Configure plug detection: latch-to-VDD_P (0x1477 bit 1 ← 1), tip-sense mode
   ← short-detect (0x1473 `[7:6]` ← 0b11), ring-sense control 0x1282 ←
   inverted + pull-up (mask 0xC0) and rise debounce 1000 ms, tip-sense control
   0x1283 ← inverted, fall 125 ms, rise 250 ms, then enable the tip/ring-sense
   block (0x1802 bit 3).
8. Set the microphone-detect threshold (0x1475) and park the headset switch
   matrix at 0xFF with `HS_DET_CTL2.SET` ← 2, and set
   `HS_CLAMP_DISABLE` (0x1813) ← 1.
9. Mask the ring-sense interrupts; leave tip-sense unmasked.

### 10.11.2 Global analogue power-up / power-down

**Power up:** `MSM_BLOCK_EN1` (0x1800) bit 0 ← 1, then `FILTP_CHARGE_CTL`
(0x181C) bit 0 ← 0 to release the FILT+ clamp so the reservoir charges.

**Power down:** wait for the VDD_P latch to report ready (polled, with an
explicit failure path), then `MSM_BLOCK_EN1` ← 0, wait for the global
power-down to complete, then `FILTP_CHARGE_CTL` ← 1 to clamp and discharge
FILT+. [Confirmed]

The corresponding CS42L83 sequence uses `PWR_CTL1` (0x1101): 0xFF = everything
down, and the power-down-done interrupt (0x1308 bit 0) is unmasked and waited
on; the published timeout for that is **235 ms** with a **65 ms** typical time
and a **1000 µs** poll interval [Confirmed, published driver].

### 10.11.3 Ordering rules that matter for pops

The governing constraint is the **FILT+ reservoir**. FILT+ reaches its
operating voltage in **under 10 ms** when a block leaves power-down, but if the
PLL and/or the headset-detect block is enabled while the ADC *and* the
headphone are both powered down, **FILT+ discharges to 0 V**, and recovering
from that can take **up to 1 second** — during which the audio path may already
be running and will distort. [Confirmed — datasheet, and encoded as two
warnings in the published driver.] Deliberately discharging FILT+ (only legal
with the global power-down asserted) takes **≈ 46 ms** with the recommended
2.2 µF reservoir.

Hence:

1. **The PLL must not be started while both the ADC and the headphone are
   powered down.** At least one of the ADC or DAC blocks must be enabled first.
   [Confirmed — stated for both parts.]
2. **`DETECT_MODE` must be 0 while both the ADC and the headphone are powered
   down**, for the same reason. [Confirmed]
3. **Every power-up sequence must start from global power-down asserted, the
   S/PDIF transmitter powered down, and the PLL stopped**, for the same reason.
   [Confirmed]
4. The bit clock must be running before un-mute, and the codec must be parked on
   its internal oscillator before the bit clock stops.
5. Un-mute is the **last** step of stream start and mute the **first** step of
   stream stop.
6. The headphone output must be muted (CS42L83 `HP_CTL` 0x2001 ← 0x0C, both
   channels analogue-muted; CS42L84 `DAC_CTL1` 0x3000 bit 0 ← 0) before the
   headset switch matrix or the headset bias is changed, i.e. **before and after
   every insertion or removal event**.
7. Before a jack insertion completes, the headset bias must be at 0 V and the
   switch matrix fully disconnected; after the type/microphone decision, the
   bias may be raised.
8. On removal the bias must be dropped to 0 V and the switch matrix restored to
   the disconnected value **before** anything else, to avoid discharging the
   bias reservoir through the user's ears.

### 10.11.4 Soft ramp and zero-cross

**CS42L84**: `HP_VOL_CTL` (0x3020) bit 1 = zero-cross update, bit 0 = soft-ramp
update. The published driver sets **zero-cross on, soft ramp off**; the host
enables **both** — it sets the soft-ramp bit for volume changes and the
zero-cross bit around DAC enable/disable, and writes 0x00 when disabling the DAC
[Confirmed]. Volume writes to the four DAC volume bytes are wrapped in the
freeze register (0x0006 bit 0) so both channels change on the same sample.

**CS42L83**: the soft-ramp rate register is `SFTRAMP_RATE` (0x100A), reset
value **0xA4**; the slow-start enable is 0x100B `[6:4]`, reset value **0x70**
(= enabled; **0b000 disables it, and all three bits must change together**).
The host explicitly writes **0x00** to 0x100B to disable slow start at one point
in the sequence and **0x70** to re-enable it, i.e. slow start is suppressed
across a specific transition and restored afterwards [Confirmed]. This is the
CS42L83's equivalent of the CS42L84's clamp/force dance.

`SFTRAMP_RATE` is two 4-bit fields — `[7:4]` for the analogue volumes
(**1 dB or 2 dB per step** on the headphone output) and `[3:0]` for the digital
volumes (**0.125 dB per step**) — each giving the number of sample periods
between steps: codes 0…15 ⇒ **1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 11, 12, 16, 22, 24, 33, 36, 44,
48, 66, 72** periods. The reset value 0xA4 is therefore analogue = 33 periods,
digital = 8 periods. [Confirmed, datasheet.]

Additional CS42L84 pop-suppression controls, all used: the headphone negative
clamp override (0x3123 bit 0), the headphone output force-on (0x3068 bit 4), the
headphone pull-down selection including the **1.1 kΩ** setting (0x3001), and the
FILT+ clamp (0x181C). The clamp override and force-on are asserted together
before an impedance measurement and released afterwards, with the previous
pull-down setting saved and restored [Confirmed].

### 10.11.5 `PowerOffAtSleep`

`PowerOffAtSleep = 1` on **every** in-scope board (and every M1–M3 board)
[Confirmed]. Consequences:

- **With it set (the actual configuration):** at system sleep the codec is taken
  through the full power-down sequence and its supply is removed. All register
  state is lost, so the twelve detection-block registers listed in §10.3.6 must
  be saved before sleep and restored after; the whole cold-start sequence of
  §10.11.1 must be re-run on resume; and jack insertion or removal **while the
  system is asleep is not detected by the codec** — the state must be
  re-evaluated by reading the tip/ring-sense status on resume. Two explicit
  conditions exist for this path: "power down for sleep" and "**wake from sleep
  with no power**" [Confirmed].
- **If it were clear:** the codec would retain its supply and its register state
  across sleep, and the wake-pin mechanism (`WAKE_CTL`, CS42L84 0x1471) could
  raise the system on headphone or microphone insertion. That register carries
  separate headphone-wake and microphone-wake masks, a wake-pin mode bit, and a
  clear bit. On these machines that capability is unused.

## 10.12 Interrupt line

Every in-scope machine routes the codec's interrupt output to a pin on the main
SoC GPIO block, and the reset input to a pin on either the main GPIO block or
the always-on "nub" GPIO block.

| SoC | Boards | Reset pin | Interrupt controller | Interrupt pin | Shared? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| t8132 | j604, j623, j624, j713, j715, j773g | `/arm-io/nub-gpio` pin **17** | `/arm-io/gpio0` | **98** | no |
| t604x | j614s, j614c, j616s, j616c, j773s, j575c | `/arm-io/nub-gpio0` pin **58** | `/arm-io/gpio0` | **106** | no |
| t8140 | j700 | `/arm-io/gpio0` pin **103** | `/arm-io/gpio0` | **104** | no |
| t8142 | j704, j813, j815 | `/arm-io/nub-gpio` pin **18** | `/arm-io/gpio0` | **100** | no |
| t605x | j714s, j714c, j716s, j716c | `/arm-io/gpio0` pin **139** | `/arm-io/gpio0` | **134** | no |

For comparison (M1–M3): M1 CS42L83 machines use nub-GPIO pin 11 / IRQ 183;
M1 Pro/Max/Ultra use nub-GPIO0 pin 4 / IRQ 180; M2 uses nub-GPIO pin 12 /
IRQ 149; M3 base uses nub-GPIO pin 17 / IRQ 173; M3 Max/Ultra use nub-GPIO0
pin 58 / IRQ 30.

- `function-reset` encodes `<gpio-controller phandle> "GPIO" <pin> <flags=1>`
  on every board. The reset input is **active low**: it is held low and released
  high to bring the part out of reset [Confirmed, published binding
  `reset-gpios = <… GPIO_ACTIVE_LOW>`].
- `interrupts = <pin> <1>` on every board. The line is **level-triggered,
  active low** [Confirmed — the published binding specifies
  `IRQ_TYPE_LEVEL_LOW`, and the host explicitly validates at start-up that the
  line is configured as a level trigger and fails if it is not].
- **The line is not shared with any other device on any in-scope board.** The
  only observed sharing anywhere in the whole set is on one M2 machine (j413),
  whose two codec nodes on different I²C buses share IRQ 149.
- t8140 is the only in-scope machine whose reset pin is on the main GPIO block
  rather than the always-on nub block, and the only one whose reset and
  interrupt pins are adjacent (103 / 104).

## Per-SoC / per-machine differences

| Aspect | t8132 (M4) | t604x (M4 Pro/Max) | t8140 (A18 Pro) | t8142 (M5) | t605x (M5 Pro/Max) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Part | CS42L84 | CS42L84 | **CS42L83** | CS42L84 | CS42L84 |
| I²C bus / address | i2c1 / 0x4B | i2c2 / 0x4B | **i2c0 / 0x48** | i2c1 / 0x4B | i2c2 / 0x4B |
| Controller aperture (absolute) | 0x3_AD01_4000 | 0x4_2901_8000 | 0x3_8501_0000 | 0x3_A501_4000 | 0x5_0501_8000 |
| Bus shared | no | no | no | **yes — one further device at 0x10** | no |
| Reset pin | nub-GPIO 17 | nub-GPIO0 58 | **GPIO0 103** | nub-GPIO 18 | GPIO0 139 |
| Interrupt | GPIO0 98 | GPIO0 106 | GPIO0 104 | GPIO0 100 | GPIO0 134 |
| Link clock supplied | none (derived) | none | **24.000 MHz** | none | none |
| Frame length | 64 bit clocks | 64 | ratio field 125, see §10.7.3 | 64 | 64 |
| Capture rates offered | 48 / 44.1 / 88.2 / 96 kHz | same | **48 kHz only** | same | same |
| `samplerate-subset` | absent | absent | **present = {48 kHz}** | absent | absent |
| Register map | CS42L84 flat 16-bit | same | **CS42L83 paged 8-bit** | same | same |
| DC impedance block | present, enabled | present, enabled | **not present in silicon** (property present but inert) [Inferred] | present, enabled | present, enabled |
| EQ block | not exposed | not exposed | **present and used** | not exposed | not exposed |
| Headset-mic capture domain | **non-secure** | **non-secure** | **non-secure** (base non-secure receive ch 2) | **non-secure** (same) | **non-secure** (same) |
| Everything else | identical across all five | | | | |

Within each SoC group every board is identical in every codec-node property
except the GPIO/interrupt numbers, which are identical within a group as listed
above. There is no per-chassis or per-model variation in codec configuration
anywhere in scope.

## Open questions

1. **Reset values for the CS42L84.** No reset value for any CS42L84 register is
   published or established here, which forces any driver to write every field
   it depends on rather than relying on defaults. *Why it matters:* read-modify-
   write on an unknown reset value is the classic source of silent
   misconfiguration, and the trim registers in §10.2.2(e) are written blind.
   *How to resolve:* hold the reset pin low, release it, wait 3 ms, then dump
   all 28 populated ranges over I²C before the host touches the part. Repeat
   after a 0x5A write to 0x0203 to separate pin-reset defaults from
   soft-reset defaults.

2. **Revision-ID values.** The byte at 0x0005 and at 0x73FE (CS42L84) and at
   0x1005 (CS42L83) is read at initialisation but never compared against
   anything. *Why it matters:* a driver cannot state which revisions it has been
   validated against, and cannot detect a future revision. *How to resolve:*
   read 0x0005 and 0x73FE on an M1 Pro machine and on an M4, M5 and A18 Pro
   machine and compare. If they differ, the "same silicon" conclusion in
   §10.2.4 needs qualifying.

3. **The DC impedance-to-ohms conversion (CS42L84).** The register block is
   established (§10.8.6) but the arithmetic that turns the four result bytes,
   the pull-down reference reading and the per-part trim into an impedance in
   ohms is **not**. *Why it matters:* without it the block can be triggered but
   its output cannot be interpreted, so the load-dependent output-level table in
   §10.2.2(g) cannot be applied and headphone output level cannot be matched to
   the load. *How to resolve:* a bench experiment — plug known precision loads
   (16 Ω, 32 Ω, 50 Ω, 80 Ω, 150 Ω, 300 Ω, 600 Ω) into the jack, trigger a
   measurement in each of the 8 range codes, and record 0x120B and
   0x120C–0x120F. Seven loads across eight ranges gives an over-determined
   system from which the offset and slope can be fitted directly.

4. **The undocumented trim registers 0x3064, 0x317B, 0x317F, 0x31AE,
   0x31B0/B1, 0x31BC/BD, 0x31C8/C9, 0x31D4/D5, 0x31E8/E9, 0x31F4/F5.** Values
   are known; meaning is not, and they lie outside the part's own decoded-range
   table. *Why it matters:* if these are mandatory analogue trims, omitting them
   may degrade output quality or damage the output stage at the 5 V charge-pump
   setting; if they are optional, a driver can skip them. *How to resolve:*
   bring the part up twice — once with the trim group applied and once without
   — and measure headphone THD+N, output swing and idle current into a 32 Ω
   load at the 5 V charge-pump setting.

5. **The CS42L84 headphone load/capacitive-load/high-voltage field encoding
   (0x3000 mask 0x74).** The field names are established, the sub-field bit
   positions and code meanings are not. *Why it matters:* it gates the
   high-voltage output mode together with 0x30D4 and 0x3826; a wrong value
   either wastes headroom or overdrives a low-impedance load. *How to resolve:*
   sweep all 8 values of mask 0x74 with a fixed digital full-scale tone and
   measure output amplitude into 32 Ω and 300 Ω loads.

6. **CS42L84 populated-but-unused register ranges**: 0x0403–0x041F (beyond the
   four plug bits and the PLL lock bits), 0x0604–0x0607, 0x0609–0x0610,
   0x0801–0x0803, 0x1203–0x1214, 0x1216–0x127F, 0x1284–0x1287, 0x1478–0x147B,
   0x1486–0x14B6, 0x2002, 0x2400, 0x2600–0x2612, 0x3008–0x301F, 0x31A1,
   0x3400–0x3401, 0x3600, 0x3800, 0x4002–0x4004, 0x4200–0x4203,
   0x4400–0x4444, 0x4800–0x4844, 0x5001–0x500F, 0x5012–0x5017, 0x5019–0x501F,
   0x5021–0x5023, 0x5025–0x5027, 0x502F–0x5067, 0x506F. *Why it matters:*
   0x2600–0x2612 is the right size and position to be a mixer/sidetone block,
   and 0x4400–0x4444 / 0x4800–0x4844 are the right size to be EQ or filter
   coefficient banks — the CS42L84's equivalent of the CS42L83's EQ. If a
   sidetone or EQ path exists it is directly useful. *How to resolve:* dump
   these ranges after reset, then dump again while a tone is playing, and look
   for registers that change; then write single bytes and watch for an audible
   or measurable effect on the analogue output.

7. **The CS42L83 registers not in the published map: 0x1401, 0x1B7B, 0x1B7C —
   and 0x1117, which is actively programmed with 0x08 / 0x09.** *Why it
   matters:* 0x1117 is written in the middle of the serial-port bring-up and
   tear-down sequence, so omitting it may produce clicks or a non-functional
   link on the A18 Pro machine. *How to resolve:* trace the I²C bus on j700
   across a stream start/stop with a logic analyser and correlate the 0x1117
   write with the analogue output; then bring the part up with and without it.

8. **Whether the CS42L83 has any DC-impedance capability at all, given
   `enable-dcid = 1` on j700.** *Why it matters:* if it does, the same
   headphone-level-matching feature could be offered on that machine. *How to
   resolve:* probe for readable registers outside the 20 decoded ranges by
   scanning every page/offset over I²C with known loads plugged, looking for a
   register that changes with load.

9. **The meaning of `mic-config = 01 00 ff ff ff ff ff ff`.** Established as an
   8-byte per-microphone table with 0xFF marking unused slots, two slots
   populated. *Why it matters:* it feeds the microphone source selection, and a
   driver that guesses wrong may route the wrong input. *How to resolve:*
   compare against the same property on machines with different microphone
   complements (the A18 Pro machine's internal digital microphones are managed
   by the same codec node, which is likely what the second entry refers to), and
   correlate with the input-source enumeration exposed to userspace.

10. **The A18 Pro link-clock discrepancy.** The serial-link descriptor gives
    24.000 MHz with a ratio field of 125, which does not reproduce the 48 kHz
    default. *Why it matters:* a driver must know the actual bit-clock frequency
    and frame length to program the codec's frame-period registers and to pick
    a PLL row. *How to resolve:* probe the serial-link pins on j700 with a scope
    or logic analyser during 48 kHz playback and measure the bit-clock frequency
    and the bit clocks per frame directly.

11. **The `function-codecinput_master` platform function's actual effect.** The
    encoding, provider and argument are established; what the provider does when
    invoked is not. *Why it matters:* it is the only mechanism by which capture
    clocking role is selected, and on M4+ the provider lives behind the audio
    coprocessor, so the effect may be a coprocessor message rather than a
    register write. *How to resolve:* trace the coprocessor mailbox around
    capture start on an in-scope machine and correlate with the codec's serial
    clock-role register 0x0608, which should remain 0x00 (slave) if the SoC is
    the provider.

12. **Whether the CS42L84 can actually be operated as serial-port clock
    provider.** The register fields exist (0x0608 `ASP_MASTER_MODE`,
    `ASP_BCLK_SEL`; 0x5000 `ASP_FSYNC_EN`) but no machine uses them and the
    internal-master-clock-to-bit-clock divider is unknown. *Why it matters:*
    only if a future design needs it; not required for any in-scope machine.
    *How to resolve:* on a development board, set `ASP_BCLK_SEL` to internal,
    `ASP_MASTER_MODE` to provider and `ASP_FSYNC_EN` to 1 with the PLL locked,
    and measure the resulting bit-clock frequency against the internal master
    clock to recover the divider.

13. **The two extra interrupt status/mask groups on the CS42L84
    (0x0401/0x0419 and 0x0402/0x041A).** 0x0402 is read during PLL bring-up, so
    at least one of them carries clock-domain events. *Why it matters:* a driver
    that masks only the plug bits may leave other sources unmasked and take
    spurious interrupts. *How to resolve:* unmask each bit individually and
    provoke the corresponding condition (stop the bit clock, over-drive the ADC,
    short the headphone output) while watching the interrupt line.

14. **Low-rate sample-rate codes on the CS42L84 (codes 1, 2, 3 and the codes for
    8 kHz, 11.025 kHz and 32 kHz).** Code 10 = 22.05 kHz is confirmed; the rest
    of the low-rate family is inferred. *Why it matters:* voice-call and
    voice-trigger paths may want 16 kHz, and the published driver cannot reach
    it. *How to resolve:* program each candidate code with a known bit clock and
    measure the frame rate at which the part actually consumes samples, or
    measure the pitch of a known tone played back through it.

15. **The ring-sense comparator threshold, and which way it fails.** The public
    counterpart's datasheet states the trim thresholds twice with different
    numbers — 0.15/0.03 · VP and 0.40/0.28 · VP in the electrical table versus
    0.10/0.05 · VP and 0.35/0.30 · VP in the register description — a spread of
    up to 0.05 · VP, and the Apple variants' values are not independently
    established. *Why it matters, concretely:* `ringsense-inverted = 1` on every
    in-scope board, so the comparator output is inverted before it reaches the
    debounce logic, and the ring conductor of a seated plug sits at the **low**
    end of the range. **If the effective high threshold is set too low (the
    0.10 · VP reading, or the low-impedance pull-up trim on a board that needs
    the high-impedance one), a seated plug reads as "not seated": ring sense
    never asserts, the fully-plugged re-detection in §10.8.5 never fires, and a
    headset is reported as bare headphones with no microphone.** The opposite
    error — threshold too high — makes an absent or partially-inserted plug read
    as seated, which triggers a microphone-presence measurement into an open
    circuit and yields a spurious "headphones" report. The first failure is the
    likely one and it is silent: audio still works, the microphone simply never
    appears. *How to resolve:* drive the ring contact from a bench supply
    through the board's own pull network, sweep it across 0 … VP, and record the
    debounced ring state for both settings of the pull-up trim and both
    polarities; the switching points give the real thresholds directly.

16. **Minimum reset-pin low pulse width.** Not published for either part, and
    not established here; only the *post*-reset wait (2.5–3 ms) is known.
    *Why it matters:* a driver that pulses reset too briefly may leave the part
    in an undefined state that only shows up intermittently. *How to resolve:*
    sweep the low time from 100 ns upward with a GPIO and, for each width, read
    the device ID and a known-modified register to see whether the reset
    actually took.

17. **Class-H rail policy on the A18 Pro machine.** The host pins the charge
    pump to the fixed ±2.5 V rail (`ADPTPWR` = 0b001) instead of the part's
    adapt-to-signal default. *Why it matters:* the fixed rail costs idle power
    but removes the ≈20 µs rail-transition and its associated artefacts; a
    driver copying the default would behave differently in both power and
    distortion. *How to resolve:* measure idle current and THD+N at low levels
    with `ADPTPWR` = 0b001 versus 0b111 into a 32 Ω load.

18. **CS42L84 headset-type-detect register positions 0x1810 and 0x1836.** These
    are inferred from block extents and from the five-register headset group
    the part exposes, not directly observed. *Why it matters:* a driver that
    wants real CTIA/OMTP discrimination rather than the assumed-CTIA shortcut
    must use them. *How to resolve:* dump 0x1800–0x1836 with an OMTP adapter and
    a CTIA adapter plugged in, and look for the register whose low two bits
    differ between the two.


---

# 11. Coprocessor-mediated paths

## Baseline

The block measured against is the always-on coprocessor of the M1–M3
generations: a small real-time CPU complex behind its own IOMMU, with a
96-bit hardware mailbox pair for host communication, its own complete
six-cluster serial audio controller, its own 32-channel audio DMA controller,
and a PDM converter/decimator front end. On M1–M3 this complex owned exactly
one audio path — the built-in digital microphone array — while the speaker,
headphone and loopback paths were driven by a **host-owned** multi-cluster
serial audio controller, a host-owned numerically controlled oscillator and a
host-owned audio DMA controller.

On the M4 generation and later the coprocessor's audio complex became the
**only** serialiser/clocking complex the platform exposes. The host-owned
serial audio controller is no longer described, its numerically controlled
oscillator is no longer addressable, and every audio stream on the machine is
declared as an endpoint of a coprocessor service. The data path did not move:
audio DMA remains host-addressable MMIO, now instantiated four times
(base/low-power × secure/non-secure). This section specifies the resulting
control interface.

**The mailbox register interface is not verified on an in-scope part.** The
register map of §11.2.2 is the published map for the block revision every
in-scope coprocessor declares (`iop,ascwrap-v6`, the same revision the M3
generation declares). Everything that concerns mailbox registers is therefore
**[Probable]** for the in-scope dies — a single line of evidence, the shared
revision string — and is listed for confirmation in *Open questions*. The
message-level protocol layered on it (§11.2.8, §11.4) is
**[Confirmed]**; only its landing on these dies rests on the register map.

**Address convention.** All MMIO addresses quoted from the platform
description are I/O-region-relative. The translation to absolute is taken from
the I/O bridge node's own `ranges` property and is, for the in-scope parts:

| SoC | I/O-region offset to absolute |
|---|---|
| t8132 (M4) | `+0x2_0000_0000` |
| t604x (M4 Pro/Max) | `+0x2_0000_0000` |
| t605x / t6050 (M5 Pro/Max) | `+0x2_0000_0000` |
| t8142 (M5) | `+0x2_1000_0000` |
| t8140 (A18 Pro) | `+0x2_1000_0000` |

[Confirmed] — read directly from the bridge `ranges` entry that covers the
audio address space on each part, and cross-checked against the coprocessor
firmware-region property, which is expressed absolutely and differs from the
corresponding `reg` entry by exactly this offset. **Addresses below are
I/O-region-relative unless stated otherwise.**

---

## Summary of differences

| Item | M1–M3 | M4 (t8132, t604x) | A18 Pro (t8140) | M5 (t8142) | M5 Pro/Max (t605x) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Always-on coprocessor | present, `iop,ascwrap-v4` (M1/M2) → `-v6` (M3) | present, `-v6` | present, `-v6` | present, `-v6` | present, `-v6` |
| Coprocessor mailbox aperture size | `0x6c000` | **`0x88000`** | `0x88000` | `0x88000` | `0x88000` |
| Mailbox block placement and register map | `+0x8000`, `0x4000` bytes | unchanged | unchanged | unchanged | unchanged |
| Mailbox interrupt inputs | 4 | 4 (t8132), **8** (t604x) | 4 | 4 | 4 |
| External-interrupt register window `reg[4]` | absent | present (t8132), **absent** (t604x) | present | present | present |
| Numbered shared-memory boot-argument slots | absent | absent | **80** | **80** | **80** |
| Coprocessor code images per payload | 1 | 1 | **2** | **2** | **2** |
| Application-endpoint numbers named in the platform description | — | — | `0x30`, `0x31`, `0x4e` | `0x4d` | `0x4d` |
| Second always-on coprocessor instance | absent | **absent** | **present** | **present** | **present** |
| Isolated-environment mailbox aperture | absent | absent | **present (×2)** | **present** | **present** |
| Audio stream description | per-cluster nodes under host serial audio controller | **single service node, no `reg`** | same | same | same |
| Host serial audio controller MMIO | present | **absent** | **absent** | **absent** | **absent** |
| Numerically controlled oscillator node | present with `reg` | **absent** | present, **no `reg`** | **absent** | **absent** |
| Audio DMA instances | 1 host + 1 coprocessor-side | **2** (base-ns, leap-ns) | **3** (+ leap-s) | **3** (+ leap-s) | **3** (+ leap-s) |
| DMA channel binding on a stream endpoint | `dma-channels` + `dma-parent` | **`dma-channels` + `dma-parent`** | **named `dma-provider-tx/rx` strings** | named strings | named strings |
| Microphone-array stream domain | non-secure | **non-secure** | **secure** | **secure** | **secure** |
| Secure loopback stream | absent | absent | absent | absent | **present** |
| Microphone injection stream | absent | absent | **present** | **present** | **present** |
| Speaker tap endpoint | absent (sense merged into speaker link) | absent | **present** | **present** | **present** |
| Audio power domains host-controllable | yes (flag byte `0x00`) | **no (flag byte `0x10`)** | no | no | no |
| Coprocessor firmware container | plain executable image | **plain executable image** | **segmented bundle** | **segmented bundle** | **segmented bundle** |

---

## 11.1 Coprocessor inventory

### 11.1.1 Which coprocessor owns audio

Three coprocessor instances appear in the platform description of the in-scope
parts. Audio is owned by exactly one of them.

| Node | `compatible` | Present on | On the audio path? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/arm-io/aop` — always-on coprocessor | `iop,ascwrap-v6` | all in-scope SoCs | **Yes.** Owns the serial audio controllers, the clock generation, the PDM front end and all stream state. |
| `/arm-io/aop2` — second always-on instance | `iop,ascwrap-v6` | t8140, t8142, t605x only | **No.** No audio function is attributed to it; its own service names describe a communications/routing role. [Confirmed] |
| `/arm-io/sio` — serial-I/O coprocessor | `iop,ascwrap-v6` | all in-scope SoCs | **No.** Its `device-type` table enumerates SPI and UART ports only. Its child `sio-dma` (`sio-dma-controller`) is not an audio DMA controller and carries no audio channel description. [Confirmed] |

The `/arm-io/iop-voicetrigger-controller` node is **not** a coprocessor: it is a
second service-client node of the same shape as the audio controller node
(`compatible = "iop-audio,controller"`, no `reg`), naming a *different service on
the same always-on coprocessor*. [Confirmed] It is present on every in-scope
board that has a microphone array and absent on the three that do not
(j773g, j773s, j575c).

### 11.1.2 Always-on coprocessor — per-SoC hardware parameters

`reg` entries are (base, size) pairs, I/O-region-relative.

| SoC | reg[0] mailbox/control | reg[1] secondary aperture | reg[2] firmware SRAM | reg[3] arbitration | reg[4] external-interrupt window |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| t8132 | `0x1_9060_0000` / `0x88000` | `0x1_9005_0000` / `0x4000` | `0x1_90c0_0000` / `0x1e0000` | `0x1_882a_8000` / `0x8` | `0x1_9062_c000` / `0x3c008` |
| t604x | `0x3_1060_0000` / `0x88000` | `0x3_1005_0000` / `0x4000` | `0x3_10c0_0000` / `0x2f0000` | `0x3_0832_8000` / `0x24` | — |
| t8140 | `0x1_0060_0000` / `0x88000` | `0x1_0005_0000` / `0x4000` | `0x1_00c0_0000` / `0x1e0000` | `0x0_f82a_8000` / `0x8` | `0x1_0062_c000` / `0x3c008` |
| t8142 | `0x1_8060_0000` / `0x88000` | `0x1_8005_0000` / `0x4000` | `0x1_80c0_0000` / `0x1e0000` | `0x1_782a_8000` / `0x8` | `0x1_8062_c000` / `0x3c008` |
| t605x | `0x0_9060_0000` / `0x88000` | `0x0_9065_0000` / `0x4000` | `0x0_90c0_0000` / `0x2f0000` | `0x0_8832_8000` / `0x24` | `0x0_9062_c000` / `0x3c008` |

[Confirmed] — identical across every board of a given SoC.

Notes:

- reg[0] is the coprocessor control + mailbox aperture. The CPU-control
  registers occupy its first `0x4000` bytes — the run bit is at
  `reg[0] + 0x44` (§11.2.7) — and the mailbox block occupies
  `+0x8000` … `+0xc000` (§11.2.1). It **grew from `0x6c000` to `0x88000`** at
  the M4 generation while the `compatible` string stayed at `iop,ascwrap-v6`
  (which first appears on M3). Whatever was added occupies the range
  `0x6c000`–`0x88000` and is **[Unknown]**; it is known **not** to contain the
  mailbox or the CPU-control registers, both of which sit below `0xc000`
  (§11.2.6).
- reg[1] is a separate `0x4000` aperture at a different base, present in
  identical relative position on every generation from M1. **Nothing in the
  published interface touches it and its contents are [Unknown].** It is *not*
  the CPU-control aperture; that is inside reg[0].
- reg[4] is a *sub-window of reg[0]* (`base+0x2c000`, length `0x3c008`, i.e.
  `0x2c000`–`0x68008`), separately described so it can be assigned
  independently. It is absent on t604x. It is the **external-interrupt register
  window** — the node's `ext-irq-reg-index` property names this `reg` index
  (§11.2.6). Its internal register layout is **[Unknown]**. It does not overlap
  the mailbox block. The same window, at the same relative offset and the same
  length, is the third `reg` entry of the second coprocessor instance — so it is
  a per-instance block, not an audio block. [Confirmed]
- reg[3] is a very small aperture (8 or 0x24 bytes) at an address **shared
  with every audio DMA controller instance on the same die** — each
  `admac-*` node carries the identical (base, 8) pair as its second `reg`.
  Functionally this is a shared low-latency-traffic arbitration/vote
  register. [Confirmed — the address is byte-identical across the coprocessor
  node and all four DMA controller nodes on every in-scope board.]
- reg[2] is the firmware SRAM window. The child nub node restates it
  absolutely in `region-base` / `region-size`. `region-base` is the absolute
  form of the same window — it equals reg[2]'s base plus the SoC's I/O-region
  translation offset on every board, with no exceptions. `region-size`,
  however, is **not** always reg[2]'s size:

  | SoC | reg[2] size | `region-size` | Relation |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | t8132 | `0x1e0000` | `0x190000` | declared region **smaller** than the aperture |
  | t8140 | `0x1e0000` | `0x190000` | declared region **smaller** than the aperture |
  | t8142 | `0x1e0000` | **`0x2f0000`** | declared region **larger** than the aperture, by `0x110000` |
  | t604x | `0x2f0000` | `0x2f0000` | equal |
  | t605x | `0x2f0000` | `0x2f0000` | equal |

  [Confirmed] — both figures are per-SoC and identical across every board of a
  given SoC. **t8142 is the only SoC in scope where the declared region exceeds
  the aperture the same node describes**, and a driver that maps only reg[2]
  there would be `0x110000` short of the declared region. See Open question 25.

  On t8132 the payload geometry settles which figure bounds the real memory,
  in the opposite direction: the per-SoC payload for t8132 declares a resident
  code size of `0x1bb000` and its highest-addressed segment ends at offset
  `0x1db000` within the firmware window. That **exceeds `region-size`
  (`0x190000`)** and fits within reg[2]'s `0x1e0000` with `0x5000` to spare.
  The per-board payload for one t8132 machine declares `0x188000` and does fit
  within `region-size`. Reading: **reg[2] bounds the memory that actually
  responds and `region-size` does not**, at least on t8132. **[Inferred]** —
  from payload geometry alone, on one SoC. It does not settle t8142, where
  `region-size` is the *larger* of the two figures. It does mean a driver must
  map reg[2] in full on t8132 or it will truncate the per-SoC payload with no
  diagnostic.
- `iop-version = 1`, `role` = a 3–4 character ASCII tag, `device_type = "aop"`,
  `power-gates` and `clock-gates` both **empty** — the host has no power or
  clock gate for this coprocessor. [Confirmed]
- `ext-irq-reg-index = 4` is carried on **t8132, t8140, t8142 and t605x** —
  every in-scope SoC except t604x, i.e. exactly the four that have a `reg[4]`.
  The correlation is exact on every board of every generation from M1 to M5:
  every board whose coprocessor node has five `reg` entries carries the property
  and every board with four carries none (14 boards with, 41 without; no
  exceptions).
  [Confirmed] t8132 and t605x additionally carry a `function-pll_off_mode`
  entry (tag reads `PLLM`) on the coprocessor node. [Confirmed]

Interrupts (raw interrupt-controller inputs, in `interrupts` order):

| SoC | Coprocessor interrupts |
|---|---|
| t8132 | `0x1b2, 0x1b1, 0x1b4, 0x1b3` |
| t604x | `0x2c7, 0x2c6, 0x2c9, 0x2c8, 0x2cb, 0x2ca, 0x2cd, 0x2cc` (**eight**) |
| t8140 | `0x187, 0x186, 0x189, 0x188` |
| t8142 | `0x1eb, 0x1ea, 0x1ed, 0x1ec` |
| t605x | `0x243, 0x242, 0x245, 0x244` |

[Confirmed]. Every in-scope part except t604x presents **four** consecutive
interrupts listed in the order (n+1, n, n+3, n+2) — one input per FIFO edge,
assigned in §11.2.5; t604x presents **eight** in two such groups, at
n = `0x2c6` and n = `0x2ca`. The doubling on t604x reads as **two complete
mailbox channel sets**, **[Inferred]** and corroborated by the display
coprocessor carrying the same doubling on t604x and t605x while carrying four
on t8132 and on every M1–M3 part. Where the second set's registers live is
**[Unknown]** (§11.2.5, Open question 29).

IOMMU: every instance's `iommu-parent` points at a mapper child of
`/arm-io/dart-aop` (`compatible = "dart,t8110"`, `page-size = 0x4000`).

| SoC | dart-aop `reg` | IRQ | `sid-count` | Audio-relevant stream IDs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| t8132 | `0x1_90f0_0000`/`0xc000` + `0x1_90f1_0000`/`0x4000` | `0x1c9` | 16 | coprocessor 0, isolated 1, base-ns 8, base-s 9, leap-ns 10, leap-s 11 |
| t604x | `0x3_10f0_0000`/`0xc000` + `0x3_10f1_0000`/`0x4000` | `0x2de` | 16 | coprocessor 0, base-ns 8, base-s 9, leap-ns 10, leap-s 11 (**no isolated sid**) |
| t8140 | `0x1_00fc_0000`/`0xc000` | `0x1ac` | 18 | coprocessor 0, isolated 1, secondary 16, secondary-isolated 17, sensor-crossbar 3, base-ns 8, base-s 9, leap-ns 10, leap-s 11 |
| t8142 | `0x1_80fc_0000`/`0xc000` | `0x210` | 17 | coprocessor 0, isolated 1, secondary 16, sensor-crossbar 3, base-ns 8, base-s 9, leap-ns 10, leap-s 11 |
| t605x | `0x0_90fc_0000`/`0xc000` | `0x268` | 17 | as t8142 |

[Confirmed]. The stream-ID assignment `8/9/10/11 = base-ns / base-s / leap-ns /
leap-s` is **identical on every in-scope SoC including t604x**, even where the
corresponding secure DMA controller is not instantiated. The mapper children
`mapper-admac-base-ns` and `mapper-admac-leap-ns` carry
`allow-subpage-mapping` (empty property); the secure mappers do not. [Confirmed]

Power domains — see §11.1.5.

### 11.1.3 The second always-on coprocessor instance

| SoC | reg[0] | reg[1] | reg[2] | Interrupts | IOMMU stream |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| t8140 | `0x1_0160_0000`/`0x88000` | `0x1_0105_0000`/`0x4000` | `0x1_0162_c000`/`0x3c008` | `0x18f, 0x18e, 0x191, 0x190` | 16 |
| t8142 | `0x1_8160_0000`/`0x88000` | `0x1_8105_0000`/`0x4000` | `0x1_8162_c000`/`0x3c008` | `0x1f3, 0x1f2, 0x1f5, 0x1f4` | 16 |
| t605x | `0x0_9160_0000`/`0x88000` | `0x0_9165_0000`/`0x4000` | `0x0_9162_c000`/`0x3c008` | `0x24b, 0x24a, 0x24d, 0x24c` | 16 |

[Confirmed]. It is a byte-for-byte structural twin of the always-on coprocessor
minus the firmware-SRAM aperture and the arbitration register. Its nub carries
`no-firmware-service` (empty) on t8140 and t8142, and `no-shutdown = 1`,
`sleep-on-hibernate`, `watchdog-enable`, `claim-wake` everywhere. It has **no
`firmware-name`** on t8140 (the host does not load it), while on t8142 and
t605x a separate firmware payload exists for it.

**Audio does not use it.** It exposes no audio service, no stream identifier
and no audio power-state tags; the services it does expose are message-routing
and system services (per-route log endpoints, a platform-expert service, a
private and a system service, and a typed message endpoint to the isolated
environment). No audio node references the second instance or its IOMMU stream.
[Confirmed]

A driver author should read the second instance as: **ignore it entirely for
audio**, but be aware that it shares `/arm-io/dart-aop` with the audio
coprocessor, so its stream IDs (16, and 17 on t8140) must not be reused.

### 11.1.4 The serial-I/O coprocessor

`/arm-io/sio`, `compatible = "iop,ascwrap-v6"`, present on all in-scope SoCs.

| SoC | reg[0] | reg[1] | Interrupts | IOMMU | Power/clock gate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| t8132 | `0x1_ade0_0000`/`0x88000` | `0x1_ad85_0000`/`0x4000` | `0x437,0x436,0x439,0x438` | `mapper-sio` under `/arm-io/dart-sio` | `0x123` |
| t604x | `0x2_29e0_0000`/`0x88000` | `0x2_2985_0000`/`0x4000` | `0x638,0x637,0x63a,0x639` | `mapper-sio` | `0x187` |
| t8140 | `0x1_75e0_0000`/`0x88000` | `0x1_7585_0000`/`0x4000` | `0x465,0x464,0x467,0x466` | `mapper-sio` | `0x120` |
| t8142 | `0x1_95e0_0000`/`0x88000` | `0x1_9585_0000`/`0x4000` | `0x4f0,0x4ef,0x4f2,0x4f1` | `mapper-sio` | `0x137` |
| t605x | `0x3_05e0_0000`/`0x88000` | `0x3_0585_0000`/`0x4000` | `0x570,0x56f,0x572,0x571` | `mapper-sio` | `0x284` |

[Confirmed]. Unlike the always-on coprocessor it **does** have host-controllable
power and clock gates, and its `device-type` property enumerates two device
classes (an SPI-like and a UART-like port set) with no audio class. Its
`dmashim` property describes two shim windows for those same two device
classes. **Not on the audio path.** [Confirmed]

Note for the record: on M1–M3 the host audio DMA controller sat in the
serial-I/O power domain (`ps_sio` was the parent of the audio register
domain). On M4 and later the audio DMA controllers no longer depend on it —
their domains hang off the coprocessor-side audio tree (§11.1.5). This is the
power-domain footprint of the ownership change.

### 11.1.5 Power domains

Decoded from the power-manager device list with the independent decoder
(48-byte entries; name at 32..47; u16 index at 26..27; flags at byte 0; u32
parent index at 4..7).

**The decisive fact.** On M1–M3 the host-side audio domains
(`AUDIO_P`, `SIO_ADMA`, `MCA0`…`MCA3`) carry **flags byte `0x00`** while every
coprocessor-side domain (`AOP_*`, including `AOP_MCA0..3`, `AOP_AUDIO_ADMA0`,
`AOP_PDMC0`) carries **`0x10`**. On every in-scope SoC there are **no host-side
audio domains left at all**: the names `AUDIO_P`, `SIO_ADMA`, `MCA0`…`MCA3` are
gone, replaced by an `AUDIO_*` set that sits inside the coprocessor's domain
tree and carries **`0x10` on every entry**. [Confirmed — holds on all six
boards decoded, across all five in-scope SoCs, and the M3 contrast holds on
the matching baseline boards.]

Complete in-scope audio domain tree (t8132 values; the tree shape is identical
on t604x, t8140, t8142 and t605x):

```
AOP_FILTER  (root of the always-on tree)
 └─ AUDIO_A                      aggregate audio domain
     └─ AUDIO_FR                 audio "fabric/reference" domain
         ├─ AUDIO_P              audio register/peripheral domain
         │   ├─ AUDIO_BASE_S_A       base-domain secure audio
         │   ├─ AUDIO_BASE_NS_A      base-domain non-secure audio
         │   ├─ AUDIO_LEAP_MCA       low-power serial audio cluster
         │   └─ AUDIO_MCA0_M … AUDIO_MCA5_M   six base serial audio clusters
         ├─ AUDIO_LEAP_A         low-power audio processor aggregate
         │   └─ AUDIO_LEAP_C     low-power audio processor core
         │       ├─ AUDIO_LEAP_S_A    low-power secure audio
         │       ├─ AUDIO_LEAP_NS_A   low-power non-secure audio
         │       ├─ AUDIO_LEAP_RX0 … AUDIO_LEAP_RX4   five receive streams
         │       └─ AUDIO_LEAP_TX0                    one transmit stream
         └─ AUDIO_SENSE_PDMC     microphone PDM converter (renamed; not a sense converter — §8 §8.8)
PDM0_AUDIO_REF, PDM1_AUDIO_REF   (no parent; PDM reference clocks)
```

[Confirmed] — parent indices resolve consistently on every board decoded.

Consequences for a driver:

1. There are **six** base-domain serial audio clusters plus **one** in the
   low-power audio processor domain — seven serialiser clusters in total,
   against four on M3 Pro/Max.
2. The base and low-power complexes each split **secure / non-secure**, and
   that split is a *power-domain* split, not merely a software one.
3. `AUDIO_SENSE_PDMC` is a **one-for-one rename of the baseline generation's
   microphone PDM converter domain**, not a speaker-sense converter, despite the
   name; it is a sibling of the audio register domain rather than a child of it.
   The speaker current/voltage sense return is **PCM over TDM on every in-scope
   machine** and is not converted in a PDM block. See §8 §8.8. [Confirmed]
4. None of these domains is host-writable. A driver cannot power the audio
   complex up; it can only ask the coprocessor to.

Per-SoC location of the entries: on t8132 the audio domains carry a
non-zero register selector in bytes 8..11 of the entry and zero in bytes
16..19; on t604x, t8140, t8142 and t605x the reverse holds, with bytes 16..19
carrying a (24-bit offset, 8-bit window index) pair in which consecutive audio
domains are spaced exactly 8 bytes apart starting at window 1 offset
`0x4000`. [Probable — the 8-byte stride matching consecutive entries is a
strong internal correlation, but the field has not been verified against
hardware.] Either way the entries are not host-writable, so the offsets are of
diagnostic value only.

---

## 11.2 Mailbox / doorbell hardware interface

The transport is a four-layer stack, unchanged in structure since the M1
generation:

1. A **hardware mailbox pair** — two FIFOs of 96-bit messages, one per
   direction, inside the coprocessor control aperture (§11.2.1–§11.2.7).
2. An **endpoint transport** layered on the mailbox, which multiplexes up to
   256 logical endpoints onto the single message stream, negotiates a protocol
   version, enumerates endpoints, negotiates shared-memory buffers for
   diagnostics, and carries power-state transitions (§11.2.8).
3. A **shared-memory ring endpoint protocol** used by every application
   endpoint, which negotiates a coherent buffer, carves two ring buffers out of
   it, and carries variable-length queue elements (§11.4.2).
4. A **framed call protocol** inside those queue elements, which announces
   named services, carries request/reply pairs with explicit correlation tags,
   and carries unsolicited reports (§11.4.3–§11.4.5).

The audio service is a fifth layer: fixed-layout **wrapped calls** carried as
one framed-call subtype (§11.4.6).

All five in-scope SoCs declare block revision `iop,ascwrap-v6`, the same
revision the M3 generation declares (t8122, t603x), and the register map
published for that revision is the same map published for `iop,ascwrap-v4`
(M1, M2).

### 11.2.1 Where the block sits

The mailbox is a `0x4000`-byte block at **offset `0x8000` within the
coprocessor control aperture** (`reg[0]` of the coprocessor node; per-SoC
apertures in §11.1.2). It is a distinct block from the CPU-control registers,
which lie in the first `0x4000` bytes of the same aperture.

[Confirmed] on `ascwrap-v4` and `ascwrap-v6`. The placement is
**generation-invariant** across every coprocessor of this family — the same
