`+0x8000` offset and the same `0x4000` size apply to the always-on
coprocessor, the display coprocessor, the storage coprocessor, the
system-management coprocessor and the serial-I/O coprocessor.

Consistency check against the in-scope platform description: the separately
described sub-window `reg[4]` covers `+0x2c000` … `+0x68008` of the same
aperture and therefore does **not** overlap the mailbox block at
`+0x8000` … `+0xc000`. [Confirmed]

### 11.2.2 Register map

Offsets are given both relative to the coprocessor control aperture (`reg[0]`)
and relative to the mailbox block base. "A2I" is the host→coprocessor FIFO,
"I2A" the coprocessor→host FIFO; both host and coprocessor see the same
register set, each using the opposite half.

| Offset in `reg[0]` | Offset in block | Name | Access | Reset | Fields | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `+0x0044` | — | `CPU_CTRL` | RW 32 | **[Unknown]** | bit 4 = run | Releases the coprocessor core. Read-modify-write: set bit 4, preserve the rest. Not in the mailbox block. |
| `+0x0048` | — | `CPU_STATUS` | RO 32 | **[Unknown]** | core idle / stopped / interrupt-pending / outbound-FIFO-empty indications; individual bit positions **[Unknown]** | Core state. Not required for message exchange. |
| `+0x8110` | `+0x110` | `A2I_CTRL` | RO 32 | **[Unknown]** | bit 16 = FULL, bit 17 = EMPTY; bits 15:0 and 31:18 **[Unknown]** | Status of the host→coprocessor FIFO. |
| `+0x8114` | `+0x114` | `I2A_CTRL` | RO 32 | **[Unknown]** | bit 16 = FULL, bit 17 = EMPTY | Status of the coprocessor→host FIFO. |
| `+0x8800` | `+0x800` | `A2I_SEND0` | WO 64 | — | bits 63:0 = message word 0 | Host write of the payload word. Does not post. |
| `+0x8808` | `+0x808` | `A2I_SEND1` | WO 64 | — | bits 31:0 = message word 1 (see §11.2.3); bits 63:32 written as zero | Host write of the tag word. **This write posts the message.** |
| `+0x8810` | `+0x810` | `A2I_RECV0` | RO 64 | — | message word 0 | Coprocessor-side read port of the host→coprocessor FIFO. Not used by the host. |
| `+0x8818` | `+0x818` | `A2I_RECV1` | RO 64 | — | message word 1 plus FIFO state | Coprocessor-side dequeue. Not used by the host. |
| `+0x8820` | `+0x820` | `I2A_SEND0` | WO 64 | — | message word 0 | Coprocessor-side write port. Not used by the host. |
| `+0x8828` | `+0x828` | `I2A_SEND1` | WO 64 | — | message word 1 | Coprocessor-side post. Not used by the host. |
| `+0x8830` | `+0x830` | `I2A_RECV0` | RO 64 | — | bits 63:0 = message word 0 | Host read of the payload word. Does not dequeue. |
| `+0x8838` | `+0x838` | `I2A_RECV1` | RO 64 | — | bits 31:0 = message word 1; bits 56:40 = FIFO state (see §11.2.3) | Host read of the tag word. **This read dequeues the message.** |

[Confirmed] for `ascwrap-v4` and `ascwrap-v6`; **[Probable]** for the in-scope
dies, on the single ground that they declare the same block revision as the M3
generation, whose map is the published one. **Reset values are [Unknown] for
every register above** — no published source states them and the platform
description carries none. See Open questions 1, 26 and 27.

A second mailbox block revision exists in this family with a different register
layout (FIFO registers at block offsets `0x50`–`0xa8`, plus explicit
interrupt-enable and interrupt-acknowledge registers at `0x48` and `0x4c` with
one bit per FIFO edge). **No Mac-class coprocessor in any generation uses it**,
and no in-scope board declares it. It is recorded only so that a driver author
who encounters the alternative offsets recognises them as a different block,
not a mis-decode. [Confirmed]

The revision used here has **no mailbox-level interrupt enable or acknowledge
register**. Interrupts are level-sensitive and must be masked and unmasked at
the interrupt controller.

### 11.2.3 Message format

A message is **96 bits**, carried as two 64-bit register accesses:

| Word | Bits | Field | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 63:0 | payload | Passed through unmodified. Interpretation is entirely up to the endpoint. |
| 1 | 7:0 | endpoint number | Demultiplexing key, 0…255. |
| 1 | 31:8 | reserved | Zero in all baseline traffic. **[Unknown]** whether any endpoint uses these bits on the in-scope parts. |
| 1 | 39:32 | reserved | Not written on send; not interpreted on receive. |
| 1 | 43:40 | inbound FIFO read index | Read-only FIFO state, valid on receive only. |
| 1 | 47:44 | outbound FIFO read index | Read-only FIFO state, valid on receive only. |
| 1 | 51:48 | inbound FIFO occupancy | Read-only FIFO state, valid on receive only. |
| 1 | 56:52 | outbound FIFO occupancy | Read-only FIFO state, valid on receive only. |
| 1 | 63:57 | reserved | |

[Confirmed]. Word 1 is written as a 64-bit store with bits 63:32 zero; the
FIFO-state fields are produced by the hardware on read and must be masked off
before the endpoint number is used. The message is **96 bits, not 128**: the
upper 32 bits of the second 64-bit access are hardware status on read and must
be zero on write.

**FIFO depth.** The two index fields are 4 bits wide and the inbound occupancy
field is 4 bits wide, which bounds the FIFO at **16 entries** per direction.
The outbound occupancy field is 5 bits wide. **[Inferred]** — the field widths
bound the depth, they do not state it, and the in-scope depth is **[Unknown]**.

### 11.2.4 Sending, detecting, dequeuing

**Send.** Read `A2I_CTRL`; while bit 16 (FULL) is set, wait. Then write
`A2I_SEND0` with word 0 and `A2I_SEND1` with word 1. The second write posts.
A memory barrier is required before the first write if the message references a
buffer the host has just filled.

**Detect.** Read `I2A_CTRL`; a message is pending while bit 17 (EMPTY) is
clear.

**Receive and clear.** Read `I2A_RECV0`, then `I2A_RECV1`. The second read
dequeues the entry and re-arms the EMPTY indication. A read barrier is required
after the pair and before any access to a buffer the message references. Loop
until `I2A_CTRL` bit 17 is set again.

There is no separate doorbell register and no acknowledge register: the second
access of each pair is the doorbell in each direction. [Confirmed]

Both FIFOs are multi-entry, so a driver may drain several messages per
interrupt and must, because the interrupt is level-sensitive.

### 11.2.5 Interrupt sources

Four inputs, one per FIFO edge. The platform description lists them in a fixed
order which is **not** ascending:

| Index in `interrupts` | Raw input | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | n+1 | host→coprocessor FIFO **not empty** |
| 1 | n | host→coprocessor FIFO **empty** (send space available) |
| 2 | n+3 | coprocessor→host FIFO **not empty** (message waiting) |
| 3 | n+2 | coprocessor→host FIFO **empty** |

[Confirmed] — the `(n+1, n, n+3, n+2)` ordering holds on **every board of every
generation from M1 to M5**, without exception, and matches the
published named interrupt list for the same part. Per-SoC raw values are in
§11.1.2.

A host driver needs only index 2 (message waiting) and index 1 (send space
available). Index 1 must be masked at the interrupt controller when not waiting
for space, because it is level-sensitive and asserts whenever the send FIFO is
empty.

**t604x is the only part with eight.** The eight are two
quadruples of the identical shape: `(n+1, n, n+3, n+2)` at n = `0x2c6` and
again at n = `0x2ca`. Reading: **two complete mailbox channel sets**.
**[Inferred]**, and corroborated independently — the display coprocessor on
both t604x and t605x carries the same doubled arrangement (eight inputs, two
quadruples of the same shape) while carrying four on t8132 and on every
M1–M3 part. The doubling is therefore a die-level arrangement introduced at the
M4 generation on the Pro/Max dies, not four unrelated outputs.

Where the second channel set's registers live is **[Unknown]**, and two
readings are open, so **a driver written against one channel set may silently lose
messages on a Pro/Max part**. *What a driver must do meanwhile:* use the first channel
set only — it is the one at the established offsets and the one every other in-scope die
uses — and treat a message-waiting interrupt from raw input `0x2ca+3` as a symptom that
the second set is live and is being ignored, rather than as a spurious interrupt to mask
and forget. Mask the second quadruple at the interrupt controller rather than leaving it
unhandled, and log it. The natural candidate, given that the first block occupies
`+0x8000` … `+0xc000` of a `0x88000` aperture, is the next `0x4000`-aligned
window at `+0xc000`. **[Inferred]** The competing reading is Section 5
§5.6.2's: that the second quadruple is a *secure* mailbox of the same
coprocessor, which on t8140, t8142 and t605x is broken out as the separately
addressed `0x4000` aperture of §11.2.9 and would therefore sit at its own low
address on t604x rather than inside `reg[0]` — except that t604x describes no
such node. **[Inferred]** A probe settles it either way: the two candidates are
one `0x4000` window apart from opposite ends of the address space. See Open
questions 3 and 29.

### 11.2.6 What the aperture growth did and did not touch

The control aperture grew from `0x6c000` to `0x88000` at the M4 generation
while the block revision string stayed at `iop,ascwrap-v6`. The mailbox block
and the CPU-control registers are both in the first `0xc000` bytes and are
therefore **not** in the added range. Whatever `0x6c000` … `0x88000` holds, it
is not the mailbox. [Inferred]

`reg[4]` — the separately described `0x3c008`-byte sub-window at `+0x2c000` —
is the **external-interrupt register window**. The coprocessor node carries a
property `ext-irq-reg-index` whose value is `4`, naming that `reg` index, and
the correlation is exact on every board: **every board whose
coprocessor node has five `reg` entries carries `ext-irq-reg-index = 4`, and
every board with four `reg` entries carries no such property** (14 boards with,
41 without; no exceptions). [Confirmed as a correlation; the reading of the
property name as "external interrupt register window" is **[Inferred]**.] Its
internal register layout remains **[Unknown]**.

**No host audio function depends on it.** The mailbox interrupts a driver needs are the
four named in `interrupts` and decoded in §11.2.5; nothing in the bring-up, transport or
stream path of this section reads or writes `reg[4]`. A driver should **map it if the
property is present and otherwise leave it alone** — the mapping matters only so that the
window is not handed to something else. The reason to decode it eventually is that it is
the one described window whose contents are wholly unaccounted for on four of the five
in-scope SoCs.

`ext-irq-reg-index` is present on **t8132, t8140, t8142 and t605x** — every
in-scope SoC except t604x. t604x is the one in-scope part with no `reg[4]` and
no external-interrupt window, and it is also the one in-scope part with a
doubled mailbox interrupt set.

### 11.2.7 Releasing the core

Read `reg[0] + 0x0044`, set bit 4, write it back. The coprocessor begins
executing the resident code in its firmware window and, within a bounded but
**[Unknown]** interval, sends the first management message.

The CPU-control register is at **`reg[0] + 0x44`**, i.e. in the first `0x4000`
bytes of the control aperture — not in `reg[1]`. `reg[1]` is a separate
`0x4000` aperture at a different base, present in identical relative position
on every generation from M1; nothing in the published interface touches it and
its contents are **[Unknown]** (§11.1.2).

### 11.2.8 Transport initialisation and the management handshake

All management traffic is on **endpoint 0**, which needs no start step and is
usable from the moment the core is released.

The 64-bit payload word of a management message is:

| Bits | Field |
|---|---|
| 63:60 | reserved, zero |
| 59:52 | message type |
| 51:0 | type-specific |

**Message types.**

| Type | Direction | Payload fields | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `1` | coprocessor → host | bits 15:0 = minimum protocol version; bits 31:16 = maximum protocol version | Version advertisement. First message after release. |
| `2` | host → coprocessor | bits 15:0 and bits 31:16 both = the selected version | Version selection. |
| `5` | host → coprocessor | bits 39:32 = endpoint number; bit 1 = 1 | Start endpoint. |
| `6` | host → coprocessor | bits 15:0 = requested coprocessor power state | Set coprocessor power state. |
| `7` | coprocessor → host | bits 15:0 = new coprocessor power state | Coprocessor power-state acknowledgement. |
| `8` | coprocessor → host | bits 31:0 = endpoint bitmap; bits 34:32 = bitmap base; bit 51 = last fragment | Endpoint map fragment. |
| `8` | host → coprocessor | bits 34:32 = bitmap base echoed; bit 51 = 1 if acknowledging the last fragment, else bit 0 = 1 | Endpoint map acknowledgement. |
| `0xb` | host → coprocessor | bits 15:0 = requested host power state | Set host power state. |
| `0xb` | coprocessor → host | bits 15:0 = new host power state | Host power-state acknowledgement. |

[Confirmed]. Types `8` and `0xb` are each used in both directions with
different field meanings; direction disambiguates.

**Version handshake.** Protocol versions **11 and 12** are the established
supported range. On receiving type `1`, the host computes
`selected = min(12, advertised maximum)`; it aborts if the advertised minimum
exceeds 12 or the advertised maximum is below 11, and otherwise replies with
type `2` carrying `selected` in both fields.

**[Probable]** for the in-scope parts: the version the in-scope firmware
advertises is **[Unknown]**, and a driver must negotiate rather than assume. A
driver that hard-codes 12 will fail on firmware that requires a higher minimum.
See Open question 30.

**Endpoint discovery.** The coprocessor then sends one or more type `8`
fragments. Each fragment carries a 32-bit bitmap and a 3-bit base; endpoint
number `32 × base + i` exists for every set bit `i`. The base field is 3 bits,
so the map covers endpoints `0` … `255`. The host must acknowledge **every**
fragment, echoing the base and setting bit 51 on the last fragment or bit 0 on
any earlier one.

After acknowledging the last fragment, the host must **start every discovered
system endpoint** (§11.4.1). The coprocessor does not complete its own boot
until they are started.

**Starting an endpoint.** Type `5`, with the endpoint number in bits 39:32 and
bit 1 set. There is no per-endpoint acknowledgement at this layer; the endpoint
becomes usable and, for application endpoints, begins its own bring-up
(§11.4.2). Attempting to start an endpoint that was not advertised is an error
the host must catch itself.

**Power-state transitions.** Two independent state variables — one for the
coprocessor, one for the host side of the link — each with the same value
space:

| Value | State | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `0x0000` | off | The coprocessor cannot be restarted from this state. |
| `0x0001` | sleep | Restartable. |
| `0x0010` | quiesced | Running, no communication. |
| `0x0020` | on | Normal operating state. |
| `0x0201` | idle | Sleeping, state retained. Low byte matches `sleep`. |
| `0x0220` | init | Transient state used to re-initialise after the core is released. Low byte matches `on`. |

Comparisons are made on the **low 8 bits**, so `0x201` tests as `0x01` and
`0x220` tests as `0x20`. The link is usable when both variables read `0x20` in
their low byte and no crash has been reported. [Confirmed]

| Operation | Sequence |
|---|---|
| Boot | Wait for the endpoint map to complete; wait for a type `7` acknowledgement; send type `0xb` with `0x20` and wait for its acknowledgement. |
| Wake | Send type `6` with `0x220`, then perform the boot sequence. |
| Shutdown | Send type `0xb` with `0x10`; then type `6` with `0x01`; then re-initialise the host-side state and restart the mailbox. |
| Idle | Send type `0xb` with `0x201`; then type `6` with `0x201`. |
| Quiesce | Send type `0xb` with `0x10`; then type `6` with `0x10`; then re-initialise. |
| Power off | Send type `0xb` with `0x00`; then type `6` with `0x00`. **Unrecoverable without a SoC reset.** |

[Confirmed]. Every transition that sends a set message waits for the matching
acknowledgement and verifies that the reported state equals the requested one.

**Readiness is this handshake, not a register bit.** The coprocessor is ready
and the audio service usable when the last endpoint-map fragment has been
acknowledged, a type `7` acknowledgement has been received, and the host power
state has been set to `0x20` and acknowledged. There is no readiness bit to
poll.

A host with no power gate for this coprocessor (§11.1.2, §11.10) therefore
still has a defined way to quiesce it, to put it to sleep, and to
re-initialise it — by the power-state messages, not by a register. It is not a
reset: the coprocessor's own software state survives a quiesce, and only
`0x00` is unrecoverable.

### 11.2.9 Mailboxes belonging to the isolated execution environment

The in-scope platform description carries **separate mailbox nodes for an
isolated (secure) execution environment**, distinct from the coprocessor node
above.

| Node | `compatible` | SoC | `reg` | Interrupts | IOMMU |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `aop-exclave-mailbox` | `iop,secure-rtbuddy-proxy` | t8140 | `0x3_5067_c000` / `0x4000` | `0x18d, 0x18a` | isolated mapper, sid 1 |
| `aop-exclave-mailbox` | `iop,secure-rtbuddy-proxy` | t8142 | `0x3_d067_c000` / `0x4000` | `0x1f1, 0x1ee` | isolated mapper, sid 1 |
| `aop-exclave-mailbox` | `iop,secure-rtbuddy-proxy` | t605x | `0x2_d067_c000` / `0x4000` | `0x249, 0x246` | isolated mapper, sid 1 |
| `aop2-exclave-mailbox` | `iop,secure-rtbuddy-proxy` | t8140 only | `0x3_5167_c000` / `0x4000` | `0x195, 0x192` | sid 17 |
| `aop-exclave-ioreporting` | `iop,secure-rtbuddy-ioreporting` | t8142, t605x | no `reg` | — | — |

[Confirmed]. Properties of note:

- Each carries `exclave-assigned` (empty), `claim-wake` (empty) and a `role`
  string that marks it as the isolated-environment side of the coprocessor.
- The reporting node carries **`exclave-endpoint = 0x4d`** — a concrete
  endpoint number for the isolated environment's telemetry channel. [Confirmed]
  (It is the only endpoint number the platform description states outright, for
  any endpoint, anywhere.)
- The aperture is `0x4000` — one-fifth the size of the main mailbox aperture,
  and at an address nowhere near the coprocessor block. This is a **second,
  physically separate mailbox instance**, not a window into the first.

What they are for: they carry the traffic between the isolated environment and
the coprocessor for the audio paths the isolated environment owns (the
microphone array on the M5 generation and A18 Pro, and the secure loopback on
t605x — §11.8). **A normal-world driver neither can nor should use them**: they
are marked assigned to the isolated environment, their IOMMU stream is a
separate stream ID, and on t8132 and t604x they do not exist at all while audio
still works. Their register layout is **[Unknown]**.

**These are absent on t8132 and t604x.** On those SoCs there is no isolated
mailbox and no isolated audio stream. That is the single biggest
generation-internal difference in this section.

---

## 11.3 Shared memory

### 11.3.1 Where it is and how it is discovered

There are two distinct memories to keep separate.

**(a) The coprocessor's own firmware SRAM.** Described directly by the
coprocessor node's `reg[2]` entry, and restated absolutely by the child nub's
`region-base` (u64) and `region-size` (u64) properties. Sizes per SoC in
§11.1.2. Discovery is purely by reading the platform description; there is no
enumeration step. The host copies the firmware payload into this window
before releasing the core. Alignment is the IOMMU page size, `0x4000`.
[Confirmed]

**(b) Host DRAM shared with the coprocessor.** This is *not* described by any
`reg` property. It is allocated by the host, mapped through
`/arm-io/dart-aop` on the coprocessor's own stream ID (0), and its address is
communicated to the coprocessor over the mailbox. The platform description
supplies only the IOMMU parameters needed to build the mapping:

| Parameter | Value | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| IOMMU | `/arm-io/dart-aop`, `compatible = "dart,t8110"` | [Confirmed] |
| Page size | `0x4000` (16 KiB) | [Confirmed] |
| Coprocessor stream ID | 0 | [Confirmed] |
| Isolated-environment stream ID | 1 (absent on t604x) | [Confirmed] |
| Per-stream VM windows | declared per stream ID as `vm-base-<n>` / `vm-size-<n>` pairs on the IOMMU node | [Confirmed] |
| Other IOMMU options | `flush-by-dva = 1`, `manual-availability = 1`, `avoid-tlbi-in-map` (empty), `no-sleep` (empty), `dart-options = 0x65` | [Confirmed] |
| Size and internal structure of the shared region | **[Unknown]** | |

On t605x the coprocessor's default VM window is `vm-base = 0x100_0000_0000`,
`vm-size = 0x300_0000_0000`; the DMA-stream windows (`vm-base-9`, `-11`,
`-16`, and `vm-base-0`) are `0x100_4000_0000` with size `0xffff_0000` or
`0x20_0000_0000`. A driver must map the shared region inside the window that
belongs to the stream ID it is using. [Confirmed]

### 11.3.2 The physical-description blob

The isolated buffer device node and the isolated stream proxy nodes each carry
a `physical-descriptions` property: **24 bytes, six little-endian 32-bit
fields**:

| Offset | Size | Field | Observed values |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | u32 | Buffer capacity, in frames | `0x3de0` = 15 840 (48 kHz paths); `0xfa00` = 64 000 (16 kHz low-power path) |
| `0x04` | u32 | Sample rate, Hz | `0xbb80` = 48 000; `0x3e80` = 16 000 |
| `0x08` | FourCC (byte-reversed) | Format tag | reads `lpcm` on every instance |
| `0x0c` | u32 | Format flags | `9` on the 48 kHz paths; `0x14` = 20 on the 16 kHz low-power path |
| `0x10` | u32 | Bytes per frame | `0x0c` = 12 (3-channel); `0x08` = 8 (2-channel) |
| `0x14` | u32 | Transport packet size, bytes | `0x320` = 800; `0x220` = 544; `0x318` = 792; `0x218` = 536 |

The packet-size field is fully explained by
`packet = header + 64 × bytes_per_frame`, with `header = 32` on the 48 kHz paths
and `header = 24` on the 16 kHz low-power path. Solving the four observed
(bytes_per_frame, packet) pairs across two rates gives 64 frames per packet
exactly, in both cases. [Confirmed — four independent data points, two
channel counts × two rates, all consistent.] The two header sizes correspond to
the two audio packet formats the transport defines, selected by a type field in
the packet header. [Probable]

Observed instances:

| Node | SoC(s) | Capacity | Rate | Flags | Bytes/frame | Packet |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| isolated low-power buffer device | t8142, t605x, t8140(j700) | 64 000 | 16 000 | 20 | 12 (8 on j700) | 792 (536 on j700) |
| microphone-array isolated stream proxy | t8142, t605x | 15 840 | 48 000 | 9 | 12 | 800 |
| microphone-array isolated stream proxy | t8140 (j700) | 15 840 | 48 000 | 9 | 8 | 544 |
| secure loopback isolated stream proxy | t605x | 15 840 | 48 000 | 9 | 8 | 544 |

[Confirmed]. Note that the A18 Pro machine declares a **two-channel**
microphone array where every other in-scope machine declares three; this is
consistent with its `/product/audio` channel masks (`0x3` versus `0x7`).

Reading the fields as frames rather than bytes is **[Inferred]**: it is the
only reading under which the 48 kHz proxies share a single value (15 840)
while their bytes-per-frame differ. At 16 kHz, 64 000 frames is exactly
4.0 seconds of history, which matches the always-listening role of that
buffer; at 48 kHz, 15 840 frames is 330 ms.

### 11.3.3 The machine-level use-case format records

On the M5 generation and A18 Pro only, `/product/audio` gains
`use-case-client-format` (96 bytes) and `use-case-dsp-in-format` (64 bytes):
arrays of **32-byte records**:

| Offset | Size | Field |
|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | FourCC (byte-reversed) | use-case tag — observed `hist`, `siri`, and one further tag |
| `0x04` | u32 | sample rate, Hz (`0x3e80` = 16 000, `0xbb80` = 48 000) |
| `0x08` | u32 | channel count (3, or 2 on j700) |
| `0x0c` | u32 | `0x400` = 1024 (frames per buffer) |
| `0x10`–`0x1f` | 16 B | zero |

Accompanied by `use-case-struct-version = 1`. Absent on t8132 and t604x.
[Confirmed]

---

## 11.4 Endpoint transport, service resolution and message framing

### 11.4.1 Endpoint numbering, service naming and the management layer

| Range | Class | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | Management | Always present; never needs starting. |
| `0x01` | Crash reporting | Must be started if advertised. |
| `0x02` | System log | Must be started if advertised. |
| `0x03` | Debug | Must be started if advertised. |
| `0x04` | I/O reporting | Must be started if advertised. |
| `0x08` | Operating-system log | Must be started if advertised. |
| `0x0a` | Trace | Must be started if advertised. |
| `0x05`–`0x07`, `0x09`, `0x0b`–`0x1f` | Reserved to the management layer | None observed in use. Treat an advertised endpoint here as an error rather than starting it blindly. |
| `0x20`–`0xff` | Application endpoints | Services live here. |

[Confirmed]. **`0x20` is the first application endpoint number**, and the
management layer owns everything below it. The coprocessor will not finish
booting unless the advertised system endpoints are started, so a driver cannot
skip them even if it discards their output.

**Endpoint numbers are not constants and must never be hard-coded.** The
application endpoint numbers in use on the M1–M3 parts all fall in
`0x20` … `0x2e`; that window is a property of those generations, not a hardware
bound. The in-scope platform description itself names application
endpoints outside it — `0x4d` on t8142 and t605x, `0x4e` and `0x30`/`0x31` on
t8140 — for the isolated environment's channels (§11.2.9). [Confirmed]
A driver for the in-scope parts must scan the **full advertised map**
(§11.2.8), not a fixed window.

The audio service's own endpoint number is **[Unknown]** and **is not a value
that needs to be known**: §11.4.4 resolves it by name at run time.

**How the platform description names services.** The audio controller node and
the voice-trigger controller node each carry a property
`iop-audio-service-name` whose value is an ASCII string naming a service inside
the coprocessor firmware. They both point at the **same** coprocessor; only the
string differs. [Confirmed]

The coprocessor's own nub subtree mirrors this: it has one child per service,
each with `compatible = "iop-audio,aop-service"` and a `device_type` giving
the service's lower-case channel name. On every in-scope board these are:

| Service child `device_type` | Role |
|---|---|
| `aop-audio` | audio control service — **this is the audio path** |
| `aop-voicetrigger` | always-listening / voice-trigger service |

[Confirmed]. The voice-trigger child additionally carries `name-override`,
whose value is the same string the voice-trigger controller node's
`iop-audio-service-name` carries — i.e. the platform binds a client node to a
service by string match on that property.

On the M5 generation and the A18 Pro **four** audio-related service channels
exist rather than two: the two above plus a **secure variant of each** (same
names with an `-s` suffix); further non-audio
channels exist on the same transport. The secure variants are reached only from
the isolated environment. [Confirmed — present on the M5 generation and A18 Pro,
absent on M4 and earlier.]

There is **no service-registry endpoint and no lookup request**. Services
announce themselves once their endpoint has started (§11.4.4); the
announcement is the registration.

### 11.4.2 Bringing up an application endpoint

Every application endpoint runs the same shared-memory ring protocol. The
64-bit payload word carries an opcode in bits 63:48.

| Opcode | Direction | Other fields | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0x80` | either | — | Initialise. |
| `0xa0` | host → coprocessor | — | Initialise acknowledgement. |
| `0x89` | coprocessor → host | bits 31:16 = size in 64-byte units | Buffer request. |
| `0xa1` | host → coprocessor | bits 47:0 = device address of the granted buffer | Buffer grant. |
| `0x8a` | coprocessor → host | bits 31:16 = size in 64-byte units; bits 47:32 = offset in 64-byte units | Transmit-ring descriptor (host writes into this ring). |
| `0x8b` | coprocessor → host | same layout | Receive-ring descriptor (host reads from this ring). |
| `0x8c` | coprocessor → host | — | No action required. Must not be treated as an error. |
| `0xa3` | host → coprocessor | — | Start. |
| `0x86` | coprocessor → host | — | Start acknowledgement. |
| `0xa2` | host → coprocessor | bits 47:0 = new write pointer | Data posted to the transmit ring. |
| `0x85` | coprocessor → host | — | Data available in the receive ring. |
| `0xc0` | host → coprocessor | — | Shutdown. |
| `0xc1` | coprocessor → host | — | Shutdown acknowledgement. |

[Confirmed].

**Bring-up order.** After the management-layer start (type `5`, §11.2.8), the
host sends `0x80`. The coprocessor replies with `0x80`, which the host
acknowledges with `0xa0`. The coprocessor sends `0x89`; the host allocates a
**coherent buffer** of the requested size, mapped through the coprocessor's
IOMMU mapper, and replies `0xa1` carrying its device address. The coprocessor
then sends `0x8a` and `0x8b`, in either order, describing two rings **inside
that one buffer**. When both have arrived the host sends `0xa3` and the
coprocessor replies `0x86`. The endpoint is then live.

**Buffer size bound:** the size field is 16 bits in 64-byte units, so a single
endpoint buffer is at most `0xffff × 0x40` = 4 MiB − 64 B. The address field of
the grant is 48 bits. In practice the coprocessor's addressing is narrower — a
**42-bit device address mask** constrains allocations. [Confirmed]

**Where the buffer may live.** It is host DRAM, allocated coherently and mapped
into the coprocessor's device address space through a mapper child of the
coprocessor's IOMMU (stream 0; §11.1.2, §11.3.1). It need not be physically
contiguous from the host's point of view, and it must be contiguous and
correctly aligned in the device address space. It is *not* placed in the
coprocessor's firmware window.

**Ring-buffer layout.** Each of the two rings occupies `size` bytes at `offset`
within the granted buffer. Within a ring:

| Offset within ring | Size | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | u32 | `bufsize` — the size of the data area in bytes |
| `1 × block` | u32 | Read pointer, a byte offset into the data area |
| `2 × block` | u32 | Write pointer, a byte offset into the data area |
| `3 × block` | `bufsize` B | Data area |

where `block = (size − bufsize) / 3`. The three pointer/header blocks are
separated by a full `block` so that each lands in its own coherency granule.

Producer rule: write the element at the write pointer; advance the write pointer
by the element length **rounded up to a multiple of `block`**, modulo
`bufsize`. If the element will not fit between the write pointer and the end of
the data area, wrap to offset 0 and write it there instead. The consumer
applies the same rule in reverse and must re-read the header at offset 0 if the
declared element length would overrun the data area.

Ordering: a barrier is required after reading the pointers and before reading
data, and after writing data and before publishing the new write pointer.

### 11.4.3 Queue elements and the framed call header

Each ring element is a 16-byte queue-element header followed by a payload.

| Offset | Size | Field | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | 4 B | Tag | Four ASCII bytes. Elements the host produces carry `IOP `; elements the host consumes carry either `IOP ` or `AOP `. Any other value is a framing error. |
| `0x04` | u32 | Payload length in bytes, excluding this header | |
| `0x08` | u32 | Channel number | Selects the service within the endpoint. |
| `0x0c` | u32 | Element type | `0` for calls, replies and reports. Other values **[Unknown]**. |

[Confirmed]. Byte order is little-endian throughout.

The payload of an element of type `0` begins with a 40-byte call header:

| Offset | Size | Field | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | u8 | Header version | `2` |
| `0x01` | u16 | Sequence number | Per endpoint, incremented on every request, wrapping. Not used for correlation. |
| `0x03` | u8 | Padding | |
| `0x04` | u32 | Reserved | Zero |
| `0x08` | u64 | Timestamp | Zero on requests the host sends; populated by the coprocessor on the messages it sends. Units **[Unknown]**. |
| `0x10` | u32 | Payload length | Bytes following this header. |
| `0x14` | u8 | Sub-header version | `2` |
| `0x15` | u8 | Category | See below. |
| `0x16` | u16 | Subtype | See below. |
| `0x18` | u16 | **Correlation tag** | 1-based. See §11.4.5. |
| `0x1a` | u16 | Reserved | Zero |
| `0x1c` | u64 | Padding | Zero |
| `0x24` | u32 | Inline payload length | Zero on requests the host sends. Its use is **[Unknown]**. |

[Confirmed].

**Categories.**

| Value | Category | Direction |
|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | Report — unsolicited, no reply expected | coprocessor → host |
| `0x10` | Notification — a request | host → coprocessor |
| `0x20` | Reply | coprocessor → host |

**Subtypes.**

| Category | Subtype | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Report `0x00` | `0xc0` | Service announcement |
| Report `0x00` | `0xc4` | Unsolicited device report |
| Reply `0x20` | `0x84` | Status only |
| Reply `0x20` | `0xa0` | Status followed by a return payload |
| Reply `0x20` | `0x8a` | Status followed by a text payload |
| Notification `0x10` | `0x20` | **Wrapped call** — the audio service's framing (§11.4.6) |
| Notification `0x10` | `0x0a` | Read a coprocessor property |
| Notification `0x10` | `0x04` | Write a sensor-service property |

[Confirmed]. Subtypes `0x0a` and `0x04` are listed because they establish that
the subtype space is **per-service, not global** — two other services on the
same transport use their own subtype numbering, and `0x20` is not reserved
across services. A driver must dispatch on (service, subtype), not on subtype
alone.

**Reply payload.** The first 4 bytes of a reply payload are a u32 status word;
`0` means success. For subtype `0xa0`, the remainder is the requested return
data, truncated to whatever length the requester asked for. For subtype `0x8a`,
the remainder is text.

### 11.4.4 Resolving a named service to an endpoint

Immediately after an application endpoint starts, the coprocessor emits one
report (category `0x00`, subtype `0xc0`) per service it hosts on that endpoint.
The payload is 44 bytes:

| Offset | Size | Field |
|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | 20 B | Service name, NUL-padded ASCII |
| `0x14` | u32 | Reserved |
| `0x18` | u32 | Status |
| `0x1c` | u32 | Reserved |
| `0x20` | u32 | **Channel number** |
| `0x24` | u32 | Reserved |
| `0x28` | u32 | Reserved |

[Confirmed].

**A service reference is the pair (endpoint number, channel number)** — an
8-bit endpoint and a 32-bit channel. The endpoint is the one the announcement
arrived on; the channel is the field at `0x20`. Every subsequent request to the
service carries that channel in the queue-element header (§11.4.3) and is sent
on that endpoint. The reference has no further internal structure. [Confirmed]

**Name matching.** The announced name is a plain ASCII string. On the baseline
generations the audio service announces itself as `aop-audio`, the two sensor
services as `als` and `las`. The in-scope platform description gives the same
strings as the `device_type` of the coprocessor nub's service children
(§11.4.1), so **a driver can predict the string it must match from the platform
description alone**. [Confirmed for the baseline generations; **[Probable]**
that the in-scope firmware announces the same string for the audio service, on
the ground that the in-scope nub still carries `device_type = "aop-audio"` on
that child.]

Two complications specific to the in-scope parts:

- The voice-trigger service child carries a `name-override` property whose
  value is a different, longer string, and the voice-trigger *client* node's
  `iop-audio-service-name` carries that same string. The audio service child
  carries **no** `name-override`, yet the audio controller node's
  `iop-audio-service-name` carries a longer string too. Which of the two
  strings the audio service actually announces on the in-scope parts is
  therefore **[Unknown]** (Open question 34). A driver should match on either,
  or on a prefix, and must not fail closed on a single exact match.
- Service announcements arrive **asynchronously after the endpoint starts**.
  A driver must start every advertised application endpoint and then wait for
  announcements; it cannot ask for a service by name.

### 11.4.5 Correlation, concurrency, unsolicited events and timeouts

**Correlation.** The call header's tag field at `0x18` (§11.4.3) is the
correlation key. It is **1-based**; a tag of zero in a reply is invalid. The
requester allocates the lowest free slot, the reply carries the same tag, and
the slot is freed when the reply arrives. The constant `0xFFFFFFFF` at offset
`0x04` of the wrapped-call body (§11.4.6) is **not** a correlation slot —
correlation happens one layer up, in the call header.

**Concurrency.** Eight outstanding requests per endpoint, tags `1` … `8`, is
the established working limit. Whether the coprocessor imposes a lower limit is
**[Unknown]**; 8 is a host-side allocation and is not negotiated. Replies are
**not** required to arrive in request order — they are matched by tag.

**Unsolicited events.** Category `0x00`, subtype `0xc4`, on the service's own
(endpoint, channel). The payload is service-defined and its layout for the
audio service is **[Unknown]** (Open question 35). Two other services on the
same transport use this path to deliver sensor samples, with a service-specific
fixed byte offset into the payload identifying the value of interest — which
establishes that the report payload is a flat, service-defined structure with
no further generic header. [Confirmed]

The voice-trigger service, the second audio-related client on this transport,
delivers a trigger event on the same path, carrying an event structure and a
score, in two payload versions (an original and a v2). [Probable] Their layouts
are **[Unknown]**.

**Timeouts.** Three distinct limits, only one of which is hardware-facing:

| Wait | Established limit | Nature |
|---|---|---|
| Send FIFO full (mailbox layer) | 500 ms, polled at 100 µs intervals in atomic context | Host-chosen. A FIFO that stays full for 500 ms means the coprocessor has stopped servicing it. |
| Management-layer acknowledgement (version, endpoint map, power state) | 1 000 ms | Host-chosen. |
| Framed call reply | **none defined** | The interface imposes no reply deadline. |

[Confirmed]. **A driver must impose its own reply timeout**: nothing in the
interface bounds a framed call, so a wedged audio service will hang every
caller that does not. No coprocessor-imposed limit is established, so the value
a driver picks is a policy choice, and the correct value for the in-scope parts
is **[Unknown]** (Open questions 5 and 38).

### 11.4.5a Crash, log and diagnostic endpoints

These three endpoints all negotiate a shared-memory buffer using a **common
request format**, distinct from the ring-endpoint buffer negotiation of
§11.4.2. The message type is in bits 59:52 of the payload word.

**Buffer request (type `1`) on endpoints `0x01`, `0x02`, `0x04`:**

| Bits | Field |
|---|---|
| 59:52 | message type = `1` |
| 51:44 | size in units of 4096 bytes |
| 43:0 | device address |

If the address field is **non-zero**, the coprocessor has already placed the
buffer in its own memory and the host must map it there and send **no reply**.
If the address field is **zero**, the host allocates the buffer, and replies on
the same endpoint with the same type, the size in 4096-byte units in bits
51:44 and the device address in bits 43:0.

Bounds: the size field is 8 bits, so at most **255 × 4 KiB = 1 020 KiB** per
buffer; the address must fit in **44 bits**. [Confirmed]

**Buffer request on endpoint `0x08`** uses a different, larger encoding —
the type is in bits **63:56**, the size in **bytes** in bits 55:36, and the
address **in units of 4096 bytes** in bits 35:0 (giving a 48-bit address). The
reply uses the same layout. [Confirmed]

**Endpoint `0x04` additionally requires that message types `8` and `0xc` be
echoed back verbatim.** A host that ignores them stalls the coprocessor.
[Confirmed] Their meaning is **[Unknown]**.

**System log (endpoint `0x02`).**

| Type | Fields | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `1` | as above | Buffer request |
| `8` | bits 7:0 = number of entries; bits 31:24 = message size in bytes | Log initialisation |
| `5` | bits 7:0 = entry index | One log line is ready |

Entry stride in the buffer is `0x20 + message size`. Within an entry: 8 reserved
bytes, then a 24-byte NUL-terminated context string, then the message. **The
host must echo the type-`5` message back verbatim** to release the slot.
[Confirmed]

**Crash reporting (endpoint `0x01`).** Type `1` is used twice over: the
**first** type-`1` message, arriving before any buffer exists, is the buffer
request; every later type-`1` message is a crash notification, and the
negotiated buffer holds the dump. A driver must take a private copy of the
buffer before using it, because the coprocessor may continue to write it.
[Confirmed]

The dump itself is a tagged, sectioned blob. A driver should copy it and hand it
on without interpreting it. [Confirmed]

One section carries a **timestamped history of mailbox traffic in both
directions**, which is useful when bringing the transport up: a driver author
can provoke a crash and read back the exact message sequence the coprocessor
saw, which is a cheaper instrument than a hypervisor trap for the message layer
specifically.

**Where a crash dump lands**, therefore: **in a host-supplied buffer negotiated
at boot on endpoint `0x01`**, in host DRAM behind the coprocessor's IOMMU — not
in the firmware window and not in an undescribed region. [Confirmed for the
baseline generations; **[Probable]** for the in-scope parts.] What the platform
property `coredump-enable = 0x40` configures remains **[Unknown]** (§11.10.1,
Open question 18).

### 11.4.6 The audio service

**Framing.** An audio-service request is a framed call with **category `0x10`**
and **subtype `0x20`** on the service's (endpoint, channel), whose payload is a
packed, little-endian, fixed-layout structure. The reply is category `0x20`,
subtype `0x84` or `0xa0`, whose first 4 bytes are the status word; `0` means
success. [Confirmed]

#### Device identifiers

Stream and device identifiers are 4-character codes carried byte-reversed in
the platform description's `identifier` property (i.e. the property prints
reversed relative to the readable form).

| Readable FourCC | Platform node | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `spkr` | `audio-speaker` | speaker playback (and, where present, sense return) |
| `cout` | `audio-codec-output` | headphone/jack playback |
| `cin ` | `audio-codec-input` | headset-microphone capture |
| `hpai` | `audio-hp` / `audio-hp-mic` | high-power audio input = built-in microphone array |
| `lpai` | `lp-mic-device` | low-power audio input = voice-trigger microphone |
| `lpbk` | `audio-mca-loopback` | base-domain loopback |
| `lilb` | `audio-leap-internal-loopback` | low-power-domain internal loopback |
| `sllb` | `audio-secure-leap-loopback` | **secure** low-power loopback (t605x only) |
| `tap ` | `audio-speaker-tap` | speaker tap (M5 gen / A18 Pro only) |
| `lpij` | `lp-mic-injection-device` | low-power microphone injection (M5 gen / A18 Pro only) |
| `adpx` | `lp-mic-io-buffer-device` | isolated buffer device for the low-power path |
| `lai ` | `siri-listening-device` | client-manager device for the listening path |
| `vtcm` | `audio-vt-device` | isolated voice-trigger device |
| `pdm0` | (no platform node on M4+) | pulse-density front end configuration target |

[Confirmed]. **`spkr`, `cout`, `cin ` and `lpbk` are accepted by the
coprocessor from the M4 generation onwards and were not accepted on M1–M3**;
`hpai`, `lpai` and `lai ` are accepted on every generation (§18 §18.11). That is
the sharpest single expression of the M3 → M4 delta: the coprocessor acquires
the loudspeaker and the jack codec as devices it owns.

`pdm0` has **no node of its own** in the in-scope platform
description — on M1–M3 it was `/arm-io/audio-pdm2`. It had no platform node of
its own on the baseline generations either: it is attached and configured by
identifier alone, exactly as in scope, so its absence from the in-scope
platform description is **not** evidence that it is gone. Whether the in-scope
firmware still requires the attach and the coefficient upload is **[Unknown]**
(Open question 8).

#### Call types

| Call type | Purpose | In scope? | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0xC3000001` | probe device — returns device id, format FourCC, sample rate, channel count, bytes per sample | **no** (baseline generations only) | [Probable] for M1–M3 |
| `0xC3000002` | **attach device** — must precede configuration of a device FourCC | yes | [Confirmed] |
| `0xC3000003` | **[Unknown]** | **no** (baseline generations only) | [Probable] for M1–M3 only |
| `0xC3000004` | **get device property** | yes | [Confirmed] |
| `0xC3000005` | **set device property** | yes | [Confirmed] |
| `0xC3000006` | **[Unknown]** — the only call type addressed to the service rather than to a device | yes | [Confirmed present, meaning Unknown] |
| `0xC3000008` | **[Unknown]** — used by the low-power-microphone and voice-trigger devices | yes | [Confirmed present, meaning Unknown] |

The in-scope set is exactly `0xC3000002`, `0xC3000004`, `0xC3000005`,
`0xC3000006`, `0xC3000008`, and it is **identical on all five in-scope SoCs**.
Neither `0xC3000001` (probe) nor `0xC3000003` is in use in scope, although both
are on M1–M3; `0xC3000007` is in use on no generation. [Confirmed] The two
unknown call types are not resolved here — see Open question 6.

#### Attach-device request

Total 48 bytes sent; the embedded length field says `0x2c`.

| Offset | Size | Field | Value |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | u32 | Reserved | `0` |
| `0x04` | u32 | Reserved | `0xFFFFFFFF` in every request |
| `0x08` | u32 | Call type | `0xC3000002` |
| `0x0c` | u64 | Reserved | `0` |
| `0x14` | u64 | Reserved | `0` |
| `0x1c` | u32 | Padding | `0` |
| `0x20` | u64 | Length | `0x2c` |
| `0x28` | u32 | Device identifier | Four-character code, above |
| `0x2c` | u32 | Padding | `0` |

[Confirmed].

#### Set-property and get-property request

The header is **`0x34` bytes**, followed immediately by the property payload.

| Offset | Size | Field | Value |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | u32 | Reserved | `0` |
| `0x04` | u32 | Reserved | `0xFFFFFFFF` |
| `0x08` | u32 | Call type | `0xC3000005` to set, `0xC3000004` to get |
| `0x0c` | 8 B | Reserved | `0` |
| `0x14` | 8 B | Reserved | `0` |
| `0x1c` | u32 | Padding | `0` |
| `0x20` | u32 | Total length | payload length + `0x30` |
| `0x24` | u32 | Padding | `0` |
| `0x28` | u32 | Device identifier | |
| `0x2c` | u32 | **Property key** ("modifier") | |
| `0x30` | u32 | Payload length | |
| `0x34` | n B | Property payload | |

[Confirmed] — the layout and the `0x34`-byte header size are exact.

#### Property keys

**The key space is per device.** The same numeric key addressed to two different
device identifiers is two different properties — key `200` is a 632-byte
front-end configuration on the pulse-density device and a 4-byte state query on
a serial-audio stream endpoint. [Confirmed]

| Key | Target | Payload | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 200 | `pdm0` | pulse-density front-end configuration, 632 B (below) | [Confirmed] |
| 200 | serial-audio stream endpoint | current device state, 4 B FourCC | [Confirmed] — §18 §18.2.2 |
| 202 | any device | power setting, **48 B** (below) | [Confirmed] |
| 203 | — | **[Unknown]** | |
| 210 | `pdm0` | standard decimator configuration, 496 B, 32-bit coefficients (below) | [Confirmed] |
| 212 | `pdm0` | high-rate decimator configuration, 8 200 B, 64-bit coefficients (below) | [Confirmed] |
| 301 | `lpai` | low-power input channel configuration, 16 B (below) | [Confirmed] |
| 302 | — | format descriptor: format FourCC, sample rate in Hz, channels, bytes per sample, 16 B | [Confirmed] — §18 §18.11 |
| 401, 402 | serial-audio stream endpoint | the two upper state codes this endpoint uses, 4 B each | [Confirmed] — §18 §18.2.3 |
| 508 | serial-audio stream endpoint | routing-switch request, u32 | [Confirmed] — §18 §18.2.2 |
| **701** | serial-audio stream endpoint | **serial-audio cluster configuration, 109 B** — slot masks, slot and sample widths, frame geometry, clocking | [Confirmed] — **§18 §18.3** |
| 702 | serial-audio stream endpoint | serialiser/FIFO reset, u32 = 1 | [Confirmed] — §18 §18.2.2 |
| 703 | serial-audio stream endpoint | master-clock enable, u32, bit 0 | [Confirmed] — §18 §18.2.2 |
| 704, 705 | serial-audio stream endpoint | capability probes: routing validation, configuration immutability | [Confirmed] — §18 §18.2.2 |

The keys from `401` upwards are the **playback and link-geometry vocabulary**.
They are specified in full in **Section 18**, which is also where the 109-byte
key-`701` record is laid out field by field. Their key numbers are [Confirmed]
on t604x, t8140 and t605x and [Probable] on t8132 and t8142.

The pulse-density payload layouts below are **[Confirmed for the baseline
generations]** and their values are baseline constants; the layouts carry over
to the in-scope parts, the *values* must be rederived per machine. Key `203`
remains **[Unknown]**.

Further properties are defined but their numeric keys are **[Unknown]** (Open
question 7): audio latency in frames; audio latency; force-enable;
microphone-disable status; microphone-disable warning status; current power
request; callback configuration; a configuration-buffer size;
descriptors-since-start; frames-written; latest capture timestamp;
bytes-copied-since-power-up; use-non-secure-DMA-controller. The last of these is
present only on the M5 generation and is directly relevant to §11.9.

**Three entries of that list are now identified and removed from it:**
**master-clock enable** is key `703`; **set-audio-configuration** is key `701`;
and **channel mask** is the pair of 64-bit slot masks inside the key-`701`
record (§18 §18.2.2, §18 §18.3.1).

#### Property payloads

**Key `202` — power setting.** **48 bytes.** Sent to the device whose power state
is being changed; the device identifier appears both in the request header at
`0x28` and again at payload offset `0x00`.

| Offset | Size | Field | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | u32 | Device identifier | Four-character code |
| `0x04` | u32 | Cookie | Monotonically incremented by the host, starting at `1`, one sequence per device |
| `0x08` | u64 | **Host timestamp** — one 64-bit quantity, not two reserved fields. [Probable], §18 §18.2.4 | |
| `0x10` | u32 | Reserved | `0` |
| `0x14` | u32 | Target power state | Four-character code; the value before the host fills it in is `err `, which is therefore never a legal target |
| `0x18` | u32 | **Direction mask** — bit 0 = receive, bit 1 = transmit | See below |
| `0x1c` | 20 B | Reserved | `0` |

[Confirmed].

Power-state codes: `idle` (off, the state at reset), `pw1 ` (powered, not
streaming), `pwrd` (streaming). Sequence up is `idle → pw1 → pwrd`, down is
`pwrd → pw1 → idle`. The voice-trigger path adds `cnfg` and `runn`. The flag at
`0x18` is `0` on the transitions `idle → pw1 ` and `pw1 → idle`, and `1` on
`pw1 → pwrd` and `pwrd → pw1 `. [Confirmed] **Its meaning is now established: it
is a direction mask**, bit 0 = receive and bit 1 = transmit, carrying the set of
directions being started or stopped by this transition (§18 §18.2.4). The
baseline observation is the special case of a capture device, which starts only
the receive direction. [Confirmed]

**Key `301` — low-power input channel configuration.** 16 bytes, sent to the
low-power audio input device.

| Offset | Size | Field | Baseline value |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | u32 | Channels enabled, bitmap | `7` (three channels) |
| `0x04` | u32 | Channels supported, bitmap | `7` |
| `0x08` | u32 | Voice-trigger channel index | `1` |
| `0x0c` | u32 | **[Unknown]** | `7` |

[Confirmed for the baseline generations]. The values are baseline constants for
a three-microphone array and **must be rederived per machine** in scope from
the microphone count (two on j700, three elsewhere — §11.3.2).

**Key `200` — pulse-density front-end configuration.** 632 bytes.

| Offset | Size | Field | Baseline value / units |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0x000` | u32 | Bytes per sample | `2` on M1/M2, **`3` on the M3 generation and later** |
| `0x004` | u32 | Clock source selector | Four-character code `pll ` |
| `0x008` | u32 | Bit clock | 2 400 000 Hz |
| `0x00c` | u32 | Controller clock | 24 000 000 Hz |
| `0x010` | u32 | Slow clock | 24 000 000 Hz |
| `0x014` | u32 | Fast clock | 24 000 000 Hz |
| `0x018` | u32 | Channel polarity select | `256` (bit 8) |
| `0x01c` | u8 | Reserved | `0` |
| `0x01d` | u32, unaligned | Channel phase select | `0` |
| `0x021` | u8 | Reserved | `0` |
| `0x022` | 496 B | Embedded standard decimator configuration (key `210` layout) | Zero-filled on parts that use the high-rate decimator |
| `0x212` | u32 | Microphone turn-on time valid | `1` |
| `0x216` | u32 | Microphone turn-on time | 20 ms |
| `0x21a` | 16 B | Reserved | `0` |
| `0x22a` | u32 | Microphone settle time valid | `1` |
| `0x22e` | u32 | Microphone settle time | 50 ms |
| `0x232` | 69 B | Reserved | `0` |
| `0x277` | 1 B | Padding | `0` |

[Confirmed for the baseline generations]. The structure is **not naturally
aligned** — the channel-phase field straddles a 4-byte boundary — and must be
emitted byte-exactly.

**Key `210` — standard decimator configuration.** 496 bytes; the same layout is
embedded in key `200` at offset `0x022`.

| Offset | Size | Field | Baseline value |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | u32 | Latency | `15` |
| `0x04` | u8 | Stage 1 decimation ratio | `15` |
| `0x05` | u8 | Stage 2 decimation ratio | `5` |
| `0x06` | u8 | Stage 3 decimation ratio | `2` |
| `0x07` | u8 | Padding | `0` |
| `0x08` | u32 | Packed per-stage filter lengths | `0x0054_2C47` |
| `0x0c` | u32 | Coefficient count | `120` |
| `0x10` | 480 B | Up to 120 signed 32-bit coefficients | 100 populated |

**Key `212` — high-rate decimator configuration.** 8 200 bytes. Used on the M3
generation and later instead of key `210`, therefore on all five in-scope SoCs.

| Offset | Size | Field | Baseline value |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | u32 | Latency | `36` |
| `0x04` | u8 | Stage 1 decimation ratio | `10` |
| `0x05` | u8 | Stage 2 decimation ratio | `5` |
| `0x06` | u8 | Stage 3 decimation ratio | `3` |
| `0x07` | u8 | Padding | `0` |
| `0x08` | u32 | Packed per-stage filter lengths | `0x00D9_4960` |
| `0x0c` | u32 | Coefficient count | `1023` |
| `0x10` | 8 184 B | Up to 1 023 signed 64-bit coefficients | 386 populated |

[Confirmed for the baseline generations].

**Decoding the packed filter-length field.** The u32 holds three 8-bit tap
counts, least-significant byte first. For the standard configuration that is
71, 44 and 84 taps; for the high-rate configuration 96, 73 and 217 taps.
**[Inferred]**, on arithmetic that closes exactly in both cases:

- High rate: `96 + 73 + 217 = 386`, which is exactly the number of 64-bit
  coefficients populated. The three stages therefore store **full** tap sets,
  laid out consecutively.
- Standard: `ceil(71/2) + ceil(44/2) + ceil(84/2) = 36 + 22 + 42 = 100`, which
  is exactly the number of 32-bit coefficients populated. The three stages
  therefore store **half** tap sets, i.e. the filters are symmetric and only
  one half of each is transmitted.

A driver that needs to change the microphone decimation must respect this
difference: the two configurations do not use the same coefficient convention.

**Sample-rate reconciliation is [Unknown].** The bit clock is 2 400 000 Hz and
the capture device advertises 48 000 Hz, requiring a total decimation of 50.
Neither ratio triple's product is 50 (both are 150), although the first two
stages of the high-rate triple are `10 × 5 = 50`. Whether the third ratio
selects a further stage, a bypass, or an alternative path is **[Unknown]** and
is a concrete thing to measure (Open question 37).

### 11.4.7 Configuring and starting a stream — the complete sequence

Steps 1–7 correspond to Section 15's state S6; steps 8–12 to S7. Every step is
a framed call unless stated otherwise.

| # | Step | Layer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Patch the firmware boot-argument table; release the core (`reg[0]+0x44` bit 4). | §11.5.4, §11.2.7 |
| 2 | Complete the version handshake, acknowledge every endpoint-map fragment, start every advertised system endpoint, wait for the coprocessor power-state acknowledgement, set the host power state to `on` and wait for its acknowledgement. | §11.2.8 |
| 3 | For every advertised application endpoint (the **whole** advertised range, not `0x20`–`0x2e`): send the management start, then run the ring bring-up of §11.4.2 to completion. | §11.4.2 |
| 4 | Collect service announcements; record the (endpoint, channel) pair for the audio service. | §11.4.4 |
| 5 | Attach every device identifier the stream needs, one `0xC3000002` call each. For the microphone path the baseline generations attach the pulse-density front end, the high-power input and the low-power input, and on the M3 generation and later additionally the low-power internal loopback. | §11.4.6 |
| 6 | Set key `301` on the low-power input device (channel configuration). | §11.4.6 |
| 7 | Set key `200` on the pulse-density front end. On parts using the high-rate decimator, leave the embedded decimator block zero. | §11.4.6 |
| 8 | Set key `210` (standard) **or** key `212` (high-rate) on the pulse-density front end. | §11.4.6 |
| 9 | Set key `202` on the stream's device with target `pw1 ` and flag `0`. | §11.4.6 |
| 10 | Acquire the DMA channel named for this stream, allocate its buffers, and program the transfer with a **source port window of 4**. | Section 4 |
| 11 | Set key `202` with target `pwrd` and flag `1`. **Data now flows.** | §11.4.6 |
| 12 | Teardown: key `202` target `pw1 ` flag `1`; release the DMA channel; key `202` target `idle` flag `0`. | §11.4.6 |

[Confirmed for the baseline capture path]. Step ordering is load-bearing:
attachment must precede any property call for a device, the channel and
front-end configuration must precede the first power transition, and the DMA
channel must be running before the device reaches `pwrd`.

**Stream parameters the baseline capture path presents to the host:**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Direction | Capture |
| Channels | 3 |
| Sample rate | 48 000 Hz, fixed |
| Sample format | 32-bit float, little-endian, interleaved |
| Minimum period | 256 B |
| Maximum period | `0x4000` B |
| Minimum periods | 2 |
| Reported FIFO depth | 16 |
| DMA source port window | 4 |

[Confirmed for the baseline generations]. These are per-machine on the in-scope
parts and **must be taken from the per-stream endpoint descriptors of §11.7**,
not from this table.

**What this sequence covers, and where the playback sequence is.** The sequence
above is the **microphone capture path**. The corresponding sequence for a
**serial-audio stream** — speaker, jack output, jack input, loopback or tap — is
given in **§18 §18.6.1**, and it differs: it uses property keys `401`, `402`,
`508`, `701`, `702` and `703` in place of keys `200`/`212`/`301`, and its two
key-`202` transitions carry a **direction mask** naming the directions being
started. In consequence:

- The property keys that set a **playback** stream's slot geometry, frame
  geometry and clocking are **no longer [Unknown]**: they are key `701` for the
  geometry and clocking and key `703` for the master clock (§18 §18.3, §18
  §18.4). Their key numbers are [Confirmed] on t604x, t8140 and t605x and
  [Probable] on t8132 and t8142.
- There is **no separate sample-rate property at all**; the rate is implied by
  the frame geometry and the divider (§18 §18.4.3).
- The **stream start is the key-`202` transition to the code reported by key
  `402`**, with the direction mask set — there is no distinct start call on the
  serial-audio path either. [Confirmed] (§18 §18.10). The meaning of call types
  `0xC3000006` and `0xC3000008` remains **[Unknown]** (Open question 6).
- The speaker path uses the same ladder, but with the **two upper state codes
  read from keys `401` and `402`** rather than assumed (§18 §18.2.3).

### 11.4.8 Three consumers, and which parts are generic

The same transport carries at least three unrelated services on the in-scope
parts — the audio service, and two sensor services whose `device_type` values
appear in the same coprocessor nub subtree as the audio service child. Their
overlap establishes what is transport and what is audio:

| Element | Generic to the transport | Audio-specific |
|---|---|---|
| Mailbox registers, 96-bit message, endpoint field | ✔ | |
| Management endpoint, version handshake, endpoint map, power states | ✔ | |
| Ring-endpoint bring-up, ring layout, queue-element header | ✔ | |
| Call header (version, sequence, category, subtype, tag) | ✔ | |
| Service announcement, (endpoint, channel) reference | ✔ | |
| Correlation by tag, 8 outstanding requests, reply status word | ✔ | |
| Unsolicited report path (category `0x00`, subtype `0xc4`) | ✔ | Payload layout is per-service |
| **Subtype numbering** | | Per-service: `0x20` for audio, `0x0a`/`0x04` for the sensor services |
| Wrapped-call body, call types, device identifiers, property keys | | ✔ |

[Confirmed]. The practical consequence: **a driver should implement layers 1–4
once, as a transport, and the audio service as a client of it** — the same code
serves the voice-trigger service, which is a second client on the same
coprocessor.

---

## 11.5 Bring-up sequence and readiness

### 11.5.1 Firmware payloads

| SoC / board | Payload tag scheme | Second-instance payload |
|---|---|---|
| t8132 | per-SoC-class tag | none |
| t8132, j773g (Mac mini) | **per-board tag** | none |
| t604x | per-SoC-class tag | none |
| t8140 (j700) | **per-board tag** | **none** (node carries `no-firmware-service`) |
| t8142 (j704, j813, j815) | **per-board tag** | per-board tag |
| t605x | per-SoC-class tag | per-SoC-class tag |

The tag is carried verbatim in the `firmware-name` property of the
coprocessor's nub child; the host resolves it to a payload in the boot
file set. [Confirmed] A driver must read `firmware-name` rather than derive it
from the SoC identity: j700, j704, j773g, j813 and j815 all break the
per-SoC-class rule.

### 11.5.2 Container format

**Two different containers are in use across the in-scope range.** Both
describe the payload container a driver must parse in order to boot the
coprocessor.

**(a) t8132 and t604x (M4 generation): a plain 64-bit executable image.** The
M4-generation payload is a standard 64-bit AArch64 executable image: parse its
segment table and copy each segment to its recorded load address inside the
firmware SRAM window.
[Confirmed]

**(b) t8140, t8142, t605x (A18 Pro and M5 generation): a segmented bundle.**
This is new and must be parsed explicitly.

Container header:

| Offset | Size | Field | Observed |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | u32 | format/version word | `0x14000200` on every payload |
| `0x04` | u32 | reserved | 0 |
| `0x08` | 4 B | magic, byte-reversed FourCC | reads `BUND` |
| `0x0c` | u32 | flags | `0x00040000` |
| `0x10` | u32 | version | 1 |
| `0x14` | u32 | **segment count** | 11 or 14 |
| `0x20` | u64 | offset of first segment / header size | `0x10000` |
| `0x48` | u64 | — | `0x8000` |
| `0x60` | u64 | — | 3 |
| `0x88` | u64 | segment count, repeated | matches `0x14` |
| `0x90` | 16 B | format identity constant | identical in every payload |
| `0xa0`–`0x27f` | 480 B | load-address / size descriptors; contents **[Unknown]** | |
| `0x280` | n × 24 B | **segment table** | |

Segment table entry, 24 bytes:

| Offset | Size | Field |
|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | u32 | type/permission flags |
| `0x04` | 4 B | segment tag, byte-reversed FourCC |
| `0x08` | u64 | offset of segment data within the container |
| `0x10` | u64 | segment length in bytes |

Segments are contiguous — each segment's offset equals the previous offset plus
the previous length — and the first begins at `0x10000`. A zero length is
legal and means the segment is declared but empty. [Confirmed — the
contiguity relation holds exactly, for every segment.]

Segment tags observed, in table order:

| Tag | Flags | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `ktxt` | `0x0000000a` | |
| `rtxt` | `0x0000000a` | |
| `utxt` | `0x0000000e` | |
| `kdat` | `0x00000011` | |
| `rdat` | `0x00000011` | |
| `udat` | `0x00000015` | |
| `nold` | `0x00000114` | zero length on the always-on coprocessor; populated on the second instance |
| `dsro` | `0x00000044` / `0x00000014` | |
| `dsrw` | `0x00000045` / `0x00000015` | |
| `uetx` | `0x00000026` | absent from the second instance's payload |
| `uedt` | `0x00000045` | absent from the second instance's payload |
| `usdt` | `0x00000085` | absent from the second instance's payload |
| `ubdl` | `0x00000045` | |
| `oslg` | `0x00000104` | **offset 0, length 0** — declared but not carried by the payload; it is backed at run time by shared memory, and a loader must allocate it rather than copy it |

[Confirmed] for the tags, their flags and their lengths. What each tag denotes
is **[Unknown]** and a loader does not need it: the entry's flags, its length
and the one zero-length entry above are the whole of what loading requires.

The second coprocessor's payload uses the same container with 11 segments.

### 11.5.3 Ownership and handshake around the load

| Step | What the platform description says | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| Before load | The coprocessor has **no host power gate and no host clock gate** (`power-gates` and `clock-gates` are both present but empty). The host therefore cannot power-cycle it. | [Confirmed] |
| Before load | The nub carries `watchdog-enable` and `coredump-enable = 0x40` on **every** in-scope board. `no-shutdown = 1` and `claim-wake` are present on t8132, t8140, t8142 and t605x and **absent on t604x**. See §11.10. | [Confirmed] |
| Load | The payload is copied into the firmware SRAM window described by `reg[2]` / `region-base` / `region-size`. Alignment `0x4000`. | [Probable] |
| Before release | The host may patch the typed boot-argument table the resident code carries in its own firmware window (§11.5.4). | [Confirmed] on the M4 parts |
| Release | The core is released by setting bit 4 of `CPU_CTRL` at `reg[0] + 0x44` (§11.2.7). | [Probable] — see §11.2.2 |
| After load | The version handshake, the endpoint-map exchange and the power-state exchange occur over the mailbox before any service is usable. Their message layout is given in §11.2.8. | [Confirmed] for the layout; [Probable] for the version the in-scope firmware advertises |
| Readiness | Readiness is the completion of the management handshake — last endpoint-map fragment acknowledged, coprocessor power state acknowledged, host power state set to `on` and acknowledged (§11.2.8). It is a message sequence; **there is no register-level readiness indication and none is needed**. | [Confirmed] |
| Route binding | The nub carries a `routes` property (a phandle on t605x/t8142 pointing at the isolated mailbox node; a small integer on t8140). | [Confirmed] |

**No published access-control filter covers the firmware-load window.** On every
in-scope board the window described by `reg[2]` / `region-base` / `region-size`
(§11.1.2) lies outside every protected address range published anywhere in the
platform description, including the fabric inbound address-protection filter of
§3 §3.4.5, whose nearest range is more than 32 MiB away from any coprocessor load
window. The load step above is therefore not gated by an address-protection filter and
this sequence stands as written. **[Confirmed]** against every published table. One
residual: on t605x that filter is enabled and locked with **no** range table published
(§3 §3.4.5), so an *undescribed* range cannot be excluded there — a bring-up attempt
that faults on the copy on an M5 Pro/Max machine must not be read as refuting this
result. See Open question 23.

**No ownership handshake exists for the audio complex itself.** Because no
audio power domain is host-writable (§11.1.5), the host cannot take the audio
hardware before the coprocessor is running, and the coprocessor is the only
agent that can bring the serialisers and clocks up. The practical bring-up
order for a driver is therefore fixed and non-negotiable:

```
load coprocessor firmware  →  patch the boot-argument table  →  release core
  →  management handshake (version, endpoint map, power states)
    →  start every advertised endpoint and run its ring bring-up
      →  collect service announcements, take the audio service's
         (endpoint, channel) pair  →  attach device FourCCs
        →  configure each device (set-property)  →  power each device idle → pw1
          →  program the host DMA channel  →  power the device pw1 → pwrd
```

Fully expanded, with the layer that owns each step, this is the twelve-step
sequence of §11.4.7.

### 11.5.4 The firmware boot-argument table

Before the core is released, the host may patch a table of typed arguments that
the resident code carries in its own firmware window.

| Offset in firmware window (`reg[2]`) | Size | Field |
|---|---|---|
| `+0x22c` | u32 | Byte offset of the argument table, relative to the base of the firmware window |
| `+0x230` | u32 | Length of the argument table in bytes |

The table is a packed sequence of records:

| Offset in record | Size | Field |
|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | 4 B | Key, four ASCII characters stored **byte-reversed** relative to their readable form |
| `0x04` | u32 | Value length in bytes |
| `0x08` | n B | Value, little-endian |

To patch, walk the table and overwrite the value in place; lengths are fixed by
the resident code and must not be changed.

**[Confirmed] on the in-scope M4 parts** — the table header is at the same
window offset on t8132 and t604x, per-SoC and per-board payloads alike, and
every key the baseline generations patch exists with the same value length.

Keys a host is expected to set, with the value lengths established on the M4
generation:

| Key (readable) | Length | Meaning | Baseline values |
|---|---|---|---|
| `EC0p` | 8 B | Coprocessor-visible base of an externally supplied window | `0x20000` on the M1 and M2 base dies and the M1 Pro/Max die; `0x0100_0000_0000` on the M2 Pro/Max die |
| `nCal` | 1 B | Suppress use of stored calibration | `0` when the host supplies calibration itself |
| `alig` | 4 B | Shared-buffer alignment in bytes | `128` on the M1/M2 base dies, `64` on the M1/M2 Pro/Max dies |
| `AOPt` | 4 B | Platform variant selector | `1` on the M1 base die, `0` elsewhere |

**The correct in-scope values for all four are [Unknown]** (Open question 31).
The platform description supplies only one of them, and only on base dies of
the M1 and M2 generations: a property `aop-memory-alignment` on the
coprocessor's child nub node with value `0x80`, matching the `alig` value of
128 for those parts. **No in-scope board carries that property, or any other
property that supplies any of these four values.** [Confirmed by absence across
all 14 in-scope boards.]

---

☠ **HAZARD — a wrong `alig` value boots successfully and then mis-parses every
ring, silently.**

`alig` is the shared-buffer alignment, in bytes, that the resident code applies
when it lays out the shared-memory rings of §11.3 and §11.4.2. It is consumed
**after** the core is released and **before** any ring is used, and nothing
validates it: the value is a host-supplied alignment, not a checksum or a magic
number, and every value that is a plausible power of two is structurally
acceptable.

**The failure mode, precisely.** The core releases. The management handshake of
§11.2.8 completes — it runs over the mailbox, not over the rings, so it is
unaffected. The endpoint map is returned. The rings are then created, and host
and coprocessor lay out the same buffer with **different strides**. From that
point every ring index the two sides exchange refers to a different byte offset
on each side. There is no error, no status bit, no unsolicited report and no
mailbox failure, because as far as both sides are concerned each is reading a
correctly framed structure — at the wrong address.

**Why it is worth calling out separately from the other three unknown
boot arguments.** `nCal`, `AOPt` and `EC0p` fail loudly or not at all: a wrong
`nCal` changes whether stored calibration is used, a wrong `AOPt` selects a
platform variant that will not match the hardware and fails early, and a wrong
`EC0p` names a window the coprocessor cannot reach and faults. `alig` is the one
of the four whose wrong value produces a **working-looking coprocessor that
returns corrupt data indefinitely.** It will present as a transport bug — the
wrong endpoint answering, message bodies that decode as nonsense, a service that
resolves and then returns garbage — and every one of those symptoms points away
from the boot argument that caused it.

**What a driver must do.**

1. **Set `alig` explicitly. Never leave it at whatever the payload carries.**
   The baseline values are 128 bytes on the M1 and M2 base dies and 64 bytes on
   the M1 and M2 Pro/Max dies; the in-scope values are **[Unknown]** and this is
   Open question 31, which §17 places first in phase 1 for this reason.
2. **Validate the rings before trusting them, not after.** After the rings are
   created and before any audio call, issue a framed call whose reply content is
   known in advance — the management handshake's version exchange or a property
   read whose value the platform description also states — and compare. A
   mismatch at that point is the only cheap signal that the layout is wrong.
3. **Treat a first-boot transport failure as an `alig` problem until proved
   otherwise.** If the handshake completes and ring traffic does not decode,
   re-try the whole bring-up with each candidate alignment before investigating
   the transport layer itself.

---

Further keys exist in the table on every generation. Their keys and lengths are
stable across generations, their semantics are **[Unknown]**, and none of them
appears to need patching.

**New on the M5 generation and A18 Pro:** the table additionally carries **80
numbered base/size argument pairs**, indexed `0` … `79` by a single trailing
ASCII character (`0x30` … `0x7f`), each value 8 bytes. They are **absent from
every M1-, M2-, M3- and M4-generation payload**. The reading is a table of
shared-memory window slots the host is expected to fill; **[Inferred]**, and
their use is **[Unknown]** (Open question 32).

**What a driver must do with them meanwhile: leave every one of them alone.**
The count (80), the indexing (a single trailing ASCII character), the value
length (8 bytes) and the base/size pairing are established; **which index means
which window, and whether any of them must be filled for a plain audio bring-up,
are [Unknown]**. The rule of §11.5.4 — walk the table and overwrite values in
place, never change a length — makes leaving them at their payload values the
safe default, and the four keys above are the only ones this document establishes
a host is expected to set. A driver that finds audio working on t8132 and t604x
and not on t8142, t605x or t8140 should treat these pairs as a candidate cause
and should say so in its diagnostics, because they are the one boot-time
difference between the two generations that this document cannot resolve.

**Also new on the M5 generation and A18 Pro:** the payload carries **two**
argument tables rather than one; the M4-generation payload carries one. The second is consistent
with the secure service variants described in §11.4.1, which exist only on
those parts. [Confirmed that there are two; **[Inferred]** as to which is
which — Open question 33.] The second coprocessor instance's payload (§11.1.3)
carries one.

Because those payloads are containers, the table's offset within the *loaded*
window on the M5 generation and A18 Pro is **[Unknown]** (Open question 39).

---

## 11.6 What is reachable directly, and what is not

This is the section's central output. "Direct" means the host can do it by
MMIO write or I2C transaction without the coprocessor's cooperation.

### 11.6.1 Inventory

| Capability | t8132 (M4) | t604x (M4 Pro/Max) | t8140 (A18 Pro) | t8142 (M5) | t605x (M5 Pro/Max) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Stream start / stop (data movement)** | **Direct** — host DMA MMIO | Direct | Direct | Direct | Direct (except isolated streams) |
| **Stream start / stop (serialiser gating)** | **Coprocessor only** | Coprocessor only | Coprocessor only | Coprocessor only | Coprocessor only |
| **Sample-rate selection** | **Coprocessor only** | Coprocessor only | Coprocessor only | Coprocessor only | Coprocessor only |
| **Sample format / word width** | **Coprocessor only** | Coprocessor only | Coprocessor only | Coprocessor only | Coprocessor only |
| **TDM slot / routing configuration** | **Coprocessor only** | Coprocessor only | Coprocessor only | Coprocessor only | Coprocessor only |
| **Bit- and frame-clock generation** | **Coprocessor only** | Coprocessor only | Coprocessor only (oscillator node exists but has **no `reg`**) | Coprocessor only | Coprocessor only |
| **Master-clock (MCLK) enable/rate** | **Coprocessor only** | Coprocessor only | Coprocessor only | Coprocessor only | Coprocessor only |
| **Audio power/clock domains** | **Coprocessor only** | Coprocessor only | Coprocessor only | Coprocessor only | Coprocessor only |
| **Amplifier register access (volume, mute, gain, protection, TDM slot on the amp)** | **Direct** — host I2C | Direct | n/a (amplifier has **no control bus**) | Direct | Direct |
| **Amplifier shutdown / reset GPIO** | **Direct** — host GPIO | Direct | Direct | Direct | Direct |
| **Amplifier speaker-ID strap read** | **Direct** — host GPIO | Direct | n/a | Direct | Direct |
| **Jack codec register access (volume, mute, jack detect, headset type)** | **Direct** — host I2C | Direct | Direct | Direct | Direct |
| **Digital volume / mute in the audio path** | **Coprocessor only** (no host mixer exists) | Coprocessor only | Coprocessor only | Coprocessor only | Coprocessor only |
| **Speaker sense capture (I/V return)** | **Coprocessor only** for capture setup; data lands via host DMA | as t8132 | Coprocessor only; separate `tap ` endpoint | Coprocessor only; separate `tap ` endpoint | Coprocessor only; separate `tap ` endpoint |
| **Built-in microphone-array capture** | Coprocessor only; **non-secure**, host DMA | Coprocessor only; **non-secure**, host DMA | **Isolated environment only** | **Isolated environment only** | **Isolated environment only** |
| **Headset-microphone capture** | Coprocessor only; non-secure, host DMA | same | same | same | same |
| **Loopback (base domain)** | Coprocessor only; non-secure | same | same | same | same |
| **Loopback (low-power domain)** | Coprocessor only; non-secure | same | same | same | non-secure **plus** an isolated variant |
| **Microphone injection** | absent | absent | Coprocessor only, non-secure | Coprocessor only, non-secure | Coprocessor only, non-secure |
| **Digital display (HDMI/DisplayPort) audio** | not described here | not described here | not described here | **separate per-display DMA controllers**, host MMIO | **separate per-display DMA controllers**, host MMIO |
