| **Device power state (idle / ready / streaming)** | **Coprocessor only** | Coprocessor only | Coprocessor only | Coprocessor only | Coprocessor only |

[Confirmed] for every row — no host MMIO aperture and no host-writable power
domain exists for any capability marked coprocessor-only.

### 11.6.2 The conflicts a driver must plan around

**(a) The amplifiers and the jack codec are host-owned but the bus feeding them
is not.** Every amplifier and codec control node remains a child of a host I2C
controller (`/arm-io/i2c1`, `i2c2`, `i2c3`), each with its own host `reg`
aperture, its own interrupt, and the full M1–M3 property set intact
(`speaker-config`, `speaker1`…`speakerN`, `bop-config`,
`amp-dcblocker-config`, `amp-tx-zd-config`, `find-speaker-id`,
`function-speaker-id0/1`, `valid-speaker-ids`, `function-reset`,
`speaker-protection`, `iboot-audio-volume`). The `function-aop-device-control`
property that on M1–M3 marked a block as configured *through* the coprocessor
appears on **no node at all** on any in-scope board. So a Linux driver can
still program the amplifier and codec registers exactly as it does on M1–M3 —
**but it cannot produce the bit clock, frame clock or master clock those parts
need, and it cannot choose the TDM slot geometry the amplifier must be
programmed to match.** Volume and mute in the amplifier are reachable; volume
and mute anywhere upstream of it are not. [Confirmed]

**(b) The host could in principle drive the DMA, but the coprocessor also owns
the stream.** The audio DMA controllers are fully host-addressable
(`0x34000` apertures, unchanged size), and the platform hands the host their
interrupts and IOMMU streams. But the descriptor the DMA engine consumes is
only meaningful once the serialiser has been configured to the matching frame
geometry, and only the coprocessor can do that. Starting a DMA channel without
a prior coprocessor stream configuration will move bytes into or out of a
serialiser that is unclocked. Conversely, the coprocessor owns the stream's
lifecycle and rejects configuration changes on a stream that is already
configured. Racing it is a real hazard. [Probable]

**(c) The serial audio controller hardware exists and is unreachable.** Six
base-domain clusters plus one low-power cluster are enumerated as power
domains — but no node anywhere in the platform description gives that hardware
a host MMIO aperture. Its registers
are presumably still at their architectural addresses and might be reachable by
a driver that computes them; whether the fabric permits a host access to them
is **[Unknown]** and is a first-order probing target.

*Narrowed, not closed.* Two always-on access-control blocks bear on this and neither
settles it (§11.6.3). The register-path filter enumerates no addresses and no agents,
so it cannot express a per-master permission and cannot answer the question at all. The
fabric inbound address-protection filter does enumerate ranges, and on t8140 and t8142
its complete published set **omits the serial audio controller** aperture predicted at
`0x…_1360_0000`, **the PDM converter group** at `0x…_1350_0000` and **the island global
configuration blocks** at `0x…_13C0_0000` / `0x…_13C1_0000` (§3 §3.4.5). **[Confirmed]**
as a statement about that filter's published table: if a host access to the serial audio
controller is refused on t8140 or t8142, that block is not what refuses it. It is a
narrowing and not a closure for three reasons. (i) The filter's allow/deny polarity is
**[Unknown]**; on a deny-by-default allow-list reading, omission would mean *blocked*,
which is the opposite conclusion. (ii) t605x publishes no range table at all, so the
argument does not extend to M5 Pro/Max. (iii) The register-path filter's source-side
global word is non-zero on exactly the A18 Pro and M5 parts and its semantics are
unresolved. Its destination-side words are zero on every in-scope board including all
four M5 Pro/Max boards; *if* zero means "no target-side register filtering configured",
inbound register accesses into the always-on island are unfiltered everywhere and this
question resolves to "reachable, subject only to power" — but the polarity is
**[Unknown]** and this must not be asserted. **This question remains open**: Open
question 10 here; §3 Open question 28 settles the fabric filter's polarity and Open
question 21 here settles the register-path filter's.

**(d) On t8140 there is no amplifier control path at all.** The A18 Pro
machine's amplifier family has no control bus (`num-channels = 2`, a
`audio-control,max98360` node with no I2C address), so *every* speaker control
— including any gain or mute — is upstream of the amplifier and therefore
coprocessor-only. That machine also routes its speaker stream through the
low-power domain rather than the base domain (§11.7.2), which is unique in the
range.

---

### 11.6.3 Always-on access-control and routing blocks

Four blocks appear in the always-on complex on the M4 generation and later and on no
M1–M3 board. Two bear on audio, two do not; all four are recorded here so that a
reader who meets them in the platform description knows what they are.

**The fabric inbound address-protection filter** (`aop-gapf-filters`) is the one with
audio bearing. It is present on t8140, t8142 and t605x, absent on t8132 and t604x, and
every range it protects is an audio DMA controller memory or register. It is
programmed, enabled and locked by pre-kernel firmware, so a host driver inherits it and
cannot change it. It is specified in full in **§3 §3.4.5** — presence per board,
control-register addresses, record layout, decoded ranges, and the agent lists —
because its targets lie inside the audio island. Note there that on t605x the filter is
enabled and locked while publishing no range table at all.

**The always-on register-path filter** (`/arm-io/aop/iop-aop-nub/aop-pio-filters`) sits
on the register (non-DMA) path of the always-on complex, upstream of every block in the
island: the power manager's always-on filter domain is the parent power domain of the
always-on GPIO, static-RAM, fixed-rate and IOMMU domains on every SoC, which is where a
register-path ingress filter would have to sit. **[Probable]** It is present on four of
the five in-scope SoCs and **absent on t604x**; on t8132 it is present with all three
words zero, so the first part on which it is configured non-trivially is t8140. The
node has no `reg`, no `compatible` and no `device_type`, and no register aperture is
published for the block itself.

| Property | Width | t8132 | t604x | t8140 | t8142 | t605x | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `pio-src-filt-global` | u32 | `0x0000_0000` | — | `0x0000_0002` | `0x0000_0002` | `0x0000_000A` | Global configuration word for the **source-side** (initiator-side) register filter. Bit-valued: bit 1 set on A18 Pro and M5, bits 1 and 3 on M5 Pro/Max. Field meanings **[Unknown]**. |
| `pio-dst-filt-global` | u32 | `0` | — | `0` | `0` | `0` | Global configuration word for the **destination-side** (target-side) register filter. Zero on every in-scope board. |
| `pio-dst-filt-fr-global` | u32 | `0` | — | `0` | `0` | `0` | Second destination-side word, for the always-on **fixed-rate partition**. Zero on every in-scope board. |

**[Confirmed]** for the values and for their per-SoC invariance — all boards of a given
SoC carry byte-identical values. **[Inferred]** for the source/destination and
fixed-rate readings: `src` and `dst` are the fabric's standard initiator and target
sides, and the `-fr-` suffix matches the always-on fixed-rate power domain, a sibling
of the GPIO and static-RAM domains under the filter domain and the parent of the
always-on I²C, SPI and SPMI domains.

**What this block cannot do.** Three global words are the whole of it. There are no
address ranges, no agent or master identifiers, no permission words, no lock bit, no
register address and no per-range table in this node on any board. **It therefore
cannot express a per-master permission**, and no statement of the form "master *X* may
or may not reach address *Y*" can be derived from it — in particular it does not decide
whether the host may reach the serial audio controller (§11.6.2(c)). **[Confirmed]** —
this is an exhaustive enumeration of the node's properties, not a sample.

**The always-on signal crossbar** (`aop-scm-xbar`, present on t8140 with no routes and
on t8142 and t605x with two routes in each direction between the main GPIO block and
the always-on sensor-control module) has **no established audio bearing**: no pin
number appearing in `gpio-to-scm-muxsel` or `scm-to-gpio-muxsel` is claimed by any
audio node, any I²S/TDM pad, any amplifier, any codec, the speaker identification
straps or the speaker reset line on any board. **[Confirmed]** for the absence of any
audio claimant; **[Unknown]** for what the module-side endpoints are (Open question 24).

**The additional always-on IOMMU stream mapper** (`/arm-io/dart-aop/mapper-scm`, a bare
stream-mapper node with `compatible = "iommu-mapper"`, `device_type = "dart-mapper"`,
a single `reg` giving stream index **3** on t8140, t8142 and t605x, and no aperture, no
interrupt and no consumer node anywhere in the platform description) has **no audio
bearing**: stream 3 is disjoint from the audio streams 8, 9, 10 and 11 and from the
coprocessor streams, so an IOMMU-managing driver must know it exists and must not reuse
index 3, but it shares no stream, no aperture and no interrupt with any audio block.
**[Confirmed]** This mapper is **not new to these SoCs**: it is present on t8103,
t8112, t8122 and t603x with stream indices 1, 6, 4 and 4 respectively, absent on t600x
and t602x, absent across the **whole** M4 generation (t8132 and t604x), and returns at
A18 Pro and M5 as stream 3. **[Confirmed]**

---

## 11.7 The per-stream endpoint model

### 11.7.1 Node shape

```
/arm-io/iop-audio-controller          compatible = "iop-audio,controller"   (no reg)
    iop-audio-service-name = <service name string>
  └─ <stream endpoint>                compatible = "iop-adma-stream,mca"  or  "iop-adma-stream,leap"
        identifier    = <FourCC, byte-reversed>
        device_type   = "iop-audio-ns"  or  "iop-audio-s"
        (M4)   dma-channels, dma-parent, function-admac_powerswitch, external-power-provider
        (M5/A18) dma-provider-tx, dma-provider-rx  (strings naming DMA channel nodes)
      └─ <data descriptor node>        compatible = "audio-data,<part>" or "audio-data,external"
            reg           = 36-byte serial-audio configuration blob
            data-sources  = capture source descriptor (capture directions only)
            device-uid, device-name, audio-stream-formatter, input-data-selectors, …
  └─ lp-mic-device                    compatible = "iop-audio,lp-mic-device"
  └─ lp-mic-io-buffer-device          compatible = "iop-audio,io-buffer-device"   (M4)
                                                or "iop-audio,isolated-io-buffer-device"  (M5/A18)
  └─ siri-listening-device            compatible = "iop-audio,client-manager-device"
```

The two `compatible` suffixes classify the endpoint by **which serial-audio
complex carries it**: `,mca` = the base-domain cluster array,
`,leap` = the cluster in the low-power audio processor domain. The
`device_type` suffix classifies it by **security domain**: `-ns` = normal
world, `-s` = isolated. These are orthogonal: `hpai` on the M5 generation is
`leap` + `-s`; `sllb` on t605x is `leap` + `-s`; `lilb` is `leap` + `-ns`;
`spkr` is `mca` + `-ns` (except on t8140). [Confirmed]

### 11.7.2 Endpoint inventory per machine

Direction is given as (tx, rx). DMA bindings are the named channels on the M5
generation and the A18 Pro; on the M4 generation the same channels are given
numerically in `dma-channels` (§11.7.5) and are listed here in the same
notation for comparability.

**t8132 (j604, j623, j624, j713, j715)** — 6 endpoints:

| Endpoint | FourCC | Complex | Domain | TX ch | RX ch |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `audio-speaker` | `spkr` | mca | ns | base-ns tx 0 | base-ns rx 0 |
| `audio-codec-output` | `cout` | mca | ns | base-ns tx 2 | — |
| `audio-codec-input` | `cin ` | mca | ns | — | base-ns rx 2 |
| `audio-mca-loopback` | `lpbk` | mca | ns | base-ns tx 3 | base-ns rx 3 |
| `audio-hp` | `hpai` | leap | ns | — | leap rx 0 |
| `audio-leap-internal-loopback` | `lilb` | leap | ns | leap tx 4 | leap rx 4 |

Plus `lp-mic-device` (`lpai`), `lp-mic-io-buffer-device` (`adpx`, **not**
isolated on this SoC) and `siri-listening-device` (`lai `).

**t8132 / j773g (Mac mini M4)** — 4 endpoints: `spkr`, `cout`, `cin `, `lpbk`.
No microphone array, no low-power endpoints, no voice-trigger controller node.

**t604x (j614s, j614c, j616s, j616c)** — identical set to t8132 notebooks.
**t604x / j773s, j575c** — identical to j773g: 4 endpoints, no microphone path.

**t8142 (j704, j813, j815) and t8140 (j700)** — 9 endpoints:

| Endpoint | FourCC | Complex | Domain | TX ch | RX ch |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `audio-speaker` | `spkr` | mca (**leap on j700**) | ns | `base-ns-adma-tx-0` (**`leap-ns-adma-tx-0` on j700**) | `base-ns-adma-rx-0` (**none on j700**) |
| `audio-speaker-tap` | `tap ` | mca | ns | — | `base-ns-adma-rx-1` |
| `audio-codec-output` | `cout` | mca | ns | `base-ns-adma-tx-2` | — |
| `audio-codec-input` | `cin ` | mca | ns | — | `base-ns-adma-rx-2` |
| `audio-mca-loopback` | `lpbk` | mca | ns | `base-ns-adma-tx-3` | `base-ns-adma-rx-3` |
| `audio-leap-internal-loopback` | `lilb` | leap | ns | `leap-ns-adma-tx-4` | `leap-ns-adma-rx-4` |
| `lp-mic-injection-device` | `lpij` | mca | ns | `base-ns-adma-tx-5` | — |
| `audio-hp-mic` | `hpai` | leap | **s** | — | **`leap-s-adma-rx-0`** |
| (t8140 only, secondary) `audio-speaker` control node | `spkr` | — | — | — | — |

Plus `lp-mic-device`, an **isolated** `lp-mic-io-buffer-device`, and
`siri-listening-device`.

**t605x (j714s, j714c, j716s, j716c)** — 10 endpoints: the t8142 set plus

| Endpoint | FourCC | Complex | Domain | TX ch | RX ch |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `audio-secure-leap-loopback` | `sllb` | leap | **s** | `leap-ns-adma-tx-5` | **`leap-s-adma-rx-5`** |

This endpoint carries `is-development-only` (empty) on the data node and
`proxy-is-development-only` on its DMA proxy, and its DMA channel node carries
`channel-is-development-only`. [Confirmed] A shipping driver should not depend
on it.

`audio-speaker-tap` additionally carries `clock-domain` with the byte-reversed
value reading `main` — it is slaved to the main (base) clock domain even though
it is a capture-only endpoint. [Confirmed]

`lp-mic-injection-device` carries `terminal-type-output` reading `injm` on its
data node, and its `data-sources` tag is the endpoint's own FourCC rather than
a generic path tag — i.e. it is a synthetic source injected into the low-power
path rather than a physical input. [Confirmed]

### 11.7.3 The 36-byte serial-audio configuration descriptor

Every data-descriptor node carries a `reg` property of **exactly 36 bytes** on
every board of every generation from M1 to M5. This is the **default serial
audio (I2S/TDM) configuration for the endpoint**. An endpoint whose descriptor
is absent, short or internally inconsistent is unusable. Its structure is therefore **unchanged from M1–M3**; what changed
is which nodes carry it and what the values say.

> ☠ **This subsection is the single authoritative decode of the 36-byte
> descriptor.** Two earlier partial decodes elsewhere in this document have been
> reduced to cross-references and must not be used as field layouts: §1 §1.12
> (which retains only a per-endpoint value inventory) and §2 §2.3 (which retains
> only the per-link value table, relabelled against this layout). Where an
> earlier decode named a field this one does not, the surviving field is carried
> forward below and marked. **A bit clock derived as "descriptor word 2 ÷
> descriptor word 3" — the superseded model — yields 192 kHz instead of 48 kHz
> on the A18 Pro jack link, and loses the data-delay and direction-mask fields a
> key-`701` record needs (§18 §18.3.1).** Use the table below.

| Offset | Size | Field | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | u8 | Descriptor version | `1` on every instance, every generation |
| `0x01` | u8 | Interface class / capability flags | observed `0x02`, `0x12`, `0x13`, `0x42` — see below |
| `0x02` | u16 | Reserved under this reading; a master-clock mode selector and a bit-order byte under the other — see below | 0 |
| `0x04` | u8 | **Link channel count** (frame slot count the masks are validated against) | 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 15 |
| `0x05` | u8 | **Bits per slot, frame-wide default** (`0` = derive from the per-direction fields) | `0x00`, `0x10` = 16, `0x20` = 32 |
| `0x06` | u8 | **Data delay, transmit and (unless byte `0x01` says otherwise) receive** | **bit clocks** after the frame-sync edge; `1` on the speaker link |
| `0x07` | u8 | Reserved | `0` everywhere — **[Unknown]** |
| `0x08` | u32 | **Master clock frequency, Hz** | 0, 6 000 000, 12 000 000, 12 288 000, 24 000 000 |
| `0x0c` | u16 | **Frame length, in bit clocks** (`0` = derive from the geometry) | 0x40=64, 0x7d=125, 0xc0=192, 0xfa=250, 0x100=256 |
| `0x0e` | u16 | **Frame-sync pulse length, in bit clocks** | 1 on every in-scope link |
| `0x10` | u16 | **Sample-rate numerator, kHz** | 0 = derive, 0x10 = 16, 0x30 = 48 |
| `0x12` | u16 | **Sample-rate denominator** | rate = numerator × 1000 ÷ denominator, and the division must be exact |
| `0x14` | u32 | **Transmit channel/slot mask** | bit *n* = slot *n* active |
| `0x18` | u32 | **Receive channel/slot mask** | bit *n* = slot *n* active |
| `0x1c` | u8 | **Transmit channel count** | |
| `0x1d` | u8 | **Receive channel count** | |
| `0x1e` | u8 | **Transmit bits per channel** | 0, 16, 24, 32 |
| `0x1f` | u8 | **Receive bits per channel** | 0, 16, 24, 32 |
| `0x20` | u8 | **Direction mask** — bit 0 = receive active, bit 1 = transmit active. Runtime field, excluded from the immutability comparison of property key `705` | 0, 1, 2, 3 |
| `0x21` | u8 | **Receive data delay**, in bit clocks; used only when byte `0x01` marks a separate receive delay | 0, 1, 2 |
| `0x22` | u8 | **Transmit bits per slot** (0 = same as bits per channel) | 0, 24, 32 |
| `0x23` | u8 | **Receive bits per slot** (0 = same as bits per channel) | 0, 16, 32 |

[Confirmed] for `0x08` and `0x14`–`0x1f`: these are forced by cross-machine
comparison (speaker mask width tracks amplifier count exactly; tx/rx channel
counts track the known topology exactly; the sense masks are exactly twice the
amplifier count on every machine that has sense and zero on every machine that
does not). **[Confirmed]** for `0x04`, `0x05`, `0x06`, `0x0c`, `0x0e`, `0x10`,
`0x12`, `0x20`, `0x21`, `0x22` and `0x23` — the geometry, clock and rate model
of §18 §18.4 closes exactly on every in-scope link under these readings, and the
values a host derives from them are the values the coprocessor's own built-in
records carry (§18 §18.7). **[Unknown]** for `0x07`.

**Fields carried forward from the superseded decodes.** Two observations that
only the earlier decodes recorded are retained here rather than dropped, because
neither is derivable from the table above:

- **`0x04` is the channel count of the *wider* direction on every endpoint
  except one.** On every in-scope endpoint `0x04` equals `max(tx channel count,
  rx channel count)` — and on the speaker endpoint that is the receive (sense)
  side, 12 on a six-amplifier machine, not the 6 playback slots. The exception
  is the base-domain loopback endpoint, whose `0x04` is a **board-independent
  constant `0x0f` = 15** on every board of every generation while its transmit
  and receive channel counts are both 2 and both masks are `0x3`. **The `0x0f`
  is [Unknown]** — it is neither a channel count nor a slot count on that
  endpoint. A driver must not derive a channel count from `0x04`; take the
  per-direction counts at `0x1c`/`0x1d` and the masks at `0x14`/`0x18`.
  Open question 40.
- **Byte `0x05` correlates with link family**, `0x10` on the speaker and
  base-domain loopback endpoints and `0x20` on the jack-codec endpoints of the
  t8132/t604x/t8142/t605x boards, `0x00` elsewhere. The earlier decode read that
  correlation as a port-group or SERDES-pairing tag. It is **not** one: `0x05`
  is the frame-wide default slot width and the correlation is a consequence of
  those two families using 16-bit and 32-bit slots respectively. Where `0x05` is
  `0x00`, the per-direction slot widths at `0x22`/`0x23` (or, where those are
  also zero, the sample widths at `0x1e`/`0x1f`) supply the width. [Confirmed]

☠ **`0x0c` is a count of bit clocks, not of master clocks.** The two coincide
only when the master-clock-to-bit-clock divider is `1`, which it is on every
in-scope link except the A18 Pro jack link, where the divider is 4. That is what
resolves the apparent 4× discrepancy this section previously recorded as
Open question 12: 24 000 000 ÷ 4 = 6 000 000 Hz bit clock, and 6 000 000 ÷ 125 =
48 000 Hz exactly. [Confirmed] — §18 §18.4.5. **The A18 Pro jack link was the
only in-scope link that did not divide out under the old model, and the only
in-scope link with a non-unity divider; that it now divides out to exactly
the advertised rate is strong corroboration of the reading rather than merely
consistent with it.**

**Related, and stated here because it is the same class of error:** the frame
field on a speaker link reads **250** and means 250 **bit clocks**, giving
12 000 000 ÷ 250 = 48 000 Hz. The per-direction data-bit counts (192 on a
six-amplifier machine, 128 on four, 32 on one) are **not** frame lengths; the
remainder of the frame is idle. See §18 §18.4.4, and §1 §1.4.4, §3 §3.7.3,
§7 §7.6.2 and §16, which state it the same way.

**Bytes `0x00`–`0x03` are [Unknown], and two readings exist.** The reading
tabulated above — byte `0x00` a descriptor version, byte `0x01` an
interface-class byte — accounts for every observed value. So does a second
reading in which `0x00` is a link-flags byte (bit 0 = a master clock is present,
bit 4 = drive the master clock out of the pin group), `0x01` a framing-flags
byte (bit 0 = frame-sync active edge, bit 1 = frame-sync pulse polarity, bits
5:4 = serialiser clock-edge mode, bit 6 = a separate receive data delay is
supplied at `0x21`), `0x02` a master-clock mode selector and `0x03` a
per-direction bit-order byte. **The observed values do not discriminate between
them**, and the difference matters: under the second reading byte `0x01` carries
link framing a driver must reproduce, and under the first it does not.
See §18 §18.12 and §18 open question 16.

Interface class byte (`0x01`) observed values:

| Value | Used by | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| `0x02` | `spkr` (mca machines), `tap `, `lpij` | base-domain stream, no master clock owned |
| `0x12` | `lpbk` | base-domain stream, immutable configuration |
| `0x13` | `cout`, `cin ` (all machines); `spkr`, `tap `, `cout`, `cin ` on t8140 | master-clock-owning stream |
| `0x42` | `hpai`, `lilb`, `sllb` | low-power-domain stream |

Bit 6 (`0x40`) marks the low-power complex, bit 0 (`0x01`) marks a
master-clock-owning link, bit 4 (`0x10`) marks a link whose configuration is
immutable (the condition property key `705` reports — §18 §18.2.2). [Inferred]

Worked example — the six-amplifier speaker link on t605x:

```
01 02 00 00 | 0c 10 01 00 | 00 1b b7 00 | fa 00 01 00 | 30 00 01 00
3f 00 00 00 | ff 0f 00 00 | 06 0c 18 10 | 00 00 20 10
```
12 link channels of 16 bits, data delay 1 bit clock, master clock 12 000 000 Hz,
frame 250 bit clocks with a 1-bit-clock frame-sync pulse, rate 48 × 1000 ÷ 1 =
48 000 Hz — and with the divider at 1 the bit clock is the master clock, so
12 000 000 ÷ 250 = 48 000 Hz frames, consistently. Tx mask `0x3f` (six slots),
rx mask `0xfff` (twelve slots), 6 transmit channels of 24 bits in 32-bit slots,
12 receive channels of 16 bits in 16-bit slots.

That last line is the important one: **the speaker endpoint is bidirectional and
its receive side carries exactly two 16-bit channels per amplifier** — the
current and voltage sense return — inside one endpoint. On M1–M3 the identical
descriptor appeared but with a link channel count of 6 rather than 12, because
transmit and receive were separate cluster nodes there. [Confirmed]

Per-machine speaker descriptor summary:

| Machine class | Link ch | tx mask | rx mask | tx ch × bits | rx ch × bits |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6-amplifier notebooks (all in-scope Pro/Max, j715, j815, j704) | 12 | `0x3f` | `0xfff` | 6 × 24 in 32 | 12 × 16 in 16 |
| 4-amplifier notebooks (j713, j813) | 8 | `0x0f` | `0xff` | 4 × 24 in 32 | 8 × 16 in 16 |
| 4-amplifier iMacs (j623, j624) | 4 | `0x0f` | `0x00` | 4 × 24 in 32 | none |
| 1-amplifier desktops (j773g, j773s, j575c) | 1 | `0x01` | `0x00` | 1 × 24 in 32 | none |
| t8140 (j700) | 2 | `0x03` | `0x00` | 2 × 32 in 32 | none (sense is on the `tap ` endpoint) |

[Confirmed]. The iMacs and desktops have **no sense return at all**, exactly as
on M1–M3.

### 11.7.4 The capture source descriptor (`data-sources`)

Present on capture directions only; absent from pure playback endpoints. Its
structure is **unchanged from M1–M3**.

| Offset | Size | Field |
|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | 4 B | source-path tag, byte-reversed FourCC |
| `0x04` | u32 | source flags |
| `0x08` | u16 | channel count |
| `0x0a` | u16 | **rate count** |
| `0x0c` | (rate count) × 8 B | one (u32 reserved, u32 sample rate in Hz) pair per supported rate |
| … | NUL-terminated ASCII | source name |

[Confirmed — the rate count at `0x0a` predicts the blob length exactly on every
instance on every board.]

Source-path tags observed: `ap2a` (low-power/leap analogue path), `ap2c`
(base-domain codec path), `ap2s` (low-power speaker path, t8140 only), `ispk`
(speaker tap), and the endpoint's own FourCC for the injection endpoint.

Rate sets observed: the headset-microphone input advertises **four** rates —
44 100, 48 000, 88 200, 96 000 Hz — on every t600x-and-later machine including
all in-scope ones; every other capture endpoint advertises a single rate,
48 000 Hz, except the injection endpoint which advertises 16 000 Hz.
[Confirmed]

### 11.7.5 The `dma-channels` record (M4 generation only)

On t8132 and t604x the endpoint carries `dma-channels` (**128 bytes**) plus
`dma-parent` (phandle of the DMA controller) instead of the named-channel
strings used later. The blob is **four 32-byte records**:

| Offset in record | Size | Field |
|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | u32 | flat DMA channel index, or `0xFFFFFFFF` = direction absent |
| `0x04` | u32 | record tag: `0x21` for the first pair, `0x22` for the second |
| `0x08` | u32 | reserved, 0 |
| `0x0c` | u32 | buffer allocation, bytes |
| `0x10` | u32 | secondary allocation, bytes |
| `0x14`–`0x1f` | 12 B | reserved, 0 |

Record order is (transmit, receive) for tag `0x21` then (transmit, receive) for
tag `0x22`. The flat channel index follows the audio DMA controller's own
numbering: **even = transmit, odd = receive**, engine number = index >> 1.
[Confirmed — decoding the M4 `dma-channels` indices this way reproduces, for
every endpoint on every M4 board, exactly the named channel that the M5
generation gives the same endpoint (e.g. index 4 ⇒ `…-adma-tx-2`, index 5 ⇒
`…-adma-rx-2`, index 8 ⇒ `leap…-tx-4`). Two independent generations agree.]

The buffer-allocation field is, on almost every endpoint, exactly one
millisecond of the stream at the maximum sample rate its channel declares
(speaker: 48 frames × 24 bytes = 1152; codec output at 96 kHz: 96 × 8 = 768;
microphone array: 48 × 12 = 576; base loopback: 48 × 4 = 192). The low-power
internal loopback breaks the pattern (768 transmit, 960 receive), so this
reading is **[Probable]**, not Confirmed.

### 11.7.6 Named DMA channel nodes (M5 generation and A18 Pro)

From the A18 Pro onward each DMA controller node gains child nodes, one per
allocated channel, named `<role>-adma-<dir>-<n>` and referenced by string from
`dma-provider-tx` / `dma-provider-rx`. Each child carries:

| Property | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `compatible` | `audio-dma-channel,v4p0` |
| `reg` | four (base, size) pairs: a `0x200`-byte channel window plus three 4-byte doorbell/status words |
| `max-channel-count` | maximum audio channels the engine will carry |
| `max-bit-depth-bits` | 16 or 32 |
| `max-sample-rate-hz` | 16 000, 48 000 or 96 000 |
| `dma-stream-type` | byte-reversed, reads `ISOC` |
| `role` | byte-reversed, reads `BANS`, `BASS`, `LENS` or `LESS` (base/low-power × non-secure/secure) |
| `direction`, `index`, `channel-buffer-size` | present but empty — the name carries the information |
| `service-exclave_proxy` | present **only** on channels owned by the isolated environment; names the proxy node |

[Confirmed]. DMA controller instances:

| Instance | Role tag | Aperture | `#dma-channels-tx/rx` | `channel-buffer-allocation` | t8132 | t604x | t8140 | t8142 | t605x |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `admac-base-ns` | `BANS` | `0x34000` | 13 / 13 | `0x1e00` | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `admac-base-s` | `BASS` | `0x34000` | — | — | absent | absent | absent | absent | absent |
| `admac-leap-ns` | `LENS` | `0x34000` | 9 / 9 | `0xe00` | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `admac-leap-s` | `LESS` | `0x34000` | 9 / 9 | `0x300` | absent | absent | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |

[Confirmed]. Base addresses (I/O-region-relative): base-ns at
`<die>+0x3800000`, leap-ns at `<die>+0x3300000`, leap-s at `<die>+0x3200000`,
where `<die>` is `0x190000000` (t8132), `0x310000000` (t604x), `0x100000000`
(t8140), `0x180000000` (t8142), `0x090000000` (t605x). The aperture is
`0x34000` on every instance — **unchanged from M1–M3**.

Note the discrepancy worth flagging: the IOMMU declares a `base-s` stream ID
(9) and a `mapper-admac-base-s` child on **every** in-scope SoC, but **no
`admac-base-s` controller node exists anywhere**. Either the secure base-domain
controller is present but undescribed, or the stream ID is reserved. **[Unknown]**

On the M5 generation a fifth class appears: per-display audio DMA controllers
(`admac-disp0`, `admac-dispext0`…`admac-dispext3`, each with a companion
`-ced-ssw` node). These are host MMIO, are not children of the audio controller
node, and carry no coprocessor binding — the digital-display audio path is
**not** coprocessor-mediated. [Confirmed]

Finally, `admac-aop-ced-ssw` (t8142, t605x) is a supervisory block covering all
four audio DMA controllers: `#dma-controllers = 4`, `dma-controllers` listing
the four role tags in order, per-controller tx/rx channel counts, two `0x4000`
apertures and its own interrupt. Its function is escalation detection on
low-latency traffic. [Probable]

### 11.7.7 Concurrency — endpoints open at the same time

The ordinary case is more than one endpoint open at once: speaker playback with
a headset microphone captured, or jack playback started while speakers run. What
follows is what the hardware description settles and what it does not.

**Established.**

- **The data paths are disjoint and statically assigned.** Every endpoint on
  every in-scope board names its own DMA channel indices, and no index is named
  by two endpoints in the same direction: `spkr` tx-0/rx-0, `tap ` rx-1,
  `cout` tx-2, `cin ` rx-2, `lpbk` tx-3/rx-3 on the base instance; `lilb`
  tx-4/rx-4 and `sllb` tx-5/rx-5, `hpai` rx-0 on the low-power instance;
  `lpij` base tx-5. On t8140 the speaker endpoint's channel is
  `leap-ns-adma-tx-0` instead of `base-ns-adma-tx-0`; the rest are the same.
  No two endpoints can therefore contend for a DMA channel, a descriptor FIFO or
  a completion FIFO. **[Confirmed]**
- **The clocking objects are disjoint between the four independent link
  families.** The coprocessor's built-in records (§18 §18.7.1) bind the speaker
  family to `mck0`/`ckg0`/`syn0`, the codec family to `mck2`/`ckg2`/`syn2`, the
  low-power family to `mck3`/`ckg3`/`syn3` and the injection family to
  `mck5`/`ckg5`/`syn5`. A rate or frame-geometry change on one family therefore
  cannot disturb another. **[Confirmed]**
- **`cout` and `cin ` are two directions of one link and share every clocking
  object and the same serialiser unit (`ms02`).** They are not independent:
  their frame geometry, bit clock and frame rate are one setting. A driver must
  not configure the two endpoints to different rates or frame lengths, and a
  reconfiguration of either stops both. **[Confirmed]**
- **The speaker tap shares the speaker link's clock and frame-sync generators
  and uses a *different* serialiser unit** (`ms01` against the speaker's
  `ms00`, and `ms12` on t8140). The tap is therefore a passenger on the speaker
  link: it cannot set the link's rate or geometry, it carries data only while
  the speaker link is clocked, and stopping the speaker link stops it.
  **[Confirmed]**
- **Configuration immutability is reported, not assumed.** Property key `705`
  reports whether an endpoint's configuration may still be changed (§18
  §18.2.2), and descriptor byte `0x01` bit 4 marks endpoints whose configuration
  is immutable from the outset (§11.7.3). A driver must read key `705` before
  reconfiguring any endpoint while another is running, and treat a
  not-changeable report as authoritative. **[Confirmed]** for the reporting
  mechanism.

**Not established.** ☠

- **Whether an attach of a second endpoint while a first is running is accepted,
  refused, or accepted with the first silently retargeted.** **[Unknown]** —
  Open question 41. The eleven-step start sequence of §18 §18.6.1 is written for
  one endpoint and says nothing about a second.
- **What happens when two endpoints name overlapping cluster objects** — for
  example an attempt to move the codec link onto `ckg0` while the speaker link
  runs on it. **[Unknown]** — Open question 41. §18 §18.5.3 establishes that the
  coprocessor reports no error when the *slot map* is inconsistent; whether it
  reports one when the *clock binding* is, is not established, and the
  consequence of a silent acceptance is a running link whose rate changes
  underneath it.
- **Whether the outstanding-call window is per endpoint, per service channel or
  per coprocessor.** **[Unknown]** — Open question 42.
- **Whether starting `cout` while `spkr` runs requires any ordering at all.**
  Nothing in the interface expresses a dependency between the two, and their
  clocking objects are disjoint, so no ordering is expected — but this is
  **[Inferred]** from the object bindings, not established, and it is the exact
  event a jack insertion during speaker playback produces (§14 §14.6.5).

**What a driver should do until Open question 41 is answered.** Attach and
configure every endpoint it intends to use *before* starting any of them; read
property key `705` on each endpoint after each configuration step and abort if a
previously changeable endpoint has become not-changeable; and treat a failed
second attach as requiring a full teardown of the first rather than a retry.

---

## 11.8 The isolated execution environment

### 11.8.1 What it is at the hardware level

A second, mutually distrusting execution context runs on the same always-on
coprocessor, with:

- **its own IOMMU stream ID** on `/arm-io/dart-aop` (stream 1; stream 17 for
  the second coprocessor on t8140), reached through a dedicated mapper child;
- **its own mailbox instance** at a separate physical aperture (§11.2.9);
- **its own segments in the same firmware payload** — the three entries
  §11.5.2 records as absent from the second instance's payload;
- **its own service channels** on the coprocessor transport (the `-s` variants
  named in §11.4.1), with further non-audio channels alongside them;
- **its own DMA controller instance** (`admac-leap-s`) and **its own power
  domains** (`AUDIO_BASE_S_A`, `AUDIO_LEAP_S_A`).

Enforcement is by the IOMMU and by the coprocessor's own privilege separation:
a normal-world master using stream 8 or 10 cannot reach a page mapped only on
stream 1, 9 or 11, and the normal-world service channel cannot issue the
secure channel's calls. [Confirmed — the stream IDs, mappers, separate
controller instance and separate power domains are all in the platform
description; the separate service channels and the separate segments are in
§11.4.1 and §11.5.2.]

The secure-side interface the isolated environment exposes to the coprocessor
comprises, functionally: report-parking-state, report-use-case-ready,
update-audio-state (non-secure side); get-audio-latency, set-boolean-control,
set-power-state, verify-low-power-microphone, verify-proxy (secure side);
set-DMA-transfer-context (low-power microphone device); and, on the
voice-trigger side, get-language-model-CRC and update-language-model.
[Confirmed present as a typed interface in the M5 and A18 Pro payloads;
absent from the M4 payloads.] Their wire encodings are **[Unknown]**.

### 11.8.2 Which streams are isolated, per machine

| Stream | t8132 | t604x | t8140 | t8142 | t605x |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Built-in microphone array (`hpai`) | normal world | normal world | **isolated** | **isolated** | **isolated** |
| Low-power / voice-trigger buffer (`adpx`) | normal world (`io-buffer-device`) | normal world | **isolated** | **isolated** | **isolated** |
| Voice-trigger device (`vtcm`) | **isolated** | **isolated** | **isolated** | **isolated** | **isolated** |
| Secure low-power loopback (`sllb`) | absent | absent | absent | absent | **isolated** |
| Everything else | normal world | normal world | normal world | normal world | normal world |

[Confirmed].

### 11.8.3 The capture consequence — read this carefully

**The stream that is isolated on the M5 generation and the A18 Pro is the
built-in digital microphone array, not the headset microphone.** The endpoint
is named `audio-hp-mic` (on the M4 generation, `audio-hp`); its identifier is
`hpai`, "high-power audio input"; its data node's `device-uid` and
`device-name` both read `Digital Mic`; and its `input-data-selectors` list the
three internal microphone elements. The headset microphone is a different
endpoint, `audio-codec-input` / `cin `, and it is `iop-audio-ns` — normal
world — on **every** in-scope machine. [Confirmed]

The practical consequences:

1. **On t8132 and t604x (all M4 machines) the microphone array is reachable by
   a normal-world driver.** Its endpoint is `iop-audio-ns`, its buffer device
   is the non-isolated variant, there is no isolated mailbox on the SoC at all,
   and there is no isolated stream proxy node. A Linux microphone driver for
   M4 is a direct continuation of the M1–M3 one.
2. **On t8140, t8142 and t605x the microphone array is not.** The endpoint is
   `iop-audio-s`; its receive channel is on the secure DMA controller
   (`leap-s-adma-rx-0`), whose node carries **no `iommu-parent` at all** — the
   platform does not give a normal-world master a mapper for it; and the
   endpoint's data node carries `isolated-audio-service-input`, a phandle to an
   isolated stream proxy. A normal-world driver cannot program that channel,
   cannot map its buffer, and cannot open the secure service channel. **Capture
   from the built-in microphone array on M5-generation and A18 Pro machines is
   behind the isolation boundary.**
3. **Headset-microphone capture is unaffected on every in-scope machine** —
   normal world, base-domain DMA, four advertised sample rates.
4. **Speaker sense capture is unaffected** — normal world on every machine,
   either as the receive side of the speaker endpoint (t8132, t604x) or as the
   separate `tap ` endpoint on `base-ns-adma-rx-1` (M5 generation, A18 Pro).
5. The `sllb` stream on t605x is isolated *and* development-only; ignore it.

Whether the isolated environment exposes a normal-world-visible copy of the
microphone stream (for example by having the secure side copy decimated frames
into a normal-world buffer) is **[Unknown]** and is the single most important
question for capture support on the M5 generation.

---

## 11.9 Proxy nodes

Four distinct proxy node classes appear, all of them consequences of one agent
owning hardware that another agent must still see. None of them has audio
function of its own.

### 11.9.1 DMA-channel proxy (`admac-ec-proxy`)

Present on t8140, t8142 and t605x. One per isolated stream.

| Property | Meaning | Example (t605x, microphone array) |
|---|---|---|
| `compatible` | `admac-ec-proxy` | |
| `device_type` | `admac-proxy` | |
| `reg` | the **whole** `0x34000` aperture of the secure DMA controller | `0x2_d320_0000` / `0x34000` |
| `use-case` | FourCC of the stream this proxy serves | `hpai` |
| `dma-channel` | the engine number within that controller | 0 |
| `function-iommu_handler` | phandle + tag reading `sdpr`, pointing at the shared-mapper proxy | |
| `exclave-assigned` | empty; marks the node as owned by the isolated environment | |

[Confirmed]. The hardware arrangement: **the DMA engine is real host MMIO, but
the isolated environment owns it.** The controller's aperture is
host-addressable and the proxy node repeats it, but the channel is driven by
the secure side. The matching channel node inside the controller carries
`service-exclave_proxy` naming this proxy.

**What a driver must do:** treat the whole `admac-leap-s` instance as
unavailable. Do not claim its aperture, do not touch its channel registers, and
do not attempt to map buffers for it. Note that its node deliberately carries
**no `iommu-parent`** — the platform is telling you there is no normal-world
mapper for it.

### 11.9.2 Isolated stream proxy (`iisaudio,isolated-stream-proxy`)

Present on t8140, t8142 and t605x. One per isolated stream.

| Property | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `compatible` | `iisaudio,isolated-stream-proxy` |
| `device_type` | `iis-ec-proxy` |
| `identifier` | FourCC of the stream (`hpai`, `sllb`) |
| `physical-descriptions` | the 24-byte buffer/format descriptor decoded in §11.3.2 |
| `release-arbiter-shared-mem` | empty; present on the loopback proxy only |
| `exclave-assigned` | empty |

[Confirmed]. This node is the **normal-world-visible stub of a stream that lives
in the isolated environment**. It publishes the stream's format and buffer
geometry so a normal-world agent can size and describe it, without giving
access to it. The stream endpoint node under the audio controller points at it
by phandle through `isolated-audio-service-input`.

**What a driver must do:** use it as a description of what exists and is not
yours. Do not try to open it.

### 11.9.3 Shared IOMMU-mapper proxy (`audio-shared-dart-proxy`)

Present on t8140, t8142 and t605x. Exactly one per machine.

| Property | Meaning | Example (t605x) |
|---|---|---|
| `iommu-parent` | **two** phandles: the secure base mapper and the secure low-power mapper | (base-s, leap-s) |
| `usecase-dart-map` | array of 8-byte records: (FourCC use case, u32 mapper selector) | `adpx`→0, `hpai`→1, `sllb`→1 |
| `exclave-assigned` | empty | |

[Confirmed]. On t8140 and t8142 the map has two entries (`hpai`→1, `adpx`→0);
on t605x it has three (adding `sllb`→1).

The hardware arrangement: the two secure IOMMU streams (9 = base-s, 11 =
`leap-s`) are shared between several isolated use cases, and something has to
arbitrate which use case gets which mapper. The `usecase-dart-map` is that
arbitration table, expressed as data: selector 0 selects the first
`iommu-parent` (base-s), selector 1 the second (leap-s). [Inferred from the
consistent correspondence between selector value and which complex each stream
belongs to: `adpx` is the base-domain buffer device, `hpai` and `sllb` are
low-power-complex streams.]

The DMA-channel proxies reference this node through `function-iommu_handler`,
i.e. **all isolated audio DMA mappings funnel through this one node.**

**What a driver must do:** nothing, except not claim streams 9 and 11. Note
that the isolated buffer device names this proxy through
`external-named-power-provider`, so it is also the power dependency for the
isolated buffer path.

### 11.9.4 Power-provider indirection

Every M4-generation stream endpoint carries `external-power-provider` (a
phandle to the DMA controller node) and `function-admac_powerswitch` (phandle
plus a 4-byte tag reading `aPSC`). On the M5 generation these are replaced by
the audio controller node's `external-named-power-provider`, a **string**
naming a power provider rather than a phandle. [Confirmed]

The hardware arrangement: the stream's power dependency is on the DMA
controller's clock/power domain, which is itself in the coprocessor's power
tree and therefore not host-controllable. **What a driver must do:** treat the
DMA controller as always-available once the coprocessor is up, and do not
attempt to implement the power switch itself.

---

## 11.10 Watchdog, crash and restart

Section 15 §15.5 lists "coprocessor restart" as the fault class that invalidates the whole
stream configuration. This is what the platform description establishes about it, and what
it does not.

### 11.10.1 What platform firmware states

| Property | Node | Value | Boards |
|---|---|---|---|
| `watchdog-enable` | nub | present (boolean) | **every** in-scope board |
| `coredump-enable` | nub | `0x40` | **every** in-scope board |
| `no-shutdown` | nub | 1 | t8132, t8140, t8142, t605x — **absent on t604x** |
| `claim-wake` | nub | present (boolean) | t8132, t8140, t8142, t605x — **absent on t604x** |
| `power-gates`, `clock-gates`, `clock-ids` | the coprocessor node itself, not the nub | present but **empty** | every in-scope board |

**[Confirmed]** — checked on all twenty in-scope board descriptions. The second coprocessor
instance's nub carries `watchdog-enable`, `no-shutdown` and `claim-wake` on t8140, t8142 and
t605x, but it is not on the audio path (§11.1.1) and its watchdog has no audio consequence.

Read from this:

- **A watchdog exists and is enabled on every machine in scope.** **[Confirmed]** that the
  platform description asks for it; the timeout period, what it is fed by, and whether its
  expiry resets only the coprocessor or something larger are all **[Unknown]**.
- **The host cannot power-cycle the coprocessor.** `power-gates` and `clock-gates` are empty,
  so there is no host gate to toggle. **[Confirmed]** A host-initiated recovery by power is
  not available on any in-scope machine.
- **`coredump-enable = 0x40` means a crash-dump mechanism is configured.** What the value
  `0x40` selects — a size, a region index, a set of flags — is **[Unknown]**. No separate
  crash-dump memory region is described on the nub beyond `region-base` / `region-size`,
  and none is needed: **the dump lands in a host-supplied buffer negotiated at boot on
  endpoint `0x01`** (§11.4.5a), in host DRAM behind the coprocessor's IOMMU, never in the
  firmware window and never in an undescribed region. [Confirmed for the baseline
  generations; **[Probable]** for the in-scope parts.] The dump's own header and section
  format, including the timestamped mailbox message history a crash preserves, is in
  §11.4.5a.
- **The t604x difference is real and is the only per-SoC difference here.** On the six
  t604x boards the nub does not claim wake and is not marked no-shutdown, so on those
  machines the coprocessor's behaviour across system sleep may differ from the rest of the
  scope. What that difference *is* is **[Unknown]**.

### 11.10.2 Initiation, detection and observables

| Question | Status |
|---|---|
| How a host **quiesces, sleeps, idles or re-initialises** the coprocessor | **Established.** By the management-layer power-state messages of §11.2.8 — type `0xb` for the host side, type `6` for the coprocessor side, each waited on for its acknowledgement. This is not a register and not a reset: the coprocessor's own state survives a quiesce, and only the `0x00` (off) state is unrecoverable without a SoC reset. [Confirmed] |
| How a host **requests a restart of a coprocessor that has stopped answering messages** | **[Unknown]**. The power-state path of §11.2.8 needs a live message loop; there is no register write or doorbell that forces a restart, and the host has no power or clock gate to use instead. |
| How a host **learns** that the coprocessor crashed | **Established.** A crash notification arrives on the crash-reporting endpoint `0x01` and a dump is written to the host-supplied buffer negotiated there at boot (§11.4.5a). A host that answers the buffer request at boot is told; one that does not is not. [Confirmed for the baseline generations; **[Probable]** in scope.] |
| Whether a restart is announced **before** it happens | **[Unknown]** |
| What the coprocessor's state is afterwards | **[Unknown]** at register level; at service level Section 15 §15.5 requires re-entry at S5, i.e. the transport, the service, every device attachment and every stream configuration are gone. |

The watchdog period and the scope of its reset remain **[Unknown]** (Open question 16), as
does whether a wedged coprocessor can be restarted at all (Open question 17).

### 11.10.3 What a driver can observe without any of that

Three host-side signals are available and none of them requires the coprocessor's
cooperation. All three are **[Inferred]** as restart indicators — each is established as a
mechanism in its own right, but none is a documented restart notification:

1. **The coprocessor→host FIFO stops.** `I2A_CTRL` at `reg[0] + 0x8114` reports
   FULL/EMPTY (§11.2.2); a service that was producing messages and stops is the
   earliest sign. **[Probable]** that the offsets still hold on the in-scope parts.
2. **`CPU_STATUS`** at `reg[0] + 0x0048` reports core idle/stopped indications
   (§11.2.2). **[Probable]** on the same basis, and **its individual bit positions are
   [Unknown]** — which means a driver cannot test a named bit here. *What it can do
   instead:* sample the whole register periodically while the coprocessor is known
   healthy, keep the value as a per-machine reference, and treat **any change** from
   that reference as a state change worth correlating with signals 1 and 3. That is
   enough to serve its role in the chain below, which is confirmation of a condition
   signals 1 and 3 have already raised, not primary detection. **Never** use
   `CPU_STATUS` alone as a restart trigger, and never write it. Open question 27.
3. **The audio DMA channel starves or overruns.** The coprocessor owns the clocks; when it
   stops, the serialiser stops draining, and the host sees `CHAN_INT_STATUS[i]` bit 1 on
   its own channel (Section 5 §5.2.4). This is the fastest indication on a running stream,
   and it is indistinguishable at that instant from an ordinary underrun.

### 11.10.4 Required response, and why its order is fixed

Because signal 3 above cannot be told apart from an ordinary underrun, and because an
underflowing serialiser's output is **[Unknown]** (Section 3 §3.6.11), the response to a
suspected coprocessor restart begins with the same action as the response to any other
audio fault:

```
assert the shared amplifier shutdown line   (host-owned, Section 6 — do this first)
  → confirm by the queue-status and CPU-status signals above
    → stop and reset the host DMA channels          (Section 4 §4.10.1)
      → re-enter the coprocessor chain at S5          (Section 15 §15.5)
```

The host-side results — board identity, calibration selection, IOMMU mappings — survive and
must not be redone (Section 15 §15.5). The amplifier register files also survive, because
they are reached over host-owned I²C, but the shutdown line asserted in step 1 has taken
their output stages down, so they return through S8 like any other shutdown-line event.

---

## Per-SoC / per-machine differences

**t8132 (M4: j604, j623, j624, j713, j715, j773g).**
Six stream endpoints on notebooks and iMacs, four on the Mac mini. No isolated
audio anything: no isolated mailbox, no isolated DMA controller, no isolated
stream proxy, no shared-mapper proxy, no DMA-channel proxy. The microphone
array is normal-world. No second coprocessor instance. Coprocessor firmware is
a plain executable image. Endpoints bind DMA numerically via `dma-channels`. The
`/arm-io/nco` node is absent entirely. j773g uses a per-board firmware tag.

**t604x (M4 Pro/Max: j614s, j614c, j616s, j616c, j773s, j575c).**
As t8132, with three differences: the coprocessor presents **eight** interrupts
instead of four — two complete mailbox channel sets, **[Inferred]**, of which
the second set's aperture is **[Unknown]** (§11.2.5); it has **no reg[4]
sub-window** and correspondingly **no `ext-irq-reg-index`**, the only in-scope
part without either; and it has **no isolated IOMMU stream ID** at all (the `exclave-sid` property is absent, and there is no
`mapper-exclave-aop`). No isolated stream exists on this SoC. The three desktop boards (j773s, j575c and, on t8132, j773g) have
no microphone path, no low-power endpoints and no voice-trigger controller node.

**t8140 (A18 Pro: j700).** The outlier in almost every respect.
- The speaker path runs through the **low-power** complex
  (`leap-ns-adma-tx-0`), not the base complex — unique in the range.
- The speaker link is **2 channels of 32 bits with MCLK 12 288 000 Hz** and no
  sense return on the speaker endpoint; sense is a separate `tap ` endpoint.
- The jack link declares **MCLK 24 000 000 Hz** with a clock ratio of 125, the
  only in-scope instance where the master-clock-to-frame relation does not
  yield the 48 000 Hz the source descriptor advertises. **[Unknown]**
- The microphone array is **two** channels, not three
  (`/product/audio` channel masks `0x3`).
- `/arm-io/nco` is **present with a `compatible` value and no `reg`** — the
  oscillator exists and is not host-addressable.
- It is the only in-scope part with **two** isolated mailbox instances (one per
  coprocessor) and with `mapper-exclave-aop2` / stream ID 17.
- Its second coprocessor has **no firmware payload** and carries
  `no-firmware-service`.
- Its amplifier family has **no control bus**.

**t8142 (M5: j704, j813, j815).**
Nine endpoints. Isolated microphone array and isolated low-power buffer.
Second coprocessor present with its own payload. Per-display audio DMA
controllers appear. Per-board firmware tags for all three boards. j704 and j815
are six-amplifier machines, j813 is four-amplifier; j813's speaker tap is 4
channels, j704's and j815's 6.

**t605x / t6050 (M5 Pro/Max: j714s, j714c, j716s, j716c).**
Ten endpoints — the t8142 set plus the isolated, development-only secure
loopback. Four per-display DMA controllers plus the main one. Per-SoC firmware
tag. Its coprocessor's second aperture sits at block+`0x50000` inside the
coprocessor block rather than at a separate low address as on t8132/t8140/t8142
— an addressing difference a driver must not paper over.

**Every in-scope machine, without exception:** no host-addressable serial audio
controller; no host-controllable audio power domain; audio DMA aperture
`0x34000`; amplifier and jack codec on host I2C with their full M1–M3 property
set; one audio service and one voice-trigger service on one coprocessor.

Transport facts, per SoC:

| Item | Value | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| Mailbox block offset and register map | Identical on all five in-scope SoCs | [Probable] |
| Mailbox interrupt order in `interrupts` | `(n+1, n, n+3, n+2)`, all five | [Confirmed] |
| Mailbox interrupt count | 4, except **t604x = 8** | [Confirmed] |
| Second mailbox channel set | t604x only | [Inferred] |
| External-interrupt register window `reg[4]` and `ext-irq-reg-index = 4` | Present on t8132, t8140, t8142, t605x; **absent on t604x** | [Confirmed] |
| Boot-argument table at firmware window `+0x22c` / `+0x230` | Present in the t8132 and t604x payloads | [Confirmed] |
| Boot-argument values a host must supply | Not carried by any in-scope board's platform description | [Confirmed absent] |
| 80 numbered shared-memory boot-argument slots | t8140, t8142, t605x only | [Confirmed] |
| Two coprocessor code images per payload | t8140, t8142, t605x only | [Confirmed] |
| Application endpoints above `0x2e` named in the platform description | t8140 (`0x30`, `0x31`, `0x4e`), t8142 and t605x (`0x4d`); none on t8132 or t604x | [Confirmed] |
| Audio service announce name | `aop-audio` on the baseline generations; in-scope value not established | [Probable] |
| Decimator configuration key | `210` on M1/M2; **`212`** on the M3 generation and later, therefore on all five in-scope SoCs | [Probable] |
| Pulse-density front-end bytes per sample | `2` on M1/M2; **`3`** on the M3 generation and later | [Probable] |
