## Open questions

Each entry states what is unknown, why a driver needs it, and what to capture.
The transport itself is now specified end to end (§11.2, §11.4) and the
playback and link-geometry property vocabulary is specified in Section 18; what
remains below is confirmation of the register map on an in-scope die, the
per-part values no published source carries, and confirmation of Section 18's
key numbers on t8132 and t8142. The
recommended capture is: a hypervisor-level trap on the coprocessor's `reg[0]`
aperture, logging every 64-bit access with its offset, value and timestamp,
from reset through a full playback and a full capture session, plus a trap on
the audio DMA controller apertures and on the I2C controllers, timestamped on
the same clock so the three streams can be interleaved.

1. **Mailbox register map on an in-scope part — residual only.** The map is now
   given in full in §11.2.2: offsets, widths, access, bit meanings, message
   format, doorbell, detect-and-clear, and the interrupt assignment of §11.2.5.
   Its confidence is **[Probable]** for the in-scope dies, on the single ground
   that they declare the same block revision (`iop,ascwrap-v6`) as the M3
   generation, for which the map is published. What remains **[Unknown]** is:
   the reset value of every register in §11.2.2; the true FIFO depth, which is
   **[Inferred]** at 16 from field widths only; and whether the M4 aperture
   growth moved anything, which it did not for the mailbox (§11.2.6). *Why it
   matters:* every layer above depends on the map, and a single moved offset
   makes the whole stack silently inoperative. *Capture:* the recommended trap
   above is now a **confirmation** run, not a discovery run — see Open
   questions 26, 27 and 28 for the three specific checks.

2. **What occupies `0x6c000`–`0x88000` in the coprocessor aperture, and what the
   internal register layout of `reg[4]` (`+0x2c000`, length `0x3c008`) is.**
   `reg[4]` is now identified as the **external-interrupt register window**,
   established by an exact correlation with `ext-irq-reg-index = 4` on every
   board
   (14 boards with, 41 without, no exceptions — §11.2.6); its register layout
   is still **[Unknown]**. `0x6c000`–`0x88000` is still entirely **[Unknown]**,
   but it is now known **not** to contain the mailbox block or the CPU-control
   registers, both of which lie below `0xc000`. *Why it matters:* it is a third
   of the aperture and it is new. *Capture:* trap the range; if the host never
   touches it, trap the coprocessor's own accesses via the IOMMU fault path, or
   read it after boot and diff against reset.

3. **The eight interrupts on t604x.** Now **[Inferred]** to be **two complete
   mailbox channel sets**, not four unrelated outputs: the eight are two
   quadruples of the identical `(n+1, n, n+3, n+2)` shape at n = `0x2c6` and
   n = `0x2ca`, and the display coprocessor carries the same doubling on t604x
   and t605x while carrying four on t8132 and on every M1–M3 part (§11.2.5).
   The second block's aperture is **[Unknown]**; `reg[0]+0xc000` is the
   **[Inferred]** candidate. *Why it matters:* the driver consequence is now
   concrete — on t604x, unmask and service both quadruples, or plan to poll, or
   messages delivered on the second set are lost on six machines. *Capture:* as
   Open question 29.

4. **Endpoint numbers — resolved as a mechanism, not as a number.** The
   numbering rules, the management-reserved range `0x00`–`0x1f`, the
   endpoint-map discovery message and the name→(endpoint, channel) resolution
   are all **[Confirmed]** (§11.2.8, §11.4.1, §11.4.4). The audio service's
   endpoint number is *by design* not a constant and must not be hard-coded,
   and the scan window must be the **full advertised map** — which the in-scope
   platform description itself proves by naming application endpoints at
   `0x30`, `0x31`, `0x4d` and `0x4e`, all outside the `0x20`–`0x2e` window the
   baseline generations use. **Residual:** the exact ASCII string the in-scope
   firmware announces for the audio service is **[Unknown]** — see Open
   question 34, which is what is left of this entry. *Capture:* log the low 8
   bits of the second 64-bit word of every message in both directions for a
   whole boot, and the 20-byte name field of every service announcement.

5. **Timeout and retry behaviour.** The three distinct waits are now separated
   (§11.4.5): a 500 ms send-FIFO-full wait polled at 100 µs, and 1 000 ms
   management-layer acknowledgement waits, both host-chosen; and **no timeout
   at all on a framed service call** — the interface imposes none, so a driver
   must impose its own or a wedged audio service hangs every caller.
   **Residual:** how long a legitimate audio call may take on the in-scope
   firmware is **[Unknown]**, so the value a driver picks is unfounded.
   *Why it matters:* too short a timeout breaks a slow but correct start; none
   at all hangs the audio path forever. *Capture:* as Open question 38.

6. **Meaning of call types `0xC3000006` and `0xC3000008`.** Two
   of the five call types in use in scope are unidentified; `0xC3000006` is
   addressed to the service rather than to a device, and `0xC3000008` is used by
   the low-power-microphone and voice-trigger devices. *Why it matters:* one of
   them is very likely the stream start/stop or the latency query a driver
   needs. Separately, the M1–M3 probe and detach call types (`0xC3000001`,
   `0xC3000003`) are not in use in scope — establish
   whether the firmware still accepts them, because probe is the only way to
   ask the coprocessor what format a stream actually runs at rather than
   asserting it. *Capture:* trace the shared-memory request buffer alongside
   the mailbox and read the call-type word and payload for each; correlate
   with the moment audio starts flowing.

7. **Which further property keys exist, and what their payloads are —
   substantially narrowed.** Keys `200`, `202`, `210`, `212` and `301` are
   **[Confirmed]** with complete byte-level payload layouts, and keys `302`,
   `401`, `402`, `508`, `701`, `702`, `703`, `704` and `705` are now specified
   in Section 18 — which also identifies three of the previously unnumbered
   properties: **master-clock enable** is key `703`, **set-audio-configuration**
   is key `701`, and **channel mask** is the slot-mask pair inside the key-`701`
   record. **Residual:** key `203` remains **[Unknown]**, as do the numeric keys
   of audio latency in frames, audio latency, force-enable, microphone-disable
   status, microphone-disable warning status, current power request, callback
   configuration, a configuration-buffer size, descriptors-since-start,
   frames-written, latest capture timestamp, bytes-copied-since-power-up, and
   use-non-secure-DMA-controller; and Section 18's key numbers are
   **[Probable]** rather than [Confirmed] on t8132 and t8142. *Why it matters:*
   what remains are the latency and telemetry knobs, not the knobs for rate,
   format and routing — those are now known. *Capture:* trace the wrapped-call
   bodies in the transmit ring during a latency query and a stop, and read the
   key field at offset `0x2c` of each.

8. **Whether the pulse-density front end must still be attached and configured
   on the in-scope firmware.** The `pdm0` device has no platform node on any
   in-scope board — but it had none on the baseline generations either, where
   it is attached and configured by identifier alone (§11.4.6). Its absence
   from the in-scope platform description is therefore **not** evidence that it
   is gone, which removes the reason this read as a bring-up risk. **Residual:**
   whether the in-scope firmware still requires the attach and the coefficient
   upload is **[Unknown]**. *Why it matters:* if it must still be configured and
   the decimator coefficients must still be supplied, a driver that omits them
   gets silence. *Capture:* trace the attach calls during microphone bring-up on
   an M4 machine and list the device FourCCs attached.

9. **Whether a normal-world path to the built-in microphone array exists on
   t8140/t8142/t605x.** §11.8.3. *Why it matters:* it decides whether built-in
   microphone capture is implementable at all on M5-generation machines.
   *Capture:* on an M5 machine, trace the normal-world DMA controllers during a
   microphone recording. If any normal-world channel carries microphone frames,
   a path exists; if all microphone traffic is on the secure controller, it does
   not. Also check whether the `lpij` injection endpoint can be made to carry
   the array's output.

10. **Whether the serial audio controller registers are reachable from the host
    at their architectural addresses.** The hardware exists (seven clusters
    enumerated as power domains) but has no described aperture. *Why it
    matters:* if it is reachable, a driver could in principle bypass the
    coprocessor for the speaker and headphone paths entirely. *Capture:*
    compute the cluster base from the M1–M3 relative layout against the
    in-scope audio block base and attempt a read under the hypervisor; a fault
    or a read-as-zero answers the question. Do this only with the coprocessor
    running, since the domains are coprocessor-powered. **Narrowed, not closed:**
    the one always-on filter that enumerates address ranges does not list the
    serial audio controller on t8140 or t8142, but its allow/deny polarity is
    **[Unknown]** and t605x publishes no range table — see §11.6.2(c) and
    §11.6.3.

11. **Settled, except for two bytes — the descriptor fields left Unknown.**
    Byte `0x05` is the frame-wide bits-per-slot default, `0x06` the transmit
    data delay in bit clocks, `0x0e` the frame-sync pulse length in bit clocks,
    `0x10`/`0x12` the sample-rate numerator in kHz and its denominator, `0x20`
    the direction mask and `0x21` the receive data delay (§11.7.3, §18 §18.4).
    The guess recorded here — that one of them was the data delay and one the
    frame-sync pulse length — was right on both counts.
    **Residual:** byte `0x07` is **[Unknown]**, and bytes `0x00`–`0x03` have two
    readings that the observed values do not discriminate between (§11.7.3,
    §18 §18.12, §18 open question 16). *Capture:* on an endpoint whose byte
    `0x01` is `0x13`, get property key `701` and compare the returned frame-sync
    edge and polarity bytes against what each reading predicts; they differ.

12. **Settled — the clock model.** The descriptor field at `0x0c` is a count of
    **bit clocks** per frame, not of master-clock periods, and the master clock
    reaches the bit clock through a divider of 1…31 carried at offset `0x1c` of
    the key-`701` record. The two readings coincide only when the divider is 1,
    which it is on every in-scope link except the A18 Pro jack link, where the
    divider is 4: 24 000 000 ÷ 4 = 6 000 000 Hz bit clock and 6 000 000 ÷ 125 =
    **48 000 Hz** exactly, matching the advertised rate. The invariant is
    `master clock = frame bit clocks × frame rate × divider`, checked exactly
    (§18 §18.4.2, §18 §18.4.5). **[Confirmed]** — the coprocessor's own built-in
    record for that link carries divider 4. The A18 Pro jack link was the only
    in-scope link that did not divide out, and the only one with a non-unity
    divider, so its dividing out to exactly the advertised rate is
    strong corroboration of the reading. The same correction settles §2 open
    question 10 and §8 open question 11: a speaker link's frame field of 250
    means 250 bit clocks at 12.000 MHz, and the per-direction data-bit counts are
    not frame lengths. *Retained as a confirmation measurement:* measure the
    master clock and the frame clock on the j700 jack link.

13. **The buffer-allocation field of the M4 `dma-channels` record.** The
    "one millisecond at maximum rate" reading holds for every endpoint except
    the low-power internal loopback. *Why it matters:* it sets the DMA ring
    size a driver must allocate. *Capture:* read back the DMA channel's
    configured ring size after the host driver has set the stream up.

14. **The missing secure base-domain DMA controller.** The IOMMU declares
    stream 9 and a mapper for it on every in-scope SoC, and the power-manager
    declares `AUDIO_BASE_S_A`, but no controller node exists. *Why it matters:*
    an undescribed bus master is a correctness and a security hazard for any
    IOMMU-managing driver. **Narrowed on location:** the instance demonstrably
    exists and its aperture is established at `0x…_1370_0000` (§3 §3.4.3,
    §3 §3.4.5), so a driver now has an address to avoid or fault-trap. Why no
    controller node describes it remains **[Unknown]**. *Capture:* watch for IOMMU
    faults on stream 9, and probe `<die>+0x3900000` and `<die>+0x3700000` for a
    `0x34000`-shaped aperture.

15. **The isolated environment's wire protocol.** The typed secure interface is
    known by function (§11.8.1) but not by encoding, and the isolated mailbox
    register layout is entirely Unknown. *Why it matters:* only to decide
    whether a normal-world driver can ever negotiate with it. *Capture:* trap
    the isolated mailbox aperture on an M5 machine during microphone bring-up.

16. **The coprocessor watchdog: period, and whether expiry resets only the coprocessor
    or a wider domain.** (§11.10.) `watchdog-enable` is present on every in-scope board.
    A crash *is* reported to a host that answered the buffer request on endpoint `0x01`,
    and a dump is produced (§11.4.5a), so the "whether the host is told" half is
    **answered** for a crash. What remains **[Unknown]** is the timeout, what feeds it,
    and the scope of the reset. *Why it matters:* the timeout decides how long an audio
    outage can last before a driver must stop waiting and silence the amplifiers itself —
    a driver needs a number to set its own liveness timeout above. The scope decides
    whether a watchdog expiry invalidates the host's IOMMU mappings and DMA state too, or
    only the coprocessor's.

    *Three probes, in increasing cost, and each answers part of it.*
    (a) **Bound the period from above without provoking anything**: with a stream
    running, measure the longest interval between consecutive coprocessor→host messages
    over an hour of normal operation. The watchdog period must exceed it, and this is
    free.
    (b) **Provoke it by starving the return path**: stop servicing the coprocessor→host
    FIFO — leave the not-empty interrupt masked and do not pop — for progressively longer
    intervals, doubling each time, and watch for a restart (detected by signals 1 and 3 of
    §11.10.3). This is the one deliberate provocation the host *can* perform, because the
    return FIFO is the one coprocessor resource the host alone drains. Whether a full
    return FIFO is what feeds the watchdog is **[Unknown]** and is itself part of what
    this establishes: if no restart occurs at any interval, the watchdog is fed by
    something internal and (b) cannot provoke it.
    (c) **Determine the scope** by, immediately after an induced restart, reading back a
    host IOMMU mapping and a DMA channel's configuration registers and testing whether
    they survived. A wider-domain reset will have cleared them. Do this with the shared
    amplifier shutdown line already asserted (§11.10.4).

    *If (b) never provokes a restart*, the period is not host-measurable and this entry
    reduces to (a)'s bound plus (c) performed on a crash induced some other way. Record
    that outcome rather than leaving the entry open indefinitely.

17. **Is there any host-initiated restart of a coprocessor that has stopped answering
    messages — and if not, say so.** (§11.10.2.) §11.2.8 gives the host a defined,
    register-free way to quiesce, sleep, idle and re-initialise a coprocessor **that is
    still servicing its mailbox**. That path needs a live message loop; the host has no
    power gate, no clock gate and no doorbell for this coprocessor. *Why it matters:* if
    the answer is "none", the only recovery from a wedged audio service is a system
    reboot, and **a driver must state that plainly to userspace rather than retry
    forever**. A negative result here is a deliverable, not a failure.

    **This entry is a bounded search over three named candidates, not an open-ended one.**
    Test each in order on a coprocessor deliberately wedged by loading a payload with a
    corrupted segment:
    (a) **`CPU_CTRL` bit 4 at `reg[0] + 0x44`** — the run bit used at release (§11.2.7).
    Determine whether it is writable while the coprocessor is running, and whether
    clearing and re-setting it re-enters the reset vector or has no effect. This is the
    single most likely mechanism and the cheapest to test.
    (b) **The coprocessor's power-manager domain**, if one is exposed on the machine under
    test — read its control register and determine whether a host-initiated power-state
    change is accepted. On the SoCs where no coprocessor power-domain address is published
    this candidate is closed by inspection.
    (c) **A management-endpoint message that precedes a restart**, observed by watching
    endpoint `0x00` traffic during a restart induced by the watchdog (entry 16 probe (b)).
    If one exists, the host can send it; if the restart is preceded by no host-visible
    message at all, it does not.

    **If all three are negative, close this entry as a negative result** — "there is no
    host-initiated restart; recovery from a wedged coprocessor requires a system reset" —
    and record it in §11.10.2 and in §15 §15.5 as such. *Dependency:* candidate (c)
    depends on entry 16 probe (b); (a) and (b) do not and can be done first.

18. **What `coredump-enable = 0x40` configures.** (§11.10.1.) Where a dump lands is
    now established — a host-supplied buffer negotiated at boot on endpoint `0x01`, in
    host DRAM behind the coprocessor's IOMMU, with the header and section format of
    §11.4.5a — so the memory-corruption hazard this entry used to raise does not arise
    provided the host answers the buffer request. **Residual:** the value `0x40`'s own
    fields are **[Unknown]**. *Why it matters:* it may select a size or a set of flags
    that changes how much of a dump survives. *Capture:* compare the negotiated buffer's
    contents after an induced restart against the declared dump size, and watch for IOMMU
    faults from the coprocessor's stream during one.

19. **Why t604x alone omits `no-shutdown` and `claim-wake`.** (§11.10.1.) The six t604x
    boards are the only ones in scope without them. §11.2.8 now supplies the transition
    set those two properties presumably select between, which makes the difference
    testable rather than merely observed. *Why it matters:* it may mean the
    coprocessor is shut down across system sleep on those machines and not on the others,
    which changes what survives a suspend/resume cycle for audio. *Capture:* on a t604x
    machine and a t8132 machine, compare `I2A_CTRL` and `CPU_STATUS` immediately after
    resume, and check whether the audio service must be re-opened.

20. **What do the always-on register-path filter's three global configuration words
    configure, and where are its registers?** (§11.6.3.) No aperture is published for
    the block, the field meanings of `pio-src-filt-global` are **[Unknown]**, and
    whether zero in the two destination-side words means "no target-side register
    filtering configured" or something else is **[Unknown]**. *Why it matters:* this is
    the block most likely to be the actual gate on host register access into the audio
    island, and its source-side word is the only always-on access-control value that
    changes across the M4 → M5 boundary; its polarity decides §11.6.2(c). It is also the
    cheapest probe in the area. *Capture:* locate the block by scanning the always-on
    peripheral pages around always-on island base + `0x82_8000` for registers reading
    `0x2` (t8140, t8142) or `0xA` (t605x) alongside two reading `0x0`, then correlate
    against the published words; then attempt a host register read into the always-on
    island with each word as found and, if it is writable, with it cleared.

21. **Why is the register-path filter absent on t604x?** (§11.6.3.) Every other in-scope
    SoC describes it; the always-on filter **power domain** exists on t604x as on every
    generation from M1, so absence of the node is not absence of the block.
    *Why it matters:* if the hardware really is absent there, t604x is the one in-scope
    part with no register-path filter at all and therefore the natural first target for a
    direct serial-audio-controller read (§3 Open question 17 already proposes that read
    on t604x). *Capture:* compare the always-on power-domain trees across the SoCs, then
    attempt the direct read on a t604x machine with a stream running and compare the
    outcome against the same read on t8132.

22. **Does an undescribed protection range cover the coprocessor firmware-load window on
    t605x?** (§11.5.3, §11.6.3.) No published table on any in-scope board covers any load
    window — **[Confirmed]** — but t605x carries the fabric filter enabled and locked
    with no range table published, so an undescribed range there cannot be excluded and
    is **[Unknown]**. *Why it matters:* it is the one remaining way the documented
    bring-up of §11.5.3 could fail, and it would fail at the very first step.
    *Capture:* on an M5 Pro/Max machine, write and read back one word of the load window
    from the normal world before the coprocessor is released.

23. **What is the always-on sensor-control module, and what do the crossbar's
    module-side selectors (7, 14, `0x18`, `0x34`) address?** (§11.6.3.) It is a
    DMA-capable master on the same IOMMU as the audio path, with a reserved stream and
    its own power domain on every generation since M1, and it has never been described.
    *Why it matters:* only to bound it — to be able to state positively that it is not an
    audio path rather than merely that no audio node references it, and to be sure an
    IOMMU-managing driver need not arbitrate with it. *Capture:* watch for IOMMU faults
    on stream 3 while exercising audio; toggle the two main-GPIO pins named by
    `gpio-to-scm-muxsel` and observe what changes.

24. **What is the middle, always-zero word of each crossbar routing record, and is word 0
    of `gpio-to-scm-muxsel` a pin number or a register offset?** (§11.6.3.) The middle
    word is zero in all eight records on all seven boards that carry routes, and the two
    readings of word 0 are not distinguished by any board; both are
    **[Unknown]**. *Why it matters:* only to complete the bounding in Open question 24 —
    a pin-number reading is what supports the statement that no audio pin is involved.
    *Capture:* as Open question 24.

25. **Why does t8142's declared firmware region exceed the aperture the same node
    describes, and which figure bounds the real memory?** (§11.1.2.) On t8142
    `region-size` is `0x2f0000` while `reg[2]` is `0x1e0000` — the declared region is
    `0x110000` **larger** than the aperture, and t8142 is the only SoC in scope where
    that is so (t8132 and t8140 declare less than their aperture; t604x and t605x
    declare exactly it). Which of the two bounds the memory that actually responds is
    **[Unknown]**, as is whether the excess is a second, separately-addressed block or
    the same block with a larger aperture than `reg[2]` admits. *Why it matters:* a
    driver that maps only `reg[2]` on t8142 is `0x110000` short of the region the
    platform description declares, and a firmware payload larger than `0x1e0000` would
    be truncated at the map boundary with no diagnostic; conversely a driver that maps
    the full `region-size` may be mapping addresses that do not respond. *Capture:*
    map the full `0x2f0000` from `region-base` on an M5 machine and walk it in
    `0x4000` steps, recording where reads begin to fault or alias; compare the
    boundary against `reg[2]`'s end, and check the declared size of the largest
    coprocessor payload shipped for that SoC against both figures. **Narrowed from the
    payload side:** on t8132 the per-SoC payload does not fit within `region-size` and
    does fit within `reg[2]`, so `reg[2]` bounds the real memory there (§11.1.2).
    **[Inferred]** That does not settle t8142, where `region-size` is the larger figure.

26. **Do the mailbox register offsets hold on an M4-, A18-Pro- or M5-class die?**
    The map of §11.2.2 is **[Probable]**, resting on the shared block revision
    string `iop,ascwrap-v6` with the M3 generation. *Why it matters:* every layer
    above it depends on it, and a single moved offset makes the whole stack
    silently inoperative. *Capture:* after setting the run bit, trap the aperture
    and confirm that the first host write pair lands at `+0x8800`/`+0x8808`, that
    the first host read pair lands at `+0x8830`/`+0x8838`, and that the 32-bit
    polls between them hit `+0x8110` and `+0x8114`. One boot answers it. This is a
    five-minute confirmation, not a discovery exercise.

27. **Reset values of the mailbox status and CPU-control registers.** **[Unknown]**
    for every register in §11.2.2. *Why it matters:* a driver that attaches to an
    already-running coprocessor must distinguish "FIFO empty" from "block not
    clocked", and the run bit must be set read-modify-write because the rest of
    `CPU_CTRL` is unknown. *Capture:* read all four status registers before and
    after the run-bit write on a cold boot.

28. **FIFO depth in each direction.** The occupancy and index fields bound it at
    16 entries inbound; the outbound occupancy field is a bit wider.
    **[Inferred]** *Why it matters:* it sets how many messages a driver may post
    before it must wait, and therefore whether the 500 ms send wait is ever
    reached in normal operation. *Capture:* post messages to a started endpoint
    that does not drain them and count how many are accepted before `A2I_CTRL`
    bit 16 sets.

29. **Where is t604x's second mailbox channel set, and does the audio service use
    it?** **[Inferred]** to exist (§11.2.5); its aperture is **[Unknown]**.
    *Why it matters:* a driver that services only one set will lose every message
    delivered on the other, on six machines. Section 5 §5.6.2 reads the second
    quadruple as a *secure* mailbox instead, which on the other in-scope SoCs is a
    separately addressed `0x4000` aperture — so the two candidate locations are at
    opposite ends of the address space and a probe must try both. *Capture:*
    unmask all eight inputs, drive one known exchange, and record which fire; then
    probe `reg[0]+0xc000` for a second copy of the four status/FIFO registers, and
    if it is absent, scan for a standalone `0x4000` aperture of the shape
    §11.2.9 describes.

30. **What protocol version does the in-scope firmware advertise, and is it within
    11–12?** **[Unknown]**. *Why it matters:* a version above the established
    supported range may change management message layouts, and the handshake of
    §11.2.8 aborts rather than degrading. *Capture:* log the first management
    message after the run-bit write and read bits 31:0 of its payload word.

31. **What values must the four host-supplied boot arguments take on the in-scope
    parts?** `EC0p`, `nCal`, `alig` and `AOPt` are present in the in-scope
    payloads with fixed lengths (§11.5.4), but **no in-scope board's platform
    description supplies any of them**, and the established per-SoC values cover
    only M1 and M2. **[Unknown]**. *Why it matters:* the alignment argument in
    particular governs how the coprocessor lays out the shared buffers a driver
    must then parse, and a wrong value will produce a coprocessor that boots and
    then mis-parses every ring. *Capture:* read the four values back out of the
    firmware window immediately after a known-good boot, before the run bit is
    set again.

32. **What are the 80 numbered shared-memory boot-argument slots on the M5
    generation and A18 Pro for, and must a host fill them?** They are absent on
    every earlier generation (§11.5.4). **[Unknown]**. *Why it matters:* if the
    audio service's buffers are declared there rather than negotiated on an
    endpoint, the whole of §11.4.2 is bypassed on those parts. *Capture:* read
    the slots back after a known-good boot and check whether any holds an address
    inside a region the host allocated.

33. **Which of the two coprocessor code images in an M5-generation or A18-Pro
    payload is loaded where, and by whom?** **[Confirmed]** that there are two;
    everything else is **[Unknown]** (§11.5.4). *Why it matters:* the load step of
    §11.5.3 assumes one image and one window. *Capture:* compare the firmware
    window's contents after boot against both images.

34. **What ASCII string does the in-scope audio service announce?** The nub child
    still carries `device_type = "aop-audio"`, but the audio controller node
    carries a different, longer service-name string and the voice-trigger child
    demonstrates that an override mechanism exists (§11.4.4). **[Unknown]**.
    *Why it matters:* a driver that matches exactly on the wrong one will start
    every endpoint, receive the announcement, and silently ignore it.
    *Capture:* log the 20-byte name field of every service announcement for a
    whole boot.

35. **What are the audio service's unsolicited report payloads?** Category `0x00`,
    subtype `0xc4` is **[Confirmed]** as the path; the audio payload layout is
    **[Unknown]** (§11.4.5). *Why it matters:* jack detection, headset type,
    thermal throttling of the speaker path and stream-underrun notification are
    all candidates, and a driver that cannot parse them cannot react to any of
    them. *Capture:* log every report on the audio service's channel while
    inserting and removing a headset and while provoking an underrun.

36. **Answered — the property vocabulary for a playback stream.** Section 18
    specifies it: property keys `401` and `402` (the two upper state codes the
    endpoint reports), `508` (routing request), **`701` (the 109-byte record
    carrying slot masks, slot and sample widths, frame geometry and clocking)**,
    `702` (reset), `703` (master-clock enable) and `704`/`705` (capability
    probes), with the ordered start sequence in §18 §18.6.1 and §18 §18.10.
    There is **no separate sample-rate property**; the rate is implied by the
    frame geometry and the divider. **The stream start is the key-`202`
    transition to the code reported by key `402`**, carrying a direction mask —
    there is no distinct start call. **Residual, and it is what keeps this entry
    open:** the key numbers are **[Confirmed]** on t604x, t8140 and t605x but
    only **[Probable]** on t8132 and t8142; the pairing of record bytes
    `0x37`/`0x38` to bit order and clock edge is **[Probable]** (§18 open
    question 4); and call types `0xC3000006` and `0xC3000008` are still
    **[Unknown]** (Open question 6). *Capture:* trace the wrapped-call bodies in
    the transmit ring during a speaker stream start on a t8132 machine and read
    the property key at body offset `0x2c` of each — confirming the numbers on
    those two SoCs closes this entry.

37. **How does a 2 400 000 Hz bit clock and a three-stage decimation reach a
    48 000 Hz capture rate?** The ratio triples of keys `210` and `212` both
    multiply to 150, not the 50 the rates require, although the first two stages
    of the high-rate triple are `10 × 5 = 50` (§11.4.6). **[Unknown]**.
    *Why it matters:* a driver that changes the capture rate must know which field
    to change. *Capture:* measure the pulse-density clock on a machine with the
    microphone array running, and re-read the front-end configuration the host
    actually sent.

38. **Does the coprocessor impose any limit on outstanding framed calls, and what
    is the longest legitimate service-call latency?** The host-side limit of 8 is
    not negotiated; the coprocessor's limit is **[Unknown]**, as is the timeout a
    driver should apply (§11.4.5). *Why it matters:* too short a timeout breaks a
    slow but correct start; no timeout hangs the audio path forever. *Capture:*
    issue 9 or more concurrent property reads and observe whether any is dropped;
    separately, time the slowest call across a full start/stop cycle on each
    in-scope machine class.

39. **Are the M4-generation payload's boot-argument table offset and record format
    the same on the M5 generation and A18 Pro?** The table exists in the M5 and
    A18 Pro payloads with the same key vocabulary, but those payloads are
    containers and the table's offset within the *loaded* window is **[Unknown]**
    (§11.5.4). *Why it matters:* the patch step of §11.5.4 needs the offset.
    *Capture:* read the two words at `+0x22c` and `+0x230` of the firmware window
    on an M5 machine after the payload is loaded and before the run bit is set.

40. **What is the board-independent `0x0f` at descriptor byte `0x04` on the
    base-domain loopback endpoint?** Every other endpoint's `0x04` equals the
    channel count of its wider direction; the base-domain loopback carries `15`
    on every board of every generation while both its directions carry 2
    channels and both masks are `0x3` (§11.7.3). **[Unknown]**. *Why it matters:*
    a driver that validates slot masks against `0x04` — which is what the field
    is for on every other endpoint — will reject or mis-size the loopback
    endpoint. *Capture:* attach the base-domain loopback endpoint, read property
    key `701` back, and compare the slot-count field of the returned record
    against both `2` and `15`; then start the loopback with a 2-slot frame and
    confirm it runs.

41. **May the speaker, codec-output and codec-input endpoints be attached and
    running simultaneously, and what happens when two endpoints name overlapping
    cluster objects?** §11.7.7 states what is established and what is not.
    **[Unknown]** for the arbitration rule. *Why it matters:* playing to speakers
    and to a headset, or starting jack playback while speakers run, is the
    ordinary case, and the failure mode of a refused or silently retargeted
    second attach is not recoverable without a full teardown. *Capture:* attach
    `spkr` and start it; then attach `cout` and start it, and read property key
    `705` on the speaker endpoint before and after. Repeat with `cin ` added, and
    repeat with two endpoints deliberately configured onto the same clock
    generator, recording which call fails and with what status.

42. **Is the 8-outstanding-call window per endpoint, per service channel, or per
    coprocessor?** The host-side limit is a host choice (§11.4.5); which scope the
    coprocessor's own limit has is **[Unknown]**. *Why it matters:* it decides
    whether two open streams may each issue calls freely or must share one credit
    pool. *Capture:* with two endpoints attached, issue 8 concurrent property
    reads on each simultaneously and observe whether the second endpoint's calls
    are delayed, dropped or completed.
