Capture bring-up follows the same shape with S8 and S10 reduced to the jack
codec alone, or omitted entirely for the built-in microphone array, which has no
discrete part on the control bus.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 15.2 States

Each state is given as a precondition, the hardware actions that effect the
transition, and the observable signal that the state has been reached. Nothing
here prescribes how a driver should be structured.

### S0 — Cold

**Precondition.** None. No assumption may be made about audio state at entry.
This is not a theoretical caution: every board in scope carries a boot-time
audio volume setting in its platform description, which means boot firmware
plays audio through the speakers before the operating system is reached. At
handoff the shared shutdown line may already be released, the amplifiers already
configured, and the clocks already running (Section 14).

**Hardware actions.** Assert the shared amplifier shutdown line. This is the
only action that is safe without knowing prior state, and it is safe precisely
because it silences every amplifier on every bus at once.

**Exit signal.** None available. This is an unobservable state by construction.

> **Ordering reason.** The shutdown line is shared across all amplifiers on both
> control buses (Section 6). Asserting it first guarantees a known-quiet
> starting point before any register is touched. The cost is that all amplifier
> register state is subsequently indeterminate and must be written fresh — see
> S8.

### S1 — Control bus ready

**Precondition.** S0.

**Hardware actions.** Bring up the host I2C controller instances that carry
audio parts, and the GPIO controller instances that carry the audio lines.
Enable any supply or power-enable line the machine associates with the audio
parts, and observe its settling time. Deassert each part's reset line where one
exists distinct from the shared shutdown line.

**Exit signal.** The I2C controllers accept transactions and report no bus
fault.

> **Ordering reason.** The codecs and amplifiers do not answer on the control
> bus until their supplies are up and reset is deasserted. This state is
> independent of the audio complex: the I2C and GPIO blocks are in host power
> domains and are unaffected by the coprocessor's ownership of the audio
> domains. That independence is what makes the two-chain structure possible.

### S2 — Parts identified

**Precondition.** S1.

**Hardware actions.** Address each amplifier and the jack codec and read its
identification and revision registers. On the machine whose amplifier family has
no control bus, this step covers the jack codec only and the amplifier
population must be taken from the platform description.

**Exit signal.** Each expected part acknowledges its address and returns an
identification value consistent with the part the platform description names.

> **Ordering reason.** Identification must precede configuration because the
> register map, the gain field position and the temperature scaling all differ
> between the counterpart parts (Section 7). Programming a gain field at the
> wrong bit position is a half-gain or double-gain error.

### S3 — Machine identified

**Precondition.** S2.

**Two separate identities are involved here, and they come from different places.**

1. **The board code** — which machine this is — is read from the root-node identity
   properties of the firmware-supplied hardware description (`target-type`,
   `target-sub-type`, `compatible`, `model`; Section 1 §1.2.1). It is available from
   S0 onward, needs no bus and no power domain, and is what selects the per-machine
   tables of Sections 1, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 16 — including the amplifier count, the I²C
   addresses, the slot map and the amplifier output level. A driver should read it
   before S1, since S1 and S2 already need to know which buses and which parts to
   expect.
2. **The speaker-module variant within that board** is read from the
   speaker-identification strap lines (Section 1 §1.10), which is what this state
   waits on.

**Hardware actions.** Read the speaker-identification strap lines where the
machine provides them. Select the protection limits and calibration constants
for this board code and this speaker identity.

**Exit signal.** A valid identity value is read, or the machine is one that
provides no straps and the identity is implicit. The board code is by then already
known and is not an exit condition of this state.

> **Ordering reason.** The straps select among speaker module variants with
> different electromechanical parameters (Sections 1 and 9). Choosing protection
> limits before reading them risks applying the wrong excursion and thermal
> limits. On machines that carry no straps the identity is fixed by the board,
> and a driver must not fall back to a default set of limits on a machine where
> straps were expected but unreadable — that is a fault condition, not a
> default.

### S4 — Transport mapped

**Precondition.** S1. Independent of S2 and S3.

**Hardware actions.** Establish IOMMU mappings for the audio DMA controller
instances that this machine's streams use, and allocate the DMA buffers.

**Exit signal.** Mappings are installed and the IOMMU reports no fault.

> **Ordering reason.** Mappings must exist before any descriptor referencing
> them is submitted. This state has no dependency on the coprocessor or on the
> discrete parts and may be reached at any point after S1.

### S5 — Coprocessor running

**Precondition.** S0. Independent of S1–S4.

**Hardware actions.** Load the coprocessor firmware payload for this board into
its firmware memory window, **patch the boot-argument table** (Section 11 §11.5.4),
and release the core. Complete the transport-level handshake.

**Exit signal.** The transport reports the coprocessor alive.

> ☠ **The boot-argument patch is part of this state, not an optional refinement,
> and one of its four values fails silently.** A wrong `alig` — the shared-buffer
> alignment — produces a coprocessor that reaches this state's exit signal
> normally, because the management handshake runs over the mailbox and not over
> the rings, and then mis-parses every ring from S6 onwards with no error
> anywhere. **Exiting S5 successfully is not evidence that the boot arguments
> were right.** Section 11 §11.5.4 states the failure mode and the validation
> check; the correct in-scope values are **[Unknown]** (§11 open question 31) and
> §17 places that entry first in phase 1 for this reason. Do not interpret a
> failure at S6 or S7 as a transport defect until the alignment has been varied.

> **Ordering reason.** The host has no power gate or clock gate for this
> coprocessor and therefore cannot power-cycle it (Section 11). If it is already
> running when the driver attaches, the driver joins an existing instance rather
> than starting one. The container format of the payload differs between the M4
> generation and the A18 Pro and M5 generations (Section 11.5.2).
>
> **There is no register-level readiness bit, and none is needed.** Readiness is
> the completion of the management handshake itself: the version exchange, every
> endpoint-map fragment acknowledged, the coprocessor power-state
> acknowledgement received, and the host power state set to `on` and
> acknowledged (Section 11 §11.2.8). The core is released by setting bit 4 of
> the CPU-control register at `reg[0] + 0x44` (§11.2.7); the interval from that
> write to the first management message is bounded but **[Unknown]**, so the
> wait on the first message needs a driver-chosen timeout.
>
> The mailbox register map this rests on is **[Probable]** for the in-scope
> dies, not Confirmed: it is the published map for the block revision they
> declare, and it has not been read on an M4-, A18-Pro- or M5-class part
> (Section 11 §11.2.2, Open questions 1 and 26). Everything above the register
> map is **[Confirmed]**.

### S6 — Audio service open

**Precondition.** S5.

**Hardware actions.** Three sub-steps, in order (Section 11 §11.4.7 steps 3–5):

1. **Start every advertised endpoint and bring its ring up.** For each endpoint
   the coprocessor named in its endpoint map — the **whole** advertised range,
   including the management-reserved numbers `0x00`–`0x1f` — send the
   management start message (type `5`), then run the shared-memory ring
   bring-up of §11.4.2 to completion: initialise, acknowledge, answer the
   buffer request with a coherent buffer mapped through the coprocessor's IOMMU
   mapper on stream 0, accept both ring descriptors, send start and wait for
   the start acknowledgement.
2. **Collect the service announcements.** Each started endpoint emits one
   report per service it hosts (category `0x00`, subtype `0xc0`), carrying a
   20-byte ASCII service name and a 32-bit channel number. Match the audio
   service by name and record the pair **(endpoint number, channel number)** —
   that pair is the service reference and it has no further structure
   (§11.4.4).
3. **Attach the device identifiers** for the streams this machine provides, one
   `0xC3000002` wrapped call each, on that (endpoint, channel) (§11.4.6).

**Exit signal.** A reply (category `0x20`, subtype `0x84` or `0xa0`) whose
leading 32-bit status word is `0`, for each attach call, correlated to its
request by the 16-bit tag at offset `0x18` of the call header.

> **Ordering reason — endpoints before services.** The coprocessor **does not
> finish its own boot** until every advertised system endpoint has been started,
> so a driver cannot skip the management-range endpoints even if it discards
> their output. And endpoint numbers are not constants: `0x20` is the first
> application endpoint, but the in-scope platform description itself names
> application endpoints at `0x30`, `0x31`, `0x4d` and `0x4e`, outside the
> `0x20`–`0x2e` window the baseline generations use. A driver must scan the
> full advertised map, never a fixed window (§11.4.1).
>
> **Ordering reason — announcements before lookup.** There is **no service
> registry and no lookup request**. Services announce themselves asynchronously
> after their endpoint starts; the announcement *is* the registration. A driver
> therefore cannot ask for a service by name — it must start every advertised
> application endpoint and then wait (§11.4.4).
>
> **Ordering reason — attach before configure.** No property call for a device
> is valid before that device has been attached (§11.4.7).
>
> **Named limitation — the announce string.** The service child in the platform
> description still carries `device_type = "aop-audio"`, but the audio
> controller node carries a different, longer service-name string, and the
> voice-trigger service demonstrates that an override mechanism exists. Which
> of the two the in-scope firmware actually announces is **[Unknown]**
> (Section 11 Open question 34). A driver must match on either string, or on a
> prefix, and must **not** fail closed on a single exact match — the failure
> mode is silent: every endpoint starts, the announcement arrives, and it is
> ignored.
>
> **Named limitation — call timeouts.** Nothing in the interface bounds how long
> a framed call may take; the only established waits are host-chosen (500 ms on
> a full send FIFO, 1 000 ms on a management acknowledgement). A driver must
> impose its own reply timeout or a wedged service hangs every caller, and the
> correct value for the in-scope parts is **[Unknown]** (Section 11 Open
> questions 5 and 38).

### S7 — Stream configured

**Precondition.** S6, and S3 if the stream is a speaker stream whose slot
geometry depends on the amplifier population.

**Hardware actions.** A sequence of set-property wrapped calls on the audio
service's (endpoint, channel), each a `0xC3000005` call carrying a device
identifier at body offset `0x28`, a property key at `0x2c` and a payload from
`0x34` (Section 11 §11.4.6), followed by the first of the two device power
transitions.

Two sequences exist, one per stream class, and a machine uses both.

For a **serial-audio stream** — speaker, jack output, jack input, loopback or
tap — the sequence is given in **§18 §18.6.1**, and its property calls are:

| Step | Call |
|---|---|
| 1 | Get keys `401` and `402` on the endpoint — the two upper state codes **this endpoint** uses. Do not assume `pw1 `/`pwrd`. Get keys `704` and `705` — routing-validation and immutability capabilities. |
| 2 | Get key `701` — the current 109-byte record, which is the only way to learn which cluster objects and pad routing the endpoint is bound to. |
| 3 | Set key `702` (u32 `1`) — reset the stream's serialisers and FIFOs. |
| 4 | Set key `508` (u32 `0xFFFFFFFF`) on a non-secure endpoint; failure is tolerated. |
| 5 | Set key `701` — the merged record: master-clock frequency and source, divider, the two frame-sync phase counts, per-direction slot mask, slot width, sample width, data delay, bit order and clock edge. The merge rule is §18 §18.3.3; the validity rules are §18 §18.3.5. |
| 6 | Set key `703` — master-clock enable — **only if** step 2 showed a master clock and a non-zero master-clock routing mask. On most in-scope endpoints the master clock is not routed to a pad and this key is absent. |
| 7 | Set key `202` with target = the code from key `401` and **direction mask `0`**. |

There is **no sample-rate property**: the rate is `master clock ÷ (divider ×
(phase 0 + phase 1))` and is expressed entirely through the fields of key `701`
(§18 §18.4.3). Step 5 must precede step 6 — the coprocessor rejects an enable
before a configure (§18 §18.10).

For the **capture** path through the pulse-density front end this sequence is
established in full (§11.4.7 steps 6–9):

| Step | Call |
|---|---|
| 1 | Set key `301` on the low-power input device — channels enabled, channels supported, voice-trigger channel index. 16-byte payload; the values are per machine and follow the microphone count (two on j700, three elsewhere). |
| 2 | Set key `200` on the pulse-density front end — the 632-byte front-end configuration: bytes per sample, clock source, bit clock, controller/slow/fast clocks, channel polarity and phase, microphone turn-on and settle times. On parts using the high-rate decimator the embedded decimator block at payload offset `0x022` is left zero. |
| 3 | Set key `212` on the pulse-density front end — the 8 200-byte high-rate decimator configuration (three decimation ratios, packed per-stage tap counts, 386 populated 64-bit coefficients). Key `212` is the one used on the M3 generation and later, therefore on **all five in-scope SoCs**; key `210` is its M1/M2 predecessor. |
| 4 | Set key `202` on the stream's device with target power state `pw1 ` and flag `0`. |

The key-`202` call is the step that reaches the hardware: on it the coprocessor
raises the audio power domains, configures the serial audio controller cluster
and its serialisers, and starts the bit and frame clocks.

**Exit signal.** A reply whose leading 32-bit status word is `0` to the key-`202`
call, with the device at `pw1 `. **The clocks are now running** — this is the
observable that gates S10.

The second power transition — key `202` with target `pwrd` and flag `1`, which
is what actually starts data moving — is **not** part of S7. It is issued after
the DMA channel is armed; see S9 and ordering constraint 9a.

> **Ordering reason.** This is the single step the host cannot perform or
> bypass. Every audio power domain on every SoC in scope is marked as having no
> host-drivable power control, so there is no sequence of host register writes
> that reaches the same state.
>
> The geometry chosen here is what the discrete parts must be programmed to
> match, which is why S8 cannot precede it.
>
> **Ordering reason — configure before power.** The channel configuration and
> the front-end and decimator configuration must all precede the first key-`202`
> transition. The coprocessor applies them when it raises the domains and starts
> the clocks; a property written after that transition is written to a block
> that is already generating clocks.
>
> **The playback property vocabulary is no longer the limitation it was.**
> Everything above this state is shared between capture and playback and is
> **[Confirmed]**: the mailbox, the endpoint transport, the ring protocol, the
> framed call header, service resolution, the attach step, correlation by tag,
> and the power ladder itself. The property **keys** that set a playback
> stream's slot geometry, frame geometry and clocking are now specified —
> key `701` and key `703`, with keys `401`, `402`, `508`, `702`, `704` and `705`
> around them (Section 18 §18.2, §18.3, §18.6.1). Three residuals are named and
> are all narrower than the original gap:
>
> * the key **numbers** are **[Confirmed]** on t604x, t8140 and t605x and
>   **[Probable]** on t8132 and t8142, where the same keys are present but are
>   corroborated at one end of the interface only (Section 11 Open question 36);
> * the pairing of record bytes `0x37`/`0x38` and `0x54`/`0x55` to **bit order**
>   and **bit-clock edge** is **[Probable]**, and reversing them produces noise
>   rather than silence (Section 18 Open question 4);
> * the meaning of call types `0xC3000006` and `0xC3000008` is still
>   **[Unknown]** (Section 11 Open question 6). Neither is needed to start a
>   stream: **the start is the key-`202` transition to the code reported by key
>   `402`**, carrying a direction mask, and no distinct start call exists on
>   either path. [Confirmed]
>
> The rate remains pinned to 48 kHz by the platform description on every machine
> in scope (§15.6), and the slot geometry is declared per endpoint in Section 11
> §11.7; a driver can now **assert** both rather than accept whatever the
> coprocessor has.

### S8 — Parts matched (rendezvous)

**Precondition.** S3, S7.

**Hardware actions.** Program each amplifier and the jack codec: the slot
assignment for the sense return direction and the receive slot for the playback
direction — both taken from that amplifier's own `speaker-config` record, whose
**structure is [Confirmed]** but whose **record-to-transducer binding is
[Probable] on the MacBook Pro 14/16-inch chassis** and [Confirmed] elsewhere;
on that chassis the binding must be confirmed by reading `TDM_CFG3` (and
`TDM_CFG5`/`TDM_CFG6`) back after the coprocessor has configured the link, and
☠ **no speaker may be driven until it has been** (§8 §8.2.3) — the data format and
word width, the sample-rate-dependent configuration, the analogue
output level for this machine, the DC-blocker and filter configuration, the
brownout and limiter configuration, the sense-path enables and the transmit-pin
drive configuration. Load the per-speaker protection limits. Leave every
amplifier muted and still in shutdown.

**Exit signal.** Register read-back matches what was written, and no fault
status bit is set.

> **Ordering reason.** The slot assignment programmed into an amplifier must
> match the geometry the coprocessor configured in S7, or the amplifier will
> sample the wrong slot. Because S0 asserted the shared shutdown line and
> because that line is shared, this programming must be complete for **every**
> amplifier before any of them is released — a partial configuration followed by
> a shared release enables an unconfigured amplifier.
>
> Protection limits are loaded here rather than later because between S10 and
> the first valid sense data there is a window in which host-side modelling has
> nothing to work with, and only the amplifier's own autonomous protections
> apply. That window is narrower in coverage than it appears: the per-machine
> configuration supplied by platform firmware leaves **thermal foldback
> disabled** on every machine in scope (Section 8), so the amplifier does *not*
> autonomously reduce gain as its die heats. The supply-tracking **limiter is
> disabled too** — no platform-supplied configuration writes registers 0x0B, 0x1B
> or 0x1C, and
> `LIM_CFG0` resets with `LIM_EN` = 0; **[Probable]**, from the counterpart
> datasheet's reset value and not yet read back, so assume no limiter until
> `LIM_CFG0` has been read from a live part (§7 §7.7, §9 §9.8.1). Overcurrent,
> brownout prevention and the hard over-temperature shutdown remain active;
> thermal protection of the voice coil does not exist in hardware and is
> entirely the host's responsibility.

### S9 — DMA armed

**Precondition.** S4, S7.

**Hardware actions.** Program the DMA channel bound to this stream: the bus
attribute fields, the FIFO configuration, the descriptor submission, and the
interrupt mask for the host's interrupt destination. Start the channel. Then,
and only then, issue the second device power transition — set-property key
`202` on the stream's device with target `pwrd` and flag `1` (Section 11
§11.4.6). **Data moves from that reply onward.**

**Exit signal.** The channel reports itself running and the completion path
begins reporting progress; the key-`202` reply's status word is `0`.

> **Ordering reason.** A descriptor is only meaningful once the serialiser it
> feeds has been configured to a matching frame geometry, so S7 must precede
> this. Starting a channel against an unclocked serialiser moves bytes into a
> block that cannot consume them.
>
> **Ordering reason — channel before `pwrd`.** The device must not be taken to
> `pwrd` until the DMA channel is already running (constraint 9a). On a capture
> stream the coprocessor begins pushing frames at that transition and a channel
> that is not yet draining overruns; on a playback stream the serialiser begins
> requesting frames and a channel that is not yet supplying them underruns, and
> what a starved transmit serialiser emits is **[Unknown]** (Section 3 §3.6.11).
>
> The host's interrupt destination index differs from the M1–M3 baseline
> (Section 5); arming the wrong destination produces a channel that runs but
> never reports.

### S10 — Output enabled

**Precondition.** S8, S9.

**Hardware actions.** Release the shared shutdown line. Wait the amplifier
power-up and ramp interval. Do **not** unmute yet — unmuting happens in S10a,
after the sense return has been validated, on machines that have one.

**Exit signal.** No fault status bit is set after the ramp interval has elapsed.

> **Ordering reason, and this is the one that damages hardware if inverted.**
> The bit clock must already be running before an amplifier leaves shutdown.
> These amplifiers raise a clock-loss fault when the serial clock stops while
> they are out of shutdown, and a driver that releases shutdown first and
> configures clocking second will provoke that fault on every start. S7 therefore
> strictly precedes S10.
>
> Unmuting before the ramp interval has elapsed produces an audible transient.
> The interval is a property of the part and, on at least one machine, is also
> stated by the platform description (Section 14).

### S10a — Sense validated

**Precondition.** S10 entered, amplifiers released but **still muted**.

**Hardware actions.** On machines with a sense return, read the sense channels
and check each against an expected impedance window before unmuting. On machines
without one, this state does not exist and S10 proceeds directly to unmute.

**Exit signal.** Every sense channel returns a value inside its expected window.

> **Ordering reason.** There is no handshake anywhere in the path that declares
> the sense stream valid (Section 8). A sense channel that is silent, stuck, or
> bound to the wrong physical driver looks exactly like a quiet speaker, and
> host-side protection built on it will then permit unlimited excursion on the
> driver it is not watching. A positive validity check is the only thing that
> distinguishes the two, and it must happen while the amplifiers are still muted
> because it is the last point at which a failure is harmless.

### S11 — Running

**Precondition.** S10a.

**Exit signal.** Steady-state. Validated sense data is arriving and host-side
protection modelling is active.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 15.3 Required orderings, collected

Each entry states the constraint and the hardware reason. A driver may reorder
anything not listed.

| # | Constraint | Hardware reason |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Shared shutdown asserted before any amplifier register is written | The line is shared; prior state is unknown at entry |
| 2 | Supplies up and reset deasserted before control-bus probing | Parts do not answer otherwise |
| 3 | Identification before configuration | Register map, gain field position and temperature scaling differ between counterpart parts |
| 4 | Speaker identity read before protection limits chosen | Straps select among modules with different limits |
| 5 | IOMMU mappings before descriptor submission | A descriptor names an address the IOMMU must already translate |
| 6 | Coprocessor running before any audio power domain is raised | No audio domain has host-drivable power control |
| 7 | Stream configured before amplifier slot programming | The amplifier must match the geometry the coprocessor chose |
| 8 | Every amplifier configured before the shared shutdown line is released | A shared release enables all of them at once |
| 9 | Stream configured before DMA channel start | An unclocked serialiser cannot consume a descriptor |
| 9a | DMA channel running before the device is taken to `pwrd` | `pwrd` is the transition at which frames start moving (Section 11 §11.4.7); a channel not yet draining overruns on capture, and one not yet supplying underruns on playback |
| 10 | **Clocks running before shutdown release** | Otherwise the amplifier raises a clock-loss fault |
| 11 | Ramp interval elapsed before unmute | Otherwise an audible transient |
| 11a | ☠ **Sense channels validated before unmute**, on machines that have a sense return | No handshake declares the sense stream valid; an unvalidated channel is indistinguishable from a quiet speaker, and protection built on it watches nothing |
| 12 | Shutdown asserted before clocks are stopped, at teardown | The inverse of 10 |
| 13 | A sample-rate change performed as a stream release and re-open, not in place | No in-place rate-change message is established (Section 11 Open questions 7 and 36), and the amplifier's rate detector re-runs across a clock stop/start, not during one (§15.6) |

Constraint 12 is the teardown mirror and is listed because it is the one most
easily missed: stopping the stream before silencing the amplifiers reproduces
exactly the clock-loss condition that constraint 10 exists to avoid.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 15.4 Teardown

Teardown is not the reverse of bring-up, because constraint 12 forces the
amplifier silencing to happen before the clock removal that would otherwise be
its mirror image.

```
  mute amplifiers
    → wait ramp-down interval
      → assert shared shutdown
        → key 202: target pw1, flag 1        (data stops here)
          → stop DMA channel, wait for it to quiesce (bounded), then reset it
            → key 202: target idle, flag 0     (clocks stop here)
              → tear down IOMMU mappings
```

The two key-`202` calls are the exact inverse of the two in S7 and S9, with the
flag values as given: `1` on the `pwrd ↔ pw1 ` transitions and `0` on the
`pw1 ↔ idle` transitions (Section 11 §11.4.6, §11.4.7 step 12).

The DMA channel must be stopped and quiet before the stream is released, because
releasing the stream removes the clock that drains the serialiser; a channel still
running at that point stalls with data in flight.

**There is no established idle bit to poll, so this step needs a fallback.** Whether the
channel control register carries a DMA-engine-idle status bit is **[Unknown]** (Section 4
§4.3.3, §4.10.1; Section 5 §5.2.6). Teardown must therefore proceed as:

1. Clear the channel's enable bit in the controller's transmit- or receive-stop register.
2. Poll `CHAN_AXI_OUTSTANDING` (channel block `+0x60`) until it reads 0 and the completion
   FIFO stops advancing (`REPORT_FIFO_STATUS`, `+0x74`, EMPTY set). **[Inferred]**
3. **Bound the wait with an explicit timeout and proceed on expiry.** The correct value is
   **[Unknown]**: no quiesce time has been measured on any in-scope part, and the only
   figure this document carries for this path is the 5000 ms *fault* deadline of Section 4
   §4.10.1, which is a failure deadline and not a latency target. Until a figure is
   measured, derive the timeout from the stream the driver itself programmed — the
   descriptor period in use, plus margin — rather than from a constant, and treat expiry
   as a fault to be logged, not as normal. See Section 4 Open question 24.
4. Pulse the channel reset (`CHAN_CTL_STATUS` bit 0) whether or not the wait succeeded.
   The reset clears the FIFOs, so a channel that never reports quiet is recovered by
   resetting it rather than by waiting longer.

Only then release the stream. If the wait expired, treat the channel as having been in an
unknown state and reprogram every non-surviving register (Section 4 §4.10.2) before it is
used again.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 15.5 Recovery

Three re-entry points cover the fault classes a driver will meet.

| Fault | Re-enter at | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Amplifier fault status set (overcurrent, overtemperature, brownout, clock loss) | S8 for the affected amplifier | Fault handling may reset part of the register state; the safe response is to re-establish the full configuration rather than to clear the bit alone |
| Shared shutdown line asserted for any reason | S8 for **every** amplifier | The line is shared, so all amplifiers lost their output stage together and the configuration of each is indeterminate |
| DMA channel error or stall | S9 | Per-channel ring reset does not disturb the serialiser configuration the coprocessor owns. Note that this is the **only** reset a host driver still has: the shared controller reset available on M1–M3 is no longer within host reach, and the audio DMA power domains cannot be cycled by the host either, so any fault state that survives a ring reset is not host-recoverable (Section 14) |
| Coprocessor restart | S5 | Everything downstream of the transport is lost, including the stream configuration, so the whole coprocessor chain repeats; the host chain's results (identity, calibration selection, IOMMU mappings) survive and need not be redone |
| System sleep and resume | S8 for the jack codec and every amplifier; S9 for every channel; **not** S4 | The jack codec loses its entire register file at every system sleep, and DMA channel configuration is not retained. The audio IOMMU, by contrast, is explicitly not taken down at sleep on any SoC in scope: its mappings survive and must **not** be rebuilt on resume (Section 14). GPIO pin state is restored on wake, but the amplifier register file is not — the two are independent, so a restored shutdown line does not imply a restored amplifier |

A coprocessor restart is the only fault that invalidates the stream
configuration, and therefore the only one that forces the amplifiers back
through S8 by way of S7.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 15.6 Changing the sample rate of a running stream

The pieces of this are spread across Sections 3, 7, 10 and 11; assembled, they say that on
every machine in scope a rate change is a **stream release and re-open**, not an in-place
adjustment.

**Why it cannot be done in place.**

- The bit clock and frame clock are the coprocessor's on every SoC in scope; the host has
  no clock register to write (Section 11 §11.6). **[Confirmed]**
- Whether the audio service accepts a rate change on an open stream at all is **[Unknown]**
  — the property key that would carry it is not established (Section 11 §11.4.6, Open
  questions 7 and 36).
- The amplifier's rate detector runs with auto-rate **enabled** on every in-scope machine
  (`TDM_CFG0[4] AUTO_RATE = 0`) and **re-detects across a clock stop/start**, not during
  one; a rate that moves under a running link latches `INT_LTCH4` bit 1 ("sample rate
  changed on the fly") or bit 0 ("ratio changed on the fly"), and an out-of-window
  combination latches bit 2 ("invalid ratio/rate") — all of which are faults, not
  transitions (§7 §7.3.1, §7.9.4). **[Confirmed]** for the bit meanings.
- Stopping the clock while an amplifier is enabled is exactly the clock-loss condition
  constraint 10 exists to prevent.

**When it does not arise at all.** The speaker path is pinned to **48 kHz** by the platform
description on every machine in scope (`samplerate-subset` on the speaker stream, §7 §7.9.4,
Section 1 §1.11). A driver has no rate choice to make there. The rates that vary are on the
jack path: jack capture advertises 48000, 44100, 88200 and 96000 Hz on every board except
j700, which advertises **48 kHz only**; `samplerate-default` is 48000 Hz everywhere
(Section 1 §1.9.2, Section 10). **[Confirmed]**

**The procedure.**

1. Reject any rate not in that endpoint's advertised set. The set is per endpoint and per
   board, not per machine class.
2. Mute digitally and wait the ramp interval — **33.33 ms** for a full-range ramp at the
   ramp rate every in-scope machine uses (§7 §7.4.2).
3. Assert the shared amplifier shutdown line **before any clock stops** (constraints 10 and
   12). On the jack path, take the codec's output stage down by its own block enables first
   (Section 10).
4. Stop and quiesce the DMA channels, then reset them — the bounded procedure of §15.4,
   including its timeout, because there is no idle bit to poll.
5. Release the stream through the coprocessor and re-open it at the new rate: re-enter at
   **S7**. The transport, the service and the device attachments survive; only the stream
   configuration is redone.
6. Reprogram everything whose value is rate-dependent, at **S8**:
   * the amplifier's `TDM_CFG0[3:1] SAMP_RATE`, and `CLOCK_CFG[5:2] SAMP_RATIO` if
     auto-rate has been disabled;
   * the **high-pass corners**, because the corner table scales with the rate family: the
     same code is 1.0884× lower in the 44.1/88.2 kHz family than in the 48/96 kHz family,
     so code 1 is 2 Hz at 48 kHz and 1.84 Hz at 44.1 kHz (§7 §7.4.3);
   * the jack codec's clocking, PLL and sample-rate code (Section 10);
   * the slot and word-width programming, if the new geometry differs.
7. Re-arm the DMA channels (**S9**), release the shutdown line (**S10**), re-validate the
   sense channels on machines that have them (**S10a** — this is not optional after a
   reconfiguration, because the sense stream's validity is never declared), then unmute
   (**S11**).
8. **Confirm, do not assume.** Read `CLK_CFG` (page 0 `0x68`, read-only) back from each
   amplifier and check the detected rate and ratio against what was programmed, then read
   and clear `INT_LTCH4`. A rate change that the detector rejected leaves the part silent
   and reports nothing on any other path (§7 §7.9.5).

**What remains [Unknown]:** whether the coprocessor supports a faster path than this — an
in-place rate change on an open stream — and, if it does, whether it stops the bit clock
while performing it. Until that is established, the release-and-re-open sequence above is
the only one a driver can rely on. See Section 11 Open questions 7 and 36.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Per-SoC / per-machine differences

| Machine class | Difference in the state machine |
|---|---|
| A18 Pro machine | S2 and S8 cover the jack codec only. The amplifier family has no control bus, so there is no amplifier register programming, no identification read, no protection register loading and no sense path. S0 and S10 still apply: the shutdown line is the only amplifier control the host has. Every other speaker control is coprocessor-side. |
| A18 Pro machine | S10a does not exist: there is no sense return of any kind, no fault line and no status register. The amplifier self-protects only at a die-temperature limit that a voice coil can exceed by a wide margin, so no state in this machine's bring-up establishes that the speakers are safe. See Section 8. |
| A18 Pro machine | The speaker stream is bound to the low-power audio processor's DMA rather than the base DMA, so S4 and S9 address a different controller instance than on the other machines. |
| A18 Pro, M5, M5 Pro/Max | The built-in microphone array is behind the isolation boundary; its capture path has no S4 or S9 reachable by a normal-world driver. Headset-microphone capture is unaffected and follows the ordinary path on every machine in scope. |
| M5 and M5 Pro/Max | Digital display audio has its own per-display DMA instances, reached by a separate instance of S4 and S9 with no S8 at all, since there is no discrete part. |
| Machines without speaker-identification straps | S3 is implicit. A driver must not treat a machine that should have straps but does not answer as equivalent. |
| Four-amplifier machines | S8 covers four parts rather than six; constraint 8 is unchanged in force. |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


## Open questions

1. **Answered, with three residuals — the property vocabulary for a playback
   stream.** S7 is now specified for **both** stream classes: the pulse-density
   capture calls in Section 11 §11.4.7, and the serial-audio calls — keys `401`,
   `402`, `508`, `701`, `702`, `703`, `704`, `705` — in Section 18 §18.2, §18.3
   and §18.6.1. There is no separate sample-rate property, and **the stream
   start is the key-`202` transition to the code reported by key `402`**, with a
   direction mask; no distinct start call exists. **Residuals, all narrower than
   the original gap:** the key numbers are **[Probable]** rather than
   [Confirmed] on t8132 and t8142; the bit-order / clock-edge pairing of record
   bytes `0x37`/`0x38` is **[Probable]** (Section 18 Open question 4); and call
   types `0xC3000006` and `0xC3000008` remain **[Unknown]** (Section 11 Open
   question 6). *Why it matters:* a driver can write S7 today on t604x, t8140
   and t605x, and on t8132 and t8142 should confirm the key numbers before
   trusting them. *How to resolve:* trace the wrapped-call bodies in the
   transmit ring during a speaker stream start on a t8132 machine and read the
   property key at body offset `0x2c` of each (Section 11 Open questions 6, 7
   and 36).

2. **Whether the host can reach the serial audio controller's registers directly
   is [Unknown].** If the fabric permits it, an alternative bring-up exists that
   bypasses S5–S7 entirely; if it does not, the coprocessor chain is mandatory.
   This is a first-order probing target: attempt a read of a cluster register at
   the address Section 3 derives, on a machine where the audio domains are
   powered, and observe whether it faults.

3. **Whether the coprocessor rejects or races a host-initiated DMA start on a
   stream it considers configured is [Unknown].** Section 11 records that the
   coprocessor rejects configuration changes on a stream that is already
   configured. Whether that extends to noticing host DMA activity determines
   how much of S9 a driver can perform independently.

4. **The settling time after enabling the audio-part supplies is [Unknown]** on
   machines that carry a supply-enable line. Until it is measured, a driver must
   use the largest published settling time for the parts concerned.

5. **Whether any state in the discrete parts survives a coprocessor restart is
   [Unknown].** The recovery table assumes it does, because a coprocessor restart
   does not touch the host-owned control bus — but if a restart also cycles the
   audio power domains in a way that affects the parts' clock inputs, the
   amplifiers may fault and need the full S8 treatment. Observable by asserting a
   coprocessor restart while a stream is running and reading amplifier fault
   status afterwards.

6. **Can a driver join an already-running coprocessor stream, or must it force the
   stream back through S7?** **[Unknown]**, and it is the normal case at handoff: every
   board in scope carries a boot-time audio volume setting, so boot firmware has already
   played audio through the speakers before the driver runs (S0). *Why it matters:* if the
   existing configuration can be adopted, the driver can reach S11 without an audible gap
   and without re-running the amplifier programming of S8; if it cannot, every attach
   produces a silence of whatever duration S7→S11 takes, and the driver must plan for it.
   *Probe, in this order, none of which disturbs the coprocessor:*
   (a) read the live slot map and level back from each amplifier over host I²C — page 0
   `TDM_CFG3` (0x0C), `TDM_CFG5` (0x0E), `TDM_CFG6` (0x0F), `CHNL_0` (0x03) and
   `MODE_CTRL` (0x02) — and compare against the per-machine table of Section 16 for this
   board; (b) read the audio DMA controller's `TX_EN_SET` / `RX_EN_SET` (`0x0000` /
   `0x0008`) and each live channel's `CHAN_BUF_CFG` (`+0x50`) to see which channels the
   previous owner left running and what carve-out they hold; (c) read the shared shutdown
   line's level through the GPIO controller. Then attempt to open the audio service by
   name **without** releasing the existing stream and record whether the service accepts
   the open, reports busy, or silently reconfigures. *Measure:* the duration of output
   silence from the first service call to the first sample reaching the amplifier, for
   both paths — that number is what decides whether adopting is worth implementing.


---

# 16. Per-machine appendix

> ## ⚠ Read this before using any table below
>
> **The transducer role must be taken from the per-machine table, never inferred
> from the slot group number.** Slot group 2 is a *tweeter* on the MacBook Air
> 15-inch and 13-inch chassis and the iMac, and a *second woofer* on the MacBook Pro
> 14/16-inch chassis. Applying woofer excursion and thermal limits to a tweeter can
> destroy it — on the 15-inch Air the tweeters have roughly three times the thermal
> resistance of the woofers, so the error is not marginal.
>
> **On the MacBook Pro 14/16-inch chassis the slot group of the tweeter pair is not
> settled.** The platform hardware description places the tweeters in slot groups 4
> and 5; the published, hardware-tested device trees for the predecessors of that same
> chassis place them in groups 2 and 3. The tables below follow the platform
> description. See Open question 1 — this must be verified on hardware before
> per-transducer limits are applied on those machines.

## Baseline

Measured against the per-machine audio topology of the M1–M3 boards as described by
their own platform hardware description and by the published Asahi Linux device trees
for the same machines. The per-machine facts that changed at the M4 boundary are
enumerated in Section 1; this appendix is the tabular form of the result, one block
per board, intended to be transcribed directly into a device-tree description.

`speaker-config` and `amp-tx-zd-config` are byte-identical on every six-amplifier
machine from the M1 Pro generation through the M5 Max boards. On four-amplifier
machines `speaker-config` is byte-identical from the M2 boards onward, while
`amp-tx-zd-config` is byte-identical only from the **M3** boards onward — the M2
four-amplifier boards store different padding bytes, which crop to the same
effective mask (Section 1 §1.8.3). That fixes the slot **geometry**
across generations — slot count, slot widths, sense slot numbers, idle masks. It does
**not** fix which transducer sits in which slot: that is a per-chassis property and is
carried by the amplifier node names, not by the blob.

## Summary of differences

Everything here is per-board, so the summary is the cross-machine quick reference
below rather than a per-SoC list. The structural outliers are **j700** (different
amplifier family with no control bus, different jack codec, speaker path on the
low-power audio processor), **j623/j624** (multi-amplifier array with the sense
return deliberately not wired), **j773g/j773s/j575c** (single amplifier, no
microphones) and **j813** (speaker identification dropped relative to its M4
predecessor).

The one per-machine electrical change in scope is the **M4 Mac mini amplifier output
level**: j773g and j773s carry level code 0x0f = 18.5 dBV where every earlier Mac
mini and every Mac Studio board carries 0x14 = 21.0 dBV. See the note under those
two machines.

## How to read these tables

- Every address, pin number, slot number and register value is taken from the
  platform hardware description of that exact board and is **[Confirmed]** unless
  annotated otherwise. That **[Confirmed]** covers the *record structure* — which
  byte of `speaker-config` is the playback slot, which bytes are the sense slots,
  and what the values are. It does **not** cover the *binding* of a record to a
  physical transducer: on the MacBook Pro 14/16-inch chassis that binding is
  **[Probable]** (§1 §1.3.2, §8 §8.2.4), and on every other machine in scope it is
  **[Confirmed]**. **On a MacBook Pro chassis machine, read `TDM_CFG3` and
  `TDM_CFG5` / `TDM_CFG6` back from every amplifier and confirm the binding before
  any speaker is driven** — a wrong binding delivers woofer content to a tweeter,
  upstream of every protection mechanism. The sense-slot columns carry the
  same qualification, for the same reason: both come out of the same record.
- **Playback slot** is the amplifier's receive slot on the serial link, 32 bits wide,
  carrying a 24-bit left-justified sample. **Sense slot A** and **Sense slot B** are
  positions on an 8-bit slot grid in the transmit direction, each carrying a 16-bit
  word; the two together occupy the same 32-bit region of the frame as that
  amplifier's playback slot. **A** is the lower slot (`4n`) and is written into
  amplifier register `0x0E`; **B** is the upper slot (`4n+2`) and is written into
  `0x0F`. ☠ **Which of A and B carries voltage and which carries current is
  [Probable], not Confirmed** — the published upstream trees write the two
  exchanged into the same two registers, and the coprocessor cannot distinguish
  them. Under the mainline naming A is voltage and B is current. See Section 1
  §1.4, §8 §8.2.1 and the third hazard in §00.
- **Level** is the amplifier's analogue full-scale output level, decoded from the
  second byte of that amplifier's `speaker-config` record as 11.0 dBV + 0.5 dB × code.
  Full scale is the corresponding r.m.s. voltage into the rated load. Note that the
  full-scale *sense* quantities are part constants and are **not** scaled by this
  code.
- **Frame** is stated as a length in **bit clocks**, which is the quantity the
  frame-sync generator's phase counters and the amplifier's bit-clock-to-frame-rate
  register both take. On every `sn012776` machine in scope it is **250 bit clocks at a
  12.000 MHz bit clock** — 12 000 000 ÷ 250 = 48 000 Hz exactly — irrespective of
  amplifier count; on j700 it is 256 bit clocks at 12.288 MHz. The per-direction data
  figures quoted alongside it (192, 128, 32 bits) are counts of **data bits in one
  direction**, not frame lengths, and the remainder of the frame is idle. See
  §18 §18.4.4 and §11 §11.7.3.
- **Link** A carries the even-numbered slot groups (the left-hand drivers) and link B
  the odd-numbered ones (the right-hand drivers); both links carry the full-width
  frame. This split is unaffected by the slot-group question above, because the
  contested pair of addresses is on the same side either way. Which serial audio
  cluster drives each link is **[Unknown]** on every board in scope — see Section 1
  §1.5.
- **DMA TX / RX**: on t8132 and t604x boards the binding is a flat channel index in
  the endpoint's `dma-channels` blob, where even = transmit and odd = receive, so
  flat index *n* is channel *n*/2 in direction *n* mod 2; the equivalent named channel
  is given in parentheses. On t8140, t8142 and t605x boards the binding is the channel
  name string itself.
- **Ref clock / Frame**: from the 36-byte `reg` descriptor on the stream data node,
  decoded per Section 11 §11.7.3. "Ref clock" is the descriptor's **master-clock
  frequency** field (`0x08`); "*N* bclk/frame" is the descriptor's **frame length
  in bit clocks** (`0x0c`). The two relate through the master-clock-to-bit-clock
  divider, which is **1 on every in-scope link except the A18 Pro jack link**,
  where it is 4 and is stated in the row. Where no master-clock frequency is
  stated, the bit clock is supplied by the link's clock generator and only the
  frame length is fixed by the descriptor.
- `bop-config` is byte-identical on every board that has it and is not repeated per
  machine; see Section 1 §1.8.2 for the full 24-register table.

## Slot group to I²C address — universal

The platform hardware description binds slot groups to I²C addresses identically on
every board, M1 through M5, on both chassis families:

| Slot group | Playback slot | Sense slot A (→0x0E) | Sense slot B (→0x0F) | I²C address (6-amp) | I²C address (4-amp) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | 0 | 2 | 0x38 | 0x38 |
| 1 | 1 | 4 | 6 | 0x3b | 0x3b |
| 2 | 2 | 8 | 10 | 0x39 | 0x39 |
| 3 | 3 | 12 | 14 | 0x3c | 0x3c |
| 4 | 4 | 16 | 18 | 0x3a | — |
| 5 | 5 | 20 | 22 | 0x3d | — |

## I²C address to transducer — per chassis, NOT universal

| Address | MacBook Pro 14/16-inch | MacBook Air 15-inch | MacBook Air 13-inch / iMac 24-inch |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0x38 | Left woofer 1 | Left woofer 1 | Left woofer |
| 0x39 | **Left woofer 2** | **Left tweeter** | **Left tweeter** |
| 0x3a | **Left tweeter** | **Left woofer 2** | — |
| 0x3b | Right woofer 1 | Right woofer 1 | Right woofer |
| 0x3c | **Right woofer 2** | **Right tweeter** | **Right tweeter** |
| 0x3d | **Right tweeter** | **Right woofer 2** | — |

| Chassis | Boards in scope | Tweeters at slot groups |
|---|---|---|
| MacBook Pro 14/16-inch | j604, j614s, j614c, j616s, j616c, j704, j714s, j714c, j716s, j716c | **4 and 5** per the platform description; **2 and 3** per the published trees for the predecessor boards — see Open question 1 |
| MacBook Air 15-inch | j715, j815 | **2 and 3** — both sources agree |
| MacBook Air 13-inch, iMac 24-inch | j713, j813, j623, j624 | **2 and 3** — both sources agree |

The address-to-transducer table is **[Confirmed]** on two independent sources: the
amplifier node names in the platform hardware description, and the published device
trees for the predecessor of each chassis, which agree with them address for address
on both chassis families.

Every amplifier and codec bus in the table requests an SCL period of 2500 ns, i.e.
**400 kHz** fast-mode nominal. That is the requested ceiling: the controller's
divider yields **375 kHz** actual (§6 §6.1.4). Both figures are given in the
per-machine tables below.
The amplifier shutdown line and the amplifier interrupt line are **shared by all
amplifiers on the machine** on every board.

### Speaker amplifiers

| Slot group | Driver | I²C bus | 7-bit address | SCL period | Playback slot | Sense slot A (→0x0E) | Sense slot B (→0x0F) | Level code | Level | Full scale | Link |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Left woofer 1 | `i2c3` | 0x38 | 2500 ns (375 kHz actual, 400 kHz nominal) | 0 | 0 | 2 | 0x0f | 18.5 dBV | 8.41 V rms | A (left) |
| 1 | Right woofer 1 | `i2c3` | 0x3b | 2500 ns (375 kHz actual, 400 kHz nominal) | 1 | 4 | 6 | 0x0f | 18.5 dBV | 8.41 V rms | B (right) |
| 2 | Left woofer 2 | `i2c3` | 0x39 | 2500 ns (375 kHz actual, 400 kHz nominal) | 2 | 8 | 10 | 0x0f | 18.5 dBV | 8.41 V rms | A (left) |
| 3 | Right woofer 2 | `i2c3` | 0x3c | 2500 ns (375 kHz actual, 400 kHz nominal) | 3 | 12 | 14 | 0x0f | 18.5 dBV | 8.41 V rms | B (right) |
| 4 | Left tweeter | `i2c3` | 0x3a | 2500 ns (375 kHz actual, 400 kHz nominal) | 4 | 16 | 18 | 0x0f | 18.5 dBV | 8.41 V rms | A (left) |
| 5 | Right tweeter | `i2c3` | 0x3d | 2500 ns (375 kHz actual, 400 kHz nominal) | 5 | 20 | 22 | 0x0f | 18.5 dBV | 8.41 V rms | B (right) |

`speaker-config` raw: `000f0002010f0406020f080a030f0c0e040f1012050f1416` — byte-identical to the record carried by the 14-inch MacBook Pro boards of the M1 Pro/Max, M2 Pro/Max, M3 and M3 Pro/Max generations, level byte 0x0f on every one of them. The scoping that holds is chassis family across generations, **not** amplifier count: j713 and j623 are both four-amplifier machines and carry different records, and the level byte (byte 1 of each record) is 0x0f on the portables and the M4 Mac mini, 0x12 on the M4 iMac and 0x14 on the Mac Studio. The slot *geometry* is therefore unchanged across generations **within this chassis family**; the transducer sitting in each slot is **not** implied by that and is taken from the node names of this board. **Never infer a transducer role from a slot group number.**

**Chassis pattern: MacBook Pro 14/16-inch.** The left tweeter is the part at 0x3a and the left woofer 2 the part at 0x39 (the reverse of the 15-inch Air). **The slot group of the tweeter pair on this chassis is contested:** the platform description places the tweeters in slot groups 4 and 5, as tabulated above, while the published hardware-tested trees for this chassis's predecessors place them in groups 2 and 3 and the second woofers in 4 and 5. The record *structure* is **[Confirmed]**; the *binding* of each record to a transducer on this chassis is **[Probable]** — the platform-description reading is adopted here; see §8 §8.2.4 for the role-order reading that would reconcile every source, and for the `TDM_CFG6` / `TDM_CFG3` readback that settles it. **Read those registers back and confirm the binding before any speaker is driven on this chassis**, and do not apply per-transducer excursion or thermal limits until you have. See Open question 1.

Frame: **250 bit clocks at a 12.000 MHz bit clock**, giving 48 kHz (12 000 000 ÷ 250 = 48 000 exactly). Of those, **192 carry playback data** (6 slots × 32 bits) in the transmit direction and **192 carry sense data** (12 slots × 16 bits) in the receive direction, with **58 idle** bit clocks in each. Playback samples are 24-bit left-justified in 32-bit slots; each sense quantity is a 16-bit word, two words per amplifier (slot A then slot B) occupying the same 32-bit region of the frame. **[Confirmed]**

Frame: **250 bit clocks at a 12.000 MHz bit clock**, giving 48 kHz (12 000 000 ÷ 250 = 48 000 exactly). Of those, **128 carry playback data** (4 slots × 32 bits) and **122 are idle**; there is no receive direction on this board. Playback samples are 24-bit left-justified in 32-bit slots. The nominal sense slot numbers in the table above are not used. **[Confirmed]**

`speaker-config` raw: `000f0002` — **not** byte-identical to the record carried by the earlier Mac mini boards: the slot bytes are unchanged but the level byte dropped from 0x14 to **0x0f** at this generation (see the note below). The sense slot numbers above are nominal. This board also has no built-in microphones: no built-in-array capture endpoint, no `lp-mic-device`, no `siri-listening-device` and no `/arm-io/iop-voicetrigger-controller`.

**Amplifier output level changed at this generation.** The level code is 0x0f = **18.5 dBV** here, where every earlier Mac mini board and every Mac Studio board — including j575c, which is in scope — carries 0x14 = **21.0 dBV**. That is a 2.5 dB reduction in full-scale output voltage, 11.22 V rms → 8.41 V rms. A driver that carries a level value forward from an earlier Mac mini will over-drive this machine. **[Confirmed]**

Frame: **250 bit clocks at a 12.000 MHz bit clock**, giving 48 kHz (12 000 000 ÷ 250 = 48 000 exactly). Of those, **32 carry playback data** (1 slot × 32 bits) and **218 are idle**; there is no receive direction on this board. Playback samples are 24-bit left-justified in 32-bit slots. The nominal sense slot numbers in the table above are not used. **[Confirmed]**

`speaker-config` raw: `000f0002010f0406020f080a030f0c0e040f1012050f1416` — byte-identical to the record carried by the 14-inch MacBook Pro boards of the M1 Pro/Max, M2 Pro/Max, M3 and M3 Pro/Max generations, level byte 0x0f on every one of them. The scoping that holds is chassis family across generations, **not** amplifier count: j713 and j623 are both four-amplifier machines and carry different records, and the level byte (byte 1 of each record) is 0x0f on the portables and the M4 Mac mini, 0x12 on the M4 iMac and 0x14 on the Mac Studio. The slot *geometry* is therefore unchanged across generations **within this chassis family**; the transducer sitting in each slot is **not** implied by that and is taken from the node names of this board. **Never infer a transducer role from a slot group number.**

**Chassis pattern: MacBook Pro 14/16-inch.** The left tweeter is the part at 0x3a and the left woofer 2 the part at 0x39 (the reverse of the 15-inch Air). **The slot group of the tweeter pair on this chassis is contested:** the platform description places the tweeters in slot groups 4 and 5, as tabulated above, while the published hardware-tested trees for this chassis's predecessors place them in groups 2 and 3 and the second woofers in 4 and 5. The record *structure* is **[Confirmed]**; the *binding* of each record to a transducer on this chassis is **[Probable]** — the platform-description reading is adopted here; see §8 §8.2.4 for the role-order reading that would reconcile every source, and for the `TDM_CFG6` / `TDM_CFG3` readback that settles it. **Read those registers back and confirm the binding before any speaker is driven on this chassis**, and do not apply per-transducer excursion or thermal limits until you have. See Open question 1.

Frame: **250 bit clocks at a 12.000 MHz bit clock**, giving 48 kHz (12 000 000 ÷ 250 = 48 000 exactly). Of those, **192 carry playback data** (6 slots × 32 bits) in the transmit direction and **192 carry sense data** (12 slots × 16 bits) in the receive direction, with **58 idle** bit clocks in each. Playback samples are 24-bit left-justified in 32-bit slots; each sense quantity is a 16-bit word, two words per amplifier (slot A then slot B) occupying the same 32-bit region of the frame. **[Confirmed]**

`speaker-config` raw: `000f0002010f0406020f080a030f0c0e040f1012050f1416` — byte-identical to the record carried by the 16-inch MacBook Pro boards of the M1 Pro/Max, M2 Pro/Max and M3 Pro/Max generations, level byte 0x0f on every one of them. The scoping that holds is chassis family across generations, **not** amplifier count: j713 and j623 are both four-amplifier machines and carry different records, and the level byte (byte 1 of each record) is 0x0f on the portables and the M4 Mac mini, 0x12 on the M4 iMac and 0x14 on the Mac Studio. The slot *geometry* is therefore unchanged across generations **within this chassis family**; the transducer sitting in each slot is **not** implied by that and is taken from the node names of this board. **Never infer a transducer role from a slot group number.**

**Chassis pattern: MacBook Pro 14/16-inch.** The left tweeter is the part at 0x3a and the left woofer 2 the part at 0x39 (the reverse of the 15-inch Air). **The slot group of the tweeter pair on this chassis is contested:** the platform description places the tweeters in slot groups 4 and 5, as tabulated above, while the published hardware-tested trees for this chassis's predecessors place them in groups 2 and 3 and the second woofers in 4 and 5. The record *structure* is **[Confirmed]**; the *binding* of each record to a transducer on this chassis is **[Probable]** — the platform-description reading is adopted here; see §8 §8.2.4 for the role-order reading that would reconcile every source, and for the `TDM_CFG6` / `TDM_CFG3` readback that settles it. **Read those registers back and confirm the binding before any speaker is driven on this chassis**, and do not apply per-transducer excursion or thermal limits until you have. See Open question 1.

Frame: **250 bit clocks at a 12.000 MHz bit clock**, giving 48 kHz (12 000 000 ÷ 250 = 48 000 exactly). Of those, **192 carry playback data** (6 slots × 32 bits) in the transmit direction and **192 carry sense data** (12 slots × 16 bits) in the receive direction, with **58 idle** bit clocks in each. Playback samples are 24-bit left-justified in 32-bit slots; each sense quantity is a 16-bit word, two words per amplifier (slot A then slot B) occupying the same 32-bit region of the frame. **[Confirmed]**

`speaker-config` raw: `000f0002` — **not** byte-identical to the record carried by the earlier Mac mini boards: the slot bytes are unchanged but the level byte dropped from 0x14 to **0x0f** at this generation (see the note below). The scoping that holds is chassis family across generations, **not** amplifier count: j713 and j623 are both four-amplifier machines and carry different records, and the level byte (byte 1 of each record) is 0x0f on the portables and the M4 Mac mini, 0x12 on the M4 iMac and 0x14 on the Mac Studio. The sense slot numbers above are nominal. This board also has no built-in microphones: no built-in-array capture endpoint, no `lp-mic-device`, no `siri-listening-device` and no `/arm-io/iop-voicetrigger-controller`.

**Amplifier output level changed at this generation.** The level code is 0x0f = **18.5 dBV** here, where every earlier Mac mini board and every Mac Studio board — including j575c, which is in scope — carries 0x14 = **21.0 dBV**. That is a 2.5 dB reduction in full-scale output voltage, 11.22 V rms → 8.41 V rms. A driver that carries a level value forward from an earlier Mac mini will over-drive this machine. **[Confirmed]**

Frame: **250 bit clocks at a 12.000 MHz bit clock**, giving 48 kHz (12 000 000 ÷ 250 = 48 000 exactly). Of those, **32 carry playback data** (1 slot × 32 bits) and **218 are idle**; there is no receive direction on this board. Playback samples are 24-bit left-justified in 32-bit slots. The nominal sense slot numbers in the table above are not used. **[Confirmed]**

This board retains level code 0x14 = 21.0 dBV, the maximum the field can express, and is the only board in scope that does — the M4 Mac mini boards dropped to 18.5 dBV. This board also has no built-in microphones. **[Confirmed]**

Frame: **250 bit clocks at a 12.000 MHz bit clock**, giving 48 kHz (12 000 000 ÷ 250 = 48 000 exactly). Of those, **32 carry playback data** (1 slot × 32 bits) and **218 are idle**; there is no receive direction on this board. Playback samples are 24-bit left-justified in 32-bit slots. The nominal sense slot numbers in the table above are not used. **[Confirmed]**

| 0 | Left woofer 1 | `i2c3` | 0x38 | 2500 ns (375 kHz actual, 400 kHz nominal) | 0 | 0 | 2 | 0x0f | 18.5 dBV | 8.41 V rms | A (left) |
| 1 | Right woofer 1 | `i2c3` | 0x3b | 2500 ns (375 kHz actual, 400 kHz nominal) | 1 | 4 | 6 | 0x0f | 18.5 dBV | 8.41 V rms | B (right) |
| 2 | Left woofer 2 | `i2c3` | 0x39 | 2500 ns (375 kHz actual, 400 kHz nominal) | 2 | 8 | 10 | 0x0f | 18.5 dBV | 8.41 V rms | A (left) |
| 3 | Right woofer 2 | `i2c3` | 0x3c | 2500 ns (375 kHz actual, 400 kHz nominal) | 3 | 12 | 14 | 0x0f | 18.5 dBV | 8.41 V rms | B (right) |
| 4 | Left tweeter | `i2c3` | 0x3a | 2500 ns (375 kHz actual, 400 kHz nominal) | 4 | 16 | 18 | 0x0f | 18.5 dBV | 8.41 V rms | A (left) |
| 5 | Right tweeter | `i2c3` | 0x3d | 2500 ns (375 kHz actual, 400 kHz nominal) | 5 | 20 | 22 | 0x0f | 18.5 dBV | 8.41 V rms | B (right) |

`speaker-config` raw: `000f0002010f0406020f080a030f0c0e040f1012050f1416` — byte-identical to the record carried by the 14-inch MacBook Pro boards of the M1 Pro/Max, M2 Pro/Max, M3, M3 Pro/Max, M4 and M4 Pro/Max generations, level byte 0x0f on every one of them. The scoping that holds is chassis family across generations, **not** amplifier count: j713 and j623 are both four-amplifier machines and carry different records, and the level byte (byte 1 of each record) is 0x0f on the portables and the M4 Mac mini, 0x12 on the M4 iMac and 0x14 on the Mac Studio. The slot *geometry* is therefore unchanged across generations **within this chassis family**; the transducer sitting in each slot is **not** implied by that and is taken from the node names of this board. **Never infer a transducer role from a slot group number.**

**Chassis pattern: MacBook Pro 14/16-inch.** The left tweeter is the part at 0x3a and the left woofer 2 the part at 0x39 (the reverse of the 15-inch Air). **The slot group of the tweeter pair on this chassis is contested:** the platform description places the tweeters in slot groups 4 and 5, as tabulated above, while the published hardware-tested trees for this chassis's predecessors place them in groups 2 and 3 and the second woofers in 4 and 5. The record *structure* is **[Confirmed]**; the *binding* of each record to a transducer on this chassis is **[Probable]** — the platform-description reading is adopted here; see §8 §8.2.4 for the role-order reading that would reconcile every source, and for the `TDM_CFG6` / `TDM_CFG3` readback that settles it. **Read those registers back and confirm the binding before any speaker is driven on this chassis**, and do not apply per-transducer excursion or thermal limits until you have. See Open question 1.

Frame: **250 bit clocks at a 12.000 MHz bit clock**, giving 48 kHz (12 000 000 ÷ 250 = 48 000 exactly). Of those, **192 carry playback data** (6 slots × 32 bits) in the transmit direction and **192 carry sense data** (12 slots × 16 bits) in the receive direction, with **58 idle** bit clocks in each. Playback samples are 24-bit left-justified in 32-bit slots; each sense quantity is a 16-bit word, two words per amplifier (slot A then slot B) occupying the same 32-bit region of the frame. **[Confirmed]**

`speaker-config` raw: `000f0002010f0406020f080a030f0c0e` — byte-identical to the record carried by the M2, M3 and M4 13-inch MacBook Air boards, level byte 0x0f on every one of them. The scoping that holds is chassis family across generations, **not** amplifier count: j713 and j623 are both four-amplifier machines and carry different records, and the level byte (byte 1 of each record) is 0x0f on the portables and the M4 Mac mini, 0x12 on the M4 iMac and 0x14 on the Mac Studio. The slot *geometry* is therefore unchanged across generations **within this chassis family**; the transducer sitting in each slot is **not** implied by that and is taken from the node names of this board. **Never infer a transducer role from a slot group number.**

**Chassis pattern: MacBook Air 13-inch.** Four drivers; the tweeters are the parts at 0x39 and 0x3c and sit in **slot groups 2 and 3**, as on j713 and its M2/M3 predecessors. **[Confirmed]**

This is the only four- or six-amplifier board in scope with **no speaker-identification mechanism**: `find-speaker-id`, `valid-speaker-ids`, `function-speaker-id0` and `function-speaker-id1` are all absent, although `speaker-protection` is 1. Its M4 predecessor j713 has the mechanism on pins 4 and 13. A driver written against j713 will find no straps here, and the calibration lookup must fall back to a single module variant. **[Confirmed]**

Frame: **250 bit clocks at a 12.000 MHz bit clock**, giving 48 kHz (12 000 000 ÷ 250 = 48 000 exactly). Of those, **128 carry playback data** (4 slots × 32 bits) in the transmit direction and **128 carry sense data** (8 slots × 16 bits) in the receive direction, with **122 idle** bit clocks in each. Playback samples are 24-bit left-justified in 32-bit slots; each sense quantity is a 16-bit word, two words per amplifier (slot A then slot B) occupying the same 32-bit region of the frame. **[Confirmed]**

| 0 | Left woofer 1 | `i2c1` | 0x38 | 2500 ns (375 kHz actual, 400 kHz nominal) | 0 | 0 | 2 | 0x0f | 18.5 dBV | 8.41 V rms | A (left) |

`speaker-config` raw: `000f0002010f0406020f080a030f0c0e040f1012050f1416` — byte-identical to the record carried by the 14-inch MacBook Pro boards of the M1 Pro/Max, M2 Pro/Max, M3, M3 Pro/Max, M4 and M4 Pro/Max generations, level byte 0x0f on every one of them. The scoping that holds is chassis family across generations, **not** amplifier count: j713 and j623 are both four-amplifier machines and carry different records, and the level byte (byte 1 of each record) is 0x0f on the portables and the M4 Mac mini, 0x12 on the M4 iMac and 0x14 on the Mac Studio. The slot *geometry* is therefore unchanged across generations **within this chassis family**; the transducer sitting in each slot is **not** implied by that and is taken from the node names of this board. **Never infer a transducer role from a slot group number.**

**Chassis pattern: MacBook Pro 14/16-inch.** The left tweeter is the part at 0x3a and the left woofer 2 the part at 0x39 (the reverse of the 15-inch Air). **The slot group of the tweeter pair on this chassis is contested:** the platform description places the tweeters in slot groups 4 and 5, as tabulated above, while the published hardware-tested trees for this chassis's predecessors place them in groups 2 and 3 and the second woofers in 4 and 5. The record *structure* is **[Confirmed]**; the *binding* of each record to a transducer on this chassis is **[Probable]** — the platform-description reading is adopted here; see §8 §8.2.4 for the role-order reading that would reconcile every source, and for the `TDM_CFG6` / `TDM_CFG3` readback that settles it. **Read those registers back and confirm the binding before any speaker is driven on this chassis**, and do not apply per-transducer excursion or thermal limits until you have. See Open question 1.

Secure low-power loopback endpoint present; jack-codec reset on the main pin controller. **[Confirmed]**

Frame: **250 bit clocks at a 12.000 MHz bit clock**, giving 48 kHz (12 000 000 ÷ 250 = 48 000 exactly). Of those, **192 carry playback data** (6 slots × 32 bits) in the transmit direction and **192 carry sense data** (12 slots × 16 bits) in the receive direction, with **58 idle** bit clocks in each. Playback samples are 24-bit left-justified in 32-bit slots; each sense quantity is a 16-bit word, two words per amplifier (slot A then slot B) occupying the same 32-bit region of the frame. **[Confirmed]**

| 0 | Left woofer 1 | `i2c1` | 0x38 | 2500 ns (375 kHz actual, 400 kHz nominal) | 0 | 0 | 2 | 0x0f | 18.5 dBV | 8.41 V rms | A (left) |
| 1 | Right woofer 1 | `i2c3` | 0x3b | 2500 ns (375 kHz actual, 400 kHz nominal) | 1 | 4 | 6 | 0x0f | 18.5 dBV | 8.41 V rms | B (right) |

| 4 | Left tweeter | `i2c1` | 0x3a | 2500 ns (375 kHz actual, 400 kHz nominal) | 4 | 16 | 18 | 0x0f | 18.5 dBV | 8.41 V rms | A (left) |

`speaker-config` raw: `000f0002010f0406020f080a030f0c0e040f1012050f1416` — byte-identical to the record carried by the 16-inch MacBook Pro boards of the M1 Pro/Max, M2 Pro/Max, M3 Pro/Max and M4 Pro/Max generations, level byte 0x0f on every one of them. The scoping that holds is chassis family across generations, **not** amplifier count: j713 and j623 are both four-amplifier machines and carry different records, and the level byte (byte 1 of each record) is 0x0f on the portables and the M4 Mac mini, 0x12 on the M4 iMac and 0x14 on the Mac Studio. The slot *geometry* is therefore unchanged across generations **within this chassis family**; the transducer sitting in each slot is **not** implied by that and is taken from the node names of this board. **Never infer a transducer role from a slot group number.**

**Chassis pattern: MacBook Pro 14/16-inch.** The left tweeter is the part at 0x3a and the left woofer 2 the part at 0x39 (the reverse of the 15-inch Air). **The slot group of the tweeter pair on this chassis is contested:** the platform description places the tweeters in slot groups 4 and 5, as tabulated above, while the published hardware-tested trees for this chassis's predecessors place them in groups 2 and 3 and the second woofers in 4 and 5. The record *structure* is **[Confirmed]**; the *binding* of each record to a transducer on this chassis is **[Probable]** — the platform-description reading is adopted here; see §8 §8.2.4 for the role-order reading that would reconcile every source, and for the `TDM_CFG6` / `TDM_CFG3` readback that settles it. **Read those registers back and confirm the binding before any speaker is driven on this chassis**, and do not apply per-transducer excursion or thermal limits until you have. See Open question 1.

Secure low-power loopback endpoint present; jack-codec reset on the main pin controller. **[Confirmed]**

Frame: **250 bit clocks at a 12.000 MHz bit clock**, giving 48 kHz (12 000 000 ÷ 250 = 48 000 exactly). Of those, **192 carry playback data** (6 slots × 32 bits) in the transmit direction and **192 carry sense data** (12 slots × 16 bits) in the receive direction, with **58 idle** bit clocks in each. Playback samples are 24-bit left-justified in 32-bit slots; each sense quantity is a 16-bit word, two words per amplifier (slot A then slot B) occupying the same 32-bit region of the frame. **[Confirmed]**
