## Per-SoC / per-machine differences

The per-machine blocks above are the differences. The cross-cutting patterns worth
stating once:

| Pattern | Boards |
|---|---|
| Slot **geometry** (slot count, widths, sense slot numbers, idle masks) | **identical on every machine of a given amplifier count, M1 Pro through M5 Max** — no in-scope board differs |
| Slot group → I²C address | universal: 0→0x38, 1→0x3b, 2→0x39, 3→0x3c, 4→0x3a, 5→0x3d |
| I²C address → **transducer** | **per chassis** — 0x39/0x3a and 0x3c/0x3d carry opposite roles on the MacBook Pro chassis versus the Air chassis |
| Amplifier GPIO pins identical across every board of the same SoC | all five t8132 boards (reset 15, interrupt 14, straps 4 and 13); all six t604x boards (54, 55, 52, 53); all three t8142 boards (151, 150) except that the straps differ per board; all four t6050/t605x boards (107, 106, 136, 137) |
| Amplifiers split across two I²C buses | every Pro/Max-die board (t604x, t605x); never on a base-die board |
| Amplifier output level changed | **j773g, j773s only** — 21.0 dBV on earlier Mac mini boards, 18.5 dBV here |
| Jack codec address | 0x4b on every board except j700 (0x48) |
| Jack codec reset on the always-on nub controller | t8132, t604x, t8142 |
| Jack codec reset on the main controller | t6050/t605x and t8140 |
| Speaker sense captured | every board with `speaker-protection = 1`; never on j623, j624, j773g, j773s, j575c, j700 |
| Playback tap endpoint present | t8140, t8142, t6050/t605x only |
| Low-power microphone injection endpoint present | t8140, t8142, t6050/t605x only |
| Built-in microphone array capture behind the isolation boundary | t8140, t8142, t6050/t605x; normal-world on t8132 and t604x. Headset-microphone capture through the jack codec is normal-world on **every** board |
| Secure low-power loopback endpoint | t6050/t605x only |
| Per-display audio DMA instances | t8142, t6050/t605x; shared serial-I/O DMA on t8132, t604x, t8140 |
| Second always-on coprocessor | t8140, t8142, t6050/t605x |
| Boards sharing an `acoustic-id` | j623/j624 (both 24-inch iMac), j773g/j773s (both Mac mini); every other machine has a distinct value |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Open questions

1. **Which slot groups the tweeters occupy on the MacBook Pro 14/16-inch chassis.**
   **Safety-critical, and unresolved.** The two available sources disagree, and they
   disagree only on this chassis:

   | Source | 0x39 (left woofer 2) | 0x3a (left tweeter) |
   |---|---|---|
   | Platform hardware description (amplifier phandle chain + node names) | slot group 2, sense slots 8/10 | slot group 4, sense slots 16/18 |
   | Published hardware-tested trees for this chassis's predecessors | slot group 4, sense slots 16/18 | slot group 2, sense slots 8/10 |

   Both sources agree on which *part* is the tweeter — it is the one at 0x3a on this
   chassis — and both agree completely on the 15-inch Air chassis and on every
   four-amplifier machine, where the tweeters are at slot groups 2 and 3. The tables
   in this appendix follow the platform description. **Why it matters:** if the
   published trees are right, then applying this appendix's map would send slot group
   2's content and limits to a tweeter that this document labels a woofer, and woofer
   excursion and thermal limits applied to a tweeter can destroy it. **Resolve by**
   muting one amplifier at a time over I²C while capturing the sense return and
   observing which capture channel pair falls silent, and independently by reading the
   receive-slot and sense-slot registers back from the parts at 0x39 and 0x3a after
   the platform has configured the link. Do not apply per-transducer limits on this
   chassis until this is done.

2. **Speaker module variant per unit.** Every table that lists speaker-identification
   straps names two pins and the valid code set {0, 3}, but nothing states which
   physical module each code denotes or which parameters change between them. The
   calibration tables in Section 9 must be indexed by `{board, code}`.
   **Resolve by** reading both straps on physical units of the same model and
   correlating with the per-unit configuration store.

3. **Link-to-cluster mapping per machine.** Each table assigns amplifiers to link A
   or link B from the bus-keeper masks, but which of the six base serial audio
   clusters drives link A and which drives link B is not stated on any board.
   **Resolve by** gating `AUDIO_MCA0_M` … `AUDIO_MCA5_M` individually while a stream
   runs; the power-domain tree in Section 1 §1.5.3 shows these are siblings of the DMA
   domains, so gating one should stop exactly one link without disturbing DMA.

4. **Whether the nominal sense slots on the no-sense boards are wired.** j623, j624,
   j773g, j773s and j575c carry sense slot numbers in `speaker-config` while
   declaring no receive channels. If the amplifier's sense output is physically
   connected but simply not captured, a driver could enable protection on those
   machines; if it is not connected, attempting to would hang the capture.
   **Resolve by** enabling the amplifier's sense transmitters over I²C and probing the
   transmit line.

5. **Why the M4 Mac mini output level dropped.** j773g and j773s carry 18.5 dBV where
   every earlier Mac mini carries 21.0 dBV, with no other amplifier-configuration
   change on those boards. Whether this reflects a different driver, a different
   enclosure loading, or a thermal limit matters for anyone deriving a protection
   bound for those machines. **Resolve by** comparing the per-unit calibration records
   of an M2 and an M4 Mac mini, and by measuring the amplifier's output at full
   scale on both.

6. **j700 channel assignment and fixed gain.** With no control bus, no interrupt and
   one shared shutdown line, the left/right assignment and the analogue gain of the
   two amplifier channels are set by board strapping that no table here can fill in.
   **Resolve by** playing a single-channel test signal, and by reading the strap
   resistors on the board.

7. **Units of the inline speaker power limits on j700.** `speaker-cpms-bgd_100ms`
   carries the pair (1363, 5453) with the instantaneous and one-second variants set to
   no-limit. Without units these cannot be used as a protection bound.
   **Resolve by** correlating against measured amplifier power at known drive levels.

8. **Per-unit calibration record format.** `/product/audio` names the configuration
   store keys for the per-unit speaker driver parameters, speaker gain trims and
   microphone gain trims, but the record layout behind each key is not described by
   the platform hardware description. In particular, whether a record is ordered by
   slot group or by transducer role is exactly the question in Open question 1 and
   must not be assumed. **Resolve by** reading the store on physical machines of
   several models and correlating the field count and ordering against the amplifier
   tables here. Cross-reference Section 9.

9. **Meaning of `acoustic-id`.** The value is distinct per model (shared only between
   the two iMac boards and the two Mac mini boards) and is clearly a selector into a
   tuning set, but nothing states what the set contains or whether a driver needs it
   for anything other than diagnostics. **Resolve by** comparing the processing
   configuration used on two machines with adjacent identifiers.

10. **Whether the shared amplifier interrupt can be attributed.** One level-sensitive
    line is shared by up to six amplifiers, and the platform description offers no
    per-amplifier status path other than the parts' own registers. Because the
    amplifier's own thermal foldback is disabled on every machine in scope, voice-coil
    thermal protection exists only in the host, so the latency of detecting and acting
    on a fault is a real bound. **Resolve by** measuring the interrupt-to-mute latency
    achievable on a six-amplifier machine.


---

# 17. Open questions — consolidated index, dependency structure and execution order

## What this section is

Sections 1 to 16 and Section 18 each end with an `Open questions` list. Together
they hold **315 entries**, and they are the work plan for the tracing and probing that follows this
document. Read individually they do not say what to do first, what is blocked behind
what, or what must be resolved before hardware can safely be driven. This section is
that view. It adds no new hardware facts; every entry below is stated in full in its
own section, and the numbering here is that section's numbering.

## The single most important planning fact

**The document's largest single dependency has changed shape.** Section 11 open
questions 1 and 4 — the coprocessor mailbox register map and the endpoint numbers —
were the gate on most of this document. Both are now closed in substance. §11.2 gives the
mailbox register map, the 96-bit message format, the doorbell and the interrupt
assignment; §11.2.8 gives the version handshake, the endpoint map, endpoint start and
the power-state transitions; §11.4 gives the shared-memory ring protocol every
endpoint runs, the framed call header, name→(endpoint, channel) service resolution and
the audio service's own request framing, device identifiers, call types and property
payloads; and §11.4.7 gives a step-by-step configure-and-start sequence for a stream.
A driver can be written against that.

What stands in their place is smaller and specific:

- **§11 #26 — confirm the register offsets on an in-scope die.** The map is
  **[Probable]**, resting on the block revision string the in-scope parts share with
  the M3 generation. One boot with the aperture trapped settles it. This is a
  confirmation run, not a discovery run — but until it is done, every class-C entry
  below rests on an unverified map.
- **§11 #36 — the playback property vocabulary — now answered, with residuals.**
  Section 18 specifies it: property keys `401`, `402`, `508`, `701`, `702`, `703`,
  `704` and `705`, the 109-byte key-`701` record that carries slot geometry, frame
  geometry and clocking, the clock invariant, and the ordered start sequence. There is
  no separate sample-rate property, and the stream start is the key-`202` transition to
  the code reported by key `402`. **What is left is confirmation, not discovery:** the
  key numbers are **[Confirmed]** on t604x, t8140 and t605x and **[Probable]** on t8132
  and t8142 (§18 #1 and §11 #36), the bit-order / clock-edge byte pairing is
  **[Probable]** (§18 #4), and two call types remain **[Unknown]** (§11 #6).
- **§11 #31 and #34 — two per-part values nothing carries.** The four host-supplied
  firmware boot arguments, and the ASCII string the in-scope audio service announces.
  No published source and no in-scope board's platform description supplies either.

The class-C count below is therefore no longer a count of entries that cannot be
attempted at all. It is a count of entries that need the transport **exercised** — and
the transport is now specified, as is the property vocabulary that rides on it
(Section 18), so exercising it is implementation work rather than research. Section 18
adds 18 entries of its own, 15 of them class C, and almost all of them are read-back
confirmations of a specified interface rather than open searches.

Counted by the resolution each entry states for itself:

| Class | What resolving it needs | Entries | Share |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | Nothing beyond what is already available: the platform hardware description, the public counterpart datasheets, host-owned I²C and GPIO with the parts powered but no audio stream, or bench measurement of a discrete part | 96 | 30% |
| **B** | A live machine with audio **already running** — answerable by observation of a system that is already playing or capturing, without the observer being able to start it | 110 | 35% |
| **C** | The coprocessor transport itself: exchanging or decoding messages, or opening and configuring a stream | 109 | 35% |

Shares are rounded to the nearest per cent.

So: **109 entries (35%) require the transport to be exercised**, and **219 entries
(70%) cannot be closed by the driver under development until a stream runs**, because
it cannot otherwise put the hardware into the state the probe requires. The transport
is specified, so those 109 are now implementable rather than blocked; what they still
rest on is §11 #26, the one-boot confirmation of the register map. **[Inferred]** —
the classification is taken from the resolution each entry states; entries whose
resolution admits more than one route are placed in the most demanding class.

## Dependency structure

```
       §11.2 + §11.4 specify the transport; §11.4.7 specifies the start
                            |
        §11 #31  the four firmware boot arguments  (set alig before anything)
                            |
        §11 #26  confirm the register offsets on an in-scope die  (one boot)
                            |
                 the transport runs
                            |
        +-------------------+--------------------+
        |                   |                    |
   §11 #27,#28,#29     §11 #34             §11 #16,#17,#18
   reset values,       announce string       watchdog, restart
   FIFO depth,                               and crash behaviour
   t604x 2nd set
        |                   |                    |
        +---------+---------+--------------------+
                  |
        a CAPTURE stream can be opened and a link runs
                  |
                  +------ §11 #36, §15 #1, §18 #1/#4/#15  confirm the
                  |        playback vocabulary's key numbers on t8132/t8142
                  |
  +---------------+---------------+---------------+---------------+
  |               |               |               |               |
 §3 serial      §2 clocking     §4/§5 data     §8/§9 sense     §12 capture
 controller     and power       path timing    and protection   and isolation
 behaviour      behaviour       under load     under load
```

Three groups sit **outside** this tree and can be worked in parallel from day one,
because they need no coprocessor cooperation:

- **The discrete parts.** Everything reached over host-owned I²C — the amplifier
  register file and the jack codec register file — belongs to the host on every machine
  in scope except the A18 Pro machine, whose amplifier has no control bus at all.
  Sections 7 and 10 are largely closable without the transport.
- **Platform-description decoding.** Section 16's per-machine entries, Section 1's
  property decodes and Section 6's pin maps are answered from the firmware-supplied
  hardware description and from board inspection.
- **Public documentation lookups.** A number of entries in Sections 7, 9 and 10 are
  closed by a vendor datasheet section rather than by probing at all.

## On tracing the coprocessor's own bus activity — read before planning §3, §11 or §18 work

Several entries concern registers that the **coprocessor** programs and the host does
not: the per-cluster clock and frame-sync generator resets (§18 #8), the serialiser
shift-buffer block (§18 #10), the low-power-complex agent fields (§18 #13), and parts of
the serialiser map (§3 #4, #5, #6, #7). It is worth stating plainly, because it shapes
the plan:

**There is no established method for tracing the coprocessor's own MMIO accesses.**
Host-side trapping — the technique every other probe in this document relies on — sees
accesses made by the application processor. The coprocessor reaches the audio island over
the fabric and not through anything the host mediates, so a host-side trap does not
observe it. No entry in this document should be written as "trace the coprocessor", and
the four that were have been rewritten.

**What is available instead, and its exact limits.** Three methods, in order of
usefulness:

1. **Host read-back of the same registers, differenced across a coprocessor-initiated
   change.** Stop a stream, snapshot the block; start it through the coprocessor,
   snapshot again; change one quantity at a time and snapshot after each. This gives
   register *contents* and, by differencing, field *positions* — it does not give
   ordering, and it does not show a write that the coprocessor later overwrites.
   **Available only on t8132, t8140 and t8142**, whose serial-audio region address is
   published (§3 §3.4.2) and whose `AUDIO_P` power-state register the host can reach
   (§3 §3.4.1). **Not available on t604x or t605x**, where no power-domain address is
   published — entries resolvable only this way are therefore **unresolvable on the
   Pro/Max dies** and must be answered on a base-die machine and carried across at
   **[Probable]**.
2. **Observation at the pins.** A logic analyser on the I2S/TDM lines gives frame length,
   frame-sync pulse width, bit-clock frequency, data delay and slot occupancy directly,
   without any register access at all. This is the authoritative method for everything
   about the *waveform* and is independent of method 1.
3. **Read-back through the interface itself.** Property key `701` returns the
   coprocessor's own current stream-configuration record (§18 §18.3.1), and key `705`
   reports whether it may still be changed. For any field that appears in both the
   message and a register, this answers the question without touching the register.
   Prefer it: it is available on every SoC in scope, including t604x and t605x.

**Plan accordingly:** an entry whose only route is method 1 is gated on §3 #1 (confirming
the serial audio controller base address) and is restricted to three of the five SoCs.
Entries answerable by method 3 are not gated on §3 at all and belong in phase 3.

## Recommended execution order

### Phase 0 — before any hardware is driven (blocking, safety)

The 25 entries marked ☠ must be resolved for the machine in question before its
speakers are driven. They are not ordered with the rest: they are a precondition on
output, not a step in the investigation.

| Entry | Subject |
|---|---|
| §7 #1 | The gain strap on the t8140 machine (j700). |
| §7 #2 | Whether the in-scope generations still require the undocumented amplifier writes to avoid an unrecoverable over-current failure. |
| §7 #3 | Whether the sense stream's raw-sample-to-physical-units convention is as assumed. |
| §7 #4 | What the platform's amplifier level should be if `speaker-config` cannot be read. |
| §7 #6 | Which of the two sense slot bytes is current and which is voltage — **[Probable], not settled**. |
| §7 #18 | Whether the supply-tracking limiter is in fact disabled. |
| §8 #1 | Which amplifier does each `speaker-config` record describe, and does the coprocessor's serialiser assignment agree with it? |
| §8 #2 | is the sense stream actually valid before the host trusts it? |
| §8 #3 | what values belong in `MISC_CFG1[5] OCE_RETRY`, `LIM_CFG0/1`, `LIM_MAX_ATTN` and `ICLA_CFG0/1`? |
| §8 #4 | On j700 only — what is the unit of `speaker-cpms-bgd_100ms`, and is 1363 / 5453 per channel or for the pair? |
| §8 #5 | on j700 only — what are the actual driver parameters? |
| §8 #6 | the per-unit Thiele–Small calibration record layout. |
| §8 #7 | Which of the two 16-bit words per amplifier is current and which is voltage. |
| §8 #8 | which capture channels carry the tweeters on the six-amplifier MacBook Pro chassis? |
| §9 #4 | The trim-gain index mapping. |
| §9 #5 | Which sense slot is current and which is voltage — the same question, from the calibration side. |
| §9 #6 | Per-transducer thermal parameters for the 13-inch MacBook Air M4 and M5. |
| §9 #9 | The GAIN_SLOT strap value on the A18 Pro machine. |
| §9 #12 | Whether the displacement/excursion model is ever enabled at runtime on the closed-loop machines. |
| §9 #13 | Numeric limit values for the A18 Pro machine's loudspeaker model. |
| §14 #7 | Does the post-resume sense-stream defect observed on M1–M3 persist on M4 and later, and what state is not restored? |
| §14 #13 | What are the addresses of the CS42L84 registers that are established as existing but not publicly located? |
| §14 #16 | What is the coprocessor's power-state value set on M4-and-later firmware, and does the quiesce/sleep/idle transition table still hold? |
| §18 #17 | Which of an amplifier's two sense slots carries voltage and which carries current. |
| §18 #18 | Whether the coprocessor's built-in record and the host's derived record can ever disagree on a machine's slot geometry. |

Phase 0 also includes the two readbacks this document names as mandatory rather than
as questions: the amplifier receive-slot and transmit-slot readback on a MacBook Pro
chassis machine before any speaker is driven, and the per-channel impedance check
before the first unmute on any machine with a sense return.

**§7 #6, §8 #7, §9 #5, §18 #17 are one question seen from four sides** — which member
of each sense pair carries voltage. They are settled together by one bench measurement:
drive one amplifier into two different known load resistances and observe which
received channel changes. Until then, do not mix this document's slot map with the
channel labels of an existing published speaker-protection configuration; see the third
hazard in `00_intro.md`.

### Phase 1 — stand the transport up (do this first, everything else waits on it)

The transport is specified (§11.2, §11.4, §11.4.7), so phase 1 is now implementation
plus a short list of confirmations and missing per-part values, in this order:

1. **§11 #31** — the four host-supplied firmware boot arguments, `alig` first. **This is
   ahead of the register-map confirmation deliberately.** No in-scope board's platform
   description carries these values, and a wrong shared-buffer alignment produces a
   coprocessor that boots, handshakes, and then mis-parses every ring with no diagnostic
   at all — a failure that presents as a transport bug and will consume more time than
   everything below it put together. Settle it, or at least pin a candidate and a
   validation check (§11 §11.5.4), before interpreting any transport result as a register
   problem.
2. **§11 #26** — confirm the mailbox register offsets on an in-scope die. One boot with
   `reg[0]` trapped. Everything after this rests on it.
3. **§11 #27** — reset values of the status and CPU-control registers, read in the same
   boot, before and after the run-bit write.
4. **§11 #34** — the ASCII string the in-scope audio service announces. A driver that
   matches the wrong one fails silently.
5. §11 #29 (and #3) — t604x's second mailbox channel set, since a driver written for one
   set loses messages on Pro/Max parts.
6. §11 #28, #5, #38 — FIFO depth, and the reply timeout a driver must impose because the
   interface defines none.
7. **§11 #36, §15 #1, §18 #1, §18 #15** — confirm the playback property vocabulary on
   the die you are targeting. The vocabulary itself is specified in Section 18; what
   needs doing first is a get of keys `401`, `402`, `704`, `705` and `701` on the
   endpoint, which returns the endpoint's state codes, its capabilities and the
   concrete cluster objects it is bound to in one exchange. On t604x, t8140 and t605x
   this is a confirmation; on t8132 and t8142 the key numbers are **[Probable]** and
   should be confirmed before they are trusted. Capture does not need this;
   **speaker output does**, so schedule it before phase 4.

Items 1–6 gate phases 3 to 6. Item 7 gates playback specifically.

### Phase 2 — in parallel with phase 1, needing no transport

The class-A entries, which are the ones that can absorb effort while phase 1 is in
progress: Section 10 (11 of 18 entries), Section 16 (6 of 10), Section 13 (10 of 15),
Section 4 (10 of 25) and Section 3 (12 of 33). Most of Section 7's amplifier questions
are host-I²C work and belong here too.

### Phase 3 — once a stream can be opened

Section 3 (serialiser behaviour under load, FIFO depth, underflow semantics),
Section 2 (clock tree and power-domain behaviour), Section 5 (interrupt causes that
only a running channel raises), Section 4's load-dependent entries, and the bulk of
Section 18 — which is almost entirely read-backs of a running endpoint's key-`701`
record and its capability probes.

### Phase 4 — once a stream runs reliably

Section 8 and Section 9 — the sense path and the protection model. These are the
entries with the highest consequence of error and they need a stable stream to
measure against, which is why they come after phase 3 despite their priority.

### Phase 5 — capture, isolation and display audio

Section 12 and Section 13. Section 12's isolated-capture entries may prove
unresolvable from the normal world; that outcome is itself a deliverable.

### Phase 6 — power, sleep and fault behaviour

Section 14 and the remainder of Section 15. These need every other layer working,
because they are about what survives a transition.

## Open questions

This section is an index; the entries it indexes carry their own open questions. Two
belong to the index itself. A third — which entries the always-on fabric access-control
blocks close — is **settled**: those blocks close §3 #26 and §4 #14 (the secure base
DMA controller aperture), narrow §4 #2, §11 #10 and §11 #14, and add twelve entries of
their own across Sections 3, 4 and 11. The counts above include all of that.

**Section 18's effect on the counts is also included.** It adds 18 entries; it answers
§11 #36 and §15 #1 down to three narrow residuals, settles §11 #12 (the clock model),
§2 #10 and §8 #11 (the speaker frame is 250 bit clocks at 12.000 MHz) and most of
§11 #11 (the link descriptor's fields), narrows §11 #7 and §12 #8, and
promotes §7 #6, §8 #7 and §9 #5 from "settled" back to open and **☠** — the
voltage/current attribution rests on a single family of sources and cannot be settled
from the controller side at all.

1. **Whether the class-B set really is answerable by observation alone.** Class B
   assumes a machine can be brought to a running-audio state by means other than the
   driver under development, and that the relevant registers and buses can be observed
   in that state. Where that turns out not to hold for a given entry, it belongs in
   class C and the phase-1 dependency grows. *How to resolve:* attempt one class-B
   entry per section early and record which were actually answerable.
2. **Whether any entry is unresolvable in principle rather than merely unresolved.**
   Several capture-path entries concern hardware behind an isolation boundary with no
   normal-world translation path at all (§11 §11.8, §12). An entry that cannot be
   answered from the normal world should be marked as such rather than left in the
   queue indefinitely. *How to resolve:* review §12 and §11 #9/#15 after phase 5 and
   reclassify the ones that proved closed to observation.

# 18. Coprocessor firmware ABI — speaker, clocking and slot geometry

## Baseline

Three things this section is measured against.

1. **The M1–M3 serial audio controller**, documented upstream in Linux
   (`sound/soc/apple/mca.c`): six identical clusters, each carrying a
   master-clock gate and divider, a frame-sync generator with separate high and
   low period counters, four serialiser units each with a configuration word, a
   data-delay word and a pair of slot-mask register halves, and a per-cluster
   output-pin routing group. On M1–M3 the **host** owns that block through its
   own MMIO aperture and programmes every one of those registers directly.
2. **The M1–M3 always-on coprocessor**, which already contained a second,
   complete serial-audio complex and its own DMA engine (§3 §3.9), but whose
   host-facing interface exposed only the pulse-density microphone front end
   (§11 §11.4.6).
3. **The public counterpart of the speaker amplifier**, TAS2764, whose TDM slot
   and level registers are the destination of the per-amplifier half of the slot
   map (§7 §7.2).

Section 11 establishes the transport — mailbox, rings, framed calls, service
resolution and the request framing of the audio service. **This section is what
rides on top of it:** the property and call vocabulary a stream endpoint
accepts, the single message that replaced the serial-audio cluster's register
set, the clocking and slot-geometry models that message expresses, the register
interfaces the coprocessor drives on the far side of it, and the configuration
the coprocessor holds built in. It does not restate the transport; every
transport-layer fact referenced below is given in §11 §11.2 and §11 §11.4.

## Summary of differences

| Element | M1–M3 | t8132 / t604x | t8140 | t8142 / t605x |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Serial-audio cluster programming | direct MMIO writes by the host | **one 109-byte configuration message per stream endpoint** (property key `701`) | same | same |
| Frame-sync generator programming | two host-written period registers | two 32-bit phase counters inside key `701` | same | same |
| Serialiser slot mask, per direction | two 32-bit register halves, of which only the low half is programmed; slots-per-frame field 4 bits, so at most 16 slots addressable | both halves programmed, slots-per-frame field **6 bits** — the mask is effectively **64 bits** and a 64-slot frame is expressible | same | same |
| Slot-width encoding | 16 / 20 / 24 / 32 bit | **plus 8 bit** (a fifth, previously undocumented code) | same | same |
| Master-clock-to-bit-clock divider field | 4 bits, only the value `1` ever written | **5 bits**, legal range 1…31, plus a new source-select field in the same register | same | same |
| Master-clock pad routing | none — one selector for bit clock and frame sync together | **second, independent 3-bit master-clock pad selector** | same | same |
| Synchronised multi-serialiser start | absent | **new aligned-enable block**: set/clear masks plus a single trigger | same | same |
| Receive data-input select | at serialiser block `+0x04` | moved to serialiser block `+0x14` | same | same |
| Receive loopback source select | not in the published register map | **new**, serialiser block `+0x18` | same | same |
| Numerically controlled oscillator | host-programmed increments through its own aperture | coprocessor-owned; the host names a **frequency in hertz** and a **source class** and nothing else | same, and the oscillator node is still enumerated without a `reg` | same |
| Stream device identifiers `spkr`, `cout`, `cin `, `lpbk` | not accepted by the coprocessor | accepted | accepted | accepted |
| Built-in default stream configuration set | absent | **present, one record per stream family, per SoC** | present | present |
| Speaker protection, limiting, excursion, thermal or gain computation on the coprocessor | absent | **still absent** | still absent | still absent |
| Per-amplifier slot assignment | host, over the control bus | **host, over the control bus — it never crosses the coprocessor interface** | n/a (no control bus) | same |

One sentence: **the serial-audio cluster's register set was replaced by one
fixed-layout message carrying the same fields, and the binding of a slot to a
physical loudspeaker never travels over that message at all.**

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 18.1 Scope, ownership and confidence basis

### 18.1.1 Confidence basis — read this before using any annotation below

Confidence in this section is assigned as follows.

- A fact that travels in a message is visible from **both ends of the
  interface**. Where both ends agree, that is two independent lines and the fact
  is **[Confirmed]**.
- Facts about registers inside the serial-audio complex, which no host on an
  in-scope SoC can read at all (§11 §11.6.1), carry **one** line. They are
  marked **[Confirmed]** only where the same field also has a published M1–M3
  counterpart that agrees; where the field is new at the M4 generation they are
  **[Probable]**.
- A fact taken from a **single published convention** is one line, not two. The
  voltage/current attribution of the two sense slots is such a fact and is not
  asserted here (§18.5.5, §8 §8.2.1).
- Every entry names the SoCs it is established for. The presence of the same
  vocabulary on a further SoC is **[Probable]** for that SoC, never
  **[Confirmed]**.

The public serial-audio implementations target **M1 through M3**. Nothing that
rests on them alone is established for the SoCs in scope.

### 18.1.2 Where the control boundary lies

Per stream endpoint of the coprocessor-side audio controller. **[Confirmed]**
for t8132, t604x, t8140, t8142 and t605x.

| Function | Owner | How |
|---|---|---|
| Serial-link geometry: slot count, slot width, sample width, transmit and receive slot masks, data delay, bit order, clock edges | coprocessor | key `701` |
| Frame-sync period and duty | coprocessor | key `701` (two phase counters) |
| Master-clock frequency and source selection | coprocessor | key `701` (frequency in Hz + source four-character code) |
| Master-clock-to-bit-clock divider | coprocessor | key `701` (one byte) |
| Output-pin routing masks | coprocessor | reported through key `701`; the host supplies them only as a compatibility constraint |
| Master-clock output enable | coprocessor | key `703` |
| Serialiser and FIFO reset | coprocessor | key `702` |
| Stream power and run ladder | coprocessor | key `202`, target states named by keys `401` / `402` |
| Audio power-domain and clock-gate sequencing | coprocessor | implicit in the key-`202` ladder; the host has no power control over any audio domain (§2 §2.6, §11 §11.6.1) |
| DMA channel programming, buffers, IOMMU | **host** | direct MMIO (§4) |
| Amplifier register programming — playback slot, sense slots, level, DC blocker, brown-out, over-power | **host** | control bus (§6, §7) |
| Jack-codec register programming | **host** | control bus (§10) |
| Loudspeaker-module identification pins | **host** | GPIO (§6) |
| Sense-return data path | **host** DMA; the coprocessor only serialises it | §8 |

**Nothing amplifier-specific, and no protection or limiting parameter, crosses
the host↔coprocessor interface on any in-scope SoC.** [Confirmed] — §18.6.2.

### 18.1.3 Resource identifier space

Every clock, generator, serialiser and pad group inside the serial-audio complex
is named by a **four-character code**. These codes are the only handles that
cross the interface: there are no indices and no addresses in the message.

| Code form | Object | Index encoding |
|---|---|---|
| `mck`*d* | master-clock generator of cluster *d* | one decimal digit, `0`…`5` |
| `ckg`*d* | bit-clock generator of cluster *d* | one decimal digit, `0`…`5` |
| `syn`*d* | frame-sync generator of cluster *d* | one decimal digit, `0`…`5` |
| `ms`*dd* | serialiser unit | **two** decimal digits, value 10·*d₁* + *d₀*, range `00`…`23` |
| `nco`*d* | numerically controlled oscillator instance | one decimal digit, `0`…`3` observed |
| `xi0 ` | fixed reference oscillator | — |
| `anco` | oscillator *class* — any instance | — |
| `i2s`*d* | pad-group clock input of port *d* | one decimal digit |
| `imk`*h* | master-clock output of pad group *h* | one **hexadecimal** digit, `0`…`f` |
| `isc`*h* | bit-clock and frame-sync output of pad group *h* | one hexadecimal digit, `0`…`f` |
| `null` | unpopulated slot in the record | — |

[Confirmed] for t8132, t604x, t8140, t8142 and t605x: the index rule is
arithmetic in the identifier itself, and the same identifiers appear in the
built-in configuration set of §18.7.

**Serialiser numbering is two-dimensional.** Twenty-four units numbered `00`…`23`
correspond to six clusters of four units each: unit *u* belongs to cluster
⌊*u*/4⌋ and is unit *u* mod 4 within it. This matches both the four-serialiser
cluster layout of the M1–M3 block and the six master-clock power domains the
platform description enumerates per SoC (§2 §2.3). [Confirmed]

A serialiser **need not belong to the cluster whose generators drive it.** The
A18 Pro speaker bus uses serialiser `12` — cluster 3, unit 0 — driven by
cluster 0's bit-clock and frame-sync generators. Cross-cluster binding is what
the source-select fields of §18.8.1 and §18.8.2 and the pad multiplexer of
§18.8.3 exist for. [Confirmed] t8140.

### 18.1.4 The identifier-subset binding rule

A requested code is accepted for an object **iff every bit set in the requested
code is also set in the object's own code**:

```
(requested_id & ~object_id) == 0
```

Because the codes are ASCII with NUL padding, a class name is a strict subset of
any instance name that extends it — `ckg` (`0x636B6700`) binds to `ckg0`
(`0x636B6730`), `ms` (`0x6D730000`) binds to any `ms`*dd*, and `nco`
(`0x6E636F00`) binds to `nco0`…`nco3`. The special code `null`
(`0x6E756C6C`) marks an unpopulated slot and is exempt. [Confirmed] — visible
from both ends of the interface.

Two consequences a driver must respect:

- **Sending a class name is the correct way to say "any instance."** The get of
  key `701` after the set returns the concrete instance the coprocessor bound.
- **Sending `0` is not the same thing.** Zero is a subset of everything and is
  the host's "leave as is"; it does not request a binding.

A code that matches no object is rejected silently: no error is returned
against the field that named it.

## 18.2 Call and property vocabulary

The framing of a call, its header layout, the `0x34`-byte get/set property header
and the reply status word are in §11 §11.4.6 and are not restated. What follows
is the **vocabulary**: which call types and which property keys exist, on which
generations, and what each payload contains.

### 18.2.1 Call types

| Call type | Purpose | Established for |
|---|---|---|
| `0xC3000001` | probe device | **M1–M3 only**; not in use on any in-scope SoC |
| `0xC3000002` | **attach device** — must precede any property call for a device identifier | M1–M3 **and** all five in-scope SoCs [Confirmed] |
| `0xC3000003` | **[Unknown]** | **M1–M3 only**; not in use in scope |
| `0xC3000004` | **get device property** | in scope, all five [Confirmed] |
| `0xC3000005` | **set device property** | in scope, all five [Confirmed] |
| `0xC3000006` | **[Unknown]** — addressed to the service, not to a device | in scope, all five [Confirmed present, meaning Unknown] |
| `0xC3000008` | **[Unknown]** — used by the low-power-microphone and voice-trigger devices | in scope, all five [Confirmed present, meaning Unknown] |

Unchanged from §11 §11.4.6; reproduced because the property table below is read
against it. The whole serial-audio vocabulary of this section travels on
`0xC3000004` and `0xC3000005` only.

### 18.2.2 Property keys

**The key space is per device.** The same numeric key addressed to two different
device identifiers is two different properties — key `200` is a 632-byte
front-end configuration on the pulse-density device and a 4-byte state query on
a serial-audio stream endpoint. [Confirmed]

Keys addressed to the **pulse-density front end and the low-power input device**,
established for the baseline generations; their *layouts* carry over, their
*values* must be rederived per machine (§11 §11.4.6):

| Key (dec) | Key (hex) | Target | Direction | Payload | Size | Established for |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `200` | `0xC8` | `pdm0` | set | pulse-density front-end configuration | 632 B | **M1–M3**; layout carries over, source on M4+ **[Unknown]** |
| `203` | `0xCB` | — | — | **[Unknown]** | — | **M1–M3** |
| `210` | `0xD2` | `pdm0` | set | standard decimator configuration, 32-bit coefficients | 496 B | **M1–M3** (superseded by `212` from the M3 generation) |
| `212` | `0xD4` | `pdm0` | set | high-rate decimator configuration, 64-bit coefficients | 8 200 B | M1–M3 **and** in scope |
| `301` | `0x12D` | `lpai` | set | low-power input channel configuration | 16 B | **M1–M3**; layout carries over |
| `302` | `0x12E` | — | get | stream format descriptor | 16 B | M1–M3 [Probable]; in scope [Confirmed] — §18.11 |

Keys addressed to a **serial-audio stream endpoint** (`spkr`, `cout`, `cin `,
`lpbk`, `lilb`, `hpai`, `tap `, `sllb`). These are **established for the SoCs in
scope** and have no M1–M3 counterpart, because on M1–M3 the host programmed the
equivalent registers itself:

| Key (dec) | Key (hex) | Direction | Payload | Size | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `200` | `0xC8` | get | four-character code | 4 B | current device state (the `idle → pw1 → pwrd` ladder of §11 §11.4.6) |
| `202` | `0xCA` | set | power setting | 48 B | state transition — §18.2.4 |
| `401` | `0x191` | get | four-character code | 4 B | the state code meaning *clocks and registers on, no data* |
| `402` | `0x192` | get | four-character code | 4 B | the state code meaning *data flowing* |
| `508` | `0x1FC` | set | u32 | 4 B | routing-switch request; written `0xFFFFFFFF` once at attach time, failure tolerated |
| `701` | `0x2BD` | get **and** set | serial-audio cluster configuration | **109 B** | §18.3 — the centrepiece |
| `702` | `0x2BE` | set | u32, value `1` | 4 B | reset the stream's serialisers and FIFOs, and restore it to the built-in record of §18.7 |
| `703` | `0x2BF` | get and set | u32 | 4 B | master-clock enable; **bit 0** = enabled. On a set, the value returned is the resulting state |
| `704` | `0x2C0` | get | u32 | 4 B | capability: non-zero = this endpoint performs routing validation |
| `705` | `0x2C1` | get | u32 | 4 B | capability: non-zero = this endpoint's configuration is immutable |

**[Confirmed] for t604x, t8140 and t605x** — the key numbers and the 109-byte
length are corroborated at both ends of the interface. **[Probable] for t8132
and t8142**: the same keys are present and the record layout is identical on all
five, but the key numbers are corroborated at one end only.

Notes:

- Key `701` is **read-modify-write**. A get returns the coprocessor's current
  record; a set must carry a record *compatible* with it (§18.3.3); the set
  returns the merged record.
- Keys `704` and `705` are capability probes. An endpoint reporting `705`
  non-zero rejects any key-`701` set whose record differs from the one it
  already holds in any byte except the direction byte. That is how a shared
  cluster — for example a loopback endpoint listening on another endpoint's bus
  — is protected from a second configurer.
- Key `703` is meaningful only on an endpoint whose configuration names a master
  clock **and** whose master-clock pad-routing mask is non-zero. Elsewhere the
  key is absent and the get fails.
- A get of key `701` with a buffer shorter than 109 bytes fails; the payload
  length field of the property header is in/out.

### 18.2.3 State codes are discovered, not assumed

Unlike the capture path, whose ladder `idle → pw1 → pwrd` is fixed (§11
§11.4.6), a serial-audio stream endpoint **reports the two upper state codes it
uses**: key `401` for *clocks and registers on, no data*, key `402` for *data
flowing*. `idle` remains the fixed bottom of the ladder and is the only code the
host compares against literally.

A driver should read `401` and `402` at attach time and use the returned codes.
**[Confirmed]** that the codes are read from these keys; **[Inferred]** that
they are `pw1 ` and `pwrd`, by agreement with the capture ladder. See open
question 15.

### 18.2.4 Key `202` — power setting, 48 bytes

This refines §11 §11.4.6, which records the payload as 44 bytes with an
unexplained flag. The table there already spans 48 bytes; **48 is the correct
length**, and two fields are now identified.

| Offset | Size | Field | Bits / units | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | u32 | device identifier | four-character code | agrees with the baseline |
| `0x04` | u32 | request sequence number | monotonic per device, first request = `1` | agrees with the baseline |
| `0x08` | u64 | **host timestamp** | one 64-bit quantity, not two reserved fields | **refines** the baseline. [Probable] |
| `0x10` | u32 | reserved | `0` | agrees |
| `0x14` | u32 | target state code | four-character code; default before the host fills it in is `err `, which is therefore never a legal target | agrees |
| `0x18` | u32 | **direction mask** | **bit 0 = receive, bit 1 = transmit**; bits 31:2 reserved | **refines** the baseline's unexplained "flag". [Confirmed] |
| `0x1c` | 20 B | reserved | `0` | agrees |

The direction-mask reading subsumes the baseline observation that a capture
device uses `0` on the way to the intermediate state and `1` on the way to the
streaming state: the value is the set of directions being started or stopped,
and a capture device starts only the receive direction. [Confirmed]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 18.3 The stream-configuration record — property key `701`

This single message replaced the serial-audio cluster's entire register set at
the M4 generation. It is **109 bytes** (`0x6D`), **packed with no internal
alignment**, little-endian for all integers.

Every four-character code field holds the code with its **first character in the
most-significant byte** of the little-endian 32-bit word, so the four bytes
appear on the wire in reverse reading order. This is the same convention as the
device identifier at body offset `0x28` of the enclosing call (§11 §11.4.6) and
the same convention the platform description uses: a code that reads `mck` is
the word `0x6D636B00` and occupies the bytes `00 6B 63 6D`.

### 18.3.1 Layout

| Offset | Size | Field | Units / encoding |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | 4 B | cluster / configuration object id | four-character code. Written `0` by the host; the coprocessor fills it in |
| `0x04` | 4 B | **master-clock** object id | `mck` when a master clock is present, else `0` |
| `0x08` | 4 B | master-clock **source** id | `xi0 `, `anco`, `nco`, `null` or `0` — §18.4.1 |
| `0x0c` | u32 | master-clock frequency | **Hz** |
| `0x10` | u32 | master-clock pad-routing mask | bitmap over pad groups; `0` or `0xFFFFFFFF` from the host |
| `0x14` | 4 B | **clock-generator** object id | `ckg` or `null` |
| `0x18` | 4 B | clock-generator **source** id | `mck` or `null` |
| `0x1c` | u8 | **clock-generator divider** | master clock ÷ this = bit clock. Range **1…31** |
| `0x1d` | u32 | bit-clock pad-routing mask | bitmap over pad groups; `0` or `0xFFFFFFFF` from the host |
| `0x21` | 4 B | **frame-sync generator** object id | always `syn` |
| `0x25` | 4 B | frame-sync **source** id | `ckg` when a master clock is present, `i2s` when it is not (clock-consumer mode) |
| `0x29` | u8 | frame-sync active edge | `1` = rising, `0` = falling |
| `0x2a` | u8 | frame-sync pulse polarity | `1` = high pulse, `0` = low pulse |
| `0x2b` | u32 | frame-sync **phase-0 count** | **bit clocks** — the assertion length |
| `0x2f` | u32 | frame-sync **phase-1 count** | **bit clocks** — the de-assertion length. Frame length = phase 0 + phase 1 |
| `0x33` | 4 B | **transmit serialiser** object id | `ms` (NUL-padded) or `null` |
| `0x37` | u8 | transmit bit order | `1` = LSB first, `0` = MSB first |
| `0x38` | u8 | transmit clock edge | `1` = rising, `0` = falling |
| `0x39` | u32 | transmit data delay | **bit clocks** after the frame-sync edge |
| `0x3d` | u64 | **transmit slot mask** | bit *n* = slot *n* is transmitted. Zero-extended from the 32-bit platform descriptor field |
| `0x45` | u8 | transmit **slot width** | **bits** — 8, 16, 20, 24 or 32 |
| `0x46` | u8 | transmit **sample width** | **bits**; `0` when equal to the slot width |
| `0x47` | u32 | transmit serialiser pad-routing mask | bitmap over pad groups |
| `0x4b` | u32 | transmit loopback-pin routing mask | written `0` by the host on every in-scope endpoint |
| `0x4f` | u8 | reserved | written `0` |
| `0x50` | 4 B | **receive serialiser** object id | `ms` or `null` |
| `0x54` | u8 | receive bit order | `1` = LSB first, `0` = MSB first |
| `0x55` | u8 | receive clock edge | `1` = rising, `0` = falling |
| `0x56` | u32 | receive data delay | **bit clocks** |
| `0x5a` | u64 | **receive slot mask** | bit *n* = slot *n* is captured |
| `0x62` | u8 | receive **slot width** | **bits** |
| `0x63` | u8 | receive **sample width** | **bits**; `0` when equal to the slot width |
| `0x64` | u32 | receive serialiser pad-routing mask | bitmap over pad groups |
| `0x68` | u32 | receive loopback-pin routing mask | bitmap; non-zero on at least one endpoint |
| `0x6c` | u8 | reserved | written `0` |

[Confirmed] for the layout and every field offset. [Confirmed] for t604x,
t8140 and t605x;
[Probable] for t8132 and t8142 (§18.2.2).

**Legal slot and sample widths are 8, 16, 20, 24 and 32 bits.** Every other
value is rejected. The 8-bit code is new at the M4 generation (§18.8.4).
[Confirmed]

**Neither the frame rate nor the bit-clock rate is carried.** Both are implied:

```
frame_rate     = frequency@0x0c / (divider@0x1c * (phase0@0x2b + phase1@0x2f))
bit_clock_rate = frequency@0x0c / divider@0x1c
frame_bits     = phase0@0x2b + phase1@0x2f
```

[Confirmed]

### 18.3.2 The four flag bytes

Bytes `0x29`, `0x2a` (frame sync) and `0x37`/`0x38`, `0x54`/`0x55` (per
direction) are the only bit-level fields in the record, and each is a whole byte
carrying one boolean in bit 0.

| Byte | Value `0` | Value `1` | Drives |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0x29` frame-sync active edge | falling | rising | frame-sync generator configuration, bit 9 (§18.8.2) |
| `0x2a` frame-sync pulse polarity | low pulse | high pulse | frame-sync generator configuration, bit 10 (§18.8.2) |
| `0x37` / `0x54` bit order | MSB first | LSB first | serialiser configuration, bit 11 (§18.8.4) |
| `0x38` / `0x55` clock edge | falling | rising | serialiser configuration, bit 10 (§18.8.4) |

**The polarity bytes and their register bits run in opposite senses.** A message
byte of `0` corresponds to the frame-sync configuration bit **set**, and a byte
of `1` to it **clear** (§18.8.2). [Confirmed] for that correspondence; the
physical sense of each bit is [Probable].

**The pairing of `0x37`/`0x38` and `0x54`/`0x55` to bit order and clock edge is
[Probable], not [Confirmed].** There are exactly two such flags per direction on
both sides of the interface and they drive the serialiser's bit-order and
bit-clock-edge fields, which corroborates the *set* but not the *order*; and on
every in-scope link the value of the byte at `0x38`/`0x55` also tracks the
port's clock-provider role, which is hard to reconcile with a pure edge
setting.
Getting them the wrong way round inverts either the sample bit order or the
sampling edge on every slot — audible as noise, not as silence. See open
question 4.

### 18.3.3 The merge rule for a key-`701` set

A set is **not a blind overwrite**. The host reads the current record and, for
every object-id field (`0x04`, `0x08`, `0x14`, `0x18`, `0x21`, `0x25`, `0x33`,
`0x50`), the record it sends must satisfy the subset rule of §18.1.4.

The pad-routing masks (`0x10`, `0x1d`, `0x47`, `0x4b`, `0x64`, `0x68`) are
compared only for **presence** — zero versus non-zero, not value — and only when
the endpoint reports key `704` non-zero.

The merged record takes these fields from the **requested** record:

`0x0c` (master-clock frequency), `0x1c`, `0x29`–`0x2a`, `0x2b`–`0x32`,
`0x37`–`0x38`, `0x39`–`0x3c`, `0x3d`–`0x44`, `0x45`–`0x46`, `0x54`–`0x55`,
`0x56`–`0x59`, `0x5a`–`0x61`, `0x62`–`0x63`.

Everything else — the object ids, the six routing masks and the reserved bytes —
is retained from the **coprocessor's** record. [Confirmed]

### 18.3.4 Correspondence with the M1–M3 register set

Every field of the message has a counterpart in the register set the host
programmed directly on M1–M3. This is the concrete form of the delta: **the same
quantities, moved behind a message.**

| Message field | M1–M3 counterpart |
|---|---|
| `0x04`, `0x10` | cluster master-clock enable and its pin-group enable |
| `0x0c`, `0x1c` | the cluster's master-clock divider field plus the oscillator's programmed rate |
| `0x08`, `0x18` | the frame-sync generator's clock-source selector and the port clock selector |
| `0x2b`, `0x2f` | the frame-sync generator's high-period and low-period counters |
| `0x29`, `0x2a` | the frame-sync polarity bits |
| `0x37`, `0x54` | serialiser configuration, LSB-first bit |
| `0x38`, `0x55` | serialiser configuration, bit-clock polarity bit |
| `0x39`, `0x56` | transmit / receive serialiser data-delay ("bit start") register |
| `0x3d`, `0x5a` | transmit / receive serialiser slot-mask register pair (widened, §18.8.4) |
| `0x45`, `0x62` | serialiser configuration, slot-width field |
| `0x46`, `0x63` | serialiser configuration, channel-count field together with the DMA-adapter padding fields |
| `0x10`, `0x1d`, `0x47`, `0x4b`, `0x64`, `0x68` | the per-cluster port enable, port clock select and port data select registers |

[Confirmed] for the correspondence.

### 18.3.5 Validity rules the record must satisfy

Checked before any transaction. A record that fails is refused without reaching
the hardware.

1. Slots per frame in 1…32 as expressed by the platform descriptor; the
   serialiser itself now accepts up to 64 (§18.8.4).
2. The index of the highest set bit of either slot mask must be **less than** the
   slot count.
3. popcount(mask) ≥ the corresponding channel count, per direction.
4. Sample width ≤ slot width, per direction.
5. (highest set slot index + 1) × slot width ≤ frame length, per direction.
6. Data delay < frame length; frame-sync pulse length ≤ frame length.
7. An explicitly given frame length must be ≥ slots × bits-per-slot and ≥
   channels × slot-width in both directions.
8. The master-clock invariant of §18.4.2 must hold exactly, with no remainder.
9. The frame-sync generator's source identifier and the clock generator's own
   identifier must be **equal** — a record naming `syn0` with `ckg1` is
   rejected. [Confirmed]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 18.4 Clocking path

### 18.4.1 Accepted master-clock frequencies and their sources

The host names a **frequency in hertz** and a **source class**. The coprocessor
selects the physical source, programmes it, and rejects any frequency outside a
fixed table of **nine**. The table is identical on t8132, t604x, t8140, t8142
and t605x. [Confirmed] — the same nine-entry table applies at both ends of the
interface, entry for entry.

| Master clock (Hz) | Required source id | Family |
|---|---|---|
| 24 000 000 | `xi0 ` | fixed reference |
| 12 288 000 | `anco` | oscillator, 48 kHz family (256 × 48 kHz) |
| 12 000 000 | `xi0 ` | fixed reference ÷ 2 |
| 6 144 000 | `anco` | oscillator, 48 kHz family (128 × 48 kHz) |
| 6 000 000 | `xi0 ` | fixed reference ÷ 4 |
| 5 644 800 | `anco` | oscillator, 44.1 kHz family (128 × 44.1 kHz) |
| 3 072 000 | `anco` | oscillator, 48 kHz family (64 × 48 kHz) |
| 3 000 000 | `xi0 ` | fixed reference ÷ 8 |
| 2 822 400 | `anco` | oscillator, 44.1 kHz family (64 × 44.1 kHz) |

**The pairing is exhaustive and enforced.** A request for an oscillator-family
frequency with the fixed-reference source, or the converse, is rejected; so is a
request whose named source cannot produce the requested frequency. [Confirmed]

The clock-generator source field at `0x18` additionally accepts the shorter form
`nco`, which the subset rule of §18.1.4 makes a prefix of `anco`. [Confirmed]

**The oscillator is addressed by name and frequency only.** No increment,
accumulator, coarse or fine ratio, or divider value crosses the interface, and
none is derived from the request beyond the frequency itself. The programming
model the M1–M3 oscillator exposed to the host
(`drivers/clk/clk-apple-nco.c`) is entirely internal from the M4 generation
onwards. [Confirmed] — corroborated by the platform description, which omits the
oscillator node entirely on t8132, t604x, t8142 and t605x and carries it on
t8140 with a `compatible` value and `clock-ids` but **no `reg`** (§2 §2.2).

### 18.4.2 The frame-geometry-plus-divider model, and the invariant

There are three programmed quantities and everything else follows from them: the
**master-clock frequency in Hz**, the **divider** (1…31), and the **two
frame-sync phase counts in bit clocks**.

```
bit_clock  = master_clock / divider
frame_bits = phase0 + phase1
frame_rate = bit_clock / frame_bits
```

and the invariant checked before any transaction, which must hold with **no
remainder**:

```
master_clock_Hz  ==  frame_bits  x  frame_rate  x  divider
```

[Confirmed] for the invariant and for the divider range. The division is
performed exactly and a non-integral result is rejected.

The realisable frame rates on an in-scope SoC are therefore exactly the set

```
rate = master_clock_Hz / (divider * (phase0 + phase1))
```

with `master_clock_Hz` drawn from the nine-entry table of §18.4.1, `divider` in
1…31, and `phase0 + phase1` the frame length in bit clocks. [Confirmed]

### 18.4.3 There is no sample-rate call

**No message anywhere in the interface carries a sample rate as a settable
quantity.** A rate request is expressed entirely through the geometry and
frequency fields of the key-`701` record:

1. The requested rate and the slot geometry give `frame_bits`.
2. Where the endpoint's platform descriptor pins a master-clock frequency, a
   driver takes that value and derives the divider as
   `master_clock / (frame_bits × rate)`; the division must be exact.
3. Where the descriptor leaves the master-clock frequency unpinned **and** the
   cluster's clock generator is sourced from the oscillator, a driver derives
   the required frequency as `frame_bits × rate × divider`; it must appear in
   the table of §18.4.1 **with the oscillator as its source**. A rate for which
   no exact solution exists cannot be expressed through key `701`.
4. The record is merged against the coprocessor's current record (§18.3.3) and
   set with key `701`.
5. The master clock is then enabled with key `703`.

The host specifies the master-clock frequency, the master-clock source by name,
the divider, the two phase counts, and the per-direction slot and sample widths.
It never specifies a bit-clock frequency or a frame rate directly. [Confirmed]

The **only** rate-shaped quantity that crosses the interface in the other
direction is the stream format descriptor returned by key `302` — four-character
format code, sample rate in Hz, channel count, bytes per sample, 16 bytes
(§18.11). That is a report, not a control.

### 18.4.4 Frame lengths the amplifier side can accept

The controller will produce any frame length the invariant admits. The
**amplifier** is the binding constraint on a speaker bus: its bit-clock-to-frame
ratio register takes one of fourteen codes.

| Frame (bit clocks) | Code | | Frame (bit clocks) | Code |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 16 | `0x00` | | 128 | `0x18` |
| 24 | `0x04` | | 192 | `0x1C` |
| 32 | `0x08` | | **250** | `0x30` |
| 48 | `0x0C` | | 256 | `0x20` |
| 64 | `0x10` | | 384 | `0x24` |
| 96 | `0x14` | | **500** | `0x34` |
| **125** | `0x2C` | | 512 | `0x28` |

[Confirmed] — the register and its codes are published for the counterpart part,
and the geometry the coprocessor's own built-in records carry (§18.7) selects
exactly these codes. The presence of the three **non-power-of-two** entries 125,
250 and 500 is what makes a 12.000 MHz fixed reference usable at 96 / 48 /
24 kHz, and it is independent corroboration of the frame length below.

**The six-amplifier speaker frame, stated unambiguously.** At 48 kHz it is
**250 bit clocks long**, the bit clock is **12.000 MHz** (the 12.000 MHz master
clock with divider 1), and of those 250 bit clocks:

| Direction | Data bit clocks | Content | Idle bit clocks |
|---|---|---|---|
| transmit (playback) | 192 | 6 slots × 32 bits, 24-bit samples left-justified | 58 |
| receive (sense) | 192 | 12 slots × 16 bits, 16-bit samples | 58 |

`12 000 000 ÷ 250 = 48 000` exactly. **[Confirmed]** on two independent lines:
the coprocessor's own built-in record for that stream family carries phase 0 = 1
and phase 1 = 249 with divider 1 (§18.7.1), and the amplifier's frame-ratio
register takes code `0x30`, which is the table entry for 250, on the same
machines.

**Do not derive a bit clock from a data-bit count.** The per-direction data
figures — 192 bits on a six-amplifier machine, 128 on a four-amplifier machine,
32 on a single-amplifier machine — are counts of **data bits in one direction**.
They are not frame lengths, they are not the quantity the frame-sync phase
counters or the amplifier's frame-ratio register take, and adding the two
directions together (384 on a six-amplifier machine) produces a figure with no
physical meaning at all, because the two directions are separate wires. §1
§1.4.4, §3 §3.7.3, §7 §7.6.2 and §16 state the frame the same way as this
subsection; this settles §2 open question 10 and §8 open question 11 in favour
of 250.

The same arithmetic holds for the other in-scope speaker links: **128 data bits
per direction in the same 250-bit-clock frame** on a four-amplifier machine
(122 idle), **32 data bits** on a single-amplifier machine (218 idle), and on
the A18 Pro machine **64 data bits** (two 32-bit playback slots) in a
**256-bit-clock frame at 12.288 MHz** with no receive direction. [Confirmed]

### 18.4.5 What this resolves in Section 11

Section 11 §11.7.3 reads the platform-supplied 36-byte link descriptor's `0x0c`
field as *master-clock periods per audio frame*, and records that the relation
`master clock ÷ that field = frame rate` holds on every link **except** the
t8140 jack link, where 24 000 000 ÷ 125 gives 192 000 against an advertised
48 000 (§11 open question 12).

**The field is a count of bit clocks, not of master clocks.** With the A18 Pro
jack link's divider of 4, the bit clock is 24 000 000 ÷ 4 = 6 000 000 Hz and
6 000 000 ÷ 125 = **48 000 Hz** exactly. The two readings coincide only when the
divider is 1, which it is on every other in-scope link. [Confirmed] — the
divider is carried explicitly at record offset `0x1c` and the coprocessor's own
built-in record for that link (§18.7.1) carries divider 4.

**That the one link which previously did not divide out now divides out to
exactly the advertised rate is strong corroboration of the reading, not merely
consistent with it.** The A18 Pro jack link was the single counter-example to
§11's clock model on any in-scope link; a wrong reading of the frame field
would have had to produce an exact integer rate on every other link *and* fail
on precisely the one link that carries a non-unity divider. It does not: the
same formula, with the divider included, gives 48 000 Hz on every in-scope link
without exception.

The same model identifies three further descriptor fields §11 §11.7.3 leaves
**[Unknown]**, and those rows are corrected in place there.

## 18.5 Slot geometry path

### 18.5.1 The positional rule — stated exactly

What the coprocessor receives, per direction, is: a **64-bit slot mask**, a
**slot width in bits**, a **sample width in bits**, a **data delay in bit
clocks**, and a **frame length in bit clocks**. What it does with the mask is
purely positional:

> **The *k*-th least-significant set bit of the slot mask carries the *k*-th
> channel of that direction's DMA stream, counting both from zero.**

[Confirmed]

The mechanism is the serialiser's *skip-masked-slots* behaviour (§18.8.4,
bit 12), which is set for every stream configured through this interface: a
masked-out slot consumes no FIFO word, so set bits and stream channels
correspond in ascending order with no gaps. [Confirmed]

There is **no per-slot, per-channel or per-device routing table** anywhere in
the message or in the register interface. The mask is the whole of the mapping.

### 18.5.2 The coprocessor never learns which amplifier occupies which slot

**On no SoC in scope does any part of the coprocessor interface, or any register
the coprocessor drives, name a loudspeaker, an amplifier, a transducer role, or
a physical quantity.** [Confirmed]

This is the resolution of a question the document flags as safety-critical
elsewhere (§8 §8.2.3, §1 §1.4.2, §8 open question 1). It does **not** say the
slot map is safe; it says where the map lives, and it is not here.

Four independent properties of the interface establish it:

1. **The record has no per-slot field.** Per direction its entire content is a
   serialiser identifier, two flag bytes, one data delay, one 64-bit slot mask,
   one slot width, one sample width, two pad-routing masks and one reserved
   byte. Every one of those is a whole-stream attribute. There is no array, no
   pairing, no ordering hint and nowhere to put a per-channel quantity.
2. **The serialiser register block has no per-slot register.** Seven registers
   per unit (§18.8.4); every field that mentions a channel is a *count* or a
   *mask*. The only per-channel storage anywhere in the complex is the
   shift-buffer bank of §18.8.6, which holds no state across a configure, so it
   carries no identity.
3. **No computation runs on stream data in either direction** (§18.6.2). Samples
   are moved between the DMA ring and the serialiser unmodified.
4. **The sense return has no device identity of its own.** It is the receive
   direction of the `spkr` device, so not even the device-identifier vocabulary
   (§11 §11.4.6) separates one sense channel from another.

### 18.5.3 Where the binding is actually made

**Host-side, over the control bus, one amplifier at a time.** The coprocessor is
told only which slots are active, how wide they are, and — implicitly, by
position — in what order the DMA stream's channels map onto them. Binding a slot
number to a *physical loudspeaker* is done by writing a slot number into each
amplifier's own registers over the host-owned control bus (§6, §7 §7.6).

| Amplifier register | Field | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `0x0C` bits 3:0 | receive (playback) TDM slot number | byte 0 of that amplifier's `speaker-config` record |
| `0x0C` bits 7:4 | second receive slot | written `1` |
| `0x03` bits 5:1 | amplifier output-level code | byte 1 of the record |
| `0x0E` bit 6 / bits 5:0 | sense transmit enable / slot **A**, in **8-bit units** from the start of the frame | byte 2 of the record |
| `0x0F` bit 6 / bits 5:0 | sense transmit enable / slot **B**, in **8-bit units** | byte 3 of the record |
| `0x0A` bits 3:2 / bits 1:0 | receive sample width / receive slot width | 16 → `0`/`0`, 20 → `4`/—, 24 → `8`/`1`, 32 → `0xC`/`2` |
| `0x60` | bit-clock-to-frame-rate code | table of §18.4.4 |

[Confirmed] — the register numbers and field positions agree with the public
counterpart part's published register map, and the values agree with the
platform-supplied records on every in-scope board.

☠ **Consequence.** A driver that programmes the coprocessor correctly and the
amplifiers incorrectly produces a **fully functional but mis-routed bus, with no
error anywhere.** There is no readback, no validation and no per-slot identity
in the coprocessor interface that could detect it. Playback mis-routing is
destructive: see §8 §8.2.3 and the readback requirement in §8 §8.2.4.

**The sense arithmetic closes independently on the coprocessor's own geometry.**
Bytes 2 and 3 of a `speaker-config` record are `4n` and `4n+2` for amplifier
*n*, in 8-bit units. The sense return is configured as 16-bit samples in 16-bit
slots, so amplifier *n*'s two sense words land in **receive slots 2n and 2n+1**,
and six amplifiers fill receive slots 0…11 — exactly the receive mask `0xFFF`
that the coprocessor's built-in record for a six-amplifier machine carries
(§18.7.1), and `0xFF` for four. Any other unit for bytes 2 and 3 places the
highest amplifier's sense words outside the 250-bit-clock frame. [Confirmed] —
reached from the platform description on one side and from the coprocessor's
built-in geometry on the other, and the two agree exactly.

**Four consequences a driver must respect.**

1. Programming the coprocessor and the amplifiers from different maps produces a
   silently mis-routed bus (above).
2. **DMA channel ordering must match ascending slot order.** The coprocessor
   will not reorder.
3. **The transmit slot mask must be contiguous from bit 0** for the
   sample-to-slot mapping to be the identity. Every in-scope machine uses
   `(1 << amplifier_count) − 1`.
4. On a machine with no sense return the receive mask is `0`, the amplifier's
   sense-slot registers are left at their reset values, and the receive
   serialiser is not configured at all.

### 18.5.4 Byte 0 is a slot number, not an index

Byte 0 of a `speaker-config` record is the amplifier's **playback slot number**
and not the record's position. On one baseline machine the four records carry
the non-trivial permutation `0, 2, 1, 3`. On every machine in scope byte 0
happens to equal the record index, but a driver must use byte 0. [Confirmed]

Byte 1 is the **amplifier output-level code**, `11.0 dBV + 0.5 dB × code`, not a
selector (§7 §7.5.1). [Confirmed]

Bytes 2 and 3 are **both sense slots**, so sense occupies **two** slots per
amplifier, not one. [Confirmed]

### 18.5.5 The two sense channels are indistinguishable to the coprocessor

The two sense slots of an amplifier are written into two adjacent amplifier
registers, `0x0E` from byte 2 of the record and `0x0F` from byte 3.

**Which of them carries the voltage sense and which the current sense is not
determined by anything on this interface, and this section takes no independent
position on it.** The attribution used elsewhere in this project comes from the
published driver headers of the counterpart part and its sibling — one family of
sources sharing one convention, not two independent lines — and the published
upstream device trees for the baseline machines write the **exchanged** values
into the same two registers. The attribution is therefore not asserted here. The settled
position, both readings, and the bench test that resolves it are in §8 §8.2.1.

What **is** established is that the coprocessor
**cannot tell the two apart and therefore cannot detect an exchange** — the four
properties of §18.5.2 apply verbatim to the sense pair. [Confirmed]

Nothing between the amplifier pin and host memory has an opinion about which
channel is which. That is the concrete mechanism by which a divergence between
two published conventions can persist undetected all the way to the protection
computation, and it means **the question cannot be answered from the controller
side by anyone**. It is a bench measurement. See open question 17 and §8
§8.2.1.
