## 18.6 Speaker path

### 18.6.1 What crosses the interface for a speaker stream

This is the **entire** speaker vocabulary, in an order a driver can use:

1. Attach the `spkr` device identifier (call type `0xC3000002`).
2. Get keys `401`, `402`, `704`, `705`; get key `701` to learn the bound objects
   and the pad routing.
3. Set key `702` (value `1`) to reset the stream.
4. Set key `508` (value `0xFFFFFFFF`) on a non-secure endpoint.
5. Set key `701` — the merged 109-byte record: transmit slot mask and widths,
   receive slot mask and widths for the sense return, frame geometry, clocking.
6. Set key `703` — master-clock enable — **only if** step 2 showed a master
   clock, a non-zero master-clock routing mask, and a readable key `703`.
7. Programme the amplifiers over the control bus (§7 §7.6, §18.5.3).
8. Programme and start the DMA channels (§4).
9. Set key `202`, target = the code from key `401`, direction mask `0`.
10. Set key `202`, target = the code from key `402`, direction mask = the
    directions being started. **Data now flows.**
11. Teardown: key `202` to the `401` code with the direction mask of the
    directions being stopped; stop DMA; key `202` to `idle` with mask `0`.

**Which of those orderings is required, and what requires it.**

| Constraint | Requirement it follows from |
|---|---|
| Step 1 before every later step | no property call is accepted for a device identifier that has not been attached (§18.2.1) |
| Step 2's get of key `701` before step 5's set | a set is a merge against the record the coprocessor currently holds, so the record to be sent cannot be composed without it (§18.3.3) |
| Step 3 before step 5, on any endpoint previously configured | a serialiser's configuration registers may not be rewritten until it has been reset and the reset observed complete (§18.8.4, §18.10) |
| Step 5 before step 6 | a master clock cannot be enabled before it has been configured; a key-`703` set that precedes the key-`701` set is rejected (§18.10) |
| Step 8 before step 10 | the DMA channel must be running before the stream reaches the `402` state, which is the point at which data moves (§11 §11.4.7) |
| Step 9 before step 10 | the interface enforces configure-data before start-data and rejects the transition taken out of order (§18.10) |

Whether the placement of step 4 relative to steps 3, 5 and 6 is constrained at
all is **[Unknown]**; no requirement is established for it. The orderings
tabulated above are **[Confirmed]** for t8132, t604x, t8140, t8142 and t605x.
No ordering is established among steps 7, 8 and the coprocessor calls other than
the one tabulated. On an endpoint reporting key `705` non-zero, step 5 may only
re-send the record byte for byte except the direction byte.

**No amplifier count, no amplifier address, no gain, no excursion or thermal
limit, no calibration value, no brown-out threshold and no per-loudspeaker
identity is ever sent.** [Confirmed]

### 18.6.2 Nothing computes protection, limiting, excursion, thermal or gain

**No speaker-protection, excursion, thermal, limiting, gain or dynamics
computation runs on the coprocessor, on any SoC in scope.** [Confirmed] — this
is a negative result and it matters, because it tells a driver author that the
entire protection loop is theirs to implement (§9). It rests on three
independent lines:

1. **Nothing in the message vocabulary carries a protection parameter.** The
   109-byte configuration is entirely link geometry and clocking; the only other
   keys on a stream endpoint are a state query, the power ladder, two state-code
   queries, a routing request, two capability probes and the master-clock enable
   (§18.2.2). There is no key, and no field of any key, in which an excursion
   limit, a temperature, an impedance, a limiter threshold or a per-unit
   calibration value could be expressed.
2. **No protection concept appears anywhere in the coprocessor's control
   interface on any in-scope SoC** — no excursion, displacement, temperature,
   impedance, limiter, compressor, Thiele–Small or per-unit calibration
   quantity — while the equivalent quantities are abundant on the host side
   (§9 §9.3).
3. **No computation runs on stream data in either direction.** The sense return
   reaches host memory unmodified: no scaling, no per-channel gain, no unit, no
   filtering and no pairing. The coprocessor does not inspect it, does not act
   on it, and does not report on it.

This **confirms** the existing statement that protection runs on the host
(§9 §9.1). The per-unit calibration data model is host-resident, and the sense
return arrives as ordinary receive DMA on the speaker endpoint's own channel.
[Confirmed]

Two things that could be mistaken for protection and are not:

- **The amplifier's own brown-out and over-power protection**, programmed over
  the control bus from platform-supplied tables (§7 §7.3, §8 §8.7). That is
  inside the amplifier part, not the coprocessor — and per §8 §8.7.1 thermal
  foldback is disabled on every machine in scope.
- **The serialiser's disable-output-when-idle bit** (§18.8.4, bit 14), which
  tri-states the data pad between the slots a unit owns. That is a
  bus-contention measure, not an audio one.

### 18.6.3 The mute and ramp machinery belongs to the microphone privacy path

A mute/unmute ramp applies on the **microphone privacy path**: a register write
inside the low-power complex, with mute and unmute ramp-time increments and
hold-off delays. It is easy to mistake this for a speaker control and it is not
one.

It is driven by microphone-status notification and by no audio stream, and by no
speaker event. [Confirmed] — it is reachable only through the microphone-disable
path (§12 §12.4.4) and no speaker stream reaches it.

A driver must not expect the coprocessor to ramp, mute or soft-start a speaker
stream. Mute and ramp on the speaker path are amplifier-side controls
(§7 §7.4) and host-side digital volume; §14 §14.4 gives the sequencing.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 18.7 The built-in per-SoC configuration set

The coprocessor holds, **per SoC**, a set of complete stream configurations —
one record per stream family. Each names its master clock, bit-clock generator,
frame-sync generator and serialiser units by the identifiers of §18.1.3, and
carries the frequency, divider, frame geometry, slot widths, slot masks and
pad-routing masks. A stream is restored to its record by property key `702`; a
separate index-valued property selects among several records for the low-power
complex, but that property's numeric key is **[Unknown]** (open question 11).
[Confirmed]

| Family | Meaning | Present on |
|---|---|---|
| low-power | low-power complex internal link | all five in scope |
| speaker | loudspeaker bus | all five |
| codec-out | headphone/jack output | all five |
| codec-in | headphone/jack input | all five |
| injection | low-power audio injection link | t8140, t8142, t605x only |
| speaker tap | playback-bus monitor | t8140, t8142, t605x only |

### 18.7.1 The records

All frame rates below are exact. The frame-sync pulse is **one bit clock** in
every record — phase 0 = 1, phase 1 = frame length − 1.

| SoC | Family | Master clock | Source | Divider | Bit clock | Frame (bit clk) | Rate | TX mask (slot width) | RX mask (slot width) | Bound objects |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| t8132, t604x, t8142, t605x | low-power | 12.000 MHz | fixed ref | 1 | 12.000 MHz | 250 | 48 kHz | `0x3` (16 bit) | `0x3` (16 bit) | `mck3`/`ckg3`/`syn3`/`ms03` |
| t8140 | low-power | 24.000 MHz | fixed ref | **2** | 12.000 MHz | 250 | 48 kHz | `0x3` (16 bit) | `0x3` (16 bit) | `mck3`/`ckg3`/`syn3`/`ms03` |
| t8132, t604x, t8142, t605x | speaker, 6 amplifiers | 12.000 MHz | fixed ref | 1 | 12.000 MHz | 250 | 48 kHz | `0x3F` (32 bit) | `0xFFF` (16 bit) | `mck0`/`ckg0`/`syn0`/`ms00` |
| t8132, t8142 | speaker, 4 amplifiers | 12.000 MHz | fixed ref | 1 | 12.000 MHz | 250 | 48 kHz | `0x0F` (32 bit) | `0xFF` (16 bit) | `mck0`/`ckg0`/`syn0`/`ms00` |
| t8132, t8142 | speaker, 4 amplifiers, no sense | 12.000 MHz | fixed ref | 1 | 12.000 MHz | 250 | 48 kHz | `0x0F` (32 bit) | — | `mck0`/`ckg0`/`syn0`/`ms00` |
| t8132, t604x, t8142, t605x | speaker, 1 amplifier | 12.000 MHz | fixed ref | 1 | 12.000 MHz | 250 | 48 kHz | `0x01` (32 bit) | — | `mck0`/`ckg0`/`syn0`/`ms00` |
| t8142, t605x | speaker tap, 6 channels | 12.000 MHz | fixed ref | 1 | 12.000 MHz | 250 | 48 kHz | — | `0x3F` (32 bit) | `mck0`/`ckg0`/`syn0`/**`ms01`** |
| t8142 | speaker tap, 4 channels | 12.000 MHz | fixed ref | 1 | 12.000 MHz | 250 | 48 kHz | — | `0x0F` (32 bit) | `mck0`/`ckg0`/`syn0`/`ms01` |
| t8140 | speaker | **12.288 MHz** | **oscillator `nco0`** | 1 | 12.288 MHz | **256** | 48 kHz | `0x03` (32 bit) | — | `mck0`/`ckg0`/`syn0`/**`ms12`** |
| t8140 | speaker tap | 12.288 MHz | oscillator `nco0` | 1 | 12.288 MHz | 256 | 48 kHz | — | `0x03` (32 bit) | `mck0`/`ckg0`/`syn0`/`ms01` |
| t8132, t604x, t8142, t605x | codec-out | 3.072 MHz | oscillator class | 1 | 3.072 MHz | **64** | 48 kHz | `0x03` (32 bit) | — | `mck2`/`ckg2`/`syn2`/`ms02` |
| t8132, t604x, t8142, t605x | codec-in | 3.072 MHz | oscillator class | 1 | 3.072 MHz | 64 | 48 kHz | — | `0x01` (32 bit) | `mck2`/`ckg2`/`syn2`/`ms02` |
| t8140 | codec-out | **24.000 MHz** | fixed ref | **4** | 6.000 MHz | **125** | 48 kHz | `0x03` (32 bit) | — | `mck2`/`ckg2`/`syn2`/`ms02` |
| t8140 | codec-in | 24.000 MHz | fixed ref | 4 | 6.000 MHz | 125 | 48 kHz | — | `0x01` (32 bit) | `mck2`/`ckg2`/`syn2`/`ms02` |
| t8140, t8142, t605x | injection | 3.072 MHz | oscillator `nco3` | 1 | 3.072 MHz | **192** | **16 kHz** | `0x07` (t8142/t605x) / `0x03` (t8140), 32 bit | same mask | `mck5`/`ckg5`/`syn5`/`ms05` |

[Confirmed] for every row.

**Pad-routing masks in the records.** The bit-clock and frame-sync pad mask is
`0x00` for the low-power and injection links (internal, no pad), `0x03` for the
speaker link (pad groups 0 and 1) and `0x04` for the codec links (pad group 2).

**The master-clock pad-routing mask is `0` in every record on every SoC: the
master clock is never driven to a pad on any in-scope machine.** [Confirmed]
This is consistent with both the amplifier part and the jack codec deriving
their internal clocks from the bit clock, and it is why key `703` is absent on
most endpoints (§18.2.2).

### 18.7.2 Reading of the set

1. **The set is per SoC, not per machine.** The set is a property of the SoC:
   every machine of a given SoC presents the identical record set. What varies
   per machine is *which* record applies, and that is decided by the host.
   [Confirmed] for t8132 and t8142.
2. **The records' slot masks and widths are exactly the per-machine values the
   host derives from the platform description and sends in key `701`.** The
   coprocessor's built-in geometry and the host's derived geometry agree field
   for field, which confirms the per-machine geometry table of §11 §11.7.3 and
   the internal consistency of the interface. [Confirmed]
3. The set is therefore a **menu of the bus shapes that SoC's machines use**, not
   a per-machine binding. Six-, four- and single-amplifier shapes coexist in the
   same per-SoC set.
4. The speaker tap is a **receive-only** stream on a *different* serialiser unit
   from the speaker transmit unit, with the same frame and 32-bit slots and a
   receive mask equal to the speaker transmit mask. It captures the playback
   bus, not the sense return — which is the coprocessor-side confirmation of
   §8 §8.9. [Confirmed]

## 18.8 Register interfaces the coprocessor drives

These are the registers on the far side of the message. **A driver on an
in-scope SoC never touches them** — there is no host aperture (§3 §3.5, §11
§11.6.1) — but the translation is the contract: it fixes what values are legal,
what a field means in physical units, and in what order the blocks must be
touched.

Offsets below are **relative to the block named in each heading**. Where those
blocks sit inside the audio island is §3 §3.4.3 and §3 §3.6; the field names are
the functional names §3 §3.6.2 and §3 §3.6.3 already use, so that the two
sections describe one register set.

Confidence throughout this subsection follows §18.1.1: **[Confirmed]** where the
field also has a published M1–M3 counterpart that agrees, **[Probable]** where
the field is new at the M4 generation, and always naming the SoCs each entry is
established for. Nothing here is established for t8142 or t605x beyond **[Probable]**
except where stated.

### 18.8.1 Bit-clock generator — one per cluster

| Offset | Name | Access | Fields | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | `CLOCK_GEN_CONTROL` | RW | bit 0 = `RESET` | Present on t8142 and t605x. **[Unknown]** whether the register exists on t8132, t604x and t8140 — open question 8 |
| `0x04` | `CLOCK_GEN_CONFIG` | RW | bits 2:0 = `CLOCK_SELECT`; bits 12:8 = `DIVISOR` | bit clock = selected source ÷ `DIVISOR` |

- **`DIVISOR`** is a plain integer divisor, **5 bits**, legal range **1…31**.
  On M1–M3 the equivalent field is **4 bits** at the same bit position and the
  published driver only ever writes `1`. The widening is a real generational
  change. **[Confirmed]** for t8132 and t604x; the same range is
  established at the message end of the interface (§18.4.2).
- **`CLOCK_SELECT`** names the master-clock generator that drives this
  bit-clock generator. Encoding: an **on-cluster master clock** maps to
  `index + 1`; **no source** maps to `0`; **any other source class** maps to
  `index + 7`. The `+1` and `+7` bases partition the selector between
  on-cluster master clocks and off-cluster or pad sources. **[Probable]** for
  t8132 and t604x — both base values are in use; one further source class also
  maps to `0` and is distinct from "no source", which is **[Unknown]** (open
  question 9).
- There is **no equivalent selector in the M1–M3 register set**; on M1–M3 the
  parent clock is chosen through the platform clock tree. **new**

This resolves the baseline's open question about the unexplained low nibble of
the M1–M3 master-clock configuration register: it is a **clock-source
selector**, and §3 §3.6.2 already reads it that way at **[Probable]**. The
offsets and widths above are what that reading was missing.

### 18.8.2 Frame-sync generator — one per cluster

| Offset | Name | Access | Fields | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | `SYNC_GEN_CONTROL` | RW | bit 0 = `RESET` | Present on t8142 and t605x; **[Unknown]** on t8132, t604x, t8140 — open question 8 |
| `0x04` | `SYNC_GEN_CONFIG` | RW | bits 3:0 = `CLOCK_SELECT`; bit 9 = `BIT_CLOCK_POLARITY`; bit 10 = `FRAME_SYNC_POLARITY` | |
| `0x08` | `FRAME_PHASE_0` | RW | u32 | **written as phase 0 − 1**. Frame-sync assertion length, in **bit clocks** |
| `0x0c` | `FRAME_PHASE_1` | RW | u32 | **written as phase 1 − 1**. Frame-sync de-assertion length, in **bit clocks** |

- Frame length in bit clocks = phase 0 + phase 1; frame rate = bit clock ÷
  (phase 0 + phase 1). The message carries the two phases directly (§18.3.1,
  `0x2b` and `0x2f`) and the **minus one** is applied here. This is exactly the
  M1–M3 convention for the equivalent high-period and low-period registers, so
  a 50 %-duty frame is phase 0 = phase 1 = frame ÷ 2 and a one-bit TDM pulse is
  phase 0 = 1. **unchanged in semantics, moved in layout.** [Confirmed] for
  t8132 and t604x.
- The two polarity bits are **set when the corresponding message byte is zero**
  and cleared when it is `1` (§18.3.2). [Confirmed] for the inversion; the
  physical sense of each bit is [Probable].
- `CLOCK_SELECT` uses the same `+1` / `+7` / `0` base rule as §18.8.1, keyed on
  the clock generator named at message offset `0x25`. [Probable]
- The **reset** register is new relative to the published M1–M3 map, where the
  frame-sync generator has no reset of its own. §3 §3.6.2 records the same
  addition at [Probable]; here it is **[Confirmed] for t8142 and t605x** and
  **[Unknown] for t8132, t604x and t8140**.

### 18.8.3 Pad clock routing — one per I2S pad group

In the cluster infrastructure block.

| Offset | Name | Access | Fields | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `0x64` | `PAD_CLOCK_SELECT` | RW | bits 2:0 = `MASTER_CLOCK_SELECT`; bits 11:8 = `BIT_AND_FRAME_CLOCK_SELECT` | `0` in either field = that pad group drives nothing from that source |

- **`BIT_AND_FRAME_CLOCK_SELECT`** (bits 11:8) is the direct successor of the
  M1–M3 port clock selector, at the same bit position and with the same
  `+1` / `+7` source encoding. **unchanged.** [Confirmed] for t8132 and t604x.
- **`MASTER_CLOCK_SELECT`** (bits 2:0) is **new**: the master clock can be
  routed to a pad group independently of the bit clock and frame sync, with its
  own 3-bit selector encoded as *master-clock index + 1*. On M1–M3 there is no
  independent master-clock pad routing. **[Probable]** for t8132 and t604x —
  single line, no baseline counterpart. This is the register behind §3 §3.6.2's
  split of the baseline's single port clock selector into two independent
  fields.
- **The two pad-routing masks in the message are bitmaps over pad groups.** Bit
  *h* set means pad group *h* is programmed: each set bit selects exactly one pad
  group, and bit *h* selects pad group *h*. The serialiser pad masks at message
  offsets `0x47` and `0x64` work the same way. [Confirmed] for the bitmap
  reading; the **pad-group numbering
  and which physical pins each bit covers are [Unknown]** — open question 2.

### 18.8.4 Serialiser — one block per unit

The transmit and receive halves have **identical offsets for the first four
registers** and diverge after that. This is a change from M1–M3, where the
receive view's data-input selector sits at block offset `0x04`.

| Offset | Transmit | Receive | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | `CONTROL` | `CONTROL` | RW | bit 0 = `RESET`, self-clearing; a companion reset-pending indication reads busy until the reset completes. Both must read clear before the unit is reconfigured |
| `0x04` | `CONFIG` | `CONFIG` | RW | field table below |
| `0x08` | `DATA_DELAY` | `DATA_DELAY` | RW | u32, **bit clocks** from the frame-sync edge to the first data bit |
| `0x0c` | `CHANNEL_MASK` high | `CHANNEL_MASK` high | RW | **inverted** mask for slots 32…63 |
| `0x10` | `CHANNEL_MASK` low | `CHANNEL_MASK` low | RW | **inverted** mask for slots 0…31 |
| `0x14` | `OUTPUT_ENABLE_MASK` high | `DATA_SELECT.DIN_SELECT` | RW | TX: inverted output-enable mask, slots 32…63. RX: **6-bit** pad-group selector |
| `0x18` | `OUTPUT_ENABLE_MASK` low | `LOOPBACK_DATA_SELECT.SERDES_SELECT` | RW | TX: inverted output-enable mask, slots 0…31. RX: **17-bit** internal-loopback source selector |

[Confirmed] for t8132, t604x and t8140; the same register set is present on
t8142 and t605x at **[Probable]**.

**Mask polarity.** All four mask registers are written **inverted**: a *zero*
bit selects the slot. A 64-bit mask *M* is written as `~(M >> 32)` to the high
register and `~(M & 0xFFFFFFFF)` to the low register. This is the same polarity
the published M1–M3 driver uses. **unchanged.** [Confirmed]

**Two independent 64-bit masks on transmit.** `CHANNEL_MASK` selects which slots
consume data from the transmit FIFO; `OUTPUT_ENABLE_MASK` selects which slots
the pad actively drives. A single transmit mask in the message reaches **both**
registers, so the two cannot be made to differ through key `701`. On M1–M3 the
published driver writes
the *cropped* mask — only the first *n* set bits, *n* = channel count — to the
first pair and the full mask to the second, so the hardware supports driving a
slot with silence while consuming no FIFO sample for it. **unchanged in
hardware, exercised differently.** [Confirmed] — and see open question 12, which
is where this matters for bus contention with an amplifier's idle-slot mask
(§8 §8.6.2).

`CONFIG` register fields:

| Bits | Field | Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| 5:0 | `CHANNELS_PER_FRAME` | slots per frame **− 1**. **6 bits on M4 and later (up to 64 slots)**; 4 bits on M1–M3 |
| 9:6 | `BITS_PER_CHANNEL` | slot width index: `0` = **8 bit**, `1` = 16 bit, `2` = 20 bit, `3` = 24 bit, `4` = 32 bit |
| 10 | `CLOCK_EDGE` | set when the message's edge byte is `0` |
| 11 | `DATA_ENDIAN` | set = LSB first |
| 12 | `SKIP_MASKED` | set in every configuration in scope — §18.9 |
| 13 | `AUTO_RESTART` | set in every configuration in scope — §18.9 |
| 14 | `DISABLE_OUTPUT_WHEN_IDLE` | set on transmit units, clear on receive units — §18.9 |
| 15 | `DISABLE_MASTER_MODE_LOOPBACK_CLKSEL` | set on receive units, clear on transmit units — §18.9 |
| 18:16 | `SYNC_AND_BCLK_SELECT` | source of the bit clock and frame sync for this unit |

[Confirmed] for t8132 and t604x.

Deltas from M1–M3:

- **`CHANNELS_PER_FRAME` widened from 4 to 6 bits.** A 64-slot frame is now
  expressible. Together with both mask halves being programmed, this is the
  sense in which the slot mask is 64 bits wide on M4 and later where it was
  effectively 32 before. [Confirmed]
- **`BITS_PER_CHANNEL` is an index, and index `0` is a fifth, previously
  undocumented value: 8-bit slots.** The field occupies the same bit positions
  as the published M1–M3 width mask, and that driver's four width constants are
  exactly `1`, `2`, `3` and `4` shifted left by six. [Confirmed]
- **Receive data-input select moved** from block offset `0x04` to `0x14`, so the
  receive block's first four registers now match the transmit block's.
  **changed.** [Confirmed]
- **Receive loopback source select is new** at block offset `0x18`: a 17-bit
  selector choosing an internal transmit unit as the data source instead of a
  pad. There is no M1–M3 equivalent in the published register map. **new.**
  [Confirmed] — this is the register §3 §3.6.2 names
  `LOOPBACK_DATA_SELECT.SERDES_SELECT` and §3 §3.6.2 places, at [Inferred], at
  one of the two unwritten receive offsets. The offset is now established.

### 18.8.5 Synchronised multi-serialiser enable — one global block

New at the M4 generation. It starts or stops several serialiser units and one
frame-sync output multiplexer **on the same frame boundary**.

| Offset | Name | Access | Value written |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0x100 + 4·m` | `SYNC_OMUX_SEL`[*m*] | RW | frame-sync generator index **+ 1** |
| `0x140` | `SYNC_OMUX_ENABLE_SET` | W | `1 << m` |
| `0x144` | `SYNC_OMUX_ENABLE_CLR` | W | `1 << m` |
| `0x150` | `RX_ENABLE_SET` | W | bitmap of receive serialiser units |
| `0x154` | `RX_ENABLE_CLR` | W | bitmap of receive serialiser units |
| `0x160` | `TX_ENABLE_SET` | W | bitmap of transmit serialiser units |
| `0x164` | `TX_ENABLE_CLR` | W | bitmap of transmit serialiser units |
| `0x170` | `ALIGNED_ENABLE_TRIGGER` | W | `1` |

[Probable] for t8132 and t604x — new at this generation, one line, no baseline
counterpart. §3 §3.6.3 records the same field set at [Probable]; the
**offsets** above are what that inventory was missing.

☠ **Ordering is load-bearing.**

- **To start:** the multiplexer selector must be valid, and
  `SYNC_OMUX_ENABLE_SET`, `RX_ENABLE_SET` and `TX_ENABLE_SET` must all have been
  written, **before** `ALIGNED_ENABLE_TRIGGER`.
- **To stop:** `SYNC_OMUX_ENABLE_CLR`, `RX_ENABLE_CLR` and `TX_ENABLE_CLR` must
  all have been written **before** `ALIGNED_ENABLE_TRIGGER`.

The trigger is what makes the accumulated set and clear operations take effect,
and it applies all of them on one frame boundary — which is why every set or
clear belonging to a transition must precede it. [Probable] No ordering among
the set and clear writes themselves is established, and whether any is required
is **[Unknown]**.

The `+1` bias on the multiplexer selector matches the `+1` bias in the clock
source selectors of §18.8.1 and §18.8.3: **selector value `0` universally means
"no source"** across this block. [Confirmed] for the consistency of the
convention.

The nearest M1–M3 construct is the per-cluster port-enable register, which has
**no synchronised trigger**. **new**

### 18.8.6 Serialiser shift-buffer block

One 32-bit word per channel, in two banks:

| Offset | Bank |
|---|---|
| `0x000 + 4·i` | transmit channel *i* |
| `0x200 + 4·i` | receive channel *i* |

Only the first 16 entries of each bank are in use; they are cleared as part of
stream configuration. Whether entries above 15 exist is **[Unknown]**. Function
is **[Unknown]** — a per-channel shift/alignment or hold register is the
plausible candidate. The bank holds no state across a configure, so it carries
**no per-channel identity** (§18.5.2). **new**, no M1–M3 equivalent.
[Probable] for t8132 and t604x. See open question 10.

**What the unknown function costs a host driver: nothing on any in-scope SoC.**
The block is inside the serial-audio register file, for which platform firmware
describes no host aperture on t8132, t604x, t8140, t8142 or t605x (§3 §3.2), and
the coprocessor clears it as part of stream configuration without the host being
involved. It is documented here so that a tracing observer can identify the
accesses and so that a bare-metal bring-up driver that takes the block over knows
the bank must be cleared before a configure. **A host driver on a stock machine
neither reads nor writes it.**

### 18.8.7 Low-power-complex stream agents

The low-power audio complex wraps each serialiser and DMA stream in an *agent*
with its own configuration register. Offsets relative to the complex's
miscellaneous block.

| Offset | Block |
|---|---|
| `0x8000 + 4·i` | serial-audio **transmit** agent *i* |
| `0x8800 + 4·i` | serial-audio **receive** agent *i* |
| `0x680 + 4·i` | frame-generator delay for agent *i* |

Agent configuration register:

| Bits | Field | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 4:0 | `CHANNEL_COUNT` | channels the agent moves per frame |
| 8 | `LOW_LATENCY_MODE` | mode select |
| 16 | `FLUSH` | write `1` to flush |
| 31 | `AGENT_ENABLE` | |

Reset value of the whole register is `0`.

Frame-generator delay register:

| Bits | Field | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | `DELAY_ENABLE` | |
| 13:4 | `DELAY` | 10-bit delay value, units **[Unknown]** |

[Probable] for t8132 and t604x — new at this generation, one line.

An agent's programmable state is a delay, a channel count and a mode select.
[Probable]

Also present in the low-power complex and driven by the coprocessor: a
frame-generator divider (a value field plus an enable), a frame-generator source
multiplexer, a pulse multiplexer, a per-core frame-packer multiplexer and a
timestamp block. Their offsets are index-scaled within the same block;
individual field positions are **[Unknown]** beyond the delay register above,
and the unit of the 10-bit `DELAY` field is **[Unknown]** — bit clocks and frame
clocks are both plausible and they differ by the frame length. Open question 13.

**What that costs a host driver: nothing on any in-scope SoC**, for the same
reason as §18.8.6 — the low-power complex has no host aperture and the
coprocessor programs these agents itself as part of attaching a low-power stream.
The consequence of the unknowns is confined to interpreting a trace and to a
bare-metal bring-up. **A host driver must not attempt to set the frame-generator
delay**: with the unit unknown, a wrong value shifts every low-power capture
stream's data relative to its frame sync by an amount that is not detectable from
the host side, because the host sees only the decimated PCM.

### 18.8.8 Power-manager clock-generator interface

The coprocessor also drives the platform clock generator that feeds the
serial-audio cluster master clocks. These are power-manager registers, not audio
registers; one 32-bit register per clock node, in four shapes.

| Shape | `ENABLE` | `PENDING` | Other fields |
|---|---|---|---|
| simple gated multiplexer | bit 31 | bit 30 | bits 27:24 = `SOURCE_SELECT`; bit 12 = `AUTO_DISABLE` |
| divider | bit 19 | bit 18 | bits 9:0 = `DIVIDER` |
| pre-divider | — | bit 31 | bits 25:24 = `SOURCE_SELECT` |
| final multiplexer | bit 31 | bit 30 | bits 25:24 = `SOURCE_SELECT`; bits 29:26 = `BYPASS`, written `1 << selector` |

[Probable] for t8132 and t604x.

**Protocol: write the field, then poll `PENDING` until it reads zero** before
treating the change as effective. `AUTO_DISABLE` is the inverse of automatic clock
gating: enabling automatic clock gating clears `AUTO_DISABLE`. [Probable]

The divider shape carries a **10-bit** divider. That is the coarse divider of
the platform clock tree and is **distinct** from the 5-bit serial-audio
bit-clock divider of §18.8.1; confusing the two gives a bit clock wrong by the
ratio of the two dividers. [Probable]

## 18.9 Four serialiser configuration bits — newly established names

Bits 12 to 15 of the serialiser `CONFIG` register are recorded in the published
M1–M3 material as unknown: three carry no name at all and the fourth carries
only a provisional one. The published driver sets bits 12, 13 and 14 on a
transmit unit and bits 12, 13 and 15 on a receive unit, unconditionally, with no
stated reason.

**These names are established here, not carried over from any published
source.** The same bit pattern, with the same per-direction asymmetry, applies
on the in-scope SoCs and on the baseline, so the names hold for both.

| Bit | **Newly established name** | Meaning | Direction | Published M1–M3 status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 12 | **`SKIP_MASKED`** | a masked-out slot consumes or produces **no FIFO word** | both | unnamed |
| 13 | **`AUTO_RESTART`** | the unit restarts itself after an error or stall rather than staying stopped | both | unnamed |
| 14 | **`DISABLE_OUTPUT_WHEN_IDLE`** | the data pad is released (tri-stated) during slots the unit does not own | **transmit only** | unnamed |
| 15 | **`DISABLE_MASTER_MODE_LOOPBACK_CLKSEL`** | suppresses the clock-select path used when the unit receives an internally looped-back stream | **receive only** | provisionally named for a data-feedback function |

[Confirmed] for t8132 and t604x — the assignment is corroborated by the
published driver setting the identical bit pattern per direction, which is two
lines for the *pattern* even though the *meanings* are established here.

Three consequences:

1. **Bits 14 and 15 are not one field seen from two sides.** Each is meaningful
   only in its own direction, which is why the published driver's asymmetric
   programming is correct rather than arbitrary. This resolves the ordering
   ambiguity §3 §3.6.2 records for bits 12 and 13 and the open reading of bits
   14 and 15.
2. **`SKIP_MASKED = 1` is the mechanism behind the positional rule of §18.5.1.**
   Because a masked slot consumes no FIFO word, the *k*-th set bit of the mask
   carries the *k*-th DMA channel. A driver that ever cleared this bit would
   change the slot-to-channel mapping from positional to absolute — which no
   in-scope configuration does, and which the key-`701` record cannot express.
3. **`DISABLE_OUTPUT_WHEN_IDLE` is a bus-contention control, not an audio
   one** (§18.6.2). On a shared transmit line it is what keeps two serialisers,
   or a serialiser and an amplifier's sense output, off each other's slots
   (§8 §8.6.2).

## 18.10 Ordering the coprocessor requires

The interface enforces an order among six operations; an out-of-order request is
rejected rather than silently reordered.

| # | Bring-up | Tear-down (reverse) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | configure master clock | stop data |
| 2 | configure bit clock and frame sync | deconfigure data |
| 3 | enable master clock | disable bit clock and frame sync |
| 4 | enable bit clock and frame sync | disable master clock |
| 5 | configure data (serialisers) | deconfigure bit clock and frame sync |
| 6 | start data | deconfigure master clock |

[Confirmed] for t8132 and t604x.

Mapped onto the host-visible interface of §18.6.1: **steps 1–4 are the key-`701`
set followed by the key-`703` set; steps 5–6 are the key-`202` transitions to
the `401` and `402` state codes.** A driver that sets key `703` before key `701`
is rejected, because the master clock cannot be enabled before it is configured.
[Confirmed]

Within step 5 two requirements hold. A serialiser must be **reset**, and its
reset and reset-pending indications observed clear, before any of its
configuration registers are written (§18.8.4); and the receive data-input and
loopback selects apply to **receive units only**. Whether any further ordering
among the configuration registers is required is **[Unknown]**. Step 6 is the
synchronised-enable sequence of §18.8.5. [Probable] for t8132 and t604x.

**Power-domain sequencing is interleaved:** the cluster's master-clock power
domain is raised before the master clock is configured and dropped after it is
deconfigured. [Probable] This is the same ordering §14 §14.4.1 derives from the
power side.

## 18.11 Device-identifier vocabulary — generational delta

The stream device identifiers the platform description names on M4 and later
(§11 §11.4.6) are **accepted by the coprocessor from the M4 generation onwards
and not before**:

| Identifier | M1–M3 | t8132 / t604x | t8140 | t8142 / t605x |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `spkr` | **not accepted** | accepted | accepted | accepted |
| `cout` | **not accepted** | accepted | accepted | accepted |
| `cin ` | **not accepted** | accepted | accepted | accepted |
| `lpbk` | **not accepted** | accepted | accepted | accepted |
| `hpai` | accepted | accepted | accepted | accepted |
| `lpai`, `lai ` | accepted | accepted | accepted | accepted |

[Confirmed] for presence and absence; [Probable] that presence implies the
identifier is accepted in an attach call.

**This is the sharpest single expression of the M3 → M4 delta: the coprocessor
acquires the loudspeaker and the jack codec as devices it owns, which it had
never had before.** It also closes §11 §11.4.6's standing question of whether
the in-scope firmware accepts these identifiers at all.

The stream format descriptor returned by key `302` carries the same 16-byte
shape on both sides of the boundary: **four-character format code, sample rate
in Hz, channel count, bytes per sample.** [Confirmed] The 204-byte tail of the
baseline probe reply (§11 §11.4.6) is **not** explained by it and remains
**[Unknown]** (§11 open question 2).

## 18.12 Relationship to Sections 3, 8, 11 and 16 — agreements and two disagreements

**Agreements.** The message layout, the key numbers, the nine-entry master-clock
table, the per-machine slot masks, the 250-bit-clock speaker frame at
12.000 MHz, the 256-bit-clock A18 Pro frame at 12.288 MHz, the 8-bit-unit
reading of the sense slots, the fact that the per-amplifier assignment does not
cross the interface, and the fact that no protection parameter crosses it, are
each corroborated at both ends of the interface and agree exactly. Section 3's
field inventory for the serial-audio block (§3 §3.6.2, §3 §3.6.3) matches the
register set of §18.8 field for field; §18.8 supplies the offsets §3 did not
state.

**A second disagreement, now resolved and propagated.** Sections 1, 3, 7 and 16
previously gave the six-amplifier speaker frame as 384 bits (18.432 MHz) or as
192 bit clocks (9.216 MHz). Both were counts of **data** bits — the first adding
the two directions together, the second counting one — and neither included the
58 idle bit clocks. The frame is **250 bit clocks at a 12.000 MHz bit clock**,
[Confirmed] on three independent lines in §18.4.4, one of which is the platform
hardware description itself. §1 §1.4.4, §3 §3.7.3, §7 §7.6.2 and §16 have been
corrected to state the frame that way and to label the data-bit counts as data
bits per direction; their slot maps, widths and channel counts were never in
dispute and agree with this section exactly. §2 open question 10 and §8 open
question 11 are settled in consequence.

**One disagreement that is not resolved here.** Section 11 §11.7.3 reads byte
`0x00` of the platform-supplied 36-byte link descriptor as a descriptor version
(value `1` everywhere) and byte `0x01` as an interface-class byte with values
`0x02`, `0x12`, `0x13` and `0x42`. The model of §18.3 and §18.4 reads the same
two bytes as **link flags** (bit 0 = a master clock is present, bit 4 = drive
the master clock out of the pin group) and **framing flags** (bit 0 =
frame-sync active edge, bit 1 = frame-sync pulse polarity, bits 5:4 =
serialiser clock-edge mode, bit 6 = a separate receive data delay is supplied at
byte `0x21`), with bytes `0x02` and `0x03` as a master-clock mode selector and a
per-direction bit-order byte.

**The observed values do not discriminate between the two readings.** Both
account for every value seen on every board. The readings of bytes `0x04`–`0x23`
are not in dispute, and the newer reading of `0x05`, `0x0c`, `0x0e`, `0x10`,
`0x12`, `0x20` and `0x21` is adopted in §11 §11.7.3 because it closes that
section's arithmetic and its clock-model discrepancy (§18.4.5). Bytes
`0x00`–`0x03` are left with both readings named and are **[Unknown]**. See open
question 16.

| Speaker sense return | present except on j623, j624, j773g | present except on j773s, j575c | **absent** | present | present |
| Jack codec | cs42l84 | cs42l84 | **cs42l83** | cs42l84 | cs42l84 |
| Secure microphone-disable register block | present | present | **absent** | absent | absent |
| Pulse-density loopback/scramble fields | absent | absent | present | present | present |

**The A18 Pro machine is the outlier throughout.** Its speaker link is a
two-channel, 32-bit-slot, 256-bit-clock link at 12.288 MHz from the oscillator,
with **no receive mask and no sense return**; its amplifier has no control bus
and therefore no `speaker-config`, `bop-config`, `amp-dcblocker-config` or
`amp-tx-zd-config` property at all, so **every** slot and level decision on that
machine is made by the coprocessor's built-in record and nothing else; and its
jack link divides a 24 MHz fixed reference by four into a 125-bit-clock frame,
the only in-scope use of that frame length. Its speaker serialiser (`ms12`,
cluster 3 unit 0) is driven by cluster 0's generators, the only observed
cross-cluster binding. [Confirmed]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Open questions

Numbered. Each names what is unknown, why a driver needs it, and the probe that
settles it. **☠** marks an entry that must be resolved before speakers are
driven on the affected machine.

1. **Which concrete cluster-object identifiers exist on each in-scope SoC.** The
   host sends the class names `mck`, `ckg`, `syn`, `i2s`, `ms` and relies on the
   bitwise-subset match of §18.1.4 against the coprocessor's concrete
   identifiers. The forms are established (§18.1.3) but the per-SoC inventory —
   how many clusters and serialiser units are actually populated on t8142 and
   t605x, and whether any identifier outside the forms listed exists — is
   **[Unknown]**. *Why it matters:* a class name that matches nothing is
   rejected silently, with no error at the field that named it. *Probe:* get key
   `701` on every endpoint of a running machine and record the concrete
   identifiers the coprocessor returns in the eight object-id fields.

2. **The six pad-routing masks: pad-group numbering and pin coverage.** Message
   offsets `0x10`, `0x1d`, `0x47`, `0x4b`, `0x64`, `0x68`. That they are bitmaps
   over pad groups, one pad group per set bit, is
   **[Confirmed]** (§18.8.3); **which pad group is which physical pin group, and
   how many exist per SoC, is [Unknown]**. The host only ever writes `0` or
   `0xFFFFFFFF` and otherwise preserves what it read. *Why it matters:* a driver
   bringing a cluster up from cold, with no prior record to read, cannot supply
   these. *Probe:* get key `701` on each endpoint and correlate the returned
   masks against the physical link each endpoint is known to drive (§1 §1.5).

3. **Whether the host may originate a routing change.** Key `508` is written
   `0xFFFFFFFF` once at attach and never again, and its failure is tolerated.
   **[Unknown]** what other values mean and whether a cluster can be re-routed
   to a different pad group at run time, as the M1–M3 platform routing calls
   allowed. *Probe:* write other values and read key `701` back.

4. **Which of key-`701` bytes `0x37`/`0x38` is bit order and which is bit-clock
   edge** (and likewise `0x54`/`0x55`). **[Probable]**, §18.3.2. *Why it
   matters:* getting them backwards inverts either the sample bit order or the
   sampling edge on every slot — audible as noise, not silence, so it will not
   be caught by a "does it play" test. *Probe:* set key `701` twice on a
   jack-output endpoint with the two bytes swapped, capture the bit-clock and
   data pads with a logic analyser, and compare the first data bit's position
   against the frame-sync edge.

5. **The reserved bytes.** Record bytes `0x4f` and `0x6c`, and platform
   descriptor byte `0x07`. Written zero on every in-scope endpoint.
   **[Unknown]**. *Probe:* set non-zero values and observe whether the record is
   rejected or the value is preserved in the get.

6. **The transmit loopback-pin mask at `0x4b` versus the receive one at `0x68`.**
   The receive mask is non-zero on at least one endpoint and gates the
   immutability capability; the transmit one is zero on every in-scope
   endpoint.
   **[Unknown]** whether a transmit loopback path exists at all on M4 and later.
   *Why it matters:* it decides whether the loopback endpoints of §3 §3.8.2 can
   be sourced from inside the complex or only from a pad. *Probe:* attach the
   `lpbk` endpoint and get key `701`; a non-zero transmit loopback mask answers
   it directly.

7. **What key `704` actually validates.** It advertises that the endpoint
   "performs routing validation". **[Unknown]** whether that is pin conflicts
   between clusters, slot overlap between endpoints sharing a bus, or both.
   *Why it matters:* **if it validates slot overlap, a mis-assigned speaker slot
   might be catchable at the interface**, which would turn a silent destructive
   failure into an error return. This is the highest-value entry in this
   section. *Probe:* on an endpoint reporting `704` non-zero, set a key-`701`
   record whose transmit mask deliberately overlaps a second endpoint's, and
   record whether the set is refused.

8. **Whether the clock-generator and frame-sync-generator `RESET` registers
   exist on t8132, t604x and t8140.** Present on t8142 and t605x; **[Unknown]**
   on the other three (§18.8.1, §18.8.2). *Why it matters:* a driver recovering
   a wedged cluster needs to know whether a generator can be reset independently
   of the serialiser, or whether the whole stream must be torn down through key
   `702`. *Probe — by host read-back, not by tracing:* the registers are at
   offset `0x00` of each generator block. **The coprocessor's own accesses cannot
   be traced** (§17, "On tracing the coprocessor's own bus activity"); what is
   available instead is a host read-back of the same registers on the three SoCs
   whose serial-audio region address is published — t8132, t8140 and t8142 (§3
   §3.4.2, §3 §3.5). Raise `AUDIO_P`, read the word at offset `0x00` of a
   clock-generator and a frame-sync-generator block, and test for decode: a
   register that does not exist typically reads as zero on every cluster and does
   not change across a stream start, while one that does exist will show the
   self-clearing reset behaviour if written on an idle cluster. **Not resolvable
   on t604x or t605x**, where no power-domain address is published.

9. **The meaning of the clock-source class that maps to selector `0` but is
   distinct from "no source".** Two of the three source-class branches are
   understood: an on-cluster master clock maps to `index + 1`, and "none" maps
   to `0`. A third class also maps to `0`. It is plausibly "sourced from the
   pad", i.e. clock-consumer mode. **[Unknown]** (§18.8.1). *Probe:* configure a
   jack endpoint as a clock consumer — frame-sync source identifier `i2s` rather
   than `ckg` — and read key `701` back.

10. **The serialiser shift-buffer block's function.** Sixteen 32-bit words per
    direction, cleared as part of stream configuration and holding no state
    across one (§18.8.6).
    **[Unknown]**. *Why it matters:* if it is a per-channel alignment or hold
    register, a driver may need it cleared on recovery — and it is the only
    per-channel storage in the complex, so it is the only place a per-channel
    identity could hide. *Probe — by host read-back, not by tracing:* the
    coprocessor's own accesses cannot be traced (§17, "On tracing the
    coprocessor's own bus activity"). On t8132, t8140 and t8142 the block is
    reachable by host MMIO once `AUDIO_P` is raised (§3 §3.5): snapshot both
    banks with the link stopped, start a stream through the coprocessor, snapshot
    again, change one quantity at a time (slot count, slot width, data delay) and
    snapshot after each. The words that move identify the function; words that
    stay zero across every configuration are unused. **Not resolvable on t604x or
    t605x.** *Dependency:* this entry is blocked on §3 open question 1
    (confirming the serial audio controller base address) and cannot start before
    it.

11. **Whether the built-in default set is reachable by index from the host.** A
    stream is restorable to its own record by key `702`, and a separate
    index-valued property selects among several records for the low-power
    complex, but **that property's numeric key is [Unknown]**, as is whether any
    equivalent exists for a serial-audio stream. *Why it matters:* if it does,
    it is a far shorter bring-up path than composing a 109-byte record, and it
    is the path least likely to produce a geometry the amplifiers are not
    programmed for. *Probe:* sweep property keys in the `700`–`720` range on the
    `spkr` endpoint with a 4-byte integer payload, observe which are accepted,
    and read key `701` back after each.

12. **Whether the second transmit mask can usefully differ from the first.** The
    hardware supports driving a slot that consumes no FIFO sample; a single
    message field reaches both `CHANNEL_MASK` and `OUTPUT_ENABLE_MASK`, so
    **a driver cannot
    express "drive this slot with silence" through key `701`** (§18.8.4).
    **[Unknown]** whether that matters for bus contention with an amplifier's
    idle-slot mask (§8 §8.6.2, §8 open question 14). *Probe:* compare the
    amplifier's own high-impedance slot configuration against the slots the
    controller drives, on a six-amplifier machine, with a logic analyser.

13. **The remaining low-power-complex field positions** — frame-generator
    divider, source multiplexer, pulse multiplexer, per-core frame-packer
    multiplexer and timestamp — beyond the delay register of §18.8.7, together
    with the unit of the 10-bit `DELAY` field, which is **[Unknown]** and is
    plausibly either bit clocks or frame clocks.
    **[Unknown]**. Needed only for the low-power capture and injection paths, and
    a host driver does not program any of these on a stock machine (§18.8.7).
    *Probe — by host read-back, not by tracing:* the same method as entry 10 and
    subject to the same limits, applied to the low-power complex's miscellaneous
    block with a low-power capture stream started and stopped. The `DELAY` unit
    is settled separately and more cheaply: set two delay values differing by a
    known amount and measure the shift of a known capture signal relative to the
    frame, which distinguishes bit clocks from frame clocks by the frame length.
    *Dependency:* blocked on §3 open question 1.

14. **Whether a speaker frame longer than 250 bit clocks is ever used.** The
    amplifier accepts 256, 384, 500 and 512 (§18.4.4); the controller accepts up
    to 64 slots. Every in-scope machine uses 250, or 256 on the A18 Pro machine.
    If a future machine needs more than six amplifiers, **the binding constraint
    is the amplifier's sense-slot field — 6 bits of 8-bit units, i.e. 512 bit
    clocks — not the controller.** *Probe:* none needed now; recorded so that
    the 8-bit-unit arithmetic of §18.5.3 is re-checked if a frame longer than
    512 bit clocks ever appears.

15. **The state codes returned by keys `401` and `402`.** **[Inferred]** to be
    `pw1 ` and `pwrd` by agreement with the capture ladder (§18.2.3). *Why it
    matters:* it removes an inference from the start-up sequence, and a driver
    that hard-codes the wrong code cannot start a stream at all. *Probe:* get
    both keys on the `spkr` endpoint at attach time and print the four bytes.
    Cheap, and it should be done first.

16. **Bytes `0x00`–`0x03` of the platform-supplied 36-byte link descriptor.**
    Two readings exist and the observed values do not discriminate between them
    (§18.12). **[Unknown]**. *Why it matters:* one reading makes byte `0x01`
    carry the frame-sync polarity and clock-edge mode — i.e. real link framing a
    driver must reproduce — and the other makes it a class byte with no framing
    content, in which case the framing must come from somewhere else. *Probe:*
    on an endpoint whose descriptor byte `0x01` is `0x13`, get key `701` and
    compare the returned frame-sync edge and polarity bytes against what each
    reading predicts; they differ.

17. **☠ Which of an amplifier's two sense slots carries voltage and which
    carries current.** §18.5.5 establishes that **the controller side cannot
    arbitrate**: the coprocessor never distinguishes the pair, so the question
    cannot be answered from here by anyone. Two published conventions disagree
    while writing into the same two amplifier registers, and a protection model
    that forms an impedance — as distinct from a power — is inverted if the
    wrong one is adopted. *Probe, and it assumes neither convention:* drive one
    amplifier into **two different known load resistances** and observe which of
    the two received channels changes. The current channel scales inversely with
    load impedance; the voltage channel does not. See §8 §8.2.1 and §8 open
    question 7.

18. **☠ Whether the coprocessor's built-in record and the host's derived record
    can ever disagree on a machine's slot geometry.** They agree field for field
    on every in-scope machine (§18.7.2), but nothing in the interface *enforces*
    it, and on the A18 Pro machine — whose amplifier has no control bus — the
    built-in record is the **only** slot description in the system. **[Unknown]**
    what happens if a host sends a geometry the amplifiers are not programmed
    for. *Why it matters:* on machines with a control bus this is the failure
    mode of §18.5.3, silent mis-routing; on the A18 Pro machine there is no
    amplifier programming to disagree with, so a wrong host record is the whole
    error. *Probe:* on a machine with a control bus, set a key-`701` record with
    a transmit mask one slot wider than the amplifier population, start the
    stream, and record whether the set is refused, whether audio still flows,
    and what the extra slot drives.
